This game is totally worth every penny.  Not only do I have a passion for space/sci-fi genres (as well as a few others) but the fact that they give you both a campaign and free roam mode only games it better since free roam basically lets you do what you wish.  You command a ship and can do whatever you want. Become a pirate and capture other ships and their cargo, become a trader and buy/sell goods between planets and space stations, become a bountry hunter, and much more... It also helps that the Gemini System (map) is pretty damned big with constant activity.  My favorite moments involve coming upon large battles between factions, or simple skirmishes between myself and a couple other ships turn into a huge battle when other nearby factions decide to intervene to either help or harm me. Best part about the space battles is that it feels so real... ships aren't all on the same plane as if on an ocean/sea, they're everywhere at all angles. Another huge point in favor of the game is how amazing the graphics are without reducing performance (that I have noticed and have a pretty good gaming computer) though there is a lag whenever you move to another sector, but that barely effects me.
The games doesn't restrict you to certain areas... you can go anywhere and everywhere they do limit you in other ways... depending on you reputation, different sectors will be hostile to you and some sectors have high level enemies in them. One major problem (in my opinion) is the repetative nature of the side missions and very few secondary missions (those give to you by factions depending on your reputation and level.)  Another problem is how long it takes to level up and to get to the higher level so as to be able to fly around in a dreadnought or carrier.
Overall, I'd have to give this game 9/10.

Max Payne. Voted to be in the top 10 happiest video game characters ever created, now in my book monotone voice acting along with a man who has lost everything quicker than he can pop some painkillers, is an impeccable decision by Remedy. This man has no reason to be happy, and anyone who disagrees just imagine having your baby daughter and wife murdered by drug fueled thugs!
Moving on to gameplay, this game revolutionised third person shooters in general. It showed us that amongst all the happiness of Banjo Kazooie or any other animal based adventure game, that there was an ignored darkness lurking in reality and Remedy made a brave move by showing us that darkness. Moving back on topic again, The introduction to the slo-mo dive shooting mechanic really turned the tables in the event of a shootout, you could carefully pick out your targets and try to dispatch of them with care as you dive through the air. Now don't get me wrong this mechanic was not perfected straight off the bat, it was actually quite clunky in some situations, but all credit for actually bothering with something new for once rather than just another generic third-person shooter.
Let us swiftly move onto story, Well let's just say that it's not the most complex idea in the book, but nonetheless that's not always a bad thing. Basically Max returns home after a night working at the NYPD only to find a group of drug fueled thugs have broke into his house and he ends up seeing his baby daughter and wife brutally murdered, so Max being Max bent on revenge swears to kill those who did this too him, leading him down a road he was never prepared for. All in all I thoroughly enjoyed meeting new characters and having them involved with the story, it made it seem like Max wasn't so alone after all.
Finally we move onto the biggest feature of the game the main man himself - MAX PAYNE. Boy oh boy 80% of the reason I love this game so much is down to this man. Let me begin by saying that whilst you are playing the game you feel as much emotion as Max feels meaning you can relate to him on a whole other level. You genuinely feel sorry for this poor son of a ♥♥♥♥♥ and this actually makes you want to unravel the mystery about the fate of his family as well.
So for christ's sake if you are unsure whether or not to get the franchise this game introduces it exceptionally well!
7/10

This game is a gritty third-person shooter about a police officer called Max Payne. The game has bullet time elements which allow Max to pull of incredible kills and survive against the odds. The game starts with the murder of your wife and child, and doesn't ever get any happier, even at the end. The gameplay is decent but nothing too amazing due to it's age. The game is interesting, exiting, and fun as well as very engaging too. Though at points the grittiness of the game make it a bit horrible to look at, it was an artistic decision. The game has comic book style cutscenes which are nice to look at and read through and carry the story along brilliantly and much better than a "normal cutscene" would have been able to at the time of the game's release. The game is stands up to this date and you must play through it if you want to play the sequels as it allows you to not only see but feel the pain Max has been through to get where he is in the sequels. The AI in this game are difficult even though you start it on the easiest setting, but the quick save feature allows you to get round this difficulty with ease. The sound on the game isn't perfect but is bearable. It's level design is very good and allows exploring for any extra supplies such as guns, ammo, and pain killers if needed. The character of Max Payne and the story of his life full of pain and suffering are both brilliant and a real experience to go through. The graphics in this game are certainly impressive for the time of release and are no issue at all.
The game can be difficult at times and there are more engaging games out there that can keep you playing for longer sessions at a time but this game is overall pretty decent.
9/15 - "Fairly decent gritty third-person shooter about pain and suffering"

Although the temptation might be to say that it's similar to it's predecessors and lacks some of the polish of them, there's some real joy and some great new stuff in here.  A few of the boss battles weren't what I'd call fun - they felt overwrought and gimmicky at times - it has that same satisfying game loop with some new twists, well-done foreshadowing to the games you've played already.
The skill trees are clever, and powered by different actions; though some of the skill-based ones will be nearly impossible to complete if you wait too long and block forward progress; if you're looking to have all of the powers, make sure you're tracking all three of the different power-up trees early.
There's a whole new set of Riddler/Enigma collectibles.  Enigma's storyline, however, ends very disappointingly.  There's no real feeling payoff after all that effort.
Ultimately, though, it's a Batman prequel to Arkham Asylum built in Arkham City.  You've been here twice before; if you've been missing more of that, it's more, and it's a good more... but it's not going to make you feel like you've played a whole new game.

There's a lot of negative reviews and disappointment surrounding Yooka-Laylee. Overall, I think the mid-70 scores its gotten are very fair, which is a bit disappointing being a spiritual sequel to one of the greatest games ever made. But if you are a fan of old-school 3D platformers, you should enjoy Yooka, especially if you don't go into it with extremely high expectations.
I'm an extremely hardcore fan of the Banjo series, and I've been thinking a lot about why it just doesn't live up to the older games' standards, so this is my opinion of Yooka-Laylee compared to them.
First off, the positives:
The music is fantastic, as one would expect.
The worlds and character design are fantastic. Graphically, I think the whole game is beautiful, even if it has that "Unity look".
The controls are fantastic. The controls feel like it was designed to be speedran, and that's a great thing for casual play as well. Rolling kind of gimps your controls a little, but it's part of the design; of course it's harder to control when you're balancing on a ball. I think the camera was overall fine, except maybe while flying.
All of the moves are useful, easy to activate, and make sense for the characters (they're chameleon/bat-related).
I quite enjoyed the game, and it was a joy to 100% it, being a bit starved for a game of this type. But, there's just so much that could have been better. There's a lot missing that would make it a timeless classic, like BK and BT are to so many people.
I'll start off talking about some of the Kickstarter stretch goals, which I feel hindered the game, since they doomed them to have to soullessly copy some key elements of BK/BT.
Tooie did it better.
Reaching the bosses in this game just don't feel exciting compared to Tooie. It's just another pagie.
They also generally fit the "three hit" formula.
Kazooie and Tooie did it WAY better.
Furnace Fun is absolutely excellently designed, with the multiple paths you can take on the board, the different square types, the minigame challenges, the Joker questions, etc.
Tower of Tragedy is more straight-forward, but still fun, especially since you're competing against the AI.
The quiz in Yooka is like they heard people loved the end-game quiz segments in the Banjo series, and boiled it down to "answer questions about the game correctly to move on", missing out on what made them fun.
Kazooie and Tooie did it better.
All of the transformations are used solely for what they're intended for, which is usually only 1 or 2 pagies. Kazooie and Tooie had more general use transformations. None of them are like the Croc, the Bee, or the Submarine.
Nuts & Bolts did it better. Ha.
These arcade games are pretty much universally despised it seems. With the hate these have gotten, it makes me wonder how much playtesting this game had...
I think we were all expecting something more like Hero Klungo Sssavesss Teh World, an 8-bit minigame programmed by Klungo in Nuts & Bolts. Everyone loves this minigame, so much that it got a sequel in the DLC. It's incredibly good at being purposely bad, and because it's purposely bad, it's designed in a way that's fun.
The Rextro minigames just... aren't fun. They're slow autoscrollers that feel painful to sit through. You also have to do them twice, which sucks.
Everything did it better.
Yooka-Laylee has 5 enemies that appear in every world. There are single worlds in BK/BT with more unique enemies.
Kazooie and Tooie did it better.
Yooka-Laylee just doesn't have many characters involved in its challenges. The most memorable characters are honestly the Pagies themselves. The low number of unique characters you run into is a huge letdown.
Yooka has some nice one-off characters, but then it also has Generic Slot Machine #1, 2, 3, and 4. The random memorable characters like Loggo or Nabnut or the Prospector or George and Mildred Icecube are part of what really made BK/BT shine, and they have SO many of them. This game doesn't have a Character Parade like BK and BT because it wouldn't have enough to fill the time.
Kazooie, Tooie, and Nuts & Bolts did it better.
I'm fine with the main characters that appear in every world; Rextro, Dr. Puzz, Kartos. It's like Mumbo and Humba. I'm talking about the NPCs that appear in multiple worlds for no discernable reason other than laziness.
Kazooie has a great example of a recurring character; Gobi. You chase Gobi all around his own valley to ground pound his hump and use whatever's inside. He runs off to the final world of the game to get away from you, and you do the same thing to him then. Then he runs off all the way to Tooie and continue the chase there.
Tooie has a few great ones as well, like Canary Mary and the alien family. Tooie of course also has a lot of recurring characters from Kazooie.
The recurring characters in Yooka are just... there, again, completely identical. They don't act like they know you, because the devs couldn't have known if you've ever talked with them before. They're just always there, and it feels less like a good re-use of characters and more just recycling.
In Nuts & Bolts, the main cast of characters give you the different Jiggy challenges, but in each world, the characters have their own separate "role" in that world. For example, Boggy is a janitor in Banjoland, but in Terrarium of Terror, he's an alien. Pikelet, the hub area's police chief, can appear as a boss, a coach, or a mercenary. Their look is different each time.
Tooie did it better.
If you're exploring Yooka's worlds in-depth, you're going to very quickly run into things that you can't do yet. It makes you want to just rush through the worlds and get all the moves, then come back and clean things up. But there's a major issue: Flying. You gain the ability to fly at will. This eliminates a lot of the platforming challenges in earlier levels completely. But the game is designed to make you want to go learn it (and everything else) before you scour the levels to clear them out. Combining at-will flying with forced backtracking was a terrible idea.
I also don't really like just running into things in earlier levels that require you to learn a move in a future level. I feel that this was more justified in Tooie because of how Tooie's worlds were all inter-connected. The game's 8 worlds have a ton of exits between each other, and you can help characters or trigger things in one world and they have an effect in another. The best example of this is the final level, Cloud Cuckooland, which takes place in the sky above the other 7 worlds; if you fall to your death in this level, you can see a birdseye view of the entire continent. This helped justify a lot of the backtracking in Tooie.
These are the main points I had in mind. There's a lot more critiques I have with this game, which all boil down to one simple summary: It feels rushed. It lacks the polish and detail that went into Kazooie and Tooie, and made them games that stand up to the test of time. With another year of dev time, I think a lot of these problems with Yooka-Laylee could have been fixed. As it is, I hope the next big game trying to recapture that N64 magic (probably A Hat in Time) meets the expectations more.

A Hitman game for Hitman fans.
I have some very serious problems with the DRM and episodic release of this game, but I can't deny that this is the best Hitman has ever played and everything about the game itself is excellent. I've put roughly 20 hours in so far and I'm not done with it.
The gameplay returns to the sandbox format of the earlier games, with large levels full of many methods of ingress and egress as well as a complex system of security, exploitable weaknesses and NPC interactions. I'm a long time fan of the series and, honestly, the Paris level is probably the best one they've ever made in these games. I don't wanna spoil anything, if you love older Hitman, you'll love this.
If you're the sort of person who obsessively plays Hitman levels experimenting with new assassinations and pushing for a perfect rating, this is the game for you. Successive playthroughs are given context from challenges and escalations, asking you to approach the level in new and interesting ways.
If you don't like the older Hitman games, though, this probably won't change your mind. It is heavily based on trial and error gameplay without a huge amount of content to keep you going. If you don't like replaying levels, you might only get 2-3 hours out of this game before you're done.

Amusing and pretty game.  I had fun.  Once I got the hang of capturing ships, the difficulty level dropped.  To be fair, I haven't tried tackling any of the veteran bounties, yet.  I understand that those are considerably more difficult since they will actually put up a fight and deploy counter-measures.
The reputation system in this game is very simple: you gain +20 reputation for completing tasks for law-abiding factions and -20 reputation for completing missions for pirate factions.  I would expect reputation gain to drop more significantly and gain more slowly as it does in many other space sim games (e.g. Eve, X3, ...).  As it is, if you're low on cash, simply cap a ship and you'll be back in black.
Pro:
- Pretty
- Lots of ships
- Large map
Con:
- Not a whole lot of variety or depth.
- Different ships don't seem different enough (i.e. play style remains largely the same)
- Voice acting is terrible; would have been better without.
- Overly simplistic reputation system (see above).

I'll split this up into two sections because this game has a multiplayer mode as well. I'll focus on the single player first.
The main story of the game is not as long as Arkham Asylum and Arkham City. It's actually quite short if you just focus on the main objectives but it's at least enjoyable for what it is. There is a lot to visit when exploring Gotham just like you would experience when exploring Arkham City but what is in the city feels kind of trivial as you travel about. The actual story content is a lot of fun.
The gameplay and fighting feel more polished to me than Arkham City. Batman seems to react better and combat feels a lot more fun. You still get upgrades and gadgets as you progress so it always feels like you are making your way forward. Batman definitely feels a lot stronger as you come towards the end of the game. Some of the upgrades however are very situational and you'll only use them a few times, an example of this would be some of the takedowns you unlock. While situations for some of these upgraded moves may be few and far between they are still very awesome when you do get the chance to pull them off.
The graphics in this game are amazing, much better than Arkham City. There is some noticeable pop in from time to time but that usually happens with sandbox games of this scale and it's mostly forgivable. If you liked Arkham Asylum and Arkham City's graphics then this game won't disappoint you in that department.
The sound lends to the atmosphere that in a brilliant way. You definitely get that Christmas feeling as you explore Gotham and you hear certain music or quips from Alfred. The voice actors do a great job portraying Batman and the various characters. It's not the same ones from the previous games but these voice actors made their characters sound exactly just like they should.
Overall if you're a fan of Arkham City and Arkham Asylum you'll definitely enjoy the story. This game is worth it if you can find it at $20 or less.
The multiplayer is disappointing in a big way. It's broken. Connections to games are rare. The message you will see the most is Connection to Steam has been dropped. This is a big issue for anyone attempting to play the multiplayer and the developer looks like they have no intention on focusing on fixing it. If you are buying this game for multiplayer then pass on it. It's enjoyable when it works but it fails more than it works.
My verdict is if you can find this game on sale for $20 or less then pick it up. You'll get a great enjoyable story out of it which feels like an expansion to Arkham city and that's how I take it as. It's a lot shorter than the previous games but if you can find it at a lower price it is worth its fee. Avoid this game if you want it for the multiplayer though as it's broken since launch and continues to have a ton of problems.

So this was a very fun game. The idea is that it is game based on noir detective type movies/comics and it does it beautifully. The cutscenes are presented as graphic novels that look very dark and grimey as they should be and the voice over work sets the tone perfectly. The gameplay sections has a realistic, albeit very outdated, look to it. Some really nice touches are that the blood, spent ammo, dead bodies and such never disappear to give it less of a "video game" like feel. Another good thing about the game is bullet-time. It makes the game slow down so that you can have more time to think out what you are doing while in a chaotic gun fight. You can also do slo-mo dives which lets you shoot enemies while (hopefully) not getting hit yourself. Another thing about this game is that it is very difficult. You die at the drop of a hat on the easiest and this was probably done so that Payne seems more like just a regular guy with a lot of luck as opposed to being super human. Sure he racks up a huge kill count by the end but it is very easy to die to even just one enemy.
All in all very good game. I give it 5 constipated looking faces out of 5.

A Hitman game for Hitman fans.
I have some very serious problems with the DRM and episodic release of this game, but I can't deny that this is the best Hitman has ever played and everything about the game itself is excellent. I've put roughly 20 hours in so far and I'm not done with it.
The gameplay returns to the sandbox format of the earlier games, with large levels full of many methods of ingress and egress as well as a complex system of security, exploitable weaknesses and NPC interactions. I'm a long time fan of the series and, honestly, the Paris level is probably the best one they've ever made in these games. I don't wanna spoil anything, if you love older Hitman, you'll love this.
If you're the sort of person who obsessively plays Hitman levels experimenting with new assassinations and pushing for a perfect rating, this is the game for you. Successive playthroughs are given context from challenges and escalations, asking you to approach the level in new and interesting ways.
If you don't like the older Hitman games, though, this probably won't change your mind. It is heavily based on trial and error gameplay without a huge amount of content to keep you going. If you don't like replaying levels, you might only get 2-3 hours out of this game before you're done.

A strong return to form for the 3D collectathon platformer genre. Premium-quality visuals and music, a rich moveset that is used evenly throughout the game, plentiful collectibles that each serve a useful purpose, and witty dialog galore. There's just the right amount of content to keep you entertained for a long time without overstaying its welcome, and enough variety in it that it doesn't feel repetitive. And on top of that you get an impressive collection of couch-multiplayer mini-games, that have a surprising ammount of work put into them.
Be aware, though, that this is a faithful recreation of classics in the genre, including all of the same drawbacks: backtracking, a camera that gets stuck on terrain, simplistic combat, gimmick-based boss fights, and sprawling levels that can give a sense of a lack of focus. It's up to you to decide if this is something that turns you off or if you're okay with it.

So after being among the first wave of "Backers", I feel Yooka-Laylee and the Playtonic team have delivered on what was promised. They set out to make a spiritual successor to Banjo-Kazooie (one of my most beloved game series) and in my opinion they have done a very solid job. Even with the new characters and updated visuals, it felt like Hivory Towers could easily exist alongside Gruntilda's Lair.
The humor is silly, the worlds are great, and the music is outstanding. All of the charms of an old platforming collect-a-thon are there. Including a semi-wonky camera at certian points. The moves you learn and the layout of the levels in the game have a familiarity to them, even though a good portion of them are brand new.
My only gripe is that this game throws a lot of non-platforming at you, and those portions severely damage the experience. The rail sections are ok, some people may like them, but I don't. And the arcade games, ugh, can be so aggravating. Requiring near perfect runs sometimes. It felt like playing several other games and I kept wondering what they doing in my nostalgic fun-trip.
All in all however, I had an extremely enjoyable time, even among the few frustrations. Anyone who loves platformers today, and owe that love to the games of the late 90's should give this one a try.

At the risk of sounding like an ignorant fanboy, this may just be the best game I've ever played. I know people are gonna harp on me for being overly positive, but I really do love what this game has done in terms of succeeding the Banjo-Kazooie series and bringing back the 3D platformer.
I feel like this game takes some of my favorite aspects of Kazooie and Tooie and brings them to the forefront along with adding on top of it. Yooka-Laylee is filled with a lot of the simple fun of Kazooie combined with some of the complexity and interconnectedness of Tooie. When you step into one of the game's giant worlds, there is already so much to do with 25 Pagies, 200 Quills, and a few other trinkets to collect in every world . While some may call this overwhelming (especially after such games as DK64), I view it as a breath of fresh air to have another platformer which just leaves you to your own devices and play around in these giant, beautiful, and fun worlds.
As previously mentioned, the game does include some aspects of Tooie, mostly in the fact that some Pagies are unavailable until you return to one world with the moves learned in a later one. I love this as I am a big fan of returning to earlier areas with my new moves and seeing what I can now get done, and I personally feel as though it's better handled than in Tooie as there is still very little locked off to you during your first trip in the world with only about 4-5 Pagies max requiring the player to backtrack, maintaining the great feeling of freedom and exploration.
The characters are another great part of the game, with just about each one having a good bit of personality and memorability. Playtonic said they wanted to create a great universe full of unique and lovable characters and they certainly delivered. My personal favorite character was Capital B, the game's main antagonist, who delightfully trash talks the player in the hub world of Hivory Towers with a large host of corporate buzzwords.
As for presentation, this game is drop dead gorgeous. The graphics are stunning, making it pretty hard to still believe this was a Kickstarter game (even though it did raise over 2 million dollars). All the characters and worlds appear bright, cartoony, and full of dedicated detail. And the music- OH THE MUSIC. Being composed by two of my favorite composers, Grant Kirkhope and David Wise, I already knew I was going to love this OST. Grant delivers great world themes that harken back to his Banjo Kazooie days along with adding new touches of ambience and experimentation which pay off beautifully. David Wise also did a great job here, showing that between this and Donkey Kong Country: Tropical Freeze, he hasn't lost a single strand of talent. Of course there is one more composer that nearly everyone seems to just kinda forget about: Steve Burke. I honestly didn't know much about Steve going into Yooka Laylee, but after listening to his work here, I'd call myself a Burke fan. He definitely deserves as much credit as Grant and David for his contributions.
Overall, from the well-refined and open-ended gameplay to the stunning graphics to the delightful characters to the awe inspiring soundtrack, I love Yooka Laylee to bits and pieces. I was one of this games many Kickstarter backers and I;d say it was everything I wanted the day the Kickstarter launched and even more. If you enjoy 3D platformers and think we need more games holding up the genre's mantel other than the fantastic Super Mario series, I wholeheartedly recommend you purchase Yooka Laylee and give it a shot.

As of now, I have completed spec ops: the line, for the second time, a mere week ago. And funlly enough, the game (even the second time around) was always fun and even with the story being already known by me. Despite that, I was still interested in what the hell was going on in Dubai and I wanted to find out more. Spec ops: the line, doesn´t change the way you play a third person shooter, not at all. It is a competent cover based shooter with extremely fun shooting. Seriously, your enemies die in some rather, entertaining, ways. Like when you shoot a guy he falls over the railing and other action movie-ish ways. The game is also quite bloody. It´s not afraid to show you some stuff that will send shimmers down your spine and it will, couple of times. And that brings me to the theme of the game. The whole atmosphere and the story itself is very dark and that´s what makes the game interesting. Your team, comprised of three soldiers, Adams, Lugo and your ,Lt. Martin Walker, are portraid like  normal people. Yes, they do kill many, many, MANY soldiers, but they don´t feel good about it. They start questioning the things that you (as Walker) and themselves are doing. And the story surrounding this is really good. You are basically sent in to look for survivors in Dubai after a big sandstorm ravaged the city and the survivors tried to stick together and started to make shelters out of the ruins. The story is great, because it moves at a great pace and finishes with a punch to gut, twist ending that you won´t see coming. So good shooting,  good story and atmosphere and believable characters who show emotions towards the whole ´´slaughter of dozens´´ thing. Also, the game is gorgeous, it truly is and suprisingly colorful. It tunes the colors down at times to show the bleakness of the world you are destroying, but those parts are few and far between so most of the time, you´ll be lookin´ at lush colors and beautiful lighting. The multiplayer, I didn´t play nor did I care. I tried it, buuuuuuut there are no people playing it. Co-op mode, I didn´t even touch. Minor issues aside like: the cover system being pretty wonky and that the campaign can be completed in around 4-5 hours and that I don´t mind if I would find the combat fun the third time around, because the third time around, yeah, there´s only that much to it. So I strongly recommend you to pick the game up at sale, because, then? It is worth it, but would I pay 20 euros/bucks for it? Nah, bit too much for the content at hand. Still, awesome story driven game right here.

Okay, I loved this game.  The ship models are fantastic and deeply customizable.  The "Heroes" that can optionally be hunted down have curiously ordinary names and faces - I think I've been killing the developers inside their own game.  The sandbox is massive, and while most of the missions really boil down to "go here and kill this guy" and "go here without getting killed", the enemies scale well enough that you're never really assured a victory.
Until you get a titan.  I didn't play the first game, but I get the feeling that the Levithan was the final battle.  Building your own ship off of that design, then, really skews the odds in your favor.  Fortunately, this is only an option at the very end, so look forward to scurrying away from enemy reinforcements.
Long story short, this will probably devour almost a hundred hours of your life and you won't resent it for that.

I wish there was a "meh" button along with thumbs up and thumbs down.
Bought it after getting burned out on Elite Dangerous in hopes that it would scratch my space sim itch.
One one hand, the scale just isn't there. You tool around a single smallish star system littered with stations, planets, teleportation gates and even a couple black holes and nebulae for some reason. The space is also dirty, dusty and littlered - no, really - there are chunks of rock and clouds of dust constantly whizzing by (fortunately there are mods that get rid of that). There's no hyperspacing to other systems or exploring the galaxy. I guess it's a little bit like the Expanse TV series.
On the oher hand, during ship combat the scale is pretty faithful - you blast your cannons in the general direction of someone flying around you in the darkness, and all you see of the opposing ship is the big red target marker. Eventually, one of you blows up. The only way to take a closer look is to approach to boarding distance, which I have to admit is a nice touch. Between that and a rather obtuse camera, the space combat experience is underwhelming.
The game isn't bad, it's just kind of lackluster. You can tell that it was made by a tiny studio on a limited budget. I know LGM tried hard, but neither the visuals nor the sound can hold a candle to the current-gen games. After seeing the visuals delivered by Elite and even the unfinished mess that is Star Citizen, you soon notice the janky-looking engine exhaust, low-budget pewpew effects and simplistic ships.
It also has some issues outside of the weird camera, the most glaring being a graphics crash (blank screen) in full-screen mode. Since you can only save in stations, this can wipe out a lot of progress.
Let me put it this way: this is a chill spaceflight game (not a sim) in the similar vein as Rogue Galaxy, and it was worth the purchase price of $6.50 with all DLCs during the sale. I wouldn't pay more than that.

Despite its age, Max Payne remains a fun shooter with an interesting story. The game suffers, however, from some clunkiness because of when it was made and its attempts to have occasional platforming sections, that are sometimes frustrating and irritating to play. Some of them are important to the story, but could've been done without having the player make precise jumps with imprecise movement controls. There were also frequent stutters in cutscenes and keyboard lock-ups when I played (Max would be stuck in place or stuck moving or diving in one direction). Despite some of the minor issues, the game holds up because of good encounter design, fun shooting mechanics and great writing, especially in Max's thoughts. The frequent metaphors and allusions give it an almost literary quality. Recommended, but might feel a little too dated for some.

+ Max himself has a good amount of upgrades and customization
+ Random Sandstorms are very cool and feel a lot like Fury Road.
+ Races are cool.
+ Great Photo-mode, I wish every game had one like this.
+ Good Collectables, Historic Relics shows the old world, the fall, and max's thoughts

Honestly a great addition to the Hitman series, perhaps the best yet. Despite the sizeable amount of negative reviews any Hitman veterans will love the return to classic Hitman.
I also like the episodic approach, makes each level seem more special and something worth looking forward to.

In the current state of things, there are 6 levels, the first season of the game completed, second season confirmed, developers have said that there will be a third season on their Twitter. So, with 6 episodes total in the first season, we may be able to reasonably expect 18 episodes total.
So, the levels are amazing. The 6 of them, 6 main ones anyway, are enough to keep me incredibly entertained. The levels are rich. Like extremely rich. Story, environmental details, new objects and things to do with them, a very wide variety of costumes, and numerous conversations to be heard. The levels will keep you entertained, as each level has challenges and opportunities to perfect it and find more about both your targets and the level itself. Each new level presents new opportunites, and unlocks from previous levels that seemed out of place now find perfect places in specific scenarios in later levels.
But, the biggest improvement to the game has came with a more recent update: Professional mode.
The Pro mode is unlocked after completing level 20 of a level. And that's too hard to get to, really. The Pro mode brings the game back to the days of Blood Money. Guard movements are more intuitive, along with the difficulty increase, and moreover, limited saves and lack of guidance on opportunities.
I will say that there are still improvements in the mix, but I find this game much more entertaining in one aspect over Blood Money: combat. The combat in the game is interesting. It's mostly similar to Absolution, which had many improvements in terms of combat. However, combat is not entirely a part of the game, in that, you're not -really- supposed to have mass firefights and such. But it is an interesting aspect. Unlike Absolution, hiding after combat is much easier, and enemies rely on line of sight and sound effects to determine your location. As such, cramped areas and suppressed weapons are a godsend in combat scenarios.
All in all though, this a true Hitman game. Its story derives from portions of Contracts and the original two titles.
Another note: the game's hardware support is quite excellent. My critical specs follow:
CPU: i7-4790k 4.7Ghz
GPU: 980 1280Mhz 4gb
Display: Ultrawide 3440x1440 60hz
These aren't all my specs but the important part here is this: I'm running the game on max settings on my display, and the game that this was often compared to upon release was Rise of the Tomb Raider, as those were the first DX12 games. But, Rise won't run well, at all, at this resolution with my relatively underpowered GPU given the resolution I'm utilizing. This game however has drastically improved how much it taxes my hardware. When it launched I only had a 1080p display, and it actually really taxed my 980. It still pushes it really hard to get it to run 3440x1440. But it does it quite well, with hardly any stuttering, frame tearing, etc. It runs smoothly, and the ultrawide adds quite the field of view.

Gonna go ahead and resubmit my review. The writing hasn't changed, but my opinion has. Hopefully it makes sense and puts things into perspective.
Here's
to determine whether or not you will enjoy Yooka-Laylee:

Whether you should get this game comes down to a few questions:
- do you like to explore every corner of a world?
- do you want a collectathon that plays just like Banjo-Kazooie and/or Tooie?
- do you want to have fun and laugh at some hilarious dialogues?
- can you appreciate great art work and soundtrack?
- can you get over some camera issues that are far from game-breaking?
- can you get over a few improvable design choices that get forgotten quickly with the next challenge?
- can you get over or do you even like the gibberish voices?
- can you get over or even like the quizzes between worlds?
What I wanted is exactly what I got: a spiritual successor to Banjo-Kazooie. It looks like Banjo, it feels like Banjo, it plays like Banjo. The game is massive without being Banjo-Tooie-confusing massive, the humor is the same, and the 4th wall breaking is at least on par with Nuts & Bolts. This is a Kickstarter game and I had much more fun than with some other AAA titles. There definitely are frustrating parts but it's the same as with other difficult games: put down the controller, come back later and triumph. I really hope that this is just the beginning of a new franchise. I crave for more!

I'm gonna stop you right here and say that this game is the husk of Banjo Kazooie, not an honorable or nostolgic sequel to it.
I've been playing video games for the better part of 20 years, I 100% Kazooie, I got like 80% in Tooie.  I played the F out of DK64 and really any N64 game that came out at the time.  This is not those games.
Lemme break down the most obvious complaints and compare them to the Banjo and various other platformers and the relevency of them.
The Camera:
In Banjo, the camera gently kept behind the main character while using the shoulder buttons on the N64 controller to have a more hands on approach to controlling it.  In certain locations it would become fixed to help the player focus more on platforming and not on managing the camera.  This made sense back then given how controllers and in general, 3D games were back then.
In Yooka, it's essentially the same thing.  The positive thing about it is it helps cater to keyboard and mouse users.  The negative thing is everything else.  Controllers (and people) have evolved with the development of a second analog stick to manage a camera.  Not only that but most games nowadays have a section to control camera settings in the game.  This game lacks both the awareness of the second analog, and the camera settings in the option menu (as well as button remapping of all things).  Further insult is the fixed camera positions are still prevelent and cause more issues then fixes them simply because people have grown used to multitasking.
World Completing:
Remember in Banjo Tooie where you needed a ability to get a jiggy from another world so you kept having to go back and forth to complete the worlds you ran into?  No?  Well you will now.
Unlike in Banjo Kazooie where all the tools where at hand, Yooka literally forces you to backtrack to the STARTING area (the equivelent to Banjo's house) after unlocking an ability in the first world, provided you have enough quils to pay for it.  Now repeat it several times.  The backtracking is absurd in how often you have to do it.  You are better off getting the bare minimum of pagies and quils to get the world's abilities and unlock the next area until you hit the last world.  You cannot complete World 1 without unlocking World 5 for crap's sake.
Flying:
I actually have no idea if people are complaining about flying, but I sure as heck am going to.  Yes, spoiler alert you gain the ability to fly and it's like driving a semi on ice and on a tightrope.
In Banjo, you needed red feathers and a launch pad to fly, pitting the camera somewhat behind your character as you navigated.  You could glide down or use a red feather to climb higher in altitude.  The control was pretty phenomenal considering you're using a hunk of cheap plastic for a control stick.
In Yooka, the same angles apply not to mention you can take off from any location but it just doesn't work nearly as well.
Here's why:  Banjo's sillouette was narrow and flat, providing the ability to see ahead and plan your flight better.
Yooka's by comparison is a giant vertical rectangle with the camera shoved up his♥♥♥♥♥  Banjo was able to manuever for safe landings and make tight precise turns with the shoulder buttons.  Yooka has no such luck and can't even glide down making it harder to plan your route before your stamina runs out and you splat to the ground.
Enemies and other things:
Enemies, quite frankly are bad.  They are either completely dumb as a brick or cheap as hell (looking at you Bees).  They respawn super quick which makes some minigames unbearable and overall not even work confronting them unless you absolutely have to.
Speaking of minigames, none feel that great to play.  Most of the overworld minigames have a timer as well, making the camera and controls issues listed above a nightmare.  The retro games are just boring and play like a stick of butter most of the time.
The level design also feels really chaotic and messy at times.  Some worlds are better then others, then you have World 4 where you just sit at a slot machine ground pounding it with proper timing.  I don't know about you but that sounds riviting.
There are some shining moments in this game, such as the humor being like the old days (very dry and subtle).  Dying doesn't reset the quils like it did notes in Banjo, making it a bit more casual and more forgiving.
And personally I like the aesthetics of the game.  World 2 looks lovely to me, but then I'm biased to ice/snow places.
If you must try this game, wait for 80% off deals cause there is no way in hell I'd recommend the full price it wants.

Specs Ops: The Line has received much praise in weaving a horrific tale of an op gone wrong and the horrors of war. The game expertly puts you in the shoes of the main character as he teeters on the edge of sanity as his PTSD nightmare slowly consumes him. But in the end, the game's greatest strength is also its greatest weakness.
The game not only encourages, but actively pushes you towards making crazy "gamer" decisions that leads to the story spiraling out of control. Executing a downed enemy is a common video game mechanic that players have come to expect. Executing a downed enemy also gives you ammo for both weapons. However, should you choose to simply double-tap them with your gun, you will not spiral into madness at the same rate as a normal playthrough. Although there are many hidden third options to most of your choices, the game doesn't let you make any key decisions that sidestep everything.
Spec Ops: The Line does a great job of telling one story but fails to give you the other option of not succumbing to monstrosity. The gameplay is very tiresome and rather boring. Some would say that this is in part of the game trying to parody the meaninglessness of your generic modern First-Person-Shooters, but was this honestly the best way of going about this? Couldn't we have some fun going down this hellish slide?
I only wish that there were more choices that we could make that would better simulate PTSD/anxiety/paranoia. Why was there no choice to interact with the civillian NPCs in a way that would test our distrust of the local populace? Why was there no option to deal with groups that were obviously armed and cutious, yet not overtly hostile?
Overall, Spec Ops: The Line is a good game to experience but not necessarily to play. I would definitely recommend this game if you enjoy storytelling experiences.

Huge nostalgia trip!
When I stumbled across this in steam it brought back a wave of memories , back when I was 11 or 12 and used to play the demo of this game on my dad's computer. I bought it on steam, expecting it to be not as good as a I remembered, as are a lot of my childhood games I go back to.
However I was hugely surprised to find it every bit as good as I remembered. Graphics arent half bad given their age, lightsaber combat is fun and fairly varied, force powers are useful and satisfying, maps are well laid out. All in all a pretty decent game. My only complaints are lack of compass or mini map means it often takes ages to figure out where you're meant to be going, and after a while the earlier missions get a tad repetitive, combined with the very slow and sparse story telling. The story/plot is the weakest aspect of the game, but its still great fun for a light saber hacky slashy trip down memory lane.
Having just completed both endings I now find myself unwilling to leave the star wars universe just yet, so am presently downloading KOTOR :)
Definitely worth a play if you are even vaguely interested in star wars, as I'm not a massive fan but still enjoyed it a lot.

For me a lot of the problem was the tons of menus, which made many things, such as trying to play a lute in a tavern or even character creation, very very cumbersome (repeated pop-up menus). The combat also felt clunky to me. I was thrown off by the "re-release date" initially (my fault for not reading the actual game description to realize the original version was older than Morrowind by a full decade), so I didn't bother looking for and reading the manual first.
To be fair, I only managed one fight.... and killed half the party before I realized I could run away. But there wasn't anything that grabbed me here. Besides the old graphics, clunky combat, and menus I would say the one other thing that put me off was the bad voice "acting".
Edit: corrected date; as others have pointed out this is a remake, not the original. I think my point of "it wasn't very fun for me and I really wish they had spent some time during the remake to reduce pop-up screens and make menus nicer" still holds.
Edit2: @RandalMcdaniel: corrected the other date part I missed. The original version is in fact 10 years old than Morrowind. I didn't think it was that hard to figure out what I meant but I have corrected my review now. And to your point, very few of my complaints were about it being 3D/having older graphics. Did I give the game much of a chance? That's subjective, but I gave it about 3 hours to grab my interest and it failed to do so. Feel differently? Write your own review.
Edit3: I will be un-subscribing from this review thread going forward. I've fixed my f*** ups and I don't have any more time for this game right now. Schicksalsklinge hat bei mir einen  Nostalgiebonus. Ich habe seinerzeit das P&P-Originl gespielt, dann Schatten über Riva und war sofort vertraut mit den Regeln. Ich hatte immmer wieder viel über Schicksalsklinge und Sternenschweif gelesen, es aber wegen der Grafik immer nur kurz angespielt. Bis ich dann das Remake im Laden sah und die Chance nutzen wollte, diesen Klassiker durchzuspielen. Es war damals die DVD-Version 1.2x. Diese habe ich schon ohne größere Bugs durchspielen können und habe da schon das Engagement des Teams mitbekommen, doch noch ein sehr gutes Produkt machen zu wollen. Ganz großes Lob dafür!
Jetzt las ich, dass das Remake von Sternenschweif in der Mache ist und ich habe mir Schicksalsklinge nochmal auf Steam geholt um einen Spielstnd für Sternenschweif zu haben :)
Was soll ich zu den anderen teils umfangreichen Reviews hinzufügen? Ich finde die Kampf-Avatare nicht soooo schlimm. Im Gegensatz zum Original finde ich die Kämpfe sogar wesentlich angenehmer mit zoomen und drehen. Die Story ist solala, wird aber durch die Umsetzung und Aufmachung wieder wettgemacht: das Rumreisen und Entdecken, die Ereignisse, die teilweise sehr zum Schmunzeln einladen, das Gruppenmanagement, der spitzenmäßige Sprecher usw. Bugs hatte ich keine mehr mit 1.36 und durch die Mods/DLC kommt noch mal viel Content und viele Features hinzu.
Man sollte sich aber im Klaren sein, dass es wegen der Größe des Studios kein AAA-Titel (Grafik zB - nett und funktional aber halt nich weltspitze) ist. Auch ist die Lernkurve sehr steil und man sollte als Neuling bereit sein, viel zu lesen und zu lernen (Komplettlösung per ModManager, Regelwerke usw.). Dafür wird man aber mit  einem einzigartigen Spielerlebnis belohnt. In welchem anderen RPG überlegt man sonst noch, ob man es noch vor dem Winter schafft, den Bergpass zu passieren und ob man  genug Schlafsäcke hat :)?

Mir hat Schiksalsklinge HD sehr viel  Spass gemacht. Für mich sind es 8 von 10 Punkten. Sternenschweif EA ist bestellt und sieht schon sehr gut aus mit sinnvollen Ergänzungen und Verbesserungen - ich freue mich drauf :)

Also, I found some mods and tweaks that helped me get rid of things I didn't like, i.e. the narrator:
- Just rename the folder "VOICEOVER" TO "VOICEOVER-" or something like this. The game won't find the sound files and hence, you won't hear the narrator.

- Bildschoenes-Aventurien-1.0: Restores vignettes for some dialogs, i.e. when the party picks up the trail of a wild animal, etc.
- Magic_Weapon_Pictures: You can now see whether a weapon or item is magical or not.
If you find more like these, please let me know :)

Even though many people complained about the bugs and glitches in Batman: Arkham Origins, I thought the game was done exceptionally well. The story was phenomenal and the side missions were not too tedious to off put me. The new grading system helped a lot as well. In the previous Arkham games, I wasn't sure exactly how I could have improved in really "being" Batman. The grading system allowed me to see me progress, much like a report card in school. Overall, great game, great story, and great artwork.

******REVISION*******
My original opinion was that this game had major flaws that didn't let it hold up to Asylum and Arkham City. I stand by that opinion. This game STILL has some problems but a little bit of hindsight makes me realize that the other two Arkham games are phenomenal, and if I compare this to them, Origins falls short. However Arkham Origins on its own merit is a playable, enjoyable Batman game.
Some of the story in the later parts of the game is acutally quite good. It's a shame that the most interesting parts of the story are at the end where a large majority of players will never get to. There is some psychological insight into the relationship of Batman and one of his major enemies that I've not seen in quite that way before.
I said this in my original, brief review but I got a kick out of the early character models for penguin and some of the other rougues from the Batman gallery.
If you can get to the last third of the game there are some good story beats in there. The combat is flawed but you can adjust to it. I've changed my recommendation from a no to a reserved yes. You still feel like the Bat.....and that is pretty cool.
**********End Edit**************************
I paid $5 for Arkham Asylum GOTY. I paid $30 for Arkham Origins. It should have been the other way around. I'm only two hours in and things may change but it feels like this third installment is a step backwards. The fighting doesn't have quite the right rythm to it. Animations often times slide just a little bit to far from one side to the other in order to make a fight sequence work.
There are some issues that even early on just don't make sense. This is an origins story, so why does Batman have all the devices that he had in the later games?
I will say that seeing the "younger" version of some of the characters from this version of the world is neat. I'm going to continue playing but unless you're a die hard, I don't feel like I could recommend this version without a MAJOR sale.

A fair amount of games are online only now days because we are
anyways. The always online even makes sense as they are releasing the levels episodically which love or hate really encourages replaying of the same levels.
Why replay the same levels? Because they are massive and there is a TON going on at the same time. There are options everywhere. Unlike absolution which was a constant straight forward path, there is simply a wide array of options in this one.
The online mode makes sense in the fact that you need to be online to gain unlocks which work with the online part of the game. You can still play the game offline if you wish but you will be missing out on a huge part of the game which is fun, contracts. Soon to be released are elusive contracts that come with rewards, there is a catch though, you cannot lose or abuse these contracts. If you lose then the contract is lost forever. You will be able to do these contracts based on the knowledge you have of the level, every floor and every possibiliy simply by replaying. The maps really allow you to explore to your hearts content, and do things your way and the best part is that they never get old.
I'm super excited for the future of Hitman and I cannot wait for Sapienza (which looks massive mind you) next month.
If you have your doubts then just get the intro pack for 15 bucks, you get everything that is currently in the game at the moment and each episode will then be 10 bucks, it's a great pricing model albeit not very well marketed.
Yes the always online DRM sucks, but the game is pretty damn good.

As much as people are trashing this game in the reviews for things that I generally agree with I'd like to highlight some of the great things about this game.
The game is definitely a true successor to Blood Money and takes all the great gameplay and combines it with the improved mechanics of Absolution and greatly expands upon it. It's pretty much everything you could ever hope for in a Hitman franchise game, albeit the DRM and arguably the fact that it's episodic.
The Paris level is large, interesting, and provides thousands of ways to replay it. The challenges allow you to try to approach the mission in completely new ways and the sheer diversity of the level is enough to keep my interest throughout multiple playthroughs. The more you get to know the level the better you get at breaking it and finding interesting ways to complete it. In the game FTL you're pretty much replaying the same thing over and over yet it's the diversity of how you can play it that makes the game interesting. So why all the hate for Hitman?
As for the DRM it's really not as bad as everyone is making it out to be. I don't care for it but I've only been disconnected twice in 24 hours of gameplay and the game autosaves fairly frequently. The new model of gameplay encourages you to save the game at vital points anyway so what's the big deal?
As for it being episodic I really don't care. I'm a little bit disappointed but it does allow me to focus on playing one level at a time and getting the most out of it. When I get bored I'll just play something else. I am optomistic that it will give more time to the devs to make the game the best it can be. Many developers abandon games after they release them and it's nice to know that we get pretty much weekly content to keep us playing. I definitely can't fault people that feel differently.

I enjoyed myself thoroughly. There are numerous 'little quirks' that could be considered annoying, but nothing brought me close to wanting to stop playing. All in all I would heavily recommend this game to anyone who enjoyed 3D platformers of old. (Notable games: Banjo Kazooie, Super Mario 64, Spyro the Dragon, Crash Bandicoot, Super Mario Sunshine, Donkey Kong 64 etc) Do note that this game suffers and benefits from the same tropes of the aforementioned titles.



********** POSITIVES **********
- Long lasting, at least for a '2017 game' without any online multiplayer component.
- Very enjoyable
- Many little jokes, some distinctly British, others quite generic
- Great controls (unless you are a KB/M user)
- Fantastic level design, each very unique from the last
- Tons of things to do
- Rarely gets repetitive
- Final boss fight was actually kinda intense
- Wasn't too easy, wasn't too hard. It had both moments of being very easy, and moments of being very hard, but never went too far either side of the spectrum
- The music was just fantastic!
- Large move-set, each making you become noticeably more powerful as a player


********** NEGATIVES **********
- Rarely the camera got stuck when in tight spaces, this was a very rare issue
- I commonly got stuck looking for the last 1 - 10 quills. This is a common trope of games of this type and to be expected.
- A couple of pagies weren't very 'obvious' in how to obtain them, but I didn't need walkthroughs at any point.
- The flight ability that you gain near the end of the game is overpowered - When you get access to this ability you can go nearly EVERYWHERE in the game without much consequence, trivialising some pagies you previously had to pass up due to lack of required abilities.
- The instructions for this very ability were not clear. You're not TOLD when you learn the ability that pressing the jump button allows you to flu upwards. Learning this was a happy mistake and was required for a couple of quills & pagies.
- That said, this ability was a lot of fun to use, and isn't that what gaming is about? :P
- Only 5 levels
- 'only' might not be fair to say, since the levels are MASSIVE
- Some of the voices are very irritating
- Some cutscene type sections aren't skippable. I died twice vs the final boss, and having to re-hear some of his dialogue when fighting him the 2nd and 3rd time was quite irritating.
- If you don't have a controller of a modern game system (X360, XBONE, PS4 (Maybe PS3?)) Then do not buy this game. The Keyboard/mouse controls are straight-up awful and there's no control menu.
- On that note, the control display doesn't update based on what controller you're using. For example, I used a PS4 controller, but the XBOX buttons display (Press "A" to jump!)



All in all, I enjoyed myself throughout and can see myself replaying this a few times in the future, perhaps with a speedrunning mentality. 8.5/10

After completing the entire campaign on normal difficulty, I'm writing a brief review to summarize my experience. You play as Martin "military everyman" Walker, leading a team of three on a shooting spree through Dubai. The environments are unique, despite every single one of them being coated in sand. There are some light stealth elements, but I found myself firring from the hip and sticking to cover through the entire game.
The two AI partners that accompany you are competent enough, though they will run out and get themselves gunned down from time to time. You can use the environments against your enemies, making for an interesting dynamic. As achievements go, I earned more than half just casually playing through the campaign.
All in all, it isn't a beautiful game, but the tight gunplay, and interesting story hold it together rather well. Get this one on sale. Oh, and there is a TON of profanity in this game. I'm not exaggerating when I say that every sentence spoken by your team contains the "F" word. It didn't bother me at first, but it got a little old by the 8th chapter.
Final Rating: 8/10 "PTSD Simulator 2012"

Ok I tried the game again after 2 years or so. I am full of great respect how far the developers brought the game. Still. It remains an anachronistic idea in itself.
Look, I am an Arkania veteran. I began to play this game system 30 years ago and like it. But as computer game, sticking so slavishly to the Pen and Paper rules is totally BORING and horrible.
Second fight, 8 Robbers. Miss. Miss. Miss. Miss. Parry. Miss. -3 Health. Miss. Miss. Miss
It drags on and on and on. And watching it simply is not fun. Even with the top graphics of 2016 it would just be totally unfun to watch a turn based fun where 80% of the swings are misses. Yes. I know, that is exactly the DSA ruleset. It is nice when you play this with a group of people in your mind, as a Pen and Paper game. But as Single Player RPG it is a nightmare.
I congratulate the developers for bringing this game so far from the humble beginnings. Really. But I can not in good faith recommend this game. Back when the "Blade of Destiny" was new, it was the first DSA (Arkania) game ever. So of course they wanted to make it 100% true. But even then it was a Dinosaur. Computer games just dont work with total PnP ruleset conversions. A pity. But even with my really patient senses it remains unplayable for me.

I would definitely recommend picking it up, especially as it is incredibly cheap now.

Anyway story is Yooka and Laylee are chilling, Some ugly bumble bee comes along and wants to create this thing which like, absorbs books and it'll make him powerful to take over the world and stuff. Anyway, he ends up trying to take a book from Yooka and Laylee and the pages rip apart and get spread around.
So, you gotta get in this factory thing and go get em all. Catch is, They are all lost and missing in various different worlds.
The worlds are large, but fortunately you can pace yourself since they start as a small but when you get enough pages you can upgrade the world and make it larger.  As for the pages, you will be able to see them but to unlock 'em you'll be challenged to go thru a circuit, solve a puzzle, beat up a bad dude. etc etc.
Collect a bunch, you unlock new areas, unlock new moves, go back to old areas and unlock some more. So some will see it as "Lots of exploring to do" but others may see this "Going back and forth, over and over" So really the game is somewhat linear in direction but kinda not at the same time, you know?
There's a multi player aspect which has a whole bunch of mini games to play with others but I dont know anything bout it so i can't comment on that. There is also a Co-op feature when the second player plays with a swarm of bees to help collect items but thats it really.
Apart from that, Im happy with the game, I hope there's more from this group, I enjoyed it heaps.
I'm left with the idea theres still more to do even though I have invested so many hours into it. I hope there is.

Gripes:
1) The Hook
This is a weird thing to complain about, I know, but the whole "book" premise is kind of silly and doesn't make much sense to me. I'm sure it would have been taboo to reuse the damsel in distress trope from the original series, but given how muchof the game's humor embraces the cliches of the previous games, i was a bit thrown by the plot not being very traditional. It comes off as contrived, to me anyway.
2) Controls
The controls are painfully inconsistent. They are not tight and fluid like they were in Banjo Kazooie. For example, the "rolling" mechanic for fast travel and rolling up hills is clunky as hell, and it's terribly inconsistent about letting you land on a ramp and do the move instead of simply sliding down the hill the second Yooka touches it. Another example: Lizard Lash (i think it's called)---why is there no crosshair when you use this move? You basically have to guess to try and find hte middle of the screen and wing it each time you use it. Also, I've only ever been disappointed with the controls in the Rextro Sixtyfourus games. Also, not sure why the graphics in those games aren't themselves retro like Rextro Sixtyfourus himself is. These come off as just annoying minigames.
3) Confusing Overworld
This thing is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to navigate, and there are no music-note doors that tell you where you ought to go once you hit a certain number. It's also very unclear at what point you should try and go find the next level.
5) Minecart segments
There are just too many of these and they are too difficult and unforgiving. Not very enjoyable.
6) No pause theme music?! Come on...
7) Not really all that much to collect in spite of the game being supposedly a collect-a-thon. Quills are spaced out a lot and don't feel as tightly-packed and satisfying to collect as music notes were. This also gives each level a kind of empty feeling. Hopefully there will be more collectables to fill out the worlds in later ones.
8) You can get stuck in icycles and have to restart the game.
9) NPCs are consistently lame and don't fit into the levels so much. (Shopping carts in a swamp? No polar-themed animals in the ice level? I don't get it.)
Overall, I expected to be wowed a bit more. The game is good but that's about it. I am also not sure how many young folks who aren't prepared to turn the other cheek for nostalgia's sake (I might be guilty of that myself) will think of the game.

Depending on your history with Rare's original sandbox collect-a-thon games, your milage may vary with Yooka-Laylee.
As a long-time fan of the genre? Yooka-Laylee is honestly one of the weaker games that old school Rare/now Playtonic has made. Levels are massive and very open, and while this makes for fun exploring, it makes collecting all the things an absolute nightmare. On top of that there are some unfortunate bugs and camera issues, which thankfully Playtonic are currently working on. Also text scrolling seems awkwardly slow, making every dialogue exchange take a while, with no option to speed it up.
That's not to say this game is bad! Kind of like Portal 2 compared to the first Portal, just because it's not as good as the previous games doesn't mean it's necessarily bad. Controls are great, characters are fun, and Grant Kirkhope reminds the world that he can still bang out a fantastic, strange soundtrack. Levels are very colorful, and there's many improvements over the old Banjo-Kazooie formula (a quick return-to-hub option, more varied power-ups, lots of variety of things to do, etc.). Backtracking doesn't feel like a waste of time, as it's fun going back to earlier areas and finding new things. Also, for people who miss the N64 days, Yooka-Laylee certainly scratches that itch for a new "real" Rare game, and it's a delight to play.

Realms of Arkania is one of the best crash simulators I've ever experienced. Not only do you have to manually tinker with game files to even start the game in English, one must also (re)select your desired resolution and the option to not run in windowed mode everytime you start the game up. If you want to change settings in-game, then you will crash. This is one of many crashes you will experience. How about starting a new game? After selecting new game and then your difficulty, you will crash again. I will not list all of the crashes, because I don't want to ruin this awesome simulator for you guys.
Graphics - 10/10:
Seriously the menu looks amazing. So does my desktop after an error-less crash.
Gameplay - 10/10:
All crashes are instant and uncorrectable due to the lack of a way of diagnosing the crashes. This makes it much different from other games, where instead of Googling how to fix the crash, you first have to figure out how it happened in the first place. Nice to see a simulator with a puzzle element to it.
Sound - 9/10:
The sound is the only lacking feature, and it's amazing. The sound you get when you crash is so good, you won't even believe that you heard it.
Overall - 10/10:
This is seriously the best crash simulator I've ever played.

On a scale of 1 to 10 I would rate this game a 5/10, and only that high because of the mods and DLCs that make the 2015 implementation of the game somewhat tolerable.  I shudder to think of what playing the original re-release of BoD must have been like.
Pros:
-Planning your party's make-up and levelling up strategy matters (somewhat)
-A somewhat nostalgic old-school RPG flavor with emphasis on being true to the underlying game world, and story-telling/quests
-Apparently there is a second installment in the RoA series being worked on, so hopefully the party you build and grow in BoD can carry over to the Star Trail re-make (assuming the developers improve on playability in the next installment)
Cons:
-Combat is glacially slow, riddled with incessant misses, and overall just a chore.  If my characters weren't missing all the time, they would be dropping their weapons, or the weapons would break.  (Hi I'm a warrior, trained in all kinds of combat techniques and... Whoopsie I just dropped my sword on the ground and now I'm dead....) Luckily I ran across a forum post recommending to switch to computer-controlled combat.  I did that, running at a 100x time multiplier and basically just brute-forced combat encounters until I won.  (You can configure the time speed-up to use in the settings for the game.)
-A still largely opaque and broken skill system.  As an example, I'm running around with 15 in Treat Disease, and yet >50% of my Treat Disease attempts fail.  For the life of me I still don't understand why my characters miss combat hits, mis-cast spells, etc... The game sorely needs a way in-game to explain what success/failure percentages are, and how changes in base skills and talents will effect those percentages.
-Related to disease, it seems that staring at the sky (metaphorically speaking) in this game leads to your character contracting a disease.  While I did choose to play the game with the realism setting turned on, the way disease works in this game is beyond ridiculous.  I swear in at least one case a party member went from "ouch I didn't sleep well because of a pebble" to "I'm dead" in a matter of days because of the inane disease mechanic in the game.
-As noted earlier, weapons break in combat.  As in ...all... ...the... ...time...  I never did figure out how to prevent this from happening.  You can buy whetstones in shops, and repair weapons after each combat occurrence which helps to some extent.  But unless you are lucky enough to find a magical weapon, resign yourself to weapons constantly breaking in combat and your party being reduced to making like Chuck Norris (unarmed combat: go punch mummies in the face!)
-Travel becomes laborious after a while.  At first I enjoyed travelling around parts of the map, wondering what I would run into.  But once I got farther into the game, and the much larger distances that needed to be traversed, travel was an exercise in boredom and frustration.  Travel is also a great opportunity to contract disease - despite running around with cloaks, sleeping bags, campfires, etc...  I swear there is a bug somewhere in this game that is just hell-bent on making characters contract disease.
-Inventory management is, well,  unmanageable, because of the strict encumbrance system.  Luckily I could use a number of mods (listed below) to make inventory management tolerable.
*Review based on playing Blade of Destiny v1.36 with all three DLCs installed.  It is important to play with at least the latest free DLC (With Blade and Brilliance) since it includes numerous bugfixes.
*Additionally I installed a number of mods to make levelling and inventory substantially less onerous:  Packesel (pack horse), Mit Sack und Pack (storage chests for potions, books, jewellry and poisons), and erfolgreicheSteigerung (replaces random level up rolls with fixed increases and 100% skill up success).  Very important:  don't put any of the storage add-ins inside of another storage add-in.  For example if you drag and drop your pack-horse, onto the pack-horse by mistake - all of the inventory stored by the pack-horse disappears!
*Mods can be downloaded from a
.  Hint:  use Chrome for its handy translate feature if you don't speak German!
*Highly recommended to read both of the following community guides for this game so you can plan a reasonable party and know how to invest in and focus on growing your party's skills:
"The old Memories Blade of Destiny Starter Guide"   and    "A camping Guide through Arkania"

Max Payne is a really unique game, a rare gaming gem.
Back in 2001 it was a revolutionary game.
You are Max Payne, a man with nothing to lose. Your family is murdered by drug addicts, you are deep undercover in the underworld of New York. Then, your cover is blown, and the cops thinks you are one of the bad guys.
The game itself is a 3rd person shooter, with it´s best feature being the ability to slow down time. This feature added depth to the vicious shootouts, and the destruction caused by the bullets could be apreciated in detail.
Simply put, there were nothing like that around.
It borrowed many elements from The Matrix, including slow motion action sequences and many of its locations.
You just have to keep moving and keep shooting every single enemy (there is one scort mission, but it´s fairly short and thankfully not frustating at all), It could be repetitive in theory, but the shootings are so fun it never gets old.
Dodging bullets while firing your duals berettas couldn´t be more rewarding.
The story is surprisingly deep for a game of it´s kind. It involves drugs, infanticide, madness, evend the russian mafia plays it´s part, and high echelon corporate conspiracy. It´s just awesome, and told in a very dark tone.
Ultimately, it´s a tale of revenge of a broken man, alone and desperate, with no higher moral, no savior cause or anything.
It aged very well. The mechanics are still fun, the graphics might seem a bit bulky and outdated, but there are some really good textures and nice particle effects that still makes it good looking in movement. Also, any cheap PC can run it with max settings without problems.
If you dig deep, you can also find some very interesting mods, adding weapons and levels that explore more of the great shooting mechanics.
10/10
Don´t miss it.

Max Payne is a bonafide and award winning noir classic released in 2001. The game centers around a NYPD cop working undercover in the Valkyr-drug smuggling mafia seeking answers after he got his family killed. As the story unravels, Max becomes the most wanted guy by the mafia and the NYPD and discover what is hiding behind the drug Valkyr.
The story is presented to the player using comic novels artifacts which sometimes resembles Frank Miller's Sin City. Cutscenes are entertaining to watch and sucks you into it with a noir narrative. I wish Max Payne got his own comic book, because the writing is second to none immersive. There is a heavy influence of nordic mythos which adds to the bigger picture.
I love the level design. Although is set mostly in a stormy, snowy and dark NY or inside some buildings, it nevers gets repetitive. You'll be looking all over the place for clues, guns and painkillers. Max Payne has one of the best level design I've ever seen in any game. You'll never forget about those nightmare levels and shootings at the Ragna Rock night club.
The music is beautiful. It has a dark and dense mood to it, the one you'd expect from detective stories. The synth sounds go really with the ambient sounds.
The gameplay is absolutely fun. The game introduces an innovative (at the time) bullet time and bullet dodge mechanics. This is a hard game, although there is some automatic health regen don't expect miracles. You'll be craving for painkillers through out the whole game. Also, a word of advice, DON'T save if you're not sure if you're still in the middle of a bullet fest.
I can assure you the game aged gracefully.
Writing a positive review about an award winning game that eventually became the cornerstone of the 2000's age of gaming feels just like another brick in the wall. It's just another one in the bag of thousand positive reviews Max Payne got through the years.
A must have for ANY gamer.

Family Guy is an American adult animated sitcom created by Seth MacFarlane for the Fox Broadcasting Company. The series centers on the Griffins, a family consisting of parents Peter and Lois; their children Meg, Chris, and Stewie; and their anthropomorphic pet dog Brian. The show is set in the fictional city of Quahog, Rhode Island, and exhibits much of its humor in the form of cutaway gags that often lampoon American culture.
The family was conceived by MacFarlane after developing two animated films, The Life of Larry and Larry & Steve. MacFarlane redesigned the films' protagonist, Larry, and his dog, Steve, and renamed them Peter and Brian, respectively. MacFarlane pitched a seven-minute pilot to Fox in 1998, and the show was greenlit and began production. Shortly after the third season of Family Guy had aired in 2002, Fox canceled the series, with one episode left unaired. Adult Swim burned off the episode in 2003, finishing the series' original run. However, favorable DVD sales and high ratings for syndicated reruns on Adult Swim convinced the network to renew the show in 2004 for a fourth season, which began airing on May 1, 2005.
Since its debut on January 31, 1999, 282 episodes of Family Guy have been broadcast. Its fifteenth season began on September 25, 2016. Family Guy has been nominated for 12 Primetime Emmy Awards and 11 Annie Awards, and has won three of each. In 2009, it was nominated for an Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Comedy Series, the first time an animated series was nominated for the award since The Flintstones in 1961. Family Guy has also received criticism, including unfavorable comparisons to The Simpsons.
Many tie-in media have been released, including Stewie Griffin: The Untold Story, a straight-to-DVD special released in 2005; Family Guy: Live in Vegas, a soundtrack-DVD combo released in 2005, featuring music from the show as well as original music created by MacFarlane and Walter Murphy; a video game and pinball machine, released in 2006 and 2007, respectively; since 2005, six books published by Harper Adult based on the Family Guy universe; and Laugh It Up, Fuzzball: The Family Guy Trilogy (2010), a series of parodies of the original Star Wars trilogy. In 2008, MacFarlane confirmed that the cast was interested in producing a feature film and that he was working on a story for a film adaptation.
A spin-off series, The Cleveland Show, featuring Cleveland Brown, aired from September 27, 2009, to May 19, 2013. "The Simpsons Guy", a crossover episode with The Simpsons, aired on September 28, 2014.[2] Family Guy is a joint production by Fuzzy Door Productions and 20th Century Fox Television and syndicated by 20th Television.[3] In 2013, TV Guide ranked Family Guy the ninth Greatest TV Cartoon of All Time.[4]
