Dream Daddy is a kind of loving parody... it pokes fun without MAKING fun, and celebrates as much as it jokes. It's well written, frequently funny, and just as frequently unexpectedly touching. All of the dads, including yourself, are wonderfully written, affable, warm people, and your daughter Amanda is a treasure. The downside is that the three-dates-til-the-end for a route feels rushed, even for the genre, and often the kids of the other dads don't get enough time for you to feel like they're important parts of the equation. They're all cute and funny and interesting, but they're just not around enough, and in a game ABOUT dads, that's sort of weird. The parameters for getting a good romantic outcome ending with a dad seem nebulous... I got perfect S rankings on my first two dates and an A on the last one, but would just replaying that last scene fix it? Do I need to aim for explosions of eggplants and sweat as WELL as hearts, or are hearts just as good? Did I maybe need to experience a scene in someone else's route? Who knows!
On the technical side, Dream Daddy is missing some basic quality of life stuff visual novels kind of need. You can't right-click to open a save menu, said saves appear in an unhelpfully long scroll without useful thumbnails or the ability to rename them, you can't skip ahead to choices or previously unseen text (just fast-forward), the options menu is a joke, and you can't scroll back up with your mouse even to review past text. Are these necessary? Not really. But they're typical functions people tend to expect most visual novels to have, and they would have made the game feel a lot more user-friendly.
As of this writing, day of release, obviously there are some odd bugs. The game frequently lost track of who Amanda's other parent was supposed to be (male or female depending on your choice at the start of the game), character sprites would occasionally lose things like glasses or whatnot from one expression to the next. These I have no doubt will be fixed in the days to come. Ultimately, it's a very polished, sweet, heartfelt and charismatic game that any fans of well-written romantic comedies should consider picking up. The art is beautiful, the characters are great, and at the end of the day, all I really want is a game that wants to make me smile and laugh. Dream Daddy comes recommended for that alone.

THIS REVIEW WILL INCLUDE MILD SPOILERS FOR THE START OF THE GAME UP UNTIL YOU GO ON TO DATE THE DADS.
The game, while having a very rocky launch that was plagued by one delay and the game not launching until the following day of the pushed back time, is very charming and doesn't reinvent the wheel on dating sims but instead adds some nice inclusivity to a wide array of people.
The game starts with you making your 'dadsona' with a good selection of options (some little easter eggs towards the Game Grumps like Daddy Sexbang's outfit and Arin and Danny's hair) to choose from and dialogue choices lets you decide you and your one daughter's history (was your dadsona married to a man or woman/did you adopt your daughter or is she blood-related, etc) which leads to one choosing your dadsona's sexuality and if you view them as cis or trans which I think is a nice touch.
After moving to your new home in Maple Bay you run the gambit of meeting the dads you can date in the future after the first chapter/prologue finishes up in a grand barbeque rife with dad jokes galore as all the dads you can date live in the same neighborhood as you. As I haven't finish a route just yet I won't go into the dads and their overall stories (to avoid spoilers) but there will be small synopsis of each here.
Mat - The local barrista who is a fan of naming his wares after band names.
Hugo - The middle school/high school English teacher who has a bit of a problem child.
Robert - The 'Bad Boy' trope of a dad.
Brian - The lovable, jolly dad who has a daughter that is a prodigy.
Joseph - The local Youth minister at the church (and my personal favorite so far) who has 4 children.
Craig - An old college pal of the dadsona who is a fitness nut.
Damien - If Hot Topic suddenly grew legs and procreated and was into Victorian fashion.
The game is very bright and colorful and has very catching music and the writing of the game overall is charming and good and filled with dad jokes and memes galore. There are minor spelling errors that I've noticed and I have yet to encounter any bugs during my small play time so if you can get past minor spelling mistakes and enjoy dating sims and the Game Grumps (who do some of the voice work for the dads!) then I recommend this game very much!
9/10, will get a 10/10 once we get a DLC where we can hunt everyones favorite cryptics like Mothman with Robert.

Going into this game i was worried because i foolishly looked at the steam reviews first before experiencing it for myself, but after about 15 minutes i was hooked, this game is everything i could want out of a Banjo-Kazooie spiritual successor, overall i would rate this game a 9/10, the only thing this game lacks is enemy diversity and length, these two things are probably a factor because this was Playtonic Game's first creation and was mainly crowdfunded and probably did not have the time/freedom to make a full fledged Banjo-Kazooie style game. However, those things are only a personal issue as i love games with many many bosses and enemies to keep me on my toes.
As for level/ game design, they knocked it out of the park, the levels were massive and beautifully created, every level was different and intricate, and there were plenty of collectibles to explore every asect of each world. The puzzles and platforming threw me back to the old days which is exactly what a spiritual successor of Banjo-Kazooie should do.
As for the comments complaining about controls or camera view, all i can say to that is this game is highly recommended to be played with a remote of some kind, the controls and movement are very fluent and perfect for the type of game they are trying to make. The camera issues were more or less patched, i very rarely had any issues with the camera aside from somtimes getting it stuck behind an object for a minor amount of time, it is more like a minor/rare annoyance than an actual camera issue.
All i can say is that if you are a fan of Banjo-Kazooie or platformers in general, please do not judge this game based on comments or opinions, im sure if you give it a chance you will enjoy it just as much as i did. Also the hints and throwbacks to the old games were perfect, keep an eye out for little nostalgia moments like those.
I cant believe im already done the game and i absolutely cant wait for more from Playtonic Games, im hoping this is just the start of 90's throwback and retro games. Keep doing what your doing Playtonic Games.

Written Review:
Yooka Laylee is a 3D Collectathon platformer much in the same vain as the likes of Banjo-Kazooie on the Nintendo 64, which makes a lot of sense seeing as many of the staff behind this game also are responsible for that title.
The game follows the Chameleon Yooka and his Bat buddy Laylee as they progress through 5 large worlds in order to explore and locate magical page pieces called Pagies, that belong to the One book.
This One Book has the ability to offer anyone who owns it, the power to effectively rewrite the universe as they see fit.
This game is so similar in fact, to banjo-kazooie that the entire gameplay formula is exactly the same, you collect Pagies to unlock worlds, to find more Pagies, collect quills that are littered about as well as collect mysterious ghost writers that are also dotted about.
As you can guess Collecting and exploring is the aim of the game here folks, and all the main collectables; Pagies are generally hidden or locked away behind various platforming challenges, mini-games or puzzles that are littered about.
Each of these platforming challenges can range from extremely easy to potentially frustrating depending on how you adjust to the gameplay. And as a result I can see many players that are not accustomed to this gameplay style to get easily discouraged or annoyed.
As you progress through each world you will occasionally come across various characters who can give you quests or help you on your way. The most notable of which of these are Dr. Puzz and Trowzer the Snake (yes I know that name is genius).
Trowzer is the main man….err snake you go to in order to purchase new moves via the quills you collect along your journey. He changes his stock depending on how far through the game you get and you are generally able to purchase any move in any order you wish, which allows the progress of the game to be more open ended than the likes of Banjo-Kazooie.
Dr. Puzz serves as this games equivalent to Mumbo Jumbo, and she offers various transformations as you progress through each world. Each transformation look pretty brilliant in design as they incorporate both Yooka and Laylee. However the objectives you get from these leave much to be desired. As they are usually only utilised once or twice in each world for the most part and feel very under-utilised.
Not only this but the general control of the transformations themselves aren’t the best, with the Snow Plow in Glitterglaze Glacier being a major pain in the♥♥♥♥♥in particular to control, having next to zero traction.
Another notable NPC will be Rextro Sixtyfourus. A 64-bit polygonal dinosaur who offers this games mini-game challenges. These range from god awful in the event of world one’s challenge, to harmless yet not all that fun for the rest of the game. These offer two Pagies every time however, one for initially completing the mini-game…..and a second for beating the high score.
And Finally we have Kartos...the god of ore. This old minecart will offer challenges where you must ride on minecart tracks and collect gems, these challenges take a little getting used to, but once you have gotten the hang of them, they can be pretty damn fun to blast through, although i’m sad to say they don’t feel very polished and could have used a better camera angle in a lot of instances in my opinion.
Each of the worlds too are rather large in scale, offering a middle ground in size in my opinion between the worlds of Banjo-Kazooie and Banjo-Tooie and generally I never found myself getting lost and honestly found the level design to be pretty well made for the most part.
What helps with exploring is about half or more of the world is locked behind this games major gimmick, expanding worlds. As you collect more and more Pagies you will be given the option to expand a world if you so choose, allowing much more user choice in exploring and again making the game more open-ended.
The writing in the game I feel is nothing short of brilliant. The game is filled to the brim with tonnes of tongue in cheek jokes and horrible (but amazing) puns which certainly makes me happy as I always enjoy a good….bad pun.
Sound design wise the game is no slouch either with tunes being produced by some of the most talented composers in the industry such as Grant Kirkhope, David Wise and Steven Burke. The world themes themselves are seemingly less melodic than the likes of Banjo however sound brilliant nonetheless, with mini-game and Kartos challenge music being spot on for what they are trying to pull off. Going into the Kickstarter, I had high hopes for the soundtrack and I can safely say they were met.
Camera also is something I must bring up because I have seen tonnes of folk online complaining about it, and truth be told I haven’t had many issues with it at all. It just feels like a typical 3D platformer camera to me. Though I will say it did cause trouble a couple of times in my playthrough (mostly in world 3 while swimming or while using the late game flying ability) and had the occasional weird bug where I wasn’t able to adjust its y axis, it never got to the point where I died or messed up as a direct result of it.
The sound effects the characters use to talk I can see many people not liking either as the game uses the same style of gobbledegook speak as Banjo-Kazooie. However you can skip through most dialogues by simply pressing the button so I feel this shouldn’t be too much of a turn off.
I also wish the intro cutscene could be sped up or skipped in its entirety too as it does drag on quite a bit.
Ultimately this game is exactly the game that was promised during the Kickstarter and offers precisely what I expected, and while it has its faults and problems, I feel that it is a worthy successor to the Banjo series in my opinion and definitely a game anyone who’s a fan of this genre should pick up.

Pros:
-Vibrant, interesting levels
-Huge nostalgia factor
-Reasonably fun exploration
Cons:
-Awful controls and camera
-Poor pacing
-Terrible minigames
-Complete lack of polish
Overall:
I can only recommend this game if you've already played and enjoyed one of Rare's old collect-a-thons, like Banjo Kazooie or Donkey Kong 64. Even then, this game may do more to harm your opinion of the genre than is worth it.
On the good side of things, the game is pretty colorful and nice to look at. It also very much feels like an older Rareware game, in a lot of ways. However, I'd argue that the problems of the game stand out far more than the shining moments.
For one, the controls and camera are a complete disaster. Even with the launch patch, the camera regularly gets stuck on overworld objects, or snaps to positions that make controlling the character difficult and frustrating. The various special moves, of which there are far too many, generally control like garbage, seemingly intentionally as a substitute for difficulty.
There are only five worlds in this game, which is pretty slim given previous games in this style. They attempt to make up for it by having the worlds be "expandable", however it's pretty obvious that in most cases they just snipped a normal level in half to make the game feel longer.
Almost every single minigame isn't fun, whether it's rextro's stupid arcade games that feel like a middle schooler's game design project using Yooka-Laylee's assets, or the incredibly frustrating to control minecart games, the head-scratching design and control decisions that seem to have gone into the game's inception truly astounds me. How could a developer take so many steps backwards in fundamental design choices in one game?
That leads me to my final overall point: The game is unpolished as hell. Nearly every problem I have with the title, except for the low world count, should have been solved with a little TLC at the end of development. But, because this apparently wasn't done, we're left with an occasionally buggy and frustrating to play game that made me ask "What the hell were you guys thinking?" over and over.

It's an okay game. Not fantastic but worth the $9 since it came with some of the DLC. This game is somewhat similar to playing Serious Sam. Lots of point-click-shoot. The main game is quite repetitive but the DLC has some unique stuff. I find that they were unable to maximize their strengths (cool boss fights, Hyperion, Vehicles, skills) and lost a lot on repetitive shooting but it's still pasable. You can see that this game is merely an extension of an old game called Brute Force, where the characters are exactly the same (Google Brute Force to see the similarity).
PROS
1. Rare occasions of New Fighting Styles
Sometimes the game gives you new creatures E.g. Tiny Tina's Adventure (DLC) where you have healing Paladins, Necromancers who summon undead and slow you down, Sorcerors who blast, levitate and summon phoenixes, Constructors who spawn Loaders and fire missiles, Giant Loaders. 90% of the time is boring grunts and midgets. Immortal Skeleton (DLC) where you have to pull out the sword otherwise they respawn (This is actually based on a Golem fight where you have to pull out a sword but I'm okay)
2. Interesting Skill Tree
The list of skills and abilities are so interesting but most of the game is point-click-shoot which wastes the good parts of the game. So many cool upgrades with the skills and you have to grind to get anywhere cool.
3. Interesting Boss Fights
Each of the bosses are very interesting to do. Pity some of them can be cheesed. E.g. Warrior (Cheesable), Sorceror's Daughter (Cheesable)
4. Elemental Effects
Play a big deal in fights. Blue counters shields, Corrosive counters armour, Explosive counters Vehicles, Fire counters flesh, Slag adds more damage
5. Sniping.
So many weak points to exploit. E.g. You can shoot the arms off Loaders, hit the red eye in the Constructor and Loaders for Critical Damage, Headshot Orczerkers to knock off their helmets then shoot them in the head (Basically Goliaths and their tiny raging heads)
CONS
1. Weapons
I was expecting more but the way the guns are played is just wrong. So many weapons to pick up but they are all so similar. They basically fall into Pistol, SMG, Rifle, Shotgun, Sniper Rifle and Rocket Launcher.
2. Ridiculous Spawns
Monsters just keep spawning and spawning until it gets tiresome. They just spawn from some blackened wall instead of appearing for a reason.
3. Same enemy, different skin
There is a Midget model, a Psycho model, a Sniper model, a Grunt model, a Goliath model and they are repeated in many of maps. They just come with a different name and skin. E.g. Suicide Psycho vs Suicide Skeleton, different name, different skin, same attack. Skeleton Archer vs Sniper, Skeleton Midget vs Midget
Even the creatures come in the similar models. E.g. Rakk vs Spider. They attack the same way.
4. Repetitive Combat
It's so boring. Just shoot, shoot, shoot. So droll.
5. Wasted Vehicle Combat
So far, I've seen 3 types. A Light Roller, a Technical and a Sand Skift (DLC). Vehicles are mostly to get you from Point A to Point B. They can't enter towns and don't have anything beyond racing in the Badass Crater of Badassitude. Each of the 3 types come in 2 forms. One with a turret and a straight shoot, one with a turret and explosive device. Very bland.
The AI has Bikes and other vehicles but you can't get them.
6. Lifeless Environment
None of the towns have a life of their own. They are dead. Just zones filled with a neverending spawn of enemies. No NPCs except for Sanctuary.
The aesthetic is boring too. You can't interact with the environment and the only thing you touch the most are chests and vending machines. In the rare case, you may see jumping puzzles or squishy traps in Tiny Tina's adventure.
7. Hyperion
The coolest orbital platform and you can't go there. Amazing Moonshot abilities but you only use it for the boss, once. Although, if you comeplete Tiny Tina's DLC, they totured an engineer to get the access codes to Hyperion, so there might be something interesting.
8. Stupid AI
All monsters just charge at you directly if possible. They always know where you are and you have to run extremely far to lose them if they chase after you.
9. Flying Units
You have Buzzards and Blimps that can fly in-game but you can't fly even though you can spawn vehicles.
10. Boring Quests
Murder Hobo. Just kill, kill, kill all the way through each quest. Really no effort. E.g. Go to point A, kill everyhing that spawns there, rinse and repeat with a higher tier.
11. Cheesing Boss Combat
If you die, there are ways to cheese the boss. For the final boss, the Warrior can be slowly killed without taking a single point of damage by standing under the start edge and shooting the Warrior. The boss fight is so cool, but you allow players to just cheese the game.
12. Level Advantage/Disadvantage
You basically win if you're higher level than the boss. You do more damage and take less damage if your level is higher than the boss. Nothing about skill. The items you can equip every 2 levels ahead seem to do almost twice the damage 2 levels below.
13. Respawning Cutscene
The blue wormhole and the digitization is quite silly. Not to mention irritating if you die a lot.

I am sorry to have to say this, but this game is a fail. Even thought one can indeed feel that 'some' effort has been put into the game, the outcome is just a pale shadow of the original.
Truth be told, the original Blade of Destiny from 1993 had lousy graphics and even the MIDI music was very rudimentary; but everything else was excellent: the story, the user interface, the 'randomness factor' - you name it, you have it. You wish to have fights automaticaly calculated - no problem. You wish to speed things up or slow down a bit? No problem. User inventory and skills? Very simple and comprehensive. I can recommend this game heartily to any fan of a good story!
And the HD version of the same? Its a complete opposite. Graphics are better (which is not hard, considering the first version to be almost 23 years old) and the music is remastered, story is the same... But the user interface is messed up. Controls are very unintuitive, inventory as well, movement through cities and dungeons is very sluggish and tiresome, as is any other aspect of the game - starting with character generation. If you end up entering someone's house - you need to wait for the narrator to finish his line before being able to somehow get out of there. ESC doesnt work, there is no cancel key, nothing. Only the right mouse button, only after the narrator finished reading the same boring line. That is absolutely unacceptable for anyone who plays RPGs and explores every door that can be opened.
And then... the battles. They cannot be accelerated, nor speed-automated as in the original version. If your high level party gets attacked by a couple of rats, you still have to wait 15 min for the battle to be decided. Ridiculous.
The *only* improvement that I have seen in the HD version over the 1993 version is the comprehensive explanation of skills and required traits for them. And I did not know that a crystal ball can be enchanted like wands. ^_^
Its a shame really... I love the realms of arkania trilogy; it is one of my favorite games of all times, but the HD version is unplayable :(

1. Bad user interface.
2. Poor presentation (graphics, aesthetics).
3. Very bare-bones user manual.
4. There are still some bugs.
----
1. The user interface has a number of issues:
a) Some items are crammed into the corners where they are hard to reach.
b) Most menus have a tiny little X to close them in the upper right corner. A big simple OK or Cancel button would have been better.
c) Not all buttons have tooltips explaining what they do.
d) Tooltips do not tell you what the keyboard shortcut for an action is.
e) In combat, you cannot move the camera from side-to-side using the mouse. You have to use the keyboard.
f) In combat, the current active character is not highlighted in the bottom character panel. So you have to pay close attention to whose turn it is.
g) When leveling up, you cannot go back or undo skill advancement choices.
2. Graphics and presentation is way off-base too.
a) The character models are very ugly.
b) The building/town models are very ugly.
c) There are few spell or action animations in the FPS view portions of the game. Casting a spell to cast a light is instantaneous. Knocking over statues in a certain level is instantaneous.
d) The sound effects are really bad.
e) Not all weapons have appropriate animations. You swing a rapier for instance. The quarterstaff uses the same 3D model as the rapier.
f) Everything is brown and boring.
g) In general this remake has less charm than the original game for MS-DOS.
3. The ingame documentation says the PDF manual is supposed to be the place to go for detailed information, but the PDF manual is shorter adn more bare-boned than the ingame docs.
4. I have run into a few issues, but nothing super serious so far.

I can successfully say this is the beginning of the end for the Batman Arkham series. Cheap tacked on MP? Check. Lame portable game released along side console/PC release? Check. Next up, yearly releases a la AssCreed and CoD style? Probably. Can't say I'm not surprised. I'm not a fan when publishers take an already established franchise and give it to another dev to make a new game on. Let alone an origin story. Now that the Arkham series is it's own separate thing in the Batman universe, it totally ruins what made Asylum and City so great for me.
Combat is a mess.  Can't recall how many times an enemy has teleported and hit me out of a combo.  Also, doing the Aerial Attack on shielded enemies stops you combo multiplier?  Needs fixed.  Also, seems like you can be hit out of you attack animations at any point.  I remember in AA and AC you could only be hit out of the beginning/start up frames of attacks.  Also, the tracking on Ground Takedowns rarely works with Shock Fists activated.  Needless to say, there are plenty of bugs to be had, and I here there we're game breaking ones before a few patches.
Predator challenges are way to easy.  Rarely do the henchmen shoot down or rig explosives on the gargoyles.  Also, the Remote Claw takes away just about any challenge for those.
Speaking of gadgets, only two of them are new for the game (Remote Claw and Shock Fists).  Everything else was in Arkham City.  Though I think the Shock Fists may have been in the Wii U edition of Arkham City.  Can't confirm though.
Some of the boss battles had memorable moments.  The Deathstroke fight was rather entertaining, even though he was a borrowed some animation from the Ras al Ghul battle in Arkham City.  The battle with Bane started out fun, but then really fell into the classic cliche of:  fight Boss A solo > damage him > cinema > fight Boss A w/ goons.  Really hoped for something more out of that.  And the Firefly fight was rather fun too.
Online can be fun, assuming you aren't playing with a host that'll ragequit right before they lose.  Maybe if I could actually finish a match I'd have a better time with it.
Can't say I'm a fan of the story either.  Everything is♥♥♥♥♥backwards.
Sadly, 2.5 fun/interesting moments don't make up for the rest of a lackluster experience that AO offers.  It really just feels like an expansion pack, not a $50-60 game.
All I can hope for is that Rocksteady gets a chance to make a sequel to Arkham City.  If/when there's another Arkham game made by WB Montreal, I'll know that I can pass on it.

Batman Arkham Origins doesn't fix what already worked in the previous games, so Warner Bros. is playing it safe really.
The last 2 Batman games were awesome, especially the first. The second one was a bit too ambitious, throwing you into the deep way too soon. Arkham Origins fortunately doesn't do this, but it doesn't hold your hand either, which is a good thing. But the city is a bit too similar to Arkham City, and yes, even though it is Christmas time, it also feels way too empty, with hardly a civilian to be found anywhere and empty cars standing on the middle of the road.
Thankfully, there's plenty of content, with lots of sidequests and collectibles and a beefy storyline. Just like the other 2 games. And there's more than enough variety as far as the villains are concerned. Just like the other 2 games.
And, of course, there are plenty of gadgets. ... Just like the other games... Sure, there are a few new ones but most of them work the same way as some of the gadgets found in the previous games (like the glue gun).
Graphically it all looks amazing, with that dark Batman vibe dating back to Batman Returns on the SNES. The voice acting and music are also all very solid and gameplay wise it all works very well.
It's just that Origins doesn't show enough innovation. It all feels and looks very similar. They should really try and expand the game for possible sequels. Give us something new, something to get excited about.
Anyway, you will, once again, get plenty of content for your money by buying this. That's also not the thing that you should be worried about. The thing is, can you look past its flaws and enjoy a game that's basically Arkham City 2.5 ?

I like this game, and I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys Hitman games, and to people who enjoy sandbox stealth games; the fact that it's episodic means that you can just buy the the Intro Pack and if you don't like it, you haven't thrown 60 bucks out the window.
The criticisms are definitely legitimate. You can only play with an active connection to the server; it happened once (luckily in between missions) that I was disconnected from Sqare Enix's servers even though I had an active internet connection. That's very, very silly, and it's sad that publishers still insist on such intrusive DRM, even when faced with examples like Witcher 3, showing that DRM is not at all necessary for a game to be successful.
Another point that people make is that it's really only one mission. So you get about two and a half tutorial missions, and then one 'real' mission in the Intro Pack. That does sound like precious little to do, and to some people it is; but this one real mission has a *lot* of replayability. It is set in an absolutely enormous area with great details and there are a whole lot of different ways to complete it, most of which seem to have a challenge attached to them, so you have some idea of the different ways to attempt the mission. If you're the type to try and find all sorts of different secrets and different ways to take on an objective in a video game, you will definitely get your money's worth.
And this game really makes you feel like a professional hitman, if you're the type that can get immersed in a game like this.
However, if you're the type to try and find the quickest, most direct way, or you play games for the story, this game is not for you, I think. The story so far is stretched very thin, even across so little content, and seems, frankly, quite weak.
So, in summary: this is had the potential of being an amazing game, but was held back by stupid publishing and an episodic model that many people are skeptical about. If you can look past these drawbacks, there's the first part of a great game in there, and if the parts yet to be released are as good as this, it's worth getting despite the crap you have to put up with.
One last thing: I'm playing this game on Low-Medium settings, with a GTX 970, but it looks quite amazing. I can only imagine what it looks like on Ultra settings. I'm not sure what this says about more low-end hardware, but I recommend you do some research to see if it'll run acceptably on your machine.

Nostalgia is a ♥♥♥♥♥, and a fickle one at that. Take off the damn rose tinted glasses and you'll realise that the beloved games of your childhood aren't as great as you recall.
The thing about nostalgia is that it tends to only show the good parts of a fond memory, you never really remember the bad parts and that's a good thing.
When Yooka Laylee's campaign launched on Kickstarter, I pledged to it on the very first day and anxiously waited for its October 2016 release date. However when that came and went I was worried, was the game having that much trouble being bought to life? Was it that riddled with bugs they had to push it back to April 2017 instead? Thankfully the game didn't fall into development hell and finally surfaced.
Nostalgia's great and all and having a game that revels in it is a nice treat but Yooka Laylee is just a little over-nostalgic, awful camera and controls included, whilst also taking shots at modern gaming cliches. Ironic, considering it falls prey to some of these very same cliches it mocks, you can only mock something so much without sounding like a joke yourself and Yooka Laylee fails in that. It reminds me somewhat of the abysmal Duke Nukem Forever, where at one point he criticises Halo's usage of regenerating health and claims that "power armour is for♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;, Yooka does the same but is actually a decent game that won't go down in history as one of the worst.
I wouldn't have minded these jokes on behalf of modern games if Yooka had cut back on them, but they even target older games, the very ones that it is paying homage to and admittedly its odd saying it but these jokes were pretty funny. I particularly enjoyed the character Rextro Sixtyfourus, who serves as an introduction to the arcade mini-games found throughout the game and was a walking cliche of classic games, with his memory being severely limited and him lamenting about his friends moving on to online games. Even better is how throughout the course of the game he enrolls in a modern gaming course and jokes about bribing reviewers and using micro-transactions, had more of the characters been like Rextro the game could have been an instant classic.
The mini-games are.... well, I did not have fun with them, or the first one at least. In the first one you control a mine-cart from a top down perspective and have to beat two laps whilst dodging obstacles to win. Now, the first time it wasn't too bad for me, I beat it and was glad but then Rextro told me to beat the high score if I wanted another Pagie, one of the main collectibles in the game. Sure, I thought, this should be easy, my god I was wrong. The high score (which was of course set by Rextro) was 2:30 and I previously beat it in 2:50 with several crashes, so this meant I couldn't crash at all and to always grab the speed boosts whilst also having perfect precision, something that is nigh impossible when hitting an enemy costs you a whole two seconds, hitting a flame costs another two and driving off the map costs a ludicrous five seconds. As someone who is fairly competent at racing games, even this is insane to me.
The two other mini-games I got to try (I skipped two of them for now) consisted of collecting enough points and not getting hit for three minutes, which wasn't too bad and I easily beat the high score for it, the other....well the other was somewhat like Temple Run, having you dodge obstacles by either jumping over them, rolling into enemies, or changing lanes and just like the mine-cart game this one also bloody required near perfect precision. As did the optional mine-cart missions found throughout the 5 main levels of the game, after talking to Kartos (hah get it, he's meant to be a parody of that fella from the God of War games somehow....) you get access to these frankly infuriating side-quests. Sure the first one wasn't too bad and I collected enough of the gems required for a Pagie but holy♥♥♥♥♥♥the subsequent ones can burn in hell, I couldn't tell most of the time whether I needed to boost or jump and the fact that the frame rate would plummet at times during this didn't help. Add to that that some of these gems are only reachable if you fall for a split second and jump but you have to be so precise you'll die much more than actually succeed.
Easily one of the most standout moments of the game is Grant Kirkhope's score, the Rare alumni show us once again why his work is so revered, I particularly loved the jungle beat theme of the first world. The music alone cements this game's status as a spiritual successor to the Banjo Kazooie series.
But... and I hate to say this, most of the characters just aren't interesting, Yooka and Laylee are great, there's no denying that, and the two villains are hilarious with their banter and attempts to impede your progress with quiz shows, and Trowzer, the merchant of the game is a cheeky ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who gave me a good laugh with every new line of his but outside of that I didn't really care for any of the characters. Some of them were re-used again and again, so instead of new characters to interact with we just get the same boring person to talk to. Oh and the less said about Vendi the better, her design is truly horrifying, and I question who in their right mind let that into the game,♥♥♥♥♥♥looks like it came straight out of the disaster-piece movie Foodfight.
Being a love letter to the 90's, the camera and controls are just as clunky in this as it was in those classic games. Once again nostalgia conveniently made me forget how much I detested this as a child and now as an adult its even worse, half the time it felt like Yooka refused to acknowledge my inputs, especially when rolling, my god the rolling.
There's sadly not many enemy types, the only difference between worlds is how they look, apart from that they all act the exact damn same, you don't even need to fight them half the time because you can simply walk by and they don't follow you for long. Bosses however are significantly more interesting, if not more annoying. The first boss in particular was a nightmare for me until I realised you could stop mid-roll and jump for smoother maneuvering, the other 5 bosses were surprisingly easy however.
The story starts and ends rather abruptly. You go from your ship to suddenly being nemesis of Capital B but you never even meet the guy face to face until the very end! Everyone suddenly knows you as a "trouble causing duo" when you've done next to nothing before this, or have you? The game never gives any backstory on our heroes or anyone, the story seems to take a backseat in this which is a shame. I wanted to know more about Capital B and why he was doing what he did, I definitely wanted to know about his right hand man Dr Quack and why he seemed to be just a disembodied duck head floating in a jar, I guess the sequel will build on this and more, assuming we get one.
I hope we do.

This... is what a game is when you combine Nolan North (Drake from Uncharted, David from The Last of Us, Desmond Miles from Assassin's Creed, and plenty of other roles) with an Uncharted (but more hardcore) cover and combat without the parkour, and a great story written by people who know how to keep you intrigued.
Gameplay:
Spec Ops: The Line is a third-person shooter by Yager and published by 2K. Yager will make the upcoming Dead Island 2. It has great cover mechanics (on some objects, you can't go to the very side of them or the enemy will have an advantage over you, cool feature) and great choice of modern military weapons from the M9, Desert Eagle, Micro-Uzi, M4A1, Scout Tactical (Scout Elite as it's popularly known), and plenty more. Your co-op partners, which I will explain later, are actually pretty good (thank god). The gameplay will keep you interested and sometimes rage-inducing (on those final few chapters) and you'll never get bored of it until after the game. If you are into third-person shooters, pick this one up.
I haven't played Multiplayer or Co-op, so I will not rate those. I do question why there was a "Downloadable Content" option in-game, where the only DLC happens to be the Co-op mode, which comes for free with the game. I don't know if it was originally planned.
Story:
The story is one of the key parts to this game, like the single-player campaign. It will take you through Dubai as you (Captain Walker), Lugo, and Adams. Keep in mind the dialogue and the cutscenes, you'll see. It will keep you interested like the gameplay throughout the main campaign, for me, it tooks only 4 hours on Normal difficulty, so I would say it is between 4-8 hours. I wouldn't say much else because I would spoil a lot of the game. Just wait until you finish the game to look up the ending.
Price:
It depends. If you can get it for about $20.00 on a third-party vendor website, I'd pick it up. If you like third-person shooters a lot (like I do), the $30.00 seems fair for the game. Unless you have friends to do Co-op with, I'd say 1/3 (being the multiplayer) is dead. The campaign is essentially the full frontal force of this game.
Overall Rating:
$20.00-8.5
$30.00-8
Third-person shooter fans-8.75
I would personally pick it up for the $20.00s or $30.00s. Highly recommended for third-person shooter and story rich fans.

Spec Ops The Line is a game I wanted to play for a while now, since it was getting a lot of praise for its themes and portrayal of war.  Is it a masterpiece? Not sure. But it is a great experience. While the game itself is quite story and character driven, it had quite a few cutscenes, mostly just a short intro and ending to a chapter, with ocassional dialogues between characters. Most of the time you were shooting people.
The gameplay was basically a typical third person cover shooter. You get to a new section, take cover, shoot until you clear the area, proceed and listen to some dialogues between your mates, take cover and repeat. It doesn't bring anything new to the table, although shooting glass and killing enemies with falling sand was a great feature, which wasn't implemented often enough.  While I'm not that much of a shooter person, I haven't played enough games to get bored by the genre, so this game felt fresh to me and I never felt bored, nor did the game feel tedious. I was always glued to the screen, waiting to clear the next wave and continue the story.
Through the whole game you're accompanied by your two subordinates, Adams and Lugo, who were surprisingly useful on their own. A lot of games usually have terrible AI partners that rarely kill any of the enemies (notable in Call of Duty and Battlefield), but in Spec Ops The Line, the AI was really useful, and I knew I would have a safe back with them behind me. Even without ordering them to take out a target, they still do great work. It really helped me enjoy the gameplay, since it never felt like I was doing the entire work. Though I still did kill 99% of the enemy in the end, but that 1% still matters, that enemy could have easily flanked me!
The story is where this game shines. At first it seems like your typical Call of Duty/Battlefield game, you go and bring freedom to people. That's what the game initially is, until the plot expands and you aren't even sure WHO you're killing. Even at the end of the game I wasn't even sure whom I'm shooting. Am I shooting the guys that started the mess? Am I shooting the guys that are protecting the people? It was either shoot or die.
Now, a lot of people mention how they felt bad for killing people in the game, felt the weight of it etc. I could see Walker get traumatised and change because of all the deaths, but I never felt anything, aside from initially not wanting to shoot the civilian crowd (which the game forces you to do, so you don't even get an option). You are usually shooting armed people, mostly soldiers. Not really something that would make me feel bad for killing people. Or maybe it's just because I'm not American, so it's the same if I'm shooting Arabs or Americans in the game. Another thing is the soundtrack, it's just so awesome that it makes shooting people actually fun.

The game is pretty graphic, with a lot of graphic visuals of burned and killed people, showing the true colors of wars, which lots of military shooters don't show. It felt a bit overdone at times, with people hanging almost at every single map later on. I usually don't care about violence and graphic content in games, but this game really used it well to set up the story and the war. Literally the first thing you see in the game are dead bodies. And slowly you see more and more dead and rotten bodies. All of that was nothing compared to watching people get burned by phosphorus (which is often used during wars, and is a really inhumane way of killing people). The first phosphorus scene, and later the one done by you, are probably the scenes that hit me the most.
As long as you don't absolutely despise the shooting genre or story driven games, this worth playing. Buy it or pirate it, it doesn't matter, what matters is the one time experience of it's messed up story and visuals.

In terms of gameplay, it's nothing particularly special. It's a 3rd person, cover based shooter with tactical squad mechanics. There's the occasional environmental kill moment but it's usually just shoot a wall or window and sand crushes the enemy. You have two NPCs that follow you around and help in combat, which you can order to take out certain enemies, flash bang a group and that's about it. They're actually decent enough and I found them to be helpful most of the time, unlike many games I've seen where the companion AI is either worthless or does all the work for you, making you feel useless. You've got your standard military shooter array of weapons but I was surprised that the developers made the feel of the guns varied so that you don't feel like your just using the same gun with a different design. I was rather let down with stealth sections. I've played the SOCOM: Navy SEALs games and other squad based shooters where you lead a team through an area and try to remain unseen. I was never very good at them. However, with Spec Ops: The Line, the stealth sections happen very rarely and either I really sucked at them in this game as well, or they were just really easy to screw up. From what I've heard about this game, I'm kinda leaning towards the latter. I found my biggest problem with this game was most likely the lack of a difficulty curve. I'd go from one section with little to no worries and then get savagely destroyed in the next one two minutes later.
But, if you've heard much about this game you've probably heard a lot of people go on about the story. And, yes, I also thought it was really good...for the most part. I'm going to try and not mention any major events that happens in the story line, just sort of touch on elements so as to keep this review spoiler free cause I'm a sweetheart and such. It's a very dark, introspective story that delves into the morality of the responsibilities of a soldier. While this isn't anything particularly new, what with movies like Apocalypse Now and Platoon, or even in video games such as multiple entries of the Metal Gear Solid franchise. But in the current market of the video game industry with emphasis on spectacle, graphics, destruction physics, and bland multiplayer, it's nice to see that some developers still actually care about telling a decent story. The story arc of the main character, Walker, is depressing and violent and I loved it. This is one of the most human characters I've seen in a video game in a very long time. He's torn between his human values and his oathe to being a soldiers, listening to his conscious or obeying orders. HIs path turns horrid and dark as pieces of his humanity are stripped from him in his quest to accomplish his objectives. This even reflects in gameplay, such as when you get further into the game, Walker's demeanor becomes more violent and less sympathetic. In combat, he goes from sounding commanding and in control of himself early in the game, to sounding hostile to the point that he seems almost like he's enjoying slaughtering the enemies. Now, I did have one problem with the story and I already promised that I'm not going to list any specific events in the game which unfortunately leaves me unable to explain in detail why, but I just did not like the ending. More specifically, I didn't like the kind of ending it had. To use the most intentionally vague method of saying why, I've seen this type of ending several times and I feel like it just undermines so much of what happens, especially in terms of character development. It was unfortunate too, because I had adored the story up to that point.
So, I recommend this game, if for no other reason than to experience it. I was a little let down by the end, but the ride up to that point was to be remembered.

I havne't been this impressed with fighting and combat and in a video game since Mount and Blade.
For a game that is from 2003 the combat int his game is incredible, perfect. It's deceptively simplistic at first.
My inittial impressions were- "Oh no, money wasted, this is just a button-smasher, hold down the left mouse button to use my lightsaber, ugh"
But after playing for a little longer, i soon realized that the deceptive simplicity at the surface game was a mere illusion. Beyond is a huge amount of depth, and just plain simple fun. The way you move your character in cohesion with your mouse movements determine where your lightsaber goes. IN effect you indirectly control your lightsaber, but despite this system of indirect lightsaber control, the amount of diversity in what you can do with your lightsaber is outstounding.
I soon found myself combat-rolling and stabbing dudes in the gut, spinning wildly while force-jumping, fighting multiple opponents.
This is just the lightsaber gameplay. Add in force powers, and the game is amazing. The simplistic system of using q/e to select your force power, and then f to use it, is simple enough that using force powers mid-lightsaber duel is actually practical, rather than other star wars games where selecting your force powers is a far more complex process.
I personally think that if they-released this game, with the exact same core gameplay (force-powers, movement, lightsaber control), but using modern 2015 graphics, this game would fly off the shelf like hotcakes.

Starpoint Gemini 2 is easily the best space adventure game available!  Little Green Men Games did a superb job in incorporating those features that make a space exploration game enjoyable while avoiding anything that would be dull.
There is a main-story quest line to keep you engaged with multiple side quests to mix things up.  Space travel feels exciting and scenic without taking years in between events (with added wormholes to speed things up a little more).  There are space pirates, some dangerous while others are targets of opportunity for some quick cash, especially if you capture their ship to sell to a nearby friendly space station.
There seems to be just the right number of ship and weapon variety to not get overwhelmed while still feeling like you have a choice in weapon loadout and ship type.  There are even some that you acquire through quest lines or obtaining blueprints for exceptional weapon types, including torpedoes, plasma cannons, railguns, etc.
Lots of Steam achievements, beautiful scenery, fantastic spacestation design.

While this game utilmately feels a tad unpolished with a few glitches, I feel like this is a hidden gem for some who are a patient lot.
A quest system is there to help with the various factions, provide some nice money, and experience; however, it will become increasingly repetitve the more you play. The reputation with factions functions like 2 sides of a coin. Do something to help this group and it will help with all with the reputation on that side. There are also some factions whom reputation does not matter and you will never get on your side. The story is there as well as faction story quests if you so wish to pursue them but bear in mind it will probably not be the reason to spend a lot of time on the game. You honestly do not need to play the first to enjoy this game.
The ships are varied and are one of the better parts of the game. All ship systems can be upgraded at stations and planets with mostle passive bonuses. Most ships and classes have a better way to play so you have to pay attention before selling the ship have and moving on to the next. You can as many ships as you want in a garage system that can be accessed in a friendly space station.
Personal note: I find this game is best if you can make your own story and the game is filled with moments that can be great. Take this example: I was in a ship with cloaking and was pulling up to an enemy factions space station. There I saw a small ship I could easily board and sell for scrap. So I applied my tracking beam to it and started boarding and before the other ships could stop me I basically abducted the small ship, dragged it away, and sold it for easy money. Bear in mind I had good and upgraded mid class ship at the time that could easily outclass small ships like that but still it is moments like that that make the game extra special for me.
Tips:
Always manage you power output when in fights. If you are in a small ship max out speed/weapons you want to always run and against larger ships and use your speed to attack then back away repeat until dead. Stay in their blind side that has the fewest weapons. If you take a bad hit you may want to run if you can. Your speed should be able to outrun them. For the larger ships they are less manurverable so its more about positioning and damage output and soak.
You may want to go space pirate early after you get your bearings. The ships are expensive and if you do not it will take you a long time to upgrade to the next ships. I recommend get you bearings then board the smaller ships and work you way up. To board select in the context menu to board and a context menu will show up and keep sending troopers over as time permits. You cannot send troops all at once and you are limited in troops and how many to send send based on the ships and upgrades you select. I highly recommend upgrading the transporter to make the process easier. You can make upgrades and gather troopers by visiting most space stations and planets although you may need to visit several locations to find the best upgrades.
There is many more nuances to this game like hazardous areas in space that damage your ship as well as bonuses you  can buy from the factions as you acquire theur favor. Such as free repairs for this faction, bonuses for killing certain groups, or stocks that provide monthly income. Anything else I would recommend veiwing a guide on youtube or elsewhere to help you get you bearings.
This game can be frustrating at times and sometimes unbalanced but if you are the patient type and like to explore and can make your own fun flying a spacehip I think this game would be a nice suprise for some.

Back in the good old 90’s I wasn’t that much into RPGs but I really liked “Startrail” and “Shadows over Riva”. Yes, I’m leaving out Blade of Destiny. Though I played it for quite some time, I never could get really into it. It wasn’t the complex gameplay that turned me off, it was navigating the cities which frustrated me the most. Nearly every building looked the same, be it taverns or homes of important NPCs. I spent a lot of my time running into every building just to see if there was some hint left to be discovered,…which in 99% of every visit wasn’t the case.  So after quite some time I lost interest but tried to get back into the game several times.
Before you judge me, I was 10 years old back then, so maybe my attention span was shorter than today. If you ask me, “Startrail” did everything better. When I learned about the remake of “Blade of Destiny” I was quite enthusiastic. When it was finally released, the reviews were so devastating, it was hard to believe. I read many reviews, watched many videos, and I was shocked. Everything looked so unfinished. Then I learned about the many patches and finally bought the game after the release of the “revised” patch. I started it up and it looked…okay. Yes, that’s not high praise. I checked the forums and realized that the developers were still very involved in fixing the game with the help of the very active community. I decided to wait a little longer, and with the arrival of version 1.35 I finally decided to play the game. That was three days ago. Three days of which I spent 27 hours playing “Blade of Destiny HD” and simply put: I had a blast!
Of course there are many things one could criticize: The story is kind of generic (and obviously always was), the graphics are not great, the combat is clunky and the cities seem a little lifeless. Were this a completely “new” game these things would mean a lot more to me, but as a remake I think this is finally a great product. It made me feel like I felt back then, but without the constant complaining about the city navigation. And I still love the original soundtrack from the 90s version, which is included in the remake.
So, should YOU play “Blade of Destiny HD”? If you liked the original, there’s not much left that should stop you from playing this game. If you want your RPGs to be a little more accessible and modern, you should probably stay clear. But if you were remotely into complex RPGs back in the 90s or enjoy pen & paper RPGs, give it a shot. You won't regret it!

I backed this game on Kickstarter and couldn't have been more excited. 3D Mascot Platformers are a dead genre that I love. It cashes in on nostalgia in the same way Shovel Knight did, but while that game plays like how you remember NES games playing, instead of how they actually were; this game plays exactly like a N64 era platformer.
First off you can tell the developers really cared and tried to do the best job they could. This isn't another Mighty Number 9 situation.
Much has been said about the camera, and it does have issues. It's the first game in years to make me think about the camera at all, as developers have it down to a science now. But it's still not nearly as bad as actual early 3D games.
The combat is similar to other early 3D games like Mario 64. It's just more efficient to run last enemies than to fight them. Most enemies are too similar to be interesting anyway.
The sound effects and music are all on point. This game sounds incredible. The sounds the characters make are made too frequently and the retro arcade music is headache inducing. Those are the only negatives. The rest of the game is on par with all of Rares previous work.
The levels are probably too big for their own good. I find myself getting lost often because everything looks a bit too similar. Condensing them would have been a good idea. This would have made it more important to engage in combat as well.
Overall it's a bit of a mixed bag. I'd highly recommend it to anyone who played these types of games growing up as you'll be more forgiving of the flaws. But I think new players will be bored or even annoyed at how it plays. I only paid 15 as a backer and I feel 40 is a bit too much. Wait for a sale.
These types of games just aren't made anymore and it's great to see a new one come out, even if they're not exactly how you remember.

Multiplayer is kinda fun but not worth it.
BUT IF YOU LIKE BATMAN AT ALL, I WOULD PLAY THIS GAME JUST FOR THE HOTEL LEVEL. IT WAS AWESOME.

THE GOOD
What many reviews on the internet fail to mention is how cinematically impressive Arkham Origins is. I mean, sure the gameplay is heavily recycled, there's pretty much zero game changers, and the open world fails horribly, (all of this I will go into detail later on), Arkham Origins is one of the most exciting games I've ever played. period. This game made me feel like THE BATMAN even more so than the previous titles. The boss battles, though not very innovative, are impressive to look at. It makes you feel like you're a badass, and that's something only a handful of games can accomplish. Since the open world part of the game is rather dull, I've putting all my attention towards the main story. I've constantly been craving the next pre-rendered cutscene, though some would argue that that's a clear sign of bad game design. The camera angles are spectacular, the voice acting is movie-quality, and the lip syncing is spot-on.  By the end of the game, I was left completlely satisifed, impressed, awed.
Arkham Origins's strongest point lies in it's cinematic delievery. (It's almost like you're watching a movie!)
THE BAD
One of the greatest disappointments I've had with Origins wasn't the lack of innovation, but the complete absence of open world content. The exact same side missions in Arkham City are present here, but only in a different name. You're still doing awkward platforming with riddler buttons and hunting down the tyger cams (now called network relays). Only here it almost feels like everythings been dumbed down. You can no longer take down data handlers like in City. They're pretty much invincible, and you're forced to interrogate them if you plan to move on. This is such unnecessary handholding. It breaks the immersion and hinders the game's challenge.  What's even worse is that they've taken away the riddles- something that I really enjoyed in the previous games. It was the only thing in the series that made me think, otherwise, it's just a mindless brawler with stealth segments here and there. The "Crime in Progress" system is a joke. All you're doing is flying to point A and beating everybody up much like you'd do without the "quest" prompt. What they're doing doesn't matter; you're just here to beat everybody up. After the third Crime in Progress, you'll start to hear the same voice acting and see the same "scenarios" (if you can even call them that) over and over again. If you aren't farming for XP, there's absolutely no reason to complete these missions. One unnoticed flaw I'd like to point out as that the thugs in the open world don't do anything. Everyone just stands there, while only a handful strolls pointlessly around an area. After playing a good deal of AC3, I expected there to be at least SOME activity going on between the civillians. There is none.
Gotham in Arkham Origins does not feel like a living, breathing world. Side quests in this game are horribly monotonous, half of which are pretty much the same ones found in Arkham City.

I really wish I could recommend this game, but it's a buggy, unfinished mess.  I can't believe the state the developers left this in before abandoning it and moving onto their next project; Starpoint Warlords, which I would highly advise people to stay away from as well.  Aside from the persistent crashing, there are parts of the game the developer just didn't even bother to finish.  For instance, none of the equipment that was introduced with the expansions works.  None of it.  The developers are completely aware of it too, they just never bothered to finish it.  Simple things like being able to skip dialog doesn't work because of "technical reasons".  I kid you not, that's their excuse, but it supposedly works on xbox.  Many of the quests are bugged, including the final mission, and require hacking save files or reloading the mission numerous times until it works.  Voice dialog worked for maybe a third of the game, the rest of it you just have to read the dialog and then wait in silence until what should have been voiced over to finish since, again, you can't do something as simple as skip dialog.
Character/story progression is very poorly thought out.  It wasn't until I got about 10 hours in, when I was getting wrecked by even the lowliest of enemies, that I had to go to the forums to find out you shouldn't do any missions because you'll over level yourself but not have enough money to buy a new ship and essentially have to start all over or hack your save file to give yourself credits.  Nope, you're supposed to just go capture ships for money and not do any missions.  I'm not kidding, you aren't supposed to level up or do missions or you'll break your game.  I'm not even going to list out all of the other bugs the devs are aware of that they just never bothered to fix.  Stuff that was brought up back in 2014 during the beta that they said they would fix and just never bothered with.  I could probably go on for another three paragarphs listing all the issues with this game, but suffice it to say, it's a mess.
I'm hard pressed to recall any other game I've played that was left in such a sad state, it's like a beta release.  It's a huge shame too, because there is a really good game hiding underneath all the garbage, but having finished the game, the incredible amount of laziness and carelessness by the devs and the amount of frustration it causes just ruins it.  I have no tolerance for devs that abandon a game like they have here and then move on to their next cash in.  I will never purchase another game from Iceberg Interactive.

Max Payne. A name that should be brought up when talking about great video games. Always.
Max Payne is a third person shooter from 2001. You play Max Payne a NYPD detective that comes home to his wife and baby killed by a group of druggies. The only clue he has in a V symbol. Standing for Valkyr. He quits the NYPD and becomes an undercover detective. From there you get loads of shooting and running and great writing.
I am still amazed that this game has aged so well. Sure it isn't as pretty as it used to be, but the gameplay is still solid and the challenge is still there. It's a fast paced run and gun kind of shooter. You get loads of ammo and have a very small amount of health. Depending on the gun you could die from five to two shots. The level design is linear, but put togfether very well.
The only complaint I could have is that there isn't a HUGE amount of replay value. Although I think this could depend on the player. If you don't usually care to go through a story multiple times then you will probably only get six to eight hours in this game. I bet there are other players that have put in 60 hours due to higher difficulties and modes like "A New York Minute" mode.
Max Payne is still worth buying to this day. The price they ask sweetens the deal. Especially if you buy the bundle that include Max Payne 2.

Where do I begin with a game like this. Well for starters this game was made by an indie company, no big publisher backing Introversion, they have done an amazing job getting this game to where it is at this time. In short, buy this game it is an amazing experience.
For those who wish to read, I will now go over the pros and cons of this game in detail.
Pros:
Build just the way you want:
There are very few contraints when building. I'd liken it to Sims 3 from a top down perspective in terms of building. It's great fun.
Cartoony but realistic at the same time:
The game has a very distinctive art style that is unique to the game, but it deals with serious topics such as if you will execute a death row prisoner or not, or if you will keep a prisoner locked up for virtually all of his day. This game makes you think.
It's tough, but only if you want it to be/You can go at your own pace:
The aim of the game is not to amass one billion dollars, but to have the lowest reoffending rate for released prisoners, and every in game day can be marginally relaxing if you want it to. For instance you can run a low-security, generally free environment where the aim is to rehabilitate your prisoners through the use of classes you can run, or you can run a max-sec environment punishing the most hardcore of criminals. It's all up to you.
A dedicated team:
I have watched nearly every alpha video that has been published, and I can clearly see that Introversion software is very passionate about the project. There were (As of writing this it's about a day off offical release) new features each month, and it was a pleasure to watch each and every video.
If you enjoyed Sim City you'll love this. There are features very soon to be released I haven't gone over yet,  as well as features I missed,but you'll see for yourself.
Cons:
Somewhat gruelling at the start:
After putting a good 200 hours into the game as a whole, this is probably my most major complaint with the game, is that in the beginning you start with 30K and the only way you can make money is via grants, but selling your first prison is practically the only way to make cash when you're still learning the ropes.
Overall a solid 8.5/9 out of 10, certainly one of the best sim and strategy/managment games I have ever played. For $30 you will get a lot of fun out of this. Strongly recommended.

This game is very hard to get into. Yet - now that i did - i can only recommend it. It has depth and offers a interesting and enigmatic world. The story is deep - as you would wish for in a good Role Playing Game.
I can only recommend to give this game a try - and maybe watch some Youtube videos or read a guide before playing. I was very frustrated after a few tries of playing without any help (maybe because this game is originally from 1992)  and now that i consulted help, i got  into the game really well and am very happy that this game did not become one more never-really-played game-corpse in my steam library.
Well, I guess at least it is possible to actually complete the game. It'll also provide you with some good laughs. If you want to save your money though, I made a full playthrough of it:

Introduction
Hardcore fantasy turn based strategy game. This is a modern version of the original and if any of you have played that than you know how brutal this can be. Disease, hunger, dehydration all can kill you as well as enemies.
Graphics split into two sections
World  Beautiful for the most part and then just average in some areas (npc's especially females)
Combat
Its full motion turn based combat and a different engine was used (appearently) and it is ugly. They dropped the ball imo here as this is what many players complain about. The mechanics work well, but the rendered models are less than stellar. If only they had really had more time on this it could have been awesome but I guess animation full motion is probably extremely complicated. Also weapons are not diplayed correctly, for example a character with a sling is shown using a crossbow. Beleive me they took a hit on yhat one with modern gamers.
Music
Top of the line...seriuosly up there with Jeremy Soule and Two Steps from Hell
Combat and other sounds
Good to just o.k.
Interaction with world
Like in the original 99% of the NPC's serve no purpose. So whem you enter a city you'll see people in the streets etc. that you cannot talk to. Merchants and tavern keepers  say the same old things over and over. You'll find your selves quickly pushing dialouge(sp) buttons as quickly as you can.
Progression of characters
Slow and grindy. However this game is about living in a fantasy world and at level 1 all your characters are really weak (as it should be) and will fail much more often than they succeed. EVENTUALLY your heroes will start to improve but you are going to spen ALOT of time in combat. Did I mention progression is slow?
Other stuff:
Although you have healing magic, it is not gonna be enough to restore everyone to pristine condition so you are going to have to find Inns to rest in. Now you can campout overnight and heal BUT wounds can get infected. As I said this a simulation fantasy experience and it ain't gonna hold your hand. There are various diseases that can set in but they are all treatable with herbs you can search for (good ones very rare as expected) or buy. Herbs and potions are VERY VERY VERY expensive. Magic items are extremely rare but you can buy some enchanted weapons in some rare places but after seeing the prices you will probably decide "Nah I will loot some magic off foes". This is simply a pipe dream it is so rare.
There are smiths
Because your weapons get worn and can break (you better have a backup weapon for combat)
The stores, smiths, herb shops, healers, Inns etc. all have varied equipment and different prices. There is definetly some economy management to your party. You will find yourselves going from shop to shop looking for the best prices because as I may have mentioned, things are very expensive. If you are lazy and just buy from the first store that has the item you are looking for, then you may later learn you spent twice the amount of extremely important gold that could have been used elsewhere.
there is also a weak haggling system. You can try for up to a 50% dicount but be warned if you anger the shop keepers they may kick you out and refuse to deal with you until you leave town for awhile.
World size and quest
The world is vast but quest are limited. You will spend all your time on the main quest as it sends you all over the place. There are side missions too and I would reccomend doing them, but it wont be long and you will be on the main quest again. No spoilers here so that is all I will say regarding quest.
Is it linear?  Nope, you can go wherever you want, and do side quest in any order for the most part.
Bug?
Yep. got some. Most are minor like the wrong label on items are events that don't really seem to do anyrthing. I personaly have not come upon any game-breakers though.
So who will like this game?
Older D&D players who appreciate using your imgination and really want the "feel" of a true wolrd. Grognards who keep diligent notes and love a challenge. Hardcore gamers.
Who will not like this game?
Console gamers that push "a" and everything dies type gamers. Gamers that like being spoon fed. Tales of MaJael (which I also own and love) and rouge-like gamers. Probably. Its kinda the opposite of those type games. Rush players who want to quickly become powerful and complete the game.
Overall
I simply love this game. It can be tedious at times but I find myself losing hours in this world. Don't let played hours fool you as I play offline alot because my bandwidth is also split between my two sons watching movies and playing online console/computer games.
If you are a hardcore simulation type that can get past a few hiccups and use your imagination I whole-heartedly reccomend this experience. Fast players give this a pass/
Final note...The devs had some legal issues and had to stop development and updates for awhile but are now back currently working on a patch anb free DLC (Ithink) and most importantly making the game open to modders.

I'm not gonna talk too much about Realms of Arkania as a game. People who don't know the original ROA should read about it somewhere. I'm just gonna say this: its a WRPG where you have to THINK. Its a REAL RPG, where your skills are as much important inside battles AND outside.
I'm here to talk about this reboot only, assuming everyone here knows ROA.
First of all, this game was released in a very incomplete state when it came to STEAM. Almost unplayable, actually. The guys patched it intensivelly after that, but at that point, the game got some of the worst reviews ever (as bad as Big Rigs!!). The thing is: after all the patching, the game became QUITE playable... and very fun to play. But people didn't gave it a chance.
Just like the original ROA, your party has TONS of skills that are used in battles and on the field. This is what I always liked about ROA, and its all here. Just like in the original ROA, you have to take real good care of your chars. They will get sick if you are in a cold place without clothes for winter, for example. And just like in the original ROA, this is the most fun part of this game: surviving while exploring the world.
The battles in here are the weakest part though. Then again, they were not much different in the original ROA... Keep in mind that this game is NOT forgiving in the beginning. You will die. A LOT. You will miss most attacks, you will be frustrated. It was like this in ROA, and its exactly the same in ROA HD. After a while, you'll get better, and will be able to DESTROY your enemies. This version has some bad looking character models though. It seems they are just placeholders, but never replaced with real models. Your characters look awful, your enemies look awful too... The backgrounds are ok. The originals had horrible looking battle backgrounds, and they are also bad here. But are at least more detailed, and since they are in 3D, you can rotate the camera at will.
Outside battles the game look quite good; impressive for a low budget game, actually. Even though this is an indie game, the backgrounds are VERY detailed, and beautiful to look at. Specially the dungeons: they are very good looking, and varied. And since the game is in 3D, you won't move in a grid based system, like in ROA 1 and 2. You can move freely, rotate the camera at will, look up and down. Kinda like ROA3, but with a WAY more beautiful world.
At the end of the day, this is still a VERY rough release. It has some bugs and some bad looking models. But its FUN. One of the most fun RPGs I've ever played. You need patience though. This isn't a game for newbie's. If you didn't like the original ROA, you will NOT like this one. ROA HD is just ROA, but with 3D graphics.
Even if this game has issues, I recommend it for fans of the original ROA. Give this game a chance. Exploring the game world is fun now. You won't see that basic tile-based cities that all look the same anymore. You'll see a world in 3D, with detailed residences, rivers and real people walking around (the 3 ROA games didn't even had NPCs visible in the game world!!). You will learn to care for that characters, because if you don't they WILL die on you. And you will be able to do optional quests to get money and experience, or can just run around the world aimlesly for as much as you want (if you can survive, that is).
This is a great game. With more polish, it would be perfect. It's fun the way it is though, and this is what's most important in a game.

Yooka-Laylee is a fantastic 3D platformer game developed by some of the team who brought us the great N64 title Banjo-Kazooie and its sequel Banjo-Tooie. The game was crowdfunded a few years ago and easily surpassed its goal funding amount much to the delight of fans and backers alike.
The games roots are Banjo-Kazooie and it shows very much so in every aspect of the game. It is demonstrated in the collectibles, secrets, sounds, NPCs and even the menus. I found the game to be very enjoyable with the only real drawbacks being the sometimes annoying camera (getting stuck in the previous room or having a poor viewing angle), a few extremely easy collectibles and the shortness of the game with only five worlds. I got a solid 24 hours of gameplay out of Yooka-Laylee in which I collected every single collectible in the game to 100% complete it. While there was only five worlds each world had a total of 25 pagies to collect, which meant a similar amount of collectibles but less game worlds compared to the developers previous titles.
The game unlocks things progressively and gives you the choice of how you want to proceed by letting you choose which player abilities you want to unlock and in what order you like. However you will need to backtrack to previous worlds after unlocking abilities in others in order to complete challenges and collect those remaining pagies.
If you like the retro throwback to older N64 console platform titles, enjoy a good fun and wholesome game that the whole family can enjoy and like your collectibles then this is the title for you.
* This game is best enjoyed and played with a controller.
Rating: 9 / 10
