Yooka-Laylee is a good game. It's not a horrible disappointment, and it's not a life-changing experience. It's simply a good game. It's sad how much controversy this game has stirred up, people either think it's the best thing to happen to gaming in a while and will single-handedly resurrect the 3D platformer genre, or they're angry they backed another "Kickstarter failure" that tried to cash in on your nostalgia. I enjoyed the game, there were plenty of moments of both mild disappointment and genuine joy, as much as any other game.
The game is a hybrid of Banjo-Kazooie and Tooie, though primarily the former. The game has a hub world that you use to access the other separate worlds much like Kazooie, but you'll need to revisit most areas later once you have more abilities like in Tooie. Trowzer teaches you new moves in every world much like Bottles, Dr. Puzz can transform you into a unique form in each world much like Mumbo-Jumbo, Quills are the equivalent of Notes, Pagies are Jiggies, etc. Plenty of varying characters filled with tounge-in-cheek jokes and classic Rare innuendo. The formula's all there. There were plenty of creative puzzles and a few of the bosses were quite unique too.
Now as an odd point, during my whole playthrough I kept getting the urge to just play the original Banjo games instead. Not because it wasn't hitting the right marks, it's because it
hitting all the right marks and put me right back into childhood mode.
Bottomline is that this is a good game, not bad, not incredible, just good. Don't go in expecting this to surpass the originals, and you will most likely enjoy it.
Oh, and Kartos can go rot in a mineshaft for all I care.

This game got blasted in reviews for essentially being the same as Arkham City.  This is true, but I don't view it as a negative.  The game inherited a winning formula, and rather than change it unnecessarily, they kept it as-is.  As a result, Arkham Origins has a winning formula as well, rather than a broken "New Coke" design.
I feel like the story is the strongest of the Arkham games so far, and the game looks visually stunning.  Playing with PhysX especially was a revelation as to how much more convincing that tech can make a game's environments, and I really hope to see it adopted in a wide range of future titles.
Most of my complaints are things inherited from the past games.
I'm not a big fan of the overly muscled look for everyone in the game, sans Joker and women.  Nor the way Batman pinballs around the room during combat.  There's got to be a better way to represent rapid motion than that.
Though the map is larger than Arkham Asylum (and City), because you spend so much time gliding overhead, City and Origins feel much smaller to me.  The various buildings in City and Origins are largely pointless and tend to blend together in a way that the environments of Asylum never did.
The rock-paper-scissors nature of a lot of the enemies is annoying.  The game is at its best when it creates those "I'M BATMAN" moments of the player dropping into the middle of 50 guys and cleaning house - thugs that require a special gimmick to be defeated (stun the armored thug, get behind the stunner thug, etc) break that feeling.  It isn't that they're hard, but that they reduce your options in a fight down to one, and it's the same one every time.
The only complaint I have that is exclusive to Origins is that the voice actor for Batman is terrible.  I'm not a Kevin Conroy fan (I'm in the minority that prefers the Bale voice), but the new guy is terrible enough that it pulls me out of the game.  This just isn't Batman's voice coming out of Batman.
But those things aside, this is still an excellent game, and may actually be my favorite of the trilogy so far.  Walking around the Batcave, for whatever reason, is particularly enjoyable to me.  If spending an hour exploring the Batcave and trying to read every blurred text-containing texture appeals to you, put this one at the top of your wishlist.

I'm admittedly only giving this a tentative thumbs up.  Even if you're starved for more Batman: Arkham action, I'd wait for a price drop.  I myself was kind of waiting, but hey - I got it free with my new GPU, and I won't pass on a free game - plus I was still interested in playing it at some point.  But a lot of my skepticism regarding the game was true, it's more like a jumbo-sized DLC pack than a proper prequel/sequel, and it's disappointing in a lot of ways.  Firstly, it feels like a prequel solely to find a way to get Joker back.  The story actually isn't bad, in fact save for some glaring continuity issues and the disappointment of potentially having a retro-themed game (The series was inspired by the Bruce Timm TV series, why not have this one go further into its Art-Deco style?  Seriously. Missed. Opportunity.) it's actually a fairly decent story, even if it's nothing new - basically being another "Batman meets the Joker for the first time" story.  There are two new actors in the lead, and while the actor playing Joker isn't bad (Even if no one can match Hamil.) I'm not sold on Batman's new actor.  He sounds like he's trying too hard to be both Kevin Conroy AND Christian Bale at the same time; lacking the personality and character of the former or the edge and conviction of the latter.
The biggest missed opportunity though is to really get a feel for Batman's early days, there are no civilians on the street and the game uses a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥excuse for this (A Curfew) and even in such a scenario, there would be SOME civvies out there - and even though you do get to interrupt random crimes, it would be cooler if they involved saving civilians instead of just stopping more thugs from doing petty bullcrap.  It's clearly a rushed effort.
But if it's at a reduced price and you want more of what made Arkham City good, it's still fun.  The predator is still great, the action is still great, the animations are still superb (The facial animations are actually eerily good), and even the waning sheen of the Unreal 3 engine is put to good use with some nice effects, lighting, etc.  It's for diehards only, and even for diehards - I recommend waiting till it's prive is halved.

So I bought this on sale and it was one of those impulse buys, I did not get this game at all when I first tried it, but when I was in a more patient mood to learn the confusing interface I have now started playing it more and actually understand it as I read the tutorials carefully and just got used to everything, there is a learning curve with this game, but considering it's singleplayer so you don't have to worry about player population and it's a really massive space sim it is definitely worth it.
Do you remember the days of Freelancer? Well I do and I played that game to death, one of the most fun aspects for me was the huge amounts of factions, the hidden bases, the exploration and the rather limited sandbox experience when it came to trading this game has decided to focus on all of that.
I may actually even check out mining properly now, because I remember wanting to do it in Freelancer but because that game was primarily about combat it was all very limited oh and just like freelancer it looks like you mine by shooting stuff rather than having any sort of specialised ship, which, while is a bit silly I do wonder if that's a good mechanic because it means you don't have to worry so much about how to defend yourself in space sims.
So to sum this game up, it very much has a learning curve, think of it as Freelancer on steroids because even the steering of your ship is very similar, but once you get into it you'll have no problem getting through the map and the various interfaces loaded with information.
If anyone wants a possible tip on getting into the game quicker, I recommend just getting used to using the context menu which you access with the middle mouse button or clicking your scroll wheel. Unlike most context sensitive stuff on games this menu actually seems to work decently and you can use it to quickly navigate around space.

I have owned this game for quite a while now and I’ve really enjoyed driving for hundreds of hours. I myself am a vehicle fanatic so I love everything that moves on wheels 8). Here are the advantages and disadvantages of the game:
1.  The game has a huge map which will take you at least 600 hours to explore fully (including both map expansions). The map (including both map expansions) stretches from Great Britain to mainland Europe, then to the very east of Poland and the Nordic region up north. As of December 5th 2016 the 'Vive la France!' DLC completes the remainder of France that was left out in the vanilla map since it's release. It brings an extra 20,000 kms of new roads using HD textures.
2. There is a wide range of trucks to choose from. There are high end trucks made for hauling heavy stuff and smaller trucks that get the job done.
3. The customization is pretty good too because you can customize almost every aspect of the truck such as tires, engines and cabin trim. You can also apply custom paints and skins to make your truck more unique.
4. There is a huge selection of trailers to haul; even if you don’t have the Scandinavia DLC, and the High Power Cargo Pack DLC, you still get a choice to haul pretty much anything that can be transported. It ranges from Tomatoes to Excavators and if you’ve got the Scandinavia DLC, you can haul a pair of Scania or Volvo trucks.
5. It’s very realistic; the roads have the correct signs, speed limits are imposed in the correct areas and many things such as white lines, hard shoulders make the driving aspect realistic. The simulation aspect is well met with settings such as physical camera rotation to make it seem like the truck actually seem like it’s moving when you’re in the cabin and realistic fuel simulation. Also real life currencies have been implemented where the main currency is Euros and you’re able to use other currencies such as Pounds sterling or Norwegian Krona.
6. It’s fully modifiable and since it’s release the game has been host to millions of community developed mods such as free map expansions (ProMods & TruckSim Map are great examples), and it literally ranges from everything. There are mods that can change the economy of the game, mods that add trucks, mods that change cabin interiors, mods that add skins. You can really have a blast customizing the game and even making your own mods and publishing them on mod websites like ets2.lt.
7. It runs alright on low spec PC's on the lowest settings of course. My PC is terrible and I get about 30 FPS in the cabin on medium settings
8. The controls are very simple and it's easy to drive with a keyboard. Gamepads work well too and if you want the full on experience then you should get a racing wheel like a Logitech G27 because it simulates driving and it's more precise.
1.  Updates take a while to come out because the company who develops this game are a very small group meaning that map expansions like Scandinavia DLC that came out 3 years after the base game was released, were demolished by the likes of ProMods, a large group of modders who mapped out a huge part of Scandinavia over a year before the official DLC was even released.
2. The cities are extremely brief; let’s take London for example. If the city of London in-game was about the same size as it is in real life, it would take almost every city in the game combined to equal it’s size. This is because each city only has around 4 to 5 roads, a service station, a garage, and a couple of depots.
3. (Good and bad) - there’s no multiplayer. This was a problem up until late 2013 when some Polish guys got together and started piecing together a multiplayer mod that would be free to play and would give players an opportunity to transport  loads with each other, organize enormous convoys, and take screenshots. To this day it has over 1,000,000 registered users and as of now it’s growing by about 500 users per day.
Overall this game is one of the best driving simulators on the store and it’s a game I’m so addicted to even though I have no interest in trucks. Hope this review helps!

Klei's take on the popular "Colony Management Sim" style of games (Gnomoria, Craft the World, the famous Dwarf Fortress and the infamous Spacebase DF-9). You can expect the same level of dedication to quality that made Don't Starve a success and with the devs seemingly following a similar development model, there is little doubts the story will repeat itself here.
This is a game about building simple systems that interact with each others to form a more complex whole. You have to design a colony that will answer the Duplicants' basic needs (food, oxygen, comfort) all the while continually expand in increasingly dangerous terrain to avert some form of crisis. At the very beggining, you have to find a way to produce oxygen and food. Electricity then becomes a scarce commodity as you scramble to build a more robust electrical infrastructure. Overheating in the colony can then become a problem. The way one solution leads to another problem is simply brilliant.
Like Don't Starve before it, the game teaches you through trial and error. You have to discover the advantages and pitfalls of each contraptions the Duplicants can build by yourself (or have a look at the wiki !), which will most likely take you a few failures to get the hang of building a proper colony core, before you can expand to more hostile territory and use advanced techniques.
The satisfaction of building a functionnal system is pretty much the core of the game right now, as since it is still in development, there isn't really any proper plot or lore in place to encourage you to keep pushing on. Still, it's one of the more entertaining management game I've played in a while and I've no doubt that Klei will keep on improving the experience like they've already done.

Yes, I do recommend Realms of Arkania, but with a number of caveats.
Realms of Arkania is definitely "budget," definitely indie, and
rough around the edges in places. RoA still has a couple of UI glitches, and isn't always pretty to look at. The English voice acting is atrocious.
However, the game-stopping bugs present at launch
been fixed. The visuals are adequate; not great, but not terrible. The voice acting, luckily, can be disabled.
As for gameplay, RoA is almost more of a management sim than a typical RPG. I actually appreciate that. The preparation you have to put into traveling during the winter months is possibly more important than how well-equipped your party is for combat. You just don't see certain kinds of brutal gameplay concepts (exposure, thirst & starvation, exhaustion, sickness & disease) in these kinds of games anymore. Unless you play smart, your adventure can easily end during the first winter, with your frostbitten party starving to death on a mountain trail.
How many fantasy RPGs have you played lately in which a winter coat is more important to your survival than a +3 sword?
Now, I didn't buy RoA at release. In fact, I didn't begin playing it until after the final major patch was out. So I didn't experience how badly broken it was at release. My only experience of RoA is with the game in its current state.
So, how is it currently? As far as I can tell, RoA is feature-complete compared to the original Realms of Arkania game from the '90s. Every quest present and working in the
is present and working in this remake. In fact, the devs have added
bits of content to the game (quests, encounters, etc), so the game now has MORE content than the original.
Again, RoA isn't the prettiest game to look at. But the gameplay itself is just what I was looking for when I bought it - unforgiving, difficult, oldschool, and based in the Dark Eye universe.
At over 100 hours ingame, and having finished the main questline and
all side quests, I can honestly say that I got my money's worth out of Realms of Arkania. Your mileage may vary, however, depending on how tolerant you are of outdated graphics, general lack of polish, and brutally unforgiving gameplay straight out of 1992.
If you like these kind of games, it's not half bad. It's pretty good actually but it sure needs a lot of work. I hope the devs will get there eventually.

Here is a lovingly crafted work obviously created a very diehard Dark Eye following. Pick your team of champions and explore town to stock up on essentials before heading out for some serious dungeon-crawling. Are you sick of the ease with which you typically overcome early adversaries in other games? Well buckle-up, because getting through your very first battles on the higher difficulty settings will take a bit of swag, even for the most seasoned oldschool rpg vet. Deal with feeding, watering and keeping your party warm and healthy in ways that bring a whole new level of realism to roleplaying, presenting you with challenges even long before you arrive at your destination. Deal with the fickle nature of magic in a world where it is obviously more difficult to master. This is a game with a serious learning curve, but with equal share the promise of rpgasmic goodness at every turn.

As one of the backers, I was admittedly rather hyped for this game. However, I want to lay off the glasses of nostalgia as it's not entirely a Banjo-Kazooie game, which led me to be disappointed at first.
But this is actually a good thing.
Yooka-Laylee takes exactly these things from its inspiration:
-It's a 3D Platformer with a buddy duo
-Fourth wall jokes and cringey puns in just the right amount (It has fun with being what it is)
-eyes. on. everything. Even some enemies are literally just eyes that can apply themselves to things. A Rare trademark.
-Basic setup from Banjo Kazooie. You go to the lair of the antagonist and find worlds that you collect stuff in to unlock more worlds with.
And that is it. But here's the good part: It adds a lot more to the mix.
While some abilties are directly based off of its inspiration, such as talon trot/Roll, gliding and super jump, they really us the concept of the protagonists being a bat and a chameleon.
Yooka can use his tongue to slurp up health or even take on the properties of items, such as honey that makes him sticky, or cannonballs that make him heavy, in order to traverse certain areas. He can also eat berries that make him shoot whatever element it was that the berries were.
Laylee uses her sonar and is generally a pretty fun character (I like the bat, okay? She cool, despite not doing much just yet)
I am only 5 hours in, but so far the game, after a bit getting used to (it has been ages since I played anything like this, let alone with a keyboard) has been fantastic. The controls are great, the visuals beautiful and most of the dialogue is funny. There is a lot to do, with worlds being huge and secrets being tricky to find. Collecting stuff has become much more rewarding, as Quills buy you Skills and tonics with special traits can be unlocked by meeting certain requirements.
The only real flaw is a missing "Decline" or B button for keyboard users, but that is easily patched in and so far, I have managed without it.
I think it's worth the money they are wanting for it. I just think people aren't used to this type of game anymore and those that are, are too used to the good ol days.
Yooka-Laylee is a 3D platformer that takes pretty much everything I loved from the older games and spiked it with new mechanics and made it more up-to-date. Can only recommend it.

Let me start off by saying this: yes, I backed this game.  Also, I've never played Banjo-Kazooie.  I've played other 3D platformers, but not Banjo-Kazooie.  In fact, it never really appealled to me; I backed the project because the game looked fun, the concept art was beautiful, and the protagonists were going to be animals with bad reputations irl which is a notion I support wholeheartedly.  Feel like that should be mentioned, too.
Yooka-Laylee is a charming and adorable little 3D platformer, with absolutely stunning environments (I'm playing on the lowest difficulty and the game still looks amazing) and quirky characters.  Yooka and Laylee are absolutely loveable underdogs, and the little details to their animations really add a lot of character to them.  The collectibles are nicely hidden, and the puzzles pretty darn clever.  The minigames and minecart tracks were a little frustrating for me, but then again I'm just bad at minigames and racing sections in general.  Camera could be an issue for some folks, but I wasn't affected by it at all (and I can get motion sickness fairly easily).  Voice acting never felt too grating, and I'm surprised how a few squeaks and grunts could tell you exactly what the characters' personalities are like.  That takes some talent.  Boss fights were exciting and varied.  The story was simple (bad guy stole a book, good guys get it back and save the world along the way), but engaging enough to keep me hooked.  And the soundtrack has this beautiful pseudo-orchestral that really sells the whole "ADVENTURE!!" theme.
It's been a long time since a game has kept my attention for so long.  Seriously, been working on this game for close to a week now.  And I'm loving every minute of it.  It is one of the most charming and visually beautiful games I've ever played, and I am so glad that I backed it.
Might be a little to early to name a game as my personal GOTY 2017, but Yooka-Laylee is my GOTY 2017.

At it's worst this is a collectathon from the 90's coming out in 2017. The only criticisms for this game would be criticisms that could be applied to Banjo-Kazooie and Banjo-Tooie and if people are here to hate either of those games, then you shouldn't have picked this title up to begin with, end of story.

Now, while I highly recommend the game, let me say some of the cons.
Camera angles can be a bit annoying sometimes, mostly when you try to use Tongue Lash (Grapple) you have to have the camera just right or it wont work.
Many of the puzzles feel very easy and simple. I don't find myself wracking my brain on how to get through somewhere at all, except for when it comes to finding that last handful of collectibles (But they gave you a way to help find those, so it's not too bad)

I am a good chunk of the way to 100% completeing this game and I'm having a blast with it.
I understand that there are a lot of people having issues with the camera and controls but I honestly have experenced almost none of it. I have only ever experenced minor camera glitches, like if I bearly make it though a timed door the camera will show the closed door for a half a second before snapping back to the over the shoulder view it should have, and this was rare. I've less had problems with consistant controls and more just needed an adjustment period with the flight mechanic you aquire late in the game and maybe the truck transformation in the ice world. The only time I was really grinding my teeth at the controls was in one particular spot called Gloomy Gem Grotto where ice physics turned two of the rolling slope sections into nightmares.
However, in the over twenty hours I have put into the game so far, such frustrations made up maybe... fifteen minutes, a half hour if I'm being harsh with the grotto, of any level of frustration. Everything else was smooth. The running, rolling, jumping, attacking, everything feels good. In a platforming game, you should want to run around and explore simply because it feels fun to do so almost on its own, and Yooka-Laylee nails that in my opinion. The graphics are good even at low settings and absolutely gorgeous if you can handle the higher settings. Finding the collectables are fun and satisfying and, if you are having trouble finding some things, they have a tonic you can equip to help you find the last few quills or what have you to complete the area. There is not much of a completion bonus but thats not stopping me from enjoying exploring this game.
And that really is the key. If you are a person who doesn't enjoy platforming, mini challenges, and exploration this is NOT the game for you. This game is more or less built on curiosity and over coming challenge. Sure, some pagies are very easy to get, but some you have to work for. Some you will need to re-try until you master the section you're on. If you are not one who feels a great satisfaction in overcoming something like that, then again, this is NOT the game for you.
If however you do thrive in this sort of action-adventure, exploritive, collectathon environment, I can not recommend this game enough.

It's never gonna top Blood Money in terms of presentation, exposition, style, and artistic direction, but it's many many steps in the right direction.
A touch of the absurd, but no overly obnoxious characters. Nuance is the name of the game, i would have liked it more if hints and opportunities were restricted to easier difficulties (Pro, Expert, Hard, etc.) additionally, having unlimited ingame saves is certainly unbalanced. The ability to save during a mission was limited by difficulty in past games. This was a more subtle way of getting the player to devide the mission objectives into milestones, saving after acheiving a certain objective has been met, either set by the game explicitly, or a player set objectivethat after acheiving, allows the rest of their plans to unfold.
While miles ahead of "HM:Absolution", there is still an excess of hand holding as far as finding clever ways to dispatch your targets. Devs might say "intuitive", but as a veteran of Blood Money it's a bit patronizing. However you want to look at it, the tradeoff is, in exchange for streamlined access to assassination opportunities, you are robbed of the sense of eureka! -Having discovered something yourself.
I am ever a fan of that special link between player creativity and developer anticipation. In this case, devs expect you to be lost, in a world rife with exciting possibilities. That being inarguably the strongest point of the hitman franchise, it's a shame it's dampened by the need to appeal to those not already aware of how brilliant Hitman can be.
That said, i love where this new installment is going, i am eager for more, i hope all further misions are as true to the original formulae that makes this franchise stand apart from other stealth-games/shooters/free-form-assasin-games etc. I love throwing melee weapons. Gunplay is solid and allows skilled shooters to ecxel. Playground aspects of the maps i experience were plentiful, and is definitely an allure in and of itself. While initially seen as a potential gameplay imbalance, the ability to save at any time plays well into the fun of experimentation and optional mayhem.
Problems, solutions, trial and error, are all present, perhaps not to the degree of the epitome of the series, but more excitingly present than ever. J.N.Allen

Before I delve into Origins, understand that I love Asylum and City, and that you should play both of those games long before you even consider touching this one. Also understand that it is because of my love for those games that I have such a distaste for this latest entry. Why? Because Origins does absolutely nothing new, for it is a simple copy/paste job hastily cobbled together, intent on snatching the cash of Arkham fans. That isn't to say it's a terrible game, mind, but it's certainly not a good one, or anywhere near the level of the previous two games.
Some may say the "if it isn't broke..." thought process applies here, and indeed it could have if they hadn't lost and damaged things during the pasting process. The combat feels like a slightly off version of City's, by which I mean it plays exactly the same when the game actually bothers to recognize your input, where in City it almost always would, for the system was spot-on. Here, the game will only counter when you press the button if it feels like it, the game will only let you perform a ground finisher if it feels like it, the game will only hit the thing that's right in front of your damn face if it feels like it. The inverse applies as well, where enemies' hits will only count if the game fee-- I know, the phrase is getting old, but it works so well in this case I simply cannot help it: The game only bothers to reach toward the realm of "good" when it feels like it, otherwise no dice.
Oh, and when I said copy/paste, I meant it; there are numerous areas (hell, even the entirety of City's map) that have been shamelessly recycled in this game, destroying any sense of discovery and freshness that the first two had. In my case, Origin's lazy design is amplified even further by my recent replaying of City, making the issues (primarily with the combat system, which is the meat of the game and therefore my biggest gripe) that much more apparent. The final nail in the coffin for me was during an instance where I decided to take a small detour from the main mission and take care of some side business...only to find out that the area it occurs in was completely ripped from City, with nothing changed about it at all. While that may not bother some, it infuriated me, further enforcing the cash-grab nature of this project and the lack of creativity that went into it.
So, at the end of the day, I cannot recommend this game to anyone in good conscious, especially at the current $50 asking price. You would be much better served to replay City if you've already finished the first two, and if you haven't, for the love of god rectify that. At the very least, if you "must" play this game for completionist purposes, be sure to wait for a price drop; I snatched it during Amazon's Black Friday deal for $20, and while I don't have outright regret, I'm certain that my twenty could've been better utilized.

There's a lot of negativity surrounding this game, and I feel it's pretty unfounded.  The game was released glitchy but as is the case for a game with that short of a development cycle.  It was the shortest of the 3 games, and from that there is some noticeable issues that have been fixed.  The complaints about the game being too similar is a bit of a frustration because why fix what isn't broken?  The game feels more visceral, and the faster paced combat gives it a more natural feel to the combat.  The complaints I can see that are warranted would be the collectibles aren't nearly fleshed out like they were in AA and AC.  AA and AC were built by diehard comic book fans and you could tell that through the incredible attention to detail they've brought with the collectibles which were nods to all of Batman's lore and mythology.  These collectibles were really weak in comparison and I hated that.  The story I thought was a difference between Halo and Halo Reach.  It's much more personal like Reach where you care about everyone versus an epic sweeping scope of a game.  I think it's much stronger than the rage people have expressed towards it.  it still warrants hours of replay value with the challenges, and the extra costumes pays much more homage to Batman's mythology than AA and AC ever did(Dat Long Halloween Batsuit)

AO feels a bit more like an expansion pack for Arkham City as opposed to its own entirely new game. I don't mind that it's filled with some of Batman's less memorable villains. By matching Batman up against a lot of B-list villains you get more of a vibe for being Batman and having something to compare it to. So it gives you a better appreciation for the really dangerous villains down the line.

This is an extremely difficult game to rate acurately. The downside is that it looks quite dated, even the simplest of quests take what seem like an age to complete, and combat seems like a stage in a marathon. The upside is that it's absolutely huge, completely non-linear, full of secret side quests, and, perhaps absurdly, the length of time it takes to complete even the earliest of quests actually adds to the sense of achievement when you eventually make it through one adding to that "epic" feel. I strongly suggest you try normal mode before going anywhere near the "pro" setting. If slow burning games with plenty of depth that take FOREVER to play are your bag then this is for you. But if you are one of those people who like eye candy, or anything remotely "high octane" then you should probably give this a miss. If you DO chance it then don't be put off by the terrible voiceovers - there's more to this game than meet either eye or ear. It feels like exactly what it is - a graphical interpretation of a slow and complex pen and paper game. This is either a good or a bad thing depending on your perspective. 75%

text: Before I write this, I should mention that I didn't grow up with Banjo-Kazooie. It wasn't until a few years ago that I started playing classic Rareware games, and now I adore them. Which is why I was beyond excited to play Yooka-Laylee. I love this game so much! I hear complaints about the camera, but I actually have no problems with it. As long as you use a controller, you should be fine. The only issue I had was the frame rate, but that's because I have a terrible PC. I think this game is a worthy successor. It may not be anything new, but that wasn't the goal in the first place. The game is designed to be a nostalgic trip through classic Rare platformers. Buy it if you like Banjo-Kazooie, or just 3D Platformers in general. You won't regret it.

Yooka-Laylee is a wonderfully built revist to the N64-era 3D platformers. More of a "family-style" game, it walks familiar territory without being boring, and brings enough colorful environments and characters to put a few smiles on people's faces. The band that brought about Banjo-Kazooie is back in full force and they've proven that those games can still be worthwhile purchases. If you were a fan of those games, Yooka-Laylee will not disappoint. If you want a more Mario-esque approach in terms of sound design and hand-holding, or if you just didn't like 3D platformers at all, you might want to look elsewhere.
Cons first to be helpful, pros to follow:
-Not Keyboard and Mouse friendly. This may seem like a sin given that this is a review of the PC version of this game, but it was built primarily to run on most modern consoles and is based on purely console-grounded predecessors. Controller advised. I use an Xbox One S controller and the controls worked wonderfully without any issues.
-Feels short. Yooka-laylee feels more reserved than the platformers that came before it, like it doesn't want to outstay it's welcome. For some, that may be a plus. If you were looking to get 40 hours out of this game, you'd have to do multiple play-throughs. As of writing this review, I sunk 23 hours into the game to achieve 110% completion.
-Any challenge involving a ball. There's about three or four of these in the game and they all seem to be frustratingly built against the players better angels. The physics and boundaries always seem to throw caution to the wind when a ball is involved to where sometimes winning is more a matter of luck than skill. These were the only truly maddening moments with the game.
-Character voices. About 1/10th of the cutscenes are unskippable and the various chirps, grunts, groans, and quips can get on some people's nerves. The rest of the time you can just bash the A-button and ignore them. If you've played Banjo-Kazooie, Banjo-Tooie, or Nuts N' Bolts, this is not an unfamiliar con. Sometimes it's funny, sometimes it's charming, most of the time it can be agitating if left unchecked. Turning down the sound effects to half helps.
-Camera can be a little unfriendly at times. This is rare and only cropped up for me at 3 moments across the entire game. It doesn't impede enjoyment of the game, but it can prove a little unsavory at critical moments. Most the time the camera behaves like any other game really.
-This is a "collect-a-thon", a rarity in modern games it seems and not without reason. Some players find them tedious. These games appeal to explorers and treasure hunters, those that like to check every corner to find rewards. Yooka-laylee also doesn't hand out participation trophies often - it's common to struggle for just one of the games coveted 'pagies' and sometimes without any hints. This style of game is ripped from an era where player's guides were incredibly popular, and so instead a quick google search can trivialize some of the games more potent puzzles.
Pros:
-"Family style" platformer. Not too challenging for kids, but providing enough of a challenge and humor for adults to stay engaged. Good clean fun!
-Colorful and fleshed out graphics, characters, and environments. Everything looks great and polished!
-Relatively bug-free. The game is built rock-solid and with enough resources to not leave the player hanging.
-Diverse challenges. There's not many dull moments in the game, and it never tries to repeat the same trick twice without some added twists. Trials broadly range from extreemly easy to frustratingly difficult, but all of them are short lived and spaced out.
-Nostalgia-friendly. Yooka-Laylee gladly brings Banjo-Kazooie to modern platforms in a way that doesn't scorn what the older games accomplished nor is it a direct copy.
-Excellent music. Grant Kirkhope is back again and has done an amazing job. The shifts in music throughout are both impressive and pleasing.
This is a kickstarter backer review. I backed Yooka-Laylee to see the old Rare team come back together again and make another delightful platformer, and they have.

"woohoo, a Freelancer remake!"
I quickly found out, that this game is just boring. Really boring.

===
===
- Good variety of pilotable vessels for various play styles: mining freighters, battleships, fighter carriers, it's all there
- RPG elements and alignments system enable the player to take the path they wish in both terms of abilities, perks and behaivior
- Fairly good, but not excellent mind you, number of different sectors to explore
- Main quest, a load of secondary missions, contracts, bounties, random encounters, global events... really, there is a lot of stuff to actually do in the Gemini Sector...
- Decent assortment of weaponry and modifications
- Space anomalies, ion storms, radioactive nebulas, and all sorts of space disasters to endanger your ship
- It takes really long to get to high levels, get all the good ships, weaponry, kill bounty targets and such things
- Quite complex but rewarding enemy ship capture system, you can really do an awful lot of money if you get good at it...
- Overall, more than good longevity, to complete everything the Gemini Sector has to offer, DLCs included, it will take you, say around... 100 hours (i played the beta version before release in the past and did so)
===
- Trading / Mining / Gas collecting / Scrap salvaging are good for making money at low levels, game start and quite a bit after, but from say level 15/20 and above, they become very underwhelming: contracts, bounties and most of all ship boarding surpass the gains by FAR, so players that want to play a Trading type character will be severely penalized in mid/late game and will have to do epic amounts of grinding to get anything
- You cannot destroy space structures if they are not part of a specified mission that involves their destruction. Solar arrays, gas collectors, bandit space stations, trading posts, all of them are completely indestructible: their structure will drop to 0 eventually but will still be perfectly fine. This MIGHT be a game design choice to avoid players break main quests and such, BUT doing so with all space structures is really unacceptable
- You can board space structures, and plausibly get all the sweet loot inside them right? Wrong my friends. Board a mining station, a resarch center or such, and the troops will say it is captured and the loot is being ejected outside: this will not happen. Never, ever. This feature might be incomplete or never finished by developers.
- You can only save your game while docked to a space station or a planet. Not a really big deal, just a poor game design choice
- Ship's autopilot can bug and randomly fly you inside space stations, space debris, asteroids, and turn your ship in a fireball.
- The ship's targeting computer is not able to target automatically asteroids or salvage piles, if you want to be a miner, be prepared to aim at every single little piece of asteroid manually and then collect its loot. This makes mining even more painful than it already is because of the problem i explained before
- The ship's targeting computer (yes, AGAIN) is able to, thankfully, target enemies in automatic fire mode, and is pretty accurate at it, more so than you doing it manually in fact, but the big issue is: the computer will randomly fire at all enemies in its range, and will NOT stay and focus fire on the enemy you locked on. You should understand how this will do in a battle. Yes, really bad.
===
- When boarding a ship, ANY ally ship, be it random, hired mercenaries or quest companions, will STILL target the enemy ship you are trying to board, and there is NO WAY to tell them to do otherwise. This results in extreme frustration because maybe you are actually succeeding in the believe me really difficult task of capturing a ship (especially at high levels), but then some random ally blows it up making you lose time, your troopers inside it, and maybe also a mission involving the ship capture will fail. The developers said this WOULD be fixed many times on forums and steam hub, well it never was.
- Ship capture is the ONLY feasible way of making good amounts of money from mid game and above: contracts will start giving you a pittance, trading will long be worthless and selling those nice ships for money will be your only chance of making money to get better stuff and ships to actually progress in the story or freeroam, because enemies scale with your level and get better everything, and so you must do the same. Yes you guessed it, the thing i said before about boarding, it happens a LOT, so you can choose between getting ulcer from boarding, or grinding 70 contracts in say 6 hours to get 1 tier III weapon for that slot you are missing, and then again and again and again.
- There is a bug that can happen randomly, i presume it is uncommon: after completing a Main Story or DLC Main quest (Happened to me just after finishing Aethera DLC), and this is a really severe bug. What it does is simple: it RESETS the entire quest line of the main story to a random mission, so basically instead of progressing to the next quest, it says the actual active quest is one you ALREADY completed, and i found no fix for this, system cache check, restarting, even savegame editing, nothing. This has lead me to be unable to play Titans DLC because the quest is broken, and who knows what sorts of troubles will other players get from this bug.
===
Honestly, SG2 is a nice space game, nowhere near the depth of some other games like the X series, but positively much more accessible than those, but still being complex enough to not become casualized, and that is all good.
Still, many problems as you read cripple the game and prevent it from becoming truly excellent.

I have mixed feelings for this game. I wish I could make the review neutral.
It's a space sandbox where you roam Gemini system, complete easy single objective quests, get money and buy better ships and guns. The game is quite slow-paced, and you'll probably want an open book at your table, so you can read it while your ship travels to whatever waypoint you've set. The combat system is pretty simple, devs probably wanted this game to be chilling instead of intense.
Positive moments:
- Beautiful space vistas and ships.
- You can destroy enemies, you can mine asteroids, you can buy things in one place to sell in another. It's a sandbox.
- A free DLC with alternative campaign from the first game.
Negative moments:
- The story is mediocre, we've seen all this a thousand times before.
- Voice acting in campaign is pretty bad.
- My PC fits the requirements, and yet the performance is really bad. I experienced crashes in long sessions too.
- Once you get yourself a carrier class vessel, you'll find out that there's like nothing else to do. You can bother yourself with achievements, but it isn't that fun.
- Unrealistic game world. Nebulas within a solar system, asteroids gathered in clouds rather than in rings, tiny planets and stars, you only fly forward when your engines are on: your ship stops once you turned them off, like a car would. I understand that it all was done to make the game less boring and more saturated with content, but it fells just toyish.
Starpoint Gemini 2 is still fun to play, even with the flaws I listed, but I can't recommend it for the full price. If you're into space, get it when on sale.

So, I've been looking forward to DDADDS for a long time. Even before it was announced, I was incredibly frustrated with the lack of gay dating sims out there, and even more frustrated that all my choices were limited to ~pretty anime bois.~ Enter: Dream Daddy. A game full of diversity, fun, and pop culture references that makes my heart soar. The day the game was announced, I rushed to all my friends to give me emergency commissions so I could buy the limited edition physical copy. And I've got my pretty pink enamel cartridge right beside me!
I do have to say, the game was definitely worth it. The art is so charmingly loveable and well-done, the writing is humorous and amazing, and I found myself scream-laughing more often than I thought I would. Every character has this own likable charm to them, and I couldn't bring myself to hate anyone. I love that! The writing was just so fun and bouncy and cute, and I wound up loving all the characters and wanting to know more about them-even Amanda. I love Amanda to death. She's so funny and quick-witted, I'm proud that my daughter is Always Ready To Roast.
Now, this game has plenty of dads to date, and plenty of fun interactions to have. And minigames! I wasn't expecting real actual gameplay, but the golf game has me craving even MORE golf! (god, I really am turning into a dad). There isn't a single aspect of this game I didn't enjoy. Charming characters, actual gameplay, gorgeous art and music direction, it's a cavalcade of fun and enjoyment for the senses. It's definitely worth the fifteen bucks or so to pick it up.
Now...onto the negatives. Every game has them, including this. And I can't really fault this game too much! It's only fifteen dollars, and, what, has only been in development for a year? This is more than enough amazing content I could ask for...but I wish it could've been, how do you say, distributed better?
I guess what I'm saying is, for a game called "Dream Daddy: A Dad Dating Simulator", and has the word "dad" and "daddy" plastered on every single hole from which it spews "dad" stuff out of...it's very much all about Amanda. And that makes sense! As a parent, your life revolves around your kids. And Amanda's great! I love her! I'm glad that we got to spend so much time with her! But...I just wish the advertised "dad dating" didn't feel like "hanging out with Amanda, also your boyfriend is there". Again, I've only finished Brian's route, so other routes may differ. But at the end of it all, I feel like I don't really know Brian? I love him to death, but I feel like I hardly got to spend time with him or...ANYONE really.
I know "I want more" is kind of more of a complement than a criticism (which it should be, because I definitely commend the creators and I definitely want more), but I just feel like I got kind of cheesed out of the dating experience because of too much of the dad experience. When Brian and I were all alone, the game sparkled, and I really felt this connection to him. But sure enough, every date just turned into me dragging Amanda somewhere she didn't want to go and I personally didn't want her to be and just-
Blehhhhhh. Is that my only complaint? Besides that it felt too short. And I could've extended the runtime by hanging out with other dads, I know. But I really, really like Brian, and I can't help but feel like I got a bit shafted in terms of content just because I was really only interested in him. Mmmm...maybe that's not the right way to word it. I just wish I could see a bit more of me and Brian's relationship, maybe after Amanda left, just to scratch that itch.
But no, for fifteen dollars and a year and change of development behind it, Dream Daddy is a perfectly acceptable use of your money. It comes with a very, very strong recommendation, do not get me wrong. It's an A+ and fantastic game, and I'm most certainly going to be playing more of it soon. I guess I just went in with too-high expectations.
Thanks for a great game, guys.

Where do I begin with a game like this. Well for starters this game was made by an indie company, no big publisher backing Introversion, they have done an amazing job getting this game to where it is at this time. In short, buy this game it is an amazing experience.
For those who wish to read, I will now go over the pros and cons of this game in detail.
Pros:
Build just the way you want:
There are very few contraints when building. I'd liken it to Sims 3 from a top down perspective in terms of building. It's great fun.
Cartoony but realistic at the same time:
The game has a very distinctive art style that is unique to the game, but it deals with serious topics such as if you will execute a death row prisoner or not, or if you will keep a prisoner locked up for virtually all of his day. This game makes you think.
It's tough, but only if you want it to be/You can go at your own pace:
The aim of the game is not to amass one billion dollars, but to have the lowest reoffending rate for released prisoners, and every in game day can be marginally relaxing if you want it to. For instance you can run a low-security, generally free environment where the aim is to rehabilitate your prisoners through the use of classes you can run, or you can run a max-sec environment punishing the most hardcore of criminals. It's all up to you.
A dedicated team:
I have watched nearly every alpha video that has been published, and I can clearly see that Introversion software is very passionate about the project. There were (As of writing this it's about a day off offical release) new features each month, and it was a pleasure to watch each and every video.
If you enjoyed Sim City you'll love this. There are features very soon to be released I haven't gone over yet,  as well as features I missed,but you'll see for yourself.
Cons:
Somewhat gruelling at the start:
After putting a good 200 hours into the game as a whole, this is probably my most major complaint with the game, is that in the beginning you start with 30K and the only way you can make money is via grants, but selling your first prison is practically the only way to make cash when you're still learning the ropes.
Overall a solid 8.5/9 out of 10, certainly one of the best sim and strategy/managment games I have ever played. For $30 you will get a lot of fun out of this. Strongly recommended.

TL:DR Best game of its type since Theme Hospital!

Another successful addition to the Arkham franchise. With this winning formula, no developer could go wrong. A great example of one of those cases where more of the same is a good thing.
In this installment the trilogy takes a darker turn, with a story more centered around death and its consequences than before; it becomes more like The Dark Knight trilogy than Arkham. Thankfully the new voice actors fill their roles perfectly, in some cases even topping their predecessors, and the boss fights have been greatly improved, offering a much more cinematic feel this time around and do a lot to drive the story.
Sure the multiplayer isn't a whole lot of fun, but this is still a very good game.

The bottom line: It's a good game, but one that is vastly inferior to the Arkham Asylum and Arkham City.

This game apparently had a really bumpy launch, which accounts for the many negative reviews you'll find all over the web. But by now it truly deserves the label "revised," and while there's still some bugs and bugginess here and there, it's in good shape. As the screenshots will undoubtedly tell you, this isn't "Elder Scrolls Online" or "Diablo III," although there is some very nice scenery to be had. The main draw—or turn-off, depending on who you are—is the gameplay, which is utterly old school and unforgiving. Your party hit the road in winter and forgot to pack thick coats and sleeping bags? What were you thinking!? In a word, if you yearn for the level of realism that doesn't even know what an "auto-attack" is, RoA is your game. If you felt that having to repair your gear in WoW was too much micro-management, it will drive you nuts. If you're undecided, wait for another sale and give it a whirl, you might love the atmosphere and good ol' story-telling.

Before reading on, I am very obviously biased towards this game. 3D adventure-platformers are my jam.
Yooka-Laylee was a 9/10 experience for me. The look, feel and sound of Banjo are all there. Whacky characters, great music (though not as many earworms, only Rextro's theme stands out in this regard), well-placed toilet humour and platforming that provides a solid challenge, although veterans of the genre will likely breeze through the game. What keeps this from being the perfect experience is what many have already talked about, a lack of going above and beyond what can only be called previous entries in the Banjo games.
I think the camera has been overstated, it is a definite improvement on the 64 era. I did not die once to camera problems, though I admit they certainly existed. It wasn't uncommon for it to get stuck behind a door or on an object in the foreground, but pausing or pressing the zoom function would fix it easily enough. If I'm honest, issues such as this felt like problems I had developed the skills to solve throughout my childhood, along with the platforming itself. As strange as it sounds, this felt to me as much a part of the game as the game itself. Yes, the nostalgia goggles are on.
The movement is key to these kinds of games, and Yooka didn't disappoint. I loved rolling around and flapping about more than I ever did with Kazooie. Combined with the ability to take flight at any time later in the game, and getting around the much larger worlds was an absolute joy. Big tick.
Speaking of the worlds, they are huge. Much bigger than anything in Kazooie or Tooie. Considering there are 25 Pagies in each one, this is no surprise. Some of the best moments come from scaling to the top of the level and realising just how high up you actually are, particularly Tribalstack Tropics and Galleon Galaxy. The themes of the first three levels were fairly standard and somewhat rehashed, but considering how unique the last two worlds are I think this can be forgiven. They only made the ice level for the ice key joke anyway. Worth it! (Note: I expanded every world aside from the first before entering it, so I can't comment on how large they appear beforehand. I would not recommend doing this for beginners to the genre, as it may make it harder to navigate).
In terms of issues, they could have cleared up exactly which moves to use in some sections by marking it more clearly. Particularly, when to use Sonar 'Splosion, Buddy Slam and Reptile Rush. Many breakable objects could be broken by any of these, but some required a specific one that wasn't clear. This was frustrating when one move was known but others weren't. On top of that, sometimes you had to melt things with fire that looked the same again.
The other thing was the aerial attack, which I greatly enjoyed earlier in the game before Laylee could flap me over larger gaps, but which fell short in the combat area. Combat overall was what I expected, I detest platformers that rely too heavily on combat as enemies should be obstacles rather than having to kill everything you see. In this way it was fine, but there were times when I wanted to clear areas to make it easier and the bees/jellyfish were a royal pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ If the aerial attack had a bigger hit box then this would be a non-issue. Otherwise, only five enemy types (off the top of my head), despite being well down on the usual variety in these games, didn't really bother me. If that's something that falls by the wayside in a quick development, I can live with it. Hopefully it's rectified in future titles.
On the other hand, I thought the bosses were great. The level three boss, and Capital B himself, were standouts. Really enjoyable fights that reminded me of Grunty in Banjo-Kazooie and Mad Jack in DK64, some of my favourite bosses of all time.
The music was good, but not overly memorable. I do want to go back and listen to it again, however. I can't remember the exact tune, but Glitter Glaze Glacier struck me as quite beautiful.
The arcade mini games weren't great, in fact I think they put the worst one in the first level, which was a poor choice. Also, you shouldn't have to beat them twice if you get the high score on the first attempt, which I did three times. Especially when you then fail to get the high score on subsequent attempts. Doing the exact same challenge multiple times when you've already achieved it is never a good thing. I distincly remember being able to get both pages and jiggies in one go in Tooie, so I don't know why they went backwards on this. However, I loved the Kartos sections. They were the right mix of challenge and simplicity, and took some time to learn but were rewarding by the end.
Overall, I don't think Playtonic could have stuffed this up for me, but it seems for a lot of other people this hasn't worked out. A lot of the criticisms I'm seeing will probably not bother you if you love the old Rare platformers. I think if they'd taken another year to work on this, maybe it could have been a classic. Keep in mind though that they are a brand new studio who were working on growing their team and their brand at the same time. I can't wait to see what they do next.

Thank God I don't go by most reviewers these days. If I did, I probably would have passed on this game, but I don't and so I did play it and it's great. For me, it had the perfect balance between old school Banjo/DK64 from Rare and a platformer that is releasing in 2017. Best part, it's a legit 3D platformer being released on the PC with no emulation needed. I'll get the negatives out of the way first.
It does have mouse and keyboard support through the menus and gameplay, though it could be a tad better. Camera control with the mouse (I cranked the in-game sensitivity to the highest) isn't the best as the game doesn't just give you 100% control over it. Things like walking around and objects in the world will have the camera move as the game wants it to. This annoyance carries over if you're using a gamepad but it feels much more annoying with the mouse. No button remapping is also annoying, but the salt in the wound is that you can't even see a screen that tells you what all the keyboard inputs are. Another negative would be the talking sounds. It's one of the things from the classic games that I wish didn't make a return or could have been handled better like if there were much, much more unique sounds for each character. As it is, there's only 3-5 sounds per character and with the frequency of the sounds being made, it's just an assault on your ears for 90% of the characters. Thankfully you can just hit Space or A and see their full text right then and only hear their voice once per line. My last negative would be the return of another classic feature, the quizzes. The questions are still covering super small details (like the color of the first Ghost that you captured in an area) and if you have taken a break between playing a level and doing to quiz to reach the next area, it's very unlikely that you will remember such small details. I played it with almost no breaks longer than 24 hours and I still forgot some of the details asked in a couple of the questions. But the worst part about the quiz sections is just the change of pacing. I want to play a platformer and be moving and jumping around, not slowly answering quizzes.
Now onto the good, which will hopefully be a shorter section and in a good way. The gameplay, they nailed it. Such a fantastic platformer with some solid mechanics that are introduced from area to area. Some people may not like the backtracking for when you get a new ability that can be used in a previous level, but unless you're a completionist, they are easily skippable and you can just keep moving on to the new levels. Great mini-games and puzzles fill out the gameplay and it just feels so right. Also, the music is great. None of it gets annoying like the character's talking, it's just like the old Rare games and pleasing to listen to outside of the game.
Yup, that's it. Despite the negatives paragraph being so long compared to the positives, this game is fantastic and is one of my favorite platformers since DK64.

Overall I really enjoyed this game! It's a really nice dating sim with lovable characters and lots of heartfelt interactions. Dad roleplaying never felt so possible.
Pros:
+ The music is super cute and nice to play to.
+ The art style is really good! All the characters look unique and the Dad's little animated quirks are adorable.
+ Each dad's arc is complete and is super fun to play. The game also does a good job of introducing them to you all at the beginning and making sure you have a good idea of their personalities.
+ The dialogue between you and your daughter is really well thought-out and sweet. The game's emotional moments never feel fabricated, they feel real and like genuine situations that you have to deal with. Amanda is one of the best parts of the game - same goes for your real talks with the other dads. There's also a lot of funny lines and moments.
Cons:
- Each run is relatively short - going on all the dates with one dad takes about an hour or forty-five minutes depending on how long you take, so the game is pretty short overall if you immediately commit to one dad like I did the first time. Playing it a more varied way on my second playthrough made it feel more robust, but I was a bit disappointed that committing to one dad made the game go fast.
- The character creator makes a few unique dads, but most of the options are silly so you'll stick to making a few repetitive figures.
- Something about the quality of Hugo's recordings in some sections isn't that great. i'm not sure if it had to do with the way they recorded his voice or the way the audio was mixed, but there's lots of processing noise that's very noticeable.
- The dialogue occasionally bugs and references things out of order. This didn't happen a lot and wasn't game-breaking, but it was still weird to hear Robert talking about things I had never done.
I still haven't gone on all three dates with all the dads, so I am concerned about re-playability since just going on three dates with Craig was so short, but if my time with Craig and Robert was any indication you can still get plenty of time going on dates with all the Dads. Super enjoyable and cute sim!

This game is sort of a mix between a good version of Global Ops: Commando Libya and Third Person Call of Duty. Well, "How?" you ask. WELL STOP ASKING AND FRIKIN READ!
Story - 10/10 (WOULD FORGET AND PLAY AGAIN)
This game has one of the best atmospheric, psychological stories I've ever experienced in my life. This game has you playing as Captain ____ Walker (< forget the first name). Walker and his 2 of his men, Luitenant Adams and Sergeant Lugo are dispatched to a city called "Dubai" in search of people who have survived the violent sandstorms. They were not able to communicate to Dubai because a "storm wall" was blocking all comms to and from Dubai. As you play, Walker gets more and more psychologically attached to Dubai. If something can go wrong, it will. That's what this story's mostly about. I'm not gonna give too much away, because you'd wanna play it for yourself. This game has so many moments where it pulls at your heart. There's a handful of moments where it's really sad. This game is a must-get just for the story.
Gameplay - 9/10
I have decreased a point on gameplay because of the controls. Nonetheless, the mechanics of the game are pretty well done, as well as the atmosphere that this game holds. The atmosphere is the number one thing that makes this game a well done piece of work. I can see that it's been worked on. I can see that it's been revised. I can also see that the devs had a f*cking sense of humor. You'll find it for yourself once you play the game. Everything about this game is well done.
Graphics - 8.5/10
It's not the
graphics, but it's enough to make you feel and see the things Walker goes through as he journeys through Dubai. The graphics are good enough that it makes traveling to Dubai a no-no for me, let's just say that.
Controls - 6.7/10 (THIS AREA HAS BEEN GRADED FROM USING A 360 Gamepad CONTROLLER)
Clunky as hell, but manageable. I've never played it on a mouse and keyboard, but the get into cover thing and turn the corner of the cover is a bit clunky. I've managed through the clunkyness of the controls, and that's the only thing keeping the score .7 points up from being a 6. And yes, it is manageable.
Sound - 10/10
Atmospheric, realistic, and ambient. The 3 most important factors of sound and this game has them. The voice acting is impressive, too. There's also the gunshots! I love judging the realisticness of gunshots. They're pretty damn realistic, but they're ambient enough to let you know "Yep, I'm being shot at."
Replay Value - 5/10
There are "choices" you can make in this game. None of these "choices" are story-changing, but they will affect your morality as a gamer.
The only "choices" that affect the story are the ones at the end, where they affect the ending. There are, I believe 3 different endings you can get, I may be wrong.
Once you finish the game, it will never be the same for you ever, ever again.
Overall Rating Value : 8.2/10
A whopping 8.2. It's a great game overall, but the only thing dragging it down is the replay value. Without the replay value being accounted for, it's 8.84, which is not too much of a difference, but it's there. This game is atmospheric, but linear as hell, aside from the moral-affecting choices you can make during the story. I'd recommend this game to anyone who likes military games and can understand some disorders of having been through service for the country and how it can affect your day-to-day life. That
what the story is about, after all.
The fact that there is no way to change the ultimate outcome... is heartbreaking. The linear storyline creates that much more impact on the choices you make. 10/10

Mad Max is a technically gorgeous game, and it runs awesomely on my potato PC, but I don't think I've ever bounced harder off of a video game than I have with this one. Why? Simply put, the controls suck.
When using a gamepad, the buttons can't be reassigned. While I appreciate the fact that the devs provided controller support, they either should have thought harder on the resulting control scheme or given a way for the player to rebind buttons. As the button layout is set up now, you're forced to sprint (or hobble, in Max's case) using one of the trigger buttons, and firing your shotgun is done with one of the face buttons. While I can sort of understand why the "shoot" button was assigned to the front [the shotgun is used often in melee combat], why dafuq would the sprint command be assigned to one of the gamepad triggers? It's counterproductive and at odds with how virtually every other open-world beat-em-up has done it since the introduction of the genre. Considering how WB has also made the Batman Arkham games, it's all really confounding that they chose such a inadequate control scheme for Mad Max.
Oh yeah, I also kept running out of shotgun ammo because I'd constantly be twitch-hitting the shotgun button when I didn't want to - you know, typical button mashing for one of these games. That's ultimately a very frustrating experience in a game where ammo is a rarity (a problem Max's
don't have apparently).
One last thing: this is an action-driving game where
. Think about how much fun spinning donuts/drifting is in every other open-world game ever made, and then think about
doing that in Mad Max. It's a staple of the open-world racing genre, and the devs replaced it with a mounted harpoon and a wonky "bump" mechanic. Ugh.
Oops, forgot to mention that the environments are monotonous as anything I've ever seen. I only got a couple hours in, but I was already tired of looking at sand and rocks after about twenty minutes. I just don't think there's enough variety in the landscape to keep things fresh for the remainder of the game.
Just not my cup of tea overall.

I really don't get why there are so many negative reviews for this game.  What were people expecting, the second coming of Christ?.
As the game is, it is a fun, vibrant 3d platformer.  And it was DEFINITELY made by the same team behind the Banjo-Kazooie games.

First of all I want to say that this game is good. Not grate. But good. For a new entry into a genera that is pretty much dead and hasn't been touched for a while this is the genera as it was, not as you remember, but as it was.
See the problem with a kick started squeal to a popular game in a (pretty) dead genera is that people want the game they remember as a kid and not how they actually were, which is where we need to start aiming these sorts of products. Now all that out of the way let me get into my real thoughts.
Yooka-Laylee is Banjo-Kazooie 3. It's not like the Banjo Kazooie series it IS the third Banjo-Kazooie game; someone made it locked it away for 20 years and now they pulled it out gave it a new coat of paint. That's the best description I can give because it does lack allot of the evolution that games have gone through since the time of the N64. I mean they did throw out lives so that was nice, but other then that most design philosophy of the time is the exact same; which is weird because allot of those design of those games was because of limitations of memory. My primary example of this is that there is no voice acting, it's all chopped up bah, bah, bah's and well I appreciate it's for the nostalgic factor I'd much rather have had actual voice acting.
It may sound like I'm being hard on this game, and I am. But I do actually really love it, it's more of a game I liked when I was young and I got what I was expecting. The problem is that that's it. I got what I was expecting and nothing more. So if you are looking for more Banjo-Kazooie or 3D platforms then this is it. Just don't go in expecting any evolution to the formula

TLDR: It starts off really strong, and then loses steam over time until eventually it just comes to a halt.
So, I'll start with a small thing and then get to the main problem I have with this game.
So the game is riddled with all these weird inconsistencies with the mechanics. For example; at one point you get an ability that you're told can break glass, turns out it doesn't break glass, it only breaks blocks of ice with a weird flashing blue outline. The move that breaks glass, you get that later.
And then you get the ability to breath fire by eating these weird berries from certain plants, You can't burn the blue-outlined ice blocks, but you can burn ice blocks without an outline.
So that's the more minor problem, but over time it really gets annoying. Now on to the biggest problem, and most important thing for a BK-style game: The level design
The hub level and the first level are great, but the first level's the best one in the game by far. Soooo, BK and BT were known for having levels that felt expansive, but also packed with stuff to do. They felt large, but they weren't so big that you got lost in them, or took a really long time getting around them. And the first level does that very well, almost every challenge felt like it belonged in the level, and the whole thing just felt really cozy. But then you get to the 2nd level, where it starts falling apart. Each challenge feels completely seperarte from one-another, while the world just feels like a sort of backdrop for it all.
Take for example: The Witness. That game has a beautiful island to explore, but nothing to do on it but solve mundane line puzzles on a screen, which just feel completely seperated from the actual island, and take you out of the game's atmosphere. YL's levels mostly have that same problem.
Also there's just nothing memorable about it, while the first level had this huge tower you have to climb (which was a lot of fun to do) the Ice world has nothing that stands out, and the same goes for the next level; the swamp.
So the swamp is just a bunch of little bits of land dotted around a large gloomy swamp lake. It has some fun challenges in it, but once again they feel completely seperate and out-of-place in the level.
Another good comparison is to look back at a BK level, Mad Monster Mansion comes to mind. In that level there was a ghost you had to sneak by in order to get a jiggy, and a haunted hedge maze. Both are challenges that work with the theme of the level. While in YL you'll just find random metal platforms in every world, as well as other things that just don't fit.
The casino level picks things back up pretty well though, but remains inconsistent. It has large empty spots, but where there's actual stuff to do it's really neat. 2 things that stood out to me were the slot machines, and the roulette table area.
With the slot machines; each one controls differently. My favorite one required me to stop slots temporarily until they all lined up the same, and then hit a button to stop them all at once when the correct icon was showing.
And then there's a neat bit where you jump around spinning roulette tables, while dodging enemies and trying to catch one of the Ghost Writers (basically flying Jinjos) It's a fun challenge that sticks with the level's theme.
So at this point I was thinking maybe they lost it a bit with the ice and swamp level, but started getting back into the swing of things near the end with the casino level. Welp, that hope was crushed when I saw the last level.
When you first enter it, you're greeted with 2 small islands and a completely empty ocean with nothing interesting to look at. After expanding it, you get 3-4 more islands. That's it, that's the entire level. Have fun kids.
It's all soooo much more spread out than nessecary, why do the islands need to be so far apart? Why not just have 1 land mass with all the stuff on it? I just don't get it.
It seems like they went with the idea of "If it looks bigger then it's better." But if it's bigger with barely anything in it, then it's just simply empty.
Also I've fought 4 out of the 6 bosses, and only 1 was actually good (The swamp boss). The rest so far are incredibly boring and have no challenge to them at all.
One is just a square that slides on a wall and occasionally stops to shoot little bits of ice at you. All you have to do is spray fire at him, and the fight just becomes a slog, especially since it goes on for farrr too long.
Also, you get the ability to fly anywhere at anytime, meaning you no longer need to platform to get to places. Which defeats the whole point of a platformer, especially one based on exploration. Seeing a thing and having to figure out how to get to it is no longer part of the game, now you can just fly to anything you want to go to. So it just becomes busywork to get pagies.
Also the flying is ridiculously over-powered. Remember the large tower I mentioned in level 1? You can get from the bottom of it, to the very top within mere seconds.
I do plan on atleast getting to the final boss, since I only need a few more pagies to. But it's just not nearly entertaining enough to want to finish to 100%

The old pool games on Yahoo were only 2D and you weren't able to jump balls. In 3D, being able to jump the ball is quite satisfying.

Tricks with fine adjustments had a major problem. If you pressed F, the tutorial would give you a green tick even if you we aiming all over the place.

The default graphics suck. I couldn't even read the words in the tutorial, I thought Left Click was Left Shift. Tried it on 1280 * 768 resolution @ 60Hz... Much better...
3. Overhead view
As I played the game as a newbie, I realised I would never bother with trick shots. I would just use the Overhead view
4. Multiple ball collisions
The game can't show how multiple collisions work e.g. proxying a ball. If you hit the cushion to hit your ball, it will only show where the white ball goes to. This turns me off from trying more difficult shots vs winning the game. If the issue is player difficulty, perhaps the developers could create 1. Easy 2. Medium 3. Hard 4. Pro modes for players. It's a gamble when you buy an episodic game like this, because you aren't ensured of the quality of subsequent releases. However, from what I've seen of the Paris levels and the intro levels, it's pretty solid. The freeform levels like Paris are huge. The way the development works is that they create a huge setting like Paris, then create missions for it. I guess this allows the development team to focus on polishing one setting and its missions as much as possible, before moving on to the next.
Could they have simply released a $60 game all at once? Yes, but it would be out later this year. Do they get more sales from doing an episodic release? Yes, that seems like the intention of the business model. Every new episode is probably going to spike sales for a short time period.
I'm going to predict that reviews for this game will improve as more content is released. The current offering is essentially an Early Access Game, so view it as such. For an Early Access Game, it's very polished. If people are spending 40+ hours on a single level, that says a lot about the game's content and replayability.
