Mad Max is a technically gorgeous game, and it runs awesomely on my potato PC, but I don't think I've ever bounced harder off of a video game than I have with this one. Why? Simply put, the controls suck.
When using a gamepad, the buttons can't be reassigned. While I appreciate the fact that the devs provided controller support, they either should have thought harder on the resulting control scheme or given a way for the player to rebind buttons. As the button layout is set up now, you're forced to sprint (or hobble, in Max's case) using one of the trigger buttons, and firing your shotgun is done with one of the face buttons. While I can sort of understand why the "shoot" button was assigned to the front [the shotgun is used often in melee combat], why dafuq would the sprint command be assigned to one of the gamepad triggers? It's counterproductive and at odds with how virtually every other open-world beat-em-up has done it since the introduction of the genre. Considering how WB has also made the Batman Arkham games, it's all really confounding that they chose such a inadequate control scheme for Mad Max.
Oh yeah, I also kept running out of shotgun ammo because I'd constantly be twitch-hitting the shotgun button when I didn't want to - you know, typical button mashing for one of these games. That's ultimately a very frustrating experience in a game where ammo is a rarity (a problem Max's
don't have apparently).
One last thing: this is an action-driving game where
. Think about how much fun spinning donuts/drifting is in every other open-world game ever made, and then think about
doing that in Mad Max. It's a staple of the open-world racing genre, and the devs replaced it with a mounted harpoon and a wonky "bump" mechanic. Ugh.
Oops, forgot to mention that the environments are monotonous as anything I've ever seen. I only got a couple hours in, but I was already tired of looking at sand and rocks after about twenty minutes. I just don't think there's enough variety in the landscape to keep things fresh for the remainder of the game.
Just not my cup of tea overall.

Pros:
+ Beautiful graphical fidelity
+ Well made convincing Post-Apocalyptic atmosphere
+ Excellent optimization
+ Accurate to Mad Max lore
+ Simple but satisfying combat, similar to Batman Arkham Games and Shadow of Mordor (same   engine)
+ Lots of customization for your car
+ Decently long amount of gameplay (20 hours in and I'm still not even close to being done)
Cons:
- Objectives can be repetitive (not always bad, but can be boring for some people)
- Main story is a little lackluster (I often find myself skipping some long, uninteresting cutscenes)
- Car driving and combat can be frusturating to handle sometimes (only in some cases)
Overall Score [8.5/10]:
If you enjoy open world games with excelent atmosphere like Batman Arkham City or Shadow of Mordor, then you will certainly enjoy Mad Max. Fans of the series will love the game, as it is good on its own, regardless of the Mad Max universe, which just adds to its appeal. Combat is fun, albeit simple, but never bores me and introduces new abilities throughout, keeping the pace fresh. Car combat is a little finnicky at some points, but is a unique addition that works well most of the time. Customization is the most enjoyable part of the game for me. I love traveling across the map to upgrade certain parts of my car or gear, even if the tasks can be a little repetitive. The variation in camp design is more than enough to make each base unique and fun to raid. Boss fights are stupidly easy, but there isn't much emphasis put on them, so it doesn't take away from the experience very much. Apart from the gameplay, the atmosphere and feel of the game is rediculously good. The post apocalyptic feel makes for a very immersive and enjoyable world. Overall, I would reccomend this game to anyone who likes open world games. It is a must buy for Max Max fans, or when on sale.

Well. I tried to like this game. I really did. Having played the original back in the 90s on a C-64 I expected to have something comparable to that. Perhaps it's being seen through rose colored glasses, perhaps not.
What we ended up with here is a shadow of the game's former self. The cities are generic, the buildings all look the same, the NPCs (if you could call the that) have no life to them. Inns, taverns, shops, smithies, you can't tell one from the other at all except for the names.
The voice acting should have been left out entirely. It's awful. It's obvious as hell that whoever was doing it isn't a native English speaker and was dry reading from a script. Yes, it's almost 2014, but not every game is well suited to lots of voice acted stuff. This one certainly isn't.
The combat system is a major deal breaker though. I know I can't possibly be doing things SO WRONG that I screwed up two different attempts to roll up and equip a party. Every fight I've been in (which has always been the party's first) ends in defeat with us missing, fumbling, being parried, or whatever. Rarely hit a damn thing even with high stats and all the equipment our meager funding could manage. Turning things over to the auto-AI is an extremely disappointing and very LONG wait for the same result - our deaths.
I hate to say it, but this is starting to become a trend with these Indie RPGs and it's now going to make me think long and hard about parting with the money I'm spending on this stuff. I took a chance on this one and got burned - it won't happen again.
(Note to Valve: This is why refunds exist in the real world! Learn something here! I'd surely love to get one at this point!)

NOTE: For 1.34(More Then A Remake) a short addition appended below this review. 1.33 review(To Cross the Borders) appended below this review. (Delaying the Ork Invasion is 1.32 review)
*****Delaying the Ork Invasion*****
Why I chose this title? Because at the release of this game, we all were leaning towards the thoughts that the game was doomed and orks would conquer the Northlands without our intervention. The game was a mess of bugs and a graphical parody to a degree where NPCs and surroundings would make you feel like in a zombie apocalypse version of Northlands. And furthermore the game used to lack many spells, mechanics and had several other gamebreakers which is probably the reason turned off many people. But...there is always a "but"...and this time it is a good "but".
The game evolved...while I am telling you its evolved it is in the level of a pokemon evolution where you would barely recognize what it was before. Crafty Studios perhaps hired a faery who touched the game with her magical wand exorcising a nasty demon who made the game look bad and broken. Or briefly, they worked their asses off during these months releasing several patches to reach this state. But before going into detail...some screenshots from my game:
If you have the game, you will notice the major differences...if you don't have the game well you should get it while it is still on Christmas Sales, because the great leap forward which has started with 1.32 patch which is named as "Revised" will not stop till "Gold" version of the game. I presume you already looked at the screenshots. Here I will not go over change by change but mention the crucial changes which made me rather happy.
The Journey Map is in English and place names are in accordance with the original Blade of Destiny. Of course still there are no descriptions for Hjaldor Mountains and such, that is just a matter of adding a few place holders.
NPCs look good and NPCs with striped pants you can feel like you are really traversing Thorwalian towns. Also market days, opening/closing times of the shops as well as if you get caught cheating at a tavern you get punished by no entrance features integrated to the game over this time.
The new UI which provides more information to the people in a coherent way, as well as they are more versatile then the old UI which was closing a part of the main screen. Now you have a broader area of view where you can enjoy the good sights of the game.
Except Demon Summoning spells(which are not added) and a few more, most of the spells are fully functioning and ready to assist you in a dungeon as utility or perhaps to decimate your foes as fast as possible. After all, we could wait a little while longer to see a few stray/unimplemented spells.
I'm not even mentioning several optical improvements done to the environment letting screenshots talk for themselves. Though, one thing worth mentioning is the improved interiors of the buildings...especially my favourite is the inn which gave me a dark feeling and I could say I was definitely in backwater, gloomy Northlands of Aventuria.
There are also a good deal of fine tunings, bugfixes and balancings...but I'll cut to the chase. This game evolved truly and deserves a second chance. You will not regret it, especially when you buy it now at a bargain price.
Edit: Price advice was during Christmas Sale, but rest of the review is still valid since it features 1.32 patch. I will update the review, after every noticeable change.
*****To Cross the Borders*****
The anticipated 1.33 patch hit the Steam and I should say while there are still shortcomings here and there, it has been a solid improvement.
Though sadly we still have to be exposed to unpolished Battle Avatars and Sounds. This can be a major deterrent to some players. But for me it is a moment of "Eh..." since I have been more interested in content of the battles rather then nice looks. But I must point out, now spells are associated with different animations, that can be a good indication for the future polishing(One can keep hoping).
Now, one major striking point is that every temple has a different interior as well as the temple distribution on Hjaldings is accurate to the world description. So you'll find a good deal of Swafnir and Travia temples while there are no Praios or Boron temples.
About battle, there are now Battle Stances! Yes, they have finally found their way into the game. Aggressive, Balanced and Defensive. Depending on your tactical situation, now you can make use of those stances. For example, if you flanked somebody, this especially alleviates the issue where hitting is a problem. Going aggressive will increase your hit chance while reducing your parry chance, providing you more success. On the other hand, a hard pressed character can switch to defensive to hold off the enemy. Another plus is that now Necrophobia is important in battles. It'll make your characters skip a turn if undead is in the vicinity. (Necrophobia roll) Also weapon/monster re-balancing seems like it will make things quite different then before. One example is some animals are hitting twice. Also two spells Nekropathia and Abvenenum added to the game. The more, the merrier.
Heavy bugfixing as usual made the game stabler and Main Game+DLCs present a good deal of content. "For the Gods" add a number of challenging unique battles across 2 detailed dungeons and one town while "Ogredeath" adds several side quests spread through the world and one extra dungeon at Groenvelden.
Now, I should stress it again. If Battle Characters, Animations and Sounds can get an overhaul via a major patch, this game has the potential to be a true success. The game has already crossed the border of remake and now it should move forward with full force.
*****More Then A Remake*****
I wasn't expecting to update my review but surprisingly 1.34 patch hit Steam containing several additional encounters, bugfixes and fine-tunings to mechanics. Additionally some of the good mods (such as herb pouch) created by the dedicated community members of the game made formal appearance with this patch. The game still has the mediocre character models, but aside that in my eyes it has become more then a remake already.

Pool Nation is a your run-of-the-mill billiards with impressive physics and graphics.
I haven't played pool since I was at a christmas party with my relatives back around 2007, and playing this type of game brought back some nostalgia for me.
This was my first in a very long time playing a billiards video game, and I'm talking a
time...like around when Sega Genesis was still new and Sonic 3 hasn't even come out. I think I was only...what, five years old during the time?
In any case, the controls took some getting used to, but after about 10 minutes into playing "9 Ball", everything felt natural.
The camera angles give a nice sense of realism, and if adjusted correctly, you feel as if you're holding the pool stick yourself and hitting the target...with psychic eyes in seeing guidelines.
The physics in this game felt just right for me, where like real pool, speed and precision matter when banking shots, as well as how you plan to hit the ball, such as curving and hopping.
The graphics added a nice sense of realism to the game, and the crisp clear look on each ball gave the game a nice type of brilliance. The only thing I question is that every ball has a reflection, which is very awkward to me, since I know actual billiard balls aren't that reflective in real life. But I'm being anal at that point, and you might as well add scratches to the balls and pool table, and make the atmosphere bleak.
Yeah, that's
pool right there, but I'm digressing at this point.
Overall, with the different types of modes in the game, and the option to play with a friend or online, this game is pretty solid, and I would recommend this game to any of my friends that want to play a billiards game without the need of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off pool owners for scratching up the leather.

Graphics: 8/10
Music & Sound: 9/10
Gameplay: 7/10
Value (Is it worth the asking price?): 9/10
Final Score: 8/10
Now for the actual review
I was very excited to see the former Rare team coming together to make another game in the spirit of Banjo-Kazooie. So I backed £25 to the project on kickstarter. Banjo-Kazooie is my favorite game of all time so I had high hopes for it, but didn't expect it to be better than the source material. As it turns out, it wasn't. But that doesn't mean it's a bad game. Yooka-Laylee succeeds to be a worthy successor to Banjo-Kazooie with interesting characters, quirky writing and overall great level design. But there are a couple of issues and a small selection of worlds keeping this game from being an instant classic.
Yooka-Laylee's story is about Yooka the chameleon and Laylee the bat, the latter finds a magical book which ends up getting stolen by Capital B, a power hunger executive from the Hivory Towers. Capital B wants to use the book to rewrite history and rule the entire world and the buddy duo has to prevent that from happening. While the book is being sucked up all the pages fly out of it. The golden pages of the book are called pagies and they are the source of the books power. Yooka and Laylee need to collect them before Capital B can use them for his evil schemes. While the story is simple, it serves it's purpose: a goal for Yooka and Laylee to explore several different tomes to find as much pointless stuff as possible. The writing and general dialog is very similar to what you expect to find in Banjo-Kazooie. Puns, video game references, 4th wall breaking and "special" grammar are all included. Yooka-Laylee doesn't look bad either. The game feels very Nuts and Bolts like and most of the levels are full of color and just look good. The game also performs really well. With my setup (AMD FX-8350, GTX 1060 6GB and 8GB RAM) the game never dropped below 80fps at the highest settings and in 1080p with an average of a solid 120-150 fps. The game is playable for me in 4K with an average framerate of 70 but it drops severly on certain points in the game. But still this is great for a Unity game. The game is also really responsive to Alt+tabbing. I thought I would include this since some games really struggle with it but this one doesn't. The options are severly lacking though. There are only a few preset quality options and you can't rebind the controls (at least not that I know of). I've never had any problems with bugs and glitches and the texture quality is pretty decent. Some spots look a little bit rough but overall it's good. The soundtrack is a beast of it's own. Grant Kirkhope, David Wise and Steve Burk did an amazing job composing this soundtrack. It's full of catchy tunes and orchestral greatness which reminded me of Banjo-Kazooie on more than one occasion. The grunts are also back to support text in the game, and it's a mixed bag. While most of them are great and really entertaining (Laylee, Capital B, Rextro and Trowzer), some of them can get grating after a while (Yooka, Blasto and Kartos). But to be fair without them it just wouldn't be the same.
Yooka-Laylee plays very similarly to Banjo-Kazooie and Donkey Kong 64, but a bit more slippery. Jumping, running and flying feel great and are supported by responsive and tight controls. The problem for me comes in a few areas here.
1. Reptile Roll
Reptile roll is the first movement ability you unlock and it's hit or miss. Sometimes you speed though levels at high speeds and knock over all enemies in your path. Other times it feels very sluggish and slippery which caused me more than one death.
2. Combat
There is nothing wrong with the combat itself, the amount of combat move is impressive and there are a lot of ways you can deal with obstacles. The problem is that it's doesn't really feel like you are fighting something. When you hit an enemy it just doesn't feel right. There is no impacting feel from hitting and destroying enemies, so I avoided most of the combat scenarios unless it was neeeded.
3. Camera
The camera is a lot better now that they patched it, but it still struggles at some point. A great example of this is with the first boss. The camera is in a fixed position as you roll up the hill. But when you get hit and roll down from it the camera swtiches position and returns behind you, while moving back 2 meter resets the camera to the fixed position. This means that the camera messes with the controls multiple times in the span of a couple of seconds, which messes you up.
The worlds itself are pretty great, except one (which I'll talk about later). They are relativly big and have a lot of activities to do in them. World can be expanded once to make them two or sometimes even three times their original size. This is an interesting but underwhelming mechanic, although they increase the activities in one world and make you come back. These activities span from memory games, simple puzzles, platforming challenges, races and bosses. The bosses are okay I guess. None of them really stand out except the boss of world 5 and the last boss. The are not bad per se, just underwelming and boring from time to time. Each defeated boss or completed challenge yields you one of 145 pagies. Each world has 25 pagies (the HUB world Hivory Towers having 20), 200 quills, 5 ghost writers (basicly more challenging Jinjo's), a health extender, a power meter extender (a meter that drains while using some moves to stop the overpowerd ones from being used the entire game long), a Mollycool (which is used to transform into different thing mixing up gameplay) and a Rextro coin. These Rextro coins can be given to Rextro to play one of his arcade games. These are basicly minigames which earn you pagies. While some of the minigames are pretty cool, they range from boring to downright frustrating. The transformations I spoke of earlier are a lot more fleshed out than in Banjo-Kazooie. Most of them spice the gameplay up just enough for them to be fun while one or two are just confusing and hard to control. While  most worlds are pretty fun to explore, there are only five of them. One is great, three are pretty good and one of them is downright awful. Here we get to the afore mentioned world 4, Capital Casino. This world is easily the worst world in the game. The unique gameplay element in this world is that you really can't earn pagies the regular way. Instead you can get tokens by completing challenges and winning slot machines and other (sometimes chance based) games. The problem is that this makes the entire world unrewarding and confusing, since you can't really earn pagies and the needed tokens are spread around the entire place. Basicly each task which would normaly earn you a pagie now gives you 5 coins, which equals to half a pagie. This makes gameplay pretty slow in this world. On top of that the slot machines and other games grind the pace to a halt and are really not that fun to do. The token mechanic is fitting for a casino themed world and it sounds kind of cool at first, but it ends up being a really bad way to reward the player. Normally this would be that big of a deal, but there are only 4 other worlds to explore. 5 worlds is pretty dissapointing and one of them being fairly poor doesnt help. The HUB world is pretty good though. It's nowhere near Gruntilda's lair, not even as good as Isle'O'Hags, it's still pretty big and fun to explore. If you want to 100% the game, there is a lot of stuff to collect. Even if there are only 5 worlds, a complete run of the game took me around 20 hours. And I know I'm going to play it again. In my opinion, I think the £40 pricetag is reasonable.

I had to put several hours into this game to form proper thoughts and I honestly think Playtonic achieved their goal of reviving the 3D platformer. The ear candy that is the Kirkhope and Wise soundtrack bless my nostalgic ears and the silly babbling of the characters bring back the wacky cartoony looks and sounds of Rare. The worlds combine the vastness of Tooie and progress feels just like Kazooie so they could please fans of both games. the Jontron controversy is a very poor excuse to dismiss this game as he was meant to only be a minor character, but grown adults are the main target for this game i suppose.My only minor complaint is that Laylee's sound wave gets glitched and won't be seen, but it still consumes energy. Besides that minor problem, Playtonic has recreated an era of gaming in our modern times and I HIGHLY recommend this if you are yearning for a "Banjo Threeie".

I've been looking forward to this game for years and tried my hardest to find something I enjoyed about it, but even if this game had been released on the Nintendo 64 it wouldn't be recommended playing.

Although I cannot recommend this game in its current state, the devs have stated that they will release a "Gold" edition, that is what this game should have been. If you are a fan of oldschool RPGs with lots of flavor text, skills, quests, items, spells, and plot buy that when it comes out.
As it is though, it was released a few months ago as completed when it actually appeared to be an early access alpha, couldnt even be called beta.
I bought it on release, and it was so buggy I literally couldnt get past the character creation screen, or even into it for that matter. Had the devs released it as early access they would have had a horde of loyal followers. But what they released as a complete game looked worse than some small game-builds Ive seen people make for quarter-long class projects. This, obviously, torked off a lot of people, myself included.
The translation leaves a bit to be desired as well. For instance when you light a torch/lantern, the game asks you "What do you want to inflame?" For those of you that are not native English speakers, inflame has two meanings, neither of which has to do with lighting an actual fire. The most common use means "To cause strong emotions in, esp anger or lust." The other means "an infected or red and swollen wound/part of the body injured due to sickness or damage.". Needless to say the sentence cracks me up every time I try to set something on fire. As in "What would you like to make really lustful?" or "What wounds would you like to infect?"
So why am I recommending it? In short, when it works right, its *awesome*.
That and the head dev is very active on the forums, has apologized for the game repeatedly, and has made great strides in making it functional. You can play it now. There are still bugs, but they are relatively minor although annoying.
It has ok graphics, that are slowly getting better, and a decent automap. I tried to play the original from the 90s while waiting for this one to be playable. It didnt have an automap. I dont have the time to map anymore, like I did as a teenager, so thats a great improvement. The music is perfect for the setting, and really puts you in the appropriate mood. Town music is cheerful, and puts you in the mind of wandering through a small green village with exposed-woood and thatch roofs. Dungeon music is nicely dark and spooky, with weird ambient effects. Only really bad thing about non-combat sound is the ♥♥♥♥ing *awful* narrarator. He narrates *everything*. And its *terrible*. Fortunately, it can be turned off. The sound effects in battle are typical grunts, "Oof"s, "EEeee"s, slashes, spell zaps and so on. Nothing special.
The combat is action-point turn based (Fallout 1/2 style), but there is decent room for strategy with the large selection of spells, movement, combat options and so forth.
As far as content, theres a lot. You can camp, hunt, look for herbs, set watches and get attacked. In town you can talk to shopkeepers, drink, gamble, pick pocets (Although you can do nothing with the wandering NPCs - I think they are just there for flavor)Random events and side quests abound, and really make the setting come alive. I cant wait for it to be finished and fullly functional, with all content added (There are still some missing side quests).
So I future-recommend it for any oldschool RPG fan, with the caveat "Even though its not listed as Early Access, it is. Don't get it now, wait for the completed gold edition. If you don't, there will be bugs. *Most*are not game breaking *knocks on wood*, but they are there.
I also have to recommend it just because of how open and honest the devs have been, unlike so many who drop broken as hell games on Steam and then disappear while laughing all the way to the bank.

Arkham Origins isn't a bad game, but I wouldn't recommend that someone who hasn't played it play it. I've played it for about 30 hours and let me tell you it's just not worth it. I was one of the biggest fans of Arkham City, that was "my game". I loved it so much that after playing hundreds of hours on PS3 I bought it on steam and played another 50+ hours. I put a lot of faith in the new developer and they let me down. There are things that I really liked about this game, but the cons far outweigh the pros. For one, the costume designs for batman and the bosses are sick. I could tell that a lot of time was put in to designing the appearences. Batman's suit looks like he put it together himself with all the individual pieces, the straps, and the bulkiness as opposed to Arkham City and Asylum Asylum where the suit looks professionally manufactured with the whole suit being one kind of layered material, strips of it bolted down, and looks really slim. Deathstroke also looks awesome with his professional armor over the  chainmail underarmor. The story is pretty good and I cared about Batman more than I did in Arkham City due to the strong voice acting. The visual style for this game is pretty slick too with it resembling Mass Effect more than photorealism. Thats pretty much where I stop liking this game and start having problems with it. My problem with the story is that it focused way too much on Bane and Joker and not enough on the characters that are new to the series. I love Bane and Joker, but I had seen pretty much all I needed to of them in AC and AA. Previews of the game made it appear that the main villians would be Black Mask and Deathstroke, something that I was looking forward to. In the beginning, Black Mask looked like a bad♥♥♥♥♥and got me really excited for therest of the story. I spoil anything, but Black Mask gets portrayed as a complete ♥♥♥♥♥ after the big plot twist. I was expecting Deathstroke to be a complex character and have a big role in the story and to play as him in the open world like the Catwoman missions in AC. However, the only exposure you get to him is the five minute boss fight and a glimpse of him later in the game. That's it. After all the screenshots and artwork showing Deathstorke released and the build up about him being in AO, I was expecting a little more than that. Not only did that disappoint me, but the playable Deathstroke has almost all the same moves as Robin from AC. That especially♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off because of all the effort Rocksteady made to make their playable characters have unique fighting styles. Lastly is the combat. It is almost identical to AC, except it is more frustrating in a few ways. One way is that on hard, I start to punch an enemy, then another enemy begins to punch me, and the enemy that was beginning his punch will finish his before I finish mine. Another way is the addition of the new enemies. WB didnt inherit this code from Rocksteady and had to create it themselves. This where the combat can get a bit buggy. Theres a lot of confusing moments with the new enemies because sometimes their moves will work and not work when I evade/counter/stun. Rocksteady's combat was so well polished and WB didn't take the time to make their additions work correctly. I would like enemies like the martial artist more if it wasnt the same 3 counter animations being used everytime and I would have liked it even more if WB hadnt added those same counter animations to the normal enemies. Also, the challenge maps in AC were so distinct with unique environments, colors, and enemy combinations. In AO, I can barely tell any of them apart. With few eaxceptions, they are all white and grey with the same enemy combinations. I was fortunate enough not to encounter any of the game breaking bugs that many others have experienced. I would say something about the multiplayer but I have yet been able to access it. Thats pretty much how I feel about this game. I think it was a poor decision for WB to make another Arkham game just to release one before Rocksteady is finished with next game. I suggest that anyone who hasn't played this game wait until Rocksteady releases their next Arkham game.

Online DRM is an issue if you have unstable internet. This does not apply to me, but it is a cause of concern for others. The reason for online is to prevent piracy, and to provide syncing for challenges, and online scoring. I don't like this decision, but it's by and large better than Ubisoft additionally requiring UPlay.
Otherwise, this is the Hitman every one is used to, lots of freedom, replayability, creative ways in solving a mission. There are settings for Opportunities, hints and markers that pop up as you interact with the game environment. You can set it as default, minimal, or disabled. Minimal only gives you a reminder on the top left on what you might want to do. Default gives you that plus in-game markers.
Performance, stable 60fps on GTX 980, with FXAA and everything else on Ultra.
It's a gamble when you buy an episodic game like this, because you aren't ensured of the quality of subsequent releases. However, from what I've seen of the Paris levels and the intro levels, it's pretty solid. The freeform levels like Paris are huge. The way the development works is that they create a huge setting like Paris, then create missions for it. I guess this allows the development team to focus on polishing one setting and its missions as much as possible, before moving on to the next.
Could they have simply released a $60 game all at once? Yes, but it would be out later this year. Do they get more sales from doing an episodic release? Yes, that seems like the intention of the business model. Every new episode is probably going to spike sales for a short time period.
I'm going to predict that reviews for this game will improve as more content is released. The current offering is essentially an Early Access Game, so view it as such. For an Early Access Game, it's very polished. If people are spending 40+ hours on a single level, that says a lot about the game's content and replayability.
Edit 3-20: It took me 16 hours to exhaust the game of the premade content. I finished all the challenges for the yacht mission, the final test, and paris. The remaining things to do are online contracts and escalation mission.
During that time, I didn't encounter a single connection issue, never disconnected no server problems. Take that as you will, you can expect the $15 intro pack to contain 16 hours of gameplay.

I played Elite on the BBC B computer and all its subsequent upgrades. Long-time player of Eve Online, Freelancer, I War, X Wing and blah blah. Lots of them.
Happy to give credit to the developers for trying and improving. I will definitely keep an eye on the new game and hope that is more my cup of tea.
The game has a story driven content and a free roaming side. In fact even in the story mode you are quite free to roam around too which is a huge plus. It looks like to me the developers must have tacked the story line late in development as some of the beta testers much have shouted very loud "Ho, hum, what do we do exactly?"
Freelancer was the last great Space game and this is not a bad recreation of that. Just that in every aspect it is worse. It has me trying and failing to fit a DVD drive back into my PC so I could install it again.
The in-flight movement and combat of your ship is pretty good. There are a few modes and modules to use. There is innovation where you can mostly destroy an opponent and then send some ruffians over to board it. If successful you can tow the ship back to a dock for huge income. Combat is pretty satisfying with options to fire yourself or computer controlled auto-fire. All thumbs up. I am told that as you upgrade your ship the movement in flight will also change. So big cargo ships move slower than smaller fast ships.
Your pilot can improve his skills as you level up. This is also innovation for this type of game. To my rookie eye though these skills seem to be mostly +5% this and that.
Your on-board computer scans the local area and identifies bounty opportunities and exploration is positively encouraged. The computer even remembers prices of commodities in every place you have docked which makes it very easy to trade away at the beginning. Whether you can do that as a main way of attaining riches I can't say. The prices of ships are very high.
The universe itself feels slightly alive as you can pass fellow ships in your travels and scan and attack them for piracy fun. Planets and space stations have some small radio chatter that comes across.
So why the thumbs down?
Freelancer remains better and that was released years ago. It had better story line, graphics, ships, reputation system. Well, almost everything. I have hope though and if I ever play this one more will update this review.

I like this game, I do, but 35$ I feel is too steep for what it offers. At first I thought this game was like Mount and Blade in space, with so many factions, different types of outposts, and skills oriented to being a leader. That however is not the case, the game is more or less a dungeon crawler RPG without the dungeons.
The story is fairly bland, and frankly the voice acting of the main character is so outright awful I had to turn off dialogue volume, and I just quickly got bored with the story missions.
Theres no real "looting" and going out of your way to be a merchant king through cargo hauling is a waste of time, the early portion of the game is farming money to get better ships, once you have better ships you just capture enemy ships for quick cash and farm levels. Looting ships for weapons is a waste of time, as all stations are static and theres no random element to their inventories, simply fly to the station selling the best weapon of your chosen class, and buy it, everything quickly becomes a monotony of going from X to Y and repeating.
The biggest issue I have with the game is saving, the save system is abysmal. You can only save while anchored at a planet or base, if you arrive at a friendly base and find it swarming with enemies (in some sectors this happens constantly) you can find yourself trapped in a prolonged battle, or killed, when all you wanted to do was save the game and go have dinner.
You cant side with factions, or take over stations, or influence anything, so dont expect any depth with the politics of the world, you are either "good" or "bad" and that determines who is friendly, nuetral, or hostile. Good being the vast majority of the galaxy. So the dozens of factions in the game, may as well be two factions.
"Commanding a fleet" isnt as exciting as I hoped either, its not so much a fleet, as you having two hirelings, hence part of my comparison to the game as a dungeon crawler.
There is plenty of good though, the actual gameplay is fun, you are more captain than pilot, you configure power usage, set speed, battles arent about quick manuevering so much as overwhelming firepower and good positioning. In a star wars example, you are piloting a Star Destroyer, rather than a Tie Fighter. (fighter squadrons are in fact a system on later ships) Just be sure to go over the controls, I spent far too long without realizing you could activate automated fire.
Bounties are probably my favorite aspect, unlike most games, bounty targets arent static, you start the game with a full list of bounties, and they move around the galaxy on their own, when you choose to hunt them you have to go by "last spotted" information and attempt to cut them off. These are also the most challenging fights available, and shouldnt be taken lightly.
After a while though I begin questioning my goal, Its not difficult to get better equipment, at least not after a certain point, and the only thing you have to upgrade is your ship. A uninteresting campaign that I cant be bothered to finish? The bounty targets to award money I dont really need? Side missions that are much the same as the main missions?
This game could be improved by aspects of strategy (something I think Warlords addresses, though the game is very very early access so I dare not bother with it yet.) and aspects of procedural generation. Non static stores, to put more of a emphasis on looting (Perhaps ships produced by that faction are much, much more expensive, but always available and the randomly generated ships are cheaper, like buying a new car vs. used car.) and procedurally generated weapons Diablo style. A star system you can purchase as a home base, to build your own colonies, defenses, shipyards to give you more to do than just upgrade your ship.
The game has so, so, so much potential, and the team that worked on it seem dedicated and helpful to their community, the framework is here for a game unlike any other, and I am excited by where the team goes with warlords once its finished. If you can nab this for $20 or less, do it. But in the end, whats that phrase? A mile wide, a inch deep.

I have seen a lot of people talk trash about Arkham Origins, and I really don't understand it.
I have played all 3 Arkham games, and enjoyed them all immensely. The story, combat and free-roaming aspects of this game were really good and it didn't do anything wrong that the previous two did right in my opinion. I get that some people just decide to hate the game from the start because it has a different developer, but I think they did everything right in this title. It still feels like a true Arkham game, and as we know Arkham games are awesome.

Similar Games:
The previous Arkham games, Assassin’s Creed games, and every game which has
attempted to rip either of those two series off.
The Good:
Fantastic setting for a Batman game. Gotham City on Christmas Eve just screams “Batman Returns” and is iconic in its own right.
The character design and graphics are top notch, from the major (and minor) villains to the skyscrapers of Gotham.
Character animations are fluid and natural, especially in cutscenes. Copperhead, one of the eight assassins gunning for Batman, is the real standout in this aspect.
The gameplay is a rehash of the previous Arkham games, with the now standard attack/counter/stun/gadget methodology in place. The combat has always been a strength of the series, and Arkham Origins is no different, except to make Batman’s combat seem less refined and more brutal. That they managed to convey Batman’s inexperience to crime fighting through his fighting technique alone is fantastic.
Detective mode is now more involved, requires more evidence gathering, and *GASP* actually involves Batman having Alfred send the evidence to the GCPD for prosecution! It’s almost like the real world! #SARCASM
The plot twist, while obvious to anyone who was vaguely familiar with a Batman plot past his Detective Comics days, was a welcome change of pace.
The voice acting, despite having changed actors from the previous Arkham games, was still solid and believable.
The “Red Hood” section. I won’t spoil it more than that, but as a fan of the comic series, this made me very happy.
The Bad:
This game was shipped by WB Montreal one week prior to Assassin’s Creed IV: Black Flag. What this means in layman’s terms was that WB Montreal had NO wiggle room in their release date, since Assassin’s Creed (also being a stealth action/combat game with an enhanced vision mode) would almost certainly have cannibalized their sales. In business terms, they had to ship before Assassin’s Creed no matter what state the game was in – AND IT SHOWS. A number of game breaking bugs were present in both the single player and multiplayer portions of the game, including:
NOTE: MINOR SPOILERS BELOW
Multiple instances where ledges that appeared to be climbable were not. One instance occurred in Burnley Tower, after the Riddler closes off the only other exit, leaving your trapped inside the Tower FOREVER… or until you fast-travel out or reset the game. If you have time and appreciate nerd rage, just Google “Burnley Tower”.
An instance where pulling a raft in a dream-like sequence lead to being unable to drop the rope or reach the other shore. Infinite falling in certain places in the map, which really broke the immersion of the game somehow. If Batman ever runs into an enemy which can actually do this, he’s screwed.
No level or stat saving in multiplayer, which is a non-starter for obvious reasons.
Funky physics. More than once, I threw a baddie against a wall at just the right angle to make him go spirally hundreds of feet into the air. But even worse, once he landed, he got back up! Which is JUST impossible.
Occasionally, you are detected by criminals from whom you have both cover and distance. Conversely, you can fly just overhead of others and go completely unnoticed.
Batman sometimes drops combos for no reason, particularly during counters.
There was a lack of emphasis on stealth for most of the game, and often going into stealth areas, Batman enters the room through the front door. Perhaps the enemies were expecting the vents, so the door was the most stealthy option?
MINOR SPOILERS: In what is probably the worst tragedy of storytelling in this series, Barbara Gordon is portrayed as an enthusiastic teenager who somehow is allowed to access confidential police files and evidence because her daddy works for the police. Brushing aside the lack of realism there, Barbara Gordan, who became Batgirl and then, after the Joker shot her in the spine, assumed the role of Oracle, was NOT the airhead from this game. I almost stopped playing for this reason alone.
The method of unlocking certain gadgets and techniques is dependent on performing certain feats. Normally that is fine, except that these feats are very specific and must be performed in the exact order that the skill tree describes. And some of these feats are nightmarishly impossible and require specific areas and circumstances to complete… just leave it at XP, WB Montreal. Come on.
The Grapnel Accelerator, described as “experimental” in Arkham City, is mysteriously present years before in Arkham Origins. I understand why they decided to include it, but it represents an obvious break in the timeline of the games.
The multiplayer… oh the multiplayer. It requires eight people to play, real people. NOT BOTS. NO BOTS. Good luck finding eight people on the servers a month from now. Make some friends on Steam, get a group together, and it might be feasible. Otherwise, it’s a waste of install space. Also, the shooting is really hit-and-miss, but that makes sense in an engine designed for hand-to-hand combat.
Can you play it while the children are awake?:
Of course not. Corpses with rictus smiles, tons of on-screen violence, multiple murder
scene investigations, psychopathic villains… I could go on. Then again, if you are looking
for a creative way to punish them…
While I’m picking nits…
Rocksteady better be working on something damned important… like freelance work on
Half-Life 3, or (dare I wish it?) a good Superman game. I know that sounds impossible,
but before Arkham Asylum, there wasn’t a good Batman game, either. I would only
recommend this game if you haven’t played Arkham Asylum or Arkham City, and thus
can’t compare the quality. Or if you have enemies, you could recommend this game on
its multiplayer strengths.
Did I make time to complete it?:
I put 26 hours into it, primarily into the single player. I know that’s incongruous with
my criticisms above, but I was a big fan on the franchise going into Arkham Origins.
This also represents the smallest amount of time I have put into an Arkham game, and
none of the others had multiplayer. I should also mention that a number of the bugs
mentioned above have been fixed… but not all.
Recommended Purchase Price:
$19.99 (so, maybe Steam Summer Sale 2014?)
or
40% of current retail value of $49.99

The game achieves perfection in its genre.

There are two reasons I love this game. First I'll talk about the base game itself.
The base game is very intriguing, with great saber combat, accompanied by optional,  yet good, blaster combat in either 1st or 3rd person. There are multiple upgradable force powers that are actually very useful and fun to use. The story is great, following Episode 6 of Star Wars. There are even a couple of moral choices you get to make. Overall the base game is great, and is well worth the 10 bucks.
But now for the real reason I've racked up over 100 hours. (more technically)
Moviebattles 2...
What is moviebattles, you may ask? Well I'll be happy to answer that question for you. Moviebattles is a mod for Jedi Academy, that completely overhault the entire multiplayer experience. It makes lightsaber combat incredibly realistic, and makes blasters an actually pheasable weapon in multiplayer. Moviebattles has a few different modes. I'll talk about 3 of them to keep this short. The first is the most popular... Open. Open is a two team class battle. There are 6 or so classes for the republic/rebellion, and for the empire/cis. Things like Jedi, Sith, Wookies, Mandalorians, Bounty Hunters, etc. The list goes on. It's an elimination/objective game mode. The two teams fight it out until one team has no players left alive, or the attacking team successfully achieves the objective/the defending team successfully defends the objective.
The second game mode, is called Duel. It's by far my favorite. The teams in this don't matter. It's a free-for-all match in which Jedi and Sith alike use only their saber skills, and force powers to defeat each other. You can respawn in this gamemode. The only thing about it, is that it's a "Duel". Not a "massacre". Meaning you can't go around fighting people while they're fighting other people.
Overall, this mod has completely rebuilt Jedi Academy, in a way I've really enjoyed. I have at least 300 hours in this game. (seeing as they changed to their own launcher during one update, so I stopped using steam to launch the game)
Jedi Academy: 9/10
Moviebattles 2: 11/10
Both highly recommended.

HITMAN™
Episodic Action Stealth
IO Interactive
Square Enix
is an episodic action stealth game developed by IO Interactive and published by Square Enix. This is the 6th game in the Hitman franchise, and every month a new episode will be released with a different setting and target. This review contains the content of the first episode: "Paris". The game is also always online, but it can also be played offline even though some features are blocked.
Powered by Glacier (the same engine of Absolution), the game does look pretty damn good, with great attention to details in the levels and with improved animations (I especially love shooting and reloading a pistol). However, at launch this game is packed with performance issues, plus some graphical options are greyed out based on your hardware. With everything either off or on Low, I managed to get 30+ FPS inside and 24+ FPS in outside and crowded areas.
You despise the levels of Absolution, but you liked the improved controls? You loved the level of detail in Blood Money and Contracts? Then this game is just for you: gone are the Point Shooting, the dumb linear levels and the unrealistic "lower-hat-to-hide-your-identity" system.
This Hitman is closer to a 007 game: the Paris level has you infiltrate a fashion show where a secret evil auction is taking place. Around the map you can eavesdrop some conversations that will activate Opportunities, which help you achieve the slickest and most badass assassinations. For example, you can disguise as a Sheik to go to a private meeting where you can garrote your target, or dress as staff of the palace to poison your target and drown him in the toiler when he is vomiting, and so on.
You can also preplan which weapons to bring in your mission, which suit to wear, and even in which area of the map to start in (in the attic, undercover in the kitchen, in the garden...). Plus, you also get XP whenever you complete certain assassinations, feats or discoveries, increasing your Mastery of the level, and as a reward you unlock more preplanning options.
If you are tired of killing the same targets, there are also Elusive Targets (currently unavailable) and Escalation Mode. In Escalation, there are five increasing levels of difficulties, where you have more objectives to complete to finish the level.
While there is no difficulty mode, your regenarating health drains very quickly, which means that you will die pretty easily, so stealth is always the best option. The AI works also very well: there are some people called Threats that will be suspicious of your disguise if you go near them, patrolling guards will take guns that are lying around the map, and if you are found trespassing you will be taken out of the area. However, it still isn't 100% realistic, and after a while it became really easy to screw with them.
Jesper Kyd didn't score the game, but the soundtrack isn't bad but neither memorable. And the sound design and voice acting are top notch as always.
Trying to master the level will keep you engaged for many hours, and Escalation Mode will be updated every week. This will last for at least 15 hours in its current state, similarly to "Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes".
Overall, I am really glad to say that this is a great return to form for Hitman games: a big sandbox to play in, multiple ways to kill your targets, many disguises, and good customization. However, being always online and the locked graphics options will unfortunately turn off a lot of players. I highly recommend buying the Intro Pack, then maybe buy the Upgrade Pack.

As a hardcore fan of both Banjo-Kazooie and Banjo-Tooie, I have been yearning for a good 3D platformer ever since the genre started drying up. So when Playtonic announced and then successfully kickstarted Yooka-Laylee, I was just thrilled. Finally being able to play it feels amazing. The worlds are gigantic and beautiful. The characters are funny and unique, and Grant Kirkhope's musical genius really shines through. However, and it makes me really sad to say this, basic gameplay feels rushed, swimming controls are weird,
and there are far, far too many enemies (in often repeated designs dressed in different colours) to simply enjoy the game, and breathe.
What happened to moments where you could do that, and just observe? Why do some games today always have to be go go go? A moment of quiet here and there is precious. I'm only two worlds in, but these are consistent patterns I've observed so far. Banjo-Kazooie and Tooie were great because of their simplicity, and are in my opinion, masterpieces. Yooka-Laylee, however, tries to bring too many ideas on board at once, and the result is messy. Unlike many reviews online, I found no real problems with the camera, or puzzle design. My concerns lie instead in the confusing level design, which is not confusing because of the absence of a mini-map, but rather, because nothing really stands out enough to be memorable, the loading screens break immersion each time you enter a new world, and lastly, the choice to host a quiz so early without any real purpose just seems bizarre. BK was great because every note, every jiggy, every character was meaningful, things were spaced out and produced at just the right time, players weren't spoonfed information, NPCs wouldn't repeat themselves if you'd already encountered them once, and all that combined drew people in. That's what YL is missing.
TL;DR: Yooka-Laylee has stunning art and music, but is let down by mediocre gameplay and confusing level design.

I first played Prison Architect during one of its earliest alpha stages. The game was buggy, limited and filled with core problems but the base idea was still really interesting and I saw a lot of potential. Over the years the game has been polished little by little and I'd say, at this point, the game feels incredibly solid. It's refreshing to see indie developers who legitimately care about making a good game and aren't just focused on appealing to a huge audience and making money.
You play as a warden, build a prison from the ground up, and get regular paychecks to keep inmates locked away. You need to make sure the prisoners have basic needs met like food and entertainment, otherwise they'll get rowdy and start trouble (like murdering each other, or breaking things). The concept is very straight-forward. As someone who enjoys games like Sim City and Dwarf Fortress (as well as prison movies) this was very up my alley.
You can min-max the perfect prison, or you can just have fun with it and design a chaotic madhouse that's destined to fail. My favorite prison design, my own invention of course, is to have every single part of the prison connect to one center room. That center room is the "warden's office + shower" combo. Watch as the warden lives a constant life of fear while the 50+ maximum security prisoners cram their way into the showers meant for no more than 10 people at a time. The warden is sitting there with lamenated paperwork, crying, trying to get something done while all these ruthless thugs wash up. The previous warden is floating, face down in the shower water, right next to the new warden's desk. Yep. Good times.
Rating: A

27-Jul-2016 : Finished main story + extras
Equipment : MSI GT80-2QE Notebook
REVIEW :
First thing first, this is not arcade space sim combat like Elite Dangerous, this is RPG game with space sim combat. You start with a small ship and you can play it like arcade space sim combat since the RPG elements seems irrelevant at the beginning. But as your rank get higher and you get access to bigger ships, you find yourself constantly outnumbered and outgunned. Tactical combat and RPG elements (properly developed character and ship) becomes essential to win a combat.
The game is open world. To be powerful enough to progress through the main quest, you can do faction side quests, freelance quests, mining. trading, bounty hunting, pirating and capturing ships. The graphics and soundtrack is great, the story is mediocre with really bad voice acting. This game is not a high budget A-List game, so there's no fancy 3D cutscenes with motion tracking and real voice actors.
The game also really mod-friendly. You can edit stats and even your savegames using a simple text editor. This mod-friendly approach is more handy that it seems. For example, my favorite Carrier-class ship doesn't come with a cloaking device. Easy, edit the ship stats file using Notepad and add the cloaking device myself. There's also Mod Tools to build your own contents. If you're a Trekkie, make sure you try the Star Trek Ship Mods in the Steam Workshop.
The developer also generous enough to give a free DLC titled "Origins". This free DLC offers 30 storyline missions of the original Starpoint Gemini, re-envisioned and ported to SPG2 engine. So if you never play the 1st one, you can play it now without extra cost. Basically you get 2 games for the price of one.
CONCLUSION :
Recommended on full price, a must-have on sale price.

This is a re-review implementing suggestions in comments:
It's needlessly complicated, the z-axis doesn't add to the game compared to the original, and it generally isn't fun.
Let me elaborate:
-Although the single continuous world is an improvement, getting around said world is tedius and time consuming unless you happen to be near one of the shortcuts and that shortcut happens to end up where you need to be.
-The combat is underwhelming. Basically, you tell the ship it can fire, it fires, you get shot at which is absorbed by shields, who wins is basically which of the parties has better shields and guns. Really the only thing you change is your facing so different shields absorb their attacks. Doesn't sound exciting, does it?
-The user interface is complicated and it really has no reason to be. I came back to play Titans and I was constantly pushing the wrong buttons. The controls are not intuitive.
-The story (including the DLCs) is uninspired, boring, completely forgettable, short, and ends before it feels like it should.
There's only two things I enjoyed in this game:
1) Exploring the galaxy.
2) The SG1 campaign imported into SG2. This fixed a lot of the gripes I had about the original (especially having to grind to proceed) which is why I liked it.
These things don't offset all of the other problems with the game though so still not recommended.
As for why there are so many hours registered, it's most likely a product of running in the taskbar.  I repeatedly got bored of the game, alt+tabbed out, browsed the internet, and resumed later.  It does not reflect what it actuallly took to finish the game (as is the case with a lot of games).

text:
This game takes place in an alternate universe of Mad Max where the events of the movie Fury Road never took place. This is made obvious by several facts, like for example that you have your precious interceptor car with you, which was otherwise stolen by the war boys in Fury Road and destroyed during the final battle and also through dialogue and an easteregg you find later in the game

The game's designers have really tried their best to replicate the looks and feels of the 2015 summer blockbuster in game form, and their efforts really show, wonderfully optimized (seriously, if an apocalypse like this one ever does occur i'm sure you can build a rig out of scraps that's capable of running this on full graphics settings.
The game offers you the chance to build your own car, build it for speed, or build it for durability, or go full out and make it a death machine with spikes and armor that'd take a tank shell (Only, not at all)
The car combat is really great, ram, shoot, and tear your way through convoys and war parties.
Lots of exciting locations to search through (Just wish they would maybe write some lore about some of these locations, that'd be awesome).
I did feel there were some things that this game could have done differently to make it more enjoyable, mainly:
⚫Make food and water a neccessity to eat and drink to survive, and not just to regain health in combat.
⚫Have Chumbucket avalible on all the collectible cars
There's a large variety of wasteland cars in this game, but the problem with them is that only the Magnum opus has Chumbucket at hand, so if your car gets damaged (which it most certainly will) you will need to use scraps to repair it, and those repairs are expensive, especially when you are collecting to buy new tires, engines, armor and all that. Plus, you won't have Chumbucket's harpoon gun and explosive sticks, meaning you're left with only your shotgun and ramming
⚫The game is really good when you're out on the road, but you can certainly see the parts of the game that weren't given the same amount of love and detail, some of my bigger issues were:
-NPCs in strongholds are like 3 voice actors in total, and they sadly do an aweful job delivering their lines.
-When a stronghold is improved it really just hangs up a bunch of banners and cloth, there's not really much change besides that.
-The game doesn't go hard enough on you.

Mad Max has been the most worthwhile game on Steam I have purchased yet! The graphics are great, the game is fun, and the amount of content is amazing! I have been playing Mad Max for 64 actual hours now and I am only getting close to halfway finished with the game. If I feel the need to clear everything and get all the acheivements, I bet there is close to another month of gameplay left.
Some stuff is a bit repetative but what game doesn't have some repetativeness? After all the hours I have spent in the game, fighting mobs and driving around wrecking other vehicles is still fun. The difference between this game and many others is the amount of detail, time, and work the developers took to get this game in the great shape it is in. I've never had any game crashes (plenty of car crashes though) and my character or car haven't gotten stuck anywhere even once yet. The game runs brilliantly.
Every new area I go to, I feel I have to complete 100%. The leveling up of the car is really cool and there are a ton of different vehicles, cities, and mobs in this game. Also, leveling up your character is fun. There are a bunch of different bases that you can level up as well.  The boss fights could be a bit tougher and have a bit more complexity to defeating them but it's not really detrimental.
Chumbucket is your sidekick and he is an absolute blast to drive around with. Some of the things he says are hilarious and you know how in most games, after an hour you've already heard everything they have to say and wish you could just turn off their voice? Not Chumbucket! He says so many different things, I have rarely heard the same thing twice in all my hours of gameplay and continue to be surprised by him saying something new and still laugh out loud!
I can't really think of any way I could be any happier with this game other than if they happened to add more content in the future.
Mad Max gets a huge thumps up and is well worth the full price ($29.99 USD). If you can get it on sale, even better but I didn't wait and am not upset one bit.

If you've been a fan of the Batman games that Rocksteady have put out over the past few years, then you are going to find a very comfortable home with a lot of the same here.  Too much of the same in a lot of cases.  Did you like that quest where Bane sent you to blow up 6 containers?  GOOD NEWS!  We have 3 of those now!  Did you like unlocking things with your bat-digital-unlocker thing?  GOOD NEWS!  We make you pull that thing out every 100 feet.
The story feels lost.  It's broken up into how you attack each boss.  However none of the storylines really go anywhere, and are not long enough to get into a character and their modivations beyond "Somebody promised me money to kill the bat."  Batman clearly has a history with a lot of the people he encounters.  He calles deathstroke by his name, but no attempt is made to explain how they know each other.  However, Joker's storyline may be the best of the series, and it is easily the best part about this game.
And yes, that includes the combat.  The wonderful combat that has been so balanced, and for how simple it was, took so much time to master.  The flow of combat comes back.  And is wonderful, and feels great....... Right up until you get the "Shock Gloves" which then allows you to plow though every type of baddy that isn't tripple your size.  Which ruins the flow of combat by turning it into a game of whack a mole.
If you were a fan of the games, then get this.  Odds are you all ready have.  If you are new to the series, then I would strongly suggest getting the previous games first.  You'll have a better experience over all.

Buy? Likely.
Is BAO more worthy of a 7.0 than a higher score as IGN review. In my honest opinion, yes. Sure, that score comes from the same people who were happy to rate arguably the most iterative popular game series, Call of Duty, with scores of 9 or higher, which doesn't make sense when their biggest argument for the score is the lack on innovation....By that standard, BAO would get a 10/10.
My score boils down to the fact that while there is still the solid, Batman Arkham series base mechanics and design, there are many minor or moderate imperfections compared to previous games.
Number one issue is the bugginess, with the infamous Lacey Tower Glitch (now fixed), interrogation glitches, geometry collisions glitches and to me, the loss of combos or the missing of attacks more than I should have compared to previous games (this could be an issue with my controller or just me).
Number two, the total lack of detail and flair compared to the previous games - there is less color variety (mostly greys, blacks, greens, and occasional blues), practically no environmental easter eggs and references (though, you can argue the fact that the villains don't have the ability to uniquly mark their territory like Arkham City because civilians and cops are still present), no interesting items to scan (except for Anarky tags), less entertaining Riddler/Enigma quest (The interesting Riddler trophies are now just boring Grey and bright green datapacks, that some how James Gordon didn't notice on his back wall with a BLARING GREEN LIGHT. The puzzles are immensely easier than BAC and argueably kind of stupid, and makes you wonder how Enigma thought Batman couldn't get them. Admittedly, Engima is perhaps less experienced/adept and hasn't became "The Riddler" yet).
Number Three, a near complete lack of innovation and recycling of assets that makes BAO feels like a glorified DLC for Arkahm City. While it it great to see what "Arkham City" was before it was Arkham City, the vast majority of the city is a damn near copy and past of AC, but without all the interesting signs, graffiti, displays, and destruction. There are still a few neon signs and normal billboards, but the city feels ironically less alive despite the fact that cops and civilians are still present (in which you never see any hint that civilians are still in the city except for murder cases, abandoned cars, and occasional hobos). The combat is mostly the same with a couple of new gadgets: A concussion sticky grenade that stuns small groups of enemies and shock gauntlets that makes Batman overpowered. Thankfully, the camera angles are improved when you make the last hit of a fight, however, it seemed I would miss attacks or loose combos unnecessarily and the combat feels even more reliant on countering relentlessly attacking goons. Thanks to a combat bug, many times I would finish a fight with a group while one thug was still in a fight stance, but not attacking. The game would recognize the fight as complete and give you XP, but you woulld have to punch or batarang the enemy (which sometimes misses at POINT BLANK). I even had another bug where a thug got stuck in a car and I had to use explosive gel to get him out.
The mutliple problems with the game left me feel like I should breeze through the story as fast as I can to get it over with. However, the story is definitely the strongest point of this game. You get to see the character dynamics between Batman, his Bruce Wayne identity (which honestly, may have been better if explored just a little bit more), and characters such as Alfred, the Gordons, and Joker. The more cunning, Less dumb Bane of the earlier games (Which is explained in the story) and the discovery of the Joker kept me interested despite me essentially knowing what was going to happen since this is an Origin story. The problem with the origin story is though, you don't get alot of information of the pure origins of Wayne becoming Batman (the suit and gear, the first outings of The Bat, his training and pre-Batman Life) and publisher/dev made the decision to put this content in upcoming DLC, because they can and want to make money. As for the predator (stealth segments), they work exactly the same, which is fine with me, but you will be stuck in Detective mode 95% time and sometimes you wonder how goons miss Batman grapneling or sneaking right in front of them.
I have yet to mess with the multiplayer. The idea stems from a little assemetry thanks to two groups of thugs shooting each other (with apparently terrible gun mechanics from what I read) while dealing with the threats of Batman and Robin and the mission to "summon" the playable bosses Bane and the Joker.
In the end, despite my criticisms, it's still a mostly solid Batman game that fits within the Akrham series and if you're a big fan of, is still worth playing. The base mechanics of combat, gliding, stealth and exploration are still here in full force - it ticks all the marks of a Batman Arkham series game, but just does that and nothing else - which makes the game uninnovative (comapred from the shift from Asylum to City) and the city is nearly so dull and drab that it made me want to rush the game. The huge fan that I was, ordered the collectors PS3 edition and thIs PC version to download/install overnight since I couldn't pick up my PS3 version on midnight and had to wait until the next store opening - I now regret that because I've spent too much money on this. If you were waiting anxiously for the next Arkham game, then definitely get it, but if you're like Many Steam gamers with massive backlogs and can wait, then look out for a 25-50% off sale or better.

This game is an over-the-shoulder 3rd person military cover shooter game which focuses on the character you play as and his two comrades journey into an almost post-apocalyptic Dubai (terrible weather conditions have left half of the city buried in sand). The three of you are sent to recover information about the Damned 33rd squadron and locate them.
Spec Ops: The Line is my favourite military shooter game because of a few reasons:
- its linear like most others but provides you with choices along the way that shape the way your character and the two soldiers that accompany you think.
- instead of focusing on blowing up terrorists and being a "hero", the game focuses on the true horrors of war and the effect of PTSD on soldiers.
This game is definitely worth picking up whenever you can, it usually goes on sale real cheap (Around £4.99) at which point it becomes a MUST buy for anyone wanting some fun combat and a compelling story.

All things said, I recommend the game. Just keep track of how much time has passed. It is a major time sink.

Rust isn't for everyone. And as I'm stepping out from this being my primary focus game I can say it was worth the money, but wont be a "home" for the majority of players.
It's interesting. It can be very fun, but with lots of lull in between - but this only adds to the axiety and rush of action.
The biggest problem is that Rust doesn't know exactly what it wants to be. It's really not a building game. It's a horrible First Person Shooter. The reason it works for PVP is because if you do kill someone with gear it can catapult you into end game but easy come, easy go.
This environment creates a very toxic, antisocial game environment. In some level, it can be fun to know that everyone will kill you - it means you can just start fighting. But honestly, it becomes very lonely - and with loneliness comes bordom, which breeds some very bad habits. Sitting in towers sniping is rampant. Griefers and door campers abound. And there are some legitimate reasons for these tactics, but when you're new and on the recieving end it sure sucks.
The game is mostly populated by 10 year olds who fantasize about being their Youtube idols. The streamers for this game are skilless sociopaths who thrive on doing 2 weeks of footage to show the one time when their anti-social tactics pay off and they get 2 50-meter headshots with a bow and arrow. Then half the population emulates this thinking it always works. You end up with a lot of morons doing moronic things and a population greater than 50% not knowing how to do the most basic survival things, ignoring more than half of what the game offers.
But at the same time, this ridiculous bloodlust is the only thing keeping the game going. Building is relatively uninteresting. Farming sucks. Exploration is a 5-6 hour process and then you've seen everything. The morons who think that 3 stacks of cooked sulfur is the 'jackpot' are the ones that keep the game going.
Rust is toxic. Toxicity is Rust. They can no longer be seperated. So if you understand that and still want to dip your feet I highly recommend this game because it does what it does very well.
