The apeal of this game is very specific.  If you are looking for a thrilling story filled action packed game, this is NOT it!  If you are looking for an open sandbox to just play in space, this is a great game.  You can mine asteroids, take down pirates, explore space anomalies, and overall just roam the galaxy.  There is a story option, I have not tried it, I wanted the sandbox.  Controls are explained, there is no tutorial, you're just dropped in space and free to go and figure things out.  Finding an asteroid belt of rare minerals sound fun?  This is your game.  Sound dull?  Move along.

Up front:  Not deep enough or fun enough to warrant a $35 entry fee.  Definitely worth it for $10.
Pros:
+Artwork.  Ships and backdrops are pleasant enough to look at and cruising through space in your ride of choice is nice.
+Simple, easy to use interface and controls.  Love the interface.
+Straightforward missions
+Stable and nicely refined.  Have yet to run in to a "broken quest" or a significant bug of any kind.
+Decent enough sized sandbox system to play in.  It takes 15 minutes to fly across Gemini even with the fastest ship.
+Game adjusts difficulty rather well as you progress to bigger ships.
+Soundtrack is a definite plus that matches the mood of the task at hand.
+Lots of factions.  No, they don't really fight all that differently but...they are labeled differently.
+Faction loyalty.  It is simple to see who you are friends with and who you should avoid.  System is easy and intuitive.
+Decent variety of ships, loots and weapons keeps things interesting.
+Fighters and bombers can be launched from you ship.
+Perk system.  As you gain rank you can shape your fighting style and abilities.  Easy and effective without being OP.
+Steam workshop enabled.  I find looking at the hind end of an Intrepid Class is nicer than the stock ships.
Cons:
-Game progression can be very grindy at times.
-Uncompelling campaign became unbearable because of horrid voice acting.  I began playing free-roam instead.
-Ships all fly and feel the same.  A battleship handles just as well as a frigate, it just has more weapons, shields etc. :(
-Unable to target specific enemy ship systems.
-Sensor range is pitifully low.  You'll always see things before your sensors do.
-Combat feels shallow a good portion of the time.  Tactics rarely decide outcome, usually ship stats are it.
-Combat AI is downright stupid at times. As a level 18 I destroyed a level 70 pirate because they kept chasing me.  My one pea-shooter gun could hit them from 800 out, their guns could only reach 550.  As they chased me I eventually wore down their forward shield and nearly destroyed them before they turned and ran.  At that point I ran them down, overtook and finished by shooting through their non-existent forward shield.
-Controls are simple, but can be awkward at times.  No target padlock option. (Really?)
-3rd person views only.  You will never be "in your ship"and that hurts immersion.
-No sense of running a crew.  Your "crewmen" are cards with stats that don't progress.
-Game does not track ships destroyed, troops lost, total money accrued etc.  Nice touches that are easy to make.
-Small variety in mission types.  Scan something, shoot something, ferry something.  That's pretty much it.
-No ability to build up a true fleet, can just hire a couple mercs.
-No feel of actually influencing events in the game world.
-When you dock at a station or planet, all interactions are handled through a simple splash screen.
Summary:
Starpoint Gemini 2 is a nice little space romp for casual/arcade crowds.  I would personally prefer options available to transform this basic game experience into something a little more hardcore.  Replayability is hurt by lack of simulation options, inability to shape conflict and shallow combat mechanics.  Less than 20 hours in I have a dreadnought class warship, have maxed out alliances with half the factions and explored roughly 60% of the systems in the game.  I do not feel as though I will make any substantial new discoveries at this point, just find combinations of things already previously seen.  The game has begun to feel like a "digital fishbowl" but may come back if I find myself in the mood for mindless point and click with a spaceship involved.  Score: 7.5

I've been playing this game about a week, and got up to level 10.
It's not a bad little game, but don't expect too much, and don't pay more than $10 for it. The learning curve isn't too bad, but the controls aren't intuitive, so expect to stare at the screen dumbfounded a few times at the start.
The tutorial is not much. It's all reading with no in-game walkthrough. On the other hand, after only a few tries you should have the contols down pat.
The storyline is so Byzantine that you could never keep up with it, and their are no cut scenes, just cardboard cutouts in the top left of your screen trying to keep you abreast of the storyline. It's almost as if they made the game first, and then inserted a story. Also the voice acting is subpar, but to tell you the truth, there are very few games where I cared about the story (Homeworld, Starcraft, and that's about it).
The visuals are actually superb. Just flying through space and looking at the colorful planets and nebula is fun in itself. The combat is good, though there really is no dogfighting. If you are in combat and you have any kind of acceleration, you'll be miles away after only a few shots, and then you have to turn around and go back. Basically it's like the British and French during the Napolianic wars. You just stand there and hammer away at each other until one of you is dead.
Upgrading ships is practically unkown in the beginning of the game. When the next ship costs 10 million and you only have 250,000 and the missions give you a paltry 10,000, you aren't upgrading fast.
That too goes for the ship modules. Upgrading weapons, shields, propulsion, and the like is the same as upgrading ships; expensive.
The thing that I don't understand is that Freelancer was put out in 2003, and yet this game isn't a quantum leap in game play. In fact it's actually a step backward. It's like we didn't have 13 years of game development.
But, like I said, it's not a bad game, just don't expect too much and don't spend too much money on it.

I like this sandbox styled Hitman. I have a GTX760 and can play 50fps+ with console settings.

HITMAN™
Episodic Action Stealth
IO Interactive
Square Enix
is an episodic action stealth game developed by IO Interactive and published by Square Enix. This is the 6th game in the Hitman franchise, and every month a new episode will be released with a different setting and target. This review contains the content of the first episode: "Paris". The game is also always online, but it can also be played offline even though some features are blocked.
Powered by Glacier (the same engine of Absolution), the game does look pretty damn good, with great attention to details in the levels and with improved animations (I especially love shooting and reloading a pistol). However, at launch this game is packed with performance issues, plus some graphical options are greyed out based on your hardware. With everything either off or on Low, I managed to get 30+ FPS inside and 24+ FPS in outside and crowded areas.
You despise the levels of Absolution, but you liked the improved controls? You loved the level of detail in Blood Money and Contracts? Then this game is just for you: gone are the Point Shooting, the dumb linear levels and the unrealistic "lower-hat-to-hide-your-identity" system.
This Hitman is closer to a 007 game: the Paris level has you infiltrate a fashion show where a secret evil auction is taking place. Around the map you can eavesdrop some conversations that will activate Opportunities, which help you achieve the slickest and most badass assassinations. For example, you can disguise as a Sheik to go to a private meeting where you can garrote your target, or dress as staff of the palace to poison your target and drown him in the toiler when he is vomiting, and so on.
You can also preplan which weapons to bring in your mission, which suit to wear, and even in which area of the map to start in (in the attic, undercover in the kitchen, in the garden...). Plus, you also get XP whenever you complete certain assassinations, feats or discoveries, increasing your Mastery of the level, and as a reward you unlock more preplanning options.
If you are tired of killing the same targets, there are also Elusive Targets (currently unavailable) and Escalation Mode. In Escalation, there are five increasing levels of difficulties, where you have more objectives to complete to finish the level.
While there is no difficulty mode, your regenarating health drains very quickly, which means that you will die pretty easily, so stealth is always the best option. The AI works also very well: there are some people called Threats that will be suspicious of your disguise if you go near them, patrolling guards will take guns that are lying around the map, and if you are found trespassing you will be taken out of the area. However, it still isn't 100% realistic, and after a while it became really easy to screw with them.
Jesper Kyd didn't score the game, but the soundtrack isn't bad but neither memorable. And the sound design and voice acting are top notch as always.
Trying to master the level will keep you engaged for many hours, and Escalation Mode will be updated every week. This will last for at least 15 hours in its current state, similarly to "Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes".
Overall, I am really glad to say that this is a great return to form for Hitman games: a big sandbox to play in, multiple ways to kill your targets, many disguises, and good customization. However, being always online and the locked graphics options will unfortunately turn off a lot of players. I highly recommend buying the Intro Pack, then maybe buy the Upgrade Pack.

My family's favorite. This is a very meaty lasaga. We prefer it with cottage cheese, but you can easily substitute ricotta.
INGREDIENTS
FOR THE SAUCE:
1 cup extra virgin olive oil
2 medium red onions, finely diced
2 large cloves minced garlic
8 ounces pancetta, diced
Salt and freshly ground black pepper
1 ½ cups good red wine, preferably Italian
2 28-ounce cans Italian plum tomatoes
3 tablespoons tomato paste
¾ pound ground sirloin
¼ cup freshly grated pecorino Romano
2 eggs
10 sprigs fresh parsley, leaves only, washed and dried
2 large whole cloves garlic
½ cup flour
1 pound Italian sausage, a mix of hot and sweet
FOR THE LASAGA:
1 15-ounce container ricotta cheese
2 extra-large eggs
2 cups freshly grated pecorino Romano
½ cup chopped parsley
1 pound mozzarella, grated
16 sheets fresh lasagna noodles, preferably Antica Pasteria
PREPARATION
For the sauce, heat 1/2 cup oil in a large heavy Dutch oven or kettle over low heat. Add the onions, minced garlic and pancetta, and cook, stirring, for 10 minutes, until the onions are wilted. Season liberally with salt and pepper. Raise heat slightly, add the wine and cook until it is mostly reduced, about 20 minutes. Crush the tomatoes into the pan, and add their juice. Add the tomato paste and 2 cups lukewarm water. Simmer for 1 hour.
Combine the sirloin, cheese and eggs in a large bowl. Chop the parsley with the whole garlic until fine, then stir into the beef mixture. Season lavishly with salt and pepper. Using your hands, mix until all the ingredients are well blended. Shape into meatballs and set aside.
Heat the remaining oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Dust the meatballs lightly with flour, shaking off excess, and lay into the hot oil. Brown the meatballs on all sides (do not cook through) and transfer to the sauce.
In a clean skillet, brown the sausages over medium-high heat. Transfer to the sauce. Simmer 1 1/2 hours.
Heat the oven to 350 degrees. In a large bowl, combine the ricotta, eggs, pecorino Romano, parsley and all but 1 cup of the mozzarella. Season well with salt and pepper. Mix thoroughly.
Remove the meatballs and sausage from the sauce, and set aside to cool slightly, then chop coarsely. Spoon a thick layer of sauce into the bottom of a 9-by-12-inch lasagna pan. Cover with a layer of noodles. Spoon more sauce on top, then add a third of the meat and a third of the cheese mixture. Repeat for 2 more layers, using all the meat and cheese. Top with a layer of noodles, and cover with the remaining sauce. Sprinkle reserved mozzarella evenly over the top. Bake 30 minutes. Let stand 10 minutes before serving.

The attack on Pearl Harbor was a surprise military strike by the Imperial Japanese Navy against the United States naval base at Pearl Harbor, in the Territory of Hawaii, on the morning of December 7, 1941. The attack led to the United States' entry into World War II.
Japan intended the attack as a preventive action to keep the U.S. Pacific Fleet from interfering with military actions the Empire of Japan planned in Southeast Asia against overseas territories of the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, and the United States. Over the next seven hours there were coordinated Japanese *attacks on the U.S.-held Philippines, Guam and Wake Island and on the British Empire in Malaya, Singapore, and Hong Kong.
The attack commenced at 7:48 a.m. Hawaiian Time. The base was attacked by 353 Imperial Japanese fighter planes, bombers, and torpedo planes in two waves, launched from six aircraft carriers.15 All eight U.S. Navy battleships were damaged, with four sunk. All but Arizona were later raised, and six were returned to service and went on to fight in the war. The Japanese also sank or damaged three cruisers, three destroyers, an anti-aircraft training ship, and one minelayer. 188 U.S. aircraft were destroyed; 2,403 Americans were killed and 1,178 others were wounded. Important base installations such as the power station, shipyard, maintenance, and fuel and torpedo storage facilities, as well as the submarine piers and headquarters building (also home of the intelligence section) were not attacked. Japanese losses were light: 29 aircraft and five midget submarines lost, and 64 servicemen killed. One Japanese sailor, Kazuo Sakamaki, was captured.
The attack came as a profound shock to the American people and led directly to the American entry into World War II in both the Pacific and European theaters. The following day, December 8, the United States declared war on Japan.  Domestic support for non-interventionism, which had been fading since the Fall of France in 1940, disappeared. Clandestine support of the United Kingdom (e.g., the Neutrality Patrol) was replaced by active alliance. Subsequent operations by the U.S. prompted Germany and Italy to declare war on the U.S. on December 11, which was reciprocated by the U.S. the same day.
From the 1950s, several writers alleged that parties high in the U.S. and British governments knew of the attack in advance and may have let it happen (or even encouraged it) with the aim of bringing the U.S. into war. However, this advance-knowledge conspiracy theory is rejected by mainstream historians.
There were numerous historical precedents for unannounced military action by Japan. However, the lack of any formal warning, particularly while negotiations were still apparently ongoing, led President Franklin D. Roosevelt to proclaim December 7, 1941, "a date which will live in infamy". Because the attack happened without a declaration of war and without explicit warning, the attack on Pearl Harbor was judged by the Tokyo Trials to be a war crime.

Update: this review got popular so I made it a bit more detailed
For some reason dismemberment is copy protected on the steam version and will not work via the in game console, also by default the game doesn't support all resolutions via the in game options.
So to get around this we make a file called autoexec.cfg and put it in the gamedata/base folder. In the file write the following, (the autoexec file is read from bottom to top for some reason).
seta r_mode -1
seta r_customaspect 1
seta r_customwidth 1920
seta r_customheight 1080
set g_sabermorerealistic 2
set helpusobi 1
Once that is done you should see it show up like this in the gamedata/base folder
(notice how the Type for the autoexec shows up as CFG file and not a text file, this is also where you dump .pk3 files to get mods to run)
This is my autoexec for reference, it has a few more tweaks and i play at a laptop resolution because im currently on a laptop.
Now you can enjoy maximum dismemberment and the absolute best lightsaber combat in the history of video games at your desired resolution. I would suggest not touching the in game resolution settings while playing, the other options are fine though.

Yooka Laylee is enormous amounts of fun. It's by no means perfect and it is a lot easier to enjoy if you don't go in expecting it to be exactly Banjo Kazooie again. It is a slightly different creature but if you loved those games back in the day, you should love this. It's not without its problems, the Rextor minigames being a bit negative for me. Every minigame in Yooka Laylee is a tedious slog through unfun garabage and the fact you have to play all of the at least twice to get 100% makes it even worse.
That being said, almost every other element comes together really well. The music is fun, the sound effects are good but Yooka's jump sounds can be a bit grading after a while, the characters are all entertaining and memorable and the platforming and combat feel really solid.
Anyone that used to love the platformer, collect-a-thons of old will get a kick out of this, just make sure to look at it as a different game in the same genre rather than a direct followup to Banjo Kazooie and Banjo Tooie.

I'll start with a bit of background about myself as I feel it is relevant due to the nature of this title/genre. I do not have much nostalgia for Banjo Kazooie as I owned a Playstation growing up instead of Nintendo consoles. I am a big fan of other platformers like Crash Bandicoot & Spyro, which I replay almost every year. I did play Banjo & Kazooie/Tooie ~5 years ago and loved it however not as much as Crash Bandicoot or Spyro.
I LOVED Yooka Laylee. While I value the opinions and perspectives that other reviewers have given this game, I cannot say I agree.
- I had only 1 death (Rampo's camera 'shift' is a little too close to the ramp) from the camera and issues with it were barely noticable.
- The size of the levels I felt was managable, the most confusing being the first level after the expansion due to the verticality and increased use of doors on the expansion mountain. Every other level was very understandable and had clear branches which you could write off as 'completed' after you visited them once.
- I had no issues with performance but as I hear those issues were both console exclusive and have been patched.
If you have played through games like Banjo Kazooie/Crash Bandicoot/Spyro recently and enjoyed your time, you will 100% enjoy this game. If it's been 15 years since you played any of these titles, it might be best if you play those first before buying to ensure that the 3D platformer collectathon is still enjoyable to you.
Overall, it took me 21 hours to 100% the game, and I am now playing it again because I loved it so much

Having been a fan of Banjo-Kazooie before, I was most certainly excited for the new duo to come out and show what they've got to keep up with the classics.  And to my delight, it has met those expectations.  The game doesn't take itself too seriously while still offering platforming challenges along the way, and most notably I don't seem to have to fight the camera like I have in other 3D platformers, banjo-kazooie included.  It's obvious a lot of time, effort, and heart went into this game on the whole.
That being said, it's not perfect, and less so if you don't have a controller.  The game is clearly ported to the PC, so it was designed for the hardware of other consoles and then brought to this platform, the evidence being everything showing graphically like you have a controller but textually correct for those who don't.  On that note, if you don't have a controller your experience is not going to be as good.  There is no button mapping, and the escape key seems to be the B key, except when it doesn't want to be, forcing you to return to the hub world if you want out of something you don't want to continue trying.  The second thing is that the game works just fine on multi-monitor setups, except if you have something pop up to interrupt the game.  It returns in a pseudo-window mode that will let your mouse (again, not a problem with a controller) go to your other monitor, allowing you to click off the game.
Those things aside, I have had a blast playing through the game and would recommend the title to anyone who enjoyed its predecessors

Is BAO more worthy of a 7.0 than a higher score as IGN review. In my honest opinion, yes. Sure, that score comes from the same people who were happy to rate arguably the most iterative popular game series, Call of Duty, with scores of 9 or higher, which doesn't make sense when their biggest argument for the score is the lack on innovation....By that standard, BAO would get a 10/10.
My score boils down to the fact that while there is still the solid, Batman Arkham series base mechanics and design, there are many minor or moderate imperfections compared to previous games.
Number one issue is the bugginess, with the infamous Lacey Tower Glitch (now fixed), interrogation glitches, geometry collisions glitches and to me, the loss of combos or the missing of attacks more than I should have compared to previous games (this could be an issue with my controller or just me).
Number two, the total lack of detail and flair compared to the previous games - there is less color variety (mostly greys, blacks, greens, and occasional blues), practically no environmental easter eggs and references (though, you can argue the fact that the villains don't have the ability to uniquly mark their territory like Arkham City because civilians and cops are still present), no interesting items to scan (except for Anarky tags), less entertaining Riddler/Enigma quest (The interesting Riddler trophies are now just boring Grey and bright green datapacks, that some how James Gordon didn't notice on his back wall with a BLARING GREEN LIGHT. The puzzles are immensely easier than BAC and argueably kind of stupid, and makes you wonder how Enigma thought Batman couldn't get them. Admittedly, Engima is perhaps less experienced/adept and hasn't became "The Riddler" yet).
Number Three, a near complete lack of innovation and recycling of assets that makes BAO feels like a glorified DLC for Arkahm City. While it it great to see what "Arkham City" was before it was Arkham City, the vast majority of the city is a damn near copy and past of AC, but without all the interesting signs, graffiti, displays, and destruction. There are still a few neon signs and normal billboards, but the city feels ironically less alive despite the fact that cops and civilians are still present (in which you never see any hint that civilians are still in the city except for murder cases, abandoned cars, and occasional hobos). The combat is mostly the same with a couple of new gadgets: A concussion sticky grenade that stuns small groups of enemies and shock gauntlets that makes Batman overpowered. Thankfully, the camera angles are improved when you make the last hit of a fight, however, it seemed I would miss attacks or loose combos unnecessarily and the combat feels even more reliant on countering relentlessly attacking goons. Thanks to a combat bug, many times I would finish a fight with a group while one thug was still in a fight stance, but not attacking. The game would recognize the fight as complete and give you XP, but you woulld have to punch or batarang the enemy (which sometimes misses at POINT BLANK). I even had another bug where a thug got stuck in a car and I had to use explosive gel to get him out.
The mutliple problems with the game left me feel like I should breeze through the story as fast as I can to get it over with. However, the story is definitely the strongest point of this game. You get to see the character dynamics between Batman, his Bruce Wayne identity (which honestly, may have been better if explored just a little bit more), and characters such as Alfred, the Gordons, and Joker. The more cunning, Less dumb Bane of the earlier games (Which is explained in the story) and the discovery of the Joker kept me interested despite me essentially knowing what was going to happen since this is an Origin story. The problem with the origin story is though, you don't get alot of information of the pure origins of Wayne becoming Batman (the suit and gear, the first outings of The Bat, his training and pre-Batman Life) and publisher/dev made the decision to put this content in upcoming DLC, because they can and want to make money. As for the predator (stealth segments), they work exactly the same, which is fine with me, but you will be stuck in Detective mode 95% time and sometimes you wonder how goons miss Batman grapneling or sneaking right in front of them.
I have yet to mess with the multiplayer. The idea stems from a little assemetry thanks to two groups of thugs shooting each other (with apparently terrible gun mechanics from what I read) while dealing with the threats of Batman and Robin and the mission to "summon" the playable bosses Bane and the Joker.
In the end, despite my criticisms, it's still a mostly solid Batman game that fits within the Akrham series and if you're a big fan of, is still worth playing. The base mechanics of combat, gliding, stealth and exploration are still here in full force - it ticks all the marks of a Batman Arkham series game, but just does that and nothing else - which makes the game uninnovative (comapred from the shift from Asylum to City) and the city is nearly so dull and drab that it made me want to rush the game. The huge fan that I was, ordered the collectors PS3 edition and thIs PC version to download/install overnight since I couldn't pick up my PS3 version on midnight and had to wait until the next store opening - I now regret that because I've spent too much money on this. If you were waiting anxiously for the next Arkham game, then definitely get it, but if you're like Many Steam gamers with massive backlogs and can wait, then look out for a 25-50% off sale or better.

As a fan of Rocksteady's previous Arkham games, I too was skeptical - as many others were - of Arkham Origins being handed over to another studio (WB Montreal). However, at least for the most part, they've done a damn fine job. Arkham Origins thankfully stands up as a great third entry into the Batman Arkham franchise.
Gameplay remains largely unchanged from Arkham City, but why fix what isn't broken? The excellent Freeflow combat system is back and as good as ever, though enemy attacks are a LOT harder to dodge - this gets very frustrating in larger fights. I'm not sure if this was intentional, but frankly I find it annoying. That being said, I think that's literally my only gripe with the game.
The "predator" sequences, wherein you sneak around a room, slowly picking off enemies one by one, is as awesome as ever. You still feel like the Dark Knight himself throughout the entire game. And there's a lot of game here - it'll take you over 20 hours to do everything in the game, and then there's New Game Plus and the new permadeath mode: I Am The Night. Odd that a game like this has a permadeath mode, but I guess if you really want a challenge, go for it.
The story in Arkham Origins is my favourite in the series, by far. There's a lot of great twists and turns you definitely won't see coming, but it also has a few predictable moments. I really don't want to spoil anything, but every scene that involves The Joker is solid gold. Speaking of Joker, Mark Hamill stepped down from the role after Arkham City, but Troy Baker certainly does a fantastic job of filling the spot, even if he does sound like he's trying to be Hamill.
Batman also sounds way too much like Chris Redfield from the Resident Evil series, but that's because they now share the same voice actor (Roger Craig Smith). It's a real shame Kevin Conroy isn't voicing Bats here.
Overall, Arkham Origins is a great Batman game, and well worth playing for the incredible story alone. I've just finished off everything in the main game, and now I'm going straight for the challenge maps and New Game Plus.

If this game was the first or second installment of the Batman Arkham series, I would say it's a top choice. But unfotunately it's not. The game can't reach to the level set by the Batman Arkham City.
I don't want to give spoilers to people who haven't played this yet, so the only thing I would say about the story is that it's really great. (wonder if there is a not-great story exists where there is the Joker involved)
The atmosphere of the under-snow Gotham city feels also very good when you first step into it. But after an hour or two you start to feel like the city is empty. The only NPCs you see are either cops or criminals except for a few hostages in a mission. Not a single Gotham citizen is out on the streets, not even a homeless person or a poor beggar. This undermines the great atmosphere set by the city itself and the story. (again not gonna say anything about the story to prevent spoilers, just know that it's great :).
If you played previous Batman Arkham titles, you'll see that the game uses the same free-flow fighting mechanism. This sounds great at first since it's a great mechanism but the developers decided not to correct the flaws in the system. It still takes one step for the Batman to hit a guy who is 20 meters away from him. (Superbatman!)
The side quests are fun but after sometime, they start repeating themselves too and most of them are shallow. Don't expect to feel the urgent need to catch a criminal like you did on Zsasz at Arkham City. And also the detective mode you use mostly in the side quests makes solving a puzzle so much easy that you don't get even the slightest bit of a challenge.
So far I've mostly talked about negative sides of this franchise but is it a bad game? Ofcourse not. Like I said the story is great, graphics and music are of very good quality as you would expect from an AAA title. Also the multiplayer part is well done and worth playing.
In general Batman Arkham Origins is a good game. You'll probably have fun while playing through the start to the end if you're a Batman fan. But if you just enjoy action games and Batman isn't something special for you, then don't expect having lots of fun time.

The Black Ops II campaign is exactly what you would expect from a game in the Call of Duty Franchise, an okay story but one mainly focused on action. As far as the campaign goes, I was actually quite impressed by there being multiple endings and being able to make choices that led towards those endings. Overall, the campaign is as expected and I thoroughly enjoyed it. However, it's the zombie and multiplayer modes that really gave me an opinion of the game.
As with World at War and Black Ops, the zombie mode was the main seller on the game for me. The maps provided with the game are slightly disappointing, giving me an initially negetive opinion of this part of the game. Despite this, I ended up buying the season pass quite recently and have since been greatly entertained with the additional maps. While they are overcomplicated at times it does provide much to do and even if things are difficult to figure out the mode is fun despite this. All in all, I would say that the DLC maps are required for the zombies experience to stay away from extreme boredom.
Multiplayer gameplay is undoubtedly the main selling point when it comes to the Call of Duty franchise, and they all tend to be similar. As a result, I have no complaints about the similarities to past games because that's exactly what I was expecting. I first bought this game in December of 2012, knowing full well what I was getting myself into. Now, I've never been a huge CoD fan, but I would say that I enjoy the competitiveness the games provide. So while I never spent hours upon hours trying to prestige, I have played the multiplayer on and off over the course of the past two years and I've felt I've gotten my money's worth, and recently I've begun playing it a lot more. My main complaint, the reason I decided to write a review, and why I can't recommend this game is that for the past few months there has been a massive influx of cheaters. Shortly before writing this review, I spent around 40 minutes leaving and joining lobbies trying to find one without somebody using an aimbot, often getting placed into the same lobby I just left. I'm proud to say that I was successful, for the first round, of course, then a couple joined.
If you're planning on buying this game solely for the zombie mode, then sure, pick it up, but be prepared to buy the DLCs. However, if you're buying it to play multiplayer, it has become a complete and utter waste of money.

Having been a fan of Banjo-Kazooie before, I was most certainly excited for the new duo to come out and show what they've got to keep up with the classics.  And to my delight, it has met those expectations.  The game doesn't take itself too seriously while still offering platforming challenges along the way, and most notably I don't seem to have to fight the camera like I have in other 3D platformers, banjo-kazooie included.  It's obvious a lot of time, effort, and heart went into this game on the whole.
That being said, it's not perfect, and less so if you don't have a controller.  The game is clearly ported to the PC, so it was designed for the hardware of other consoles and then brought to this platform, the evidence being everything showing graphically like you have a controller but textually correct for those who don't.  On that note, if you don't have a controller your experience is not going to be as good.  There is no button mapping, and the escape key seems to be the B key, except when it doesn't want to be, forcing you to return to the hub world if you want out of something you don't want to continue trying.  The second thing is that the game works just fine on multi-monitor setups, except if you have something pop up to interrupt the game. I really want to like this game, I backed it from the Kickstarter, and I would say I had "high hopes" but I expected it to be fun.
Unfortunately it is not, this game isn't Banjo-Kazooie/Tooie, as much as it tries.
I will give credit, it does new things, you can't just re-hash an old game, they have injected a new personality into this game, but for me, I am not a fan.
My biggest gripe is the controls, there is no weight in any of my movement, especially the roll, it is very floaty, and you don't feel like you have very much precision at all.

Followed by this, you have the camera, it does not ever seem to be where you want it, it looks too far to the ground, or too high, or gets caught on walls, and you just can't seem to control it. Half the time if I want to look at something, it won’t even let me zoom in, because I'm on an edge. I read word of the devs saying they were working on a patch pre-launch, but I honestly have no idea if that has been rolled out on not.
The loading/have to retry challenges, such asa the Arcade, are just painful, you have to scoll through dialogue over and over again, for no reason, there is no reset button during these "mini-games" such as the arcade, mine cart levels and races. You either need to time out, finish, or quit, and then you need to read the intro speech again.
The Cart section is particularly infuriating, the controls have not once felt like they work, it feels random as to where I can use something, there is no indication of if you can boost, slow or attack. And if you have a bad run, you have to either die, or finish to restart, as I stated earlier, this is a huge pain.
I dislike that they have this expanded worlds feature, as to me, it feels like a way to make you backtrack through the level for no reason, I don't want to spend a couple hours on a world, trying to find everything, and realise that I need to comeback, and look everywhere again after I upgrade a tomb.
Combat is pretty bland, there are no permanent projectiles, and why do you need to have a stamina bar, it just makes navigating frustrating (albeit it isn't as bad with the plethora of health/stamina pickups around).
There are some things I like though.
I do like they have changed some of the formula; new moves are the best part.
(Couple of move spoilers here)
I like that you can alter your state depending on items you ingest, and it adds a nice puzzle solving aspect.
Being able to walk underwater in nice, as the swimming is horrid.
I like that getting new moves genuinely feel useful, but this makes me want to skip a level, just so I can learn the next move, and move on.
The game looks very nice.
As it stands, I am only 7 hours into the game, in the 4th world, but I am not having fun. Every time I load up the game, I feel like I am just grinding through, so that I can get a new move, which shouldn't be what this game is about, I should enjoy the challenges and exploring.
I want to enjoy this game, and I will get around to finishing, but I can only play this game for so long at a time, because it just frustrates me to play.
If you don't envision the old Banjo-Kazooie games and want a decent Platformer, you might have a good time, but for all else, I honestly don't think so.

First of all, I backed this game, so this review is biased. I will still attempt to be objective, however.
9/10
I really enjoyed the game overall. It really brings back the essence of Banjo-Kazooie without being exactly like it, and as such, I would absolutely recommend the game to any Banjo-Kazooie fan. It's not burdened by a lot of problems that were around in BK and BT, though it introduces a few new ones (but hey, there's no such thing as a perfect game). You can reasonably beat the game Any% without any guides. 100%, however... You'll probably need a guide (or at least a friend) at some point. I would sort of expect that.
=== POTENTIAL SPOILERS AHEAD ===
I'm going to be sort of vague and save the gory details for a longform analysis that I might do sometime in the future.
MECHANICS
The abilities are fun and occasionally make you feel like you're outsmarting the game. Having abilities on a recharging energy bar instead of depending on pads and ammo is a big improvement. The camera can be a little silly at times and a handful of challenges have an incredibly low margin of error, meaning you will probably make 15-20 attempts to beat them. The golfing challenges are especially frustrating since Yooka & Laylee (probably) have capsule collision and the balls are spheres, making it about as precise as moving a bug by peeing on it. Bosses have a good level of challenge; I only beat one of them on my first try and only because I had a massive health pool when I found it.
Most of the transformations were fun (aesthetically, at least), especially the helicopter. The snow plow was pretty awful mechanically, with the worst controls imaginable. It turns like a boat, drifts like an innertube, and can't go in reverse, making it incredibly frustrating to deal with for the platforming that (eventually) results in ONE PAGIE. Meanwhile, the helicopter gives access to at least half a dozen pagies and several other collectibles and is just downright fun and useful in exploring the level.
Loading screens are pretty minimal and never occur within individual worlds, though I wish the hub didn't have any loading-screen transitions.
LEVELS
The levels were overall solid, though a little easy to get lost in. That's pretty normal for collect-a-thons, though there were definitely times I attempted to pull out a map and then realized immediately after that there wasn't one. At times, interactable elements of levels didn't read well (especially in Capital Cashino), though you can definitely figure out a lot on your own through trial, error, and banging your head against the wall.
There is no hand-holding in this game. While it does *generally* tell you where to go, it's little more than "you need X to get to Y, so try looking in Z place first" and "Here is how you do X move" or "These are the controls for this transformation" Good level design does a lot of the tutorial work and the small amount of text tutorial given in the first ten minutes of the game does not interrupt gameplay.
STORY
The story gets the job done. It explains why you're exploring book worlds for Pagies. Do you really expect a deep story from this kind of game?
The dialogue is humourous (note the British spelling, of which this game touts shamelessly) right from the get-go. It kept me amused for the first four hours of the game while I rushed through all the levels to unlock every ability. It does an awesome job to get crap past the radar- the dialogue is littered with naughty jokes and innuendos (naugtier than Banjo-Kazooie but not as much as Conker's Bad Fur Day). There is, of course, the obligatory potty humor, though not quite as ubiquitous as it was in BK. And if you're the type for puns and plays on words, there are *a lot* of really solid ones. The game is even more self-referential than its spiritual predecessor, making reference not only to its own game, but other games and the industry as a whole. The game's humor probably only make you laugh once, but that isn't really the sole reason to play it anyway.
GRAPHICS
I'm not one to judge this as I ran the game at the lowest rendering setting with the second lowest resolution, but it actually looked surprisingly good at that resolution, with text being totally readable and no critical character detail being lost. Low settings do not detract from gameplay and still give a lot of the nice post-processing effects such as distance blur. A lot of things have oversized collision, meaning that a handful of things appear to float in midair when viewed from certain angles, which looks kinda strange. LOD-popping was very noticeable and somewhat distracting- though I suspect that had a lot more to do with my resolution than being a general graphical problem.
One of the nicest things they did for you is essentially making the main menu also the game's benchmark so that you know which settings to use. :D
AUDIO
Grant Kirkhope and David Wise are musical geniuses! I had high expectations from the composers and they absolutely delivered! The talking sound bits work well and fit completely with the Banjo-Kazooie revival aesthetic. Looping and transitions work seamlessly, adding tremendously to the gameplay. Audiowise, the game is (dare I say) perfect.

Yooka Laylee is a mixed bag. On one hand, it's a faithful spiritual successor to the Banjo Kazooie/Tooie games. On the other hand, it doesn't do much "succeeding" and in some cases it's worse or rougher around the edges. There are issues with the camera, controls, combat, level design, and overall gameplay mechanics. Many will forgive these faults and say that these issues are there because the developer was trying to remain as faithful as possible to the Banjo games or platformers in general of that time period, but the problem is that these issues come off as mere laziness or as lack of polish than faithfulness. For every good quality of Yooka Laylee, there's almost always a negative aspect to it to counteract it. While you may enjoy certain aspects one moment, the next moment you may end up being frustrated with it.
On the store page, the game is promoted as having "huge, beautiful worlds", and while it's true that the worlds are HUGE and there's a lot to explore, Yooka Laylee proves that bigger is not always better. Most of the worlds are designed in a way where it's easy to get lost due to the lack of NPCs or unique features/landmarks in the environment. After fully exploring and knowing exactly where I need to go to complete a quest or get a collectible, I still tend to roam around the level randomly in confusion until I get to where I want to be, which is a waste of time and a sign of poor level design. Reducing the size of the worlds  (possibly adding more smaller worlds to compensate this) and adding more detail or making areas more distinctive/stand out more would have easily fixed this problem. I will say that the last world is significantly improved over the others with the added warp gates and has a more pleasing atmosphere and attention to detail added to it. I also didn't mind the casino world as much but that may be because I liked the concept of it more than the others rather than it being structurally different.
The camera is reminiscent of what you'd find in games of the late 90's or early 00's. It's not quite as bad as what you'd expect, but there are moments where you'll fall to your death or fail a challenge because you're either fighting with the repositioning of the auto-camera or you're not able to control it at all due to it being locked in place in certain areas. In one of the timed trials late in the game the camera shook in place while i was sliding down a ramp causing me to fail and have to start over which may have been a bug, but I'll use it as an extreme example. The controls possess a similar fault, I often felt like I wasn't being given the precision needed to climb ramps or navigate between platforms and I'd fall off as a consequence to this which can lead to restarting from the beginning of a route.
The combat in this is atrocious and probably the worst feature of the game. It's so bad that I'd almost think that removing enemies from the game entirely (except for bosses) would be a better alternative than having them in the game. To start with, there's no lock on or strafe controls for projectiles which makes targetting with projectiles a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ You can zoom in to aim by pressing the left stick button as an alternative, but this doesn't do much good when you're getting attacked, especially for boss fights, and is really only useful when completing puzzles or quests so this makes projectiles nearly useless for regular enemies. The fact that the zoom controls aren't mentioned until you exit the first world is pretty lame, this game is deserving of a better tutorial.
Melee attacks feel either overpowered to the point where you're spamming the same thing over and over, or not very useful. The hit detection for the jump attack feels.. off. Maybe it's just the depth perception or positioning of the camera but it's harder to hit with jump attacks than it should be, so this sucks when you're against airborne enemies. The default spin attack doesn't have any inherent problems but taking out large groups with it isn't optimal and takes too long. Buddy slam (without tonic) has such a crappy range that makes it too weak for normal enemies, the tonic should have been a permanent upgrade for that move, or there should have been a lesser upgrade for it to make the base move not quite as useless. Meanwhile both buddy slam (with tonic) and sonar splosion completely wipe the floor. It just doesn't make sense to worsen combat and variety by screwing up the balance of attacks.
Most of the enemies are bland or reskins of enemies you'd find in previous worlds. There's not much variety to them so you'll be seeing the same ones in every world. Only the bosses were designed with a bit of creativity, and even then I found over half of the bosses uninspiring. I don't know if enemy design was a budget restriction or if it was a rush job, but there's very little emphasis given to them and you may find yourself ignoring/moving past them completely rather than attacking them as there's no point to a lot of the combat.
The quests/challenges and collectathon aspect are solid and I found myself enjoying that the most out of the content in the game, however this does have a downside. Playtonic thought it'd be a great idea to make most of the objects you need to break or manipulate to unlock areas/collectibles look extremely similar, so if you're like me you'll get confused as to which special move you're supposed to use to break an object (because each object is unique to each special move and the differences can be blurred). For example, ice can look exactly like glass and windows can require two different types of moves to break. This can also be a problem when you haven't obtained the move yet, leaving you confused for what you're supposed to do. Dumb decision that could have been corrected by making the objects more distinctive.. which ironically is the same issue the game has with level design. Blandness appears to be a major issue universally (worlds, enemies, and destructables).
Rextro's mini-games are tacked on and feel like a chore to complete. You have to complete them twice (once for basic completion, and the second time to get a high score) to obtain both pagies, which is nonsense when they could have made it so that you can get both pagies in one play. They seem more like a forced inclusion to stay faithful to the banjo games and to add a "multiplayer" experience, the quality is mediocre at best. The minecart challenges, similar to mini-games, even though I'm terrible at them I'll admit were competent and something you may expect out of a good standalone indie game (Joe Danger and Action Henk come to mind) so I was impressed with those. Neither Rextro's arcade games or the minecart levels give you an option to do a quick "restart" which is frustrating, and more annoying for the minecart ones because you can fail easily early on into the level so you're forced to complete it or run yourself off the track, unless you exit back to the game hub which is very inconvenient.
Yooka Laylee ran at a consistent 60 fps for me at 1080p/maxed settings with a 780gtx, and I didn't encounter any noticeable bugs. Takes about 20 hours to finish and took me 35 hours to collect everything and get 100% achievements. I was a kickstarter backer and paid $15ish for it. I would say that there's maybe $30 worth of content in this, max. $40 is a bit too high of an asking price when you factor in all of the frustrations that you might experience, and that's one reason I'm giving this a negative review. If you're a big fan of Rare platformers or the Banjo Kazooie games, I would suggest giving this game a chance and see if you can get past the flaws, for everyone else I would avoid it until it's much cheaper. You don't get 3D platformers like this anymore, so despite its flaws if you can take the good with the bad.. with enough patience, it might be worth a playthrough.

So here's the kind of stuff that happens in SG2:
I'm flying in my cloaked Freya-class stealth carrier towards a small fleet of enemy vessels. I drop to cruising speed (drawing power from engines to weapons + shields) in the middle of the ship cluster and release 1 wing each of fighters + bombers, which wreak havoc in their ranks. I lock a grappling beam on the flagship, drop out of cloak and set weapons free. Turning the ship, I shoot missile salvos from my port, bow and starboard ports, crushing the flaship's shields and bringing hull integrity to critical levels. I then use transporters to launch a boarding party, which subdues the vessel's defenders in less than a minute. All the while my guns, bombers and fighters make short work of the supporting vessels and I leave with a prize ship worth millions of credits.
That's the game in a nutshell. It's really, really, really cool and accomplishes what few games like it can... but has giant glaring holes in it. I recommend the game if you get it on sale or if you don't mind taking the good with the bad. I'm not one of those weird people who likes s***ty games and *I* played it for 55 hours and counting.
Here are my gripes:
* Capturing ships? Yeah, pretty much the only sensible thing to do towards the end game for cash.
* The system is kind of arcane. Most of it becomes intuitive after you get a chance to tweak it (for instance, I've set my mouse page Back/Forward buttons to lock on the nearest target and mark it for fighters/fleet vessels). However... it wasn't until like 40-50 hours into the game that I realized that "Power-To-Engines" didn't actually put full power to engines and you boosted speed significantly if you used the power allocation tab to set Engines to 100% while in PTE mode.
* AI is miserably weak. Boarding actions? They don't do 'em. Hacking your ship? Yeah they don't do that either. Grappling? Hahaha no. They seem to just go towards the nearest enemy and shoot. The most complicated thing they do is use items that drop mines or kill your fighters or knock out your engines. It leads to ridiculous situations like my Freya ship with 110 troopers destroying 6 Equinox-class carriers with 130 troopers each... when just two of them could almost guarantee taking my ship by boarding. Same goes when I'm wrecking a freighter with a small corvette-class fighter/bomber... and it could easily knock me out of commission by grappling me and pounding me to dust.
* The dialogue killed my parents. Seriously... this stuff comes across as written by a middle-schooler, translated to Russian-and-back, and voiced in the dumbest, least engaging way possible. Worst of all.. it's unskippable! There's a command for "skip dialogue" but it DOESN'T WORK.

Bottom line - more baddies for you to shoot, blow-up and electrocute. Better voice acting, more story, better story, and all the FPS action of the original - it's pretty much FPS of the year.

Klei once again proves that they know how to do "Early Access" correctly.  On install, the game already felt self-contained with what I thought was a feature-complete list of things to build and places to explore.  However, since I initially installed a few months ago, Klei has released a regular cadence of enhancements, each one once again feeling feature-complete.  New systems, so far, have been seemlessly integrated, rarely feeling like they are still being worked on.  On top of the releases being solid and feature-rich, Klei is nice enough to tell us, on the main menu screen, when the next major release is coming out.  It's comforting to have an Early Release game that flat out says "this is what we're working on and it will be released in 6 weeks and 2 days".
A word of warning: for those who are looking to "beat" a game, this one isn't for you.  It's essentially a giant sandbox with no end goal currently.  Your dupes (colonists? abductees?) are dropped in to a small cave with their basic skills, a few things they know how to build and no idea why they are there.  Your job is to help them survive by telling them what to research, what to build and where to dig.  The dupes will eat when they are hungry, sleep when they are tired and use the restroom (assuming you build one.  For the love of god, please build one) when they need to on their own.  If they need oxygen, they will run to the nearest pocket of air to refresh their precious oxygen supply.  Outside of basic life functions, they are aimless and need your help to improve their living situation and, untimately, thrive.
I heartily recommend Oxygen Not Included for anyone who likes games like The Sims, Cities Skylines or any kind of non-combat oriented survival game.

Dream Daddy is a great game with wasted potential. The game's story is great, the characters are loveable and relatable, and multiple-route gameplay allows the player to play the game over and over again. It has all the makings of a great game, but somewhere along the line, it falls short. It's not that long of a game, and once you get all the good endings, there's not much else to do. Content in the game files (such as the controversial cult ending) wouldn't only make the game more interesting, but would help make it a longer, more interesting experience. That being said, for it's short completion time, it's loads of fun. The art and dialogue is filled to the brim with happiness and humor, and minigames help enhance the stories (despite being hit-or-miss). And the LGBT+ representation is amazing, and helps to make LGBT+ players feel welcomed.  So overall, depsite my many problems with it, I believe Dream Daddy is good for what you get and would recommend it to any friend looking to date some virtual dads.

While Arkham Origins (AO) didn't really revolutionize the Batman gaming franchise it did provide one good thing and that was more Batman. In my mind this game was more of an extended expansion pack of Arkham City with many of the same features with a couple new ones sprinkled in here and there.
While some may have been hoping for an all new Batman experience I was content to continue on being the same old badass I had been in the previous games. As with the other games the story is well done and kept me interested. Although I do wish that some of the newer characters that were introduced were explained a bit more. As their stories were a bit lackluster. Overall though I think the story was fun.
As for the mechanics there isn't much new here if you've played any of the previous games. The same great free flow combat system is in place with a few new gadgets to play with. Overall though, combat is largely the same. I did enjoy the remake of the detective mode and all of the cool features that now come with that. It made me feel like more of an actual detective than I was in previous games.
Finally, for the online portions. I have not put that many hours into the online area yet, although from the short time I've spent there I'm not sure I will. While some what intriguing and posing a particularly interesting gameplay mechanic of having a 3 team match. The fact that that is the only game mode available makes it a lot less interesting. Combine lack of players in with that too and you have a fairly lackluster multiplayer. Overall, the ideas are interesting, but the execution is poor.
In closing, I really enjoyed the game. If you liked the previous Batman games, you'll probably like this one too.

It's like living in Mad Max: Fury Road!
This has become my 'escape from life' game for the past year, along with Fallout 3 (notice a post apocalyptic theme here? :P)
Long story short, it looks very beautiful, it's hella immersive and it handles very nicely. If you've played any of the Batman Arkham games, it's very similar in combat gameplay. The beat'em up element is very satisfying, almost anxiolytic hahaha. The car racing element is a little more frustrating as the cars handle like boats sometimes, but overall it's ok.
My only gripe is that although there's a ton of stuff to do to get 100% or even to a level where the endgame is possible (I'd say at 28 hours I'm not even halfway there yet), but the tasks out of the main story gend to get very similar/repetitive. Thad said, this is saved by the FANTASTIC locations and ambience of the game. I could spend an hour just driving around in the desert and gazing at the ruined monuments and landmarks.
It also runs very smoothly at max settings on an average rig, without any visual discounts, it really looks amazing.
Given that you can get this for less than 5 bucks in the usual grey markets, it's a MUST BUY.
Despite having no replayability, this game is excellent, and it was definitely worth the $60 I paid for it.

TL:DR If you can handle a bit of repetition, the game is a great game.
Story: Not to go into great depth, the story of Mad Max is quite interesting. Max teams up with his trusty side-kick,  Chum Bucket, a Car Enthusiast and god-tier Mechanic. Together they cause havoc across the map. With gripping combat and amazing destruction, the world comes alive driving around causing mayhem. At some points, if you don't do side-missions with the major missions, you will be forced to "clean" areas of occupying baddies. It can take from the story when you have to drive around finding side-missions and cleaning areas just to lower the terriorty threat-levels.
Combat: The combat really comes alive while in  "Fury Mode". Doing WWE moves on countless numbers of baddies can never be more fun. The developers really hit the nail on the combat in this game.
Driving: As you will mainly be driving in this game, the driving is quite good. The destruction is even better. One down-side, is that you can change your car on-the-fly. I mean, it leads to some amazing moments, but does take from the immserion when you can change a battle-ready car into a speed-demon in a matter of seconds without stopping. Apart from this small things in this game, the driving is amazing.
Optimisation / Optimization: The PC port is amazing. Running easily on Medium/High on most settings on my R7 370 4gbs GPU. Just looking at some parts of the game... they are breath-taking. Just a head-up, sometimes the physics in the game causes some issues.
Overall: The game is amazing, it looks amazing while also playing amazing. Just the odd mission requirements that require a certain terrority level. It can just take away from the game. There does come a time were repetition occurs, but if you pass that stage, the story takes over once again.

This game is getting bashed a lot because of its online-only policy and the fact that there are only three missions in it as of right now (two of them tutorial - so it's more like one full-fledged mission). Both complaints are true - in fact, I'd go as far as to say thet you shouldn't buy this game unless you have a 100% stable connection (or nerves of steel). When you lose connection to the HITMAN server, the game simply drops you out of the level and into the main menu. To add insult to injury, it doesn't even autosave before doing that. And on some occasions, the game simply doesn't connect to the servers at all - in that case, your best bet is just to restart it.
Despite all of the above, I would strongly recommend this game to any avid Hitman fan. The one level that we get for our money is huge, and doing only one playthrough would simply mean that the work of level designers goes to waste. And what work! There are lots of ways to eliminate your primary targets, and if you disable opportunity markers, there's no hand-holding at all, which is commendable all by itself in a modern game. The ability to save your game is back, so feel free to experiment with game mechanics as much as you desire.
However, no amount of freedom is enough to make someone play for hours on end on a single level, right? Wrong. The challenges are back, and this time there are a lot more of them (of course, if you don't like spoilers, I'd suggest you don't look at them before you complete them). Still, in Absolution, the challenges weren't much of an incentive. Well, this time they are, because each challenge gives you points that allow you to unlock meaningful rewards. Among the things to unlock are weapons and spawn points. In this installment of the Hitman series, you are allowed to start the game somewhere else besides the standard level entry point - and you get a free disguise in some cases (such as when you start as a waiter in the kitchen, or a cook in the staff locker room). The lore behind this is that 47 managed to infiltrate the palace before you even started playing - doesn't sound very plausible, but it does save you a lot of time in your
th playthrough.
The sad thing about the challenges and their rewards is you don't get them when offline. I'm not sure what led to this piece of outstanding corporate logic, but I imagine it's just an extra DRM layer so that people who pirate the game when (and if) it gets cracked don't get the full experience. It's a shame, really - even contracts, the mode that makes a return from Hitman: Absolution, are not playable without an internet connection. And they added a new type of contracts, as well - the so called Escalation contracts that have to be completed multiple times, difficulty increasing (in unpredictable ways - one of the Escalation contracts adds extra cameras and laser tripwires that trigger mines) with each playthrough. Those are really fun, and they add a lot of replay value to the levels.
On a different note, I'd like to point out that my very mediocre (by today's gaming standards) hardware handles the game reasonably well. I have a laptop with a GTX860M, which is way below the minimal settings - and I still get between 30 and 60 fps in 1080p on the lowest settings with medium level of detail and anti-aliasing set to FXAA. Of course, the game isn't even close to being optimised, and it did crash to desktop on several occasions, but that's to be expected with a modern multi-platform game.
I guess, the bottom line is - don't buy this unless you're absolutely sure that you love the Hitman games that came before Absolution. This game has just one, if awesome, level to offer at the moment, and we don't have a way of knowing what's in store for us in the future. Also, you don't get the full experience unless you stay connected to the HITMAN server at all times, and God knows what's going to happen if Square Enix goes out of business. Still, if you're looking for a classic Hitman game with new content, this is definitely the right game to buy - and since I fall into the second category, I'm going to give this game a recommendation.
Addicting, fun, and an overall time killer, Oxygen Not Included is by far one of the best colony/city builders out there currently.

Ok well for people wanting to buy this game I just want to let them know that first they must realize what this game consist of. First I will list the pros and cons of HITMAN.
Pros:
- They went back to the roots of hitman allowing the player more freedom to do a mission, and explore without constraints.
- You are once again alloud to customize your weapon load outs before entering a mission.
- Ai is a little more intresting, people in the game react to the way that you do things and conversations are brilliant.
- The game has a 15 dollar option if you wish to just get the early cotent.
- Key Mapping has become more expansive so you don't mix up actions in the game.
- Contracts mode is still pretty great and makes the game replayable longer.
Cons
- You must maintain a stable internet connection to HITMAN servers or it will boot you out of a game. (Hopefully saves recently)
- The game as of now only consist of 3 missions... If you Preordered you got to play the first 2 mission and then one PARIS mission on game release.   The Game is now episodic and I see this as a flaw only because I worry that we wont be getting many mission per release.  When I first though they were releasing paris I thought that ment a campaign for it with many missions... I was wrong and this was a major let down.   I am not sure how they plan to release the episodic content but if it is only one mission per month then this is a rip off. (They should have released a bigger game at launch and then after released episodic content in my opinion as DLC. )  Most people say they like the idea but I think it is rediculous, and perhaps the company got lazy and went for this approach.
- If you dont like doing the same thing over and over to approach it for achievements this game will get old.
My final opinion of the game is that the game was a weak release and I don't like this whole epidsodic thing they are doing.   I always expected a complete full game on release and they decided to give us content little by little.  On the plus side you can spend 15 dollars instead of the full 60 to play what is availible now in the game, but overall I think this approach is really stupid. Let me explain...    Lets say you know someone like me spends 60 dollars for the full hitman experience.   Ok now I have about 3 missions to toy with for a couple of weeks, little by little getting content.   Now a person that waits to buy the game can get a sale, lets say hitman hits the point where its 50% - 75% off.  At that point of sale maybe the game is just about finished releasing all it's content.  So the person that picks the game up gets the full experience at about the same time as me for a big fraction of the price.  Then I the person who bought the game in it's early stage that paid full price burned out on the game.  (Basically It is like the game is ALPHA unfinished but they call it this episodic thing)
If you love hitman and can't wait to play it and dont care that there is only 2 tutorial mission and one major mission availible then buy the game.  I have told many of my friends this without being pushy of my opinion at first and they thought this episodic and constant online thing was crap too.  I hope other games don't come in with the lazy attitude that they will release game like this and see it as acceptable.   "Release little content on launch and slowly give packs of content along the way."   Now the plus of this is maybe they can release some pretty awesome missions with alot put into them, but the down side I think is that they will not deliver many mission for each episodic release. (This is based on the original release.)
I do not recommend this game in it's current state and if you are wise you will wait for a major price drop when you can get the complete game for less money.   If you read all this and still feel you are dying to play hitman then perhaps pick up the 15 dollar pack and decide from that if you are still intrested in this.     I tried to put my opinions in the Hitman forums and got attacked by hitman diehards... I been playing hitman since the original release that was PC only,  I been a hitman fan for a long time.   However I am not defending a game I strongly do not love and this game is good but weak in content and I think this new way of delivering hitman content is bogus.

Don't buy this billiard-game for actual billiard-games.
The focus in this game has been put on "trick-shots": The (extremely 1-1 strict) tutorial even teaches spins & jumps far before the very basics, which in reality would include chaining (or "combos") & bank-shots (bouncing cue or other balls from banks).
Don't even bother playing without guidances or other "deflection angle" indicators, especially mainly because the full-power-shot hits like a unrestrained Superman, which will almost 100% guarantee send your cue-ball flying off the table.
Also a large number shots that chalk the table simply makes my cringe, especially when the tutorial forces the players to do so at least once (I.E. when pool-stick hits the carpet of the table).
So why is still getting an okay from me?
Well, like i said, this focus in this game are the indeed the trick-shots, for which the game gives all the needed tools, especially for analyzes and other calculations, which are extremely useful with the recently released optional "playground"-objects.
So if you want to try out something even crazier than those seen during artistic-pool-competitions without risk of ruining ones pool-carpet, this is a game for you.
Of course, the available amount of game-modes ("8-ball" and so on) do allow playing "normal games" too; just be prepared to do lots of trick-shots instead of "playing normally like in real-life".

TL:DR If you can handle a bit of repetition, the game is a great game.
Story: Not to go into great depth, the story of Mad Max is quite interesting. Max teams up with his trusty side-kick,  Chum Bucket, a Car Enthusiast and god-tier Mechanic. Together they cause havoc across the map. With gripping combat and amazing destruction, the world comes alive driving around causing mayhem. At some points, if you don't do side-missions with the major missions, you will be forced to "clean" areas of occupying baddies. It can take from the story when you have to drive around finding side-missions and cleaning areas just to lower the terriorty threat-levels.
Combat: The combat really comes alive while in  "Fury Mode". Doing WWE moves on countless numbers of baddies can never be more fun. The developers really hit the nail on the combat in this game.
Driving: As you will mainly be driving in this game, the driving is quite good. The destruction is even better. One down-side, is that you can change your car on-the-fly. I mean, it leads to some amazing moments, but does take from the immserion when you can change a battle-ready car into a speed-demon in a matter of seconds without stopping. Apart from this small things in this game, the driving is amazing.
Optimisation / Optimization: The PC port is amazing. Running easily on Medium/High on most settings on my R7 370 4gbs GPU. Just looking at some parts of the game... they are breath-taking. Just a head-up, sometimes the physics in the game causes some issues.
Overall: The game is amazing, it looks amazing while also playing amazing. Just the odd mission requirements that require a certain terrority level. It can just take away from the game. There does come a time were repetition occurs, but if you pass that stage, the story takes over once again.

How much do you value your previous free time and the amount of blood, sweat and tears that you may lose from being frustrated at a game? Well, regardless of what bodily fluids you may lose over playing this game, SMB is an awesome game. It is hardcore tough. Completionists may take a liking to this game because there is a lot to do and masochists...well, you get the point. This game is tough.
You play as Meat Boy, a lovable wad of meat who is trying to rescue Bandage Girl from being kidnapped by Dr. Fetus. Awesome already isn't it? You must get from point A to point B in each stage while maneuvering sometimes very difficult obstacles. There are 7 worlds to beat, usually with 20 stages each, an additional 20 stages that are more challenging, boss stages, and secret hidden levels. There are extra characters to unlock (many of them you may recognize from other games) and each with their own special ability.
If you are looking for a challenge, definitely pick this up.

A rather cinematic game , accompanied by a rare type of storytelling which involves using a comic book strip storyline. The game follows a cop who finds himself in a questionable position after his family is killed and he seeks revenge.
There is a lot of emphasis put on performing as well as possible. Absorbing a few rounds from most guns will kill you so you need to take advantage of cover as much as possible and painkillers (the medkits of Max Payne) are sparse in the levels. Luckily , Max can take full advantage of dolphin dives to move from cover to cover. This proves highly advantageous during parts of the game like in boss battles or where there are many enemies.
Given the game's age , don't expect excellent graphics but looking back on this classic , you will see some features of the game which are well ahead of the time it was made in such as acial expressions and almost ragdoll bodies.
The game did require a small bug-fix relating to the sound ingame which seems to be due to the way that the MP3 files worked on older systems. There is an official fix for this which I believe I found on the Steam forums.
Aside from that , there is very little bad to say about this title. I have only one gripe with the title - there is no way to stay lying down after the dolphin dive. Max will get up as soon as possible from the dolphin dive which resulted in me dying a great number of times. Given the game's quick save and load buttons , however , this very rarely meant repeating whole battles which I am extremely thankful for.
Also there is a villain based on an in-game comic book heroand the game is self-aware. Yep.

Pros:

This is a very good return to form for Hitman. It does everything that Blood Money did and improves upon it, but it's not without its flaws (bugs). For instance, whenever the game is loaded using dx12 as the api, it either crashes or it loads into the level with all kinds of graphical glitches that make the game unplayable. Also, I have been caught dragging a body many times, which usually happens because of my own incompitence, but sometimes I get caught dragging a body without anyone even being around to witness me dragging the body. The game then reveals that the person who spotted me is either clairvoient, or has x-ray vision. This bug seems to happen at random points in the game, sometimes at the end of the mission, as I hide the target's body. If those two bugs aren't a deal breaker for you and you're a fan of stealth games, go ahead and buy at least the Intro Pack. The gameplay is great, and when you finally pull off the perfect hit, it feels amazing. I hope that the bugs listed are fixed quickly, and that the game is better optimized for pc in the future.
EDIT: I realize now that I hadn't updated my drivers, so the game ran terribly and dx12 didn't work. The game works fine as long as your drivers are up to date.

You're tasked with assassinating some guy on a boat. After blending in at the bar, while the target converses with a women, the game crashes. So I reboot, and reload the game. I tried reloading the game 4 times, the error occurring each time. The second common graphical error that occurs for myself is that I get textures that run diagonally through rooms. So, starting in the top right corners of rooms, the texture runs, like a wall, through the middle of the room. The same error occurs on stairs, where the ceiling texture will run from the ceiling to the floor. Luckily you can walk through the textures. These errors occur most frequently on the tutorial levels for me.
There are also a few other bugs I've run into on the Paris level but are not nearly as noticeable. Such as, very rarely, sometimes if I kill someone in a room downstairs, if there is a NPC in the room upstairs right above me, will notice a crime, and proceed to sound the alarm and search for me.

I run an AMD R9 270 @ 2560x1080 and I get around 30 FPS on Paris, high 20’s if something intense is going on. Not really an issue for me, I’m just happy that it runs.
