After reading the previous reviews, I decided to take a punt and buy this. I wish I hadn't.
Don't get me wrong, the gameplay is engaging and the world is thriving and bursting with personality, but there are some serious problems.
1. The game itself runs awfully. I am running it on an Alienware 18 Gaming Laptop, dual nvidia 880M's, i7 4930MX, 16GB RAM + SSD. Yes, by comparison, my laptop is not as powerful as say, a gaming desktop, but it should certainly be aqequate to comfortably run this game on at least medium settings. I have to lower literally everything to minimum to even get 20-30fps, and that is no exaggeration.
2. The game is absolutely HEAVING with bugs. To name a few:
- The game freezes for around 5-10 seconds every 10-15 minutes. At first, this may not sound like too much of an issue but when you're in the mits of combat this becomes extremelly annoying.
- Sometimes NPCs will start a conversation and then randomly walk in different directions, yet still be able to maintain the conversation whilst several rooms apart.
- If you use you fiber wire on a standing up enemy whilst you are prone, there is a good chance you will both glitch into the floor.
3. The AI is so friggin dumb. Want to spike someone's drink? No problemo, just do it right infront of the bar staff, they might ask you what you're doing, but if you make a quick enough exit, they'll forget about it almost instantaneously.
4. Always online. Personally, I have not had any connectivity issues, but this is going to be a serious problem for a lot of gamers who game on the go. This requirement desperately needs revising.
5. Way too short for an initial release. I mean seriously, it was over in an instant.
As it stands, I cannot recomend this iteration of hitman. This isn't a game, it's a BETA demo.

I don't understand why the critics are so mixed but pointing more towards the negative. Batman Arkham Origins have done everything right to maintain a certain standard to the Arkham Series. Good story, great gameplay as usual and better graphics. And it has the same amount of replay value like it's predecessors.
The only negative aspects in my opinion is a few choices how the different gadgets work. Some of them has the same concept like in Arkham City but lacks some of the speed and the efficiency it had before. You could maybe accept or understand it due to the fact that this is a prequel but like WB Montreal said. They don't want to downgrade Batman or the gadgets, but they have sort of done that a little gameplay wise.
Another example is that Batman seems to be slower and the enemies way more agressive in New Game Plus compared to Arkham City. When you strike an enemy and another one is about to hit you, you can't counter it. Which is a dumb decision or a mistake WB Montreal have done.
And we lack the oppurtinity to use every skins from the beginning without the costume code present in Arkham City. I hope WB Montreal adds the code like Rocksteady when Christmas arrives. Another thing that is problematic is you don't start the game with skin you chose from the last playthrough. If you selects a skin, goes out in Gotham, exit the game and reload it, you won't start with the skin you chose. The developers has to fix this issue.
Overall this game is almost as great as Arkham City. It may doesn't present new mechanics, but I don't expect them to when this in a prequel to Arkham Asylum and Arkham City. The only thing I expect is that it's still an Arkham game where you feel like you are Batman, and adding some aspects from the Dark Knight trilogy is a good way to do so. They added some of the good things, but didn't exaggurated like Christan Bale sort of did with his Batman voice. Good actor, but the voice is just so wrong in many ways.
This Game gets a 8 out of 10, maybe as close as the Game reviews out there. I am definetely recommending this game. If you want to have an even better experience. Those who haven't started the Arkham series yet can just start with this game, jump over to Arkham Asylum and than over to Arkham City. Than you can go to "Good, Better and BEST!". But the choice is up to each player.

Let me start off by saying that I have been playing this since launch day the only bug I've ever encountered in this game is the Burnley Tower glitch. The game works for some people, others hate and rage. So, word of caution before you buy this game.
Gameplay wise, it's everything great about the past Batman Arkham games. The timing in free flow combat has been tweaked. You will find yourself mixing in gadgets, counters and evasions in-between your combos. Some people hate it, I personally approve of it. No more button mashing and watch Batman fly across the screen to beat down the thug. Now you have to point him to the right direction. Knock down enemies as fast as possible or you'll get swarmed. Hear that alarm? Find the bad guy tinkering with the box or you'll get blasted with holes. Survey the room first, look who you are up against and plan your attack before diving in.
Free roam is still as fun as ever. You'll sink in time trying to find the data packs, relays, anarchy tags, weapons cache and vats of poison. There's also this hidden side quest involving Cyrus Pinkney, the architect of Old Gotham that I enjoyed.
I won't got into the story much. You probably read a lot of it all over the internet, but you need to experience the whole thing in your own play through. Though I have to say, it's a real treat to meet all these characters before Batman was BATMAN.
Lastly, the game is absolutely gorgeous. If your machine can handle it, set in on Ultra. I spent most of my time atop buildings, watching the lights or trudging through the snow. Batman Arkham Origins is a great game; rough around the edges but it IS worthy to be the 3rd installment of the Arkham series. WB Montreal did a good job.

I just finished playing this game and decided to write down my immediate thoughts after doing so. You don't "win" in this game. You simply complete it. Completing this game doesn't give me a sense of satisfaction but instead leaves me feeling hollow. Nothing in this game makes you feel good about yourself. I can't say anymore for fear of spoilers but I haven't felt this way after completeing a game since This War of Mine. It's often thought of as protentious to call a game an "experience" but this game truly is one.
Now for a standard list of Pros and Cons.
Pros:
Story
Visuals
Well designed gunplay. Nothing revolutionary but is still well designed.
Cons:
Issues with controls at times and the sprint control in particular.
Difficulty spikes can be unreal but the checkpoints are fair so this can be negligable.
Do yourself a favor and experience this game. It's tone is so different from that of the stock FPS nowadays that I hesitate to put them in the same category. A well desgined game I likely won't forget for a long, long time.

In World of Tanks , I can go back of a tank to attack its weak back armor . But in this game all ships are moving too fast , and there are no weak back shield , they are the same in four directions.
7.Movement of enemise. I guess it's because the movement partten of enemise that makes them hard to find and track. I'm not sure about this , but the point is it dosen't feel good when you are trying to find and track an enemy on screen when fighting. 8.Weapon direction. Weapons have an area of turning , you need to point them to enemise . It lead to a confusing ceasefire when auto fight mod is on , because there are nothing to tell you that enemise are out of your weapons angle . In Freelancer , there is no auto fight mod , so you can see enemise fly out out your shooting angle , and you can see weapons on your ship can't turn any more . in EVE Online , there is no angle limition , only turning speed.
9.Lock. You can lock an enemy , but your weapons will choose a nearer target if you turn on auto fight mod.
That's all I can think of by now. The game is not all bad , I just don't think the fun I get worth the time I spend on it. After 17 hours I am even afraid of starting the game program again. If you are looking for a challenge, definitely pick this up.

After reading the previous reviews, I decided to take a punt and buy this. I wish I hadn't.
Don't get me wrong, the gameplay is engaging and the world is thriving and bursting with personality, but there are some serious problems.
1. The game itself runs awfully. I am running it on an Alienware 18 Gaming Laptop, dual nvidia 880M's, i7 4930MX, 16GB RAM + SSD. Yes, by comparison, my laptop is not as powerful as say, a gaming desktop, but it should certainly be aqequate to comfortably run this game on at least medium settings. I have to lower literally everything to minimum to even get 20-30fps, and that is no exaggeration.
2. The game is absolutely HEAVING with bugs. To name a few:
- The game freezes for around 5-10 seconds every 10-15 minutes. At first, this may not sound like too much of an issue but when you're in the mits of combat this becomes extremelly annoying.
- Sometimes NPCs will start a conversation and then randomly walk in different directions, yet still be able to maintain the conversation whilst several rooms apart.
- If you use you fiber wire on a standing up enemy whilst you are prone, there is a good chance you will both glitch into the floor.
3. The AI is so friggin dumb. Want to spike someone's drink? No problemo, just do it right infront of the bar staff, they might ask you what you're doing, but if you make a quick enough exit, they'll forget about it almost instantaneously.
4. Always online. Personally, I have not had any connectivity issues, but this is going to be a serious problem for a lot of gamers who game on the go. This requirement desperately needs revising.
5. Way too short for an initial release. I mean seriously, it was over in an instant.
As it stands, I cannot recomend this iteration of hitman. This isn't a game, it's a BETA demo.

In a Dutch oven, cook sausage, ground beef, onion, and garlic over medium heat until well browned. Stir in crushed tomatoes, tomato paste, tomato sauce, and water. Season with sugar, basil, fennel seeds, Italian seasoning, 1 tablespoon salt, pepper, and 2 tablespoons parsley. Simmer, covered, for about 1 1/2 hours, stirring occasionally.
Bring a large pot of lightly salted water to a boil. Cook lasagna noodles in boiling water for 8 to 10 minutes. Drain noodles, and rinse with cold water. In a mixing bowl, combine ricotta cheese with egg, remaining parsley, and 1/2 teaspoon salt.
Preheat oven to 375 degrees F (190 degrees C).
To assemble, spread 1 1/2 cups of meat sauce in the bottom of a 9x13 inch baking dish. Arrange 6 noodles lengthwise over meat sauce. Spread with one half of the ricotta cheese mixture. Top with a third of mozzarella cheese slices. Spoon 1 1/2 cups meat sauce over mozzarella, and sprinkle with 1/4 cup Parmesan cheese. Repeat layers, and top with remaining mozzarella and Parmesan cheese. Cover with foil: to prevent sticking, either spray foil with cooking spray, or make sure the foil does not touch the cheese.
Bake in preheated oven for 25 minutes. Remove foil, and bake an additional 25 minutes. Cool for 15 minutes before serving.

This game is probably the single largest surprise I've ever experienced through a lifetime of gaming.  Prior to release, all the gameplay footage I saw looked incredibly boring.  I hate Avalanche's other games (the Just Cause series) because they are incredibly boring, repetitive, and generally low quality with an incredible over-reliance on cheap gimmicks.  I can hardly stand to watch 5 minutes of the original Mad Max and thought Fury Road was an over-hyped over-indulgent action movie with lousy characters, a mediocre story, and little meaning, the kind I'd expect from Michael Bay (albiet with significantly more style.)
Despite all these things, I found Mad Max very enjoyable - to the point where I put the time in to complete every achievement and was still enjoying it at the end.  Somehow Avalanche produced a game that doesn't feel like it relies entirely on a single gimmick, doesn't feel incredibly padded to fulfill some quota for the size of the game map, has a decent story with interesting characters (I was amazed at how well-written Max's mechanic's character is,) has solid gameplay, and also runs incredibly well.  I say this as a person who is very intolerant of games that feel repetitive and grindy.
So to the gameplay: You play as Max, driving around in the post-apocalyptic wasteland in your muscle car (obviously.)  It takes the typical open world game route of scattering objectives around the map that you can complete at your leisure, along with fast travel locations that reveal nearby locations on the map and story missions.  There are only a couple types of locations but they vary significantly in size and structure which helps prevent the game from feeling repetitive, even though you're doing the same thing at each location.
The game features both car and hand-to-hand combat.  The hand-to-hand combat is similar to the free-flow system found in other games like the Batman Arkham series and Middle-Earth: Shadow of Mordor.  While Mad Max uses a simplified system with only a couple enemy types and abilities, but it works well for the most part and is satisfying to engage in.  It's not without its problems though, with some moves (that you have no control over whether execute or not) prevent you from blocking attacks from other enemies, and being hit will interrupt the move.  The prompt timing for blocking attacks also feels a bit off, similar to Batman: Arkham Asylum before they got it straightened out in Arkham City (and then broke again in Arkham Origins.)
Car combat though, is where the game really shines.  Your car is equipped with a harpoon to grab and pull pieces of other cars and hostile objects in the game world and you can upgrade your car with various equipment to make ramming more effective and add other ways to inflict damage or protect your car from damage.  Battling other cars is a lot of fun and flows very well, though fights can get quite hectic against multiple enemies and can end up devolving into jousting.
The really brilliant part though is when you go up against convoys.  Convoys have set routes on the map, and are composed of one main vehicle along with a number of guard vehicles.  They continuously drive in a loop on the convoy route and you have to destroy the main vehicle to clear the convoy and get a reward.  The continual driving keeps the pace up and taking out the guard vehicles as they split off to deal with you while maintaining proximity to the convoy (the guards will respawn if you get too far away) is incredibly satisfying.  It was so much fun that I was really disappointed when I cleared the last one on the map and realized there weren't any more.
The only real problems I see with the game besides the aforementioned hand-to-hand combat issue is that some of the map locations can feel pretty pointless.  Driving up to a pile of rubble just to pick up one pile of scrap on the ground?  What's the point?  Luckily those locations are in the minority and don't really pose much of an issue.
And so I have to conclude that Mad Max is one of the best games released in 2015.  I never thought I'd ever say that.

I had my eye on this for a while and finally said just do it, and took the plunge. Glad I did.
I have no actual experience playing billiards of any kind in the real world. But I really enjoyed an old PS1 era game called International Snooker that I found a really relaxing experience to play and I was hopeful this would provide a similar fix. It really has delivered.
The physics are very solid, to the point that with shot assist turned on (and you can turn all video game aides off in the options, if you wish), things like jump shots are pretty reliable. I will say some of the speed challenges are very, very tough playing on a laptop trackpad, I have no idea if they'd be easier with a controller. But everything is tougher on a trackpad, generally. I actually find it very, very nice in this for lining up precision shots though. So in this case my trackpad has some pros and cons, and actually works pretty well in this game overall. Any game where I don't feel particularly disadvantaged for using one definitely is a bonus.
Graphically the game is also a treat. The screenshots on the store page show off a lof of the weirder ball/table combinations though you can keep it much more realistic as well. This game has more character, as such, than you might expect from a pool simulation.
You have a decent variety of game modes, including the classic 8 ball, 9 ball, and straight pool formats as well as some others. Developers say that long term more is in the works (snooker, please and thank you). We will see, but even without it this is a complete game worthy of purchase if you enjoy pool.
I do wish there were some animations of your opponents to really add to the atmosphere, but it's really not significant or particularly important. Just would be a nice add-on but it's really something you'd have at the very end of development if at all.
This is a game I keep plugging into for 30 minutes or so at a time and there's something really satisfying about knocking a few virtual balls around the table and giving it a go.
Only big complaint is the multiplayer is really, really scarce which is unfortunate. But there's a variety of modes here, the single player has been fun thus far, and apparently there is more yet to come (the Box of Tricks appears to be on the verge of release as I publish this, with an update planned for Nov 5, 2014). Should also be noted that if you want to do hotseat multiplayer (multiple people on one PC), that capability exists here, as far as I know. Though I haven't tried it myself.
Overall other than the lack of multiplayer community, it's got everything else I could want. Really enjoyable, relaxing game. Feels like something made by enthusiasts for others with a lot of care.

It is a building/management game, but one with a twist.
Usually these are all about just good micromanagement.  Not so with Prison architect.  Planning and your own personal ethics come into play.  There is no "wrong" way to build or run a prison.  The prisoners have a form of personality which brings unpredictability to just part of the play.  As such, the management is fully management.  It isn't about just building it correct the first time, but also involves constant watch to ensure problems are not developing.
Overall, it is a fantastic builder.  Do you wish to try to reform your prisoners, or is it Do the Crime, Do the Time?   Neither is wrong...
This is a fine example of the power of a quality early access system.  They released regularily key parts of their objectives.  Every update brought new things, but more importantly, brought about bug fixes.  Result is not only is it a well made management builder, but extremely stable.  I have encountered fewer bugs with this game than many major production pieces.
Do not mistake it for some simple independent production.  It is rich and vibrant, a very fullfilling purchase.

Like snow or Christmas decorations, Call of Duty shows itself by the end of the year. Like every year since Modern Warfare. This time, it's the turn of Call of Duty: Black Ops 2, developed by Treyarch. Unlike its predecessor, the story sets in two distinct eras, the 80's and the year 2025. Two viewpoints which allow the game to offer many side roads in the story, and 8 different endings. This is a first for such a mainstream series. Of course the game's core remains the same on the basics: cinematic action, epic scenes and a percussive score. Even if Black Ops 2 reuses old recipes, it does it really well and remains a great experience. I recommend you guys to buy this Game !
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Grief mode is aptly named: It’s a four-versus-four squadmatch with zombies attacking everyone at the same time. Sure, that sounds like a cool idea, but getting into a match was nearly impossible since no one seemed to be playing it the first week the game was out. And of course, no zombie game would be complete without a “survival” mode, which has you and your squad fighting waves of zombies. This mode is simply cheap thrills, but thrills nonetheless.
The graphics look great and the game ran extremely well totally maxed out on our overclocked Core i7 Sandy Bridge system with a GeForce GTX 780 Ti at 1080p. Everything from the characters to the gun models to the explosions just looked badass. Adding to the eye candy is a whirlwind of exotic locations, including jungles in South America, deserts in the Middle East, and even the gritty streets of downtown Los Angeles.
In the end, we liked CoDBlops2 more than we thought we would. The singleplayer campaign is fun and the replay value is increased by the inclusion of multiple endings. And the overhauled multiplayer is surprisingly good.
If you’ve gotten tired of the Call of Duty games, we know the feeling. That’s exactly why developer Treyarch tweaked the formula so much this time around, and the results are largely successful. Though it’s not a perfect game, it’s one that FPS fans certainly won’t want to miss.

I have made it to World/Tome 3 before making this review and yes I will compare this to Banjo Kazooie as this was supposed to be the spiritual successor.
The quick and dirty info:
Pros –
- Amazing Soundtrack
- Great Characters
- Beautiful Visuals/Scenery
- Funny Dialog
- Good Controls
- Fun Skills/Moves
Cons –
- Cut and paste enemies
- Repetitive mini games
- None or lack of “unique” mini games
- Flat Feeling worlds
Overall, I would give it 3/5 but still find the game very fun
The specifics:
What I think the nail in the coffin for this game will be is the negatives I specified. The enemies and mini games are so freaking repetitive along with a flat world leave me wanting more. I wish and HOPE they make a sequel with all this ironed out.
Amazing Soundtrack:
The music always seems to fit the world you are in perfectly and what adds to the magic is how it changes depending on where you are like being underwater. It is these slight changes and mix-ups that make the soundtrack never feel “dull” or repeated. I felt like I was playing Banjo again because of this
Great Characters:
Yes, the characters may not feel memorable yet….game is still new and I am taking my time enjoying it. I do wish certain NPC’s gave more of a back-story, but they all feel interesting and well thought out in my opinion. I am always excited to run into a new one because I am so fascinated by what they could come up with.
Beautiful Visuals:
From the colors to models nothing looked bad to well…..look at!
Funny Dialog:
To honestly compare this to Banjo I think the dialog is exactly the same. Yooka is Banjo and Laylee is Kazooie and basically talk the same way they did. Although maybe a tad different which is not bad I loved the silly remarks made between characters and random NPC’s. Almost all the dialog maybe because of the noises they make when talking just threw me right back to the good ol’ days.
Good Controls:
I felt the characters and camera controlled very smooth and never ran into any crazy camera moments. If I did, I may be used to it? I guess if I had to complain the swimming underwater feels a bit off ….. maybe because I am use to having a fast and slow swimming option as well tilting the stick up and down to go up and down.
Fun Skills/Moves:
I have nothing bad to say for the skills, they all felt new, fresh, and fun to use. Yes some had very limited use like the Green fisher boots from banjo, but still fun. Yes again some things feel similar to the moves in Banjo but they are changed up enough that it feels new.
Cut and paste enemies:
There are maybe what? 3 different enemies in the game?! The only thing that changes between worlds are the colors and slight model differences other than that they act and do the same thing. Little to no variety.
Repetitive mini games:
If I have to do another timed loop race, it will be too soon. Enough said.
None or lack of “unique” mini games:
Stopping the chompers from eating the light bulbs, the alligator mini game, and things like that would have really prevented getting pagies feeling like a chore. Any mini game in Yooka –Laylee could be thrown into any world in this game or another like it….very sad.
Flat Feeling worlds:
As beautiful as the worlds feel they also feel very flat. With little to zero hills the only thing that changes height are structures. Other than that, it is flat ground, walls, and buildings no iconic landmarks in any world like the Snowman or Banjo Sphinx (cannot remember his name sorry).
An overall well made and enjoyable game, strong nostalgic feel to it, simple but entertaining. Some decent jokes here and there and. I would definately recommend picking up this game..

The actual gameplay is fantastic and in my opinion the best Hitman to date. To finish the content on 1st run through took me less than 3 hours. Episodic release was very clear before I purchased and whilst I am now hungry for more content, I would not have gone and explored the level this thoroughly had I had access to the full game. The idea of receiving a location and getting to master it before moving on is starting to appeal to me.
Complaints about network issues were mostly resolved after the 1st day and are typical of all online games. It should be noted that offline play is possible, however it is with limited functionality.

I don't typically write reviews - but this game is so right up my alley that I simply had to contribute to outweigh the negative reviews.
The new Hitman game is a work of art. I've played every single Hitman game, with Hitman: Blood Money being one of my absolute favorites of the genre. The level of sandboxing in that game was beyond anything previously seen. This, in turn, left me rather unhappy to see Hitman Absolution which was extremely linear and not at all a true Hitman game.
Hitman (2016?) continues the trend of Blood Money. There are tons of different ways around every single obstacle. It's beautifully sandboxy, and the mapping has so far been excellent.
People seem to complain about there only being two real maps released at this point (with only one of them being a non-training map). I find this curious, considering that I've spent close to 20 hours on that single map so far without getting tired of it. I completed Absolution in less.
I don't know how much people expect to get out of the €12.99 that you currently need to pay for the currently available material - but if you're anything like me, you'll know that 20 hours of gameplay (and counting) is way more than you should expect. I sprung for the full experience, and can't wait for new maps to become available. I'm having an absolute blast!
As for graphics/performance, I have not had any issues. The graphics (much in fact due to me not being able to run the game at High Texture settings) are still perfectly fine, and I have not had any issues with lag. Your mileage may vary of course - know that the game does require ample amounts of RAM to run well, and close to 6GB of VRAM to allow higher texture settings.

Introduction
This is the first game I've ever had the urge to write a formal review for. That may be because I enjoyed it much much more than I expected, or because I struggle with it, even as someone who's played 'hardcore' games for a very long time. This game is well worth your money.
Rating
10/10. Great combat, though a little stiff, great story and atmosphere. Well worth the money.
In Detail
Garfield Kart is an incredibly difficult, incredibly punishing game about discovery and chaotic, blood-pumping combat. To this day, I have only discovered a total of three games that give me an unforgettable adrenaline rush in the combat: Rust, Dark Souls, and Garfield Kart. It is not a game you will understand within an hour, or maybe even two. It took me just under three hours to get the full grasp of the combat, and to become a competent player. You will get angry. Garfield Kart is much like Dark Souls in atmosphere and writing style, in that nothing is handed to you through the story, you piece it together through parchment and books scattered all over the dungeon the game takes place in.
Garfield Kart is also said to be part of a larger project known as Sui Generis, been in development since November 2014 if I'm correct, and for a prototype, it's incredibly well done. Although the animations and combat movement seem a bit stiff, it is still incredibly satisfying. Garfield Kart has, probably the most satisfying combat in any game I've played. The physics-based gameplay make it possible to knock an enemy off their feet with a high-impact weapon, or occasionaly tangle yourself into them so much that they are knocked off their feet. Nothing is more satisfying than smacking someone in the face with a sledgehammer and seeing them topple to the ground in Garfield Kart.
This is all said with only barely mentioning the writing - which has a very admirable air of mystery and some, more subtle horror elements to it. It's dark, gritty and bloody, and incredibly interesting. It's unfortunate I didn't know that you could interact with items in the environment until a few hours into play.

The Pope's movement took its first public shape at the Council of Piacenza, where, in March 1095, Urban II received an ambassador from the Byzantine Emperor Alexios I Komnenos asking for help against Muslim (Seljuk) Turks who had taken over most of formerly Byzantine Anatolia. A great council met, attended by numerous Italian, Burgundian, and French bishops in such vast numbers it had to be held in the open air outside the city of Clermont. Though the Council of Clermont held in November of the same year was primarily focused on reforms within the church hierarchy, Urban II gave a speech on 27 November 1095 to a broader audience. Urban II's sermon proved highly effective, as he summoned the attending nobility and the people to wrest the Holy Land, and the eastern churches generally from the control of the Seljuk Turks.

This game is probably the single largest surprise I've ever experienced through a lifetime of gaming.  Prior to release, all the gameplay footage I saw looked incredibly boring.  I hate Avalanche's other games (the Just Cause series) because they are incredibly boring, repetitive, and generally low quality with an incredible over-reliance on cheap gimmicks.  I can hardly stand to watch 5 minutes of the original Mad Max and thought Fury Road was an over-hyped over-indulgent action movie with lousy characters, a mediocre story, and little meaning, the kind I'd expect from Michael Bay (albiet with significantly more style.)
Despite all these things, I found Mad Max very enjoyable - to the point where I put the time in to complete every achievement and was still enjoying it at the end.  Somehow Avalanche produced a game that doesn't feel like it relies entirely on a single gimmick, doesn't feel incredibly padded to fulfill some quota for the size of the game map, has a decent story with interesting characters (I was amazed at how well-written Max's mechanic's character is,) has solid gameplay, and also runs incredibly well.  I say this as a person who is very intolerant of games that feel repetitive and grindy.
So to the gameplay: You play as Max, driving around in the post-apocalyptic wasteland in your muscle car (obviously.)  It takes the typical open world game route of scattering objectives around the map that you can complete at your leisure, along with fast travel locations that reveal nearby locations on the map and story missions.  There are only a couple types of locations but they vary significantly in size and structure which helps prevent the game from feeling repetitive, even though you're doing the same thing at each location.
The game features both car and hand-to-hand combat.  The hand-to-hand combat is similar to the free-flow system found in other games like the Batman Arkham series and Middle-Earth: Shadow of Mordor.  While Mad Max uses a simplified system with only a couple enemy types and abilities, but it works well for the most part and is satisfying to engage in.  It's not without its problems though, with some moves (that you have no control over whether execute or not) prevent you from blocking attacks from other enemies, and being hit will interrupt the move.  The prompt timing for blocking attacks also feels a bit off, similar to Batman: Arkham Asylum before they got it straightened out in Arkham City (and then broke again in Arkham Origins.)
Car combat though, is where the game really shines.  Your car is equipped with a harpoon to grab and pull pieces of other cars and hostile objects in the game world and you can upgrade your car with various equipment to make ramming more effective and add other ways to inflict damage or protect your car from damage.  Battling other cars is a lot of fun and flows very well, though fights can get quite hectic against multiple enemies and can end up devolving into jousting.
The really brilliant part though is when you go up against convoys.  Convoys have set routes on the map, and are composed of one main vehicle along with a number of guard vehicles.  They continuously drive in a loop on the convoy route and you have to destroy the main vehicle to clear the convoy and get a reward.  The continual driving keeps the pace up and taking out the guard vehicles as they split off to deal with you while maintaining proximity to the convoy (the guards will respawn if you get too far away) is incredibly satisfying.  It was so much fun that I was really disappointed when I cleared the last one on the map and realized there weren't any more.
The only real problems I see with the game besides the aforementioned hand-to-hand combat issue is that some of the map locations can feel pretty pointless.  Driving up to a pile of rubble just to pick up one pile of scrap on the ground?  What's the point?  Luckily those locations are in the minority and don't really pose much of an issue.
And so I have to conclude that Mad Max is one of the best games released in 2015.  I never thought I'd ever say that.

EARLY ACCESS REVIEW
Gonna be a bit confusing, but need to write a english essay for school. Its about if the death penalty should be abloished in America. please leave any advice or suggestions you have if you have the time to look through it. many great thanks-Liam
One thousand four hundred and forty five, that’s how many lives the death penalty has consumed in America alone. The first recorded execution in America was in 1608 when Captain George Kendall was executed for being a Spanish spy. Was it just? Is it right to put someone's life in another’s hands? It's a fiery debate across the whole of America with many powerful arguments on each side. This barbaric form of punishment is harsh and brutal, but also very intriguing. It captivates people like flies swarming to rotten carcass. My view on the death penalty is that it should be eradicated and punishment for capital crime should be remodeled into a more humane alternative.
I believe in my stance on this issue because it's been proven that the death penalty does not deter crime. In fact the death penalty sometimes does the opposite of what it is intended to do. An example of this, is when comparing America and its neighbouring country, Canada. Canada has a much lower murder rate; less than half of that .Canada's murder rate per 100,000 people in 2015 was 1.68, whilst America’s was 4.88. This example clearly shows that in fact the death penalty does not deter crime and that countries without it may be better off than countries with it.
Another argument against the death penalty is that there is always a likelihood that the convicted criminal is in fact innocent. Since 1973 it's been found that 130 people have innocently been executed. In 1991 Cameron Todd Willingham was sentenced to death for the murder of his three young daughters. He allegedly set his house on fire to cover up his maltreatment of them. He died on the 7th of February 2002. However, on the 13th of March 2015 the state of Texas ordered a unexpected re-examination of the case. It was found that he was unjustifiably convicted, an innocent man had been excised from this world.
Another strong reason to oppose the death penalty, is that it is morally wrong to put the life of someone into another's’ hands. A retired executioner, from the state of Oregon, declared that after dealing with only two executions in the last fifty-four years he has made it his mission to persuade anyone he can the death penalty is a “failed policy”. He thinks that regardless of their crimes no person should have to go through what he saw. He thinks this because of his personal involvement in the executions, this forced him to have a deeper reckoning with his feelings about capital punishment. As well as this on average the death row inmates spend 15 years on death row. I think this is unacceptable as these prisoners spend more than 20 hours in isolation every day. I think that Americans should no longer accept the myth that capital punishment has a constructive role in the justice system.
My final reason for abolishing the death penalty is that it costs the American government millions of dollars every year. This is mainly due to the state having to provide services such as lawyers, judges, jury and accommodation for the accused. In 2003 a legislative audit in Kansas found the average cost of one death penalty in $1.26million whereabouts a non capital case only costs $740,000. The money that is squandered on these things could be used to great benefit in others areas to improve Americans lives.
However, one point in favour of the death penalty is that the convicted receives a fair punishment as the jury decides what will happen to the criminal. The jury is made up of a group of people with different beliefs, cultures and morals. This allows for a fair trial and a fitting punishment in their eyes. Although this is a firm argument it only highlights how shortsighted the death penalty truly is. The fault is not with the jury and people who decide what punishment is handed out, but rather with the legal system. The death penalty should not be a feasible form of punishment at all and should never have been introduced in the first place.
In conclusion, I don’t think the death penalty is a valid form of punishment. I believe this because of many different reasons such as the morality of taking another's life, the cost of having to sentence a person to death and the underlying prospect of the prosecuted being innocent. I don't think it's justifiable to have someone decide who lives and who dies like an almighty god. Nobody should have the power to end someone's life as if it was flicking a switch.

Garfield Kart takes place in the ancient city of Mapungubwe (meaning 'hill of the jackal'), an Iron Age archaeological site in the Limpopo Province on the border between South Africa, Zimbabwe and Botswana, 75 km from Messina. It sits close to the point where the Limpopo and Shashe Rivers meet. One thousand years ago, Mapungubwe appears to have been the centre of the largest known kingdom in the African sub-continent. The civilization thrived as a sophisticated trading center from around 1200 to 1300 AD, trading gold and ivory with China, India and Egypt.
Your goal is to transform this small city into a nation. Barbaric tribes will try to raid your areas, and European invaders along with other African nations will rival you for land.
The site was 'discovered' on 31 December 1932, when a local informant, Mowena, led E.S.J. van Graan (farmer and prospector), his son and three others, to Greefswald farm on Mapungubwe Hill. On the hill they noticed stone walls and on closer inspection, they recovered gold and iron artifacts, pottery and glass beads. Van Graan's son recognized the academic value of the site and contacted the head history department at the University of Pretoria, Professor Leo FouchÁƒÂƒ©. As a result of his intervention, the University negotiated with the owner of the property, E.E. Collins. In a legal agreement the University took ownership of the gold and other artifacts and secured an option and contract for excavation rights. The University also successfully requested a postponement of prospecting, mining and related activities on Greefswald. In June 1933, Greefswald was bought by the Government and excavation rights were granted to the University of Pretoria. The University established an Archaeological Committee, which from 1933 to 1947 oversaw research and excavations (read more about the excavations).
The find initially received wide publicity in the media, but soon the archaeological digs and discoveries made by the University were kept fairly secret and were only made public after 1994. Possibly because the discovery provided evidence of a civilization that existed and flourished years before European occupation.
Mapungubwe hill is 300m long, broad at one end, tapering at the other. It is only accessible by means of two very steep and narrow paths that twist their way to the summit, and yet 2 000 tons of soil were been artificially transported to the very top by a prehistoric people of unknown identity.
Archaeological enquiry uncovered the remnants of numerous dwellings, which had been built on the ruins of predecessors over many generations, resulting in a series of habitation phases. Radiocarbon dates show that the first buildings were erected below the hill at the beginning of the 11th century AD. But adjacent to Mapungubwe is the sister site of Bambadyanalo, which was settled even earlier. It seems that the centre of the state shifted from Bambandyanalo to Mapungubwe hill in about 1045 AD, when the town most probably became overcrowded. It was also at about this time that hills and mountains became associated with royalty and the noble classes began to build their structure on high ground. This is an important observation as it provided evidence of the extensive wealth and social differentiation of the people of Mapungubwe, in other words this ancient civilization was class-based.
The gold findings are also evidence of early gold smelting. A large amount of artifacts from the royal family were discovered at Mapungubwe. The best known of these objects is the golden rhinoceros. All in all, the amount of gold from this burial amounted to 7 503 ounces.
In the 1400's it appears that all the citizens of the kingdom left leaving palaces and the settlements behind. We don't know exactly why the people of Mapungubwe moved away, but the ruins give us a good idea of how these people lived and how their society and political structures grew over the years. Scholars believe that the climate in the area changed, which made it much harder to grow crops and feed animals, this might have caused the civilization to move.
Greefswald farm remained the property of the State from the 1930s. Management of the farm was taken over by the provincial Department of Nature Conservation in 1992 and control was transferred to SANParks in 1999. Mapungubwe was declared a World Heritage Site by the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO) in July 2003.

The Grief mode is aptly named: It’s a four-versus-four squadmatch with zombies attacking everyone at the same time. Sure, that sounds like a cool idea, but getting into a match was nearly impossible since no one seemed to be playing it the first week the game was out. The graphics look great and the game ran extremely well totally maxed out on our overclocked Core i7 Sandy Bridge system with a GeForce GTX 780 Ti at 1080p. Everything from the characters to the gun models to the explosions just looked badass. From invention, discovery, and personality, almost anyone can have an impact on society. But many impacting people did something negative. Just imagine walking through the streets of a city in a dark alley, and knowing that at any moment, you could be the next victim of a serial killer who is on a rampage. In the late 60s and early 70s that is what the people of San Francisco were worried about, a deranged killer only known by the alias “The Zodiac killer”. The Zodiac killer was a psychopath who committed a series of murders from 1968, to 1974. During this time, he killed at least 5 people, but that number could be into the 30s. His early life is basically unknown, but there are little details here and there. During his time as a killer, he would sent ciphers to the police and news outlets. This resulted in him exploding in the media and causing the people in the area to become paranoid, some people even evacuating. He impacted the media and subculture in several ways, and may have been the cause of other killers.
The childhood of the self proclaimed Zodiac Killer is shrouded in mystery, but trying to uncover it, is something people will not give up on. Chances are the Zodiac killer had a bad upbringing. As stated by psychologist william baker, “Chances are, the Zodiac killer probably had family and childhood dilemmas.” this makes sense, as several serial killers grow up with a dark history which may result in their twisted thoughts. Maybe the Zodiac was forced to work on a Plantation where he got constantly beleaguered by his parents. Although the Zodiac Killer was very clever, he may not have received formal education. The website “
includes all the zodiacs ciphers and the police reports. The Zodiac's letters showed that he was unable to spell simple words such as Paradise. This leads many to believe the Zodiac killer only went through some education. Although, many think that errors were intentional. The misspellings may have just been a way to taunt the police, something the Zodiac enjoyed doing. While there were misspellings the Ciphers were  complex. The ciphers, still mostly unsolved, were covered in languages from Japanese to Arabic. The book, “The most dangerous animal of them all”, states that one of the Zodiac's ciphers was encrypted in Japanese.
The Zodiac Killer's first victims had their lives taken around 1966 or 1968. According to
, His first confirmed kill was Betty Lou Jensen, and David Faraday. Books such as “The most dangerous animal of them all” state that the first victim was Cheri Jo Bates, but that is all suspicion. These first killings were thought to be revenge, and passed on by the public. But that all changed later when Zodiac sent his first message. U.S History in context states, “In July 1969 editors at three northern California newspapers received letters from an anonymous author claiming responsibility for three murders.” The killer also wanted this news to be broadcasted to the public or else he would ride around and kill people in the night, the newspaper company complied to his demands. Over time, the ego that was the Zodiac Killer slowly built up. Many around the San Francisco area were scared and paranoid that they could be the next victim. The increase in his killings didn’t help either. Years later, the Zodiac had a confirmed 5 killings. Although, he himself, stated that 37 people were actually killed. In 1974, the killings and messages suddenly stopped. Then in 2004, the case was closed. But due to some initiatives and possibly an insurrection, it was later reopened.
Although not to Catastrophic proportions, the Zodiac Killer definitely left an impact on the people of San Francisco, and possibly the world. In a short time, he grabbed the attention of the police and the media, which is something quite hard to do. Most make the claim that he provided psychological research, but he did no such thing. Since the killer was never caught, he wasn’t all that great of a source. But the killer left impacts in other ways. To start off, he killed at least 5 people. He also used the media as a weapon. His ability to force the Media to do his bidding, caused great scare among the people of San Francisco, and possibly the world. His more world based impact, is inspiring future killers. The Zodiacs method of killing and spreading his popularity gave ideas to other psychopaths. Some even commemorate him for his work. Normally, someone who wants to kill, will restrain themselves, because it is impossible to do without being caught. But the Zodiac showed it was possible since he was  never caught. Probably because he would not leave evidence or debris after he was done.. This most likely led to the Kobe killer, Richard Ramirez, and others. These people were probably inspired by the killer, leading to their actions. He also had a big impact on modern media. Several films, Tv series, and books were made about him, and countless other forms of media were inspired by him.
In conclusion, the killer has little known about his early life. Chances are he didn’t get a good education, but possibly knew a few languages. His time as a murderer started around 1968, but may have killed other victims before that. He used the media as a weapon, and taunted police. Eventually the murders stopped in the early 70s. Today, the Zodiac case is largely at rest. The are many online communities dedicated to finding this man, coalitions to find the zodiac. But, if he is caught, it will result in several legal squabbles. Not just for the Zodiac, but for others too. But in this day and age, it does not matter. Banjo-Kazooie was one of the first games I ever owned, and is the game I most often credit for starting me down the road to pursuing game development as a career. Obviously that means I hold it and games like it in high regard, and that I was over the moon when Yooka-Laylee was announced. This game finally scratches the itch that I've felt every day of the long and painful 15-year gap between Super Mario Sunshine in 2002 and this game in 2017.
Yooka-Laylee delivers exactly what it promises: a game rooted entirely in the 3D-platforming nostalgia of the 1990s. Everything you remember from Banjo-Kazooie is there: a huge lair to traverse; worlds to unlock and explore; a huge cast of weird and wacky characters; witty dialog with a bit of lewd humor snuck in; a villain who pipes up as you wander the lair to deliver short quips; and so much more. It's exactly the return to 90's Rare platforming that fans have been begging for.
Unfortunately, it's far from a perfect game. You'd think this would have been the perfect opportunity to iterate upon the classic formula with modern upgrades like a strong camera and ultra-tight controls; but Yooka-Laylee sometimes sticks a little
close to its 90's roots. The camera has quite a few places where it freaks out, flipping full 180's as the player enters or leaves a zone with a locked camera, sometimes leading to an untimely death. The controls can be a bit screwy as well, especially during mini-games (most of Rextro's arcade games have frustrating controls ranging from unresponsive to downright head-scratchingly unintuitive). Kartos's mine cart courses feel a bit out of place seeing as they actually come from Donkey Kong Country, a 2D series from several years before the games that inspired Yooka. The gem-collecting is based on a (not-well-liked) mechanic from DK64's mine cart courses, but that's about the closest tie these challengs have to the 3D platformers of old. The game as a whole panders so heavily to nostalgic Rare fanboys like me that it might alienate new players who try it out on a whim.
Even some of the modern side of the game is a bit problematic - the worlds manage to be even larger than those in Donkey Kong 64 and Banjo-Tooie, both of which were seriously pushing the limts of world size back in the N64 days, both technologically and in terms of player patience. Confusingly, this game lacks any sort of fast-travel system despite both DK64 and B-T possessing them, making traversing the levels a chore at times. They also feel hugely overscaled, making Yooka and Laylee seem to be mouse-sized within the environments. Further adding to the confusion, each level is quite monochrome, making finding your bearings at a glance extremely difficult at times.
Even with these few gripes, I still love Yooka-Laylee to death, and I'm simply ecstatic that it even exists. It's the game I've dreamt of for longer than I can even remember anymore. My fingers are crossed that it will spearhead an industry-wide resurgence of 3D platforming, bringing a prematurely-dead genre back to prevalence, much like 2D platforming dominated the indie scene for so long (to the point of becoming a cliche - let's not go quite that far with 3D platformers, please).
"A 3D Platforming Rare-vival" indeed. Highly recommended.

You will not like this game if you are not familiar with the old-fashioned 3d platformer. Having grown up with said genre, it was quite the experience—this game is an absolute love letter to a past era of gaming. It's not an industry-redefining game, and it wasn't pitched by Playtonic as such. The backers were given everything promised to them and more.
The game is strongly reminiscent of the classic collectathon, but the collectables in each level have been essentially reduced to 6 types: Pagies (used for unlocking and expanding worlds), Quills (used for purchasing moves), Ghost Writers (5 in each level, collect all and get a Pagie), Energy and Health Expanders (self-explanitory), Play Coins and Mollycools (which unlock an arcade game and transformation in each world, respectively), and Pirate Treasure (almost sickeningly-well-hidden, only used for acheivements and unlocking an ability-changing tonic). The controls are tight, the worlds and characters are pleasing to look at, the sounds and music are all top-notch, and every challenge feels unique and well-thought-out even if the concept of it is repeated. They've successfully captured the feel of the collectathon in a modern, refined package. It's very old school without feeling dated, in the sense that you're dropped into a huge area with no explicit directive, and must remember yourself where places you cannot yet explore are (i.e. no map), with refinements such as the absence of lives and the need to re-collect everything if you "die." It's a very pleasant hybrid and once again, if you have fond memories of similar games from decades past, you will undoubtedly love this game.
It's very disheartening, not just for me but certainly for the devs, to see such negativity from a vocal minority surrounding the game, mostly relating to topics that the finished product should not be punished for. If you are or were  considering this game, please consider it based on its merits (what a concept!) and of course whether or not you'd be happy with a game of this style. It's not for everyone of course, but if you want a trip through late 90s platformer nostalgia, this is the game for you.

Several aspects of the game feel unpolished and the level design doesn't come close to the brilliance of Banjo-Kazooie, which was somewhat to be expected as the original game's lead designer isn't part of Playtonic. Also, many problems that plagued Banjo-Tooie and DK64 are present here as well (e.g. bloated worlds, repetitive challenges, forced backtracking, awful minigames and lots of unnecessary dialogue that hurts both pacing and immersion).
However, it definitely succeeds at bringing back the classic "Rare collectathon" gameplay I loved so much on the N64, and that's all that mattered to me when I backed the project. The basic controls feel very natural and responsive, the soundtrack is great, the characters are charming, and the visuals are mostly good-looking and colourful despite some inconsistencies.
So yeah, it's essentially "diet Banjo". Not a perfect game by any means, but I still enjoyed many of the 24 hours it took me to fully complete everything. I'm glad I bought it early on Kickstarter though, because the current asking price is pretty damn high and doesn't even include the upcoming DLC they promised.

Yooka Laylee, for the 10+ hours I’ve played and the 50$ I’ve spent on the game, I was not disappointed. The game aims to put on modern twist on the platformers from days of old, and the developers did so rather well. The game has a terrific soundtrack; a cute and bubbly art style and a level design that makes the worlds seem that much grander.
The most pivotal part of any game is the gameplay and playstyle, and the most prominent issues that need to be addressed are the controls. The game has relatively simple control scheme, for controllers, otherwise if you attempt to play on a keyboard (like I had for the first hour) the controls aren’t too easy to follow and are a bit difficult to use.

Another key issue in the game is the camera, while the developers are currently working to fix these issues, in the games current state the camera is rather buggy. In specific places in the game the camera quickly snaps to one orientation which messes with your perspective and orientation and sometimes you get stuck in a loop of a camera going back and forth, and other times around corners you are unable to see Yooka.
In terms of Level design, the developers excelled in creating fun and enjoyable levels.  Each world or “Tome” has a distinctive theme and layout, while most worlds can easily be broken up into various segments which makes navigation easy in vast worlds full of various minigames and puzzles, each utilizing the worlds moves and skills, and also utilizing skills form previous or future worlds.
Now let’s discuss the games music, art style, and characters, parts of this game that allows this game to define itself from other games. The games music is incredible with great tracks like “Armed and Dangerous” used to express tension during a boss fight, and tracks like “Bee Bop” aimed with portraying a brighter setting for a minigame. The games art style also serves as a medium for tone expression, the colors used are brighter and more vibrant, and the googley eyes slapped on everything makes the game take a sillier majority of the time, while some parts of the game utilize dark sharp objects to create high tension and dark scenarios. And finally we discuss the characters, probably my favorite thing about the game. Unlike most games where characters are just present to give quests or to further conflicts, characters are used to give the game, well, character. Constant quirky remarks and jokes made by the characters in the game make the characters much more memorable compared to one’s form other games.
Overall the game is well done rivaling the classic Mario 64, and Banjo Kazooie, the game Yooka Laylee aimed to modernize. The game is easily worth the price and would recommend picking up if you have a controller or are okay with poor keyboard controls.

I’ve been a fan of the Arkham games since Asylum, and they never fail to impress. That being said, Origins feels like a step backwards from its predecessor, Arkham City.
Based during the early years of Batman’s career, the game focuses on a plot by the infamous crime lord, the Black Mask. I’m not familiar with the comics, so I was very happy to see a new primary antagonist replacing the Joker. The only problem was that Black Mask wasn’t the primary antagonist; it was surprise surprise, the Joker AGAIN. It was during the unveiling of this revelation that I became upset with Origins. I understand that he’s Batman’s arch enemy, but he had such a large role in the previous two games that I just wanted a break from his jokes. It became so much easier to compare the game to Arkham City, which was not a good idea.
The previous game, Arkham City, had a very deep and original setting. A prison city that was filled with Gotham’s worst criminals was very interesting. In contrast, Origins features a Gotham city roughly twice the size, but only half as interesting. Random criminals prowl the streets and no sign of other life can be found. I wanted cars, pedestrians, and so much more. I expected a living city.
There were parts of the game that impressed me though. I really liked the upgrade system. It’s still quite basic, but a definite step up from previous games that pretty much unlocked half of the upgrades from the get go. They added some cool new gadgets that I used quite often.
As for the bad guys, I felt they didn’t have enough screen time. One by one they showed up, you fought with them for 15 minutes, and that was the end of them. In particular, the fight against Deathstroke was one of the greatest boss battles I’ve ever played, but after beating it, he never made a return. What’s more disappointing was that his character was only available to play as in the boring and mostly generic challenge maps, rather than the actual campaign. Some of the other villains came and went without me really remembering them at all cough cough Electrocutioner. It kind of felt like Warner Brothers sold the game on the premise that there would be plenty of bad guys to go around, but delivered a mediocre performance from them. Quality is always better than quantity in my opinion.
The multiplayer is a new addition to the franchise and I don’t really know how to describe it. I feel as though the game didn’t need it and it was an attempt to get people to continue to play the game. There are times when it’s quite enjoyable, but I always felt as though it needed to be re-worked based on certain over-powered features such as the criminals detective vision.
Despite the uninspiring plot twist, the often annoying multiplayer, and the incredibly familiar gameplay, the game wasn’t that bad. I wasn’t too upset, but wasn’t too impressed either. I can safely say it felt like a 6/10 experience on the whole. Worth playing if you like the Joker, not so much if you wanted more.

Single Player Review:
Arkham Origins is not too bad of a game compared to the first two, Arkham Asylum, and Arkham City. It's an Arkham game, it's bigger than Arkham City, and is somewhat more challenging compared to the first two in combat. This time around it seems as if there are way more enemies trying to hit you while you're ina  big fight, so you have to pay extra attention. The only problem with this Arkham release that I have an issue with, are the boss fights. Many of them seem reused from Arkham City, and Asylum. Without giving away too much, one of the early fights is a straight rip off of one of the main boss fights in Arkham City. Yet they do bring in some fun boss fights, so it ain't too bad.
This time around, fast traveling is brought to the Arkham series. Bigger city, might as well help out the gamer with giving the option for fast travel. But fast travel is not given, you have to earn it, and it is not as simple as showing up to an area and it's unlocked. Trophies make a return, but this time they are not as challenging as the ones in Arkham City. Crime scene investigations are back as well, but this time they require you to do more than just scan an area and thats it, you're ready for the next objective. Some found this to be annoying, I actually liked it.
As for enemies out and about int the open world, this time there are more enemies armed with guns. Again, making situations more challenging. The gadgets remain the same pretty much, but instead of a line launcher, this time you get a gadget from one of the bosses that acts the same, but without the freedome of the line launcher. You do also pick up some gadgets form some of the bosses, but not all of them.
When I was done playing Arkham City, I completed my original playthrough and new game+ 100% (played City on console, and never got the calender man achievement). But this game just didn't grasp me as much as the first two. It is not a bad game, I would actually recommend it to my friends, but when I was done with the story, I didn't feel the need to continue. Another thing, this game did seem to be more violent and darker than the first two. That I did like a lot.
I played Arkham Origins on a gamepad and had no issues at all. It was smooth, and I enjoyed it all the way through. The combat is still as smooth as Arkham City, so if you have played Arkham City, you'll know that the combat in Origins is pretty good.
In the end, I enjoyed it, but the boss fights were easy, and the story was not bad. If you enjoyed the first two, then I would recommend this game. Even first timers to the Arkham series will enjoy it. But if you like Asylum over City, then I don't think you will get much out of this.
My personal opinion is AC>AA>AO.

This is the third game in the Arkham series, and a prequel designed to explain how the Arkham of Batman: Arkham City came to be. It's a tough one to recommend. It's also impossible to say it's not worth your time. This is a decision to weigh up carefully, but ultimately maybe it's strictly for the fans.
On the positive side, there's no question that this iteration of Arkham features some of the most interesting writing in the series... eventually. It has some of the most engaging combat, and certainly the toughest.
But the sense that this game lacks a soul is palpable. It does hit its stride eventually, but by then players will have been put through a good few hours of sterile, frustrating busywork and an atmosphere of deathly coldness, and I'm not talking about the Christmas setting. That's another problem with the game; its reason to exist should be to show us what that chunk of the city was like before it was walled off and turned into the prison city. I was especially excited to see that city not only with inhabitants, not only in *snow*, but also at Christmas! What an opportunity for a Batman story. Well, it turns out that these parts of Gotham were just as lifeless in their heyday as they were as an abandoned prison. There's a handwave about a curfew, but that's inadequate. Aside from a few cars and other junk, there's almost no evidence of a population there even if it is shut up indoors. With the lights off. On Christmas Eve.
Ultimately, the first two Batman: Arkham games are so great because they're fantastic games based on the comics, and Arkham Origins is a so-so edition because it's based on the Arkham games. Corey May clearly loves the comics too, but those are the things you see in cutscenes, and little of that love is allowed to flow into the game itself.
So if you've never played an Arkham game before, it would be a tragedy if you played this one and not the others: get those instead. However, if you've played those better, more stylish games, you'll like them so much that you'll probably want to see this third one simply because it exists. And if you play it to the end, you won't end up hating it... though you might if you give up before the end, and there's a strong chance you'll want to quit. So, yeah. Buy it, or don't. If you don't, you didn't miss anything major.

I don't typically write reviews - but this game is so right up my alley that I simply had to contribute to outweigh the negative reviews.
The new Hitman game is a work of art. I've played every single Hitman game, with Hitman: Blood Money being one of my absolute favorites of the genre. The level of sandboxing in that game was beyond anything previously seen. This, in turn, left me rather unhappy to see Hitman Absolution which was extremely linear and not at all a true Hitman game.
Hitman (2016?) continues the trend of Blood Money. There are tons of different ways around every single obstacle. It's beautifully sandboxy, and the mapping has so far been excellent.
People seem to complain about there only being two real maps released at this point (with only one of them being a non-training map). I find this curious, considering that I've spent close to 20 hours on that single map so far without getting tired of it. I completed Absolution in less.
I don't know how much people expect to get out of the €12.99 that you currently need to pay for the currently available material - but if you're anything like me, you'll know that 20 hours of gameplay (and counting) is way more than you should expect. I sprung for the full experience, and can't wait for new maps to become available. I'm having an absolute blast!
As for graphics/performance, I have not had any issues. The graphics (much in fact due to me not being able to run the game at High Texture settings) are still perfectly fine, and I have not had any issues with lag. Your mileage may vary of course - know that the game does require ample amounts of RAM to run well, and close to 6GB of VRAM to allow higher texture settings.

I have played many games, for many hours. But this game... This is amongst the handful of games I genuinely give a 10 out of 10!
When I downloaded this game I expected nothing of it, I laughed it away and I thought: "Hah, this will be boring". Nothing was further away from the truth. It evolved from a game into a lifestyle... And while I'm writing this I have only played 80 hours of it...
I thought that this would be a game where I drive my truck through one or two roads, attach/detach a trailer and done.
But this game is so in detail!
* Realistic graphics, definitely for an indie game! I've seen A-rated games that were graphically inferior to this!
* Realistic truck designs and driving mechanics.
* Realistic extras: Petrol stations, sleeping places, fines for breaking the traffic laws, cabin and trailer damage upon collisions, road signs in the language of the country you are in, etc...
* Being able to start your own company, hire drivers, etc..
The only 2 things I would advise as a patch or for ETS3:
- Visible damage to cabin or trailer when collided. Because even when I caused world war 3 on my way to my destination, my truck still looks unscratched.
- NPC's that also follow traffic laws. For example taking over from the right (left in UK)... I see NPC's doing this all the time to me. And when I signal that I want to go to the left lane, the cars on the left lane should slow a bit down or go to the third lane to make way. This problem caused me to collide many times in countries like Germany where the right lane suddenly turns into an exit lane.
Thank you SCS for developping this masterpiece.

There are various special items hidden around the world of Mad Max that look like scrap books. Each of these items is either a letter written to someone or a photograph of the world before it ended. It's often something sentimental, like two children playing, with a note written on the back about their day at the park. This is something that might have actually existed, and the purity of it would cause those left behind in the wake of the apocolypse to hang on to the photo.
One such photo you can find is someone who took a photo of themselves wearing a motorcycle helmet just as the world started to end. The back of the photo expresses hope that this helmet will stop them from being shot in the head. This had happend recently to a friend of his recently. After picking up the photo, Max notes that a motorcycle helmet would not due much to stop a bullet.
The thing that is most noteable about this photo, however, is that it is a selfie. In the reflection of the helmet, you can see that the man is taking the photo with his smartphone. This means that just after the fall of man, when everyone was beginning to kill each other, this person took a selfie, put it on a computer, printed the photo out, wrote on the back, and sent it to no one.

At its core this game is very simple.
You go around and collect loot, fight bad guys, complete challenges and level up. It's all very standard. What happens in it? What's the story? I don't even know anymore. I can't remember. Who cares?
But at the very least the one thing this game does right is the driving. There's just something so freeing and satisfying about driving through the vast, open, empty deserts, through the cracked, and broken Earth that sometimes splits open like a festering wound in the world. The only sounds, your thoughts and your monster engine. Let the Valkyries sing as they bring us closer to Valhalla. Freaking beautiful.
And them some spazzes try to ruin your good time by running you down with their little spiky buggies. Mediocre. So you blow them sky high with an easy shotgun blast to their fuel tank, or physically tear them out of their cars with a well timed grappling hook to the face, and drag their bloody carcasses across the burning sand. Then you pause the game and take a screenshot of their pain. Good times.
To be honest this might be one of the best movie-to-game adaptations I've played, though I haven't really played many...
Regardless, I also really like upgrading my car. Stronger. Faster. Better. Shiny and chrome. I recommend.

Super Meat Boy is a game that keeps track of how many times you die and has to invent new numbers with which to do so.  Thankfully the enthusiasm and frantic energy with which Meat Boy hurls himself into the task keeps you from getting discouraged.  Do you call it a platformer if you spend more time attached to walls or flying through the air then you do on the ground?  Whatever it is, the jumping puzzles in this game require fast reflexes and  precision timing.  A high tolerance for failure helps, too.  When you do complete the level, though, your final run will be very impressive.  The game will automatically start a replay that you can save with the press of a button.  And should you manage to fight through the main game there are plenty of unlockable characters and dark world levels to keep you playing.  The soundtrack is great, too, even after you've been listening for a track loop for thrity mintues while you're stuck on a level.

A brutally hard indie platformer. You play the Super Meat Boy, a chunk of meat that can run very fast and stick to walls, leaving a bloody trail wherever he goes.
Each level has you navigating saws, salt, maggots, rockets, lava and many other obstacles, to rescue Bandage Girl from the evil Doctor Fetus.
Each of the 250ish levels has an easy and a hard version. There are also warp zones, which often have characters from other indie games and use their moves. More special characters can be obtained by grabbing bandages, which are usually found in the trickiest of places.
Usually you will die many times on a level, but this is all part of the fun. Restarting a level is instant and the controls are excellent, so dying never feels unfair. When a level has been completed all the attempts are shown simulataneously on screen, which is very amusing to watch.
The music is very well made and fits the game perfectly.

I don't review games often but this one really smacks you in the face. When you watch a movie and you're still thinking about it days later, you know you've seen something special. I am having that same feeling with this game.
I am not a big shooter player so I won't comment in detail on the gameplay mechanics or the difficulty, I found them both great, but the story and the artwork was incredible. I found myself rationalising the protagonist's choices as if they were my own. Even as events started to spiral out of control, I found myself trying to think about what I would do if it were my boots in the sand. I couldn't ever question Walker's decisions because they were always based on a truth he had compiled from an incomplete understanding of the situation, which was something I shared with him.
It's a three dimensional look at war, imaged in breathtaking scenes and with commendable voice-acting. Oftentimes, war is not as we traditionally define it. Decisions are not always based on what is good or bad, heroic or cowardly. They are often driven by interpretation of orders and gut-feel. And when dreadful things happen, do we really fully appreciate the toll on those that felt they had to pull the trigger, squinting though the fog of war?
This is a visceral and engaging experience which I highly recommend to gamers looking for something a bit different.

I am really enjoying Starpoint Gemini 2!  Having never played the original, I was a little nervous about buying the sequel, but that isn't a problem at all!  Free roam mode gives you a blank canvas and you can do pretty much whatever you want.  The option is also available during the campaign, but I always feel compelled to stick with the story rather than go off and do my own thing for a little while.  Due to this, I have not spent much time at all on the campaign.  Doing random missions, trading, capturing enemy ships, and exploring have all distracted me from that.  However, the five minutes or so I have spent on the campaign were not all that impressive (shoddy voice acting, uninteresting writing). So, do I recommend this game?  Absolutely, just not for the story.  Get this game if you want to get lost in a space sim for hours, not for some kind of an epic drama.

I see a lot of negative reviews for this game, and while it may be a bit repetative, I can't find any 3-D space RPGs that are as easy to control and not just pure spaceflight "simulator". The story and voice-overs are what you would expect from a space rpg, however that shouldn't really be the reason you play this game.
In my opinion, I have had loads of fun warping all over the galaxy doing manuevers around large carries and owning pirates and rebels with my plasma cannons and missiles. The amount of customizibility with your ship is off the chart for this game, however once you find your playing style and the best gear for that style you are kind of set.
You can also download other peoples mods and get fan made ships or docking hangers and other cool weapons not found in-game which is pretty sweet that the devs opened it up for modding.
All in all, this is a quality game that I went back and purchased the DLC's for because I thought the price justified the entertainment. If you like space games like the original escape velocity, or games like the app galaxy on fire you will like this game a lot.
