Grand Space Sim that puts you in command of a space ship to fly, shoot, trade, save the universe, blow up stuff, do the laundry, collect files hidden in floating junk, level up, hire recruits, upgrade your ship, and do pretty much anything else your starfaring heart desires.  The game looks nice, plays well (albeit at a slowish pace), has enjoyably 'space-y' ambient music, and offers a ton of different content that may not always 'wow', but will definitely satisfy.
Starpoint Gemini 2 reminds me of a giant, sword-wielding turtle.  No, really! Just let me explain...
Waaaay-back-when, in those wonderful 8-32 bit Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtle video games, you could play as one of four characters, each with different strengths and weaknesses: Raphael, who had tiny, short-range, but superfast attacks; Donatello who was really slow but could whack-a-ninja from half a screen away with his staff; Michelangelo who specialized in... I don't know, making pizza with nunchucks? Or something?  And then there was Leonardo, who didn't attack quite as fast as Raphael, and didn't have quite the reach of Donatello, and didn't (pizza?) quite as well as Michelangelo - but hey, he was a very close second-best at *everything* and pretty dang awesome as a result.
Sooo... if space games were mutant turtles, then Starpoint Gemini would definitely be Leonardo.  Sure, some dedicated RPGs have better character development in stats and story (and DEFINITELY voice-acting), and some starfighters have more intuitive controls without the need for a gazillion tuturial screens and HUD informational windows, and some trading/exploration games have a more lifelike economy that can fully support your character as a pacifist (read: cowardly) trader... but Starpoint 2 offers ALL those types of gameplay and more, and all done extremely well - just not quite on par with the best. This enormous range of solid, enjoyable space-sim content is the essence of Starpoint Gemini 2.
All-in-all, SG2 is a huge Space-Based-RPG/Combat/Trading/Strategy/ShipBuilding/Sandbox-Simulator mashup that may be slightly flawed and a bit slow-moving compared to games that 'specialize', however the astonishingly vast scope of gameplay content is all well-done, nicely polished, and most importantly... fun!   With a large campaign and moddable freeplay mode spanning half a dozen genres, Starship Gemini 2 is second-to-none in being second-to-all - but hey, so was Leonardo, and he became the leader of the Ninja Turtles for a reason!

In space, noone can hear you get ripped off!  How often do I write reviews on a game that just failed as a game or was not professionally done?  Not often.  I purposefully avoid such games, and I typically know what to look for.  I prefer finished, professional, high-quality games, and that's what I go for.  Furthermore, I incorrectly thought that was what this was, and that I just hadn't heard about it because it was one of those undiscovered wonders.  I was incorrect. And, games that mark themselves appropriately as Indy (some dude in his basement writing a game for fun) or Early Access (some dude in his basement writing a game for fun but he's not sure if he wants to finish it)...such games should be spared criticism.  They let you know it's kind of a yard sale game (I did this painting of Elvis myself), so honestly, how can you complain, as funny as some video reviews are.  Well, this game doesn't do that, and I bought it, not smelling the rat.  I think that, in this situation, I was just too greedy for a Space Sim - there are so few good ones.  Well, I don't get got often, but here is a time I got got.  I have heard some people say that this is a faithful modern reproduction of Freelancer.  I can only assume that such individuals never played FreeLancer (or never played it properly - there are appearantly some sick, sad souls that played it third person), which was the first giant, beautifully made, open world space sim.  This is certainly not that.  And, I don't know what to say other than there isn't much here.  It's a third person ship, with limited upgrade options.  I thought that maybe this was a space capital ship sim, a la Eve (but with less blatant masochism), but it isn't that either.  It's a shooter of some kind...a really bad one.  They don't even bother to create the simple launch and land animations that Freelancer did 14 years ago.  All of your armaments look the same...balls of light that make you feel like it's 1986, and there's not much variety in ships or armaments...which is the easy part of typing numbers into databases, especially when they aren't animated separately.  Well, anyways, it's a waste of time to go over every detail, but this is clearly a not-so-professional indy space game.  As long as you know what you're getting, all is well.

This is the third game in the Arkham series, and a prequel designed to explain how the Arkham of Batman: Arkham City came to be. It's a tough one to recommend. It's also impossible to say it's not worth your time. This is a decision to weigh up carefully, but ultimately maybe it's strictly for the fans.
On the positive side, there's no question that this iteration of Arkham features some of the most interesting writing in the series... eventually. It has some of the most engaging combat, and certainly the toughest.
But the sense that this game lacks a soul is palpable. It does hit its stride eventually, but by then players will have been put through a good few hours of sterile, frustrating busywork and an atmosphere of deathly coldness, and I'm not talking about the Christmas setting. That's another problem with the game; its reason to exist should be to show us what that chunk of the city was like before it was walled off and turned into the prison city. I was especially excited to see that city not only with inhabitants, not only in *snow*, but also at Christmas! What an opportunity for a Batman story. Well, it turns out that these parts of Gotham were just as lifeless in their heyday as they were as an abandoned prison. There's a handwave about a curfew, but that's inadequate. Aside from a few cars and other junk, there's almost no evidence of a population there even if it is shut up indoors. With the lights off. On Christmas Eve.
Ultimately, the first two Batman: Arkham games are so great because they're fantastic games based on the comics, and Arkham Origins is a so-so edition because it's based on the Arkham games. Corey May clearly loves the comics too, but those are the things you see in cutscenes, and little of that love is allowed to flow into the game itself.
So if you've never played an Arkham game before, it would be a tragedy if you played this one and not the others: get those instead. However, if you've played those better, more stylish games, you'll like them so much that you'll probably want to see this third one simply because it exists. And if you play it to the end, you won't end up hating it... though you might if you give up before the end, and there's a strong chance you'll want to quit. So, yeah. Buy it, or don't. If you don't, you didn't miss anything major.

I wanted to get a few hours of play before I wrote my review, and I'm glad I did.
I played Banjo Kazooie as a kid and loved it. I even played it recently, and although dated, I still loved it. I get the same enjoyment and fun out of Yooka Laylee.
The first level is okay, but I remember being underwhelmed with Mumbo's Mountain at first in Banjo Kazooie. As you make your way through the overworld and through the worlds, you get more abilities, so you get to goof off with more movements as you walk around the world. I play Yooka  Laylee like just like I did Banjo Kazooie. I make the character's sounds match up with the upbeat music as I run around. I do the jump+attack so I can do a fast flying tumble and enjoy the animation. Sometimes I run around eating stuff because the sound effects are funny to me. I play to have fun, not to complete objectives.
I think the humor is just silly enough that it isn't bad, which matches my taste. The supporting characters are okay, but I adore the character design of Yooka and Laylee so much that I don't mind.
Yes, the camera is bad. At first, the movement made me feel a bit dizzy, but I'm also very sensitive to motion sickness. I became used to it after awhile. I'm a working adult with responsibilities, so I play in hour chunks. I usually save after getting a new move or finding an item, which triggers the auto save.
The music is good. I had to adjust my volume settings to have sound effects lowered because it was too loud to fully enjoy the music. It has the same musical transitions like in Banjo Kazooie in that the melody stays the same but the theme is different based on where you are or what you do.
I know that for me, nostalgia plays a huge role in why I enjoy this game. It makes me feel like a kid again playing games just for FUN. It doesn't hold your hand in marking the map on telling you where to go to do x, y, and z like a lot of modern games do, which sometimes leaves me feeling like a lab rat pushing the button when commanded. This game expects you to explore and experiment to figure it out. If that's what you enjoy, then you may like this game.
I paid full price for this game and I don't regret. I am having fun, and that's all that matters to me to get my worth of it.

Yooka Laylee's issues aren't it's retroness or it's "failure to deliver on it's nostalgia" as some might say; the overall problem is that it's not a very polished and realized game.
While playing the first world, Tribalstack Tropics, you can't help but feel that it's generic to the point of forgetfulness. By World 2, a world with a curiously unexplained palace in the middle of an ice world, the lack of indentity becomes evermore apparent. You'll wish the devs went the whole way and that this level in partifular was more inspired, say a fairytale frozen storybook world akin to Disney's Frozen. As it stands, most levels fall short of having their own identity beyond "ice world," "tropics" etc. Levels appear static and empty; they lack that magical look and feel, or that extra polish to make them stand out from appearing like prosaic tropes. (Note that on the final world, it's core concept is expanded on and played with and it shows positively).
Related to this is the level design in itself. The worlds are mostly awkward to navigate because they don't appear to have "central points." Even when they do, they aren't obvious and they blend in with the rest of the level. The end result are worlds that look the same almost everywhere you turn, and you have to make considerable effort on your own part to make sure you're not revisiting. (Again, at least the final world resolves this by "sectioning" off the level so that the world is easier to navigate). Similarily, the world expansion concept, while intriguing, is not executed to best it's potential. It could have been ideal (in Tribalstack Tropics), to have a volcano cause an earthquake to a new area, or a bridge form to an unexplored jungle. This fits the theme well, instead of having more random indentical floating islands just materialize. Once again, this is a lack of polish.
As I said, the retro flavour is not Yooka Laylee's pain, but with two exceptions: Kartos and Rextro. These two game modes are so hurtfully retro; 70's gaming retro, and really kill the enjoyment of the main game. At times, one's spirit sinks seeing either of these two characters. I wish these minigames were structured differently. I really do.
Finally, there are some inexcusable technical issues plauging Yooka Layee; frame rate dips as low as 16fps. Yes, it's that bad.
So why a positive rewiew?
Because the game delivered on it's expecations and then some.
At it's core, Yooka Laylee is an N64 platformer, a genre of 20 years ago, and yet it still holds fantastically well and undeniably can survive in 2017 on a gaming platform. If this game were a litmus test for how well it works today. It passed with strong marks. Even the icing on the cake, the humor and the silly Britishisms, are still a good laugh after all this time.
Yooka Layee is esentailly a great platformer game in concept and partially there in delivery, but just under lack of manpower, working hours, and deadlines it is an unpolished, and not fully realized game.
These issues aside, it's core concept is great. With more resources available the next time around, we'll have a solid game on our hands.

So... having fully completed the game now I feel in a good position to write a review.
I've never played a Banjo-Kazooie game, but I'd seen others playing it for a short time and a minimal amount of game footage on various videos. Collect-a-thons have in the past been interesting and fun so I backed the Kickstarter for this game, and it's pretty much exactly what I had imagined it would be almost two years ago.
A phrase I've seen a lot in reviews and commentaries about the game's likeness to late-90s-era Rare-style games is "warts and all", and from the little I know that seems accurate.
The camera is definitely reminiscent of late-90s 3D cameras with an unhelpful lack of automation where it's needed and an annoying attempt at automating where it's not. But patches are coming, and I'm confident Playtonic are more than aware enough of the need for a review, if not various specific instances where it definitely needs reworking.
Level design is likeable overall; it's received a bit of criticism and at the halfway point I was bordering on agreeing with some of it, but after disliking world 3 at first it seriously grew on me and is possibly my favourite of the worlds now. Some complaints are that levels are too densely-packed and others are that they're too vast and empty. I think this is a case of reviews disagreeing on what they dislike, and I personally feel the balance struck is a good one. The levels flow well and mix well with the ability progression.
Another common complaint is that the first worlds feel larger and more detailed than the later ones, but I suspect this is symptomatic of the game's upgrade system. When you first play the earlier worlds you only have a few abilities, and need to return to them when you have the rest. With the last worlds you already have all abilities so there isn't that multiple-visits feeling.
While I do like the varied level design overall, I'd have to say the Dr. Puzz transformations are a bit of a low point. Their inclusion often feels tacked on, especially in worlds 1 and 3 where they do very little and have no contribution outside of that. The world 5 transformation makes up for some of this, though it also highlights the worst example of the transformation's accessibility and inability to be easily reverted.
Rather than the level design, what did cause me frustration was the design of the hub world. Definitely detailed but I feel slightly excessive to cover 5 worlds. More to the point it is not so much a hub in the sense of being able to quickly move between worlds, but a question-mark shaped loop where traveling between opposite worlds (say, worlds 1 and 4) takes quite a lot longer than it needs to and with no quick-jump. This discourages repeatedly revisiting old worlds when you get new abilities, which is oddly frustrating for a collect-a-thon.
Postscript to the above, I've since become aware that I totally missed a shortcut in the hub world from the entrance statue to World 3. This alleviates things a little, though it's still a bit of an issue unless I've missed others as well.
I feel a highlight of the game is the boss system; bosses are not screaming "I am the boss, over here!", sitting in an obvious boss room and needing a boss key to be attempted. They're almost hidden in the worlds and encountered quite naturally while collecting everything else. In two (I think) worlds you don't even need to expand the worlds to be able to find the boss, and this is refreshing. I really liked what they did with world 4 in particular, but world 5 was neat too.
As a counterpoint the minigames are very hit and miss. Karting is... awkward, but lenient so it should only take a few retries. The arcade games probably won't be remembered so well. One per world: World 1 is decent, worlds 2 and 3 are simple but a little bland, world 5 can be a little unforgiving and world 4's Hurdle Hijinx is getting a few complaints for good reasons; it is very unforgiving and for me the direction detection was over-sensitive and the thumbstick returning to the center would move the character back.
The worst part about the minigames though is that failing is frustrating. There is no quick retry option within the games themselves, only an exit that counts as finishing the game with a failing score. After that, players are forced to go through a series of dialogue that cannot be skipped before getting the option to try again. Much like a 90s game, true, but a quick retry would very much be a quality-of-life improvement rather than an out-of-place modernisation.
As characters Yooka and Laylee themselves aren't fleshed out all that much; Laylee is occasionally mercenary and I suppose Yooka is fairly high on the do-gooder scale, but beyond that I can't think of much that defines them. Without knowing Banjo-Kazooie I don't know if this is an omission from the old or more of the same.
The support cast are a mixed bag, but generally pretty cool. Against expectations I think my favourite might actually be Kartos, but Trowzer is up there as well. Capital B makes for an interesting villain, perhaps with the capitalism/business talk dialled up a little too much. I expect the knights of Hamalot will get a very mixed reception, and Vendi is rightly getting a lot of criticism for looking like a caricature of Mrs. Pacman's ugly grandmother.
Behind all this is a generally strong collection of dialogue. There are definitely a few misses within what is a very densely-packed mix of wit and comedy, which is probably inevitable and probably slightly caused by the higher standard of most of it.
Similarly the music is brilliant. Perhaps not memorably so (a day after putting the game down I'm struggling to remember more than the world 1 track) but none of it was ever annoying and it always felt perfectly fitting to the scenery of each world.
Overall a very enjoyable game, exactly what I had expected in terms of level style, music, atmosphere and tone, and overall difficulty. Playtonic have made a little noise about future games (particularly within the game itself!) and I'd definitely look forward to a sequel.

A few notes before I begin:
1. I played Banjo-Kazooie, Banjo-Tooie, DK64, and Conker's Bad Fur Day, and I loved all of them.
2. I backed this game on Kickstarter, but I didn't follow the game very closely and wasn't particularly hyped for it.
3. I didn't finish this game, so this is more of a review of the first 2 (of 5) worlds than the game as a whole.
I don't think I need to explain that Yooka-Laylee is a game that attempts to replicate the magic of N64 Rare platformers (specifically, Banjo-Kazooie). I have seen many people say that the game needs to be judged as a spiritual successor to those games, and that's exactly how I went into the game. However, what I got was an amaturishly-designed game (strange, given the pedigree of the developers) that failed to capture my nostalgia or interest for more than a fleeting moment.
This is the one part of the game that made me feel really nostalgic. Character dialogue is represented by talking heads accompanied by short sound-bytes (a la Banjo-Kazooie). Characters look and feel like they're right out of an N64 platformer. The humor, while not laugh-out-loud hilarious, is still charming and amusing. The music is pretty good, and, while not as good as some of Grant Kirkhope's previous work, still manages to capture the Banjo-Kazooie spirit. Overall, this is the best part of the game, and why I played for as long as I did.
Once I actually started playing the game, I quickly felt like something was off. I found myself unmotivated to collect things, and unmotivated to discover new areas (which is strange, because I usually love these aspects of games). Eventually, it became clear to me: the level design is bad. The worlds feel like large, stock areas with platforming challenges shoehorned in to random corners of the map. Getting to these challenges feels like a chore, as there are rarely more than a few quills on the path from one challenge to the next (if even that).
In addition, much of the terrain has collision when it clearly shouldn't. I repeatedly found myself getting to areas I was clearly not supposed to be in with my current abilities, and I kept following ledges only to find that there was literally nothing at the end of them. It even disrupts the existing platforming challenges (one level has a mound of snow at the edge of a platform that you can bump over when rolling, eating your jump and causing you to fall to your death).
Ultimately, the levels don't feel like Banjo-Kazooie to me. They feel like a shovelware platformer (the kind made in Unity from stolen assets).
Throughout the game, you gain various abilities. Most of these feel fine, though they're marred somewhat by the fact that many of them require power to work, which doesn't really make the game more difficult as much as it makes it more tedious. In addition, much like (you guessed it) Banjo-Kazooie, each stage has a transformation that is used to solve various puzzles. However, the two that I used felt TERRIBLE to use. The first was incredibly slow and had no useful abilities (other than one that gives you a pagie when you use it in certain places). The second controls like♥♥♥♥♥and made one platforming challenge an absolute nightmare, even when done slowly and carefully. I wanted to get out of these transformations as quickly as possible (which is a bad sign for something that's supposed to be FUN). I hear that one of the later ones is fun, but I can't comment on that.
In addition, some of the puzzles have very specific, non-obvious solutions. For example, what do you think would get rid of a pile of snow? Fire? EXPLOSIONS! NO! Those don't do anything! Turns out you have to unlock a transformation that lets you get rid of them! There are several situations like this, where I found myself spamming all of my abilities to no movement/impart whatsoever, only to find out I needed an ability I didn't have. I'm fine with needing to unlock new abilities to solve puzzles. I just don't appreciate when something looks like it should work, but doesn't.
The camera is a bit of a mixed bag. While, most of the time, I found it worked fine, there were moments where it was forced into a position I didn't want, which was immensely frustrating.
I went into this game with the intent of finishing it. However, as I kept playing, I found myself not having any fun. I honestly can't even remember how many Pagies and Quills I got on each level, and I didn't even care. It was a collect-a-thon platformer where I felt no desire to collect things.
Overall, I don't think I would've paid the $20 I backed this game for, and the game DEFINITELY isn't worth $40. I'm not sure if a sequel would improve upon the game's problems, given the fact that the developers probably should've known about these issues, since they've been making games for so long.

Super Meat Boy is a game that hates you and will mercilessly laugh in your face as you die thousands of times. And yet you have no-one to blame for your failure but yourself, and you'll spend hours trying to perfect your skills. With slick controls and a great style, it's a game that will challenge all those who fancy themselves to be experts at platformers.
Old school platformer that will send you back in your childhood and your controller in the screen.

Super Meat Boy is a game that keeps track of how many times you die and has to invent new numbers with which to do so.  Thankfully the enthusiasm and frantic energy with which Meat Boy hurls himself into the task keeps you from getting discouraged.  Do you call it a platformer if you spend more time attached to walls or flying through the air then you do on the ground?  Whatever it is, the jumping puzzles in this game require fast reflexes and  precision timing.  A high tolerance for failure helps, too.  When you do complete the level, though, your final run will be very impressive.  The game will automatically start a replay that you can save with the press of a button.  And should you manage to fight through the main game there are plenty of unlockable characters and dark world levels to keep you playing.  The soundtrack is great, too, even after you've been listening for a track loop for thrity mintues while you're stuck on a level.

A brutally hard indie platformer. You play the Super Meat Boy, a chunk of meat that can run very fast and stick to walls, leaving a bloody trail wherever he goes.
Each level has you navigating saws, salt, maggots, rockets, lava and many other obstacles, to rescue Bandage Girl from the evil Doctor Fetus.
Each of the 250ish levels has an easy and a hard version. There are also warp zones, which often have characters from other indie games and use their moves. More special characters can be obtained by grabbing bandages, which are usually found in the trickiest of places.
Usually you will die many times on a level, but this is all part of the fun. Restarting a level is instant and the controls are excellent, so dying never feels unfair. When a level has been completed all the attempts are shown simulataneously on screen, which is very amusing to watch.
The music is very well made and fits the game perfectly.

This game has a lot of good stuff in it, but also some weak spots.
Brief description of the game:
You are commanding a capital class ship in either a sandbox experience or a campaign with main missions. You will be flying around undertaking side missions and smaller assignments, upgrading your ship size and firepower.
First I will start with good things:
+ Proper 3D movement, your ship rotates in all directions
+ Huge map full of objects in space, except planets and space stations space is full of ships of various factions and other space objects like solar power plants, gas collectors, prisons, etc. All of those objects come with few designs so the feeling is that most of them are unique. In addition there are clouds of radiation of electric storms.
+ In dept ship command. In addition to guns your ship also has tractor beam (you can pull enemy ships), teleport and marines (you can board enemy ships and pull them to nearest station to sell them), launch bays for fighters, slots for various consumable items (bombs, AI turrets, boosters, repair bots etc)
+ Power management. You can direct power between 3 main areas of your ship - engines, weapons and shields by default power if directed 1/3 to each, but you can channel it to one of them in order to receive +100% bonus to speed, reload, recharge etc, at a cost of -% to others.
(PRO TIP: always channel power to engines when you fast travel for +100% boost, since you cannot shoot in this state anyway)
+ Large selection of ships and weapons as well as system upgrades to tweak your ship as you like it, weapon types are really different (plasma are slow firing, slow flying, high damage, high power consumption; laser are 100% accurate, quick firing, low damage; projectile are quick firing, medium damage, fast flying) as for missiles you can get some with huge area of effect or long distance small area of effect etc.
+ Campaign is not so bad, but lack of options, alternative solutions etc makes it a less fun.
Now to negatives:
- Bad voice acting
- Poor mission reward system - if you wanna buy new ships and top weapons you better learn to board enemy ships, do it for few hours at start then start campaign fully equipped. (for example: low level assassination task will give you 4-10k credits, while if you board enemy craft, kill the crew and pull it to space station you will get 80-120k plus you will complete the mission), just doing missions for money is mindless grind and gets boring really fast.
- Not involving space combat, this will require some longer explanation.
Your ship has turrets, shields and missile weapons in 4 sectors (front, aft, port and starboard). You can manually aim turrets, but odds of you hitting a tiny little black dot on black space around you are virtually none, the only thing you can hit manually are destroyed ship husks and space station with are not moving. So in order for your turrets to do anything you set them to auto-fire then they will randomly pick a target and shoot few bursts at it, then change target and go on. In the end during combat you can only select target and manually fire guided missiles at it and rotate your ship so that more turrets and fresh shields are facing the enemy. After 10h of playing this is damn boring !!!
- Not interesting PTE (power to engines, which is a form of quick flying), as to why it doesn't set power distribution to engines for 100% and has to be done manually for a nice speed boost is a wild guess. And you don't get this fancy visuals of super fast travel like we know from movies, it is just that, your ship travels faster.
Conclusion:
I recommend this game as it is quite fun to play for space exploration for 10-20h of fun, therefore I advice get it on discount because it is not worth 40€.
Then I advice you to learn how to board enemy ships quickly so you can make some good credits and try out weapons and ships.

It's a very *loose* yes as a recommendation to play this game. If you can get it on a good sale, then it can be a fairly fun experience running around a small system of planets, doing odd jobs, buying new ships, and upgrading weapons. There's some decent stories involved and the devs have made some nice DLC's available for pretty cheap/free.
Downside: this game is buggy as hell when it comes to the control scheme, especially if you want to use a controller with the game. I happen to like using a controller; I feel like it's very relaxing and I can kick back in a chair. Using an Xbox One controller with this game, (or any controller) is going to lead to a hell of a lot of mapping issues that don't get resolved easily.
Also, loading up the DLC's can be kind of weird, since you're selectively activating them. Unlike games like Skyrim, where you can just roll up and jump into a DLC once you add it to your game with whatever save file you're using, this game like to cordon off the DLC's and have you jump sandbox to sandbox. They can be fun, but it's not always ideal.
That all being said... there's a ton of ships in this game and ways to arm them out. Whatever your playstyle, you'll eventually captain a ship that meets your needs, whether that be overwhelming destructive force, a carrier that houses a fleet, or a ship that can drop out of stealth and put the hurt on. It can be pretty addictive. It can ALSO be extrememly repetitive. You mileage may vary!
Final Verdict: yes, I'd recommend this game, but it really will appeal only to a specific type of gamer.

This game has several issues, but a few good points, which I will list.
Storyline: The campaign is your standard 'fight the Empire' campaign. It's not very interesting and honestly, is not enough to keep you locked into the game.
Missions: Escort, kill, transport, scan. That's it. There isn't much to do and not much fun in doing it unless you really enjoy grinding the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of ships.
Speaking of ships: They are expensive, as are the systems that use them. So get used to grinding for scrap material to sell for every single credit you can because my god is everything so expensive. You will be a higher grade officer on a ship that is well below your experience level. I guarantee it.
Combat: You can take control of the canons yourself. Don't know why you would though. Camera controls in that mode make it useless and the autoaim is about 10x better than you will ever be at shooting other ships.
Abilities: Marginally useful depending on the situation but unless you have the repair ability you aren't playing the right class.
Now onto the positive stuff. Mods! Lots of really good mods to alter combat, add ships, and improve the cosmetics and trading. It really does make it a lot more fun to play when your ship isn't moving like and old woman up a hill all the time. Plus it makes it easier to get good weapon systems. The problem is, modding the game makes it very unstable. You will crash more than a Bethesda game.
TLDR: If you are looking for a discount Elite Dangerous or Star Citizen, keep looking. This is not the game you want.

Pros
+ Enough complexity for you to keep learning new features, but not so much that its frustrating.
+ Great replayability.

+ The art style - I normally don't care for this, but Klei's games are expectations. They have somehow been able to give each of their games a unique style, while at the same time maintaining a consistent style across games.
I would also give an upvote to the developer. Klei is one of my favourites, and they have been able to produce high-quality games again and again.

From my time playing rust people have always cried over changes, From the Blueprint system -> XP -> Components These changes were major parts of the game but guess what? It made the game better in my eyes making it so everyone is equal. The P2 ( Pistol ) Used to be an amazing gun but it was really cheap, After it was nerfed people ♥♥♥♥♥ed over it but what do they expect due to the price of it. Also, The aimcone... In my eyes this has a positive and a negative. Positive = They made an aimcone so hackers and players have an equal chance... But the Negative = Everyone knows how to control an ak spray now.
Now don't get me wrong its not bad that everyone can do this now. But ak used to be used by skillful players who knew how to control it meaning they had the advantage. Now the ak is all Random number now due to the aimcone. But who cares, We will adapt to it eventually.
Seriously, If you buy rust you will not regret it, First hop onto a modded and learn the basics, Once you've understood the concept and how to play and maybe meet a few friends start to play vanilla ( Weekly, Bi-Weekly, Monthly ) And you will enjoy it due to everything having value and you will not just constantly roam. I suggest playing on servers like Rustafied and Rustopia personally due to them being high pop and having good wipe schedules for everyone, EU Odd ( Wipes every monday ), EU Main / Medium ( Main = 1 Week wipes on thursdays, Medium = 2 week wipes on thursdays )
Now to everyone thinking of buying rust, Buy it now and I hope to see you all around in the future. I wish you and your keyboard and mouse the best of luck...

This game is both infuriating and super enthralling at the same time. I find myself so absorbed into keeping my house fortified and weaponized, my gear modded and lethal, that I forget how many hours have passed. This is quite a game.
I've heard a few people say that the player base is toxic and cancerous, but I've had pretty good interactions all around. On day one, with no clue what I was doing, a player stopped and helped me organize my house so it wouldn't get torn down every two seconds. He also provided me with supplies and traps. Few other games have sported players that would go out of their way to do that for you. The reviews by people saying that this community is cancer are probably written by people who are cancerous themselves.
This game does have flaws, like every other early version game, but I am okay with that as long as it's core gameplay keeps me coming back for more. The A.I. is somewhat lackluster and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ right now, but the player base more than makes up for that. It's also a bit of a taxing game on your computer, so make sure you address that before you start the game. Also, this is not a game for people easily deterred by having all of their stuff broken or stolen. You have to be a little resilient to see a proper base through to completion in the game, a factor which scares many noobs away. Don't give into that, and you'll enjoy the game.
All things said, I recommend the game. Just keep track of how much time has passed. It is a major time sink.

I said some dissapointing things about Arkham Origins about four hours in.  The characters seemed lackluster, the building grappling was a bit spotty, and the combat felt out of rythym.  Then I tried to remember that this was a more or less untrained Batman, still getting the feel of taking on ten guys with knives and baseball bats at once and gliding through the city skies with nothing but a grappling hook and a fancy cape.  It actually gets pretty good about a third of the way in.
The new Crime Scene feature seems like a hassle the first time you do it, it's so slow and methodical.  Then about the second or third time around it starts to get fun.  Scrobbling back and forth on the timeline to look for clues- or just little red triangles- is kind of fun and a nice break from punching thugs and dodging machine gun fire.
It helps to think of it as more of a "Long Halloween" Batman than a follow-up to the previous Arkham titles.  Asylum and City were built around the more coloful rogues gallery with Mr. Freeze and Poison Ivy and those types.  Origins focuses more on the human angle of both the hero and the villains; their motivations and weaknesses.
The script is absolutely top notch, and the writers- Corey May and Dooma Wendschuh of the Assassin's Creed series- absolutely NAILED the Joker.  There are different takes on Batman's most famous antagonist, and these guys went for the scary as hell version.  This is the Joker that put Barbara Gordon in a wheelchair and beat Robin Number 2 nearly to death with a crowbar before blowing him up with a bomb.  It's my favorite Joker, truth be told.  I do wonder at the missed opportunity to introduce a pre-accident Harvey Dent, especially since his future self featured so prominently in Arkham City.
I know this entry in the Arkham Series was supposed to tide us over until a "proper" Rocksteady release in a year or two, but I'd play another Origins title without question.  What I'd really like to see these guys do next though is a Batgirl Origins.
C'mon guys.  Seriously, it's time for a Batgirl game.  You can get Natalie Lander fresh off her sick turn as Kinzie Kensington from Saints Row.  DO IT.

The best pool experience on a computer that I know of.
9-ball, 8-ball and Straight games are available together with a couple of for-fun modes (speed-potting, lose-a-life-when-you-miss etc.) and endurance (a "survival mode" with extra balls appearing on the table with increasing speed).
The game makes it easy to execute the shots you know how to perform in theory (e.g. swerve, jump or back-spin with the 9-ball as a secondary target - and there are tutorials for those), if you just take your time with the available features (such as first-person/top-down view toggle or fine-tuning mode for precise aiming even at table-long distances) and do the necessary adjustments of shot power, spin and butt angle. The balls rebound (from cushions and other balls) in angles depending both on their spin and speed, and the cue ball's trajectory before the first impact (including jumps) can be made visible in different degrees, depending on the novice-to-expert settings.
The default control settings turned out to be very practical once being used to, but custom key-binding can be set up. I would like the option of 9-ball games with more than 2 players, but the already available multiplayer options are very nice (whether on a single computer or over network). Whole matches can be archived for replay (I am not sure whether single shots can). Extensive trick-shot options and snooker are supposedly coming in the (near?) future.
For any pool-lover that can afford it, I would consider this game a must-have. I got it myself in 90 % discount, but would now take it even for the full price.
(Also, the visuals are great and the single-player opponents are funny at times.)

I enjoy how simple it is to build a prison, there's an option to plan it in a blueprint sort of way, or you can dive right in with building concrete walls.  In the space of 20 minutes you've build the basic necessities and a few cells. You bring in some prisoners, and everything is fine.  Then you think "I want more prisoners.  I want to build Alcatraz or Sing Sing" so you build more cells, and more cells.  You intake more prisoners, and boom you need more showers, and a bigger canteen.  By the time you know it, that "I'll just have an hour on it has turned into 6 hours, 90 prisoners, 12 murdered guards, 4 escapees, and 1 riot.  This game forces you to become addicted to it (not like that's a bad thing, not at all!) as prisoners need more stuff like a laundry or library to stop them rioting.
I'm up to 42 hrs on this game, City Skylines less than an hour.

I won this in a giveaway, and I try to play and finish every game I win. Unfortunately, the game is bug-ridden as heck.
It seems to be purely dependent on luck if the achievements do or don't unlock for you. After completing the first tutorial, the internal achievement unlocked for me, but the Steam achievement did not.
A quick look at the logfile showed a possible cause:
"TSteamManager::InitializeManager(): error: could not get key from steam. disconnecting"
Going back into the game, the internal achievement has vanished, and does not show again upon finishing the tutorial again.
As I understand it, the problems started back in 2014 when UIG changed something about their DRM. For some it works, for others it doesn't. And for those for whom the achievements do work, they unlock seemingly randomly.
UIG is infamous for their lack of support. Do not expect this to be fixed in the future.
Stay clear if you like 100% achievements on your games.

Well, here I go... Ahem, Undertale is a simplistic Comedy RPG (meaning it relies more on humor and dialogue/lore to give a story, It isn't even supposed to be a "RPG" per say.) It's kind of like Earthbound's quirky, dumb but still good younger brother. (The fanbase... Isn't really cancerous actually. I don't know how it was when you played the game, but for all I know, I had to actively search for cancer to find it, if your disturbed by all the porn then WHY THE HELL ARE YOU ON RULE 34? But chances are you had to GET ON THE INTERNET to attract that cancer. There are three endings, Pacifist/Neutral/genocide. I'm not one of those people that judges you for wich ending you chose. There are 27 seperate neutral endings, each adding on a hint of lore. There is a bunch of easter eggs (SOME of which refer to Earthbound). It isn't suppose to rely off of Traditional RPG tropes (Infact, it even makes fun of and parodies some RPG tropes). I can see how people say its "Overated" but that still doesn't particularly mean it's a BAD game, it's called perspective and preferance people. The humor, while lowbrow at times, is pretty funny. The fighting mechanics are... HORRIBLE! But the fighting mechanics aren't technically supposed to be GOOD, you see that's why it's called "The RPG where no one HAS to die." The soundtrack is phenominal, although it is heavily reliant on leitmotifs (And I mean, what videogame/movie/TV show hasn't been completely reliant on leitmotifs?) it is barely recognizable with how much reworking is put into each piece. The characters, although exagerated and over the top, have subtleties to their character that make them way more in depth and realistic/relatable. The thing I find fond most about games like these is how self-aware the games are. A little bit spoily but, the game breaks the fourth wall 10 seconds in to the game. People may argue that the Game looks super "Crappy." I have to back it up by saying, that in the Undertale Conceptual book, the creator of the game "Toby Fox" even admitted to how it looked crappy and that he wasn't trying to make a flashy extravagent game like some may lead you to believe. It's just one guy( As well as Temmie Chang) who made a silly knockoff of Earthbound that gained more funds then they expected for their kickstarter, He wasn't going for a GREAT game in the first place. And even during the developement, there was more comments about the concept art in the Undertale art book that futher proved that Toby didn't wan't to make the best looking, or greatest game on Earth. His comment was "Everyone says the protagonist's sprite looks terrible. That's right. If it looks good, you'll have a different expectation of the game." Meaning that he wasn't wanting the game to be expected of as some sort of MASTERPIECE, It's just a quirky comedy RPG that gained a little too much of a fandom. The thing I also love about this game is how it is a sad and disturbing game hidden by a facade of dumb jokes and crappy designs. I just love all the disturbing dialogue, SPOILER ALERT, like San's depression, Alphy's suicidal tendencies, The ending of ENTIRE timeline's at the hand of a demonic child, DONT EVEN GET ME STARTED ON GASTER. All these subtle undertones make the game extremely more enjoyable, throwing comic relief at you one moment, only to explain a bunch of horrific, depressing, and creepy lore the next. Along with the creepy lore and fourth wall breaking, the main attractions are the moral system and permanent consequences.(without hacking the game or redownloading it) I would recommend playing this game if your not looking for a standard RPG, because this is a comedy RPG, a genre of RPG more reliant on humor than engaging battle systems and fancy graphics. (AND THATS HOW YOU CONSTRUCTIVELY CRITICIZE WITHOUT SOUNDING LIKE AN OBSESSED FANBOY/FANGIRL OR A BLIND HATER HATING JUST FOR THE SAKE OF HATING) (Don't believe how long it says I've played this game, a glitch occured that reset all my playtime for all my game's)

Starpoint Gemini 2 is an enjoyable Space Sim, and still looks good for its age, but I wouldn't grab it for the $35 price. It's definitely a game to buy on sale though. Some key points:
1. This is a combat focused game. Don't bother trying to be a trader; it won't work, and you can't automate the process like in X3.
2. Along 1 above, the primary way you can make money in this game is capturing ships. Unless you want to end up outclassed, learn how to use your troopers and grappling beam.
3. The progression through the classes of ships is well balanced; each feels like an improvement, without any of them feeling redundant.
4. Each class of ship does feel unique, and the methodology of flying and fighting in a corvette is distinctly different than in a dreadnought.
5. The different models of ships in each class are also rather distinct from one another, and will play well with different tactics. For instance, one ship may have great overlapping fire arcs between the side and front turrets, but have hardly any coverage on the top bottom and the back, while another will offer ballanced coverage over the whole ship, but can't offer the same forward punch.
5. Ye gods, the voice acting is TERRIBLE, and the plot is a throw away at best. This wasn't a big issue for me, as the game is mostly free-roam.

This is the best example of the Hitman forumla at work. The large open sandbox style levels of Blood Money combined with the sharp stealth controls of Absolution. Combat is unfortunately not a viable option as it was in Absolution, so you might as well reload at these points. There is a lot of nay-say about the fact that this is an episodic game; but any review by a steam user that complains about this, bought the game with full knowledge of the fact and thus should not complain simply on that point alone. The arguement is whether the current offering is substantial for what you paid. If you buy the intro pack alone and hate it, then you are not going to be sold by the future missions because you have experienced what Hitman has to offer in a nutshell. I have played 7 hours thus far and completed the Paris mission in 3 different ways; yet I find myself wanting to perfect it and try every possible combination. Therefore I have every confidence that the the full experience will live to its potential when it completes this year and potentially expands into 2017. I Actually I feel that the episodic nature helps the game. It encourages you to milk every possible outcome and try each mission in multiple ways where arguably if you had the full experience on launch, you'd probably blitz through it in one sitting and not take the time to explore all of the possibilities available (or even play the game a second time). This is the way that gaming is heading unfortunately, but if other titles follow by Hitman's example they will be more refined experiences in the long run. It's a slippery slope and undoubtedly a lot of companies will abuse this model, but this game is not an example of that.

Banjo Kazooie and Banjo Tooie were my favorite games on the N64, and aside from Megaman X, Banjo is my favorite series. All the delightful weirdness and vibrance I came to associate with Rare was gone and we were left with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ uninspired driving game that tried to be Mario Kart and Vigilante 8 and Bamjo Kazooie and a Lego game at the same time but failed at everything.  I was really worried about how Yooka-Laylee would turn out because the other kickstarted spiritual successor I was looking forward to, the Mighty No. 9, was a big letdown.
I'm glad to say this is the true successor to Banjo Tooie that I've wanted since I was 10. It feels just like Banjo Kazooie, the music and atmostphere are great,  the controls are tight and responsive, the worlds are huge and the game definitely feels like it belongs in this generation. There are lots of classic Rare-style easter eggs and references to the old games, and I especially like the jokes/jabs at Microsoft (some are suble, others not so much). It sets the bar for modern platformers. Aside from Mario games, which are fun but have all felt like the same game over and over again since 2006, platforming is a dead genre. I've missed it and I'm glad that YL is such a solid addition to the genre. Maybe we'll see more AAA platformers and not be flooded with endless FPS's and open world survival games.

Surprisingly well-polished (literally, in the case of the pool balls) with a decent number of game modes and a nice amount of customisation over controls. Physics are very well done, graphics are surprisingly good, gameplay is... well, it's pool through and through.
However, the game is unfortunately currently limited to 1v1 online. Whilst it's nice to have online play available at all, the game is definitely not living up to its potential in this regard. The inclusion of 4+ player modes would be most welcome - championships, perhaps?

Recommended.
Depending on what you're looking for the single player campaigns are lacking.  There are a lot of opponents but they felt very identical to play against.  However, I wasn't working towards the challenges against each opponent and going for those could be fun, although they're usually pretty same-y (x match score, x-ball streak).  Additionally, there are actual stand-alone challenges but of the few I played they were pretty boring.  While they did break up gameplay when I found it necessary, the AI is so unpredictable  that modes like speed challenge or 3 ball just aren't that much fun.
As a 8-Ball and 9-ball simulator, though, this game is pretty excellent.  The physics work, there's a guiding shot marker to help  you learn how to shoot better (this can also be turned off, or reduced) and the game is pretty.  Pool Nations ia  large step up from those crappy flash games.
Online play seems functional.  At the very least I didn't have any issues with it.  For online play there are a lot of interesting game modes past 8 and 9 ball including 3 ball, straight, rotation, speed, and killer.  Of those I only tried killer (possibly speed in the campaign) and it was fun, though it felt more like a quick distraction between a few rounds of 8 ball.
So yes, I recommend this game.  It's much, much better for me than driving down to the Pool Hall, especially when I can't guarantee I'll have anyone to play.  This is something I needed in my life and it's nice to have, but I also recognize that it's probably not for everyone.  I've only played a handful of times and only for a few hours total.  It's definitely a pick up and play for a few rounds and then put it down for a few weeks kind of game, though that is exactly what I wanted.
Oh, and I guess there are features that haven't been implemented yet but are on their way like the box of tricks.  That mode seems fairly interesting.

I said some dissapointing things about Arkham Origins about four hours in.  The characters seemed lackluster, the building grappling was a bit spotty, and the combat felt out of rythym.  Then I tried to remember that this was a more or less untrained Batman, still getting the feel of taking on ten guys with knives and baseball bats at once and gliding through the city skies with nothing but a grappling hook and a fancy cape.  It actually gets pretty good about a third of the way in.
The new Crime Scene feature seems like a hassle the first time you do it, it's so slow and methodical.  Then about the second or third time around it starts to get fun.  Scrobbling back and forth on the timeline to look for clues- or just little red triangles- is kind of fun and a nice break from punching thugs and dodging machine gun fire.
It helps to think of it as more of a "Long Halloween" Batman than a follow-up to the previous Arkham titles.  Asylum and City were built around the more coloful rogues gallery with Mr. Freeze and Poison Ivy and those types.  Origins focuses more on the human angle of both the hero and the villains; their motivations and weaknesses.
The script is absolutely top notch, and the writers- Corey May and Dooma Wendschuh of the Assassin's Creed series- absolutely NAILED the Joker.  There are different takes on Batman's most famous antagonist, and these guys went for the scary as hell version.  This is the Joker that put Barbara Gordon in a wheelchair and beat Robin Number 2 nearly to death with a crowbar before blowing him up with a bomb.  It's my favorite Joker, truth be told.  I do wonder at the missed opportunity to introduce a pre-accident Harvey Dent, especially since his future self featured so prominently in Arkham City.
I know this entry in the Arkham Series was supposed to tide us over until a "proper" Rocksteady release in a year or two, but I'd play another Origins title without question.  What I'd really like to see these guys do next though is a Batgirl Origins.

First and foremost, unlike previous Arkham titles, Origins was not developed by Rocksteady Studios. Do not go into Origins expecting the same level of quality, as it simply isn't operating on the same level as previous titles.
Arkham Origins was developed in-house by Warner Bros. Games Montreal, a studio who's only previous development credit is the Wii U port of Batman: Arkham City.
In terms of gameplay, Batman: Arkham Origins apes Rocksteady's games as closely as possible. However, the combat and environmantal traversal systems are fundamentally broken by back-end code changes. The rhythmic, dance-like free-flow combat of past games that rewarded skill, and punished button-mashers, has been re-worked, dumbed-down and tailor-made to appease those who were never any good at Asylum and City, and will immediately irk players who've mastered combat in those games. To counter-act the watered down fisticuffs, WB Montreal has increased the number of enemies that will engage Batman in combat at any given time to ridiculous levels in some cases, which would be fine, if countering actually worked as it did in the original games. You can counter upto 3 enemies at a time, so when a group of 6 thugs all decide to attack at once, it doesn't matter how many time you hit the counter button, you're going to get hit and any momentum you've built up will be lost. You'll frequently be knocked out of a combo after multiple hits by the very assailant you're attacking or an offscreen enemy who's decided to throw something at you.
Navigating around Gotham is also a major issue that will be immediately apparent to anyone who's familiar with past titles. The areas of Gotham that eventually become Arkham City are essentialy the same, save for the fact that Batman's grapnel gun doesn't seem to work on roughly half the buildings anymore. The same goes for the areas new to Arkham Origins, which unfortunately isn't as well laid out and seems designed to be as unmemorable and bland as possible, which leads to easy confusion when trying to discern where to go next as every building looks the same.
Story wise, the game fares a little better. There are some genuinely interesting ideas at play in Arkham Origins, mostly concerning one villains psyche and relationship with Batman, but too few of them get fully fleshed-out. The entire setup of the game, the worlds best assassins all out to get Batman all at once, makes up roughly 10% of the total game and fans of certain characters (deathstroke especially) will feel cheated by how little actual screen-time they get (some aren't even featured in the main storyline at all, instead remanded to menial side-quests).
Finally, I'd be remiss for not mentioning the voice acting. By now everyone should be aware that neither Kevin Conroy or Mark Hamill reprise the iconic roles of Batman and Joker, respectively, despite the fact that they've become synonomous with those roles after playing them for more than 20 years. Replacing them are Roger Craig Smith (Ezio of the Assassin's Creed series) as Batman and Troy Baker (Booker of Bioshock Infinite/Joel of The Last of Us) as The Joker. Smith is fine as Batman, if completely bland and forgettable. Troy Baker is the star of the show here, chanelling as much of Hamill's Joker as possible while still giving it his own flare and completely owning every line. It's a remarkable highlight in an otherwise unremarkable experience. Much of the supporting cast from previous games has returned, playing the same characters (such as Martin Jarvis as Alfred and Nolan North as Penguin) and most do a respectable job with the largely terrible dialogue they're given. Special mention should be given to actress Laura Waddell, who plays Tracey (one of Penguins henchwomen) for doing possibly the absolute worst, cartoonishly awful Cockney accent ever recorded. It's astounding how bad it is, moreso considering Ms. Waddell is, in fact, british herself.
What you're left with is a game that wants so badly to be a true Arkham game, but lacks the fundamental understanding of what makes Rocksteady's entries so good. I'm sure there's a studio more than capable of equalling what Rocksteady built with Asylum and City, but WB Montreal isn't it, a sad fact that's readily apparent in nearly every aspect of Arkham Origins. Do yourself a favor, just play through Arkham City again while waiting for Rocksteady's return with their next Batman game sometime in 2014.
Addemdum: I did not mention the numerous glitches and game-breaking bugs that I was plagued with during my initial playthrough of Arkham Origins, as they've largely been fixed thanks to post-release patching. I am told the game still has it's issues, though they're relatively minor compared to what players experienced in the first few weeks of release.

A definite step down from the two amazing games set in the Arkham setting of Batmanverse. When Asylum introducted us to the great atmosphere and mechanisms of the game and Arkham City polished all of them to a perfect shine, made the explorable world bigger and yet still filled to the brim with things to do and collect and see, Arkham Origin is not only pointlessly bloated but also feel much, much more clunkier than any of the previous games - and to be honest, in every possible aspect of the game!
Free Flow Combat is somehow damaged. I can't really tell you a simple explanation why, but it just feel /off/ - Batman tend to kick and hit the air from time to time for no actual reason. Counters sometimes do not work. Double Counters do not work quite often! Deflecting sharp weaponry also rarely work well - yes, some could say "Hey, I bet you are doing it wrong!" and maybe so, but in Arkham City I had no issues with it, so I can't just blame the skills. Batman simply do not react in the free flow combat the way he used to. Not to mention the thugs are sometimes confusing to read their movements as well. Don't get me wrong, it's still a a good combat and addition of new enemy types really help to make each encounter a bit more challenging and fun, but still prefer the smooth mechanics of previous game here.
Bigger map! Yay? Nope. It is bigger, significantly so, but what about it, when a lot of the huge building aren't even crossable? Yup, the 'cold winter wind' will turn you back as soon as you try to fly over the monoliths of Gotham. Not to mentions a lot of city sections are pretty much empty and serve no purpose. I can count at least half a hundred time I had to cross the god-damn bridge. It's great they added the Fast Travel option, but it should be a help to get somewhere quickly, not the /MAIN/ tool of moving around, right?
Story is actually pretty fun and contains plenty of neat moments, but still, the point that it is a bit... Silly in it's idea, that Batman met a huge lot of his main antagonists in a single night is a lit pressing, not to mention sometimes you /feel/ in the game that the whole plot is nothing more than an excuse to throw some kind of Meanie at the Bat-pants. And it could be alright! Really! If not the raging disappoitnment that only /one/ boss battle is actually a riveting experiance. Adding random thugs to a boss fight is not making it a harder kind of challenge. It just make it frustrating... Not to mention most bosses are basically 'repeat a move, dodge their big attack, then beatdown'. Deathstroke is a joke. One of the most deadly character in the DC universe turned into a disappointing event. So is lady Shiva and Deadshot, really crappy bosses. It saddens me to the bone. It really feels like the game designers had no idea how to make a good, thrilling fight with a boss and went by the easiest solution of beating the crap out of them with Fists of Justice.
Another issue is the fact that we do not FEEL the atmosphere the game should press upon us - I, as Batman, never felt hunted by the elite assassins even once in this game. They could make this idea work, they could make Deathstroke and others harrass Bat-pants through the whole story, but no, that would be too hard, right? Instead we just meet an assasin and then kick his or her butt. Boring as it only can be. In Arkham City we felt the pressure, we felt the changes in envirnoment as the story move onwards, we felt the time ticking as Strange constantly reminded us of the hours left until his plan will be enacted. Here we do not feel anything of the sort. No thrill. No fun.

I want to start off by saying I really enjoy this game.  I have played a lot of Hitman: Blood Money and Hitman: Absolution over the years and really enjoy this series.  (Hitman Blood Money is definitely my favorite though.)
Pros:
- It has very fun gameplay.  After playing this game for a few hours I have found that I really enjoyed playing the game.  Sure it isn't as fun as Blood Money but it still is a great game.
- If you are running DX11 it performs really well and has decent graphics.  Now this is no Uncharted 4 or Witcher 3 Maxed out but it still looks and runs well.
- It got rid of the point system.  One of the things I didn't like about Absolution is the point system so I am glad they got rid of it.
- Several different ways to take people out.  One thing about Absolution is it was just to linear.  I am glad they brought back a more open map where you don't feel like you are being guided down a path.
Cons:
- The story so far has not interested me. It is only episode 1 (more on episode stuff in a second) and it has the potential to get better. However, I still believe that a story should grab you during the first part otherwise what will keep you sticking around?  Absolution had a great story, starting from the first mission, and I wish that this Hitman would be the same in that way.
- The one thing that most people don't like about this game: Episodes.  I was very opened minded about this and I thought at first it was a great idea but now I play the game I don't like it.  I just don't understand why this route was taken.  I honestly would of rather waited a few extra months and get the full experience rather than playing one mission and then waiting a month for the next.  I love episodic games like The Walking Dead S1 and 2, Life is Strange, etc. but this is not a good fit for this franchise.
- Holy crap DirectX 12 is buggy in this game.  I had to switch back to DX11 because while using DX12 (on my Windows 10 PC) it not only ran poorly but it also crashed all the time.  I couldn't get past the first training mission.  Also there was a horrible performance loss.  I ended up gaining about 30-40 fps when switching to directx11.  I am currently running an i7 3770k OC at 4.4 GHz and 2 ASUS 980's (OC Edition 4GB) [SLI] if you are curious.
Overall I would say definitely get this game but don't run DX12.  I had a lot of fun with it but it could be better.

I'm going ahead and making my first review EVER to ardently defend this game, so let that be established up-top in case somebody's looking for bias, because I might have it - I played and loved Blood Money to death, so naturally this game is directly up my alley and delivers what Absolution didn't. This review is going to take the format of a response to this game's criticisms, because my main motivation in writing this review is to illustrate my own confusion as to why this has mixed reviews.
My understanding is that people are super upset that this game is episodic and that, therefore, the first episode contains only one 'real' stage and two tutorial stages. I can understand how that would upset people who somehow thought that wasn't what they were getting...but if you're at all familiar with episodic series like Life is Strange or any of the Telltale Games, why are you upset about this? It was never presented as anything other than what it is.
Further, if game length is the concern, that basically tells us what kind of game you wanted to play. In this latest Hitman, if you are a one-and-done kind of killer, then this first episode will be done in about 2 hours - the approximate length of an episode of Life is Strange, but nobody was upset about that. Unlike Life is Strange, this game could have a great deal of replayability, should you be interested in experimentation.
The one 'real' stage is a masterpiece of level crafstmanship, with more details and methods of entry, attack and escape than were ever available in any stage of Blood Money. Fans of the series should be floored by the care that went into this one stage and the TONS of voice acting that went into bringing it to life. Instead, it seems like a lot of players just completed the level once and were done. Why? I have put in TWENTY-FIVE HOURS playing this stage, completing challenges. I haven't even really touched Contracts yet, but I plan to start making some.
The always-online DRM complaint I can understand far more than the length complaint, but that frustration just hasn't happened to affect me very much. Square Enix's servers died twice on me and booted me out, and I was and am STILL pretty salty about how saves can't be converted online to offline...but is that a dealbreaker? I don't see why it would be, unless your internet connection is prone to shorting out. I don't like it by any means, but I can deal with it, because this first episode has me very much impressed.

There are issues with always online, challanges not registering properly etc. However all of that can and will hopefully be fixed. What can not be altered after release is the core gameplay experience, which is excellent.

Solid AAA game. Sweet mixture of driving + fighting with some racing, scouting, story, drama, swear words ...
It feels like it has too much of side-content (not directly related to story or missions) and become quite repetitive at the end: defusing mines (30 encounters is waaaay too many, only first 15 mines are fun, rest 75 is booring), clearing camps, scarecrows.
Point is: you learn about 90% of game in first few (1-3) encounters and the rest is a boring repetition. Only occasionally game suprises with unexpected mechanic or encounter. E.g. one camp had elevator to move up, it took me 20 min to realise it's not non-interactive environment and I actually have to use it..
Racing is easy, but.. big but.. the balance is poor. In general all death races are VERY easy with archangels (boost + weapons), while first car in the list to beat it is sometimes VERY hard. Some routes required studying by failng race several times to find working shortcuts. Race during night is really poor experience, especially when car has NO lights.. ><
Quests: some are very unclear/poorly designed, including main quest where you have to build your first archangel. NOT a single player is capable to complete it without googling.
I must admit one good thing: encouters are varying enough. You will not notice copy/paste, because there is none. Searching for valuables is fun and sometimes hard (e.g. a symbol located on the back of the letter on the roof, or well hidden container).. though for my taste it's too easy. I'd enjoy having more puzzles, having to scout more.
On-foot combat is intuitive and simple, yet satisfactory. I generally dislike melee characters in games, but in Mad Max it was very fun.
Cinematics and story are ok. Not too impressive, but good enough.
I definitely recommend this game to everyone, who enjoy games like latest far cry, tomb raider, gta and wanted to experience something similar but in post-appocalypse word. Though I am not sure if many will decide to finish it (as it may become too repetitive).

This review is for the game ''Max Payne'',a third-person shooter video game
,developed by the video game company Remedy Entertainment.
The game was published by Gathering of Developers
(now known as Gathering,a daughter company of Take-Two Interactive) in North America
and 3D Realms in Europe on July 2001 for Microsoft Windows.
and released in Semptember 22 on 2006(in Europe).
The game can be run through Microsoft Windows,Playstation 2,Xbox,Game Boy Advance,Mac OS,iOS & Android.
The game uses the MAX-FX 1.0.
Genre(s):Third-person shooter
Mode(s):Single-player
Distribution:CD-ROM,DVD,cartridge,digital download.
Plot
The game takes place in New York city,in December 2001,where you take control of a former NYPD officer and a renegade DEA (Drug Enforcement Administration),Max Payne,who's being arrested by the police at the top of a skyscraper.
While he is being arrested he experiences a flashback which explains his life story and why he is being chased.
On August 22. 1998 NYPD detective,Max payne,just finishing his work goes home only to find his wife and his newborn daughter,Rose,brutally murdered.Max kills the junkies responsible for the murder of his loved ones but he is too late.After that incident he transfers to DEA in order to find out who is responsible and ultimately take revenge.
The game's content majority takes place during the last two days while Max is operating inside the Punchinello Mafia family,under the Don Angelo Punchinello(family's head),responsible for the trafficking of the Valkyr drug.After given a message to meet Alex(his Dea contact and Max's best friend) Max find Alex on the NYC Rosco Subway Station.His arrival at the Station results in encountering Jack's Lupino mobster group(Punchinello's crime family underboss)who were attempting an armed robbery.There he will come in contact with Aesir Corporation(just company bonds),a mysterious New York corporation,who is bound to play an important role on the story later on.
Later on Max Payne will come in contact with Alex who informs him that Max has been exposed by a mole in the Punchinello family.Seconds later Alex gets killed by a possible Killer Suit(Aesir's corporation hitmen).To make things worse Payne becomes suspect because of the fact that he is still an undercover,therefore an enemy,and is now chased by both the Punchinello crime family and also by the Deputy Chief Jim Bravura.
Succeding the Station's events he goes to a Lupino's motel where he finds and kills the Finito Brothers(Vinnie's Gognitti subordinate).After that Max travels in one of Lupino's bars,finds the diary of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥,Candy,and the fact that he sends video tapes of her and a mysterious <<one-eyed Alfred>>(an important figure later on).Eventually Max finds and kills Rico Muerte(a former hitman working for Punchinello) and Candy.In the bar Max found the location of Gognitti.
After chasing Gognitti from his apartment through the city and the subway,Max learns about a nightclub named Ragna Rok.There Max spares Gognitti and Max proceeds in killing the so called ''antichrist'' Lupino.After killing him and his men he encounters Mona Sax,Lisa's Punchinello twin sister and contract killer,who sedates Max by throwing something in his drink,telling him that she wants to kill the Don too.
After a dream about his family's death he wakes up and manages to escape the Mafia base and after that he finds himself in the bar where he earlier killed Rico Muerte.There Max finds Frank "The Bat" Niagara who had captured Max and was going to kill him.After these events Max is approached by Vladimir Lem(Russian's mafia leader and Punichinello's prime enemy) and is proposed a brief alliance.With Vlad's help Max seizes the cargo ship Charon and kills Boris Dime,a Punchinello subordinate(former Lem's subordinate),and arranges a meeting in Don's restaurant,only to bee a set up resulting in the bombing of the place and the killing of the rest of Punchinello's men(by Max Payne of course).
Max Payne,then,heads for Punchinello's residence only to find and kill the Trio(Vince Mugnaio,
Pilate Providence (AKA "Big Brother"),and Joe "Deadpan" Salem) Don's most feared hitman group.Max later finds the corpse of the Don's wife(Mona's twin sister) and discovers that the Don is just a pawn for the Aesir Corporation.The Don is killed by the agents of Nicole Horne,the Ceo,and Payne is being injected an overose of the Valkyr drug.Payne then suffers nightmares about his family but manages to survive the dosage.
The game now takes it's final course.Max finds out and underground military research complex where inside that complex Valkyr is being researched,an experiment that attempted to improve but failed to do so the stamina and morale of the U.S soldiers.The drug research was halted but Horne ,who was the leading expert of the so called Valhalla Project,after becoming the Ceo she restarted the research and used the company as a front for producing the Valkyr.Max escapes the complex after a successful destruction by the Aesir Corporation in order to destroy the evidence.
Later on Max encounters B.B who admits that was bribed by Nicole Horne to kill Max and Alex.Max then chases the traitor B.B Hensley(Payne's other DEA contact) and kills him.After doing so Max gets a phone call from Alfred Wooden(''one-eyed Alfred''),asking him to come to Asgard Building.There he learns that Alfred is a part of the Inner Circle,a powerful society with strong ties to the U.S government.The Inner Circle want to stop Nicole Horne but they can't because of
the fact that Alfred was being blackmailed by the Punchinello family over the tapes coming from the Lupino's pimp club.They ask Max to kill Horne in exchange for dropping the charges against him.Suddenly,Aesir assassins invade the building and kill everyone except Max,who manages to run away,and Woden,who pretends to have died.
In the end Max arrives at the Aesir Corporation building,kills the guards and at the top of the building confronts Nicole Horne who boards a helicopter.Max shoots wires that holds the buildin's antenna,which breaks off and crashes onto the helicopter,successfully killing Horne.While these events Mona Sax dies from a shot in the head but her body vanishes unknowningly.
In the end Max,as said in Plot's section first paragraph,gets arrested by the policemen.Max has finally taken his revenge for the death of his loved ones.Max smiles satisfied while knowing that Woden will get the charges dropped and Woden smiles as well,satisfied that Horne has been stopped.
Gameplay-Themes
Max Payne is a third-person shooter with neo-noir elements.You can use many weapons(9mm pistol,jackhammer,ingram,sniper rifle etc.).Unfortunatelly you can't use any means of transportation in the entire game.There's a useful thing you can do called Bullet-Time that you can use in order to slow time and dodge or fire at your enemy.
As for the themes the game's elements are named from figures and mythsfrom Norse mythology(Valkyr,Valhalla,Ragnarok,Woden which means Odin,Aesir,Asgard,Balder etc.).
Recap
I find this game an absolute work of art.The story,the missions,the objectives,the plot,the gameplay everything to be absolutely breath-taking and mind blowing.It has a little audio problems but can be solved in a matter of minutes.
I definitely recommend this game.Don't be fooled by the fact that it's a 2001 game.Can easily compete in fun with modern 2013-14 games in my opinion.
Thank you Remedy Entertainment and Rockstar Games for this wonderful game.
P.S Max Payne has only started his journey through the night.The pain has only just begun.More will follow.
