When this game was first announced at Kickstarter, I was estatic. Everyone knew that Rare is a shell of tis former self, with all of the people who worked on the games we loved having left, leaving only those who developed Kinect Sports titles. This is an actual game developed by the actual people who made Rare what it was back in the day!
Not only that, but unlike other kickstarter projects like Mighty No. 9, there didn't seem to be any controversy or problems going in after the game was funded and development seemed really, really smooth, so everything is smooth sailing, right? Wrong.
I've played through a bit of the first world and expanded it, but I don't know if I can stomach to get through the game anymore. The camera control is the worst part. Pressing  RB to orient yourself is a terrible idea. I find myself instinctively going to the right stick to control the camera, but it currently does absolutely nothing in the game. Meanwhile, I run around blindly, trying to orient myself. When I press RB, sometimes, the camera spins in a completely different direction than what I thought it would, and the effect of the camera whipping around gives me motion sickness.
Not only that, but the game is way too close to the player characters most of the time. The game also has a terrible tendency to snap to different camera angles at certain points, which actually made me fall down a tall tower once because the game kept changing angles. No 3d game with controls respective to the camera should have cameras that snap to different directions on its own. It's a terrible idea and it should only exist in those titles that use tank controls.
I can't help but feel that most of the humor and dialogue in the game is trying too hard. I feel the adult humor in the game is a bit too on the nose and the self-referential stuff is too often. And while the goofy voices in the original BK games were iconic and interesting back when I was a child, now these new voices are grating to my adult ears. I cannot honestly say what I would think of the BK voices if I had first heard them as an adult.
Last, but not least, let's talk about how Playtonic has been treating their customers. They caved to pressure from people who weren't even intersted in buying their game in the first place and made a minor change that many of their backers didn't like so they wouldn't be on the "wrong side of history." Yet, the controvery they were hoping to avoid has blown over like every other controvery of its type, leaving the game forever scarred by their reckless decision for something that most players had no problem with. Not only that, but their terrible attitudes made them a company I am not eager to invest in again.
Would I reccomend Yooka Laylee if it were perfect in every other way but this one bit of controversy? Certainly! But at the current state of this game, the problems all add up and outweigh the fun this game could have. I do not think it is worth your money if you're investing in nostalgia. Banjo Kazooie and Tooie are both on XBL and Rare Replay, and while that isn't available on PC, they are both great games that should be played. This is a mess, not as big as MN9, but big enough to be more frustrating and nauseating than enjoyable.

A decent capital ship combat game, but somewhat shallow.
Pros:
+ A wide variety of ships and equipment
+ Combat is a little simplistic but fun nonetheless. Reminds of Rebel Galaxy but offers more control.
+ Capturing enemy ships feels satisfying
+ Looks good enough. I somehow love the battle hud(blue ring thingie around your ship, appears on some of the screenshots) and miss it in other similar games.
Cons:
- Probably the worst voice acting in game history. Some voices are really irritiating, especially protagonist's.
- Even though all ships are capital ships, you don't feel their scale. For example if you play X3/X:Rebirth, you do feel that your massive capital ship is a massive capital ship. Here all ships are basically the same size and you don't have anything to compare them to.
- RPG elements are pretty lame
- Story progression is sometimes very confusing. Like you won't have enough crew on your starter ship to capture any other ship (and start earning significant amount of money) or you'll simetimes find that you need 10 more levels to actually pilot a ship you've just earned. Or later in the game I kept getting way more levels than I actually needed.
- Limited ship customization options. You can arbitrarily choose any weapons for your ship which's good, but its subsystems are predefined for any given hull and you can just upgrade them slightly via enhancements.
- Even though I did rush the game in the end, I have completed it(without DLC stuff) in 32 hours on the hardest difficulty which's a little underwhelming for this kind of games.
Grab this game if:
You want a little arcadish broadside-style capital ship combat driven by a campaign scenario.
Avoid this game if:
If you're looking for a very in-depth experience similar to X3/EVE or physically plausible ship controlling similar to Elite. This game has a strong indie feeling to it, don't expect anything of AAA-like scale.

TL; DR Its a trap! Great fun at start, absolutely mind numbingly boring towards the end.
You start with a gunship and the map is huge right? Then you fly around doing freelance missions (10k each) to get your first ship which costs around 200k. After a while, you notice the 200k ship is not so different then the one you have, so you start eyeing that 2m ship which is significantly better. But how can you get 2m? By boarding other ships, thats how.
The game is as long as it takes you to get that first 2m ship, philedelphia if I remember correctly. After that you resupply your marines and look for other ships. doing it will net you around 30m + some dreads. It took me 3-4 days to get that 2m ship since I enjoyed every view, mission and etc for a while. Everything was challenging. I thought the game was a little like eve. No.
Around the 5 day mark I almost had/sold/destroyed every ship in the game and I was invincible. A mission? let me just warp in to melee range and press f (auto fire). A side mission 15 levels above? No problem. Massive battle near station with 10+ enemy ships packed together + hero? Let me just warp in melee again and turn different sides of my ship since shields on one side went down to 50%.  After 5 days of casual play there was NOTHING to contest my ship and I had not even started the MAIN CAMPAIGN.
Noticing this, I immediately started the campaign and finished it in several hours. Everyone was saved, lots of joy, yay. But, nothing changed on the map. I had somehow brought the dlc's as well, and there is a bug in titans main quest which forces you to free roam. There are fixes for it but I do not have the patience to "play" this anymore.
Oh and you can't destroy enemy stations, hell the shots go right through.
Also why are there so few weapons and systems. You buy/capture a 30m ship and all you can put on them are the same measly crap that exists in almost all stations everywhere. There is no chance of variation or strategy. Why the hell would you cloak?

Many people have already mentioned the mediocre(to say the least) main campaign with the poor voice acting and the uninteresting plot.
The map on the other hand is quite large but for the most part empty except for some generic space stations( used to buy and sell loot and save the game) and mining platforms(used for nothing whatsover).
There are quite a few ship types but the way they are used is quite similar so the difference between a small gunboat and a massive carrier is relatively minimum.
There are some RPG elements where you can choose perks for your hero but they are rudimentary at best.
And as a final thought the DLC Secrets of Aethera has a "beautiful" bug that forbids you from advancing the campaign after you discover Kepler station while the Titans DLC completely lacks voiceovers even for your protagonist.

Pros:
+ Beautiful game; very nice to look at!
+ Lots of small interesting mechanics and ideas, such as boarding other ships, hacking their systems, etc.
+ Mining and trading are well implemented, although it's very hard to get rich through either

Cons:

- what REALLY pushed me away from this game:
WELCOME TO USER INTERFACE HELL!
oh my god, this game's interface makes me want to stick puppies in a blender!
--> fifty thousand menus that don't give you all the information you need
--> 'why can't I select this station? oh the waypoint marker is in the way, let me place it somewhere else for the 1000th time so I can move on with the docking procedure' (same thing applied to any static object in space you hope to interact with)
--> 'does a green price mean it's a good sell, or does it mean the price is very low?'
--> 'why can't I use the turret camera while in PTE mode?! oh, I can, but I need to press Mouse1 simultaneously. wtf?'

--> I could go on, but the point is: if this game's UI had been better conceived, SG2 wouldn't have♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off so often. I'm not saying it's a bad game, just that... it's not great fun. I guess that's enough.

I'm going ahead and making my first review EVER to ardently defend this game, so let that be established up-top in case somebody's looking for bias, because I might have it - I played and loved Blood Money to death, so naturally this game is directly up my alley and delivers what Absolution didn't. This review is going to take the format of a response to this game's criticisms, because my main motivation in writing this review is to illustrate my own confusion as to why this has mixed reviews.
My understanding is that people are super upset that this game is episodic and that, therefore, the first episode contains only one 'real' stage and two tutorial stages. I can understand how that would upset people who somehow thought that wasn't what they were getting...but if you're at all familiar with episodic series like Life is Strange or any of the Telltale Games, why are you upset about this? It was never presented as anything other than what it is.
Further, if game length is the concern, that basically tells us what kind of game you wanted to play. In this latest Hitman, if you are a one-and-done kind of killer, then this first episode will be done in about 2 hours - the approximate length of an episode of Life is Strange, but nobody was upset about that. Unlike Life is Strange, this game could have a great deal of replayability, should you be interested in experimentation.
The one 'real' stage is a masterpiece of level crafstmanship, with more details and methods of entry, attack and escape than were ever available in any stage of Blood Money. Fans of the series should be floored by the care that went into this one stage and the TONS of voice acting that went into bringing it to life. Instead, it seems like a lot of players just completed the level once and were done. Why? I have put in TWENTY-FIVE HOURS playing this stage, completing challenges. I haven't even really touched Contracts yet, but I plan to start making some.
The always-online DRM complaint I can understand far more than the length complaint, but that frustration just hasn't happened to affect me very much. Square Enix's servers died twice on me and booted me out, and I was and am STILL pretty salty about how saves can't be converted online to offline...but is that a dealbreaker? I don't see why it would be, unless your internet connection is prone to shorting out. I don't like it by any means, but I can deal with it, because this first episode has me very much impressed.

There are issues with always online, challanges not registering properly etc. However all of that can and will hopefully be fixed. What can not be altered after release is the core gameplay experience, which is excellent.

Armed with duel lightsabers, I open the door to the next room in the Imperial base. Two storm troopers lying in wait rush me, attempting to flank me. One runs face first into my saber, cutting himself from the top of his forhead to the middle of his chest dying instantly. His friend ran through my other light saber, removing his head from his shoulders. Both men fell lifelessly at my sides while I stood, lightsabers out, unmoving since I opened the door.
This game makes you respect the lightsaber in a whole new light. There's a "gore" mod you can download that shows limbs and heads fall of, making your lightsaber a terrifying, grizzly weapon, as a beam sword of pure energy would indeed be. Your lightsaber is so deadly, you dont even need to swing it to kill random storm troopers and thugs, you can simly walk into them with it, or turn your characters body, moving the buzzing beam blade of death into them.
Every lightsaber duel with other saber wielders is an action packed game of sudden death. I admit it gets a bit... infuriating when the game decides you get your head sliced off, while your opponent lives from his saber wound to the face and chest... but its the games way of balancing the light saber swings, which I admit are not perfect. For this games time though, its one of the best experiences you could ask for, if you want to feel what its like to be a Jedi. Even modern games like Force Unleashed dont hold a candle to how "Jedi" this game makes you feel, as well as giving the hallowed respect to the lightsaber it deserves.
Fun little game quirk, lightsabers remain on for awhile after the death of a Sith or Jedi, resulting in sometimes HILARIOUS death scenes. My favorite so far has been cutting a Siths arm clear off from his shoulder with a downward chop, only to have the inertia from his swing, bring the lightsaber still in his sevared arms hand, down across my neck, decapitating me. Silly mayhem-driven combatitive fun.  Up to 4-players frantically control violent - seemingly drunken - blobs out to destroy each other.  Terrain is interactive (cutting the cables on someone's elevator car to watch them plunge to their doom, is - of course - always a source of hilarity) and no game plays out the same.
In a way, Gang Beasts reminds me of Rocket League.  "How's that again?" you might ask.  Well Rocket League takes normal sports gameplay and warps it by handicapping players into using cars to have to control the ball.  Gang Beasts takes a normal fighting game and makes controlling your character somewhat tricky and unpredictable due to the sticky physics.  Much like Rocket League, the results are phenomenal and rampantly amusing.
Some small complaints are that the UI is very basic, but overall this is very much worth the money and especially for people who want to enjoy that most classic (but very rare these days) of gaming traditions, the local playing mode.
What's also nice is that some players can use controllers while another could use the keyboard (if controllers are scarce).  That's a nice touch.
Overall, I'd give Gang Beasts a solid 8.3 out of 10.

There's been a lot of controversy and criticism surrounding this game. It's not all undeserved, the game has its flaws, but it is a title worth playing and owning. I am recommending it, if not wholeheartedly.
As a fan and player of the original Rare games, I'm conflicted in writing this review. This game is good. This game is not great, and it unfortunately isn't on par with Banjo-Kazooie. It's a shame, because I think it could have been with a little more  time and work.
Anybody who's played BK or BT will know exactly where I'm coming from. The game carries the tradition forward, if not as well as its predecessor. The characters are well designed and pretty well rounded, and each has a charming personality. The levels are colorful, enticing, and every corner presents a fun activity or puzzle, and each nook and cranny has a collectible, a mere excuse to explore and interact with the world. The music, as always, is grand and compelling, a real treat, and overall, It's very clear that a lot of care and effort went into this game.
But there's something that bothers me. Something that perhaps followed Playtonic from Rare's time under microsoft. Something that stinks of Nuts and Bolts, and of gaming in general these days. These levels are massive and sprawling, and unfortunately rather sparse and somehow cold. For every minute I spent solving a puzzle or completing a task, I spent another just getting back and forth to my objectives, and it really impressed upon me just how much whitespace there seemed to be here, something that works to the game's disadvantage. Truly unfortunate.
Is it a bad game? Not at all. Is it a great game, like the ones that inspired it? No. It falls somewhere in between, worth playing for certain, but lacking. I hope Playtonic takes the lesson to heart, so that the sequel can avoid the missteps this game made.

First Impressions:
Yooka-Laylee is the return of Banjo-Kazooie. Peroid.
If you're unaware of that means, let me try to desribe it to you.
It brings back the classic RARE platforming into 2017 with modern graphics. Everything you love (and hate) about the classic games is here.
Nostalgia aside, Yooka-Laylee offers a rich, massive, platforming world. Full of secrets and collectibles, along side the cheese dialog from the 1990's.
If you're from a generation that grew up with the N64, you're going to feel right at home. However, if you're from a newer generation, I implore you to go back to the classic games (via emulator if you don't own or cannot find original copies). Or, play the Xbox 360 remasters. They're excellent and run at 60fps / 1080p
If you don't enjoy the platforming from those earlier titles, it is very unlikley you will enjoy this game. All of its shortcomings will be even further highlighted (iffy camera, annoying voice overs, etc) due to this.
And I think that's what I like most about Yooka-Laylee. It's not trying to be anything else. It's knows exactly what it is and who its market is. The downside is that it is dated to modern game development. However, I strongly belive that a lot of modern games today, lose their focus. In my honest opinion, as a gamer for almost 20 years, the gameplay is what defines a great game.
This further reinforces why Yooka-Laylee is an essential title in 2017. If you respect gaming in any form, please, check this game out.

It's certainly playable, but it's not good. Of what little I played of Banjo-Kazooie I didn't really care for, so I never came into this as a fan of previous games (unless the devs had something to do with battle toads). Despite this, I thought it looked good and wanted to give it a try.
Visually, it's very appealing. The main characters are cute, and I like designs for (most) of the NPCs. The environments range from interestingly new to outright bland.
Sometimes the jokes were good. Sometimes.
The controls are mostly good. Moving is fluid and responsive. Aiming is a pain, though. You have to enter a FPS view to aim projectiles, and before you enter your FPS view Yooka has to come to a
stop.
The camera probems that everybody complains about are somewhat true. The camera for the first portion of the game (until the first boss) didn't bother me. After that point it does start to get pretty janky. It's constantly auto-fixing itself into positions you don't want. It's a small nuisance, but the fact that it's a consistent nuisance is what makes it worth criticizing.
The framerate is mostly not an issue, but there are certainly some areas (such as where you need to spit water on moving, flaming platforms) where it's noticable and even encumbering to the player. These framerate drops usually don't make sense, either. There are plenty of areas in the game with just as many effects that don't stutter the game. Again, this is an example of a nuisance that, coupled with the poor camera, becomes a compounding problem.
Perhaps I'm nitpicking when I say this, but I think the local area transitions (entering a door, cave, etc. where the reverse-silhouette slowly blacks out the screen) take too long, too.
Certain text isn't skippable and is too slow. Perhaps I didn't notice an option for this, but I'm pretty sure you can't speed up text. Buying a new skill is tedious and there's too much unskippable text for confirming what to buy.
Another issue is that the game changes the rules randomly:
-I can't tell when I'm going to take fall damage. I've jumped from the top of the mountain in the first level and landed safely on the bottom, and there are times I didn't take damage where I thought I would. There are times I took damage when I thought I wasn't high enough to.
-There are no indicators for environmental damage. There's an area in world 2 that you'll randomly take cold damage, when there's literally no indication that area is any colder than the rest of the world. At first I just thought it was touching the ice that gave me damage.
-Hitboxes don't seem to make sense sometimes. There are these "eyeball" enemies that possess objects and attack you in the game in which sometimes your ground pound will work and make them vulnerable to your tail spin, and sometimes you'll just take damage (even when they're not attacking). As another example, the jellyfish enemies in the water will only sometimes be defeated by your ground pound attack and sometimes you'll just take damage.
Now, the above problems I listed can all be easily fixed with patches. Therefore, they are not the main reasons that I don't recommend the game.
This is a common complaint, but it's true: the environments are way too large, and without much in them. It takes way too long to traverse from one side of the map to the other, and it's not rewarding to search every nook and cranny in them because more often than not there's nothing to find. Too much of the game is just rolling from one area of the map to the other.
The game is also incredibly
. There is no reward for defeating enemies, and they're all forgettable. In fact, most enemies are just the same with a remodel to match the world they're in. Any difference between enemies is superficial. Enemies are not even obstacles, as you can usually just ignore them. The game is so easy in fact that I seldom ever payed attention to my health and didn't always care to dodge attacks. Health is littered everywhere. The only deaths I've had in this game came from environmental damage and/or instant death falls. Dying doesn't even carry a penalty. All that happens is you respawn from the last door you came from (which is often the same room where you died) with full health.
The "puzzles" lack any creativity, and don't require any critical thinking. They consist of "match the tiles on the wall" and "simon-sez icicle edition."
There are "quizzes," too. They suck.
The mini-games are tedious. It's like the devs couldn't think of
clever to put in the Rextro arcades. The first one is just a race against the clock with horrificly bad friction. The second one is just collecting feathers over platforms that occasionally sink. They're unchallenging and provide no sense of competition or urgency.
The minecart mini-game is ok, I guess. There's a bit of input lag that I don't like, though.
These problems are just inherent to the game itself. I don't see these as "fixable" without a huge overhaul of the game.
If you want it, get it on sale. I'm glad I backed the project because I only had to pay $15.

It feels like it has too much of side-content (not directly related to story or missions) and become quite repetitive at the end: defusing mines (30 encounters is waaaay too many, only first 15 mines are fun, rest 75 is booring), clearing camps, scarecrows.
Point is: you learn about 90% of game in first few (1-3) encounters and the rest is a boring repetition. Only occasionally game suprises with unexpected mechanic or encounter. E.g. one camp had elevator to move up, it took me 20 min to realise it's not non-interactive environment and I actually have to use it..
Racing is easy, but.. big but.. the balance is poor. In general all death races are VERY easy with archangels (boost + weapons), while first car in the list to beat it is sometimes VERY hard. Some routes required studying by failng race several times to find working shortcuts. Race during night is really poor experience, especially when car has NO lights.. ><
Quests: some are very unclear/poorly designed, including main quest where you have to build your first archangel. NOT a single player is capable to complete it without googling.
I must admit one good thing: encouters are varying enough. You will not notice copy/paste, because there is none. Searching for valuables is fun and sometimes hard (e.g. a symbol located on the back of the letter on the roof, or well hidden container).. though for my taste it's too easy. I'd enjoy having more puzzles, having to scout more.
On-foot combat is intuitive and simple, yet satisfactory. I generally dislike melee characters in games, but in Mad Max it was very fun.
Cinematics and story are ok. Not too impressive, but good enough.
I definitely recommend this game to everyone, who enjoy games like latest far cry, tomb raider, gta and wanted to experience something similar but in post-appocalypse word. Though I am not sure if many will decide to finish it (as it may become too repetitive).

At first, you're invincibility time frame is really small, but the more you collect the gems scattered throughout the giant maze, the longer your time frame gets.

I highly recommend this game to anyone that likes strategy games and grid-based design games. I have had 1000+ hours of literal non-stop fun so far from this game. This game LACKS the ability to be boring, as you can always restart and try again. It's extremely easy to mod and I would recommend this to anyone that wants to learn how to Lua code. It's far more stable and less buggy than Garry's Mod. Garry's Mod is a buggy mess outright in itself; I've had one or two bugs ever happen in this game (Prison Architect) over two years of playing it, with over 1,000 hours (steam/normal version combined).
This game is great for anyone, and there's tablet versions for those without their computer at hand. Introversion makes enjoyable games, Uplink and Prison Architect being my favorites, then Darwinia. If they continue work with Subversion, and they complete it to full, it could be an amazing game. Or, Uplink 2.0? That'd be cool.
Pros/Cons (Cons are exagurated, so take with a grain of salt, but they aren't that bad and the gameplay and replayability of this game is worth more than any kind of con this game has).
Pros:
Great Gameplay
Mods via Workshop
Prisons via Workshop
Community is decent (the website forum is full of ♥♥♥♥♥♥s, especially the moderators, steam community is better)
Amazing Lua capabilities
Built in computer logic set pieces ('remote control' research option)
Cons:
-Starts to lag like hell with 200+ AI's on the map (30-45fps with oc 4.1ghz fx-6300), you're going to need a decent processor (high-end i3, i5, i7, fx-6300, fx-8350)
-No multiplayer, but I can see that being a bigger issue than it would be worth (how would pathfinding be handled? servers? host? if peer-to-peer, it could kill the hosts computer from the possibility of too much AI)
-Needs better multi-threading, or 64-bit. Lag issues could be killed permanently if either of these were introduced. 64-bit would kill the lag harder than more cores, though.

I have played many games, for many hours. But this game... This is amongst the handful of games I genuinely give a 10 out of 10!
When I downloaded this game I expected nothing of it, I laughed it away and I thought: "Hah, this will be boring". Nothing was further away from the truth. It evolved from a game into a lifestyle... And while I'm writing this I have only played 80 hours of it...
I thought that this would be a game where I drive my truck through one or two roads, attach/detach a trailer and done.
But this game is so in detail!
* Realistic graphics, definitely for an indie game! I've seen A-rated games that were graphically inferior to this!
* Realistic truck designs and driving mechanics.
* Realistic extras: Petrol stations, sleeping places, fines for breaking the traffic laws, cabin and trailer damage upon collisions, road signs in the language of the country you are in, etc...
* Being able to start your own company, hire drivers, etc..
The only 2 things I would advise as a patch or for ETS3:
- Visible damage to cabin or trailer when collided. Because even when I caused world war 3 on my way to my destination, my truck still looks unscratched.
- NPC's that also follow traffic laws. For example taking over from the right (left in UK)... I see NPC's doing this all the time to me. And when I signal that I want to go to the left lane, the cars on the left lane should slow a bit down or go to the third lane to make way. This problem caused me to collide many times in countries like Germany where the right lane suddenly turns into an exit lane.
Thank you SCS for developping this masterpiece.
PS: Adding Dutch paintjobs to the game would make it sooo awesome for me!

I was late to the party with Undertale. I hate bullet hell games. Never had the reactions for them. I dislike only MOBAs more than bullet hell. First try once I discovered battle mechanics and accidentally killed a couple of characters I stopped playing because the game made me feel bad about these pixels I accidentally removed, as well as me hating bullet hell. But that's the first sign of me really getting why everyone loved this game. How it made me feel bad over some side character.
Recently, I was persuaded by a friend who loved the game to play through it again now that I knew how it worked, from the beginning. So I streamed it to him as I played a few hours every night for a week and we went through it together. Only the Pacifist run, because I hadn't the heart afterwards to play the Genocide run now that I had fallen so in love with the characters.
It is testament to Toby Fox's writing and composing that now, a week after completing this game, I am still listening to the soundtrack and crying every now and then when I remember the story. I fell in love with the characters, despite it taking me just 12 hours to beat the game. I only knew them for 12 hours, yet the knowledge of their fates at the end and the time I spent in their universe still fill me with joy and sorrow. At the end, both me and my friend were audibly crying over it, and not in a bad way.
I had a list of top 10 games I've ever played, of all time, the top two being original Deus Ex and The Witcher 3 in that order. I think storytelling is the most important part of a game, followed by soundtrack, then gameplay, then graphics. Why? Because for me the journey you are taken on is paramount for the enjoyment, and the soundtrack is what sets the scene. Forget everything else. Now, having played Undertale, it has taken that top spot. Now I honestly believe this is the best game ever made. I wish I had the power to erase my memory completely of this game so that I can once again experience that journey of getting to know these characters, laughing and crying with them, and relive for the first time again this story that has affected me so.
Toby Fox has truly created a masterpiece, making a fervent opponent of the game's bullet hell mechanics such as myself willingly and happily force my way through them just to find out what happens next, because it meant that much to me. Now that I have beaten the game, I no longer want to play it ever again because I feel that would undo the ending for each of the characters that I worked so hard to achieve, and I care about them too much to do that to them. I hate bullet hell, yet my number 1 game of all time is a bullet hell game. That is why this is the best game ever made.
TL;DR: 11/10, best game ever made in the history of gaming. Buy it, play it.

While I don't like the online requirement and I have had about 4 crashes in the game in about 6 hours gameplay I still want to give a positive review, while there are things that needs to be fixed I don't think this game deserves all the hate it has got. People also complain that there is only 1 mission, but there is really 3 main missions that can be completed in multiple ways + a lot of contracts and other modes that increase the replayability even more. For an "intro pack" I think there is well enough content in my opinion.
But on to the actual game. I have been a big fan of the Hitman series since the start and have played every game since then. While I don't feel like this edition of Hitman really brings that much new to the formula it still feels very polished and the gameplay is still as interesting now as it was in the first game. The one thing that have always impressed the most in any Hitman game is the levels, they are often huge and very believable with tons of npc:s roaming around and paths and things you can explore that take many playthrough to discover. The Paris mission here really shines in those areas and is probably one of the best in the series in scope and complexity (The Hotel mission from the first game is still my favorite though)
The biggest differance to the game this time I would say is the "challanges". Every level has a big roster of challanges to be completed, most often killing your target in very specific and interesting ways. My biggest gripe with the game however is that there is no difficulty slider this time, meaning that there is no limited saves or even penalty for saving. In the old games, if playing on the higher difficulty you where only allowed to save once or twice, or on the higest not at all. This made every moment very tense and the feeling of consequence and that anything could go wrong at any time made the game very immersive. To have an unlimited save system really destroy any tension. You no longer feel anxious while you are drowning your target in the toilet and hoping that no one will open the door, if that happens you just have to hit "reload". Because of this I prefer to play the contracts right now where no saving is allowed, especially the Escalation contracts are very fun where every time you complete the mission another requirement is added to the mission. So for example on the first go you have to kill your target. After this you have to kill your target again, but this time you also need to hack a computer, and so on, the requirements gets added for every time you complete a previous level.
All in all, I am positive for the full game, and if they just fix the save system for the main mission to make it a bit more hardcore like the contract mode is now, fix the crashing and get rid of the Online Drm, I think this could be one of the best Hitman games yet.

Mad Max is a great game.
Lots of reviewers compared it to the Batman Arkham Series, because of the combat system, and to Middle earth: Shadows of Mordor, because of the fast travel and upgrading by side quests systems.
The combat is somewhat similar to Arkham, but its more clunky, less ballet, and for a good reason: Mad Max is more brute, less classy than Batman. Max cannot counter while he is attacking, so he gets beat up too. But Max will break the other guy´s neck if he needs to.
As for the fast travel, it´s a good thing to have. You conquer a spot and then you can fast travel there. It´s useful when dealing with a huge map (it´s huge even if you have a fast car).
And the upgarde system was designed, in my opinion, to make you enjoy your stay, roam the world, with patience. You don´t want to rush through this Wasteland.
And what a gorgeous Wasteland it is. A terrifying, yet beautiful silent, desolate place, with lots of different terrain.
I reckognized other games in Mad Max. For example, the scrap collecting system reminded me a lot of Red Faction Guerrilla, not to mention the Mars-like landscape and the fact that the car will never capsize...
Also, being a loot ♥♥♥♥♥ ever since I played the Risen series, I enjoyed A LOT collecting stuff to build up my character´s abilities, something I also enjoyed doing in games like Saints Row IV.
Another game came to mind: GTA. After all, you are a badass in a land full of badasses. You go out there and beat them up, rob them, loot them, kill them. In the meantime you race like hell in the open lands. Pity there is no incidental music  like in GTA - because after the apocalypse there was no radio station. But the sounds of the games are awesome - the car running, the car idle (my favourite), the opening of the water canteen...
Max is a badass. Apart from drinking water and eating dog food, he can also eat dead-flesh-eating-maggots to replenish his health!
And talk about pimp my ride... If you like car tuning, upgrading your ride, you´ll love this gem.
There´s also the sidekick, Chum, a Gollum-like hunchback that treats cars as deities, wrenches as religious artifacts, and developed his own belief systems based on engines and combustion... which is genius, this is something that might very well happen in an apocalyptic future where survival depends on gasoline and a set of wheels.
So you have a well-know character, greatly rendered, great voice acting, awesome landscapes, lots of cool cars, mad racing, car tuning, character-building, guns, violence, badassery all around, all of which in a chaotic land with no law.
Even after completing the main storyline after 101 hours, I want to go back to the game, hop in my ride and finish the side quests I left behind... Maybe this time I´ll pump some serious rock for background music! ("Burn it Down", by Awolnation, for starters)
As for the storyline... well, you will have to see it for yourself. Hint: it´s a Mad Max game.

I really wanted to love this game. I was a huge fan of Banjo-Kazooie and Banjo-Tooie and all of the other N64 Rare games so when I heard this game was on Kickstarter, I immediately backed it. Even disregarding all of the recent JonTron drama and trying to step away from the Banjo mindset to give this game it's own chance to wow me, it just fell short.
The gameplay is pretty solid but it is lacking in a few areas. There are no moves that give you
projectiles. The only projectiles you can shoot are Laylee's sonar which is only a stun and picking up ice balls when they happen to be around for a puzzle. The movement is really solid but once you unlock the ability to fly, all platforming sections become basically flyover.
There are only 5 worlds to this game and I consider only the first and third to be anything worth talking about. This is somewhat remidied by the worlds being expanded to add more content to them. But then the worlds feel extremely large and I'm gonna miss collecting something because I didn't check every nook and cranny. The 5th world is just sad. The music is dull and the design feels extremely lazy. In world 2 there is a big strip of rooms where kickstarter backers helped design the rooms. These for the most part are mindless platforming sections or grindy puzzles. It's almost like the dev team didn't make any constructive input to help improve the rooms.
The music in this game is also pretty forgettable. Other than maybe the song in world 2, the music feels empty. I love Grant's work in BK, BT, and DK64 but here in Yooka, it feels too basic and dull. The actually sound itself sounds good. It's fully orchestrated but it just doesn't hit the mark.
I have a bunch more to say about this game but it's become hard for me to put ideas into words.
This game just fell short of being "The revival of 3D platformers". I still plan on finishing the game but I probably won't go back and 100% it. I would advise passing this unless it's heavily discounted. I'm happy I only paid $10 for this on Kickstarter.

Yooka-Laylee is a game I've been looking forward to for a very long time. I read reviews from professional reviewers and others beforehand and it honestly disheartened me quite a bit. There were a myriad of complaints, all essentially the same, and it made me worried as to whether I would get my $39.99 worth of value when I purchased this game. Thankfully I went ahead and bought it anyways. After playing it myself for a little over 15 hours now, I feel the need to defend it from much of the negativity it's received. Yooka-Laylee is exactly what Playtonic has pitched it as, and nothing more or less.
Yooka-Laylee is a spiritual successor to the Banjo series and past Rare games in every way. This is both a good and bad thing. Good because if you're a fan of Donkey Kong 64, Banjo-Kazooie, and Banjo-Tooie, stop reading this review and buy this game right now. You'll love it just as I have. Bad because it feels like it still is burdened by some of the limitations those games had because of the technology then (the camera specifically).
The majority of the complaints I've seen have been leveraged at the camera. Most devolved into many complaining about the camera needing to be manually adjusted. God forbid you need to move your mouse or right stick. But aside from that, there are some very valid complaints as the camera doesn't feel any different from the very first Banjo game released. Objects in this game don't get proper transparency when the camera is over them and it can make it feel jerky sometimes. There are also sections that can be quite frustrating because the camera angle changes entirely. If you step out of the zone of that it can be increasingly frustrating since the camera will jerk back and forth until you're a bit away from it. I feel that this is the only truly valid complaint about this game since it can be incredibly annoying at times.
Another large complaint I've seen is that the worlds feel empty. Every time I've seen this so far I have to ask if they're playing the same game as I am. There are items to collect around every corner, massive maps to explore that feel unique and interesting (yet don't overstay their welcome), a variety of interesting characters to speak to on each, and something for everyone in each and every single one. On that note, I seen many complain about the exact opposite as well. Many have complained that it's a collectathon game. Yes, it is. It was pitched exactly as such and never as anything else. If you don't like collectothons then you'll despise this game, but if you even moderately enjoy them then you'll have a lot of fun in each world.
The controls feels amazing and I've played all of what I have so far on mouse and keyboard. For me to be able to competently play a 3D platformer on a mouse and keyboard is quite amazing. I can assure you you're going to have a much better time playing this with a controller, as do Playtonic themselves, but you can play it all the same with a mouse and keyboard. However, the B button is not bound on mouse and keyboard (which they may patch hopefully soon) so you have to use a little work around to leave dialog options. You need to press and hold P, then press escape twice, and let go of P. This is a little irritating to have to do.
Performance wise, I have not had a single problem. I have not noticed any frame dropping whatsoever, I've not encountered any bugs or graphical glitches, and I've not had any inputs that don't register. Your mileage may vary here, but it seems like it will run just fine on anything.
Time to go over some subjective things now that will vary from person to person. Many people have complained about the style of voice over used in this game, the same type that was used in the Banjo franchise. If you hated it then you'll hate it now. If you're like me and quite liked it or weren't bothered by it, then you'll like it now. It's as simple as that. The writing is also witty and clever like in Rare's past games. While I don't feel it's as good as Banjo's writing, it is still quite good in my opinion. The art style is something I also enjoy, though some textures look like they are lifted straight from Banjo-Kazooie. It's jarring at times to see a beautiful texture right next to something that looks like it came from 1998. This is not common though, and I've only seen it in a couple small parts.
All in all, Yooka-Laylee is not perfect. It's a great game that has had me smiling and feeling like a kid who just booted up my N64 to play Banjo-Kazooie for the first time all over again. This is all that I wanted out of it too as did many fans of Banjo. This game is the spiritual successor that Playtonic promised it'd be, and it's exactly what you'd expect with that being said. I haven't been disappointed with it, and if you're missing out on purchasing this because a reviewer ranted about it then you're making a mistake. If you are worried about the cost of the game or can't afford it, definitely wait until it's on sale and pick it up as soon as you can. Yooka-Laylee is an amazing game that you need to give a try.

If there was one word I could use to describe this game, it'd probably be "Disappointment".
The foundation for a truly great game is there but it just didn't have the funds or the team to push that foundation into a classic status like Banjo Kazooie before it. The game will feel immediately familiar to BK veterans, but that glowing nostalgia will slowly give way to disappointment. The length of the game is the first one. Only 5 worlds and probably 35 hours later (had the game left paused in menus for a while) you're left wanting more. While you can easily 100% complete BK in roughly the same amount of time, the fact that BK has 9 worlds to YL's 5 just makes this feel like a shorter experience. And even with only 5 worlds, 3 of those are essentially similar themes to worlds in BK (Tribalstack Tropics = Mumbo's Mountain, Glitterglaze Glacier = Freezezy Peak, Moodymaze Marsh = Bubblegloop Swamp). That leaves you with only two truly unique theme worlds. Disappointment.
The lack of enemy variation is another point against Yooka Laylee. In Treasure Trove Cove in BK, you get to fight crabs, jumping clams, a giant hermit crab, a shark, and sea mines, and the enemies are completely different in each level. In YL you get to fight the corplet minions, the flying bees, the eyeballs that possess objects, and the underwater jellyfish. These 4 enemy types are pretty much the majority of the enemies you'll come across in the whole game, with the addition of the security robots and the VERY occasional large Corplet minions. Only the small corplet minions change their appearance to match their theme level. The rest are just plonked in everywhere. It doesn't really feel like much effort was put in to make the enemies match the worlds. Disappointment.
The lack of variety of the puzzles was another low point of the game. In Banjo Kazooie, in the first world alone, I had to fight a giant ape, appease a totem pole, and climb a termite mound. In Yooka Laylee, I had to hit some switches to unlock a cage, fly through some hoops to unlock a cage, or use some other moves to unlock a cage. Most of the puzzles are just in cages. When comparing that to truly stand out jiggies like lighting the christmas tree in Freezezy Peak or swimming inside a giant metal shark, the puzzles just seem lacklustre. Disappointment.
Overall there's a lot that could have improved the game. More levels, more enemy variety, more puzzle variety. In fact, lack of variety seems to be the core problem with this game. I chalk that up to the limits of crowdfunding. They got $2 million and they probably needed close to $40 million to add the variety I was hoping for. I still had fun playing this, but it was the kind of fun that was constantly making me think "if only they'd done a little more here...." It will make you want to play Banjo Kazooie again. And while it admirably reaches the tone and feel of Banjo Kazooie, it fails in the creativity and execution of that tone. It does innovate well with the welcome feature of collectibles staying collected once you leave the level. You no longer need to collect all the notes/quills in one go, which is a welcome update over Banjo Kazooie. But still, if they'd only had more funding to push this game where it needed to go, then this could have been a worthy sequel. The fact that it wasn't is just a disappointment.

Batman: Arkham Origins is an odd one. While the gameplay itself has been tightened up, for example the combat flows a lot better and enemies are generally more aggressive than they were during previous games, the innovation is seriously lacking.
The collectibles are uninspired compared to the original riddles and the main story is just downright dire, with the assassins that are supposedly after you falling more into sidequests than anything else. The copy/paste assets of Arkham City doesn't do the game any favours either, as it feels more like an expansion than anything.
Graphically the game looks great and there are a few nice touches here and there such as PhysX enabled snow and it has been optimised to hell and back so it runs fantastically (game breaking bugs aside), but it still doesn't look as good as Arkham City does.
It's a good game if you are a fan of the series, but I would hold off and get it a little cheaper unless you really have to have it.

While I don't like the online requirement and I have had about 4 crashes in the game in about 6 hours gameplay I still want to give a positive review, while there are things that needs to be fixed I don't think this game deserves all the hate it has got. People also complain that there is only 1 mission, but there is really 3 main missions that can be completed in multiple ways + a lot of contracts and other modes that increase the replayability even more. For an "intro pack" I think there is well enough content in my opinion.
But on to the actual game. I have been a big fan of the Hitman series since the start and have played every game since then. While I don't feel like this edition of Hitman really brings that much new to the formula it still feels very polished and the gameplay is still as interesting now as it was in the first game. The one thing that have always impressed the most in any Hitman game is the levels, they are often huge and very believable with tons of npc:s roaming around and paths and things you can explore that take many playthrough to discover. The Paris mission here really shines in those areas and is probably one of the best in the series in scope and complexity (The Hotel mission from the first game is still my favorite though)
The biggest differance to the game this time I would say is the "challanges". Every level has a big roster of challanges to be completed, most often killing your target in very specific and interesting ways. My biggest gripe with the game however is that there is no difficulty slider this time, meaning that there is no limited saves or even penalty for saving. In the old games, if playing on the higher difficulty you where only allowed to save once or twice, or on the higest not at all. This made every moment very tense and the feeling of consequence and that anything could go wrong at any time made the game very immersive. To have an unlimited save system really destroy any tension. You no longer feel anxious while you are drowning your target in the toilet and hoping that no one will open the door, if that happens you just have to hit "reload". Because of this I prefer to play the contracts right now where no saving is allowed, especially the Escalation contracts are very fun where every time you complete the mission another requirement is added to the mission. So for example on the first go you have to kill your target. After this you have to kill your target again, but this time you also need to hack a computer, and so on, the requirements gets added for every time you complete a previous level.
All in all, I am positive for the full game, and if they just fix the save system for the main mission to make it a bit more hardcore like the contract mode is now, fix the crashing and get rid of the Online Drm, I think this could be one of the best Hitman games yet.

More Detailed Review:
Technical: This game looks gorgeous (Especially with the graphics cranked up) and doesn't have any major gamebreaking bugs or glitches. My character got stuck under a bridge during one of the race segments, which I had to restart, but not a big deal. My game crashed once, not sure what happened, but it appears to be a one-time thing, so *shrugs* not a big deal.
Controls (Played this with a Wired 360 Controller) are mostly fine, except controlling while in ball form and
were a bit of a pain to hassle with, causing me to fall or fail a few challenges. I think a tweak to make them a little more responsive would have helped a lot with some rather frustrating parts. One particular area in World 2 I gave up on and came back later with a new ability that let me skip most of it.
Camera: For the most part, I didn;t have any major issues with the camera. A few awkward angles, but that's pretty par for the course when it comes to 3d platformers. I doubt it'd ever be completely perfect. At least having the camera mapped to Right Stick was a good move. In most cases, any minor camera issues were quickly fixed.
Worlds: The worlds are massive (especially when expanded), but there's no hints on where to go. After clearing most of the worlds' more obvious Pagies, it became rather difficult to scour them again in search of new ones. In all, I entered each world half a dozen times or so... and then needed a Pagie walkthrough to find a few missing ones in order to scrounge up enough Pagies to take on the final boss.
Favorite World: World 4 -
. I had fun with all the things to do with this place.
Least Favorite: World 5 -
. I think this place should have been presented a bit differently. It wasn't quite the themed the way I'd imagined when I saw what it was.
The quills only mean something until about the midgame. It wasn't a hindrance unlocking any of the new moves, but I do kind of wish there was something to do with the stoclpile I hads late game.
Music: The music was pretty good in most spots. One track could have belonged at home in a Banjo-Kazooie game. The rest for the most part didn't seem out of place.  If yu have a chance though, most of the under water themes are quite relaxing.
Bosses: Each of the world's boss battles are unique, and will require you a number of attempts before you beat them. The same goes with the final boss too, as it took me numerous tries before I was able to conquer it.
Story and Writing: I was personally very meh on the story. I didn;t feel that invested in it for the most part. By the time I got to the end, I just kind of wanted the game to be over with. The writing was decent, and I had some chuckle worthy moments, but most of the jokes and references I didn;' get. Maybe that's just me... or maybe I'm getting old. lol. Also, the ending felt kind of.. well...
Play it if you're a Tooie fan. A few hiccups (arcade games, camera), but well worth your time.

LONG REVIEW INBOUND.
I've been waiting to write my review for this game until I've completed it 100%.
So, about 19 hours later, I've accomplished that.
And I have many mixed feelings.
I wish there were an option between "Yes" and "No" for the recommendation, because I'm just that inbetween.
To start off, I'm a very big fan of 3D platformers. I always have been.
The original Banjo-Kazooie is still one of my favorite games to this day.
On one hand, I do feel like Yooka-Laylee game delivers that nostalgia of N64-era platformers.
It has cute characters, the worlds are big and colorful, allowing you to explore and find the collectables required to progress further in the game.
It has some pretty good music, which are a more relaxed, atmospheric take on the B-K style tunes.
Jumping and moving around as the star duo feels fine most of the time, outside of some of the transformations and loose rolling mechanics.
So, there are some redeemable aspects, and I think that those looking solely for a ride of nostalgia will find enjoyment in areas.
What killed this game for me is the lack of polish, the over-abundance of technical problems, and some downright confusing and awful level design.
Hivory Towers, the hub world of Yooka-Laylee, is clearly trying to emulate Gruntilda's Lair from Banjo-Kazooie. The big difference being that Hivory Towers is often a chore to navigate, and you'll most certainly constantly be trying to remember how to get to and from each seperated section of the hub, until you've memorized it all 10 hours into the game. It's cluttered with so much nonsense, and feels too large for the purpose its serving.
I can extend the "too large" complaint to every level in the game. I was constantly being turned-around, and unable to distinguish one area from another at times. It's the worst in the first 2 worlds of the game. There is also a lot of empty space in certain levels, namely Glitterglaze Glacier and Capital Cashino. Offering nothing more than a giant blank space seperating objectives.
And, honestly, I think there are too many collectibles, considering there are only 5 main levels, excluding the hub. I was hoping they would have taken an approach more similar to Banjo-Kazooie than Tooie. By the time I've collected 25 pagies in a level, I was sick of looking at it. And if you're missing a single quill out of a whopping 200, good luck finding it in these massive levels. I was on a hunt for a single quill I missed in Tribalstack Tropics for about an hour. Once I found it, I was ready to punch a hole in wall out of frustation, due to the asinine placement of it.
Whenever I play Banjo-Kazooie, I like to complete a world 100% before moving onto the next. Unfortuntely, for those who also like to play that way, that's simply not possible here. There are two reasons for that, and both took a major toll on my enjoyment. Those reasons being: Trowzer the Snake, and expanding worlds.
Trowzer is a snake found in each world (including the hub) that teaches you new moves and techniques, which are required to obtain many Pagies scattered throughout the worlds. You pay quills to unlock his moves, and then they're yours to use as you please. With each new world, he'll have new moves for you to purchase. This would be fine, if it weren't for late-game moves being required to accomplish tasks in the earlier levels. This is a combination that results in a large amount of back-tracking, and having to navigate through the confusing mess of Hivory Towers repeatedly. To complete just the first world 100%, you'll at least need to have learned every move up until the fourth world in the game (to re-cap, there are only 5 Grand Tome worlds in the game). In my opinion, I feel like this breaks the pace completely, and doesn't do a good job of giving the player freedom, which completely counters what it seems like the developers were trying to give to the player.
A great example of that is how you can expand worlds. Once you unlock a Grand Tome world, you can then choose to expand it by paying a certain amount of Pagies. This might sound good on paper, but once again, I feel like it breaks the pace, and at times results in confusing level design pre-expansion. For example, when you enter the first world of the game, there is a structure you can climb by dodging fire blasting out of the walls. It's not a long trek, and not very difficult, but if you reach the top, you'll realize there's nothing there. Nothing to do at all. I was left confused, wondering what I was supposed to do. Was it a glitch? Or was this whole platforming segment pointless? Well, yes and no. It IS pointless, but only until you EXPAND the world. After expanding, another structure is added onto it, giving it purpose. It felt very half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and I'm not sure why they couldn't have just taken out the building completely until you expanded the world. In fact, expanding worlds in general doesn't seem like it was thought through very logically. By the time I reached the third world, I was immediately expanding the worlds before I even began running through it, to avoid confusion.
Overall, I think the level design ranges from awful to above average. I do think the final world of the game was the most enjoyable, and the best way to finish out the adventure. But, even then, there were many instances of frustation purely due to poor design or lack of polish.
And, don't get me started on this game's camera. It is absolutely just as bad as everyone makes it out to be, and it can be very headache inducing. HOW a game in 2017 has a worse camera than a game that released in the 90's is beyond my comprehension.
Another headache is the "arcade" style games, which you play in each world by acquainting yourself with a character named Rextro. None of these I found enjoyable, and ALL of them overstay their welcome. They are all poorly designed, have incredibly janky mechanics and controls, and once again felt half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and thrown in. I can extend that to the transformations found in each world.
Man, this is a long review.
I will say, I didn't think I had this much negative stuff to say about it before I began.
This is a very unorganized review, I know. I don't usually write reviews this long.
In conclusion, I don't hate this game. I hated it at times, but when it got on its rhythm, I was having fun.
But the camera, the technical problems (weird texture tearing, clipping, audio cutting out, etc), the often bad level design and confusing worlds, the back-tracking..
This is a game that DOES feel like an N64-era platformer, but one that you wouldn't have remembered fondly,  unlike Super Mario 64 or Banjo-Kazooie. If they manage to make a sequel, I'm hoping they take their time and make something really special.
I'd wait for a sale if you're really interested.

I went into this game expecting a reiteration of Banjo Kazooie, Banjo Tooie with mixes of their other games. That's exactly what I got. I wasn't a backer. I bought this game despite negative reviews because everything that people said was a negative quality I found to be rather entertaining and a taste of what I really did want from this project, more of RARE. Now the polish on the story isn't that good and the characters voices aren't as easy on the ears as Banjo or Conker's but this game's gameplay, is fantastic and really does bring a good call-back to the titles everyone used to love. I've played old titles recently, especially older platformers on my consoles and this lives up to them, doesn't exceed them, but it's 100% a creative approach and a well done game as a result. Some puzzles will frustrate you, sometimes you'll feel clueless, sometimes you'll have to back track to beat a certain part of a level but once you get a feel for the game all of this becomes enjoyable. However it is divisive and some people it simply isn't for. If you like RARE games, you will not be disappointed, this is basically Banjo Three-ie but you can't look at them through nostalgia goggles and expect it to be perfect, this is a solid 7.5 or maybe even an 8/10 platformer. It's a good game despite the critism it's been receiving and I would recommend it to anyone who enjoyed the RARE platformers like Banjo, DK64, Conker and more. They brought back collectathons, Minecart Courses and a bunch of interesting bosses and platforming puzzles to solve. Overall I think everything aside from the Rextro games was what people wanted who knew what Playtonic was making. A good old-school platformer that doesn't change too much but keeps the same gameplay charm a niche amount of people have craved.

But is a bit more deep if you focus on pacifism. (No more deep than pokemon levels of thought process.)
Going pacifist route removes the "emotional" side of the story, making it a bit more bland. (but more realistic)
Going "Genocidal" route feels a bit more boring, due to missing out on using other strategies for "combat", but you get more emotional storyline.
It feels a bit self destructive of a design.
Thats my #2 issue with the game.
Animations/Graphics are an obvious thing to poke at, so I wont bother, thats for you to decide from the pictures/trailers.
The game is extremely short.
Only made longer by slow moving and slow everything.
The game however is an ADD kids dream come true, with constant variation in puzzles/story/mechanics thrown at you. (just wish the level design was just as varied, and I would have loved it despite the other flaws.)
No bullet h*ll boss fight will truely stop you, as there's ways to deal with just about anything. (including armor of invincibility pretty much.)
But the challenge is moderate enough to be acceptable to just about anyone. (both bad and great players)
As with most RPG Maker like games, the keyboard controls arent enjoyable, so I suggest using a controller, if ur PCs USB dont like to shut off like mine constantly.
The "fast travel" is practically non existent, except in just 1 spot, which hardly needs it. The slow walking makes back tracking horrible. (Though you dont really need to back track unless you're unable to beat some of the final bosses, and need the best armor in the game.)
Wouldnt be so bad if there was a sort of hub, you can reach every "area" from, but its a straight line from start to finish, which means u have to go through almost every single place over again, except a few small bit of shortcuts. cutting off only 40~% of the trip down. (Which is a lot of hallways of black nothingness, and an occasional rock here and there, or w/e the object is that gives the area its theme/ground color.)
But, since there moments of actual quality in the game, but only on a rare occasion, I will say the game is worth getting at $5, but not at $10.
Get it on sale if u see it on sale.
Do get it.
but dont expect perfection, just expect a short little ride, and enjoy the good bits it does have.
(I will put dont get it, solely for the current default price, will update if its price goes down permanently)
Final Rating. 5/10

New comers, WB Montreal take the well respected and loved Arkham Universe and give it an Origins story in, Batman: Arkham Origins. Knowing the weight they carried, the developers kept everything the fans loved from Arkham Asylum and Arkham City and added to it. This payed off in the game play element but yet lacked in the environment. With the same beautiful feel of the Arkham games there was an unfortunate emptiness. As enjoyable as the Origins has been, it stands out as the weakest of the three games. Recommended none the less, and a big thumbs up!!

While this game definitely has its issues in terms of mechanics and bugs, I'm almost inclined to say that its story is the best in the series. The origin story provided the developers with a lot of flexibility in how to introduce some of Batman's best villains, the Joker being the most obvious of course. The voice acting, while not Kevin Conroy or Mark Hamil, was well done overall. Troy Baker is a good replacement for Mark, and he did a great job. By far, the best part about this game is the more angry and hard Batman. That being said however, you get to see how Batman struggles with his morals and convictions as a character and a hero. This is a must play for any Batman fan, and if you aren't a Batman fan you stand to enjoy it as well.

After playing the excellent 'Arkham Assylum' and 'Arkham City' this is so dissapointing.

If you're a fan of the Arkham series you will enjoy this game. It is technically an Origin story, but the only real indications of that are in the story, most notably in that Batman has never met the Joker before at the start of the game, as well as Jim Gordon not being an ally to Batman over the course of this story. The gameplay is more or less identical to AC, but honestly, why fix what isn't broken. No game has managed to do a game of this style this well, so I have no real problems with this being a serviceable follow-up to Arkham City.
Graphically, the game is magnificent. The game looks beautiful, and runs extremely well. I had everything on max settings, with AA and all, and never dropped below 60 fps. My monitor is only 60 Hz, so I had it locked at 60, but that shows that the game is properly optimized. Loading times were extremely short, even when not loaded on an SSD, as was the case in my experience.
What the game didn't progress in combat, it progressed in plot. The story is great, right up there with Arkham Asylum, and miles ahead of City, of which a lot of the city is more or less recycled. Is it. the voice acting is universally great, and a lot of lesser known Batman villains get brought to life. While not Heath Leger, Troy Baker's rendition of the Joker hits every mark a self-respecting Batman fan would want to see, and simply steals the show in every scene he's in. I really hope that this version of the Joker sees play time in future titles.
While some people might consider this a little bit of a money grab, and potentially should have been DLC for AC, but I disagree. The play time is quite lengthy for the main story, and there is just as many collectibles as in AC. I've spent close to 20 hours on the game so far, and that was just on the main campaign, which I think is enough time
I know the game has multiplayer, but I really don't have an interest in it, and have not played it, so I will not review it.
As far as AAA games go, it's definitely solid. Is it 60 dollars solid? I personally don't think so (but I don't pay 60 dollars for games, I don't; I only own this game because it came for free with my graphics cards), but if you're looking for an iterative sequel to Arkham City, this is not a bad follow up. If you see this in steam sales in the future, I'd highly recommend it, especially if you could get it at like, say, 20 dollars.

Although it's not as innovative as the previous two Arkham games it carries the torch well. If you're like me and were craving more Arkham City this is the game for you. If you're looking for a new narrative or anything spectacular you'll probably leave disappointed. The voice acting is great, Troy Baker does a fantastic job recreating the Joker. He'll make you fall in love with the clown all over again, and then abruptly make you never ever want to hear from him again. A must have for Batman fans and anyone who just can't wait for the next Rocksteady developed Arkham game.

I bet if people didn't know this wasn't Rocksteady studios they wouldn't even know the difference. It's like asking people to tell the difference between drinking bottled water and municipal water and then asking which one tastes better.
I'll rate this game high, I don't care. There is absolutely nothing wrong with Origins. If Arkham City were the third installment and this were the first one, then people would be making same complaints. I'll settle for the Uncharted 3 argument/syndrome but there is little to no reason to downgrade this game because it more or less features same core gameplay. And WHAT IS that "same"? Refined fighting system, satisfying action, old and new upgrades (that you have to actually work for this time around by completing challenges), expanded itnel/database, enigma's games, superb voice acting, crime investigations, top notch cinematics, joker's side of the story (a clock work orange), a plethora of new and old characters each of whom require a different takedown approach, the perma-death mode, among many other things, the horror!
There's little to no innovation? Well, for starters you can't innovate much when it comes to something that happened in the past. But there are small changes there and there. You can now slide into the grates and open them. You can daze your foes with smoke and they will swing their arms at each other and punch it each by accident. Many fights are no cakewalk. Many enemies become armed towards the middle of the game, the ninjas, the martial arts experts and Bane's brawlers can make fights quite tough. The environments are also more varied. There is still no blood splatter anywhere, however. Many fights requires preparation in advance - disable guns, check; disable gun crates check; mark the ones you want to bump together, check; throw the smoke pellet in the middle of the crowd, check; swoop in and start kicking♥♥♥♥♥
The game is considerably longer than the other two. It took me 30 straight hours to beat it and I have only completed around 60% of the game. The game literally goes on and on.
The game is much more Tim Burton-y this time around. There are more highrise buildings so there is greater satisfaction of gliding and plunging down. The city is filled with gangs and crimes that you can prevent. The streets are wide so there is more maneuverability. There is more approach to targets. The old Arkham City area is filled with somewhat disturbing Christmas decorations. The art design is off the charts. I also like the fact that you are kind of on your own in a sense that cops and criminals don't really know what to make of you. The graphics are also somewhat expanded, noticably the lens flare, the smoke that adjusts to your movement and changes its shape (nonexistent on the consoles), and physx (ah, those snowflakes dancing around when you fight 10 people at the same time - the consolites are missing out), AND LET'S NOT FORGET THERE IS NO GAMES FOR WINDOWS LIVE.
Each boss fights requires a level of investigation, psychological build up and later on skill and patience - something that Arkham City wasn't too famous for later in the game (which was one of GS's gripes by the way). The ultimate bane fight was as close to the Mr. Freeze fight as it got. The uneasy alliance with Gordon was also played out pretty well.
I can only wish this was the first installment. Arkham City was pretty much a perfect game but it doesn't preclude Origins from being a great game.
P.S. Don't skip the credits scene.

So... I really, REALLY wanted to like this game.  The team that created this are the same minds behind such classics as Banjo-Kazooie and Donkey Kong 64, some of my favorite games of all time!  Sadly, they dropped the ball with this game, and rather than the sucessor to the old, grand, 3D platformers of the past we get a jumbled mess of garbage.
Now, not EVERYTHING in this game is terrible.  The main characters, Yooka and Laylee, are interesting despite feeling like a less-interesting Banjo/Kazooie pair.  Many of the moves in the game are airlifted straight out of Banjo, but there are enough new ones, or changed nuances, to keep things interesting enough.
The level design is... no, let's just leave it there.  It is.  There's nothing great about any of them.  They're large, sprawling expanses which... for the most part are totally empty.  Exploring them can be fun at times but the sheer size (coupled with how convoluted the layouts are) make finding what you're looking for difficult at times.  Sadly, the worst of all of them is the HUB world, which was designed by a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ toddler.  Finding where you need to go has never been so hard.  Who knew, the hardest puzzle in the game is FINDING the next level so you can get back to playing the game.  Thankfully, the levels are amusing and colorful enough to keep things at least mildly interesting.
Now... the bad.  Everything else, THE END!
Ok, I get the feeling that people would get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥if I reviewed it like that.  Let's take a look at some (more) of the issues this game has.
First off, the camera is♥♥♥♥♥♥  There's no other way to describe this schizophrenic mess.  It jerks around without your consent, clips on EVERYTHING, and randomly likes to zoom all over the place while you're in the middle of TRYING to platform around obstacles.  Playtonic released a patch on release day to fix it.  They failed.  Hard.  This is something that you would EXPECT them to take the time and get right for a change.  Remember the "good ol' days" of 3D platformers?  Ever wonder why they vanished?  Well, this is one of the core reasons.  If the camera keeps swinging around on its own in a platformer then YOU CAN'T PLATFORM!  The direction you're trying to move in keeps changing WITHOUT your input changing.
Next are the controls.  SOMEHOW, the controls are even worse than the camera.  The button layout is unintuitive trash, to say the lease.  Sadly, after decades of progress, it seems some people still haven't figured out how to implement basic game functions such as adjustable hotkeys.  EVEN WORSE... if you play on PC and don't decide to go drop $30 EXTRA on a controller then just give up playing this game now.  There's NO "B" BUTTON mapped to the keyboard controls, so you'll constantly find yourself unable to do a challenge cause you don't have everything you need, which leads to loops of "Do you want to try again?  Press A - Yes / Press B - No".... but there's no ♥♥♥♥ing "B" button!  You need to "Quit to HUB" to cancel out.  Even worse, if you try to expand a world and don't want to yet... you need to QUIT THE ♥♥♥♥ING GAME and reboot.
A much more minor issue, for me at least, were the characters OTHER than Yooka and Laylee.  They're boring.  One of the coolest things about games like Banjo was the DIVERSITY of the cast.  Each new world had new characters for you to interact with.  They were dynamically built into, and interacted with, the stages.  This is not the case in Yooka-Laylee, sadly.  There's almost no diversity in the characters.  In fact, there are almost NO new characters in the stages.  They introduce everyone in the very first world and they all show up everywhere.  What's worse is the fact that they don't even feel like they belong there.  They're just stapled to the floor.
The puzzles in the game are also a bit of a grab bag.  When I know what I'm supposed to do, even if it's hard to accomplish, the game is FUN (all the game-breaking issues aside).  However, there are very few puzzles like that.  MANY of the puzzles in the game are AWFUL.  You have NO IDEA what to do, none of your moves have any immediate effect, and nowhere else in the game do these mechanics come up again.  Well, I say "again", but when this♥♥♥♥♥♥just randomly pops up 3-4 worlds in then Playtonic... THE ♥♥♥♥!?  Not to mention that many of the "solutions" for these puzzles are so arbitrary to what you're trying to actually achieve that unless you go look the section up you'll never actually figure it out without spending HOURS in the same place.
The mini games (which sadly protect MANY of the pagies in the game) are trash.  They're either ABSURDLY difficult because of the controls  or they're just NOT FUN.  There were so many GOOD ideas, like the Rextro games and the mine cart challenges, that it's a real accomplishment that they managed to ♥♥♥♥ it up so badly.
Oh yea, let's go back to the controls for another quick minute.  Remember how I said they were♥♥♥♥♥♥  They're still♥♥♥♥♥♥even now.  Not only can't you change them, but you can't even VIEW them!  They TOOK OUT the feature from the Toybox which let you view the actual control layout.  Something that's been a STAPLE of gaming since the NES era.  Playtonic... THE DOUBLE ♥♥♥♥!?
So, in summary.  If you want a nostalgia trip for games like Banjo and DK64, and nothing more, you might enjoy this.  If you want a good game, go elsewhere.
In another summary.  If you want a nostalgia trip for games like Banjo and DK64, and nothing more, just go play those.  THEY'RE BETTER!  If you want a good game, sorry, you still need to go elsewhere.
