When this first appeared there wasn't anything else like it. I remember seeing a tech demo where they replicated the infamous lobby shootout from The Matrix, naturally highlighting the "bullet time" feature to great effect. Max Payne is a gritty, dark, neo noir shooter/ mystery game that still holds up remarkably well 13 years on thanks to its solid gameplay. The plot centers around some pretty dark stuff: mobs, drug addictions, prostitution, corruption etc that seems to be all in a day's work for the NYPD detective on a mission for revenge against those who violently murdered his family: permanently tense facial expression included. The bullet time feature is still a great way of scoring trick kills and the game's dark sense of humour is always appealing. Also worth mentioning is the graphic novel style cutscenes they use to advance the plot: another thing that, to my knowledge, nobody else had done at the time. You've most likely played this before, but even if you have, pick it up. I'm currently enjoying working my way through it again. Classic!

I was late to the party with Undertale. I hate bullet hell games. Never had the reactions for them. I dislike only MOBAs more than bullet hell. First try once I discovered battle mechanics and accidentally killed a couple of characters I stopped playing because the game made me feel bad about these pixels I accidentally removed, as well as me hating bullet hell. But that's the first sign of me really getting why everyone loved this game. How it made me feel bad over some side character.
Recently, I was persuaded by a friend who loved the game to play through it again now that I knew how it worked, from the beginning. So I streamed it to him as I played a few hours every night for a week and we went through it together. Only the Pacifist run, because I hadn't the heart afterwards to play the Genocide run now that I had fallen so in love with the characters.
It is testament to Toby Fox's writing and composing that now, a week after completing this game, I am still listening to the soundtrack and crying every now and then when I remember the story. I fell in love with the characters, despite it taking me just 12 hours to beat the game. I only knew them for 12 hours, yet the knowledge of their fates at the end and the time I spent in their universe still fill me with joy and sorrow. At the end, both me and my friend were audibly crying over it, and not in a bad way.
I had a list of top 10 games I've ever played, of all time, the top two being original Deus Ex and The Witcher 3 in that order. I think storytelling is the most important part of a game, followed by soundtrack, then gameplay, then graphics. Why? Because for me the journey you are taken on is paramount for the enjoyment, and the soundtrack is what sets the scene. Forget everything else. Now, having played Undertale, it has taken that top spot. Now I honestly believe this is the best game ever made. I wish I had the power to erase my memory completely of this game so that I can once again experience that journey of getting to know these characters, laughing and crying with them, and relive for the first time again this story that has affected me so.
Toby Fox has truly created a masterpiece, making a fervent opponent of the game's bullet hell mechanics such as myself willingly and happily force my way through them just to find out what happens next, because it meant that much to me. Now that I have beaten the game, I no longer want to play it ever again because I feel that would undo the ending for each of the characters that I worked so hard to achieve, and I care about them too much to do that to them. I hate bullet hell, yet my number 1 game of all time is a bullet hell game. That is why this is the best game ever made.
TL;DR: 11/10, best game ever made in the history of gaming. Buy it, play it.

I just wanted to write this down in case I die in my sleep tonite. Heed my warning: Agricultural Simulation 2013 is beyond my mortal comprehension. I have now seen the true face of evil.
The best part of this game was the menu screen, and just because it was in HD. And it had a tractor in it. I was sceptic at best, but proceeded to selection screen. "Hmm, Tuscany, that seems nice enough", I thought to myself. Without any ceremonies, the game dumps me onto a courtyard filled with chickens, multiple buildings, a dog and a tractor. In glorious 3D, except ran through multiple gaussian blur filters.
Chickens flee at my wake as I run around the yard for a while. I take my hands off the keyboard, and my farmer alter ego keeps running. I disconnect gamepad and joystick, to no avail. Dog on the yard barks as I strafe around the yard, unable to stop. I try to steer myself towards the tractor standing in the corner of the yard, but I just climb over the damn thing and keep on running. Finally, after fiddling around with sound (wtf?!) options, I manage to disable the mystical autopilot feature.
I fiddle around with tractor for a while, managing to fire it up. The farmer is walking faster than the damn machine, so I just ditch it. I start rummaging through the multitude of various buildings around. I find some supplies from the cellar of my house. Items vanish into thin air as the farmer uses his nifty jedi powers to move sacks, milk containers and crates of fruit around.
I spot some livestock on the other side of the yard. Apparently I have some cows, a horse and a sheep or two. They make funny sounds when you click them. After few clicks I realize I have now managed to lock my horse into infite rotating loop. Few short moments later all my livestock are rotating around like some ♥♥♥♥ed up experimental farm yard merry-go-round. The display is too grotesque to behold, so I close the pen behind me, jump onto my trusty Massey-Ferguson and ride out of the farm.
Massey charges forward like a crippled manatee. I manage to enable autopilot again, and the top speed settles around 10. Mph or Kph, I have no clue. Running would be faster, but I dare not to challenge the wilds by foot. I take a smoke break. Get some late night snack. Take a leak. I come back to find massey around 100m away from the farm. In my frustration, I steer right, and all the rules of physics and universe fly out of the window. Massey's nose goes up, right around it's axle, and I land the vehicle upside down. My farmer doesn't give a flying ♥♥♥♥ as the camera clips inside his skull, apparently the weight of the tractor doesn't really bother him.
At this point, I pressed escape, exited the game, uninstalled it and removed it from my Steam game list.

I got incredibly bored this week, when I had gotten almost 8 hours through Omikron and had the existential crisis of "Oh my God! I've still got so much left to do!" So I had been trying to avoid it with something fresh and new (or fresher and newer), so I decided- what the hell- I'll try Jedi Academy even though I only have gotten a little bit into Outcast, and for the better part of this week I've been hopelessly addicted to Academy.
Jedi Academy is the story about the New Republic and there's some new Sith threat (out of the  hundreds of rising and falling Sith threats that always manage to pop up in the galaxy), and it's up to your custom-made Jedi (which will go by the name Jaden, for some read) to rid the galaxy of evil. Yeah, as far as story goes, this game doesn't have the best. It's just mission after mission, with no real revelations and the big "twist"- if you can call it that- was REALLY predictable. But this game is sort of like the Mario of the Star Wars video games.
What I mean is, while the story isn't any Oscar-winner, it's really the level design and gameplay that excel over everything else. Part of the reason I hadn't gotten through Outcast yet, was because the level design is vague as hell (something I'll go into whenever I review it), but Academy makes things laid out in a line, so you can't miss the important details along the way. Does it restrict the way you approach a level? Not really, because it's all about the environment in Academy's combat system that really makes it shine. The timing of your blows, how fast you move around your opponents, and which Force powers you use are all essential to winning a battle. And sometimes, even one good slice from an opponent can end you. Which makes sense, as I don't think Jaden would be walking properly after being cut from his groin to his head with a laser.
Probably the Force power I had the most fun with was Speed, as not only Jaden speeds up but everything around him slows down making the process of slicing down Stormtroopers and Dark Jedi a whole lot easier. And when you race lazer blasts and your own thrown lightsaber in slow motion I can hear "Time in a Bottle" playing in the back of my head.
As far as gameplay and unique levels that really shine in brining new aspects of challenge to your style of gameplay. Some levels require you to stop and think more. Some require you to act fast and adapt quickly. There are honestly a lot of memorable levels just purely on their unique conecepts (Like the planet with the acid rain, the hangar where the humongoues mutated rancor is chasing you, or when you have to plant bombs and Boba Fett is chasing you down).
I do like a good mesh of gameplay and story, but if a game succeeds in the former, it still is very commendable. Of all the Star Wars games out there, I'd have to say that Jedi Academy definitely comes the closest to really making you feel like a Jedi. And if you played this and didn't have any fun, I'd be seriously concerned for your mental health.

So far, this is definitely the best Star Wars games that I've ever played. Yes, that's simply how I felt that this review should start, because it's the goddamn truth. But throughout the game, besides learning a whole lot of different skills you're also free to select which side of the force suits you better. You can make as many mistakes as you like in order to learn the best way to beat a level. Gang Beasts looked like so much fun in the Early Access stage while watching let's plays.
We all know about Early Access disasters (i.e most of them) being terrible when they go full release because they are rushed out or abandoned, but how many games are WORSE after being released fully? Gang Beasts is.
At it's core and if you can muster 2 or 3 friends to sit around your PC and somehow find ways to get everyone controllers, it can be fun, I'm sure, but online play is so laggy that you will have to stick to local and make do: when the servers aren't down, which seems very common. Don't even think about "Waves" game mode (i.e survival against AI) it's just crap.
The Ui is the worst part, however. When you launch the full release game, the resolution will be stuck on 640-480 - a resolution that I haven't seen anyone use for 20 years. I don't remember the EA version having this problem. While it can be changed, I had to google how to do it because it wasn't possible to change with the Xbox controller I have. When I found out that for that particular menu option I had to use A and D to cycle through the resolution options... which took a while and was very sluggish.
Clearly, despite being early access on PC for a very long time, Gang Beasts has had no effort put into the PC version what-so-ever: they couldn't even be bothered to replace the button icons for the PS4 control pad - again this didn't seem to be present in the Early Access game.
Buy this on PS4 if you have one, and enough friends who would want to play, I'm sure it's fine. The developers don't deserve your money if you are playing on PC until these problems are fixed, however. Avoid.

Prison Architect is a golden example of how Early Access should be handled. Having released as one of the first titles in the "Greenlight" AKA "Early Access" program on Steam. Prison Architect's name is rather self explaining. You take the role of a warden developing a privately run prison. While the title is indeed a breath of fresh air from all the recent failed 'building' titles (Towns and DF-SB 9 to name a few), theres also a certain brand of gallows humor (Pun intended) and satirical jab at the private prison industry.
Players start off with some rather straightforward options: Fog of war on or off? how big do you want your starting map to be? would you like randomly generated trees; buildings and bodies of water? Would you like to include failure conditions (Too many deaths in a day, ongoing riots or debt being the chief factors here), Would you like gangs to be able to form in your prison?
Pros:
1) Active modding community in the workshop adds to an already brilliant title.
2) The developers have improved on this game hundreds of times over in it's time in Early Access.
3) An extremely helpful community, with more guides than you can shake a stick at.
4) Randomly generated prisoners ensure no one prison is ever truly the same.
5) With notepad++ you can tailor the game to be harder or easier with very little computer knowledge and a guide.
Cons
1)  This game is all about learning from your mistakes. So it may not be for those with less paitience.
2) Sometimes  prisoners and staff behave a tad strange, however extensive patching has eliminated almost all of this.
3) As of posting this review (9th of Sept. 2015) PA will soon leave Early Access, meaning fewer updates. Having said that, theres so much content here that can easily be overlooked.
All in all, I give this game an easy 9/10

The Arkham City formula is near perfect in my opinion when it comes to game play. If you're wanting more of that, you have it in this game. The combat is just as fluid as it was in Arkham City. However if you're looking for something completely new and innovative, Arkham Origins game play wise is something we haven't seen before from the previous installments. But for me personally that was not a problem. The story is well written, but is a little shorter than the previous game's stories. Nonetheless there are still several side missions that can be accomplished, adding to the richly told story.
I would recommend this game to those who wanted more Arkham City. as this game does deliver in that regard while adding some new content to the near perfect formula.

If you're looking for something different from Arkham City, I suggest running away from this as fast as possible.
This is what one might call an "iterative" sequel. It adds virtually nothing new. HOWEVER, when you're building on what is near perfection, that's not a bad thing.
Combat is slightly more refined to what it should be, story is a lot stronger, missions are a little worse, open world is terrible, multiplayer is interesting, new detective mode is good. Oh, and the game is A LOT HARDER.
Call WB Montreal lazy, but it's still a great game.

While in my personal opinion this game is not an overall improvement of Arkham City it is still a very solid game and I recommend it to anyone who has played the previous two games of the franchise. That being said if you are someone who is looking to jump into Arkham franchise; this is a very good choice for starting with. There have been many complaints about this game being too similar to City in regards to the combat which to be fair is pretty similar to the City with a few minor changes and they use the same assets as in City. However in story driven games such as this I don’t really mind it that much so long as it gives me an interesting and entertaining story which this game does. The best part of this game has to be the new detective mode they introduced, instead of searching for some paste on the ground you attempt to reconstruct the crime scene by piecing together clues you find and rewinding and fast forwarding the crime scene as you construct it. It’s really one of the most innovative things I’ve seen in video games in a while and really brings out the “World’s Greatest Detective” in Batman. My two biggest problems with this game are actually the way it was advertised and the multiplayer (SPOILER ALERT AHEAD). In the steam page of this game you will see batman facing off against two villains, one being the crime boss Black Mask and the other the mercenary Deathstroke. If you are fan of comic books you’ll know that Black Mask is one of Batman’s most underrated villains with a fascinating back story and Deathstroke a prominent foe of the Teen Titans who is a very formidable opponent. When they announced this game they stated that Black mask would be the main villain and the first trailer of this game featured an epic fight between Deathstroke and Batman. I was very excited that these characters were going to be shown prominently outside the comics. However, Deathstroke is only involved in one fight and is never seen in the campaign again and Black Masks back story is never touched on and you only ever actually see him in one cut scene as it is reveled in a plot twist that the Joker had been masquerading as the Black Mask for the entire game. Had I never seen the trailer or followed the build up to this game I probably wouldn’t have thought anything of it, but having been led on to expect a campaign mainly featuring Black Mask and Deathstroke, I couldn’t help feeling let down by this. Now I’m not saying that the story in the game was a bad one, far from it actually, it was just something I received that I wasn’t expecting. The multiplayer on this game has its fun moments but is ultimately a pay to win game which is just really unnecessary for a game that isn’t free to play and anytime you play as a thug and not Batman and Robin, you’re really just looking forward to the moment you can play as Joker or Bane.

I have played many games, for many hours. But this game... This is amongst the handful of games I genuinely give a 10 out of 10!
When I downloaded this game I expected nothing of it, I laughed it away and I thought: "Hah, this will be boring". Nothing was further away from the truth. It evolved from a game into a lifestyle... And while I'm writing this I have only played 80 hours of it...
I thought that this would be a game where I drive my truck through one or two roads, attach/detach a trailer and done.
But this game is so in detail!
* Realistic graphics, definitely for an indie game! I've seen A-rated games that were graphically inferior to this!
* Realistic truck designs and driving mechanics.
* Realistic extras: Petrol stations, sleeping places, fines for breaking the traffic laws, cabin and trailer damage upon collisions, road signs in the language of the country you are in, etc...
* Being able to start your own company, hire drivers, etc..
The only 2 things I would advise as a patch or for ETS3:
- Visible damage to cabin or trailer when collided. Because even when I caused world war 3 on my way to my destination, my truck still looks unscratched.
- NPC's that also follow traffic laws. For example taking over from the right (left in UK)... I see NPC's doing this all the time to me. And when I signal that I want to go to the left lane, the cars on the left lane should slow a bit down or go to the third lane to make way. This problem caused me to collide many times in countries like Germany where the right lane suddenly turns into an exit lane.
Thank you SCS for developping this masterpiece.
PS: Adding Dutch paintjobs to the game would make it sooo awesome for me!

Disclaimer : I was a Kickstarter backer, so I had high expectations and they were fulfilled. But that also means I knew I'd most likely like the kind of game it set out to be, since I loved previous games of the same genre.
This game is exactly what it set out to be: a worthy spiritual successor to Banjo-Kazooie. You pretty much can't review this game without comparing it to Banjo-Kazooie, so expect a lot of that in this review.
I am a fan of Banjo-Kazooie (BK), Banjo-Tooie (BT) and Donkey Kong 64 (DK64), and I fell in love with this Yooka-Laylee. Right now, more than 15 hours in, I have 100% completion in all but one world, which I basically haven't touched, and I have not yet finished the story. If you like 3D platforming, collecting a lot of things and looking for every nook and cranny to get everything (although it's optional, that's the only way I've ever played these types of games), then you won't be disappointed. It really is a blast to the past.
It's more in the vein of BT and DK64 in how it approaches its level design. In BK you could pretty much do everything in one swing, save one Jiggy, while in the later games you had to backtrack to previous worlds after unlocking abilities to get everything. This game does involve backtracking to get everything, but you can get still progress through all the levels without backtracking and then come back to expand the worlds and get all the stuff you missed when you have all abilities, making it so that you only have to visit all levels twice. The second time you visit a level, after expanding it, there will be new areas to explore. So, basically, if you hated Banjo-Tooie or Donkey Kong 64 because of the backtracking but liked Banjo-Kazooie, you may still have some problems with the design they chose, but it shouldn't be as bad. I, for one, got bored out of playing Banjo-Tooie in my last playthrough because of how tedious it gets when you try to get everything. Yooka-Laylee doesn't have this problem.
All in all, it's a very fun game, it delivers what it advertises, and while it doesn't innovate in especially extraordinary ways, it's still not a carbon copy of Banjo-Kazooie; there are both things you'd expect and surprises to be found. There are still some parts which may be frustrating, but to me it's part of the design that I loved from the earlier games.

As a conceptual premise, this Hitman has the most potential of any of the titles. Like the devs have described, this is in fact a playground. Leaps and bounds have been made with a few setbacks from previous titles.
PROS
- Conceptually perfect sandbox, huge amount of toys, paths, possibilities, interactions etc.
- Beautiful asthetics and well optimized. No issues playing 120+ fps at 1440p most of the time.
- Challenges, masteries, achievements, are all non-invasive that add a lot of opportunity for replays.
- Pre-mission planning.
- Each level can be seen as a stand-alone mission, or part of the bigger storyline
- Player made contracts, escalation and elusive targets add more potential to each map
- LOTS of NPC's, with lots of dialogue to bring the maps alive
CONS
- AI needs a lot of work. Understandably programming huge amounts of NPC's to have 'realistic (within reason)' dynamic responses is no easy task, but it can really make the game easy or hard depending on your situation. An NPC could watch you run into a forbidden area but wont respond at all because they need to observe you for a certain period of time before a response is initiated. On the other hand, holding a screwdriver can be considered suspicious.
- Wherever you are in the world, the Morrocons, the Japanese, the Italians etc, all speak fluent English in perfect British or American accents. I'd much rather local dialect with subtitles. This really breaks immersion when you go to Bangkok and the entire hotel of Taiwanese employees were apparently born in America. Though for some reason in the Japanese hospital the computer AI monitoring the place has a Japanese accent?
Things i like to see added / minor CONS
- Small in game crafting system. Allow 47 to pick up duct tape and some wood to craft a weapon as you weren't allowed to bring one in for example.
- Keyhole looking. As i play with basically no HUD or unit indicators, being able to look through a keyhole while not terribly realistic, allows for more map interactions. This was a neat feature in previous titles.
- Slow walk speed button. 47's walkspeed is faster than everyone else. This is obviously so players can catch up to targets without running. But it looks odd at times and if you have to follow an NPC, you can't just walk behind them because you constantly catch them and must stop temporarily otherwise you will run into them.
- Inventory needs work. There is no quick weapon switch, If you want to swap out an item, you must press the inventory menu, which pauses the game, then you select which item you want through rotation.
- No briefcase. I understand this could seriously make the game very easy by allowing you to transport any(?) item across the map, in any disguise - however without, using something like the sniper can quite difficult as you can alert basically anyone who sees you; and Hitman has always been about hiding in plain sight, and not a splintercell infiltration game.
- only 2 seconds to throw a 160lb or so man into a wardrobe? Convinient and fluent sure, but small immersion break. (I get that it's a game, not a simulation)
This really is a mix of Blood Money and Absolution. Hopefully it doesn't drift towards a James Bond/spy styled series where 47 develops some sort of moral compass and wants to make the world a better place so we can hold hands and throw rose petals at each other. I also miss some of the goofy arrogant behavior of NPCs from Absolution, where they would taunt you and speak about you as some bald dude that has been working out. Oh and they changed the voice of Diana, probably gonna notice that if you're a verteran Hitman fan.

Now that the game is updated I can recommend the game.
It is now possible to override the video memory lock, and the (now "soft") limit is increased to a more sensible max. 2560x1600 for 3GB video cards. Which means I can run it at 1440p.
The huge open Paris level is a very different experience from Absolution and I think the Opportunity works well (you can turn it off if you're hardcore and want to find out stuff for yourself).
The two smaller training levels and the one big level offer enough replayability to justify the price tag (13 euros for Intro Pack) for me.
I have a stable connection, the servers disconnecting only happened to me once, and I can somewhat understand why it was necessary to make the play-only-once contracts work and ensuring the scoreboard is fair (now its filled with impossible max scores because of a (now fixed) bug with the time bonus for missions, the update log mentions an incoming highscore reset). The solution still sucks for people with bad connections, but if you have a good internet connection it's pretty much a non-issue.

Agricultural Simulator 2013 - Steam Edition, is a simulator that allows you to learn all of the aspects of running a modern farm, from the comfort of your chair. As far as simulators go, it is one of the easiest I've seen in a long time. The tutorial walks you through each step and let's you play through the process of how to hook up and unhook equipment, manage fields and livestock, maintaining your equipment, as well as much more. You are given a choice of 4 different regions to choose from, as well as three different maps. The farm equipment used in-game, is based on actual equipment farmers use,  bringing another immersive level to the game.
Campaign mode is available, aside from tutorial missions, and you can also start a new game and build your own fully functioning Agricultural Farm from the ground up with only the bare minimum. Campaign mode has several missions for you to complete, for those want a little more direction, and there are a bunch of different types of crops you can grow. They seem to have a pretty healthy selection, each with their own challenges and rewards. All in all this is a pretty fun simulator, which kind of surprised me. I didn't think farming would actually be fun, but if you like simulator games, this is a good one to try out.

To be honest I don't get what all the fuss is about regarding Undertale. I played through it including all three endings and while the writing itself isn't bad at all, the game is extremely repetitive,  and heavily biased against the player by marking him either neutral, a mass murderer or a hippie-pacifist with zero tolerance for the latter two endings. Kill literally no one or literally everyone, otherwise you're neutral. Alright.
The game by no means is bad and to some it might contain a fresh look at RPG games in general, but to me it felt like a cheap indie knock-off to Zelda but without the actual fun parts. The game is simplistic, and while the soundtrack is amazing, much of the rest is not that bad, but far from being as outstanding as reviews might suggest.
I don't really mind that this review will most likely get downvoted into invisibility, but Undertale has a hype train behind it which it by far does not deserve and a story that could have been considered great in the late 90s but falls completely short regarding current story-telling standards. Any and all plot twist are foreseeable, characters are fleshed out well but so over the top that - at least to me - they feel simply off. And gameplay wise ... well, imagine Zelda with RPG Maker battles, without the actual battles but a repetitive exhaustion of predefined dialogue choices for each enemy variation while having to dodge projectiles in very tiny bullet hell windows representing your soul force. Sounds not even interesting, plays even more lame.
Looking at the overwhelming reviews, I cannot imagine what all those people see in Undertale. Apparently I was not able to and therefore I cannot recommend this in a way that would make me upvote it.
It has a lot of content for the asking price, but I went through three playthroughs to be able to understand what people see in this title and personally feel like I simply ended up wasting a few dozen hours without being any wiser about it. This in particular is irking me, as I indeed was more than able to enjoy games like Sometimes Always Monsters, The Cat Lady or To The Moon to a fabulous degree and am a very story focused person.
Maybe it was just the setting, I don't know, but I recommend anyone unfamiliar to the game to ignore the hype train and just let this title sit there.

Super Meat Boy is that simple. You know what you need to do, the controls feel natural and somehow familar. The levels start out easy and quickly become very difficult, forcing you to learn new techniques and improve how you control Meat Boy. Most new games increase your characters stats to help deal with the increasing diffuculty in the game. Meat Boy stays the same and you have to improve yourself.
This game is inspired by old school games, which you will see in many hidden references and game design. If you die you have to start the current level over, but unlike old school games there are no lives or continues. You can make as many mistakes as you like in order to learn the best way to beat a level. The game can be beaten in a few days but the main story doesn't even scratch the surface of the available content. Collect bandages, warp zones, and extra characters. Beat the dark world and A+ times for each level.

Max Payne is a challenging thirdperson shooter with bullet time (Which unique for the time), solid story telling, an interesting gritty, dark, silly and often distrubing narrative, superb sound design  and music (You'll need a patch to fix it) all combined with some incredible set pieces and a man (who thanks to the teams experience and budget at the time) who looked like he was about to♥♥♥♥♥♥his pants named Max Payne.
Crysis this aint and while the character models are what REALLY date the game even for 2001 Max Payne is still in many aspects a great looking game considering the low budget and small team behind it. The environments are well detailed,believable and generally well laid out and I should know as I live in New Jersey and have seen New York constantly meaning if anyone can attest to the accuracy it's me. It used pictures they took themselves for loacles, reference and for the textures which really wen't a long way in terms of grounding the game and general belivability/immersion. Max himself is infact (Or at least the photo that constitutes his face is) modeled on the lead writer Sam Lake who thanks to not being low poly does not actually look like he is having lemons shoved up his♥♥♥♥♥ The environments are highly interactive and for the most part destructable too so it's not just style over substance as far as I'm concerenced. Minus the cutscenes it's like a thirdperson equivalent to Half-Life minus Xen.

Max Payne is an awesomely cinematic game, with some stunning action gameplay that goes both powerfull and very addicting. It has a GREAT story (I can't express in lines how great it truly is) that goes involving and is told in a series of graphic novel sections, narrated by the forever dramatic James McCaffrey doing Max's voice, while lead writter Sam Lake plays the role of Max on screen.
This game didn't just introduce and literally create the Bullet Time mode on videogames, it's also by far one of the best cinematic games ever made, I got into it expecting only a good Third Person Shooter, but when I finished it I came out with an entirely new appreciation for the Gaming Industry. Max Payne is a Pc classic that deserves to be played by everyone that likes action games, and everyone with a taste for truly cinematic videogames, because Remedy Entertainment achieves an amazing level of interactive story telling, creating a masterpiece that I would, with no doubts, include in my Top best games ever made.

‘Pool Nation’ is a fun, polished Billiards simulator and a bargain at its $1 pricetag (Steam Fall Sale 2014). Released as the maiden offering from Cherry Pop Games, it’s gorgeous visuals, multiple game modes, lengthy campaign and lots of unlockables will keep Pool fans coming back for more.
Gamers have the choice of playing standard 8-ball or variations like 9-ball, Rotation, Endurance, Sudden Death etc across a variety of visually stunning locations / pool halls. A lengthy campaign mode (against AI opponents) allows you to perfect your game and strive toward numerous unlockables including new locations, pool table decals, new ball styles and cue styles. Additionally, the online mode allows you to match up with friends or other online players in single matches, Tournaments or King of the Hill events. Multiple difficulty levels (from Novice to Pro), a spot on physics engine, responsive controls, and a great soundtrack make this the best Pool game to date.
In considering its biggest issues – 1. Game Stability is poor (Tabbing to windows results in an insta-crash) and 2. Online Gaming is largely dead (Bring your own friends). Additionally, the developers have pushed the previously promised ‘Trick Shot’ mode to the next release, and the lack of Co-op play is disappointing as well.
Overall, ‘Pool Nation’ is the best conception of a Billiards game to date and fans of the real game will find this a fun, polished distraction. But, even ardent fans soon realize that Pool without the smoky basement rooms, uneven cues, pitchers of beer, chatty girls, side-bets and bar-room trash talk, is a somewhat hollow experience. Recommended on Sale (Best played with Friends) - Rated (7/10)

Just to be clear: I haven't grown up with old titles such as Banjo-Kazooie or Super Mario 64. I have watched full playthrough of Banjo-Kazooie and I can see all the references in Yooka-Leylee, such as all these grunts, snarls etc. while talking, the quiz show between some worlds, all collectibles and many other things. It is more than clear that Yooka-Leylee wants to be a spiritual successor to Banjo-Kazooie. Is it really? I cannot tell since I haven't played Banjo-Kazooie. I can say though that the game does not disappoint.
In terms of gameplay you have a pretty general goal: collect everything in every world. When it comes to finishing the story you just have to find a hundread pagies, which isn't much. I believe that the game has 135 pagies but don't quote me on that. The point is that you don't have to collect everything if you just want to finish the game. The worlds are quite large in their normal state but can be later expanded to reach enormous sizes with much more stuff to do than before.
When it comes to collectibles you have previously mentioned pagies, which act as keys for unlocking and expanding worlds and in the end, the final boss. Then you have quills, which act as currency to buy abilities. The number of avaible quills is more than enough to get every ability as soon as they become avaible, so no frustration over not being able to make certain puzzle should occur. Those are the basic colelctibles, but there are other things, such as play coins, molicools, ghost writers etc.
The controls in my opinion were fine and didn't feels stiff or annoying. That is of course if we only mean Yooka and Leylee in their normal state. If you get into anything that has wheels then better get your patience ready because those parts can be infuriating. Thankfuly there are only three or so moments when that happens.

FYI, I backed this game on Kickstarter. Its a solid 8/10 game. The camera issues were fixed on launch. Its exactly what it set out to be, which is a modern day collect-a-thon, warts and all. Given that I've played Banjo Kazooie/Tooie and Donkey Kong 64, none of the warts bother me all that much.

As of 4/14/2017 I have 100%ed the game. It still lacks the N64 Shader Tonic and the 'secret' that the Toybox refers to.
I backed Yooka-Laylee as soon as I was able on it's first day on Kickstarter and I don't regret it. BUT the game is not perfect. It's got its flaws and plenty of them. It inherited the flaw that most 3D Platformers tend to have and that's a poor camera that Banjo-Kazooie and Banjo-Tooie, the games that this will naturally be compared to, also have.
This game feels like an in-between of the two. It has neither of the twos' highpoints but shares a few of their low points such as Banjo-Kazooie's unmemorable bosses and mostly arbitrary transformations and Banjo-Tooie's poor tacked-on multiplayer, though it ends up doing all of these things words than the originals did.
Minor Spoilers Will Follow
1. WORLD
The hub and the first world of the five is fantastic but the other worlds dwindle in quality and feel less alive as the game goes on. The idea of expanding the worlds really interested me and the first world's expansion is great. It feels like a real expansion to the world.
The second world's expansion unlocks a cave names Icymetric Cave due to the view that's forced on the played but the pun doesn't lighten the blow that the disappointing expansion hits the player with.
The third world's expansion is alright but the world's design seems to want to go for a Halloween feel but they drop the theme quickly and just go with "ugly" as the theme.
The fourth world looks pretty but feels incredibly barren and lacks unique challenges. You get a Pagie by trading in 10 tokens and you get 44 tokens from breaking open broken slot machines around the level and 22 from playing slot machines. That's 6 Pagies right there from doing nothing fun. And with 5 challenges that repeat in every world (excluding the bosses) that leaves you with 14 Pagies around the world (which you will get by collecting more tokens).
The final world feels a lot like a collection of unconnected things. It's got space/pirate/carnival theme going and feels disjointed but it's not bad.
2. COLLECTING
I loved collecting the Quills more than the Pagies. I think it may be to the lack of an animation that Banjo-Kazooie had. It always made collecting a Jiggy that much more cinematic and fantastic to see the duo dance. It gave them more character that Yooka and Laylee miss out on in this regard. So while the Quills and the Ghost Writers (this game's version of Jinjos) are fun to collect the Pagies feel more like a means to an end.
There are two things I have a problem with in terms of making collecting a little too easy. At a certain point in the game swimming becomes incredibly easy which may make it better in this one regard to Banjo-Kazooie and Banjo-Tooie as swimming was a chore in both of those games. HOWEVER I would rather them have found a way to make it fun rather than easy.
The other problem is flying which you get late in the game. There are no pads you have to stand on. You can fly anywhere and  your power recharges after a while so you can get to a high point and wait and then fly more if you need to. The game becomes 'too easy' in these cases.
3. TRANSFORMATIONS
The transformations are almost useless except for the one in the last two worlds. All of the other transformations are used  to get one Pagie or maybe two that are very close to each other. The only transformation that's actually fun is the last world's. Banjo-Tooie had much more important transformations. Yooka-Laylee's transformations feel like an afterthought.
4. REPEATING PAGIES
This is in regards to the Pagies that you get the same way in every world. There are 5 (excluding the boss).
i. Collect all 200 Quills
ii. Collect all 5 Ghost Writers
iii. Beat Kartos's Challenge
iv. Beat Rextro's Game
v. Beat Rextro's Game again (and beating his high score)
Only the first two are fun and that's ONLY if you like collecting things. Kartos's Challenge feels like a less tight and dumbed-down version of Donkey Kong Country's minecart levels and Rextro's games all suck.
5. BOSSES
The bosses are all unmemorable and bland. A few are okay in the moment but fail to really stand out. We get a bunch of Targitzan but no Mister Patch.
-Jontron issue. To let people know any biases I may have I disagree with Playtonic's decision to remove Jontron's voice. While I don't think that they are infringing on his right to free speech I believe it's hypocritical of them to do in regards to what some of their developers have suggested on Twitter during the 2016 election and in the long run I think it will just create more problems than it will solve. A much less messy thing they could've done was to just make a statement saying that they disagree with what Jontron said and it does not reflect on the company. While I'd like to be charitable with Jontron and think he just mispoke (I also believe he misintepreted statistics) I will impart a quote that he should follow and we could all learn from: "It's better to be thought a fool than to open your mouth and remove all doubt."
FINAL VERDICT
Unless you REALLY love Collect-a-thons like I do I can't suggest it. If you don't know how a Collect-a-thon plays then you need to go play the games that this is a spiritual successor to because they are both far superior games. And if you really love those then come back and play Yooka-Laylee. It's pretty fun.

Fundamental flaws in level and boss design, terrible pacing, and a whole lot of missed marks. Don't buy if you're looking for the Banjo experience.
From the outset ,the game looks promising, a casual sense of humor, good looking art design, and a control scheme reminiscent of other nostalgic titles, but the game begins to fall flat soon through the first world. Locations are large, but empty, with traversal becoming near meaningless later in the game with the always available ability to fly, but this only helps to make the game bearable, as locations are simply a trudge, being far too large for the scope of the characters movement.
Boss fights are a pain, instead of being creative and fun, they are more of a chore, mostly requiring you to subscribe to the school of "Don't get hit, hit it more." As well, due to their abhorrence of things like Health Pick ups mid fight and check points, already boring fights become abyssmal quickly due to multiple sections (The last boss fight has near 8 sections, all of which are still, don't get hit, hit them more.)
The pacing begins strong, the game introducing plenty to get you moving, but eventually you're just using your roll and fly to try and hurry through the massively empty levels (World 5 is ESPECIALLY bad about this)
There was plenty to build on here, but somehow they flopped. The game, when compared to nothing else, is average, but when compared to its legacy, its incredibly below average.

EDIT 28/4/16: Episode 2 is bloody amazing. I'm changing my recommendation to positive; there are already enough people boycotting the game that sales numbers are low enough for Square Enix to get the message that their always-online garbage ain't cool. Definitely glad I bought it - can't get this kind of experience anywhere else. Well, I could in real life I guess, but that has potentially unpleasant consequences, and no save-reload mechanics.
EDIT 23/4/16: This week's patch incorporated a reconnect option that allows you to reconnect to the game's servers should you happen to be disconnected during play (Thanks IO). This helps somewhat to solve the immediate frustration of having your gaming sessions disrupted, but still doesn't change the fact that the game is almost entirely single player, yet is unnecessarily hampered by draconian DRM and a pointless always-online requirement to access new equipment and unlocks. HITMAN may very well lose most of its content if the servers are shut down without the developers rectifying these issues. If the game wasn't so damn good I'd be boycotting the next episode(s) until they remove all of it completely, but I don't think I'll be able to help myself. Damn you Square Enix.

To be honest I don't get what all the fuss is about regarding Undertale. I played through it including all three endings and while the writing itself isn't bad at all, the game is extremely repetitive,  and heavily biased against the player by marking him either neutral, a mass murderer or a hippie-pacifist with zero tolerance for the latter two endings. Kill literally no one or literally everyone, otherwise you're neutral. Alright.
The game by no means is bad and to some it might contain a fresh look at RPG games in general, but to me it felt like a cheap indie knock-off to Zelda but without the actual fun parts. The game is simplistic, and while the soundtrack is amazing, much of the rest is not that bad, but far from being as outstanding as reviews might suggest.
I don't really mind that this review will most likely get downvoted into invisibility, but Undertale has a hype train behind it which it by far does not deserve and a story that could have been considered great in the late 90s but falls completely short regarding current story-telling standards. Any and all plot twist are foreseeable, characters are fleshed out well but so over the top that - at least to me - they feel simply off. And gameplay wise ... well, imagine Zelda with RPG Maker battles, without the actual battles but a repetitive exhaustion of predefined dialogue choices for each enemy variation while having to dodge projectiles in very tiny bullet hell windows representing your soul force. Sounds not even interesting, plays even more lame.
Looking at the overwhelming reviews, I cannot imagine what all those people see in Undertale. Apparently I was not able to and therefore I cannot recommend this in a way that would make me upvote it.
It has a lot of content for the asking price, but I went through three playthroughs to be able to understand what people see in this title and personally feel like I simply ended up wasting a few dozen hours without being any wiser about it. This in particular is irking me, as I indeed was more than able to enjoy games like Sometimes Always Monsters, The Cat Lady or To The Moon to a fabulous degree and am a very story focused person.
Maybe it was just the setting, I don't know, but I recommend anyone unfamiliar to the game to ignore the hype train and just let this title sit there.

While in my personal opinion this game is not an overall improvement of Arkham City it is still a very solid game and I recommend it to anyone who has played the previous two games of the franchise. That being said if you are someone who is looking to jump into Arkham franchise; this is a very good choice for starting with. There have been many complaints about this game being too similar to City in regards to the combat which to be fair is pretty similar to the City with a few minor changes and they use the same assets as in City. However in story driven games such as this I don’t really mind it that much so long as it gives me an interesting and entertaining story which this game does. The best part of this game has to be the new detective mode they introduced, instead of searching for some paste on the ground you attempt to reconstruct the crime scene by piecing together clues you find and rewinding and fast forwarding the crime scene as you construct it. It’s really one of the most innovative things I’ve seen in video games in a while and really brings out the “World’s Greatest Detective” in Batman. My two biggest problems with this game are actually the way it was advertised and the multiplayer (SPOILER ALERT AHEAD). In the steam page of this game you will see batman facing off against two villains, one being the crime boss Black Mask and the other the mercenary Deathstroke. If you are fan of comic books you’ll know that Black Mask is one of Batman’s most underrated villains with a fascinating back story and Deathstroke a prominent foe of the Teen Titans who is a very formidable opponent. When they announced this game they stated that Black mask would be the main villain and the first trailer of this game featured an epic fight between Deathstroke and Batman. I was very excited that these characters were going to be shown prominently outside the comics. However, Deathstroke is only involved in one fight and is never seen in the campaign again and Black Masks back story is never touched on and you only ever actually see him in one cut scene as it is reveled in a plot twist that the Joker had been masquerading as the Black Mask for the entire game. Had I never seen the trailer or followed the build up to this game I probably wouldn’t have thought anything of it, but having been led on to expect a campaign mainly featuring Black Mask and Deathstroke, I couldn’t help feeling let down by this. Now I’m not saying that the story in the game was a bad one, far from it actually, it was just something I received that I wasn’t expecting. The multiplayer on this game has its fun moments but is ultimately a pay to win game which is just really unnecessary for a game that isn’t free to play and anytime you play as a thug and not Batman and Robin, you’re really just looking forward to the moment you can play as Joker or Bane.

Arkham Origins is an excellent installment into the franchise to the series and definately one worth buying. I played the first two Arkhams on the Xbox 360 and plugged in a 360 controller to my computer to play this game as well, so the controls for me felt very familiar. The combat is smooth and a lot better, though the better fights also mean the fights are significantly harder, but the lack of game changing elements (other than new and better gadgets) make the fights also begin to feel repetitive at times, like little things you have to do in order to get to the sweet, wonderful boss fights. However, it's not the gameplay that makes Arkham so great, but rather it's fantastic story. Every plot point ties in with eachother beautifully and, even despite this game being a pre-quel, it creates a completely fresh and new story with many unexpected moments and incredible feats of character/character development for Batman and his villains alike. The map here works better than City's, though not due to it's size, but rather it's believability. City tried too hard to make every notable building have something going on with it, whether a side mission or just snipers on the roof, while Origins leaves many buildings just building while still adding enough features on their other buildings to feel the need to travel wisely. If you enjoyed the last Arkham games then i would definately recommend this game, to the point where the story and bossfights alone are worth it.

Mad Max is an open world action game set in a post apocalyptic wasteland. It features a blend of various gameplay mechanics into what I think is a really solid experience and worth your time if you are into these sorts of games.
The game has a lot of high points and a couple of low points. The best part of Mad Max is the vehicle portion of the game. The driving is fun with a great sense of speed and the vehicular combat is a blast. The rush of racing through the wasteland battling against a gang of vehicles in a car loaded with rockets, flamethrowers, nitro, harpoon gun, spiked rims, etc. is thrilling. The sense of speed and impact of your weapons makes every encounter a fun and engaging experience. My only criticism (and that goes for the rest of the game) is how easy it is once you upgrade your vehicle. Once I had my rockets maxed out the challenge was gone so I forced myself to mix up my weapon use in order to keep it fun.
You can upgrade your vehicle the way you want. You can have a speed demon, slow but tank like vehicle, or a mix of both by adding/removing parts such as armor, bumpers, spikes, etc. There are aesthetic upgrades available as well but it's not as robust as I would like. You only have the choice of a few decals/paintjobs/body parts.
While the hand to hand combat feels brutal it feels a little clunky. It's not as smooth as say the Arkham series or Shadow of Mordor. Maybe that's on purpose because it does feel a little 'heavier' and it could be due to design. But the problematic camera can be frustrating if you are in closed spaces. As you would have guessed from my Arkham comment the game uses a combat system similar to that game series. If you are not familiar with it it's based on pressing the attack/block/counter buttons at the right time in order to flow freely and rack up your hits. The longer your combo goes on the faster your 'fury' meter rises. Once it is filled you hit a lot harder than you normally do.
The map itself is large and filled with a lot of activities. Unfortunately, the variety is scarce and it does feel old by the time you get near the end. The tasks are really simple; destroying an enemy camp, killing snipers, destroying scarecrows, talking to random NPC's, and finding loot locations. The loot locations allow you to find scrap, parts to expand your bases, and collectibles. Scrap is used to upgrade your character and vehicle but at a certain point you are going to have an incredible amount of it so you don't need to worry about saving up.
The graphics are gorgeous and the game is very optimized. The developers did an incredible job with the PC version of the game and they should be commended. One thing you should know is people have reported heavy stuttering when playing the game on a HDD so I recommend installing it into a SSD drive. Ultrawide screens are supported and you can re-bind your keys as well.
I really enjoyed my time with Mad Max. I really hope they make a second game and I cannot believe how underrated this game is. I believe it will be a cult classic and I for one am very glad to have experienced it.

I thought this game would start off on a high note; one that would get me fired up and ready to take on the challenge set before me. I thought I would enter the world of post-apocalyptic Dubai ready for anything. But I didn't.
I thought that I would feel satisfied every time I landed a well-aimed headshot, like in CSGO. But I didn't.
I thouht I would save the civilians and kill only those who stood in the way of what was truly right. But I didn't.
I dropped white phosphorus on the civilians I was trying to save. Those men I killed with a well-aimed headshot were the true heroes. I was the villian. Anyone who wants to know what the world of war which video games have created is really like: play this game. Next to Portal 2, this is the second game to ever make me shed a tear. But this time it was for the complete opposite reason. The story was incredible.
Issues with the gameplay only lie in the fact that they were unorthodox and strange, but after an hour or two I had mastered them. Still a bit fiddly at times, though.
The graphics and visuals were great. I truly believed I was in a ruined Dubai. Even when it's destroyed and uninhabitable, the place still blew my mind. Occasionally some of the player textures would sporatically change resolution; they would look life-like one second and then potato the next, all having to do with the angle at which they were viewed. The anisotropic filtering became a noticable annoyance in some cutscenes. But even then, it was a beyond passable overall experience. Someone poured a lot of time in making it as good as possible; this much is evident, even with a few minor hiccups.
8.5/10

This is a hidden gem for people who like singleplayer games. At first glance Spec Ops: The Line looks like a generic brown military shooter set in Fakeistan. And on the surface, it is! But it's not just about the gameplay; this is an experience which will make you doubt your own actions and the actions of others. Making and releasing this game took SERIOUS cajones, but  I have to say: this is the most anti-war game about war I've ever played. If you want a game where the story and themes are so great you don't even care that the running and gunning is rather simplistic, try this. It is seriously a candidate for the notion that games are art, in a way that other "artsy" games just don't.

I paid for Banjo-Kazooie 3 and that's exactly what I got.

I walked into the jungle themed area from the starting position and, in no time, encounter a butt-stomp puzzle with no real lead-in or any clear reason as to why it was in the middle of a pathway. I completed it and was given the main currency of the game, a Pagey. I pressed B and Yooka vaguely tweened his head forward and spat his tongue out with no real force or fun applied to the animation. It looked like a non-tweaked motion that Unity's built-in animator seemed to have chucked out and nobody considered to make it look satisfying or add any cute flair to it. I looked around the zone to see where I might want to go next and had no real sense of priorities as nothing whatsoever helps guide my eye (except for the fact that some places are taller than others). I can't make out much because it's all the same browns and greens. I find none of it attractive.
A little ways away was a giant arcade cabinet just as thoughtlessly thrown into the zone as much as every other major setpiece. I consider that it would have been neat if a cave had led into it and separated it from the zone somewhat, but instead squint at how it's just out in the open too. I don't think the level was ever designed with it, or other major Pagey sources, in mind. I ignore it and climb a tower that I halfway glitch upwards in a poorly telegraphed segment that reminds me of Glover. An unlovable medieval pig is over there and he wants me to find his friends. For some reason. I think he's in every zone, as are probably all of the extremely gross looking NPCs that are arbitrarily assigned roles in what can only be a "design first, affix later" philosophy. They are just here. For some reason.
Everything is here, all at once, for some reason.
Yooka Laylee seems to go over a checklist of things that other Rare games had and hopes that you're very forgiving of it if it doesn't remember why it's doing what it does. The levels feel like they were just strung together one small chunk of land at a time and the grab bag of "necessities" was just sort of emptied out on to the landscape. If anything, it's actually even more reductive than the original Banjo Kazooie on that front. My complaints are not at all that Yooka Laylee is meant to be a pastiche or retread of old Rare platformers and that's bad, but that it fails to even be good at that so far. It's not a good standalone experience, it's not a good nostalgic experience. It's just.... nothing and I can't see this changing either. Maybe I'll get to the latter levels of the game and be shocked that they start appearing thought out. I genuinely wish it played more in the Shovel Knight vein of "this is what your childhood REMEMBERS these games being, not necessarily what they WERE" and not ..... whatever this is.
Back in jungle time, I walk up to a really gross looking cloud that looks like a Donkey Kong Country 3 render from 1996 and challenge him to a race. I groan as I remember that a fun mobility tool that makes the game more enjoyable to navigate actually costs energy to use, despite this move already "costing" an element of controllability as a fair tradeoff. I have to walk into butterflies to regain that stamina it uses. But if I hit B and do the really lazy tongue animation, I eat that same butterfly and regain health instead, actually.

Play this game, or play Russian Roulette?
REVIEW DISCLAIMER: I am human, a gamer, a loyal fan of anything Batman, and severely jilted by my experiences with this game. This review can't be completely objective, but I'll try. I DO intend to write from a first-person/casual narrative, so if you are bothered by that, look elsewhere.
Anyway, you can probably guess that this won't be a positive review. Sadly, my level of Batman fanboyism, which is pretty severe, makes it all the more bitter to write.
First, the positive points:
-New story
It's always nice to see a new story, but a pretty major bait-and-switch early on makes it tough to swallow. Also, the game's writers, Corey May and Dooma Wendschuh, aren't exactly Batman veterans. Despite that, the story DOES deserve positive marks--if only because we get more adventures of the Caped Crusader.
-New Arch-Vilains
Fighting Deathstroke was a highpoint for me; unfortunately I can't claim to have finished the game(more later), so there may be more noteworthy battles in the second half. The way the game engineers the boss battles is interesting, pitting Batman against his foes where they are at their strongest. Situations include a fight while poisoned, the aforementioned bare-knuckle brawl with Deathstroke, and the like. One boss battle is engineered for stealth(the enemy has a hostage), as well. It does seem to truly test all of the pillars that the previous games built.
...With the few Highs out of the way, let's look at where Arkham: Origins falters. Sadly, this will be the real meat of this review. Your mileage may vary, obviously, but mine, personally, was abysmal. From here on in, I'll only touch on each point briefly, as they are numerous.
Again, understand that this is subjective, I am only trying to lay out my own experiences.
My major gripes, organized into subgroups with details:
-Glitchy
---For me, the first boss fight had graphics issues/BOSS DISAPPEARED(try fighting invisi-Killer Croc, WTF)
---Enemy AI and pathfinding are broken. In ONE stealth sequence FOUR GUARDS got stuck walking into walls/corners. Stealth, meet stupid.
---Combat timing is broken. You're supposed to combo smoothly between one technique and the next, but, SURPRISE! When you begin an animation, you get decked by a guy who was ACROSS THE ROOM A MOMENT AGO.
---Again, combat is BROKEN(worth repeating). timing for counters is inconsistent and erratic, leading me to nearly punch my monitor before ragequitting. BTW, I'm good, when the game works as advertised. I had no problems free-flowing through Arkham Asylum & City.
-Repetitive
---NEW ENEMIES(except, not really, they're mini-Banes, thugs on Venom, since, y'know, those fights were such fun, right?)
---Gameplay was frequently extended using contrived methods. For example: Was that ten-minute fight over too soon? ...Not really, we're gonna throw in 15 more goons, AT ONCE. AND REPEAT TWICE MORE. This might have been less of an issue if, again, the free-flow timing worked properly.
---The leveling system is a rewardless grind with TWO SEPARATE TREES OF ARMOR UPGRADES BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE, and a whole lotta "not much" after. Obviously, it's hard to follow Rocksteady Studios' well-rounded arsenal, but the gadgets here feel tacked-on and poorly thought-out. It almost feels as if one of the developers said "Well, that's as good as it gets, so let's give them armor upgrades." Since this is a prequel, certain constraints had to be observed to respect canon/timeline, but even THAT feels like a thin excuse.
-Nothing new
---Exact same hunt/fetch/collect side missions(some of which are nearly impossible FOR NO REASON(here, go find a bomb allllllll the way across the map. You have Three minutes. Oh, and your grapple is busted/glitchy. Good luck, have fun.
---Mostly recycled map from Arkham City(Except, y'know, this game doesn't take place in Arkham City, so seeing NO civilians is jarring and immersion-breaking.
And finally:
-high probability of encountering game-breaking bugs
---My game had innumerable issues, some of which noted above, but the Pièce de résistance was when, after fighting Bane atop a hotel(minor spoiler: you fight bane, major spoilers averted), my game froze, and crashed to the desktop. This had happened several times before, and each time, I simply restarted the game, kept calm, and carried on beating thugs.
Not this time.
This particular bug, which apparently has something to do with the Wwise audio engine, was consistent. Beat Bane, Crash to desktop. I attempted the usual methods of repair, Cache verify/driver check(all up-to-date)/uninstall & reinstall, I even installed the game on a separate computer, always with the same aggravating result.
Sadly, because there's no manual save function, my whole savefile is stuck there, and I can't even return to the city without a full restart.
It should be clear by now that I feel this game is broken, and my trust in the entire franchise is now decimated. I got the game with the purchase of a new GPU, so I can't even ask for a refund. As of now, it sits in my library, un-beaten and uninstalled.
The promise of a new successor to the Arkham series was delivered as a string of thin excuses; the gadgets and skill tree had to be preserved, it's a prequel. Okay, fine. The city is RECYCLED, with no civilians, but it's a record winter storm, so they're all gone. Sigh, okay, fine. Batman can't fight, but it's because he's still getting used to his black suit. Hold up. Do you see a pattern?
To make it worse, all these excuses are laid atop a game that is physically, shamefully, broken.
I feel that WB Montreal should issue a public apology, and be shuttered over this. It makes me sad that they're still active and making excuses, while better studios like Psygnosis Studios(and later, SCE Liverpool) were shut down, and they were making incomparably high-quality product. For shame.
TL; DR:
Stay away. I don't even recommend pirating it.

Arkham City sits at one of my most favorite games of recent years, it was perfectly made and well paced. How exactly could they improve it, shortly put.. They didn't. However, I do recommend this game fully. Just not at full price.
I preordered this not expecting much, but what I did get was a dose of strong story telling and character development and is definitely worth playing if you can make it past the thirty year old man child that is our immature protagonist.
- The map is now larger, covering portions of soon to be Arkham City and New Gotham, albeit empty due to a cop out excuses of curfew. Even with this larger area, the game feels intolerably lonely and devoid of creativity that was present in the previous titles.
+ The music is more fitted to the Christmas themed enviroment, my favorite being The Joker's Theme. Which is allowing of an eerie but calming feel.
- The Boss battles fall flat, being a series of button mashes and repetition. Except Deadshot, it took me forever to beat him and I loved every single agonizing death with restart. This though does not make up for the failure which very well could have been a surpass to the fight with Mr Freeze in Arkham CIty.
+ A semi-detailed look into the canon background of The Joker, directly referencing The Red Hood. With a major plus of showing him as being what he is, the polar opposite of Batman.. being given no choice to do what he must because that is the way society has made him, just as Bruce has been made into what he is by the actions of others... mainly Joe Chill.
+ Well delivered characters especially Edward Nigma, whose appearance was more horned in than ever before, but welcomed. He made me question if what I was doing was the moral thing to do, yet Big Bad Bat Bruce seemed to ignore it, lost potential there.
- Immature Brat Bat. I understand that this is supposed to be an origin story, ignoring that Bruce crowned the cowl two years before the start, but he is such a ♥♥♥♥♥ at times. He is even straight cruel to Alfred and even endangers him time after time because of his careless nature.
+/- The newly added and changed features were some iffy choices.
- No Bruce, You cannot have gadgets seven years before the prototype was made.
+ Crime Scenes show the true detective skills that make Batman the "World's Greatest Detective." (Even if they were kinda look here click, look there click.)
- Very Eh Upgrade system, feeling more like the linear choices of Arkham Asylum.

This is a great game that has been damaged beyond use by its creators.  It has a number of mechanics that are quite fun.  There are multiple different ways to move around the universe (including surfing a wormhole) which is fun.  Ship design has enough detail to be fun.  Combat is a mix of skill (manual aiming) and equipment which is also quite fun.  The most fun you can have is capturing another ship.  This requires some amount of skill because the ship has to be damaged a lot in order for your troops to be able to overwhelm the other ship's crew and automated defenses.  All this should make for a very enjoyable game.  However, someone seems to have confused annoyance with difficulty.  When they created higher difficulty levels (normal is quite easy and, therefore, not very fun) they decided to make ship capturing more annoying.  Not harder (by making enemies stronger).  Not riskier (by increasing the chance you will get jumped by pirates looking for two ships for the price of one).  Not more expensive (by increasing the cost of troops).  Not less lucrative (by making the salvage value less or increasing taxes).  They just made it more annoying.  On any level above normal they make is so that other ships in the area continue to fire on the ship you are trying to capture.  This means that unless you are really fast, the friendlies will destroy your prize.  You cannot fight them off because they have overwhelming power and numbers.  This mindless agression is also focused on ships that you have been paid to capture.  Thats right, organizations will put a reward out for the capture of a ship so they can extract vital information, but at the same time, they let their own ships just blow the information up.  Because that makes sense.  The justification for this behavior is that ship capturing is the easiest way to make money so they wanted to make it harder.  But they just made it more annoying by having the AI troll the player.  As a strange consequence of their logic, the higher level difficulties are actually much easier.  Neutral ships will always attack "bad" ships as aggressively as possible.  This includes ships that you have been hired to kill.  So you can actually take almost any mission that is a kill mission because the neutrals will kill the enemy for you.  This is much faster than trying to capture ships and towing them back to a station.  You just wander in, let the computer do the mission for you, collect the prize money and wander away again.  Easy, but not very fun.  The creators have been defending their choices for years (there are steam forum posts from at least 2014) so don't expect it to change.  The game might be worth playing if someone has a mod for AI behavior and adjusts the difficulty in a more rational manner.  I'm not quite ready to give up on the game but I definitely cannot recommend playing it as the creators have built it.  Unless you like being trolled by your own computer.  In that case, have fun.

Brief Linux port technical review (i.e, not reviewing gameplay/story)
CPU: i7-3770k @ 4.20GHz
GPU: Nvidia GTX 970
Distro: Mint 18 x64 Cinnamon
Kernel: 4.4.0-42-generic
GPU Driver: Nvida 370.28
Right off the bat, let me say this game performs phenomenally and looks great. Running an Nvidia 970 with every setting cranked up to its highest possible value (beyond the presets), I get a solid 60-80 FPS at 1080p. The only time I've noticed the framerate drop is, oddly, around numerous latern/candles (not sure exactly how to describe them), which only bottomed out at 48fps. The issue seems to be limited to these particular objects and no other sources of fire (like burning cars) or other graphically demanding things (like giant sand storms) seems to bring it down at all.
The game, like many these days, seems to handle controllers relatively well. I plugged in my 360 controller while the game was still running and automatically detected it and instantly switched the buttons displayed on the interface upon using it, and switched it back upon using mouse/keyboard (you can swap between the two, no problem). My only complaint here, which, I know is nitpicking, but the game doesn't seem to be able to handle simultanious controller and mouse/keyboard input well. As absurd as I'm sure it may seem to some, I like to be able to use my controller to drive with one hand and my mouse to aim with the other, and while I'm using the mouse the controller input goes undetected, so I'm not able to drive and shoot as well as I'd like. The slow-mo and aim-assist makes aiming fairly easy to do with the controller, so this is a pretty minor gripe.
The audio seems to be great (using the headphone configuration), but I've had a few relatively trivial issues here as well. When opening something with the crowbar (I think it's called something else in game), the sound for when something is finally opened seems to be absent. I also had an odd experience where the audio was very slightly muffled off and on for about 15 minutes. I can't say whether or not this is normal game behavior though, just the two things that stood out as seeming odd.
Overall, this definitely seems to be a great port. The few issues I've encountered are minor to the point of being something that could easily go entirely unnoticed without looking for it. While the negatives may seem highlighted over the good things here, that's mostly an artifact of any port review - if it's done perfectly there's really nothing at all to talk about, and so much of this port seems to be that.
If the game sounds interesting to you and you're a linux gamer, I'd definitely suggest picking it up.
Edit: Here's a video showing off an example of a low-fps area. The video was captured and uploaded at 60fps (so watch at either 720p60 or 1080p60 quality). The video also shows an example of one of the audio bugs (at the start of the fight). It may potentially contain spoilers.

OK, so Undertale. I have almost 60 hours on this game and god knows why - I've run through each route multiple times. Let me tell you a bit about it.
First off, the music. The music in the game is FANTASTIC. There's a sense of nostalgia during some battles, or walking through certain areas of the game because some older tracks can be heard later on in the background. EX: 'Spear of Justice' has 'Heartache' in the background. Check the audio files :D
I wanted to mention while this game is short, you should replay it multiple times. After about 6-7 replays, you'll stop noticing anything new, but new things happen for the most part whenever replaying, and there are 3 different ways to play the game: Neutral (Kill some spare some), Pacifist (Spare all), and Genocide (Level grind and murder everyone.) I recommend you play it in this order: Neutral, Pacifist, Genocide, Pacifist. (The pacifist ending changes after playing genocide.)
This game is a work of art, and not very surprisingly, it's well received for it's comedic lighthearted top with a darker story underneath, and it's lovable unique characters. These characters aren't your bland sidekicks who support you through the game with that sudden story twist that makes their personality make sense. These are diverse characters who feel lifelike, with unique backstories, goals, motivations, etc.
Now parents, this game does have swearing (Only 2 times I think and it's very mild), and it is pretty violent if you choose the genocide route. However, I wouldn't hand it to younger kids for disturbing imagery in quite a few parts of the game. (EX: Amalgamates, The final boss in the neutral path, some other things) This game has some adult things in it, such as drinking, smoking, mild 'suggestive' content as some people put it. Older kids would be fine to play it, maybe 13+ in my opinion, as anyone younger might have trouble understanding some parts of the game. If it had an ERSB rating, which it will soon considering this game will be a PS4 game (Wooooh!), The community has debated between a T and M rating.
Another thing - This game is incredibly difficult in parts. Some bosses are fairly easy, others you can spend HOURS with little to no progress in beating them. (If you keep trying you'll get there! I've beaten every boss in 1 try, and a certain boss who leaves you with 1 hp with somewhere in the 30s.)
The battle system is also unique - every single character has different actions you can perform, from flirting with the enemy to persuading the enemy that their better than that and consoling them whenever something bad has happened and they are venting their anger on you. You can use items, fight, act (Talking to the enemy), and spare/flee. Each character must have a specific order of actions to be done in order to spare them.
If you are looking for a game with a strong backstory left up to the player for some speculation, secrets hiding everywhere within the game's code, and characters that will begin to influence your daily life and how you make choices in the real world, this is for you.
Seriously though, don't touch the fanbase. If you want to keep your soul (ayyyy puns) then don't even prod it with a stick. As a warning so you aren't curious, the fanbase is literally split into 2 portions: The good side of the fanbase, where people draw amazing art and respect the game for what it is, and the bad side, and the side of it that's just porn. Literally. Careful. Don't look up Undertail either - That's the darkest of the bad side.
