This is my all-time favourite game in my all-time favourite game series.
-It is the perfect mix of exploration, character growth and  difficulty that every adventure-rpg needs to be successful. Along with the looting and OP loadouts to strive for, while at points can be tedious to farm for, it is always worth the effort (especially considering the fact that one of the latest hotfixes boosted the attainability of rare loot by 300%).
-Now on top of the solid core of Borderlands 2 already has, the game is FULL of humour and ridiculousness that keep you coming back to play it, even after 2+ years of owning the game.
-All the characters have suprising depth under their humourous layers, with interesting and sometimes tragic backstories to their names.
-The newest entry in the series, 'Borderlands: The PreSequel' (Prequel to BL2, Sequel to BL1) cannot even begin to compare to Borderlands 2, especially with the meta-game of BL2 being some much more in depth and full of bosses and guns to find.
- The game is also beautiful in design, with it's comic book-like art style. Which I, for one, deeply feel suits the style of the game. It can be as light-hearted as a comic, but also as serious and deep as one.
-You will lose yourself in the environment of this game, so much thought and time put behind every single map, location and interaction.
-And of course, you can't have borderlands without a crap load of guns, and this one definitely doesn't disapoint. With millions and millions of guns, all with unique abilities, stats and specs, you're sure to find one that you'll love.
-Now, a game wouldn't be complete without a good enemy, right? Well, Handsome Jack takes the cake for my favourite video game baddy by far, and many agree with me. This guy is hilarious, maniacle, and will stop at nothing to get to his end-game. What that is, you'll have to play to find out.
Do I recommend this game? Hell yeah I do. Heck, I've recommended it to all of my gamer-friends, and this game has never ceased to dissapoint.
Do yourself a favour and buy this game, you will not regret it.

There has been quite the controversy around this game. Many people are disappointed because it doesn't quite live up to the greatness of the original Banjo-Kazooie and Banjo-Tooie, to which it's supposed to be a spiritual successor. While I agree with this, it's still a very fun game and it certainly scratches that itch for a collectathon 3D platformer. I don't regret backing this on Kickstarter at all two years ago.
The gameplay is immediately familiar if you've played the N64 games, the characters fit the same archetypes and the worlds are filled to the brim with stuff to do.
Unfortunately, the game as a whole is simply not as memorable due to some issues. There are only five worlds, so there is somewhat of a lack of variety because you spend a lot of time in the same places.
Also, while getting around is a challenge at the beginnign as it should be in this kind of game, some of the moves you get as you progress through the game just completely break this aspect and make going back to earlier worlds to get what you missed or skipped feel stupid, because the new moves trivialize the challenge you would have had if you had tried to do it in the "proper" way the first time. This makes it seem rather pointless to stay in a world once you have collected just enough pagies to move on the next one - which is not a lot.
Additionally, it's somewhat annoying that there is a severe lack of variety in enemies and world-inhabting NPCs - you basically run into the same ones in every world, and they don't fit the overall theme of the world either because of this. This is a severe setback from the N64 Banjo games.
The soundtrack is a mixed bag - some of the tracks are really great and memorable, while others are bland and repetitive.
These negative âspects don't stop the game from being enjoyable at all though. There is a lot of stuff to do in the worlds, the various new moves you unlock give you that "ah-ha!" moment when you remember a spot you couldn't get past earlier and are now able to thanks to that new ability, and the dialogues, animations and character sounds are as quirky and fun as ever in the Banjo games. Playtonic definitely managed to capture the atmosphere of them, so hats off for that.
Overall, if you are a fan of the N64 Banjo games, I recommend this - it does have its flaws, but Playtonic delivered on what they promised.

I wrote this review in January of 2015 on Metacritic.  I thought I posted it to Steam, but did not.  This game deserves a review.  Here's a copy/paste of my former review.  The game has only gotten better through expansions.
I am a Star Citizen backer. Want to know a dirty little secret? I love and crave 3rd person space games. En route to searching for something to fill this desire, I came across this game. "A Steam sale?" I asked. "Twenty-four bucks?" I blinked. "I spend that on 2-3 drinks at a restaurant with the wife..." So, I plucked this one out of the Steam shelf, downloaded and started playing. Eight hours later I looked up and saw it was 4am. "Woah..." The next (read: later that) day I dove into the Starpoint Gemini 2 Community and learned I was late to a really cool party.
Did you love Freelancer? Are you craving a 3rd person Space game? What are you waiting for...? Pick this gem up ASAP. There are few games that are so worth your money that you'll want to encourage others to purchase, but this is certainly one for me. In a day when space sims are seeing a great resurgence, it's refreshing to see a game that's not afraid to be 3rd person and give the player a bit of a relaxed take on space.
I feel like a Malcom Reynolds, flying around in my ship, always with my eye on a new shiny, but lovingly holding onto, in my case, "Big Red," until the time is truly right. There's dangers around every planet, but I've got a crew, a purpose, seemingly endless space to explore (certainly more than my limited time allows), and a ship. There's even a fun plot-line to follow along as you make your way in the galaxy--or don't; whatever--it's all up to you.
I can assure you that if you want a rewarding, relaxing, and immersive (but not taking itself too seriously) space game, this is it. I give it a 9 (I'd have done 9.5 if it let me) because of the somewhat outdated UI, and the graphics are not the most polished. That said, the graphics do not detract from the game too much and again, it's sort of a breath of fresh air of late with the Elite: Dangerous's and Star Citizen's of the world.
The development team has their ear to the forums and though I am new to the scene, they appear to be largely shaping the game around their community. It's mod friendly, and seemingly more so as time goes on, and there's already some great mods out there. It's much of anything you want in a fun game.
Cheers.

I would definately recommend this game... but with some notes of caution.  I consider my self a supporter of 'Little Green Men', because I've always enjoyed their games ( at least the few I have).  However... I feel this one is falling a bit short, and I'm unsure if these are problems they are having issues resolving... or have just given up.  However... the problems that I've seen thus far, are more inconvenient than Game Stopping.
There's a serious issue with early game over powering of the enemy.  While I've heard a claim by the developers that this was a Development decision, I personally believe this is a Bug that they haven't been able to resolve.  Basically, when taking a mission which is marked at a specific level, the mission turns out to be impossible to complete even though your level made be higher than the recommended level.  Option:  Run and find another mission and hope this doesn't happen too often... but it will.
Another issue deals with Enhancements which can be added to ship's equipment and weapons, but the Enhancements do not actually enhance the item.  Note:  some... not all.
Licenses, also, which should provide specific bonus do not work.  Note:  some... not all.
Other than the above I have no other negative issues with this game.  It has all of the elements of a Good Space Sim, with many choices on how one wishes to play... Fighter... Merchant... Miner... Salvager... or even pirate.  I usually don't play pirate until I get bored with a game, but don't want to stop and need a new challenge.  however, the problem with being a pirate in many space sims is the limited choices you get; often being more of a headache than anything else.  But with this game I've seen the pirates (or more correctly, the Hostile Factions) have as much territory to operate in as the 'So-Called' Good Guys.  I'm actually looking forward to trying my hand as a pirate.
The merchant side of the game is IMHO as well done as it seems to be possible based on the many games I've played, and wanted to be a Merchant.  In short... I don't feel like it's Great... but it does seem Very Good; just haven't got a decent size Cargo Ship for really trying it out.  However... for the little trading I've seen and done... it looks like it has "Very Good" Potential.
Mining for both Ores and Gases was done in a very fun and unique way... which I've been enjoying for the most part.  It doesn't really seem to make as much money as Combat... but then again, this is a Combat Game; I just like mining; with a touch of combat to give me a reason to wake up in the morning.  But you'll still need to focus on combat fairly early just to get a decent ship for mining.
Combat was a bit disappointing at first because of the mechanics used to control the ship.  I found it was best to turn on Auto-Fire on all turrets... which seemed a bit Impersonal to me.  However... as I got better with all that you can do to Protect and Enhance you ship in battle... Aiming my Laser became the least of my problems, and I was rather happy I didn't have to worry about that anymore.  But that is a matter of Personal Preference.
Also... the Skill and Perk system is fun; I like the fact that you can "Sort Of" custom build yourself for the type of Player and Character you choose.  I'm not a fan of being forced to play a specific character as is done in the Campaign (I feel disconnected to my Character while following the story line), but that, again... is just Personal Preference.  And the fact that I can build him the way I choose is far more important to me.
One of the best aspects of this game "To Me" is that Money, thus far, is maintaining it's value.  Too often in Single Player Games you find that Money loses it's value far too soon.  Once you get to your 3rd or 4th ship -or- 20th or 30th level, you find  you start ignoring ways of making money... and just focus on leveling... because there just isn't anything left to buy that you can't afford.  I'm current level 43, and still find myself occasionally trying to scrap together a few Bit Coins to buy that Blaster with the Extra Kick.  I find that once a game's currency loses any real value (or more directly; Need) the game heads down hill from there.  At the time of this writing I have roughly $17mil, and trying to get to $29mil for the next for the next ship I want; but not the last ship I'll fly.
All in all; while I got this game on sale, I would not have been disappointed if I had paid full price (assuming full price was under $40).  I definately would recommend this game; with hopes of certain issues being resolved.. but with confidence it's still a Fun and Addictive Game.

Pool Nation delivers a solid billiards simulation experience.  It makes the grade in the areas critical to this type of game:  the physics are sound,the shot-making is clean, and there's enough variety in the game types to keep things fresh for a while.  On top of that, the game is downright beautiful.
There are some flaws, but nothing game-breaking.  The most glaring (for me, anyway) was that the game feels literally empty.  When shooting, you're shooting in a seemingly deserted hall.  There's no crowd, no opponent squirming in the chair as you knock the balls down.  Speaking of your opponents, while their descriptions are modestly humorous, there's little to differentiate them from one to the next.  At times it feels a bit sterile.  Again, this isn't really game-breaking.  But part of the allure of playing at the bar or hall is the atmosphere, and the game is lacking in that regard.
All in all, though, the plusses outweigh the minuses.  If you're a billiards enthusiast, this game is just about value for money at full price and a bargain if you can pick it up on sale.

OK, so Undertale. I have almost 60 hours on this game and god knows why - I've run through each route multiple times. Let me tell you a bit about it.
First off, the music. The music in the game is FANTASTIC. There's a sense of nostalgia during some battles, or walking through certain areas of the game because some older tracks can be heard later on in the background. EX: 'Spear of Justice' has 'Heartache' in the background. Check the audio files :D
I wanted to mention while this game is short, you should replay it multiple times. After about 6-7 replays, you'll stop noticing anything new, but new things happen for the most part whenever replaying, and there are 3 different ways to play the game: Neutral (Kill some spare some), Pacifist (Spare all), and Genocide (Level grind and murder everyone.) I recommend you play it in this order: Neutral, Pacifist, Genocide, Pacifist. (The pacifist ending changes after playing genocide.)
This game is a work of art, and not very surprisingly, it's well received for it's comedic lighthearted top with a darker story underneath, and it's lovable unique characters. These characters aren't your bland sidekicks who support you through the game with that sudden story twist that makes their personality make sense. These are diverse characters who feel lifelike, with unique backstories, goals, motivations, etc.
Now parents, this game does have swearing (Only 2 times I think and it's very mild), and it is pretty violent if you choose the genocide route. However, I wouldn't hand it to younger kids for disturbing imagery in quite a few parts of the game. (EX: Amalgamates, The final boss in the neutral path, some other things) This game has some adult things in it, such as drinking, smoking, mild 'suggestive' content as some people put it. Older kids would be fine to play it, maybe 13+ in my opinion, as anyone younger might have trouble understanding some parts of the game. If it had an ERSB rating, which it will soon considering this game will be a PS4 game (Wooooh!), The community has debated between a T and M rating.
Another thing - This game is incredibly difficult in parts. Some bosses are fairly easy, others you can spend HOURS with little to no progress in beating them. (If you keep trying you'll get there! I've beaten every boss in 1 try, and a certain boss who leaves you with 1 hp with somewhere in the 30s.)
The battle system is also unique - every single character has different actions you can perform, from flirting with the enemy to persuading the enemy that their better than that and consoling them whenever something bad has happened and they are venting their anger on you. You can use items, fight, act (Talking to the enemy), and spare/flee. Each character must have a specific order of actions to be done in order to spare them.
If you are looking for a game with a strong backstory left up to the player for some speculation, secrets hiding everywhere within the game's code, and characters that will begin to influence your daily life and how you make choices in the real world, this is for you.
Seriously though, don't touch the fanbase. If you want to keep your soul (ayyyy puns) then don't even prod it with a stick. As a warning so you aren't curious, the fanbase is literally split into 2 portions: The good side of the fanbase, where people draw amazing art and respect the game for what it is, and the bad side, and the side of it that's just porn. Literally. Careful. Don't look up Undertail either - That's the darkest of the bad side.

The space combat was very straightforward. Point and shoot. You win, you lose.
Exploration was... very simple, almost entirely predictable.
There were a lot of asteroid and debri fields. I don't think I spent more than 30min fumbling around in the very first one. I could have missed out on a very important part of the game by ignoring this activity.
Trade was well thought out. Unfortunately there was no reason to participate in it. Overwhelming amounts of money had no real purpose. In other games, you could use massive fortunes to create space stations, buy sectors, buy planets, enable trade routes. I never saw that in this game (maybe I just missed it). Capturing and selling ships was more profitable, more entertaining.
Money could be used to upgrade a particular weapon, endlessly, but it felt like a lazy money-sink. Investing in it made combat too easy. You could rent wing-men, but they were largely pointless if you acquired the above weapon.
An alarming number of ships were useless in almost all situations. There didn't seem to be a way to improve a ship, if you liked it. There were modular upgrades that could be added and removed, but this seemed more like a standard approach - the upgrades must be done or this ship will be even more useless. I mention this, specifically, because I would have traded the money-sink weapon for a money-sink ship improvement system.
The acting was good enough. The story was below average (which made the acting seem a lot worse than it was). Playing the main story may actually lower your over-all opinion of this game, which isn't uncommon for a space game. You have the option, in the game, to skip the main story entirely.
There were some bugs in the game. Some of the bugs enabled exploits, so I'll avoid detailing them.

Set in a post apocalypse chunk of Australia, Mad Max is an open world action game that is quite literally, one big sandbox. As you progress through the campaign your map will quickly become littered with icons, but I never once felt overwhelmed by the amount of things I had to do in this game. One reason for that is just how fantastic this game looks. From the early morning sunrises glinting off the freshly bloodied spikes on your ever customizable whip, to the powerful sandstorms that appear full of flying cars and lightning. In the 61 hours I spent with Mad Max, I am not ashamed to admit I spent a great amount of time inside of the built in screen shot creator. What helps these visuals glow is the absolute top notch job the developers did with optimizing this title. Not once did I experience any sort of frame rate drop, which is impressive considering the amount of things you can have going on at once time. So not only is every corner of this harsh landscape breathtaking to look at, the gameplay is there as well. Mad Max implements the best vehicular combat I have ever seen in a game. The grappling hook is so satisfying, but you will need to pry off doors and wheels in order to remove the driver. Making your way to the side of a large bandit patrol to aim your shotgun, slowing time around you to line up your crosshair with the giant red gas tank attached to the back, and firing to see an explosion of car parts and limbs is quite the epic moment. Clearing one of the many camps requires you to exit your vehicle and proceed on foot, which doesn’t provide any interesting new mechanic compared to your recent action beat up games, but it does regress in anything they have done either. The characters in this game are well voice acted and very interesting, thanks to their mostly grotesque physical appearances. This world is a rough place to live in, and it shows. I did quickly grow attached to your companion and artisan mechanic, Chumbucket. He keeps the humor in line with Max. The voice acting is very well done.
The setting of this game carries the story so much, emphasizing the importance of the resources that are so precious to these survivors. Mainly gas and water. One thing I wish would have happened was actually NEEDING to keep up with managing my gas tank and hydration. Quickly your upgrades to both car and water canister make these trivial, which is a real shame. Similar to Mordor, as you play through this game you can always see the looming giant that is Gastown off in the distance. I was terrified of this place, I knew the game was working my way there but I was literally terrified. I won’t spoil anything but it wasn’t quite what I expected after having the visual of that giant bandit city.
The fact that you can get this game at such an affordable price these days should really push anyone who has the slightest interest to purchase. I can see myself coming back someday for another play through, which is something I have never done with an open world action game before. I can’t recommend it enough, it was an absolute blast to play.

Note this is for the Single Player component - I haven't really played the multiplayer at all.
It's Call of Duty, and it's the Black Ops series. That means a slightly confusing but oddly engrossing time-hopping storyline with multiple very similar protagonists. But the game is slick, has some great set piece moments, and enough little extras and challenges to keep you going for a while.
It also has the Strike Missions - a weird Ground Control-esque combination of first person and RTS views that can influence the outcome of the story. They are optional but worth playing to get the "best" ending (assuming you succeed of course...). They also showcase some of the areas of innovation over previous games in the series. Elsewhere, there's not much else to see - if you liked the previous games, you'll like this one. If you prefer the Modern Warfare subseries to the World At War/Black Ops subseries then this one may not be your cup of tea, especially with the weird future tech on display.
Graphically it's not the greatest (ie not Metro Last Light or similar) but everything looks cinematic, feels visceral and kicks hard. It runs very smoothly in its fully patched state, and for those of you who have access to a nVidia 3D Vision 2 monitor and glasses? Wow, the solidity of the graphics really sells it and it is very immersive. I really enjoyed playing it, and unusally for a CoD game I think I will go back for another play through.

I have a lot more hours on the Multiplayer and Zombies modes.
Campaign: Pretty decent. It's over kinda quick, but it's definitely much better written and more enjoyable than MW3. I definitely enjoyed the throwbacks to BO1 here and there, which also had a great storyline.
Multiplayer: I can't speak too much for online, as I haven't played a whole lot of it. I'm not very good online, generally I just end up getting killed left and right and leave the game feeling salty. Bots is fun though, if you're into that sort of thing. Just beware, they're insanely good shots with pretty much any weapon. Recruit = cutting down grass, Regular = dealing with the damn Navy Seals.
Zombies: This is the actual reason I bought this game. I love the Zombies game mode, and while most people didn't seem to care for this game's zombies, I really enjoy it. I've killed over 55 hours on Zombies since I got this, and I play Zombies a lot on my PS3 as well. I just wish the DLC prices would drop (definitely NOT paying $15 for like 1 new Zombies map). This game is also STILL full price (as of mid December 2014), which makes no sense to me. I snagged it on a sale on Amazon for $20 a few months back. Beware that this game is hard to find cheap, so if you want friends to play it with you, they'll either have to pay full price or you'll have to find a good deal somewhere.
Overall: It's not worth what they're charging for it (is any CoD game? heh), but if you can get if for $25 or less I'd say it's worth the time you'll spend on it. Especially if you like the other CoD games and the general arcade FPS style of it.

Yooka-Laylee does a fine job accomplishing what it sets out to do, revive the 3D Collect-a-thon genre. I was worried when critic reviews where mixed, until I found out they where literally docking points for it being a 3D Collect-a-thon. In terms of controls, the game plays as well the best 3D Platformers around, with no problems. Is the game as good as it's spirtual predecessor, Banjo-Kazooie? I would say no, but it's close. Even with more to collect in each world, the lack of variety from having half the number does hurt a bit. Overall, the worlds do not have the same level of character or intricate design but are still quite satisfying. With 25 Pagies per world, the methods of obtaining them suffer a bit, with 5+ being obtained the same way in each world. They also forgoe the greater complexity per major collectable of Banjo-Tooie, though some still have that Tooie feel (The hot tub comes to mind).
My most major gripe about the game is that Playtonic seems to remember how make 3D platforming as fun as ever, but almost every mini-game suffers from frustrating design and programming. The Cart challenge in each world has no where near the ploish of the Donkey Kong Country games and Rextro64's mini-games are all frustrating and feel like they where made by amateurs. They should stick to Banjo's mini-game style of not changing the style completley.
Overall, the game is solid and a must-have for fans of a genre that is woefully under-represented.
Final Score:
8.5/10

Putting aside everything that's not explicitly tied to the game itself (that is, the developers involved, the drama surrounding internet personalities, the kickstarter funds, etc.),
Aside from some very frustrating control and camera issues, the game is technically proficient and can be entertaining for at least a few hours.
This, however, makes it particularly difficult to decide if I can actually recommend the game. The game isn't bad, but it does have many problems. Most of the problems probably could have been fixed with another few months of development, but they also feel almost inexcusable when you start considering the people involved. It's also confusing that many of the new gameplay features feel like they were never fully fleshed out, as the core gameplay was perfected nearly 2 decades ago and needed no extra work to refine.
Putting this into the perspective of a small indie studio with a (relatively) small game budget, I think that the end product here is quite professionally put together. If this were a game by a bunch of nobodies, it'd likely be celebrated as the first real attempt at cartoony 3D platformers in years. What's really disappointing here, then, is that
It lacks the helpful guidance-by-items of DK64, the focused and compact level design of Banjo-Kazooie, and what edgy adult humor there is pales in comparison to Conker's Bad Fur Day. At its best, it feels like a semi-clone of Banjo-Tooie, but the poor camera design ends up holding it back from even that.
This is a classic case of "so close, yet so far", but I really I do want to see Playtonic continue to make games--I know that they can do much better than this.
(Also, please hire a writer that actually knows how to write witty and sarcastic dialogue!!)

There is a very important tip in this review! If you're going to get this game, you better read on.
I tried to return this game after five hours of trying to make enough money to even by the next better laser in order to break the asteroids faster.  And, I can tell you I'm very happy that I passed the hours played deadline for returning it! This really is a quite fun game if you know the right way to make money!  If you think you're going to make money trading or mining, you got another thing coming! Forget about anything except capturing enemy ships.
When you go to a space station, on the upper left you can select hiring troops or mercenaries. Hire as many troops as you can, and then go find an enemy ship. Find an enemy ship that has as many or less personnel than the troops you hired.  The number of personnel is listed to the right of the 'lock on' information.
Destroy most of the enemies hull, but leave about a quarter. Then from your 'center mouse button' menu select send troops. Over on the right side of your screen a small flag will appear showing your troops are boarding the ship and how many troops are left on both sides. At this point you can click on the green arrow to send extra troops, if you don't send extra troops you will probably lose the battle.  If and when you capture the ship, and you must learn how to capture ships, use the tractor lock on in the 'center mouse button' menu. Then head back to a space station and sell it.
In the beginning ships get you about $100 K, maybe a little less. But that beats the $10 K per trip of breaking rocks. Then use that money to buy better lasers, missiles, and systems upgrades. You do not get experience points for capturing ships though.(unless it finishes a mission) Destroying ships gives you experience points. Once you have upgraded your ship as much as you can, then go start doing missions to gain experience points.
Make sure you save at least one of every higher level ship to use as you rank up. If you are good enough at combat, you can capture ships larger and better than yours. Then once you rank up you can start using them instead.  I have succeeded capturing ships with one third less personnel on my ship than the enemy ship. I think the worst damage to the enemy ship the less troops you need.
Definitely read the instructions in the upper right ? Icon.

It definitely is a well-made galaxy. It's pretty, large, has lots of planets, anomalies, and wormholes. The wormholes can be a little crazy when you're in a battle and one grabs you and sweeps you away!

Some armaments work well in some situations and then do not work as well in others.

The campaign story is really good.
Cons:
Even though it has a good campaign story, the voice acting is some of the worst I've ever heard in most of the characters.  It seems like they went around from high school to high school looking for the worst of the drama students they could find to perform the stories.
The mission text portions have obviously been poorly translated. I think it was originally in German. A lot of the stories and side missions are just given to you in text form, and because of the poor translation it can be hard to understand what they are trying to say.
Considering the size of the galaxy they provide, the main campaign was too short. I did tons of side missions, finished the story, and still had half the galaxy unexplored. Since I find no point in just roaming around the galaxy for no particular reason, the rest will remain unexplored.
All in all:
It was totally money well spent! I also got the two extra campaigns which I will now go and play.

Good points -
1. Fighting, the fighting is just down right fun, you can just bounce all around your enemies and dodge everyone of their moves and feel like a complete bad♥♥♥♥♥while doing so.
2. Exploration, outside of just getting through the objectives, there are puzzles that while some might not find hard, I did get stuck on for a few minutes and they made me look around at the map and see how expansive they make these worlds, while you may not even explore them all. The secret areas from the previous games return, but unless you really need an extra health pack, and or ammo refill, you don't have much motivation for finding these areas.
Bad points -

After more than 200 hours of playing this game, here's my review.
Overall the general gameplay of this game is amazing, and giving hours of fun even though in reality you're pretty much just doing the same thing over and over again. The more missions you do the easier it becomes really to understand the game and how you should drive the truck properly and avoid damage to you, and also gaining penalties from silly little mistakes. There are a few bugs in the graphics like trees coming out from under a motorway which isn't often, but it does look fairly bad in the chances of you seeing it.
I recommend if you play this game, you install the Multiplayer modification with it because honestly the AI drives like idiots and are a general pain. The multiplayer mod allows you to play with players online and removes the silly AI traffic, but with them being removed the gameplay still feels amazing. You almost always get honked at a truck passing or getting stuck at traffic in europort.
Overall, i don't like singleplay that much. But the multiplayer mod is where my heart is.
I would recommend you pick this game up, it's something i have not regretted at all.

I write this as a £90 Kickstarter backer, and someone who has 100%ed B-K, B-T, Grunty's Revenge, N&B (including the L.O.G.'s Lost Challenges DLC), and quit out of DK64 shortly before getting to Hideout Helm, IIRC.
I do recommend this game, but with some caveats. There is a lot to like here as a nostalgia trip, but there's also a lot of polish issues, and some of the most confusing level design I've seen in a game of this type.
You've got (for the most part) visuals reminiscent of N&B, the googly eyes, the music, the colourful worlds filled with colourful characters, the abundance of things to collect... all the elements are here, it's just many aren't assembled quite as you'd expect.
If you loved the tight levels of Kazooie, but hated Tooie's more open ones... you're probably not going to enjoy Yooka much. Every level is supersized far beyond what Tooie offered, and that's without expanding them. The levels frequently lack clear landmarks, visual differentiation between areas, or strong signposting, and NPCs can be tiny specks on a broad canvas.
The world expansion system is offered as this game's main innovation over the Banjo series - you can choose to unlock new levels, or expand the ones you have, meaning they'll offer new Pagies (Jiggies) and Quills (Notes) and more. The problem is, this is a false choice - most of the collectibles in the expanded versions of the worlds need moves from the later levels, and it usually isn't clear if you're trying to do something that you can't do. Tooie was a lot better about making it clear that you cannot currently do the thing, usually by making you go from the later world where you get the move back to the earlier world, and back again.
This also presents the problem of the game's collectible curve being all over the place. I had about 35-40 Pagies when I unlocked world 5 without expanding any, and you need 100 total to unlock the final boss. I've since gone back and expanded and completed the first two worlds (now at about 75-80 Pagies), but that's still a lot of time where you're looking at fundamentally the same environments with some additions. Quills also become seemingly useless for the same reason - there seems to be no more use for them once you've unlocked world 5's move, other than granting a Pagie for collecting all 200 in a world.
For me, I would have definitely preferred a greater quantity of smaller levels than this small number of too big ones - though I suppose working at this level of visual fidelity, the asset creation would have been prohibitively expensive.
In terms of controls, they're generally alright for basic things, but they falter when speed and precision come into play. Yooka's roll is faster than the Talon Trot, but it's also a lot looser and uses up your stamina meter. It's the same story when you get the ability to fly later - it's just not as precise as Kazooie's in any respect, although being able to take off from anywhere is nice. Not helping in this respect is the camera - which again, is alright for basic platforming, but struggles in closed off interior environments, while moving quickly, or while trying to fly and look down. During certain parts, it switches orientations in a pretty nasty way, and the controls instantly change to the new angle rather than keeping your direction from before. It sometimes actively seems to fight player input, starting to turn and rebounding back to the original position.
Each level has an unlockable "arcade style" minigame. They don't control well, and the lack of AI opponents means you're just either racing the clock or going for the highest score by yourself - which is kind of boring. In game, these are branded as "Amazing Rextro's Software Entertainment" - which would have been a funny joke, if the acronym didn't sadly become an accurate descriptor. They are also required to beat twice for 100%, even when you already beat the time/score requirement on your first go. And I mean, Tooie had some dud minigames, but it also had some really fun ones. Other side activities include minecart challenges, which you'll do once if you're a completionist and/or masochist, and then never look back.
Each level also has a transformation - and from the two I've seen so far, these are definitely at the lower end of those offered to Banjo. You have a plant, which moves slow and has to traverse a significant distance to speak to some other plant NPCs to get a reward that probably isn't worth it. You also have the snow plough, which moves faster, but has zero traction control and a large turning circle... and you have to do precision platforming with it. Also you transform back if you touch water - and of course, the precision platforming section is partially over water, so you'd better be prepared to waste more time getting transformed again. Each of these is only used for one Pagie total (and in the plant's case, hints to the stamina/health bar extenders), when I feel like Banjo's worst ones at least usually got involved in two Jiggies, or helping to open the level up more.
You've also got the quiz... and there's a severe lack of understanding here of why people liked the quizzes in Kazooie/Tooie. The quizzes in Kazooie and Tooie were a way to wind down before the final boss. Kazooie's offered a board game with bits of risk and strategy (if I take this longer, more dangerous route, I can avoid those instant death spaces), while Tooie was a more straightforward case of getting the highest trivia score against opponents, Yooka has none of those elements - it's a boring room with a straight line, no one competing against you. There's too long a gap between the question being asked and your choices appearing, so you might accidentally confirm an answer trying to press A to get the dialogue to display. It feels like cheap filler someone threw in relatively late, and it happens twice - once after the first world, which is way too early for this kind of sudden gameplay shift that you have to complete or you don't get to progress.
---
Despite the length of the complaints here, it is still a love letter to a genre that doesn't really exist any more, and that matters. I just wish that they'd skewed closer to the originals in some respects, and a little more modern in others. I do want to 100% it (and probably will do so again on Switch after that version is released), but I've accepted the fact that I'm going to absolutely hate parts of it while doing that. I hope Playtonic makes a good use of feedback from Yooka for their next game.
If you've never played the originals and happen to own an Xbox One, I would strongly recommend picking up Rare Replay first if you're interested in this game. (If you own a 360, the originals are on XBLA, but picking them both up there is probably about as expensive as Rare Replay is, without the benefit of getting 28 other games with your purchase). Otherwise, go in with the expectation of a decent game that could have used a bit more polish, and you'll be alright - though it's not something I could recommend at the full asking price unless you are a huge fan of the Banjo games and willing to overlook at least some of its flaws.

I didn't want to write this review up until I had completed the game 100%, so that I could properly judge it as a whole for what it is. I've done that, so here's my review.
Yooka-Laylee is exactly what I was expecting, and exactly what I wanted from a game that bills itself as a 'spiritual successor' to Banjo-Kazooie. The tight controls, pastel color palettes and quirky British humor are all immediately evocative of late 90s Rare titles, and it's abundantly obvious the amount of love they put into this game.
It is not, however, without its flaws. The camera was not a consistent problem for me as it has been for others, but at times it wasn't as tight as I'd like a 3D platforming camera to be. I felt like the world expansion mechanic, while cool and interesting, was underutilized. Only Worlds 1 and 3 had good 'expansions'; the others were inconsistent, and ranged from okay to outright disappointing.
On the positive side, something the game executes very well is control. Yooka feels good to control, the turns are crisp and everything you want in a platformer in terms of mobility is there. The level design, while it does fall off after World 1, is still good and succeeds at not making the game feel too linear. There are A LOT of throwbacks to the Banjo series in this game, and I'd be remiss if I didn't suggest that a lot of my enjoyment of the dialogue came from, "Hey, I get it!" moments.
Ultimately, and honestly, I don't think this game is GOTY material. Nothing here is revolutionary, and it's probably not going to appeal to a lot of fans outside the platforming genre. But, it is what it is: a solid, good (but not great) platformer that delivered on its promises. It falls short in certain areas where the advancement of gaming in the past 20 years hasn't seemed to have caught up with it yet. Having said that, I enjoyed every one of the 36 hours I spent playing Yooka-Laylee, and while it isn't a masterpiece, it's the best non-Mario 3D platformer we've gotten in a long time.

Index:

Overall Thoughts:
-This game started as a promise to make a new Banjo Kazooie style game on kickstarter, did it came true of its promise? Well it is true but the reason the people are mixed about this game is the following:
People who wanted a Banjo Kazooie sequel.
People who wanted a Banjo Tooie sequel.
While Banjo Kazooie had small levels with no empty and unused parts in the level, Banjo Tooie had big worlds with lots of empty parts of the level and lots of backtracking. So if you played Yooka Laylee you will know this game is more like Banjo Tooie then Kazooie with the same style of worlds, and somewhat confusing Hub.
I liked Banjo Tooie alot so thats why I think I enjoyed this game.
Gameplay
-The gameplay is very solid for the most part for a few exceptions: The rolling which feels slippery (Do not get me started on ice physics with this) and the gamebreaking flying ability which lets you break the worlds getting to unintended areas.
-The Hub world it looks nice I give it that but this could have used some signs for where to go because its a little bit confusing.
-The transformations feel like Banjo Kazooie style transformations,  the snowplow truck that has the worst mobility in this game however.
-The swimming feels good and you have a move that lets you walk underwater, but some areas are hard to navigate through thanks to one of the worst things in this game: THE CAMERA.
-For those who have not seen it but want to know why the camera is terrible, while its good in most parts of the game but when the camera changes position to a fixed location in the world. This will make you to change your own direction you are walking towards sometimes this wil make you switch the camera to third person and the fixed position rapidly.
Characters:
-While this game has some find has some good characters (Yooka & Laylee, Kartos, Trowzers, Rextro, and Dr. Puzz) it has a ton of npc's and enemies that you will forget and don't fit the world themes. Characters like Vendi, Rextro and Dr. Puzz could have used their own building instead of being copy pasted in the world in sometimes unfitting area's.
Music:
-I love David Wise and Grant Kirkhope style for music and enjoyed the music in this game can't say much more about it.
Minigames/Bosses:
-This game has some minigames (Rextro and Kartos) while I like most of the Kartos minigames it does have some frustrating controlls. The Rextro minigames well most of them are not enjoyable. I liked the first two Kartos racing and the Ice Gladiator but the last two are just way to long and punishing to enjoy.
-The bosses only have two noticable bosses for me the Ice Block (World 2) and the Kraken (World 3).
The first world boss has makes you fall all the way down for getting hit once sometimes letting you take 1-2 extra damage on the way down.
The fourth world boss has Kartos mechanics which are hard to get used to and has to much health.
The fifth world boss well I actually liked this boss if it the fire attack was not done better.
Then there is the final boss Capital B, this is a pretty good fight but he has a bit to much health
Conclusion:
-I give this game a 8 or 7,5 out of 10 since I enjoy this style of game. But if I were new to games I would rate it with a 6,5 or 6 out of 10 because of some of the issues this game has. I hope they learn from what was wrong with this game and fix this and do it better in the DLC that was promised and if they ever make Twooka Laylee.

It's a great game. You don't have to really like the movies to have fun with the game. The story fits right in with Max. If you are looking for a deep experience, you won't find it here, though.
Car customization seems great at first, but becomes a little tiresome and simple. Character customization is the same as car customization. It's simplified down to the very basics. There are limited options. The scrap mechanics in this game get extremely tedious early on. It is, however, pretty easy to start heaping in piles of scrap quickly if you focus on that at the beginning. The enemies, camps, and objectives are super repetitive and a bit too easy. It never felt like it got too challenging. There are a certain variety of enemies and that is pretty much it. Each have their own ways of fighting and appearance. The boss battles are all pretty much the same too. They slapped a different texture and mask on them, set them up in a different location, and called it a day. They all fought in the same manner. They all had relatively the same weapon or equipment on. They all had the same voice.
Fighting isn't as deep as Tomb Raider or Sleeping Dogs, but it is pretty solid. It is pretty satisfying dispatching enemies with the tools/moves you are given. The double barrel shotgun is extremely satisfying for this. Setting up enemies for complete destruction in this game is fun work too. Try some improvisation by clearing a minefield using enemies on foot and not your clippers.
The story itself is pretty linear. There's no feeling of freedom to do what you really want without a mission failing. Lack of options. Only one way to finish/end a mission or the story itself. With that in mind, there's no real replayability for any of it. You can, however, go for completion of everything. There isn't an extreme amount of side missions or stories to sort through that would make this too time draining. I can't see myself coming back to this game after it has been beaten. Great fun. Bought it on sale. No regrets. Beat it in a weekend, more or less.
Overall, it's a great action game, and worth playing through once.

Starpoint Gemini 2 (SP2) is a sort of tactical space-combat simulator with RPG elements. At the start of the game you pick a character avatar and name, a class and one of three starter ships. Then it plops you down in the newbie-friendly area of Planet Trinity and gets you started with some context-sensitive tutorials.
Gameplay is fairly straightforward. You have a map of the universe, and as you fly around various missions become available. You can accept any of these missions; they can be a number of things: straight Assassination missions (destroy the target), Escort or protection missions (preserve an allied target and destroy enemy targets), repair missions (fly to a structure and use the middle-click context menu to repair it), taxi missions (fly VIP from point A to point B), smuggle missions (fly contraband cargo from point A to point B). Each mission provides some cash, experience and either positive or negative reputation.
The reputation system is not spectacular. There are "bad" factions and "good" factions. Doing missions for the good factions, or blowing up the ships of bad factions, rewards positive rep. Vice-versa for the bad factions. If you want to work with the "bad" factions, you need to acquire negative rep. However, there are a handful of "fanatic" factions that you can never join, and destroying them ALSO rewards positive reputation,
. I tried a couple playthroughs; the first time I didn't pay any attention to rep and within a few hours I was close to maxing out my positive rep (+2500 points). The next day I attempted to build negative rep, not knowing how the rep system worked (it's not explained well in the tutorials or anywhere else) and it took many hours of trial and error, and reading the Steam discussion forum, to figure out what was going on. In short the game is heavily balanced in favor of working for the "good" factions. The only way to change reputation outside of missions and combat is to find a "good" or "bad" structure and kill it (actually disable it, it's still there in a deactivated state) by holding down the fire button for a solid minute or two.
Making cash in the game is equally frustrating. Most missions provide piddly amounts of cash, and the biggest incentive to earn money is to buy a bigger, badder ship. Missions also award experience, however, and raising your level tends to raise the level of threats you face. At level 10 there is a rather steep increase to the difficulty of missions involving combat. You are probably still in your gunship, when your targets become freighters and destroyers. This is even in the easiest area of the map (areas of the map are "leveled" in some aspect; how exactly is somewhat opaque). Effectively this locks you out of the most fun and rewarding missions, those involving combat. Inquiries to the devs on the Steam forums as to how this leveling-scaling works were ineffective.
Ironically, the best way to make money is to simply pirate other ships. This is not inherently a "bad" move: as long as you are pirating the ships of the "bad" factions, you will gain positive reputation. Pirated ships call sell for between 100k to a million or more, depending on the ship and it's cargo. Capturing a ship is a fairly simple game of "who has more troopers". Even with extensive buffing of your troopers strength via skills and perks, it's effectively impossible to take a ship that has more men; taking one with equal numbers is a roll of the dice. There are videos available on the interwebs explaining this in more detail. Again, none of this is addressed in-game.
There is more to talk about, such as the levelling, the exploration aspect, and the "sideline" missions that advance some sort of story in freeroam (it seems to be a "good" centric story, unfortunately for people hoping to be an enterprising space pirate; it is however completely optional). But I don't want to go on for ages. Is this game worth $42.00 (core game + DLC)? Absolutely not. It's a fairly amateur product that is struggling with balance and weird game-crashing bugs years after it's debut. The dev company is by their own admission very small, and their players seem to know the game better than them; unfortunately the wiki is highly underdeveloped, leaving brand-new players in the dark. This game was bought while it was on sale at 80% off; $10 is a perfectly reasonable price for a game that will entertain for about a week. If you're interested in deep simulation and RP opportunities, look elsewhere. If you want a pretty simple, fun game that looks good and doesn't take a lot of research to grasp, this may be the title for you.

Spec Ops: The Line is a third person shooter who takes a warfare story telling aspect, and mixes in gritty realism, coupled with very solid cover-based-game play.
How do you talk about the story in this game without giving away any great details? The story goes in a very unorthodox direction from most Shooter games I've played. Additionally there are choices that you make throughout the game, and it's not just "go right or go left" as the saying goes "indecision is a choice".
In the words of William T. Sherman we hear the well known quote "War is Hell" To be quite honest not very many shooter games run with that concept, in Spec Ops: The Line, you will see far more gritty details of consequences of warfare... and the people effected.
Spec Ops: the line is a cover-based third person shooter, meaning while you're being shot at you will move from cover to cover, most of the mechanics are quite straight forward, but do take some getting used too, you can jump over cover, change cover quickly by looking or pressing a movement key in that direction THEN pressing Space, there is a fair bit of learning to be had.
It should be noted that the controls will take some getting used too, I had already played a few third person shooters so those old controls were messing me up while I was trying to learn the new ones. Once you learn the controls the rest of the game is quite enjoyable to play through.
Even if you're unfamiliar with cover-based-shooters the starting difficulty is friendly enough that you can get the hang of it while gunning down your foes. (I would still recommend getting used to hiding behind cover)
There are 50 Achievements in Spec Ops: The Line, after my first play through I had 33 of those achievements, there are four achievement category types: Find the lintel (collection), Get kills or special kills with weapons, Make this choice in the story, and standard story quests.
Spec Ops: The Line is priced at $29.99, by this point most people should be used to games (especially shooters) being priced there, as I always say "I recommend waiting for a sale".
Spec Ops: The line will appeal most to people who enjoy the two qualities of "Third person shooter", and "story telling". If you just want a shooter where you run in and pew pew pew, this isn't the right game for you. If you like playing games with meaningful stories, making hard ethical decisions while gaming or just looking for a change of pace this game will provide it.
To quickly recap: Story - Outstanding story telling methods. Game Play - Controls might be a bit tricky at first, but the cover based combat is very good. Achievements - Pretty Standard, there are a few tricky looking achievements though. Price - Standard, wait for a sale.

A story about a three-man squad in an apotalyptical Dubai, covered by sand. An epic plot of insanity intwined with deadly choices. The question is, what path will you choose?

This review is only for the single player campaign on normal difficulty.
Pretty well everything about this game was exactly what I would want out of a FPS campaign.  There was a decent variety of guns, some of them had secondary fire options, a few gernade choices and a melee option.  The best thing about the guns was that there wasn't one or two that were obviously the ones you had to take with you, you had the choice to pick whatever two you liked and make your way through the game.  Of course there were times that one gun was much more useful than another but for the rest of the time you could run with what you want, till you ran out of ammo anyways.
Enemies were not to difficult for the most part outside of a few areas that were tricky.  Later game enemies did start presenting a bit more of a challenge.  They used cover surprisingly well and did attempt flanks and the like.
The setting, enviroment, graphics, etc... were all top notch, there is pretty well nothing that I could complain about in that department.  From the beauty of the open spaces in destroyed dubia to the smaller areas were unspeakable horrors abounded, everything was just so well presented.
And the story.  Without getting into spoilers because this is a game that should be experienced spoiler free.  I loved the story, I'm still not sure I entirely got everything that there was to get from the story, but thats the great part.  The game did leave some choices to make, as to what exactly those choices decided at the end of the day, well thats why I want to play the game more than once, and I can't really think of any FPS single player campaings that made me want to come back for more.
The only big gripe that I had with this game was with your AI teammates and their use of cover, or well lack of cover I guess.  The two AI teamates that you travel the game with are better than a lot of other AI teamates other games have stuck you with, these guys actually can kill an enemy or two but they tend to walk stupidly out of cover every now and then.  They would end up dying foolishly and you'd have to break cover to revive them or mission failure.
But to sum it all up.  This is exactly what I've wanted out of a FPS single player campaign.  Everything was presented beautifully.  There was a decent selection of weapons to keep the shooting interesting and a story that above all else makes the game stand out far above a lot of other FPS campaigns and is something that I would whole heartedly recommend to almost any FPS fan.

This game is fun, but the most recent update seemed like a significant downgrade. The new Football mode is a great idea that is executed very poorly, and the odds of actually finding a match for it are slim to none. The new Waves mode is another great idea that would be a lot better if your teammates would respawn after every wave or few waves.
More importantly though, the game looks better in a lot of ways, but the camera seems waaaay too zoomed in. It's hard enough to play this game with the weird physics, which have also changed substantially, but now it's hard to see where I'm even going sometimes. Also, the game seems to have a bit of frame lag, regardless of what the FPS counter tells me. I've tried changing settings, even going to all lows, but it stays the same.
Additionally, some maps have changed for the worse. The floating mechanic in Buoy is nice, but it takes the difficulty out of the map. If I can land in the water and not die for a few seconds, it doesn't really matter that I'm slipping around on ice. But far worse than this is Grind, which used to be one of the best maps. Now, the map is far too congested to enjoy.
One more issue I have with this update is some general changes that were made. Namely, the physics feel a bit off, and people are both too easy to knock out and too quick to get up. If you are not perfect with the game mechanics, you will have a hell of a time eliminating anybody in this update, because as soon as you can manage to grab them without grabbing a wall or the floor by accident, they'll likely have woken back up already. These mechanics absolutely did not need to change, and should be reverted or reworked.
I'm very glad to see that this game is still being worked on, but this was a step back, rather than a step forward. While I love playing this game, I can't recommend it until the glaring issues have been resolved.

Yooka-Laylee is a game promised to be a revival to the old days of collect-a-thon platformers - which it achieves handily - but struggles from the fact that it tries so hard to be a revival of such games that it never establishes its own identity and is held back by its own nostalgia in the process.
Yooka-Laylee triumphs in a great many ways. Game feel, controls, atmosphere, it really does get what it means to be a collect-a-thon platformer. Anyone who enjoys this genre as much as I do will find enjoyment in Yooka-Laylee. YL's biggest draw is its five expansive worlds that can be expanded to be even larger by spending additional shiny main collectables aka Pagies. In doing so the worlds almost double in size, adding additional challenges and collectables to collect. Every world does a great job standing out both in atmosphere and in direction, as a result there's never really a "bad" world that you'll have to work through. In fact, if you wanted to, you could completely skip one of the five worlds (given you stop in it briefly to pick up the required moves) and attempt to collect everything in three of the worlds and most of everything in the fourth. Not that this is a particularly smart choice. While five worlds may seem a little underwhelming, given that you'll be collecting collectables normally spread out in two individual worlds in other games, it manages to hit the "quality over quantity" mark pretty well. However Yooka-Laylee isn't a great game nor is it the revival the developers are probably hoping for.
Probably the biggest miss that collect-a-thon veterans - like myself - are going to notice is that despite the wonderful lively atmosphere filled with all sorts of precious things to discover, there's a remarkable lack of polish to it all. Gameplay-wise the mark is hit, there's a framework they're following, it works. However the music and sound design feels inconsistent as does the difficulty, there's no gradual increase or anything that holds steady here. One moment the variable mix and the challenge works, suddenly the song seems a little... off and the difficulty becomes either null or a bit overbearing (with the former being much more likely than the latter, the latter being more frustrating design choice over difficulty). Cutscenes occur with the game's normal soundtrack playing behind it, character animations feeling slightly out of place like they're tacked on, sadly derrives a perfectly fine ending with it. These things feel so minor that I question just how much work would be necessary to fix it up.
Now you're probably wondering where I was going with the nostalgia thing, especially since I took a paragraph to rant about the game's polish. Well, I'd like you to look at the title, the box art, the character speaking sound effects, the random quiz sho- Yes, this is a game trying really really hard to be Banjo-Kazooie without actually being Banjo-Kazooie. Mighty Number 9 did something similar, being cosmetically different enough from the original but clearly HEAVILY inspired by the concept. As a result, Yooka-Laylee has difficulty standing up on its own since despite looking good and playing pretty well, it's the inferior product to older titles. You can experience just about everything Yooka-Laylee has to offer - albiet better - in the older N64 titles. It doesn't take nostaliga and harnesses it to create its own identity like Shovel Knight, it looks at nostaligia and tries to mimic it without learning what makes these games so dated and AGONIZINGLY TEDIOUS today. Like seriously devs, you thought putting 200 individual quills in every level was a smart idea and STILL had the gall to hide them in REALLY out of the way places that blend in way too well? I know you're trying to give us vets a knowing nod but spending a literal hour combing every inch of a level for that last quill isn't challenging, it's tedious, it's frustrating. Banjo-Kazooie could get away with it because the levels were small enough and there were only 100 notes to find rather than 200. And even then the sequel side-lined a lot of the note finding process to focus on making Jiggies more challenging to collect, which was a brilliant idea if I may add. At least you were smart enough to not attempt Donkey Kong 64 levels of backtracking every-square-inch-searching agony.
If for some reason you frequent my reviews, you'll probably see that I'm pretty hard on games I want to like or games I do like pretty well. Hell I'd say I'm hard on all sorts of games. At the end I liked Yooka-Laylee and was happy with the 15 hours I sunk into 100%-ing it because that's just something I do really. If you take away the tedium of hunting every last shiny thing, the game plays very well and is fun from beginning to end. It's just if you're hoping that Yooka-Laylee becomes a classic is where you're going to be disappointed. I don't want this to be the first and final note of Yooka-Laylee, I do want a sequel. And given that the game is loaded with hints to a sequel I hope they're actually planning it rather than being cocky enough to think that the game deserves it. Both outcomes are likely. BUT, and this is a big damn but, a sequel will only succeed if the developers are brave enough to do different things rather than just embrace the flaws of nostalgia with a sort of dejected "well that's just how it is" mentality. There's potential and talent here, they just have to use it for something more than just a prettier remake-but-not-really of classic games.
Recommended for full price if you're a collect-a-thon vet, if you're casually interested I'd just wait for a sale of 33%. $40 isn't a ton of money for the amount of quality game you're getting but if you don't like collect-a-thon platformers this game won't change your mind.

Yooka-Laylee is a modern revisit to Banjo-Kazooie, warts and all.
Graphics are colorful and appealing, and the music is topnotch. Sound design is serviceable, though more than a few of the gibberish voices get grating (Looking at you, Yooka). When the game lets you explore the worlds, collecting goodies and solving puzzles, it's a fun and rewarding experience.
However, you'll soon come to hate both Rextro and Kartos. Rextro's mini-games are poorly-designed and go on for far too long to be any fun. The mine cart sequences... let's just say they're not Donkey Kong Country.
Controls are loose and slippery at times, but I felt there were only a few sequences where it caused frequent failure. I didn't feel the camera was that bad when you could control it freely, but many of the fixed-angle areas cause massive problems, and good luck if you're surrounded by objects; the camera needs to be patched so it can go through the scenery.
However, most of the game's jankiness is something that can be fixed with some patches and elbow grease. I still had fun more often than not, even if some choices made during development baffle me. Still, I'd be interested in a Tooka-Laylee.
If you can play Banjo-Kazooie or Banjo-Tooie and still enjoy it, you'll probably like this. Just watch out for its rough edges.

As an early backer on Kickstarter, I can't really recommend this game in good conscience. Firstly, I don’t think supporting Playtonic is a good idea. They’ve made several promises, I don’t think they delivered on. It’s important to remember that this Kickstarter received over 10 times the original goal. As such any excuse of lack of funds is simply unacceptable. Firstly, they cancelled one of the versions that they promised. The game was originally supposed to be released for the Wii U, only for Playtonic to cancel this version shortly after the announcement of the Switch, essentially screwing over fans who backed the game in the belief that they would play it on the Wii U.  Secondly, they promised that those on PC would be the first to play the game. This was simply untrue. The console version of the game released a full day before the Steam and GOG versions. This means backers could go to the store to buy the game for a console, but couldn’t play the game on the PC which they already payed for.  Again, Playtonic failed to deliver on their promise here. Overall, this shows a lack of respect and appreciation for the Kickstarter backers who made this game possible.
Beyond all that, the game itself just isn’t very good.  I would say the biggest flaw is the game’s level design. While the game was billed as a spiritual successor to Banjo-Kazooie and Banjo-Tooie, Yooka-Laylee failed in one of the most fundamental aspects in a platformer. Simply put, the level design is bad. Filled with incredibly poor design choices leaving large areas empty and boring, only to have tiny corners of levels overflowing and cramped and incredibly difficult to navigate.  Instead of thought out level design, it seems as if the designers made a giant empty space and then later ploppe3d in obstacles, collectables, and enemies haphazardly.  The location of these things seemed like and after thought, making the levels feel disjointed. The leaves the gameplay often feeling boring or downright frustrating.  Other issues include strange locations, that are easy to get to but impossible to leave without purposefully jumping off the edge of the map and dying. As such the player never knows if they have found a secret area where an elusive collectible might be hidden, or if they found an area that is a point-of-no-return. A collect-a-thon platformer that discourages exploration fails one of the most fundamental aspects of the genre.
Another part of Yooka-Laylee’s core gameplay are the various mini-games disperses throughout the levels and hub-world. These include trivia quizzes, mine-cart sections, and retro-style arcade games. All three of these mini games are terrible. The quizzes are incredibly frustrating and unfair, asking questions so specific that you would need to have a photographic memory to get them right. One question even asks how long you have been playing the game, down to the exact minute, with all the options being relatively close to each other.    The Mine-cart sections are also frustrating, this time due to poor controls and design. But perhaps the worst offender are the retro-style arcade mini-games. These games are simply broken, poorly designed messes that offer little to no fun for the player.
Two more things of note. The camera and the sound design. While many people complain that the camera is not good, I, personally, never found it to be too much of a problem. Without a doubt, it could and should be better, but it never felt outright broken to me. Another big complaint is the annoying sounds the characters make when they talk. This is a direct hold-over from the Bajo games, so while I do find them to be incredibly annoying, I understand why they are there. I do wish there was a way to shut them off though.
Now, despite all the game’s flaws there are some things the game does right. There is a sarcastic wit and humor throughout the game that does offer some genuine laughs.  The controls are tight and responsive, for the most part. There are some fun obstacles and puzzles and the soundtrack is generally good if not great.
Overall, Playtonic failed to make a genuinely fun game. As a backer, I do plan to finish the game (although I probably won’t go back to hunt for all the collectables) despite its many flaws. Hopefully, Playtonic’s sophomore outing will be a much better and more polished experience. But for now, I would give this game a pass unless heavily discounted.

Mad Max game is a great game without a doubt. Post apo world presented in the game is true rough and dangerous. Story line is fairly short and not very thrilling, might even say it's a cliche although the last parts of the story are quite heavy. Game itself is well presented with visible great motion capture, beautiful graphics (if you can call wastelands the beautiful place). World is filled with places to visit and scavage jung and water along with collectables which are scraps of history. Collecting and visitig those places might seem boring and repetetive but its not, all the places scatered in the world look different and makes us want to know a little bit more about title Max's memories and point of view. In the game we can also find small RPG elements implemented, such as upgrading your ride Magnum Opus, Max's gun and the rest of his tools. For a long time I haven't experience such a rewarding and satysfying combat system in sandbox games, it's similar to Batman or Assassins Creed franchise, but we still don't feel too overpowered as sometimes enemies can be a real hussle and get on your nerves. On the wasteland we can take over the regions from the enemy and lowering their influence by taking down enemy camps where game gives you few approaches, you can either sneak close to the camp and suprise your opponents or go old fasion way thorugh the main entrance or disable most of the defences from far away using your sniper rife on the back of your car. Also to lower the influence you can destroy small towers made from human bodies and scraps of metal, disarm mine fields and by couple other ways. Game offers plenty of side activities such as death races and wasteland stranger quests. Mad Max content will last easly for about 60 hours for 100% completion. The whole world presented in this game is really heavy, depressing, showing the struggle of humanity after the apocalypse when water on entire planet dissapeared along with sealife. Now people are fighting for oil, water, food and junk which is by the way the main currency, everyone are driven to madness to the point where it's hard to say who's normal. I think that WB and Avalanche Studio did the great job with presenting the Mad Max universe. As the game is not perfect and has it's flaws I can surely call it a great game worth picking up.

All memes aside, I am not going to recommend this game to most people. If it works for you as an .io fan, sure. If it also works for you as an emoji fan, then yes. But does it work for the most part? No.
Emoj.io is just another .io game, but with a twist. Instead of the typical .io fashion of a big space occupied by heaps of players and points, it takes the form of a tightly spaced Pac-Man mosh pit. Each area has a bunch of points that'll be taken by other players that surround you.
The main premise of the game is just like the other .io games. Just collect more points, build up your meter, gain a power-up, and kill all players around you to collect ever more points and so on. There is no real strategy to this game, other than trying to find the power-ups for you to collect. That's if there is nobody camping the power-up beside it. I could give it a few more points if there was some sort of challenge to this game, where if you would bump into players (power-ups or not), you would die. After all this is a Pac-Man esque clone right?
The sound design and graphics are another story. First off, let's start with the sound design. The sound design is pretty much non-existant. I have heard nothing but bleeps and bloops from collecting points and killing other players. There is nothing much but silence completely with short bursts of noise, so you'll just be better off ♥♥♥♥ing muting the game. Music in this game doesn't seem to be there, as it is probably the thing that keeps me playing the game without fear of sensory deprivation.
The graphics in this game are plain and simple, with character assets taken from an emoji website. The point graphics are just random colored diamonds that attract all and any emoji nearby. Everything in this game is very colorful and it's quite the choice for a game like this. Even the power-up effect is quite astonishing for seconds on end. Would have to give them credit for this.
But the most ♥♥♥♥est of all that I have seen in this game, is the unlocks. There is a place where you can buy separate emoji packs for a dollar each. Yes, you have heard that right. In order to get the complete emoji packs that your heart ever desires, you would have to pay for the entire pack for 1 dollar. Like I would ever do that. However, I am much more forgiving that you do not have to pay for EACH emoji at a time. The system that makes up for this is a button you get after dying in the game. It's a big green button that says "Free Emoji" and it gives you a random emoji from one of the packs. The one that I got was a skull and crossbones. Pretty much an anology on how I got that and I was already thinking of how short my life was. However, you can only get a free emoji every hour. There is no real way around this, other than waiting for the next emoji you can get. I doubt that you will wait that long to gather up every single emoji for free, as many people would go ahead and quit the game. In order to get all of the emojis for free as estimated it would take you about 30 hours to get every single one. I think I might have left a pack out, but this is only if you are willing to put in that amount of life-wasting and sad time.
Overall, emoj.io is pretty much a borefest with short bursts of excitement. Tension only exists when you rub your emoji skin across the wall from trying to run away from big crying face emoji that's trying to kill you. Do I still recommend this game to everyone? Not really, but kids could certainly find some fun in this for about 30 minutes before going back outside or going back to playing Minecraft on the Xbox One. I would probably have about as much fun as trying to shove a remote up my♥♥♥♥♥ The fact that I have actually spent time writing this review is quite the saddest thing that any man has had to do, and I was one of those people.
