The Diary of a Vietnam Soldier:
----------------------------------------------
This long day began like all the rest - hot and humid.
My day began, like all the rest, with a trip to the latrine. Just as I was getting ready to leave, a tremendous blast blew me out the door onto the dusty ground outside. Realizing I was not wounded, I rose quickly and ran toward the site of the explosion as the sirens screamed red alert - incoming rounds.
As I neared the smoking, black crater I felt warm liquid running across my shoulders and down my arms. Still feeling no pain of my own, it dawned on me that body parts were raining down from the sky, landing on my head and shoulders.
I stopped, overcome. To my right lay a torso heaving one last, reflex-driven sigh. To my left writhed a screaming man clutching the remains of his arm.
Feet pounded by as braver men than I ran to assist their fallen comrades. I could not move.
In time, two of my men led me to the shower for the first of several I took that day as I tried to wash from my body the remnants of corpses that still stain my memory.
The telegram went out that evening to six sets of devastated parents and spouses with the dreaded introduction; "We regret to inform you that your son, (name of deceased), was killed in combat operations in the Republic of Vietnam in the service of his country...."
But it was not an incoming enemy mortar round that caused the carnage I witnessed that day. A despondent GI, very high on pure heroin, chose to commit suicide and in the process, take some of his comrades with him.
He was cleaning his weapon by a table with five other soldiers returned from a night of duty on our defensive berm. The self-destructive 18-year-old removed a hand grenade from the case in the center of the table, pulled its pin, then put it back in the box, detonating the entire batch.
During the nightly drinking scene in our officers' club made of sandbags, we decided that the telegram sent home should have been modified. It should have read: "We regret to inform you that your son died needlessly in a conflict that should not have happened, at the hands of a person under the influence of a powerful drug taken to anesthetize the pain of separation from his family and confusion for his participation in this stupid war."
Even today, we can and should dishonor that war without dishonoring the warriors.
The movie, "Saving Private Ryan" confirms one difference between World War II and Vietnam. The war we won inflicted great pain on innocent children as the battle ebbed and flowed across Western Europe. The war we lost produced two new classes of child victims: Amerasian babies and political refugees. On Sundays, when the Viet Cong went home to tend crops, an informal truce occurred between their side and ours. On those days, I oversaw the provision of food, medical supplies and later, clothing, to an orphanage in My Tho city on the Mekong River near our base in Dong Tam. The effort boosted our morale as much or more than of that of the two Vietnamese nuns who operated the facility populated by over 200 orphans and disabled persons ranging in age from a few months to some well into their 80s.
The many troops trucked to the orphanage on those Sunday afternoons returned to the war with pieces of their souls repaired. I soon learned that the nuns were not without their political skills. They had the older children make sure that at least one of their number latched on to a GI each afternoon to encourage our continued support. I fell in love with the eight-year-old who regularly attached herself to me over those 10 months. Tears came one day when she greeted me wearing a T-shirt with "Bowdoin, Class of 19??" printed on it. The shirt came in a "CARE" package sent by my parents' church in Belmont, Mass. who became involved in the clothing component of this mercy mission. I'd graduated from Bowdoin.
These orphans may have differed from those wandering Europe, however, in that many were the issue of unions of American soldiers with Vietnamese women. You can imagine, then, how outraged I became at the American colonel in Saigon who ordered me to leave the kids unsupported and unprotected when my unit, the 9th Infantry Division, was redeployed to Hawaii and Ft. Lewis as part of President Nixon's first troop removal. This event capped my transition from a defender of U.S. policy in Asia to ardent critic. The cultural bias toward mixed-race children combined with the hatred of anything touched by Americans, spelled doom for those children, including the young girl whose affection kept me at least partially sane those long 10 months of incessant combat conditions.
Thanh Tran, who arrived at Salem State College via Andover Academy, Everett High School, and a virtual child slave camp in Hong Kong, personifies the second kind of causality. Tran is a so-called boat child, exiled to Hong Kong and later to the U.S. because his father fought on the side of the United States during the war. As an officer in the South Vietnamese army, his father was taken prisoner following the removal of U.S. troops and later died in a "re-education" camp.
This story is particularly moving to me as his father served with the 9th ARVA division alongside my unit in the delta region of South Vietnam. Through Tran, I have learned a good deal about how new immigrants experience our citizenship process. Angered by the inexcusable delays in processing his application, I asked Senator Ted Kennedy for his help at an event in Salem last March. But even the ranking Democrat on the Subcommittee on Immigration of the Senate Judiciary Committee cannot expedite the interminable process to which applicants are subjected by the Immigration and Naturalization Service.
Thus the offspring of our deceased former allies must wait with all citizenship wannabes while our country decides whether or not to hang a "no vacancy" sign around the Statue of Liberty's neck. A mother's pain is a mother's pain whether we win or lose the war. As we celebrate Speilberg's triumph in his film about the invasion of Normandy a half-century ago, let's not lose its meaning. The damage war inflicts continues long after the bullets stop flying.

I obtained this game in early April 2016 during a great sale. The TL;DR is this: simple enough to pick up, complex enough not to put down. For me The game is marred only by its poor save mechanic and truly terrible voice acting.
I was a bit surprised at how good this game was. Others have called it “Eve Light” and guess what? Its good enough comparison. Like other games such as “evochron Mercenary”, the Various “X” games like X3:Terren Conflict” , Freelancer etc, you fly around and do stuff for folks and get money from that. You can mine, salvage, build an economic power house, play taxi, attack the meannies, etc.
What sets this game apart from the rest is a mix of easier to use controls, a good mix of things to do, good pace and an active community. If you think many space games are just too complicated without a joystick and throttle then you may like this game. Since I am not a pilot in real life, do not have a us$200 joystick, and have no desire to learn an intricate set of controls, I think this game is much easier to play and enjoy then many others of the same genre.
Pros
-	Controls are easy to learn but hard to master without needing an expensive joystick and throttle
-	Enough choice to feel in control
-	Good selection of mission types
-	Fun achievements
-	Good mix of things to do
-	Fun exploration
-	Developers are active in the community
-	Enjoyable forum community
-	Single player offline goodness.
-	Survives repeated alt-tabbing out of the game.
-	A slower pace then some space games
-	Enough choices to feel in control without being so overwhelmed that you cant wrap your head around where to even begin
-	Long tutorial campaign is kind of fun but not mandatory you can start it and pick the main campaign back up when you want to.
Cons
-	Really poor voice acting. Seriously BAD. Its cringe worthy how poor the voice acting is.
-	Poor save game mechanic you can’t just save when you want to.  you’ll have to fly back to a station so its not the right choice for busy life if you can’t set aside a block of play time. This sis not a game that you can start to play if there is much chance of interruption since you may often find you cant save for another 5 or 10 minutes.
-	Boring choice of ships in the start – just your own ship, nothing compares for some time into the game. There is nothing wrong with your starting ship but you can’t just swap it out for another other until much later in the game the other choices are simply too weak compared to what you start out using.
-	Often inscrutable choices – you’ll need to use google allot to get a hang of what is going on. It’s a good thing that alt-tab does not break the game. It is a good thing the community is so active and there is plenty of information out there.
-	Tutorial is bit thin you’ll need to google allot. it will help if you have played other space games like Eve Online, Freelancer, etc before this game.
-	If you have played other space sims and want an immersive dog fighting, pirating power house this is not the right game for you.
-	Single player may be a snooze fest if you are used to the pace of online games
Highly recommend this!!!  So fun and such a great price right now in the holiday sale.  Very realistic and while I never thought I could get into this it's highly addictive!

Basically Freelancer.
Similar to Sid Meier's Pirates but in space. Huge space.
Ship customization similar to Mechwarrior's mech customization.
Mine asteroids, hunt bounties, play with the market, buy better ships, better equipment, etc.
Streamlined user interface.
Combat is good. There's several weapon types for you to try out. Rockets, laser beams and plasma cannons to name a few, each with their own properties and upgrades. Get on your gunship and chase enemies by their tail or line up your battleship and bombard them mercilessly. Your choice.
Exploration is good. The game gives the player a huge world to explore. Planets, space stations and shipyards that offer different products depending on their region. Planets and space stations act as hubs, you can't set foot on them and explore. Not as huge as Elite Dangerous but huge nonetheless.

Music is good. Too bad there's not much to go around. If you have a space exploration playlist then add this game's music to that playlist and play that instead.
Economy is there. Trade clean goods or contraband. You can take advantage of rising and falling prices of materials but the economy isn't deep enough to make it an engaging enterprise. You can mine asteroids or scavenge space junk while going about your trade route, I guess.
CAN'T FORM A FLEET. You can capture enemy ships. You either sell them, keep them or scrap them. Keeping them puts them in your garage. You can switch between ships YOU CAN ONLY USE ONE SHIP AT ANY TIME. The closest to a fleet you'll get is by hiring mercenaries to fly with you for a price. Even then you can't command them. This is probably the worst negative point of the game in my opinion.
Light RPG elements.
A good space game overall but if you're into trading, playing with the economy or empire building then this game won't satisfy you.

This review is only for the single player campaign on normal difficulty.
Pretty well everything about this game was exactly what I would want out of a FPS campaign.  There was a decent variety of guns, some of them had secondary fire options, a few gernade choices and a melee option.  The best thing about the guns was that there wasn't one or two that were obviously the ones you had to take with you, you had the choice to pick whatever two you liked and make your way through the game.  Of course there were times that one gun was much more useful than another but for the rest of the time you could run with what you want, till you ran out of ammo anyways.
Enemies were not to difficult for the most part outside of a few areas that were tricky.  Later game enemies did start presenting a bit more of a challenge.  They used cover surprisingly well and did attempt flanks and the like.
The setting, enviroment, graphics, etc... were all top notch, there is pretty well nothing that I could complain about in that department.  From the beauty of the open spaces in destroyed dubia to the smaller areas were unspeakable horrors abounded, everything was just so well presented.
And the story.  Without getting into spoilers because this is a game that should be experienced spoiler free.  I loved the story, I'm still not sure I entirely got everything that there was to get from the story, but thats the great part.  The game did leave some choices to make, as to what exactly those choices decided at the end of the day, well thats why I want to play the game more than once, and I can't really think of any FPS single player campaings that made me want to come back for more.
The only big gripe that I had with this game was with your AI teammates and their use of cover, or well lack of cover I guess.  The two AI teamates that you travel the game with are better than a lot of other AI teamates other games have stuck you with, these guys actually can kill an enemy or two but they tend to walk stupidly out of cover every now and then.  They would end up dying foolishly and you'd have to break cover to revive them or mission failure.
But to sum it all up.  This is exactly what I've wanted out of a FPS single player campaign.  Everything was presented beautifully.  There was a decent selection of weapons to keep the shooting interesting and a story that above all else makes the game stand out far above a lot of other FPS campaigns and is something that I would whole heartedly recommend to almost any FPS fan.

*As someone who loved Banjo-Kazooie and Banjo-Tooie I will say I had fun 100%ing this, however I only recommend this to people who are die-hard fans of the series or someone who is interested in trying something like this out on sale. The devs worked for 2 years on this and that is very impressive that they got something this massive out that fast and I'm impressed by that. This will be a spoiler-free review I will try and be as vague as possible. I was a kickstarter backer and I'm disappointed in the missed potential this has.
* Let's start with the music it's very much a throwback to the good old Banjo-Kazooie and Tooie music very nice and atmospheric as well as having its serious tones from time to time so that is done very well. Next we will go over the atmosphere of the levels is that they're absolutely gorgeous and everything to me looks very nice and well polished if you like the pretty cartoon aesthetic. The moveset is definitely there although my biggest problem is that one of the moves completely gets overshadowed by another move and past the area you use it you will pretty much never use it. Level design is pretty nice except for the fact that one level in particular seemed very confusing didn't gate you properly and you got to a segment where you couldn't solve it at that time. I would be fine about not solving it but not being gated and having to do a fairly annoying segment seems like pretty bad stage design to me. One thing I will say about the level design is that the levels are absolutely massive and don't feel like they have too much in them aside from clones of NPCs making you do arbitrary tasks which is fine except in Banjo Kazooie and Tooie we didn't have clones we had fairly memorable characters who were fun and interesting like Boggy for example. The bosses felt very bland and not very unique except for maybe the 3rd boss and the 5th boss. There wasn't too much challenge to them which is fine but there wasn't anything with a wow or fun factor to them either. The enemies weren't really all that different from each other I felt like they needed a bit more variety to them. The story really doesn't matter in the grand scheme of things you don't really play these for the story but the main villian. I felt he didn't jab at our heroes that much. I liked the dynamic of Yooka and Laylee felt a lot like Banjo and Kazooie.
* Let's get into the really big problems of the game now: Rextro and Kartos these two characters are the most infuriating characters in the game, because of the tasks they make you do. Rextro's old school arcade games aren't fun, aren't challenging, and they just feel completely tedious and uninteresting like they were thrown there just cuz. You have to beat each of them twice and my biggest problem with this is the second time you're supposed to achieve a highscore, but what if you already achieved that highscore I hear you ask well the game doesn't recognize it so you're forced to do it again. Kartos is the hardest thing in the game minecart segments that have really clunky controls a speedup and slowdown on cooldown and a shoot on cooldown which is fine if it didn't feel super clunky and super frustrating you're just collecting gems avoiding obstacles and shooting them hoping you don't fall down a pit. I know they were trying to throwback to the old minecart segments, but they could've done that in a challenge that makes you feel like you achieved something rather than being glad it's done and over with and you don't ever have to do it again. There are glitches galore from losing your ability to attack, softlocks, my graphics card crashed, and I had a massive issue in area 4 when I talked to rextro all the textures spazzed out. I feel like there aren't any really unique or memorable challenges in this like as infamous as she was Canary Mary I will remember her for the rest of my life or the fun of the ufo shooting, or hatching Eyerie the Eagle, battling Nipper, and many more. Instead you go through rings lots and lots and lots and lots of rings. The controls on most transformations are clunky, awful, and require you to do a round about method just to use. A lot of sounds in the game are very loud and in your face and caused me to have a headache at some points.
* I feel like there's a lot of potential here and Playtonic could rework it to be more interesting and more polished. I look forward to the next game they put out, but all things considered and this is being lenient as a die-hard fan this game gets a 6/10 and keep in mind that's from a 100% playthrough experiencing everything this game has to offer.

This game has been an absolute delight to play, and absolutely feels like the Banjo-Kazooie spiritual successor promised. It is familiar, but sufficiently different from its predecessors. The game is beautiful, with great music and humor.
I can't say that the experience is perfect. There are a few bugs and the camera can be annoying at times. I've also found that it seems to require too little progress to unlock later worlds, and some of the later moves can trivialize challenges in early ones. Despite a few issues, this is a great 3D platformer.

There is so much to explore and I spent over 16 hours on the game before reaching the final boss. There is so much to do in the game.
I loved most of the collectable challenges you had to complete. There were some that are more trouble than their worth, but  for the completionist, it makes the game that much more challenging. Overall though, this really is the spiritual successor to the Banjo-Kazooie series and I look forward to what else Playtonic will do!

Games good! It is solid in its own little indie way. But it is good. I dont know where all the negative salt is coming from. I absolutelly do not understand how some people manage to find such huge gripes with the game.
Good graphics, gameplay is great, not hard, a bit too easy but yeah it is solid and it does great at key areas. Which is ofcourse gameplay.
My faults torwards the game goes to the story, ending, camera and levels.
THE BAD
Story
Characters just dont have that much impact. They do not click against or with eachother as much. Most of the supporting characters are great, but between the main baddie and yooka/layle there is not much to bounce off of. Where I do like the story is when the world does the talking, or when the character personality does the talking. The other half of what I think is bad is the constant 4th wall breaking. Other than that, its just annoyingly close to being a solid story.
Camera
Gameplay wise, the only thing I hate about the gameplay is the camera. I honestly do not know why they havent found a solution to it but eh... I can live with it.
Levels
The levels are pretty big, a bit too big. I wish they could cut the levels into 2 pieces. Basically, there are 5 worlds, and each world can be expanded. What sucks is that you only have 5 worlds, whats great is that these worlds are pretty flipping big actually. I just think it would be better for more worlds and have them be smaller. This is like, unnecesary big. Its so big that I can see what they tried to go for, but it just does not do the trick. They did not have to go for this scale.
I rather have smaller worlds but more of them.
One of the arcade mini-games features the 1st world assets but makes it feel like a beach setting. If anything, they should have made more worlds utilising the same assets that way. Heck the many worlds have diversive areas. The swamp worlds has industrial assets in one section, that could have been its own world. Rusty bucket bay all the way.
THE GOOD!
Gameplay
Freedom in gameplay by a long shot. I am surprised that they let me go this far with what I can do. I also feel like some glitches in the game or exploits are left in there on purpose, like if you attack just before you fall off a ledge, you will do that attack floating in midair. Something about that makes me think of Gex. I felt like sometimes I was going into places I shouldnt go, but then whadya know... there is a quill.
Music
Yess the music! So good, it feels so good! I do not know what else to say! I wish there were maybe more worlds but smaller. That way, the repetetive music is not so repetetive and you would then have more music! aw yeah!
Graphics
Loving the way they made the game look. It does not look bad at all. Honestly, I somtimes felt like I was playing a nintendo game. However, there are some effects and other things that just does not have an impact enough. But I still only have one question in my head, and that is if this game would actually look better with a cell shaded look. I like the realistic lighting, but with such realized technology today, i think aesthetically it is best to go with something that fits this game and its cartoony style. But they made that choice long ago, im just dreaming here.
OVERALL
about 7/10. I hate to be that honest to this game but a 7/10 is what it honestly truly is. I would give it an 8 or 9 with other surrounding games that just are not as solid as this one that also have the same score or more. But in reality, as solid as this game is. It really is a good 7/10.
Also the whole jonthing. I still think that was not a good move playtonic. Shame on you...

Though I never had the opportunity to play Banjo Kazooie as a kid, one N64 game that I did cherish was Donkey Kong 64, and I'd say that Yooka Laylee does a fine job in brining me back to the collectathon days. The worlds are large and fun to explore, the music is catchy and exciting, and the characters and their dialog are quirky and a pleasure to read (though maybe not always so much to listen to). I encountered a few performance issues, and a the odd rendering glitch around the first world's boss, however in my experience that hardly made the game any less fun. I'm very impressed with Playtonic's work, and I hope to see more great games from them in the future!

I’m generally not a major fan of FPSes. I’m more of an RPG sort of guy. And yet, I found myself interested and intrigued by the
series. When the series went on sale not long ago, I canvassed some friends’ opinions, whether I should get the first game, or the second. I had, admittedly, enjoyed watching the
videos of the latter. Having been told to get the second game, that’s what I did, getting the Game of the Year edition. But was it worth it? **** the hell,
Five years have passed since the opening of the original Vault. The Hyperion Corporation, led by the egotistical and petulant tyrant Handsome Jack, has begun to tighten its grip on Pandora, killing bandits and the normal populace alike, all in the name of ‘taming’ the border world. As rumours of a new Vault spread, Jack makes the call for new Vault Hunters, only to kill them. But that was a mistake. A new group of Vault Hunters will rise, team up with old ones, and embark on a quest to stop Handsome Jack. But they have a hard task ahead of them, as Jack has more than one trump card up his sleeve…
I enjoy games with a good story, and one thing that Borderlands does very well is the story. It’s like the mutant offspring of
and
, with a touch of
(or
, if you need a more modern show) thrown into the mix. Funny, full of references, and yet serious and full of pathos when it needs to, it’ll certainly have some shocks for fans of the first game. It’s also populated with a cast with the good, the bad, and the fugly. The storylines of the DLC ones are fine enough, though the real star storyline of the DLC campaigns is that of
. It’s also one of those rare sequels that you can enjoy fully without any knowledge of the previous game.
The graphics of the
series are very distinctive, being pseudo-cel shaded. They’re also pretty damned good, giving the right style and vibe to this world. There’s also a variety of landscapes, from desert and arid lands, to tundra, to cities, and even verdant mountains. The
series shows that realistic graphics aren’t always the way to go, that stylised graphics can often be better than the more realistic stuff some games seems to want to tend towards.
Sound-wise, the game is superlative. The music is spot-on, albeit not as spectacular at times as I want it to be. The voice-acting, however, is something else, with particular praise going to Dameon Clarke as Handsome Jack, Cherami Leigh as Gaige, Jason Douglas as Krieg, Brina Palencia as Moxxi, Chris Rager as Torgue, Colleen Clinkenbeard as Lilith, Scarlett, and Tannis, David Eddings as Claptrap, and Ashly Burch as Tiny Tina. They, along with so many others, make this game wonderful, giving life to characters that make us laugh, cringe, and cry.
But a game would be nothing without gameplay, and as far as FPSes are concerned,
****ing
. While I am not enticed by the series’ claims of ‘87 bazillion guns’, procedurally generated (though the elemental properties are certainly enjoyable), the hybridisation of an FPS and an RPG is considerably more interesting. Each character is given a unique attack ability or Action Skill, as well as a variety of abilities you can invest points in, RPG style, to customise your character’s abilities. The game itself can get a bit grindy at times, but thankfully, it’s one of the games that will have you having fun while doing so most of the time. The four DLC campaigns also add some substantial playtime to the game, and the two DLC characters are bloody good. Not only that, but it’s a game that you may very want to play through again, right from the beginning, which is why the True Vault Hunter mode may appeal to those who do want to do so.
If you had to get one FPS to play in your entire life, then I would have to recommend
, hands-down. Get the Game of the Year edition. You won’t regret it.
EDIT: Nominated this for the "Five More Minutes" Award for the Steam Awards 2016.

Good, fun game if you like base-simulation games like I do.
It's always interesting to see what your little dupes decide to do to obey your commands and what you then have to do to save them from themselves.
Be aware that the dupes have the sense of self-preservation of terminally depressed lemmings.

Oxygen Not Included has a really tense atmosphere to it despite the cute & silly drawings.
Having to micromanage your crew in order to sustain your base from starving to running out of power.
Although times can be tough, it feels very rewarding when you fix an issue in your base, such as finishing an airvent system to filter out pollution into an empty room while pumping your hydrogen to your hydrogen generators to keep the system running.
One cool aspect of the game is the research system. By supplying workers and resources to a research system you can unlock new technologies to upgrade your base with. This may be gas pumping for the air, liquid filtration, or even sanitary systems.
This game has a lot of potential and I hope to see the devs keep pumping out new tech to the tech tree!

Update after 160 hours!
Prison Architect is "sandbox" builder par excellance.
I have had the pleasure of seeing it grow and improve over the last half a year and it draws me back in every time. There are no cons, just so you know :P
But what's Prison Architect?
You are the Boss. Your prison, your rules, your design.
Start from scratch and work your way up the ladder until you can house the most dangerous criminals. Or go into the unlimited fund mode and just build your personal dream prison.
Prison Architect offers a variety of complex mechanics that work neatly with each other to create a living, changing prison environment.
Building: classical square-based, bird eye sandbox.
Environment: day and night cycle, proper shadows, chances of lakes and woods to be incorporated into your design. grass and flowers will grow uncontrollably and need to be trimmed.
Gangs: criminals will now sometimes have gang affiliations. they will fight you and other prisoners and even take over your prison!! They come in all shapes and sizes, and some are even docile.
Needs: prisoners have several needs they shout at you, from the easy 'Bladder' to the more difficult to reach 'Safety'. Family visits will do a lot to release stress. it's a constant fight to keep them happy, but understanding their needs is key for running a tidy prison.
Contraband: Ah, you can try, but you will have a hard time preventing smuggling inside your prison. Your prisoners steal, have help from their families or have packages thrown over the fences. Fight back with metal detectors, routine searches and confidental informants.
Wiretap the phones for additional insight and shake down your prison every once in a while (or daily :D )
Guards: Regular, Armed and Dog Handlers, plus an extra Riot Unit to call in emergencies. station them on posts, let them patrol or teach each of them how to use tazers. they're not the smartest, but loyal to the death.
Dog Handlers will sniff out smelly contraband or tunnels, while armed guards are great at keeping your inmates surpressed. be sure to plan their routes properly and concentrate forces at critical points.
Rooms: a large variety of rooms, from different cell types (holding cells, solitary, regular) to security stations and armories to libraries and laundries for the prisoners. build a dog pound, common room or even a chapel for the those that want to find salvation in the arms of the lord.
Cells have a quality, directly incluencing the inmates' behaviour. always good to have an eye on that ;)
Staff: Psychologists for intimate group seminars with the prisoners, grounds keepers, cooks and, of course, a lawyer and accountant. Let them research, clean and fend off annoying lawsuits or loss conditions. I told you, you are the boss :P
Prisoners: now, they are the true heroes of this game. quite clever and crafty little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. They will stop at nothing to try to escape you or send the prison spiraling down into a muderious abyss of blood and mayhem.
building tunnels together with other prisoners. stealing the appropriate tools from around the prison. shanking suspicious inmates in the shower. initiating riots when a prisoner dies.
Prisoners come in all forms and shapes. from the mid 20 stoner, in for possession, to deathrow inmates with multiple murders. some have abilites, some are even legen-wait for it-dary. and you decide their security level ;)
Snitchs and Ex Law Enforcement inmates are a painful joy. not fast enough in identifying them? see them shanked to death in the shower, yard or laundry.
There's a huge variety of prisoners, crimes and reputation skills, and each prisoner is indeed somewhat of an individual.
Intelligence: recruit confidental informants, check the history of contraband and control your gangs. but be careful, the more you rely on your informants, the more likely they are to be killed by their fellow inmates.
Logistics: still a bit of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥to get around with, but you can control who is washing which wings' clothes, preps their food etc.
Size: as they say, it doesn't matter. try to manage a small prison with few but maybe violent inmates, or go ballistic with hundreds of prisoners, likely suffocating in their own filth. Prison architect is fun from small to big. But always a challenge.
Random Events: Fires, floods, virus outbreaks and surprise prisoners, all the things you need to ruin your day.
While a burst pipe is easily taken care of, a fire can surely burn down large parts of your prison and kill many an inmate or staffer.
Be sure to have either a quarantine ward ready for outbreaks, or to isolate the affected prisoners in their cells quickly.
Prison Policy Events: You can't run a prison without some politician or the other trying to boss you around. They will ask you to serve your prisoners the lowest grade food or to remove all work out benches from the yards, because some one clearly does not want your prison to be peaceful.
ignore it and get annoyed by phone calls every few ingame hours, or just do as they ask and deal with the fallout. probably by bashing in heads and locking up half your prison
Campaign: a lovely little story revolving around betrayal, murder and mayhem, also serving as a perfect tutorial for the sandbox mode. The campaign introduces the mechanics in an understandable and easy to grasp way for new comers, and even after 100 hours, it still offered insight for my gameplay.
There is so much more going on, but seriously, 110 hours into the game I feel like I barely scratched the surface of what Prison Architect really has to offer.
Even now, after 160 hours, it still sucks me in for 5 -10 hours a time. From the urge to build more and better wards to just observing the prisoners and try to keep the place calm, there is much to do and even more to observe.
Get it. This game is worth every Euro and Stotinki and will make you forget about everything else.
There's still some bugs left, but the devs are still putting out updates, and so far the game as steadily improved.

I love space sims. I don't even know how much time I sank into freelancer or the x3 games. Yet this one I am dropping after a bit more than 10 hours of playing.
Let's start with what I like about this game: The graphics are good, the different ships with their various layouts are cool, you can customize your ship through enhancements and hiring officers, the energy transfer management (engine, weapons, shields) is interesting, and on the surface the game feels like it is trying to marry the best parts of freelancer with those from the x series (which means many things immediately make sense if you have played those games before).
However. Somehow the game feels like a chore; something I am willing myself to play in the hope that if I continue a bit further it will finally become exciting and turn into the great game it has the potential to be.
The story is inherently boring. Fly from A to B, listen to some terrible voice-overs, destroy a target (ambushes being optional), get an (uninteresting and unusable) item and no real information other than "fly to XYZ to get more info". But you need to grind a few side missions first to level up enough for that. Rinse and repeat. I have lost all interest in the main story and there is just nothing that compels me to continue playing it.
The other sidequests and missions are okay, but also very repetitive. The difficulty rating of these is useless, as some missions (e.g. science, maintenance, taxi, ferry) are childishly easy, whereas others (e.g. assasination, station defence) become really hard quickly unless you sink all your money into your fighting capabilities. Importantly the missions don't pay enough in my eyes to make them worthwile. I found boarding other small ships much more lucrative. And flying through space feeling like you are a towing service is just not fun for long. These side missions quickly turn into mindless grinding.
There are many other things that bug me (not even to mention the numerous bugs I encountered already) that make this game a "no" for me:
The fighting is super boring; most of the time I just sit there with my turrents firing automatically and I don't do anything other than watch. Ships feel very small and their speed and maneuverability do not seem to decrease with size as far as I can tell (there is no "speed" property you could check when buying a ship). There is no good fast travel: gates are too expensive, wormholes regularly throw you out at the wrong location (and what is it with that terrible, terrible animation you are shown after you have flown into a wormhole?) and those "green highways" seem a bit pointless; most importantly while all of these move you long distances quickly they don't allow to quickly travel to something that is say halfway of that distance. Factions have no character and no individual story making them pointless really. The energy transfer management can only be used effectively by dragging it around with your mouse; there are no customizable settings to be activated through a button, e.g. a "hit and run" (50% engine, 50% weapons). Skills have no real impact: I have put all my skillpoints into one particular tree (beam weapons) and I still can't tell the difference before and after I activated the skill, with the promised increase in range definitely not working. The game cannot be played effectively with a joystick: some button commands cannot be changed (e.g. closing window, using skill, cycle through tabs in the store) while others simply are not recognized or don't work; also you can't use a mouse to quickly navigate say the store and star map.
There are many more things that have added to me not liking this game, but those are probably too specific to me to be really useful for other players.
Tl;DR: Repetive missions, bad main story, boring fights, lots of mindless grinding, terrible voice acting, the whole universe feels characterless and the joysticks can't be used effectively. While it is trying to combine the best things of previously succesful spacesims (freelance, x3) it does not get it right.

Spec Ops: The line... ah, only the name of the game already reminds me of that great experience I had when I was playing it. In Spec Ops: The Line, the player controls Captain Martin Walker, who is sent into a post-catastrophe Dubai with an elite Delta Force team on a reconnaissance mission, where they find dead American soldiers. Upon the finding, Walker declares that the team's mission has changed, and that they will search Dubai for survivors. An online multiplayer mode, developed by Darkside Game Studios, is included with the game, allowing players to engage in both co-operative and competitive gameplay.
The writers stated that the premise of the game is influenced by various novellas, including Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness, with Konrad replacing Kurtz. Video game critics gave Spec Ops: The Line generally positive reviews. Praise focused on its narrative and themes, while criticism was targeted particularly at the online multiplayer mode and generic third person gameplay. Spec Ops: The Line also won, and was nominated for, several industry awards, including Best Narrative at Machinima's Inside Gaming Awards.

In  STAR WARS™ Jedi Knight - Jedi Academy™, you play as, well whoever you want. The cool thing about this game is that just like the Knights of the Old Republic, you get to choose how your character looks, the problem howevers is that it's left to 3 choices, your head, torso, and legs but along with this you get to customize your own Lightsaber and later on in the game you even get to choose between a double bladed saber or dual lightsabers.  In my review of the story i'll be sticking with the Human Male persona. Star Wars Jedi Academy takes place after Jedi Outcast and for all who haven't played Jedi outcast first why not? Second it's alright becuase you'll be able to understand the story without previous knowledge of the previous games.
Story -In this game you play as Jaden, a new student at the Jedi Academy hand picked by luke Skywalker becuase Jaden was able to build a Lightsaber without previous knowledge. While on the ship to the academy he befriends a unlikeable douch named Rosh and then the ship is shot down leaving Jaden to find a way back to the academy with Rosh. After this, Jaden is set on a set of missions to destroy a cult and many other stuff. Each set contains 5 missions were Jaden can upgrade his powers after every other mission with a interlude mission after each set.
Gameplay- Jedi Academy is actually pretty much the same gameplay wise with some new things added in. THe lightsaber action in this game just feels so awesome creating some memorable moments when you put up against a army of enemies. Also the force powers in this game in this game just make you feel like a true jedi, especially later on in the game when your powers become really upgraded, It just makes you feel like a badass. To be honest, the main force powers you'll be using is force push, pull, heal, lightning, and sometimes sense. While the other powers aren't horrible, you probrobly won't be using them 'till the end of the game when you just become stacked with enemies upon enemies.
Multiplayer- The multiplayer is probrobly one of the best parts about this game. There is still a large community in this game and they are a cool community to. You'll have alot of fun trust me. Also you can play as any playermodel that is in the game or just customize.
Overall- this game is in my opionion one of the best star wars games there is being beat by Jedi Outcast. This game has some flaws but they can be over seen with all the awesomness of this game. Overall you should get it.

It's got 300 levels of which at least 220-230 are really well made and it throws probably a solid 100 mechanics at you (of which almost all work--the repulsor magnets are pretty much just miserable). It really does it well, too, like a great student of all the great platformers. Each mechanic is presented in some surface level fashion, but a few levels later it'll come up again, and this time it'll be trickier. The replays are perfect, the game trimmed as much cruft as possible to make retrying a level an enjoyable experience, the Dark World levels are some of the best remixes in gaming and reminded me of games like Eversion that explore these concepts. The controls are dead-on, most of the extra characters feel as good to use as Meat Boy, and the game is tough but very rarely frustrating.

If your are an idealist who is against the "always-online" cancer that has caught on with some major games, then this game is not for you. Hitman requires constant internet connection, and if you lose connection while playing a story mission, it kicks you to the main menu, requiring you to reconnect and reload your game (with hopes you saved recently since once you lose connection there isnt a way to save).
Now, having said all of that, I love this game. if you have good internet, you wont really notice it. yet, I havent encountered a game with such a focus on replayability. There are only 3 maps, and thats being generous. really only 1 map. but within this 1 map, i could replay this mission again and again until my fingers fall off. Never have I had so much fun messing up while performing a choke-hold, throwing a body off a railing and alerting the guards below, and spending the next 15 minutes shooting my way out and engaging in costume-stealing shenanigans while i desperately try to justify calling myself a "professional hitman".

Spec Ops: The line... ah, only the name of the game already reminds me of that great experience I had when I was playing it. In Spec Ops: The Line, the player controls Captain Martin Walker, who is sent into a post-catastrophe Dubai with an elite Delta Force team on a reconnaissance mission, where they find dead American soldiers. Upon the finding, Walker declares that the team's mission has changed, and that they will search Dubai for survivors. An online multiplayer mode, developed by Darkside Game Studios, is included with the game, allowing players to engage in both co-operative and competitive gameplay.
The writers stated that the premise of the game is influenced by various novellas, including Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness, with Konrad replacing Kurtz. Video game critics gave Spec Ops: The Line generally positive reviews. Praise focused on its narrative and themes, while criticism was targeted particularly at the online multiplayer mode and generic third person gameplay. Spec Ops: The Line also won, and was nominated for, several industry awards, including Best Narrative at Machinima's Inside Gaming Awards.
Now that you're familiar with the game itself- let's talk about pluses and minuses this game has.
One and the biggest flaw- it feels like a generic 3rd person shooter with nothing original in it, all it has- he have seen before. You'll say "Shotyyy, but there is the sand and destruction", well my friend, no- the send and destructable objects are strictly in scripted spots which are encountered very rarely.
But, this game is awesome no matter what I've said above! Both following pluses redeem all the boring gameplay! First- story: It's very interasting and very humane, you feel bad for the negative actions of the characters as, at most cases, you have a choice, you get tied to them and feel sorry for everything they do wrong. You don't lose grip of the story until it ends- all that was unclear- becomes clear and understable, leaving you shocked with any of multiple endings it has. Second plus- game's setting. It's set in beatiful Dubai after the serious damage was dealt to the city. Every step you make- you enjoy the view. It's interesting and full with small details making it very original and not boring.
So, to sum up, if you don't care about gameplay and came to hear an interesting story- grab it, don't hesitate, it's a great game holding you from start to finish. But there is one big BUT. If you came relax and shoot some bad guys up- wrong place, pal. Lack of gameplay doesn't make it bad, it's great and worth the small amount of money it costs these days.

Story line is fairly short and not very thrilling, might even say it's a cliche although the last parts of the story are quite heavy. Game itself is well presented with visible great motion capture, beautiful graphics (if you can call wastelands the beautiful place). World is filled with places to visit and scavage jung and water along with collectables which are scraps of history. Collecting and visitig those places might seem boring and repetetive but its not, all the places scatered in the world look different and makes us want to know a little bit more about title Max's memories and point of view. In the game we can also find small RPG elements implemented, such as upgrading your ride Magnum Opus, Max's gun and the rest of his tools. For a long time I haven't experience such a rewarding and satysfying combat system in sandbox games, it's similar to Batman or Assassins Creed franchise, but we still don't feel too overpowered as sometimes enemies can be a real hussle and get on your nerves. On the wasteland we can take over the regions from the enemy and lowering their influence by taking down enemy camps where game gives you few approaches, you can either sneak close to the camp and suprise your opponents or go old fasion way thorugh the main entrance or disable most of the defences from far away using your sniper rife on the back of your car. Also to lower the influence you can destroy small towers made from human bodies and scraps of metal, disarm mine fields and by couple other ways. Game offers plenty of side activities such as death races and wasteland stranger quests. Mad Max content will last easly for about 60 hours for 100% completion. The whole world presented in this game is really heavy, depressing, showing the struggle of humanity after the apocalypse when water on entire planet dissapeared along with sealife. Now people are fighting for oil, water, food and junk which is by the way the main currency, everyone are driven to madness to the point where it's hard to say who's normal. I think that WB and Avalanche Studio did the great job with presenting the Mad Max universe. As the game is not perfect and has it's flaws I can surely call it a great game worth picking up.

This game makes me feel like I'm wandering a post-apocalyptic wasteland blowing the hell out of War Boys and that's exactly what I wanted.
I had two major problems with the game.  First, the boss fights are all stupid, except for the penultimate one.  Fortunately, they don't make up a majority of playtime, but since (as you'd expect) the game ends with one, it's pretty anticlimactic.  Secondly, and a slightly bigger problem, the difficulty scales poorly.  Early in the game, with not much of a car, no skills, and weak attributes, survival is a real struggle.  By late game, you're a superpowered killing machine.  The sweet spot between the two is vanishingly small, though.  It may work out better if you don't (as I did) complete a lot of optional side quests along the way, or if you leave them for the end.
These problems do nothing to sully the fact that the game lets you wander a post-apocalyptic wasteland blowing the hell out of War Boys.  Highly recommended.  (The game's pretty as hell, too.)

Handling a yearly franchise such as Call of Duty is no easy task, as you always have to come up with fresh ideas that will make everyone believe that you didn’t make just another Call of Duty game, or an improvement over the last year’s game, but a new and fresh experience overall that brings everything fans love about the franchise and mixes that up with a great story and a fresh take on a first person shooter’s campaign. The story the game wants to tell is profound, detailed and amazingly well executed, shifting between the past stories that follow the protagonists Alex Mason and Sgt. Frank Woods from the first Black Ops game and the present story that takes place in 2025, following David “Section” Mason, Alex’s son and his squad. Black Ops II is not another game that puts a random villain in it taking you one step closer to killing him from a mission to another, but instead it makes you understand the reasons of the game’s villain, Raul Menendez as he tries to take revenge on the United States and its people. Every mission takes you closer to understanding what Menendez’ intentions truly are and even when you think you have it all figured out, in the next sequence a plot twist will wipe that impression and you’re back at the start with no clue on how it’s all going to end. The past missions are a delight as they will instantly bring back some nostalgia to the fans of the first Black Ops, while still keeping those new to the franchise up to date by telling some of the previous stories as you make your way to the next objective. Each character has its own spotlight and you will have plenty of opportunities to find out more about each individual as you play through the missions, but the real magic begins when all those stories come together at once into what is without doubt one of the most apocalyptic sceneries seen in a Call of Duty game before, but even with all that the story that Black Ops II wants to tell isn’t about destruction or taking control, but instead about losing, revenge and the meaning of a person’s life. Whoever said that first person shooters no longer care about the story was wrong, and Black Ops II proves that more than anything, managing to deliver a touching story that breaks any barriers of time or protagonists, leaving you with the emotion you want to feel as there are multiple endings and different choices that will affect the outcome later, all that while still keeping an addictive and diverse first person shooter feel.
Since Call of Duty: Modern Warfare, Multiplayer has kept growing in size from one game to the next one, introducing more features and content than ever before and becoming an essential component of any Call of Duty game. Black Ops II is no different, pushing the boundaries of competitive multiplayer even forward, with more maps, modes and weapons than ever before, all wrapped up with a ranking system that makes it interesting and exciting to unlock more content as you level up, and make multiplayer feel refreshing even after you've familiarized yourself with all the maps and modes. It all comes together in a well crafted rank mechanic, which allows your character to level up and unlock new weapons, slots and gear, as well as the weapons themselves, which will unlock new attachments such as silencers, scopes or additional ammo slots. There are tons of gadgets, weapons and scorestreaks to unlock, and even if by the end of level 55 you should be able to unlock everything, the Prestige mode allows you to reset your entire progress in exchange for a new special rank and additional slots or unlock tokens, so you can try out new things the next time, while still getting rewarded for your progress made so far. League Play is where Black Ops II gets competitive, as it was meant to be the perfect place to sustain eSports activities without limiting access to professionals only, as anyone can take part in placement games, after which they will be placed in a division with players with a similar skill level to theirs and play in ladder matches so each and everyone has a chance to occupy a place on the ladder
The Zombies mode from Black Ops I and Call of Duty: World at War before it makes a return as a standalone experience for the first time, bringing with it more features, maps and of course zombies. Just like in the original Black Ops the story follows a different group of four survivors: Abigail "Misty" Briarton, Marlton Johnson, Samuel Stuhlinger, and Russman, surviving the events following the destruction of Earth in Richtofen's Grand Scheme in the American South-West, players being given the ability to choose between them when playing. There are three different maps in which the players can choose to survive against multiple waves of zombies, Bus Depot, Town & Farm, with the fourth map named TranZit that will spawn an Undead Bus which will travel all of the previously mentioned maps, allowing you to take items from each of the locations and move on to the next one shortly after, as well as throwing in a couple of other activities, quests, items that you can take from each location and Easter Eggs that can be discovered along the way.

If you can get it on sale, definitely get it. It's a good pool sim, but I wouldn't say the best. It has some little things that irk me especially having played other pool games like Virtual Pool, and of course real life pool (in which I suck lol).
The graphics are beautiful, though at times it may be a little too shiny, like everything is made of chrome. With some balls it's difficult to distinguish between the stripes and the solids due to how the light shines on them at some angles. It also has a tendency for the FPS to shoot up too much if you have a decent gaming rig, so be sure to use VSync or have some kind of frame limiter program like RTSS. The problem with the FPS shooting up is that it makes it harder to aim as how quickly the mouse moves is affected by it. There are no advanced graphics options adjustments except for VSync and anti-aliasing. An option to reduce shininess or even brightness/gamma would've been great.
Cue and ball control are fairly good. It may take some getting used to how noticeably slow the rails and the table are if you're coming from other pool games. The speed of the table and whatnot are not adjustable in this game. However, they feel somewhat similar to real life pool tables so that's not a bad thing. The only other odd thing I've noticed is that the side pockets are very open. You can pocket shots into them from angles that you just can't do in real life. Pocket size can't be adjusted either.
The UI and interface are very nice. I love the UI sound effects particularly. A minor issue about the interface is that it seems to have been optimized for play with a controller, however due to how slow and inaccurate you are with the controller when playing pool, it's much more comfortable to play with mouse and keyboard anyway. Because it was optimized for controller, the interface options can be a little confusing when playing on mouse and keyboard. Things like a "select" button to go forward/continue and they ask you to press "start" to view your completed challenges. Again it's a minor issue since these are mapped properly by default to certain keys and mouse buttons, but still something they could've addressed.
The music is nice, but short and repetitive, and I wish they would've given us more of that. I ended up turning the music off entirely within the first hour and I just play music in the background via iTunes. It's odd, because with a shiny, cool-looking pool game like this you would think they'd have a bit of good music to go with it. Casual games often do.
One more issue that bothers me about this game is that you watch your opponent taking the shot as if you're the one at the table taking the shot. This probably won't bother some people, but because of how quickly the AI thinks and how they move the cue, it can be very jarring. I wish they would give us the option to automatically switch to a fixed camera angle when it's the opponent's turn. I like the way Virtual Pool does it, where you're off to the side as if you're physically standing aside while your opponent takes their turn. An option for that would've gone a long way for me.
And lastly, I need to comment on the game's AI. It's probably the worst part of it, and you have no choice but to play against it to unlock things like cue stick skins and ball sets. The AI seems to be suffering from a pre-programmed failure algorithm. You can watch even the low level AI make fantastic trick shots or amazing safety placings at the start of their turn, but then they'll suddenly miss on easy shots late in the turn, often on the last ball itself. After having played hundreds of matches against the AI, it feels like a pre-determined failure chance to make sure the player gets a chance at the table. It gets so bad that sometimes you'll miss on the 9-ball and it rattles in the pocket, and it'd go in if anybody sneezes, yet the AI somehow misses it too. As a testament to how rushed the AI feels, the AI never changes its shot (such as moving the ball or changing the angle at least) on the break. I'm an original backer as well as an avid fan of both the Banjo-Kazooie/Tooie games and DK64. Played them multiple times shortly after their release, continually revisit them, and can honestly say Yooka-Laylee is the first game I've played since then that brought those same feelings back. Playtonic Games has truly created something special here and I believe negativity towards the game is derived mostly from players neglecting to remember the gaming-standard when BK/T and DK64 were modern.
Starting from best to worst, Kirkhope has proven his absolute genius in composing once again - it sounds exactly like the originals. The characters are just as we remember, quirky, vibrant and always a little raunchy. Dialogue is hilarious and will keep you smiling throughout the game - Playtonic took some risks and it paid off very well. Gameplay is extremely smooth (I used a Logitech controller) and found little to almost no issues with the camera which apparently was an issue for others playing early on.
I see a lot of reviews complaining about the camera angles and something about "glitchy bosses". I watched the video mentioned, and can say that I saw absolutely nothing of the sort during my time spent in Yooka-Laylee (22hrs+). Playtonic released a performance patch right as the game released and it seemed to fix a large amount of issues; again I experienced maybe one or two very small areas throughout the entire game which I had what I can hardly even call trouble adjusting the camera.
Others are commenting that the gameplay is too difficult and I can see why this is a valid point if you are comparing this to modern gaming. What others aren't realizing is this game was based entirely off a title released in 1998, the difficulty standard for games back then was much, much different than it is today. Challenges would take multiple attempts, and they were not all easy by any means. This game has reinvented that same aspect of difficulty and I feel that a lot of older fans have forgotten that's how it used to be. I recall a specific challenge in DK64 with an arcade game *AHEM* that I don't think anyone who's played that has ever forgotten (took some people hours to complete). While I didn't find anything in Yooka-Laylee so far that has taken anywhere near that long to master, there are still some very difficult areas that you will have to traverse.
Lastly, I will cast a slight amount of criticism on the minigames placed into Yooka-Laylee. I found that after the second world the minigames (5 total in the worlds) became rather boring and very lengthy, it gave off the feeling of not redoing the minigame for fun but simply because you knew you needed to retrieve the reward at the end. Along with that, I feel that if you scored highly enough on the first run to meet the criteria for the second reward, it should be awarded rather than instead of having to finish the game a second time (topping a set score this time).
Overall, this game truly is a re-visit to the classic buddy-duo from long, long ago. Everything you loved still exists albeit modernized to a certain extent. With a good amount of the original developers and team working to create this title, I can strongly say it's a great addition to the series for anyone who actually remembers how those games were almost 20 years ago.
P.S There is a STRONG amount of foreshadowing for a sequel, and I'm incredibly excited to learn more of it!

Disclaimer/Disclosure: I backed this on the kickstarter at the £10 tier for the finished game. Furthermore I have NEVER played a Banjo Kazooie game - not even Nuts and Bolts - nor have I owned an N64 or played any games like it to my knowledge. So I went into this pretty much blind. The only reason I kickstarted is because I have friends who adored the BK games and I felt maybe it needed a second chance with this successor.
So! Rapid review so far in the first five hours.
Looks great, sounds nice and fun, music's good and chirpy and not obnoxious, gameplay is pretty rock solid so far.
CONTROLS are good, CAMERA is not so much. It really needs work. It sometimes just ignores you without warning and sometimes gets stuck on scenery resulting in slipping off things. very frustrating at times.
Also unskippable cutscenes.
Other than that, so far, the humour is fantastic and silyl and fun, and not all that odious. It's charming in a silly, childish, puerile way without being overly gross or mean spirited about anything. It's a lovely, innocent, cheerful game full of smiles and laughs and good clean honest fun. I can't hate it. It's too good and nice so far.
The gmaeplay is at its most bsaic, collecting pickups. that's pretty much it. You solve puzzles and explore for secrets to find the major macguffin things (the Pagies) so you can unlock worlds, and then expand those worlds, and you spend the little coin analogues (quills) on new moves to help you solve puzzles and explore for more secrets to unlock and expand more worlds to get more quills and...well, so on and so forth. :)
Story is pretty much an excuse plot, some cute little digs (not all that subtle either) at corporations and capitalism and suchlike, which is pretty fun and not too obnoxious, and the main characters are fun. "Voice Acting" is all done with silly little sounds for each character, rather than actual voice acting of any kind, in keeping thematically with the era of games it's evoking (think the original SNES Starfox 'voice acting' in a way though that's earlier in gaming history than this game is aiming for obviously).
Aside from the ever present explora-collectathon, there's some great little minigames peppered about that are pretty cool, and the puzzles are nice and fun and engaging, and intuitive without handing you the solution with a "clue" that pretty much just gives it away immediately.
I got this on the cheap as a result of the KS pledge, but I genuinely think it's probably worth its price of £35. It's pretty well crafted and really enjoyable.

More or less the Banjo-Threeie I've been waiting for ~
The only major problem I have is that some of the mini-games you play for Pagies feel very iffy, namely the Kartos stuff you go through in roughly every world. Other than that I think the controls feel fine when they need to be, and the camera (for the most part) was responsive enough. The game does have its charm too, especially with the new protagonists Yooka & Laylee.
Very abridged thoughts, but I personally recommend it. Only thing I'll urge is that, don't go into this expecting anything more than what's essentially the third Banjo game.

On close look, it's not as polished and the worlds are not nearly as complex as they were in the Banjo Kazooie games and therefore it's a really easy game.
Still, collecting everything feels great and it's fun to use the new moves and meet new characters. If you don't expect too much, it does feel like playing a new Banjo Kazooie.
If you like this kind of game, I don't think you can wrong with Yooka-Laylee. If not, don't expect this to change your mind.

Despite my earlier review on Borderlands 1.  Borderlands 2 does more than just set things right.
Instead of rehashing the whole story and game mechanics in a cookie cutter fashion Borderlands 2 achieves looting/shooting, questing, characters and storyline much better this time around.
Borderlands 2 succeeds by giving a more living, breathing environment than the first game. In which there wasn't much life and at times felt downright static.  The beginning sequence felt like you jumped right in the chaos whereas in BL1 you jumped off a bus.
The funny and comedic entries on just about every character makes the game all the more enjoyable.  While we all hate the main villain, Jack.  You can't help but laugh at just about everything he throws at you and the characters throughout the game.  They give an actual villain this time and not just some vault alien.  It really makes you feel motivated to progress the game's story.  You feel like 'this is personal' 'we must stop jack' ' stand against hyperion'.  There's a sense of satisfaction how the whole game plays out.
Taking it's place after BL1 I must admit though the weapons are pretty good they did make specific changes to each manufacturer (ex. Dahl : burst fire while zoomed etc).  While there aren't any real aggressive changes what bothers me the most are the loot drops/shops.  In the previous borderlands the chances of rare items was better and so was being able to buy them at a vendor.  Marcus now mostly sells white/green items which was a disappointing change from the previous game.
What I do miss about BL1 is that they didn't do so well in this one (imo) was the boss battles.  I wish BL2 including more boss fights throughout the game and to me they ran pretty scarce this time around.  To some, you guys/girls might agree that they are well placed and better scripted but it was one of the perks of BL1 I liked so much.
Slag, the new elemental dmg in the game is pretty lame and boring at times.  I don't like the switching between weapons so much.  Not that I'm lazy or anything but it does make combat more tedious unless your slag weapon could really deliver the pain to your enemies. Or if you feel the need to induce more damage.
Overall, I think BL2 brings back all the old stuff that was good from the original Borderlands and delivers it so much more better.  The interactions between the original 4 playable characters from BL1 definitely feel satisfying.  Combat system feels great and much more fluid than ever despite the menus not being my favorite thing in the game.  But I definitely recommend this game to anybody who might be interested.  That's coming from me who generally hates FPS-games but I suggest giving this one a go and maybe BL1 if you haven't already (for better backstory) given it a shot.
Overall 8/10.

+ Voice acting is mostly passable, with a few notable exceptions
+ Visuals, animations, and effects are decent for year of release, so it's hard to justify counting them against the game; they didn't necessarily age well, but certainly not to such a degree as to hold it back
+ Movement and platforming feels smooth and organic; this is particularly evident when 'force jumping'
+ Environmental puzzle elements are well-designed, and work well with the use of the player's core 'force abilities'
+ Dark side/ Light side orientation can be chosen, but isn't necessarily influenced by dialogue, as in many other titles
+ Audio design is ripped directly from the films, and does well to complement the final product
+ Melee and FPS transition works seamlessly; both are fun in their own right, and neither serves to detract from the game's enjoyment
+ Combat is both fun and engaging; this, clearly, was the primary focus of the developers, and the combat system is easily that which works best in the title
+ Secret areas are available, offering tangible rewards for one's mission
+ Controls are intuitive and adequately explained in the tutorial missions; however, there is seemingly no controller support to speak of
+ Plot is nothing sensational, but it measures up fairly well to the rest of the franchise, and doesn't divorce itself from the established nuances of the Star Wars universe
- Vehicle controls, notably turning, can prove a bit clunky in practice
- Enemy AI is positively atrocious

Great game, apart from the physics.
It's the game Freelancer could have become if Microsoft hadn't killed it. The artwork is impressive, the variety is good, and in general I liked it.
The only issue I have with the game, and this is a major issue for me, is the flight physics. It's a SPACE sim. That means that when I turn off my engine, I expect to keep going until I say otherwise. Not here. In this game, they've decided that space is really just air-based fighters where you can't fall down. Turn off the engine? Immediate stop. Try to coast so you can move in one direction but face another? Not possible - you only move forward. Freelancer had this right. These guys? Not at all.
I initially recommended the game, but find that I can't honestly do that. If you want a jet fighter game set in space then yes, I'd strongly recommend this game.  If you're expecting a SPACE game look somewhere else, as I'm doing.
I'm still searching for a game that was as elegant as Freelancer, with newtonian* physics, simplified flight systems (so Evochron Mercenary, with its ridiculously overcomplicated flight systems and 90's inspired console graphics doesn't really do it for me either), and a decent single-player campaign but sufficiently creative random campaigns to keep things interesting afterwords. Drop me a note if you have any suggestions.
======
* After reading several reviews, I see that "newtonian" needs to be defined. "Newtonian" physics is simple. It means that if I put my ship in motion on a specific vector, I will remain on that vector unless I do something to change it. Turning off the engines should NOT stop me cold in "space". I should just keep going until I do something to change my vector. That "something" includes turning on docking assist, braking thrusters, or what-have-you. I'll accept "slowing down slowly" (space dust, donchaknow) but not "stops as if stuck in mud". If I wanted to play "cars in thick mud" I'd play a land-based game.
Enjoyable game - worth a shot!

I recommend Star Wars Jedi Knight: Jedi Acadamy. The combat is usually fun and being a psycho lunatic laser sword butcher is fun. It's always fun enough to keep playing, but there are some things holding the game back. I have some big reservations about this game. The voice acting was really terrible. It's the kind you'd expect from a cheap cartoon for ten year olds. The same goes for the plot.  At one point it is revealed the recruit who was obviously going to turn on the jedi from the moment he was introduced at the beginning of the game has in fact turned on the jedi. In his defense, though, the dark side did have two hot dark jedi chicks that liked to party. The Jedi Academy run by Luke just had some old coots nagging you to keep a good attitude while you're doing their work. Being a Star Wars title there's plenty of jibber jabber about sides of the force. I don't really see how the jedi can claim to be so morally superior when they kill everyone that stands in the way of their goals. It's just because they're not♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off or scared when they're doing it that keeps them from turning to the dark side of the force? There are a good solid 18 levels or so and took around 12 hours to finish game. While they do a reasonably good job of mixing of the objectives and scenery of the varied locations. It all really boils down to fighting most enemies with guns or dark jedi with a light saber and doing a lot of often crazy platform jumping. Towards the end of the game I was getting so tired of fighting light saber duels. I just stopped fighting them whenever possible  and kept running ahead until they stopped chasing me. It was a largely successful strategy for speeding up the game. The light saber fighting is maybe about as good as one can realistically expect. There are a couple of types of slashes and the light saber can be thrown like a boomerang. The fights seemed like they just came down to spamming the button until enough hits connect. When winning a duel the game will go into slow motion and you can see a cool shot of the fatal blow and bodies do get sliced up.  The worst part about them is that it's expected to use force powers during duels and it can be hard trying to move my characater and hitting the function keys at the same time. The best part, hands down, is using the force push to throw enemies off of cliffs. Hilarious every time.  As the game progresses the main character is completing his jedi training and he becomes more powerful as the game procedes. By the time the game is ending your character can jump five stories high and the light saber is almost heat-seaking.  You can also choose optional force powers to upgrade at the end of each level. So there are some very minor RPG elements to the game.The music in the game is just classic Star Wars soundtrack and it still sounds fantastic. The boss fights are really tough and time consuming. They deliver big damage quickly and so most of the time I'd spending running around avoiding them while I recharge my health and then engage them again for a minor skirmish before I run away again to heal up. The game isn't overly difficult. I did save a lot, though. Jedi Acadamy is fun, it just lacks that certain something should have taken it to the next level.

This game. This game! This is how a shooter is supposed to be made. Engaging characters and story, excellent gun-fighting and gameplay, and a twist that made me sick with disgust at myself and Captain Walker. I loved it!
After the half-way point, things go to $#!t. A spiral of madness and death opens up that you walk to the end. Even the loading screens after Chapter 10 or so start to take the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you by passive-agressively insulting all you've done in the game when you're reloading after being killed. Plus, unlike most shooters, it has multiple endings depending on the choices you make!
This game is a must for fans of shooters, horror, and war games. At only $20, this game is a better deal than any CoD or Modern Warfare game out on the market. It has replay value, fun gameplay such as zip-lining, commanding your troops to snipe or bomb enemies, and interesting enviroment kills such as the standard "shooting fuel tanks to make them explode" but also a new "shoot out glass to drop sand and stun enemies." It has numerous weapons, and while ammo is sometimes hard to come across, the enemies drop weapons with each one you kill, so you can their bodies. You can only carry 2 guns at a time, but this doesn't take much away from the game, giving you incentive to try out the various firearms and find the ones you like best. My only real complaint gameplay wise is that the Sticky Grenade can be more trouble than it's worth, as it has a smaller explosion range and distance to be thrown than a Flash Bang or Frag, and no bounce. It is fun to stick them onto a foe and watch them flail around, though.
As for the characters, Spec Ops makes you sympathise with all of them. Even the villains have understandable motivations, and you wonder if you'd act any differently in this situation. Captain Walker, Lieutenant Adams, and Sergeant Lugo are people, with feelings and emotions that they display through both cutscenes and in-game banter. They are far superior to the burly, no-name, buzz-cut scrubs of the current FPS.
This game gripped me like no other. I got it (from a friend) on March 1st. It is now March 4th, and I have been playing almost non-stop to finish it. I had to see the ending. I had to experience what was the culmination of Captain Walker's actions and struggles. I had to. This game is the most engaging thing I've played all year, and I'd argue it is going to be an all-time favorite, right up there with the other games of my childhood I remember fondly.
With FPS's pedalling boring stories, gameplay and characters that are little more than cardboard cutouts, Spec Ops: The Line makes me hopeful for the future of gaming, and sick to my stomach for the in-game atrocities I witnessed and committed. You want a good game? Buy this one.
Without spoiling anything, Spec Ops: The Line seems like a mediocre shooter. Let me tell you though, it's anything but that.
