Review: Yooka Laylee seeks to be a spiritual successor to a series of games from the 1990's, specifically the Banjo Kazooie series. This series includes Banjo Kazooie, Banjo Tooie, and Grunty's Revenge. There are several other games in the series as well, but those games diverged from the formula and are not going to be discussed because they are so different and not what Yooka Laylee was seeking to recapture. The goal of these games is to explore silly cartoonish worlds and collect a lot of little widgets to earn new abilities, unlock new levels, or enable certain in-game changes. You do this by completing platforming challenges, mini games, exploration, and solving environmental based puzzles.
These sorts of games had slower game play than what is found in contemporary games. They really focused on exploration and environmental puzzle solving instead of action. Combat was never there as a major challenge or obstacle. Enemies simply served to spice things up, keep the landscape interesting, or to keep you moving forward. This is very important to understand. If you enjoy third person exploration that focuses more on platforming exploration and collecting things instead of action or combat you will likely enjoy this game. Otherwise, you will find this sort of game to be slow moving and uninteresting.
I cannot stress this enough. This game does not embrace contemporary sensibilities and never even tries to. Everything about this game is a love letter to the sort of 1990's/early 2000's platformers that defined an era. If you are looking for formula improvements, new game play mechanics, or an evolution of the genre you will not find it here. What you will find is a lovely game that feels exactly like a Banjo Kazooie title, whether you find that to be a good or bad thing in 2017. This game was pitched as a "1990's style platformer" which many seem to have taken to mean "an innovative new next-gen platformer that raised the bar and evolved the formula." If this is your expectation you will be sorely disappointed. This game was never intended to be that. It was intended to be another game extremely similar to the design sensibilities of the platformers of the 1990's. The game accomplishes this well. It really does feel like Banjo-Threeie, which is exactly what I wanted.  If it wasn't for the updated graphics and reskinning of the characters you wouldn't even know this wasn't a Banjo Kazooie game. If you did not want Banjo-Threeie as designed as a 1990's platformer, this game may not be for you.
With this though does come some issues. As a 1990's-styled platformer it inherits the strengths and weaknesses of these sorts of titles:
For one thing, you have to manually control the camera. Cameras in games have become so sophisticated these days that we often don't even recognize them any more. Not so for these retro games. In these games you have to manually swing the camera around and point it where you want to look. If you don't have experience with sort of thing there is a possibility that it can sour your experience by ruining your immersion. However, having grown up with manually controlled cameras, I am still enjoy it. If I were a young person now who had never experienced this sort of thing and only had experienced modern games, I may not be able to enjoy it. So let that serve as a warning. Many reviewers are reporting issues with the camera, however I have not really experienced any troubles with it at all. In fact, the reported issues are somewhat baffling to me. The camera controls quite well in my experience and I have only encountered two problem areas during my play time. Both of these areas were solved with a little bit of patience. But the vast majority of my play time has not been impacted by any negative camera performances. I can only report my experiences though. And in my experience the camera has had a 95% success rate of performance.
Others are also reporting frame rate lags and performance problems. Again, I have not experienced any of these at all except for one or two very small areas that have a lot of particle effects. I do not know if this is because of my PC or not. For the record, here are my PC's technical specifications:
Intel Cor i7-3630QM CPU @ 2.40 GHz
8 GB Ram
NVIDIA GeForce GTX 670MX
I do not know if the reported technical performances are happening on those with lower specifications or not, but for what its worth my game runs very smoothly on the specs above.
I think my biggest concern though is the size of the levels. They are huge. I mean HUGE. This can be a problem for people who don't really enjoy 1990's platformers or who have issues navigating large areas in a 3-D space without serious signposting and land marks. Personally, I have not encountered any problems winding my way through the levels or getting lost. But I will always prefer small, tighter, deeply-designed levels as opposed to huge sprawling ones that take a while to traverse. Also, these levels really need warp pads. Banjo Tooie had some levels that were even larger and more labrynthian than those found in Yooka Laylee (Grunty Industries was a nightmare), but the use of warp pads in that game made them much easier to digest and explore at your own pace. From where I stand there really is no excuse for the lack of warp pads, and I think the size of the levels would be more embraced by the community if warp pad functionality was added in by a content update.
Some of the Pagies (the primary collectible) are frustrating as hell to get, but considering that 31% of them are completely optional I don't really see what the problem is. You can just forget about it and obtain another one. However, for those who are compulsive completionists I can see it being maddening. I've never had the desire to 100% my video games so this really isn't a problem for me. But a word of warning to completionists: this game might drive you insane if you must 100% it. Many of the puzzles are cryptic and require abilities earned later in the game. Again, as I am not a completionist this doesn't bother me. I just move on and keep on having a grand old time.
Finally, you absolutely must use a PC controller to play this game. And I do not mean that is my opinion (which it is, btw, I couldn't even conceive of playing a game like this with a mouse and keyboard), but you literally cannot complete the game without a controller due a glitch (the "B" button does not work) and the lack of key binding options. Honestly, this error is inexcusable, but the developers have already stated they are working on a patch to fix the problem. I am not justifying it though, there really is no reason for this particular problem to exist. In my play through I am using an XBOX 360 controller via USB and I have not seen any problems.
The controls are tight and very responsive on the 360 controller. I have experienced no problems.
With all that said, I personally believe this is a very fun platformer that delivers everything that was promised. It fully embraces the design choices of 1990's/early 2000's platformers without feeling the need to redefine the formula or spice things up. If that is what you need to be satisfied with the game you will not find it here. However, if you are looking for Banjo-Threeie as it might have been designed in 2001 you will surely enjoy this game.
If I had to put a numerical rating on it I would do so as follows:
If you have experience with 1990's platformers and love them: 9/10
If you are a new-comer to the genre and did not play, or do not enjoy 1990's platformers: 7.5/10

These are somewhat uncommon and are usually short enough to not sour the overall experience, but the worst moments of the game feel incredibly amateurish and even embarrassing. The game's budget was likely never comparable to any of Rare's past work though, so I think it is unfair to judge them on the same exact merits. I will say I think the pacing is greatly improved over Banjo-Tooie and DK64 -- I personally strongly prefer Yooka-Laylee over those particular releases, too.

"On release players have access to the Intro Pack content - Prologue Mission, the Paris Sanguine Fashion Show, full access to Contracts Mode, Escalation Mode, elusive targets and other live content. Remaining content will be available as six releases periodically throughout 2016, starting April 2016".
Anyway, I've only managed to put about 5hrs or so into Hitman, what with the Division on XBONE and PC still taking the majoirty of my time. That said, I have rather enjoyed those 5 hours. The game runs well on my system (max settings on a 3.3ghz i5 and GTX 970).
The episodic release isn't a new concept, but is rather unique in its application to a Hitman game. If the game relied solely upon its main 'hit' and the prologue missions, even for £11 you'd be lucky to get a positive review. However, its the returning 'Contracts' mode from 'Absolution' that keeps me coming back. Not just playing the many varied contracts from the community, but scrouring the depths of the huge Paris fashion-show level for the most obscure targets and intricate ways in which to mark them for death is pure joy. If the future 'episodes' feature such rich in-depth locations (which I'm sure they will), I can see this game milking even more time out of my Division-based gaming scheduel.

I am absolutely loving this game. I can understand the negative reviews this game is getting, because I partially agree with the complaints, but we can't just judge this game based on content that's not even available. Let's talk about the elephant int he room first.
This game's release schedule is beyond stupid. They are releasing ONE level every month. That means this game currently has one actual level to play. That being said, the level is fantastic and easily one of the biggest and more complex levels available in the entire Hitman franchise so far. It's a huge french palace with 4 stories with every room being accessible either by doors or windows, making for an incredible sandbox that requires a lot of replay to really understand. There's tons of options to assassinate and neautralize the AI and it's a lot of fun to experiment with. I'm really looking forward to the rest of the levels they plan on releasing this year if this level is anything to go off of.
Next thing, the always online DRM. Now this IS TERRIBLE. I've had it happen twice now where the Hitman servers went offline, and the game gives you a warning message with no other option but to quit your current session and go back to the main menu. This is a single player only game... forcing me to go back to the main menu just because the game can no longer track my online stats is incredible annoying and a major flaw in this game's design. Hopefully IO Interactive changes this as soon as possible.
And finally, the last major issue with this game, optimization. This game runs decent enough to the point where it's playable, but there are some spots in the map where the framerate drops as low as 40fps, and I have a very high end machine (gtx 980ti, 16gb Ram, i5 3750k 3.4ghz processor). I originally thought it might be my processor bottleknecking my system, but I have had no issues like this with other games, and several players with lower end machines are reporting terrible framerates which are simply inexcusible. I think this game suffers from the same problem Fallout 4 has where it renders shadows the player can't even see on the other sides of buildings and drops your performance significantly. A higher end processor should, in theory, improve framerate significantly. But this could also be solved by simply optimizing the game so that unnecessary features aren't putting increased load onto the system when they're not even visible.
Edit: I can confirm that after upgrading my processor to an i7 6700k, that I have recieved at least 20fps more. However, after a more recent patch, performance has taken a nose dive, giving me performance I used to get with my old i5 3570k processor. IO Interactive really needs to get their crap together.
Ok, now that we talked about the 3 major gripes, let's talk about why I'm actually recommending this game. It's the perfect Hitman game. It keeps the great control scheme from Hitman Absolution (and the graphics) and blends it together with the open ended freedom of older Hitman games like Hitman Blood Money to make a virtual assassination sandbox that's a ton of fun to keep replaying and learning. Even the two tutorial levels featured before the main paris level are fun to play, with tons of options to try out for eliminating your target. For example, you can dress up as a mechanic, sabatage a military jet, and have your target test the ejector seat on the plane just to have him fly up through the cieling and kill himself. Or alternatively, you can sneak into his private quarters, drug his glass of vodka, and then wait for him to go the bathroom, and then drown him in the toilet bowl. The main mission in Paris is even larger with far more options. My favorite was trying to take out both targets undetected without ever changing my disguise. It took me a long time to figure out and it was really rewarding. I love how the game will reward you with new gear, new entry points, and new hidden caches to retrieve extra weapons/gear, making it perfect for setting up the perfect kill. I liked sneaking into the auction on the top floor dressed in a tux with no weapons, and retrieving my silenced pistol in the upstairs toilet and then overflowing the bathroom sink so that the target would investigate, and then shooting her right as she looked up from the sink at the mirror. The game feels like a true Hitman game and has really shown how much the series has grown and evolved.
So I highly recommend this game, however, if you don't like the idea of only getting one level to experience right now, I suggest waiting until the full experience is available this fall.

Before I say anything I will say there are some bugs. Nothing that has been game breaking for me but others will tell you that there are some nasty bugs and glitches.
They have done some 'tweeking' with Arkham Origins that has changed the timing of counters or critical hits. That will have you swinging at air a bit more than in AC. As far as the gadgets go it's pretty much a wash.  Except for the remote claw which is overpowered but still hilarious just to sling two foes into each other. As far as multiplayer goes I can't comment on that. I'm not a big fan of online multiplayer.
Overall, I like Origins a little bit more than City. Whether it's because it's newer and the graphics are nicer (that DX11 snow is wicked), the city seems more fleshed out and brighter, the story having more villains, less Nolan North or the fact that Batman isn't wearing his underwear on the outside (yet).
At the end of the day I would give this game a 8.5/10. Without really bringing anything completely new to the table I can't give it a much higher score. It's still definitely a must play for comic and Batman fans.

But I don't honestly feel like I can recommend it, especially not at a $20 asking price. The full release of Gang Beasts is quite clearly rushed. It's still extremely buggy

I Kickstarter backed this so be warned this cannot be an entirely unbiased review. I'm going to break it down by game elements in order from most important to least.
GAMEPLAY: Gameplay is more important than story because it's how the players interact with everything. Some games can have next to no story and still have engaging gameplay. See examples like LIMBO and INSIDE for example.
Unfortunately Yooka-Laylee gets a couple dings here for me. Not because of camera controls like everyone else seems to say. I found the camera worked just fine. No my big complaint if for some of the movement mechanics. Rolling as a ball, turning in Snowplow form, adjusting direction while flying... all just seemed to have this weird turning problem that felt unresponsive and I was fighting against each time.
That said, however, the rest of the controls were great. Tight, focused, responsive, and flowed quite fluidly. I never felt like the core controls were ever fighting me and every attack flowed strong and smooth. I do think the flying mechanic kinda breaks the challenge a lot of the worlds have, but considering it's the last move you get in the game I only think it's fair since it helps you explore and find everything you missed up until then.
CHARACTERS: There's not much to say about most of them here. Yooka comes off as a bit more intelligent than Banjo did, though Laylee is still the wisecracking smartmouth of the pair like Kazooie. The villains are about stock standard for a game like this with their own evil goals in mind. Although there are a couple twists right at the end I won't reveal. The supporting cast are all interesting. Trowzer was amusing, and I really liked Rextro 64 as a nice shout out to old-school games.
STORY: The plot was nice and simple. Villain wants all the worlds books but there's a deeper meaning behind it. Yooka and Laylees recently found book is stolen, turns out to be special, and they have to go and recover all the escape pages. It's a basic plot that never tries too hard to be complex or psyche you out. A classic simple setup straight from the Nintendo 64 era of games.
GRAPHICS/SETTING: The worlds that Yooka and Laylee visit are fairly stock standard on the surface. Jungle, ice world, swamp, casino, and outer space. However they're boosted by two important factors in my opinion. First, all of them are drop-dead gorgeous in look. Second, they are freaking HUGE. Even before expanding a world with more pages, some like the 'Cashino' (which incidentally is my personal favorite) are gigantic for this sort of game.  And all of them are well designed with few invisible walls and generally a large free roaming element to them.
SOUND/MUSIC: Yooka-Laylee earns a solitary ding here for a slight overuse of some sound effects in places. That 'iris out' slide whistle every time you go through a door can be a bit bothersome in some areas where you might hear it a four or five times a minute. That being said though the music in games words was beautiful and fit all wonderfully. Though I did feel the jungle stage a bit too reminiscent of the Banjo-Kazooie games.
Overall I found the game to be wonderful fun, but I would be remiss if I didn't close out with my biggest annoyances. And I have three (not counting the stuff mentioned above).
First (and least annoying) the worlds are so big that finding any singular small item you might have missed can be a reail pain. However this can be fixed if you but Vendi's tonic 'Hunter', which, even if you don't have a rumble function on a controller, will still give you a whistle when you get close. I wish I'd known about how it worked since I spent a good hour looking for the last couple quills in one world before I used it.
Second and more annoying, The final boss fight drags on way too long, and there's no indication on what to do most of the time. I do like that you're supposed to intuit a few things, but with so many moves you get through the game a clue on which ones to use at times would be nice. And a nice mid battle checkpoint would be wonderful so restarting the whole thing when you die doesn't make you want to chew on something hard.
Lastly, Rextros game on Gallion Galaxy. Most of Rextros minigames are alright if a little tricky but they aren't too hard to master. This one though is particularly annoying and took me a dozen attempts to get through. Not only do you have to keep tapping the jump button to fly, not only does every flap push you forward slowly so you constantly have to pull back to keep from getting too close to the edge of the screen, but ALSO one hit on anything and you drop something like half the quills you've collected. It made beating the high score an exercise in frustration that nearly had me chewing on my own tongue.
Still in a game as big as this those flaws are just a few dings on an overall amazing experience and I am so glad this game exists. Please if ou've taken the time to read all this, consider getting this game. Because it's something the games industry needs to see more of again.
TL;DR – A few minor problems here and there but overall a great game that's lots of fun.

Got to say this is a bit of a tough one, keep in mind that my feelings are heavily influenced by nostalgia for Kazooie and Tooie. In a lot of way this feels like a step back. It's still largely a good game, but it feels somewhat lacking. The worlds don't feel as fleshed out (or as large as Tooie), the 4th wall breaking isn't done very well, the innuendo that was subtle and cheeky in the Banjo games is very in your face here, the characters so far aren't nearly as amusing or memorable, the enemies aren't threatening in the slightest, the story isn't engaging, and some of the new stuff like the move salesman just being in one place per level isn't an improvement on how Tooie handled it. (It's very clear to me that many of the problems with nuts and bolts are not at all the fault of microsoft) All in all it feels a bit more like a Banjo rip off rather than Banjo's spirtual successor. Though keep in mind these are impressions after only 5 hours of play.

It's just like Banjo Kazooie. If you loved Banjo Kazooie, you'll love this. If you didn't, you probably won't. If you haven't tried any Banjo games, chances are you'll like it either way; I've not played Banjo games as much as some, and I love this game.
Edit: now that I've got a few more hours in the game, here are some updated thoughts.
You'll definitely love this game if you're a completionist. The collectibles are fun to find and often have enjoyable challenges behind them, not tedious and bothersome like some games can be with their collectibles.
The camera is mostly issue-free for me for all parts of the game except for the first boss. It changes position depending on if you're in a specific 2D-style platforming section or similar, which I don't have a problem with.
The first level is doubtlessly the best. It feels very Banjo-Kazooie-like. All the other levels are also great, though. I especially like the soundtrack of the second stage.
Speaking of the soundtrack, it's made by Grant Kirkhope. Of course it's good! Sound effects are also just what you'd expect from a Banjo game, goofy and lighthearted.
Graphics are usually great, especially for the characters. Some textures feel a bit low.
One complaint I do have is that the basic enemies of all the levels are weak and basically reskins of each other. Slightly smaller in size than Yooka, armed with a very basic AI. Banjo games were known for creative enemy designs, something this game doesn't have, outside of the googly eyes that possess objects they position themselves on. Bosses are enjoyable though, with the exception of the first.
There are glitches, but they are few and far in between.
It's not flawless, but it sets the bars high for future 3D platformers (and I really hope there will be future 3D platformers).

If you want a good old fashioned 3d platformer though, this is the real thing.

I've been following Yooka-Laylee ever since it was announced, and even before then, I followed the 'MingyJongo' Twitter account years before it went on to become Playtonic Games.
I backed the Kickstarter on day one, in hopes of a "clone" of Banjo-Kazooie that felt like a true spiritual successor, and that's definitely what I got.
----------------------------------------------
I'll start off by saying that the level design in the game is pretty good overall.  None of the worlds felt too big or too empty (With the exception of world 2 IMO), and there's a ton of stuff to do in each world of course.  I never felt like it was a chore to complete every challenge, find every collectible, and so on.  Additionally, the cast of characters in the game feels like they were taken right out of the Banjo universe, in a good way.
The game is also very visually appealing, and the soundtrack, with the combined talents of Grant Kirkhope, David Wise, and Steve Burke, is certainly a masterpiece.
----------------------------------------------
Now, the game isn't perfect.  There are a handful of camera issues, namely in areas with fixed camera angles.  Some of the dialogue is a bit mediocre as well honestly (Especially Yooka's), but it's not a big factor in my enjoyment of the game personally.
There are also some challenges/obstacles where it might be extremely unclear on how to solve them.  For example, there are glass blocks in the game that look exactly like ice, so you try and melt them, but it just doesn't work.
Those are pretty much the only complaints I have with the game, and they really didn't impact the game that much, at least for me.
----------------------------------------------
Overall, I'd say that if you're a fan of the Banjo-Kazooie series, you should really give Yooka-Laylee a try.

Unlike most of the reviewers complaining about performance I'm not trying to run the game on a potatoe and have not had any issues thus far. Also unlike most of those negative reviews complaining about the game being "unfinished" and "only one level", I actually read news about the episodic release structure months ago (before STEAM pre-orders went live). I also have functioning eye-sight allowing me to read the FIRST PARAGRAPH of the store page that states:
"On release players have access to the Intro Pack content - Prologue Mission, the Paris Sanguine Fashion Show, full access to Contracts Mode, Escalation Mode, elusive targets and other live content. Remaining content will be available as six releases periodically throughout 2016, starting April 2016".
Anyway, I've only managed to put about 5hrs or so into Hitman, what with the Division on XBONE and PC still taking the majoirty of my time. That said, I have rather enjoyed those 5 hours. The game runs well on my system (max settings on a 3.3ghz i5 and GTX 970).
The episodic release isn't a new concept, but is rather unique in its application to a Hitman game. If the game relied solely upon its main 'hit' and the prologue missions, even for £11 you'd be lucky to get a positive review. However, its the returning 'Contracts' mode from 'Absolution' that keeps me coming back. Not just playing the many varied contracts from the community, but scrouring the depths of the huge Paris fashion-show level for the most obscure targets and intricate ways in which to mark them for death is pure joy. If the future 'episodes' feature such rich in-depth locations (which I'm sure they will), I can see this game milking even more time out of my Division-based gaming scheduel.

Literally millions and millions and guns due to randomly generated modifiers that change each gun. Effects can go from simple aesthethic changes, to massive damage multipliers, or even mods that make the weapons useless. The random nature of the the guns is one of the strongest elements to the game. Moreover, the actual guns themselves are amazing. If you're new to Borderlands you'll quickly be attracted to the number and types of guns availible. Many claim that some weapon types are overpowered. This is simply not true. Any person could complete the whole game using any type of weapon they choose. One will not be forced to use assault rifles simply because assault rifles are "overpowered." Rather, one can use snipers, pistols, rocket launchers, a combination of several gun types, etc. The choice is up to you. Whats more fun is that the guns you obtain from the game can be wacky, over the top, or simply cool to look at. Many joke weapons exist throughout the game that are compltely useless but I still find myself amused when I obtain such weapons. The actual usable weapons you obtain are equally fun to obtain. Its good to know that there are countless weapons, shields, grenades, class mods, etc. that are very rare.  Obtaining any type of rare weapon and realizing that it kicks♥♥♥♥♥when you use it for the first time simply is a fantastic feeling. I often found myself researching rare items up in wikis and trying to find how I could obtain them myself. Sometimes, I had to farm enemies for hours on end simply to try to obtain rare loot. This will be one of the only games that I would willingly do this kind of thing in. In my opinion however, this happens to be one of the biggest weaknesses of the game.  Drop percentages for some loot are ridiculously low and I didnt even bother trying to obtain some items simply due to the amount of effort and time I would potentially have to put in to obtain what I wanted. However, if I did go on one of these ventures and managed to obtain something I wanted, it truly would be worth it and any potential regrets I had about the time I "wasted" would be washed away.
Gameplay
The gameplay is amazing. The numerous amounts of enemies you face and the techniques you need to use to fight them can seem overwheleming at first. But after a few hours of gameplay you realize that there really is no technqiue to fighting enemies. Just kill them, no matter what the means. whether this means bum rushing the enemies with your bullet-sponge build character, or sending in reinforcements to do the work for you, Many will be surprised that the replay ability for this game is very strong even though you are simply playing the same story over and over again. This is due to the fact that it takes 3 playthorughs to get your character to full level (excluding DLCs). Each playthrough gets exponetially harder, but you will have learned how to kill effiecientally and quickly by this time. Plus, you'll get way better loot. It may not sound fun on paper, but trust me you will be intrigued to play it over again. In addition to better loot and enemies, the player will be able to level up more in these extra playthroughs. Leveling up allows you to pick abilites that your character can do. Essentially, each character has three skill trees, and starting from level 5, one point can be put into any skill tree of your choice. This allows you to create a character with any mix of skills you want. Make your own build and see if it works for you. If it doesnt simply pay some petty in-game money and re-spec your skills however many times you want. What makes this special is that you can tweak you skill trees prior to any boss fights or dungeons you enter, and simply change it back afterwards. And with the the dlcs that add 20 level, along with class mods that give you even more abilities, you can create a very powerful character. Whenever an enemy is hit with your weapon, a damage number is displayed (even for every bullet that hits them), Its fun to see this number rise from the 10s when you just begin to millions when your full level, The world of Pandora is truly amazing and open world. There are many secrets and easter eggs to be found at your own pace, or not all if you never happen to learn about them. Many of the most memorable side quests are found in unusual places, which serves as an incentive to explore. Moreover, loot and loot chests are scatters everywhere. The world is truly massive every bit of it has something unique and interesting to it.
Story
The story is kind of cliche to be honest. However, what makes it special is the atmosphere and mood that any typical Borderlands game creates. At the beginning, you see that your just a person stuck in a world filled with crazies and psychos. But sooner than later you'll realize that you're not any more sane than the people your killing. The dialogue, the unique quests  and the integration of the characters from the first game make the game's story enjoyable. Handsome Jack, is beautifully voiced and played. The characters you meet each have soemthing unique about them and force you not to forhet them. Many consider him one of the best video game villians, and rightfully so. Side quests and main quests are rarely the generic, cookie cutter ones you see from most video games, and this makes you compelled to do as many sidequests as you can. On any repeat playthorughs, the story might become boring, as with any game, but the improved loot and weapons keep players wanting to play more and more, so this con should not be an issue.
Verdict: Meh, it was ok

I am absolutely loving this game. I can understand the negative reviews this game is getting, because I partially agree with the complaints, but we can't just judge this game based on content that's not even available. Let's talk about the elephant int he room first.
This game's release schedule is beyond stupid. They are releasing ONE level every month. That means this game currently has one actual level to play. That being said, the level is fantastic and easily one of the biggest and more complex levels available in the entire Hitman franchise so far. It's a huge french palace with 4 stories with every room being accessible either by doors or windows, making for an incredible sandbox that requires a lot of replay to really understand. There's tons of options to assassinate and neautralize the AI and it's a lot of fun to experiment with. I'm really looking forward to the rest of the levels they plan on releasing this year if this level is anything to go off of.
Next thing, the always online DRM. Now this IS TERRIBLE. I've had it happen twice now where the Hitman servers went offline, and the game gives you a warning message with no other option but to quit your current session and go back to the main menu. This is a single player only game... forcing me to go back to the main menu just because the game can no longer track my online stats is incredible annoying and a major flaw in this game's design. Hopefully IO Interactive changes this as soon as possible.
And finally, the last major issue with this game, optimization. This game runs decent enough to the point where it's playable, but there are some spots in the map where the framerate drops as low as 40fps, and I have a very high end machine (gtx 980ti, 16gb Ram, i5 3750k 3.4ghz processor). I originally thought it might be my processor bottleknecking my system, but I have had no issues like this with other games, and several players with lower end machines are reporting terrible framerates which are simply inexcusible. I think this game suffers from the same problem Fallout 4 has where it renders shadows the player can't even see on the other sides of buildings and drops your performance significantly. A higher end processor should, in theory, improve framerate significantly. But this could also be solved by simply optimizing the game so that unnecessary features aren't putting increased load onto the system when they're not even visible.
Edit: I can confirm that after upgrading my processor to an i7 6700k, that I have recieved at least 20fps more. However, after a more recent patch, performance has taken a nose dive, giving me performance I used to get with my old i5 3570k processor. IO Interactive really needs to get their crap together.
Ok, now that we talked about the 3 major gripes, let's talk about why I'm actually recommending this game. It's the perfect Hitman game. It keeps the great control scheme from Hitman Absolution (and the graphics) and blends it together with the open ended freedom of older Hitman games like Hitman Blood Money to make a virtual assassination sandbox that's a ton of fun to keep replaying and learning. Even the two tutorial levels featured before the main paris level are fun to play, with tons of options to try out for eliminating your target. For example, you can dress up as a mechanic, sabatage a military jet, and have your target test the ejector seat on the plane just to have him fly up through the cieling and kill himself. Or alternatively, you can sneak into his private quarters, drug his glass of vodka, and then wait for him to go the bathroom, and then drown him in the toilet bowl. The main mission in Paris is even larger with far more options. My favorite was trying to take out both targets undetected without ever changing my disguise. It took me a long time to figure out and it was really rewarding. I love how the game will reward you with new gear, new entry points, and new hidden caches to retrieve extra weapons/gear, making it perfect for setting up the perfect kill. I liked sneaking into the auction on the top floor dressed in a tux with no weapons, and retrieving my silenced pistol in the upstairs toilet and then overflowing the bathroom sink so that the target would investigate, and then shooting her right as she looked up from the sink at the mirror. The game feels like a true Hitman game and has really shown how much the series has grown and evolved.
So I highly recommend this game, however, if you don't like the idea of only getting one level to experience right now, I suggest waiting until the full experience is available this fall.

Martin Walker, Delta Force Operative send to Dubai after natural disaster, right after loosing contact with 33rd Battalion, which was sent there first. With two other operatives, your mission is to find any survivours in Dubai. That's the story outline. The game itself isn't thats special - it's a typical TPS - with cover system, a bit of tactics, bunch of weapons, and thats it. What makes it special is story - this is one of the few games that don't show the player that you are Good Guy and kill Bad Guys to save Poor Guys. Here is diffrent - and thats a big plus. True face of War isn't the one shown by CoD or other Battlefield. War is a big human tragedy - and that is what the game shows. To add more, player actions DO matter - and it isn't always clearly shown where you can decide, which allows you to play it as you would in case that happens. Recomened mostly for players, who pay antention to the story.

A truly fantastic open world 3rd person action game revolving around Max and his quest to get his car back and take down the guy who took it from him.  The story is OK, not brilliant but it is fun.
The setting for this game is what makes the game great, the world feels alive yet desolate and sticks to the Mad Max film formula really well.  It is beautiful to look at and visually stunning in certain lights and times for example when a storm is rolling in.
The main bulk of the gameplay is mission objectives, drive to certain place, take out enemies and return however on the way you will need to perform some optional side quests to gain scrap which allows you upgrade your cars and Max. Without these upgrades you will not survive in the harder areas of the world.  Side quests range from racing from point to point, locating scrap, doing missions, destroying fortifications and taking down bandit camps.
The upgrade system is really good and if you complete a decent amount of side quests allows you to upgrade nearly everything in a single playthrough.  Car upgrades are the usual attack and defense stats as well as performance.  There are a decent selection of cars to drive and all accessible once you have unlocked the upgrades/car bodies.  Max upgrades are similar, you can upgrade his health, combat and weapon stats.
The combat is really well done and although its similar to the recent Batman games you do have to at least point Max in the direction you want to punch, the combat feels punishing though and his punches always look to be doing damage which really adds to the gameplay.
The only real negative i can give this game is there isnt much variation in the side quests and in general its a bit grindy, especially once you have got towards the end however dont let this put you off a really excellent game.
Steam Controller support is a little terrible to be honest, apparently when the game first launched it worked fine with Mouse/Gamepad input but an update was put out which broke that.
As such you can either setup the controller for Keyboard/Mouse input and tackle the on screen prompts being incorrect or go full gamepad and deal with Mouse-Like Joystick or Joystick Camera.
In reality its not a twitch based shooter so having the slower reacting trackpad wasn't much of a hindrance once I got used to it.
Game works fine over the Steam Link with no noticeable drops in performance although i only played a few hours like that.

I've been following Yooka-Laylee ever since it was announced, and even before then, I followed the 'MingyJongo' Twitter account years before it went on to become Playtonic Games.
I backed the Kickstarter on day one, in hopes of a "clone" of Banjo-Kazooie that felt like a true spiritual successor, and that's definitely what I got.
----------------------------------------------
I'll start off by saying that the level design in the game is pretty good overall.  None of the worlds felt too big or too empty (With the exception of world 2 IMO), and there's a ton of stuff to do in each world of course.  I never felt like it was a chore to complete every challenge, find every collectible, and so on.  Additionally, the cast of characters in the game feels like they were taken right out of the Banjo universe, in a good way.
The game is also very visually appealing, and the soundtrack, with the combined talents of Grant Kirkhope, David Wise, and Steve Burke, is certainly a masterpiece.
----------------------------------------------
Now, the game isn't perfect.  There are a handful of camera issues, namely in areas with fixed camera angles.  Some of the dialogue is a bit mediocre as well honestly (Especially Yooka's), but it's not a big factor in my enjoyment of the game personally.
There are also some challenges/obstacles where it might be extremely unclear on how to solve them.  For example, there are glass blocks in the game that look exactly like ice, so you try and melt them, but it just doesn't work.
Those are pretty much the only complaints I have with the game, and they really didn't impact the game that much, at least for me.
----------------------------------------------
Overall, I'd say that if you're a fan of the Banjo-Kazooie series, you should really give Yooka-Laylee a try.

A new game in the vein of Banjo-Kazooie, by the original creators! Surely this can't go wrong, right?
Well, it did go wrong. It's not a complete disaster, but in the time since the N64 I guess they lost a bit of their old magic.
Now, I bet some people will immediately complain that the game "shouldn't be compared to Banjo-Kazooie", but since the Yooka-Laylee Kickstarter's entire point was to make a new game for fans of the Banjo games I feel it's more than fair to compare them.
Overall the game's pretty similar in structure to both N64 Banjo games. Collect pages called "Pagies" (jiggies), use them to open a new world and collect more pages, as well as quills (music notes) and new moves that allow you to get further through the main hub world and reach new world entrances.
I think most people will agree that Banjo-Tooie (as well as Donkey Kong 64) suffered from too much bloat, every level was a confusing mess with a billion collectibles and it took an eternity to get anywhere and do anything.
The levels in Yooka-Laylee aren't quite as big and confusing as those, but I don't think they're anywhere close to as tightly designed as Banjo-Kazooie's either. When you first enter each world they're arguably just the right size, but you can then spend some of your pages to "expand" the world and make it even bigger, which makes them about twice as large and lets you access double the amount of collectibles.
If you ask me it would've been much better if every world stayed its original size and they simply added some additional worlds for more variety. Yooka-Laylee only has five worlds total, and none of them are particularly special, which is quite a big problem considering how long you'll be spending in each one.
That's the main gist of the game, but I have many more issues with it which I'll just make a list of (And yes, a lot of these are comparisons to Banjo-Kazooie):
-The hub world, even though it's not as big as Grunty's Lair, is a confusing mess and there's several points where it's really unclear where you should go next.
-A disappointing soundtrack. I don't know what happened, but it seemed like Grant Kirkhope just tried to imitate his old work without actually trying to make the music memorable, just kind of loud and "epic". I played the game for 15 hours and I honestly don't remember a single one of his tracks. The few songs David Wise did are excellent though, as expected.
-The camera can be terrible sometimes. If you're airborne and trying to get out of a place with a fixed camera, good luck once you hit the edge and it keeps switching back and forth. It also gets stuck on geometry a lot.
-Controls during certain moves and transformations, in particular flight and the world 2 transformation, are incredibly imprecise and annoying. It's particularly bad when you happen to fly into an invisible wall or ceiling and start flying backwards.
-Wonky hit detection every now and then. It can also be really hard to tell when certain enemies are vulnerable and when they're not.
-Tons and tons of places where you can get stuck or clip through the level geometry. I actually usually kinda like this kind of stuff in games because it makes for interesting speedruns, but there's way, way too many in this game which just makes it look incredibly unpolished.
-Too many places where you can use tiny ledges, edges of rocks and the like to get up to places you shouldn't and trivialize any challenge.
-You gain the ability to fly (ANYWHERE, unlike Banjo-Kazooie) halfway through the game which takes away any remaining challenge.
-Moving into an invisible wall or ceiling won't simply prevent you from advancing, it'll also awkwardly launch you into a random direction which looks incredibly janky.
-The stamina bar serves as nothing more than an annoyance and should've been removed.
-Transformations are for the most part useful for getting two or three pages and then completely irrelevant. This was a problem in Banjo as well, but they didn't really do anything about it.
-Every world has an arcade game you have to play to earn a page. All of them are incredibly boring, and the game makes you play every one of them twice. Also, they don't even look like arcade games, they have the exact same graphics as the rest of the game.
-Puzzle solutions are sometimes very counterintuitive. There's a shout attack you learn which the game says is so loud it "shatters glass", but it only breaks a very small amount of very specific glass panels. Likewise, there's a bunch of ice cubes you'd THINK would be meltable with fire attacks, but they actually have to be broken with the aforementioned shout attack and THEN molten down.
-Another example of the above, you gain an ability that lets you absorb fire and other things to alter Yooka's body and give him some extra attributes. Why can you only absorb fire from very specific braziers and not the dozens of torches hanging on the walls?
-Another one, if you enter world 2 before expanding it (which you probably will) you'll find two big locks with a keyhole on them. Now, where could that key be hidden? The answer is that it's not hidden anywhere, you literally can't find it unless you exit the world and expand it. A better idea would've been to not even have those locks/doorways until the expansion.
-World 2's isometric area. You'll know why.
-Lack of enemy variety. There's about 3 types of enemies and they're all incredibly basic.
-The quiz shows are absurdly easy and straightforward, and all of them are multiple choice questions. B-K had a gigantic quiz show/board game near the end with all sorts of different question types and gameplay challenges, so this is very disappointing.
-Banjo (the character) was always pretty generic and I guess Yooka kinda takes after him, but Laylee isn't anywhere near as funny as Kazooie.
-Completely unmemorable villains, they're not interesting, intimidating or funny. I didn't so much as chuckle at any of their dialogue, they're just sorta there.
-Complete letdown of a final boss.
-Actually, most bosses are pretty disappointing and/or annoying.
-No extended ending or for getting 100% which means there's literally no incentive to collect everything besides achievements.
-No unlockable fun cheats to mess around with. Tonics (which slightly boost some of your attributes) are a neat idea but aren't very useful.
-Every world has a secret item to find, but they don't actually do anything except unlock achievements.
-There's far more pages and quills than are required to access/unlock everything. There should've been SOMETHING to use these on.
That said, there are a handful of things I do like which helped redeem the game somewhat:
-Quills stay collected when you exit the level or die, unlike the notes in Banjo-Kazooie, so you don't have to get all of them in one visit/life.
-A few interesting/funny side characters in specific worlds.
-The mine cart minigames are challenging and fun, though some of them move a bit too fast.
-World 4 as a whole has an interesting gimmick which I quite enjoyed.
-While most bosses were a letdown, the world 4 boss is pretty cool and easily my favourite. Just another reason world 4 is good.
-Some of the transformations are pretty fun, as limited in use as they are. It's mostly the later ones though, because the first two in particular are terrible.
-David Wise. Should've let him do the whole OST.
Overall, I did enjoy the game a bit, but the entire time I was pretty much thinking how I'd rather be playing Banjo-Kazooie instead. I do hope they make a sequel, but they'd need to change a lot of things to improve the experience.

Don't let my time played fool you, I bought this game when it came out before I ever owned steam and this might be my 4th reply.
So, if we're all serious here. Max Payne is a pretty silly name and makes me think of a comedic, bad video game that tries to be super macho but this game is not that. It has cutscenes told as a comic strip and the story grips you from almost the moment you begin. Let me tell you why this game is so darn good. And why it has dated oh so well.
Max Payne, I don't know where to start, I love this trilogy so much (Even though I love two first games much more)
Max Payne centers around...well..Max freaking Payne, a tragic character who's family has been murdered in cold blood. Max decides to go for a revenge, and one good revenge at that.
Sounds cliche? Well, things are not as they might seem, the game knows it, heck, Max knows it, the game is self-aware while still taking itself seriously, this strange blend of humor and drama makes the game date better. Max himself is a very likeable chap, you'll hear his voice a lot, and he monologues quite often.
This helps the player to understand Payne more, his personality, his feeling at that very moment. He tends to speak in a very monotone voice.
Story is being told through gameplay, comic artworks and cut-scenes, cut-scenes are not used very often, they don't tell the story most of the time actually, they're there only to show you the place and some enemies coming to get you. The game rarely takes the controls away from you.
You get to also play Max's nightmares, and nightmares they are indeed, they are most likely one of the creepiest levels you encounter in non-horror game. And yes, this indeed is quite genius. This makes us think about Max more, trying to make up our thoughts about the visuals before us.
Game has amazing voice acting, every character is voiced perfectly, the only problem some people might have is strange acting which can be seen in comics. They look silly most of the time; Sam Lake really knows how to make the weirdest faces. But then again it is most likely intentional, I wouldn't be surprised, the game really doesn't take itself too seriously, well, it does, but at the same time it laughs at itself, at its cliches etc. Not to mention Max's model has this smirk throughout the whole game, Max is most likely thinking like this:
He knows how his quest silly sounds, he knows how cliche it sounds, he knows his quest is impossible, that self awareness is what makes the game date oh-so well.
Soundtrack is top-notch as well; the main theme is truly heaven to ears as it pretty much presents Max Payne's personality.
Gameplay is extremely fun and addicting, the main mechanics this game explores are bullet time and shoot dodge. They work well and smoothly, you will not find a franchise which does this better. Even Matrix games got it wrong. The game IS challenging when you start, you'll need to learn how to use these mechanics to your own good.
Spamming shoot dodge won't get you anywhere; you can't spam it, if your bullet time runs out Max cannot use it anymore. So you better thing before using it.
Max Payne can heal himself using painkillers; he can have up to eight painkillers which he can use whenever he wants. They encourage the player to explore for them.
Game has 3 difficulties, only one being avaible at the beginning, that being the easiest one, which is still not quite easy. Luckily the game has quick saves, if that's too "cheap" for you then play on the hardest difficulty which limits your saves. Even with quick save though the game is no cake walk, game will spam a lot of enemies at you, but the game is fair, it is not unfair.
Level design offers the player to explore a lot of areas, there are many weapons painkillers to be found which make Max's journey through madness much easier.
The game never feels repetive, even though you do just shoot guys in the face, it's most likely the levels, they're done so well.
At the end, Max Payne not only has dated well, but feels quite refreshing, this is no cover shooter, it's quite the opposite, this is not about hiding, this is about going into the open, shooting everyone up, quick thinking.
The game can be completed around ten hours, depends on your skill level. But the fun doesn't have to stop there, there is a "New York Minute" mode for the speed runners who wish to run through the game as quickly as possible, it has a timer on every level, you score more and more time the more enemies you kill. The mod community offers quite a lot of content to enjoy, complete game changers, minor changes. And it's really easy to install them.
Guys at Remedy, I love you.
Thank you.

Starpoint Gemini 2 is to space exploration games what Skyrim is to fantasy adventure games. Vast, full of lore and play styles and activities for everyone, and just so beautiful to stroll through and appreciate the scenery. The long list of buttons and actions appear daunting at first, but are easy to learn and facilitate a rich level of interactivity that makes an enjoyable experience for both the casual gamer and the hardcore strategist. Stats, activities and tricks offer a healthy challenge for micromanagement fiends, and movement and combat are simple yet satisfying enough for someone who has an actual job and no time to micromanage in a virtual world. Also like in Skyrim, the voice acting is endearing and the accents are so thick you could cut through them with a knife. It's not often I play a game with just the right balance of exploration, story, environment, gameplay and general polish that I don't mind playing all day on a day off. Also like with Skyrim, STEAM WORKSHOP! Can't wait to find some funny mods in the future. Little Green Men Games nailed it. 10/10, would buy for the wife and kids.

I'm 60+ hours into the game as I write this review. I have to say that I haven't played space sims for a while but do have fond memories of Freespace 2, Wing Commander, Privateer, Freelancer and Darkstar 1. The good news is that SG2 has some interesting elements. Could it be better? Sure, but let's get to the nitty-gritty. There are 3 things I'll comment on: RPG elements, SIM elements, and GAMEPLAY elements.
RPG:
·	Not great -- voice acting is poor, and I don't really care much about the storylines (I have Origins, Aethera and Titans DLCs), which I feel could be better or more compelling.
·	Not enough random events by NPCs, etc. The universe is constantly changing economically, politically but it doesn't feel ALIVE. The characters seem dead.
·	There is a points/perk system where you can improve your character but that's about it.
·	You get some credits and blueprints for completing campaign missions (no medals or other perks). The blueprint reward system is interesting but really tough to complete a whole set, so what's the point, really?
·	The NPCs you deal with are flat and uninteresting. Oh and the voice acting sucks. Or did I mention that already?
SIM:
·	This is supposed to be a space sim, but many controls are lacking. e.g. You can't coordinate attacks with wingmen or give them specific orders.
·	Other sims even let you contact NPCs/wingmen over comms; not here.
·	Combat is simplified -- which may or may not be a good thing. i.e. You have an auto-fire button for your light weapons, and a key for your heavy weapon. You have to be facing your opponent appropriately before other non-frontal weapons will fire. Sometimes the AI fires at other targets even when you're locked on the nearest one.
·	There doesn't seem to be full support for my Thrustmaster -- I can't map the buttons, nor does it allow me to use a Joystick / keyboard combo. There is a turret cam view that can be useful, but without my joystick, it's pretty pointless.
GAMEPLAY:
·	Pretty graphics
·	Fun sandbox (free play) mode. I actually spent more time here than on the campaigns.
·	These are cool: Space stations, T-gates, T-drive travel, worm hole travel, boarding ships,
officers and mercs you can hire
·	Lots to explore
·	Faction/reputation tracking system
·	Very useful star map with overlays and filters
·	Game seems skewed towards battle; i.e. hard to get rich through the economic model
Overall:
The game world is pretty. While the devs try to create a decent economic model, I'm not quite sure it succeeds. You can't really make much cash that way. The quickest way is to board and capture ships with your troopers, then sell the vessel, or through bounty-hunting. This skews the game towards a combat model -- not complaining, mind you, but if you want to have a robust economic model, well, then make it workable. Players should be able to make MORE money through mining, gas clouds, and trading. There's a fair bit of grinding involved if you want to play a merchant. This is a shame because there is an excellent transport infrastructure -- i.e. you can travel vast distances using T-gates, rifts, worm holes, etc.
I like the fact that there's sandbox mode and campaign mode. Having hangars and your own fighters/bombers is a nice touch; and being able to beam your troopers to enemy vessels to try capturing them is fun.
All in all, SG2 is an entertaining and pretty game, but it falls short of being great -- more RPG elements would help, and of course, proper joystick support... and yeah, the voice acting sucks! I would recommend getting it only if it's on sale.

Batman. The one comic book hero almost any comic book fan will like.
The Arkham series, heavily based on the Bruce Timm DC Universe, has been one of the best series of comic book hero games to date. With great fighting mechanics, tons of lore and back story and of course, you get to play as the God Damned Batman. What more could you want?
So where does Arkham Origins fit in with the others? In m opinion it is a solid entry into the franchis and WB Montreal did a decent job. I would give it a 8/10.
Apart from some bugs, only a few that everyone experienced, the game itself was just as good as Arkham City. It ties in with the other two and exposes you to events that start the cascade of Arkham Asylum and ultimately what happens in Arkham City. It introduces some new villians and uses some older ones while tying the story together in a neat christmas package.
The graphics are about the same as Arkham City except there were no performance issues to start.
The voice actors are great and do a good job of portraying a younger Batman and Joker, although I still prefer Kevin Conroy and Mark Hamill as they have defined those two for almost 20 years.
The gameplay is as good as Arkham City, better than Arkham Asylum but the thugs are not as scared so they will react faster. This means you have to watch and react faster to counters and especially the harder enemies.
The story over all is a good story to tie in with the Arkham Universe. It shows how all the madness begins while also filling you in on more back story of the characters.
Overall, it is a good game. I found it worth the $50 dollars but I am also a big DC fan so those that are not as big of DC fans might want to get it on sale, but either way it needs to be played.

My short version of the review is that Arkham Origins is everything we loved about Arkham City but refined. The core gameplay is still there but they added more great features to it. There is a whole new story and it's just as strong as the last 2 games and for a prequel there are some big bold twists and shocking moments that explain characters in the other games better. In 15 hours, I didn't even see any serious glitches, just small stuff like a beaten thug floating up a wall once. I can't fathom how so many critics gave it a 6/10 for being everything you could want from a prequel and on the Akrham City engine.

As a die-hard fan of the series, and the characters at play, this game was a delight. It doesn't quite surpass the progression and expansion of the series as Arkham City did, but it'll deliver enough to keep you gleeful while living out your Batman fantasies...or just wait for the original developer RockSteady to do it better in 2014-2015.

If you are more than just a fan of Batman or absolutely loved the past two Arkham titles, this is a must get, but if not, it's just more of the same with less polish as Warner Brothers continue to try to milk the IP for profits but falls short of the previous two titles.
Not as good as Batman Arkham Asylum and City, probably because it wasn't made by Rocksteady, but it's still a decent game to play. Now, bring on Arkham City sequel!

The inspiring story of a Vietnam Veteran diagnosed with terminal liver cancer who goes on a mission to experience the world for himself. Seeking a purpose to life, he becomes an illegal street racer and drug dealer. The tale progresses along the game and reaches emotional heights that are unreal for a videogame. I found myself in a rollercoaster of feelings, personally relating to all the characters depicted with so many layers of depth and elaboration. With a moving story and fast-paced, dynamic, demanding and high intensity gameplay, this masterpiece of a game has stunning visuals, a wonderfully realized soundtrack that instills heartbreak and brings tears to my eyes, yet at times shows a ray of hope and joy, and finally, presents gameplay so innovative and original, I would say it beats the creativity of most big studios like Nintendo. Buy this game. It is the cheapest, and best value triple A title out there, and possibly the best game of all time.

ADOLF HITLER: EARLY YEARS, 1889–1913

How to cite this article
Baptized a Catholic, Adolf Hitler (1889–1945) was born on April 20, 1889, in the Upper Austrian border town Braunau am Inn, located approximately 65 miles east of Munich and nearly 30 miles north of Salzburg.
His father, Alois Hitler (1837–1903), was a mid-level customs official. Born out of wedlock to Maria Anna Schickelgruber in 1837, Alois Schickelgruber changed his name in 1876 to Hitler, the Christian name of the man who married his mother five years after his birth. Alois Hitler's illegitimacy would cause speculation as early as the 1920s—and still present in popular culture today—that Hitler's grandfather was Jewish. Credible evidence to support the notion of Hitler's Jewish descent has never turned up. The two most likely candidates to have been Hitler's grandfather are the man who married his grandmother and that man's brother.
LINZ

In 1898, the Hitler family moved to Linz, the capital of Upper Austria. Seeking a career in the visual arts, Hitler fought bitterly with his father, who wanted him to enter the Habsburg civil service. After his father's death, Hitler eventually persuaded his mother, Klara Hitler, née Pölzl, to permit him to pursue his dream to become an artist. As she lay dying of breast cancer in the autumn of 1907, Hitler took the entrance exam to the Vienna Academy of the Arts and failed to gain acceptance. In early 1908, some weeks after Klara's death in December 1907, Hitler moved to Vienna, ostensibly in the hope of renewing efforts to win acceptance in the Academy of Arts.
VIENNA

Hitler lived in Vienna between February 1908 and May 1913. He had grown up in a middle-class family, with relatively few contacts with Jewish people, in a region of the Habsburg state in which many German nationalists had been disappointed that the German Empire founded in 1871 had not included the German-speaking regions of the Habsburg Monarchy. Yet the legacy of the Vienna years is not as clear as Hitler depicted it in his political autobiography. His impoverishment and residence in homeless shelters began only a year after his arrival and after he had frittered away a generous inheritance left by his parents and rejected all arguments of surviving relatives and family friends that he embark upon a career in the civil service.
By the end of 1909, Hitler knew real poverty as his sources of income dried up. That winter, however, helped briefly by a last gift from his aunt, he began to paint watercolor scenes of Vienna for a business partner and made enough to live on until he departed for Munich in 1913. It is likely that Hitler experienced and possible that he shared the general antisemitism common among middle-class German nationalists. Nevertheless, he had personal and business relationships with Jews in Vienna and was, at times, dependent in part on Jews for his living. This may have been a cause for discretion about his actual feelings about Jews. It was not until after World War I that Hitler can be demonstrated to have adopted an “antisemitic” ideology.
INFLUENCES UPON HITLER IN VIENNA

Hitler was genuinely influenced in Vienna by two political movements. The first was the German racist nationalism propagated by the Upper Austrian Pan-German politician Georg von Schönerer. The second key influence was that of Karl Lueger, Mayor of Vienna from 1897 to his death in 1910.
Still in power when Hitler arrived in Vienna, Lueger promoted an antisemitism that was more practical and organizational than ideological. Nevertheless, it reinforced anti-Jewish stereotypes and cast Jews as enemies of the German middle and lower classes. Finally, unlike Schönerer, who was always more comfortable with the elitist nationalism of the student fraternities, Lueger was comfortable with big city crowds and knew how to channel their protest into political gain. Hitler drew his ideology in large part from Schönerer, but his strategy and tactics from Lueger.

Garfield Kart is a racing game developed by Gravity Europe releasing on PC in November 2013. The game has also been released on Nintendo 3DS previously as well.
We have all come to know what to expect from kart racing games from the likes of Mario Kart in the past. Most kart games that have come out to try and rival Mario Kart have often fallen flat on their face. Prior to playing Garfield, I had played another kart racing game on Steam, Coffin Dodgers and sadly that didn’t live up to the mark. Garfield Kart is almost an identical game to that of Coffin Dodgers.
Gameplay is going to be simple when it comes to kart racing, simply beat your opponents in the race around a circuit. There are 16 different courses to race around with 8 different powerups to collect around the circuits too. The game’s tutorial is back to front when it comes to explaining the controls; whether they did it with a different controller in mind I am not sure, but the controls on an Xbox controller were the complete opposite to shown on the screen. Garfield Kart has three different game modes to play, Grand Prix, Single Race and Time Trial. Grand Prix is the more structured part of the game, where you take part in 4 or 5 races at a time in a league, depending on where you finish in the races will determine how many points you get. Single Race is more like the “free mode”, whilst you can gain money from competing in races here; there aren’t any huge rewards for winning. Time Trial is what you would expect from a Kart Racing game; nothing too exciting and certainly the least interesting of the three modes.
There is one final game mode which is where Garfield does something a little different to the rest of the Kart Games on Steam. A daily challenge mode is included, complete the set task and you will get a reward at the end of it. This is a really easy way to gather better upgrades for your car without having the need to grind out money by replaying previous tournaments.
Graphically, Garfield Karts looks really nice. It looks like one of the cartoons, with some really nice modelling, textures and animations on show. The game’s environments are all very nicely designed as well. The sound effects do let the game down a little bit; it can sometimes seem too quiet at times. Your engine noise can almost seem too quiet for it to seem realistic which something which felt really odd when playing is. The sound track is really catchy though.
Garfield Kart has three levels of difficulties. Whilst you are not able to choose the difficulties per race, you choose which bracket of difficulty race to take part in; 50cc, 100cc and 150cc. Obviously the higher the number the more powerful the rest of your opponents cars will be. In order to even be competitive in the 100cc and 150cc bracket, you will have to completely upgrade your car using the upgrade system; you are able to purchase items for your car which will improve three criteria of performance, speed, handling and power. You will also be able to choose from a selection of helmets which will also grant you a specific bonus for individual power ups which you can collect. Whilst I really liked the upgrade system, it does feel very much like a grind to unlock items as you have to replay previously won competitions in order to get anywhere close to being able to buy anything. I would have personally liked to have seen a reduction in the price set on the items so you aren’t forced to replay already played content if you don’t want to. The daily challenge mode helps with this, but only if you play the game in small doses.
I have been playing for over an hour so far and I have just completed the first bracket of races whilst also taking part in the daily challenge and a couple of time trials. There is easily another 3 or 4 hours of content from this game. Sadly the game will have very little staying power and I will more than likely not play the game again after completing the three stages of difficulty. With the lack of any multiplayer mode, the developers have really shot themselves in the foot of making game out of a genre which is so perfectly crafted for any type of multiplayer action.
As the Steam page says for this game, there is only partial controller support for this game. The gameplay itself works well with a control, however you have to navigate menus with your mouse, making a bit awkward to play on a couch setup. There is a wide selection of resolutions to play on, right the way up to 4k, with minimal graphic options to change.
To sum up, Garfield Kart is purely an OK game. There aren’t any glaringly obvious negative points; it’s just not going to blow your socks off with exciting game play moments and hilarious local multiplayer. The only thing that resembles Garfield in this game is the character models; there is no story, no voice acting, and nothing else that makes this game any different to a generic kart racer. Luckily the game is priced low at £5, 59, and for that price you will get some enjoyment out of it, just don’t go into it expecting all the bells and whistles of Mario Kart. I’ve marked it down as a 3 on my scale, it’s not the best game, but it certainly isn’t a bad game either. If you can get it less than the sale price, you will want to consider checking it out for an hour or two of action.

At first, Spec Ops seems like an effective war story. It clearly encapsulates the message that "war is hell" and also tackles American neo-colonialism. However, there is another level to the story as well. By the end it becomes clear that the game is as much about video games as it is about war.
Spec Ops does an incredible job of marrying gameplay with storytelling. While the game at first feels like a generic cover based shooter, this was an intentional choice. While this decision will turn many players away, those who stay around will be treated to an intelligent conversation about player agency and modern games.
Ultimatly, the ending doesn't quite land, but its impossible to deny Spec Ops' great narritive.

An open world, slightly repetitive, surprisingly addicting game.
You drive around, you collect scrap, you beat B*tches up. That's pretty much it.
Honestly, I didn't like this game until at least 6-7 hours in. Maybe it's because I loved the movie so much...or maybe it's because I have a man-crush on Tom Hardy....I'm not sure. Either way, It's disappointing how little they build up the "bad guys" and things are very repetitive, especially in the beginning.
However, it's a beautiful game, and it gets more interesting as you progress. Loot locations and oil camps get more complex/unique, combat gets way more fun, and you open up a lot of different mechanics with your vehicle(s).
The game does an acceptable job of capturing the emptiness of the movie, but not really the craziness...and it misses the mark on character development wildly. But all-in-all it was still a very entertaining game, even if it really could have been so much more.

I honestly went into this game thinking that it was going to be a fairly typical car-chase / beat-em-up game. It turned out to be much deeper than I'd expected.  While it certainly has its fair share of speeding around in cars, and a melee combat system which is pretty similar to the Batman games, it has shades of Skyrim, with its huge, detailed environment and no shortage of NPCs to worry about.  Sure, it doesn't have the Workshop support, but there is a hell of a lot of game wrapped up in this package.
The game plays very nicely using Mouse/Keyboard, though I'm sure that it was really designed for a controller.
The environment is about as atmospheric as it is possible to get in a computer game, and the voice acting is exceptional. When you get stuck in a dust storm, with your mechanic clinging desparately to the bonnet of your car as he tries to hammer your engine back to life, while you try to hug the cliff-face as closely as possible, you really get a feel for just how hostile the place is.
The missions (it's open world, but you get 'quests' to do if you want to advance the story) aren't too hard... and are essentially about driving to a wreck somewhere, fighting your way inside, and looting the hell out of the place.  You can also steal or find other vehicles, and take them back to base to add to your collection.
If you're one of those people who has to 100% everything, you'll love this. You'll also love it if you're an explorer. There are enough cool things to see to keep you busy for a while... such as the enemy base made out of aircraft parts, with wings forming bridges over a deep cloud-filled chasm... or the ruined light-house which has become home to a rag-tag bunch of misfits.
You can upgrade everything, including yourself... though if I had a complaint about anything, it was that sometimes it's a bit obscure to see what you can upgrade. I was hours into the game before I realised I could level up Max to be a more effective fighter, for example. Up to that point, I thought I was just supposed to add improvements to the car.
In short, this game is a lot of fun. While I might balk at the full price, that's probably just me. I got it on (I think) 80% discount during one of the Steam sales, and I've easily had my money's worth out of it.

Wow. Amazing game worthy of the Mad Max name. The wasteland really has a distinctive feel. Great graphics, good acting, vehicle combat is cool and the the story is very unique. It's a game for sandbox completionist fans. The plot is paper thin. There are bugs ranging from crashes to objectives that don't spawn without a reload. The vehicle handling (at least with keyboard+mouse) fishtails constantly. The growth is mostly passives like more damage or better armor or faster acceleration, but nothing really groundbreaking. The characters are one dimensional. But if you want to slowly chip away at a map and watch the good guys regain control... if you want to clear out bases and take down convoys... if you want to find collectables and biographies... if you want to seek that glorious 100% in assorted categories... this is the game for you. For me, it was just enough to make me keep going until I turned the whole map green.

There have been a lot of sandbox games to come out in the last few years, and Mad Max checks of almost every open-world cliche there is, but there is something undeniably special about this game. The graphics are astounding, the story and characters fit the universe well, and the vehiclular combat is in a league of its own. I keep coming back to this month after month, completing the odd side quest here and there, just for fun.
