A fun, but sometimes tedious, casual stroll through an open world of the wastelands.
Never have the unforgiving wastelands of the post-apocalypse been so, well, forgiving... I never died in combat once during my playthrough. Whether through the rock'em sock'em "click X a bunch of times" fist fights or the bashing car chases I just never felt in danger. And really wasn't. All my deaths were stupid human errors and accidental falls because of them. So we have ourselves a very very tame game here which doesn't quite fit the desperate theme. But while missing the true challenge it still delivers loads of fun and a story that sticks to the Mad Max character quite well in my opinion. And as a fan of the movies, that story polished the gaming experience for me on a very high note despite some infuriatingly tedious gaming moments along the way.
The story both plays it safe and dares enough to stand on it's own. Any references (some awesome subtle ones) to the quartet of movies are vague enough to not insult and keeps everything at a safedistance. This can easily be considered its own entity and universe with the same set pieces and character. It doesn't HAVE to be considered part of the movies. And that's where they did enough to do a still complete story that didn't hang itself on adhering to the movies. All while still culminating in the Max I know and love. It worked well. Nothing award winning or something but; I liked it!
From a gameplay standpoint things get a little muddier and average. I really cannot understate how easy this game is. Go here, get that, bash a button to beat up guys in the way, earn scrap, buy new upgrades to make your bashing a button look more awesome, crash a car or two, bam you're the Road Warrior legend! Its weird to call a game of this scope and this well constructed "average", but it just is. The combat really is just one button with another to block and another to roll. Combos are more or less automatic based on timing rather than actual pattern input or anything resembling skill. And as long as you do a little grinding and side missions your car handles itself in battles just as easily. There is still a feeling of satisfaction to both situations though. So again, it works. The missions are mostly elaborate fetch and grab missions. Level designs of areas don't do anything new. There's nothing hard to find or difficult to beat. Its average. But that isn't to be mistaken with "not good".
Another issue needing mentioning was the pacing of the play. Getting over the idea of never feeling threatened you want to move things along a little quicker since you're awesome and basically the Ayatollah of Rock n' Rolla. But this game absolutely assaults you with tedium and parts that are entirely unnecessarily slow. And I mean sloooow. I'm old so I don't mind "smelling the roses" and I'm not some kid with no attention span. This game is legitimately slow in parts. It can burn you out bad in long sessions. Anybody who has played it shudders if you mention hot air balloons, mine fields, or ' ! ' encounters to them. Words cannot express all the little things this game does to numb your brain by slowing the pace. So just a fair warning there.
The game ran well on my toaster with no need for setup beyond turning off motion blur as a personal preference. It ran exactly how I like my games to; It just did! Never dipped in framerate or required any more effort than plugging in a controller (I can't speak to the K&M controls) and clicking play. It wasn't without a bug or two of course. But nothing more than could be expected in an open world game of this scope. Weird things are just going to happen in a game like this and anything too jarring is solved with a game restart in every case I ran into. A guy gets stuck on a wall, or a sound effect doesn't play, stuff like that. Nothing big or game breaking.
All in all I had loads of fun. I'm a sucker for the wastelands and they are well represented in their desolate dangerous beauty here. I never felt in danger of course, but I felt like I was still in the wastes. There were some greatly satisfying moments of play and the story delivered on all points to seal the deal and make me (mostly) forget the tedium. It is priced more than fairly compared to games of similar scope, but can be found on sales often enough to save the money and wait for one. Mindless fun in the best setting that I can definitely recommend!

I may be one of the people who strongly disagrees with playtonic's choice to get political with their IP, shaft pc players  with launch day release time, and have exceptionally incompetent forum moderation, but I'll keep this review exclusively about the game and not the company... because boy is there plenty wrong with the game.
I finished it in about 17 hours, but could have finished it sooner (in about 13 hours) had I gone straight to the last boss as soon as it was unlocked. Keep in mind, I was playing with a mouse and keyboard, but I'll mostly point out things that have nothing to do with my choice of gameplay equipment.
Most of the levels are enormous, and suffer from a very non-cohesive level design where big chunks of the world have a few pagies in one corner, and a large chunk has some in another. There isn't a whole lot of free roaming possibilities with a lot of the worlds because of how large they are. If you go roaming without an intended goal, you'll come across things to do, sure. But about half-way through completion of that world, any roaming you do is more likely to make you feel like you're wandering aimlessly, rather than exploring to find something to do. This is
for an exploration platformer. The level design itself has some problems though. There are places where the player can get stuck and be forced to die in order to get unstuck based on the moves they currently have available to them. Granted you really have to try, but if you're desperate looking for something, it's bound to happen. The game seriously needs a new tonic that adds a wayfinder arrow pointing to regions of the level/collectibles you have not found. It's THAT big and THAT boring to revisit places trying to find the last collectibles.
The camera is a nightmare. More-so than I think any platformer I have ever played. If it has no room to move in a direction you want, it simply won't. It won't snap to the player, it won't turn the player invisible if it's forced to get right up close next to the back of the player's head. It won't clip through solid objects and turn them invisible to try and keep providing the player with a view of what's happening, it just refuses at times, but jumps around more quickly than the player was expecting at other times. Not to mention way too many areas in the game where the camera is forced into a specific perspective that it doesn't need to be in, much like it's trying to give you a 2d-platformer camera when you wouldn't actually want one. There wasn't nearly enough work put into the camera, and the worst experience I had with it was while underwater. If you try to swim down, you would want to LOOK down to see where you're going. But with Yooka Laylee's camera, it will constantly snap back up and forward directly behind the player (which effects how the player can move) over and over again. It's a terrible nightmare of poorly-coded frustration.
If you're playing on a keyboard, they literally didn't bind "B" to cancel to any key, meaning players were getting stuck in challenges they could not refuse to try again on if they failed, because P is pause, and ESC is pause, so you have to double tap P and then hit ESC as a hotfix to try and select cancel.
For some reason you can collide with scenery foliage and ferns in the ground, as well as debris from breakable objects, which get you stuck for a couple seconds until they disappear. Very annoying if enemies are nearby.
This happened to me several times. If you don't clear the area of nearby enemies before talking to an npc, they are likely to run up to your occupied player characters as you talk to said npc, and as soon as you stop talking, you will take unavoidable damage.
Even Banjo Kazooie had it so nearby enemies automatically and instantaneously de-agro'd on you when you lost control of your character. How was this overlooked!?
The pink butterflies act as both health pickups and energy pickups, but not in one. Eating a butterfly gives health, touching them like a collectible gives energy, but not vice versa. In races, this is exceptionally annoying because it's hard to gauge where the butterfly is that you have to touch while in motion. They also don't cast shadows AND float around unpredictably, so it's way more difficult than it ever should be.
Player can take unavoidable damage from certain unskippable cutscenes if the cutscene ends at just the wrong time, especially with world 1 boss.
Mostly with world 2 transformation. You can't move backwards, and it's a
transformation. You also cannot move left or right without moving forward, and are required to do precise platforming as this transformation. Unfair and nightmare-inducing. The 'tarnsform back' feature for this transformation is also broken, can be interrupted and result in a spastic seizure pulsation of the character if you hold shift and then attack.
Lizard Lash is the ability Yooka starts out with that is used to grab on to things with his tongue, such as butterflies or powerups. It can be done while jumping, but not while doing the bat flutter move, which you will feel as though should be easily possible, when it's not. Later moves that upgrade Lizard Lash are TERRIBLY inconsistent, mostly in world 3 where the functionality of the move is just ALL over the place and results in unfair damage/death.
Some are fun and straight forward, others are horrendously broken, unfair, pointlessly frustrating, and make you despise Rextro more than any other character. World 1 arcade game is more frustrating than fun, as is world 4 and 5 arcade games, but world 4 "Capital Cashino" especially. The controls are literally broken. It's called Hurdle Hijinx, you run straight forward and dodge obstacles by changing lanes. If you change lanes too fast, the game gets confused and LOCKS YOUR ABILITY TO CHANGE LANES, guaranteeing death, and making the second pagie for a high score next to impossible without surgical precision and 15 tries later.
Certain challenges such as world 4 transformation escort missions don't have their target rings removed if you fail and then refuse the challenge, meaning the ring stays there for the rest of the tim you're in the world, but does nothing, confusing new players into thinking it activates something when it doesn't. There are many oversights like this where the devs just didn't pay close enough attention to how they coded it.
The Hunter tonic makes lone collectibles whistle periodically when you are near them to help you find them, but ONLY if you've missed them beforehand, and left the area, which the tonic doesn't specify.
Some characters/enemies sound thematic for what they are, others are just a guy in his 30s making monster sounds as though he's entertaining children, and it sounds obnoxious and ridiculous, instead of stylistic.
Certain tunes sound like they are from a poorly-produced 80s children cartoon, while others sound on par with the rest of the soundtrack. It's very off-putting.
Overall, it's not worth 40 dollars, even if you LOVE Banjo-Kazooie. Wait for it to be 25 or less on sale, or don't bother. I adore Banjo-Kazooie, but have to give this a 6/10 and not recommend it for $40 in its current state. Too many incompetent design-choices that come at the expense of the player.

I was foolish enough to ignore this game when it first came out years ago and only bought the double pack last year. What a fool I was, 2001 me would have loved this game.
Set in a snowed in New York in 2001 you play as a Burnt out cop Max Payne who's out for revenge after his wife and newborn child are killed by rampaging drug addicts. Pretty grim stuff eh? well it only gets darker from here on out.
The level design and sound is brilliant, although it has aged I would argue it aged rather well. The atmosphere it gives off is incredibly bleak and noir at its best. The gunplay is great with rounds going off all around you as you fly through the air in slow motion, and yes corpses and bulletcasings (including empty mags and shotgun hulls) stay around. You can really see the carnage you caused. The TV shows playing on random tv sets dotted around the levels are brilliant too, this was continued in Payne II.
Unfortunely for most with modern machines this game will not work from the get go, but there is a series of fixes and widescreen mods floating around on the web. It took me about 5 minutes to get it running on nice resolutions.
In conclusion if you like 3rd person quality shooters that have strong atmosphere and fun gunplay look know further, this game is a classic.

TL:DR version: Arkham Origins is a not very innovative, but not a complete messup either. The boss fights are greatly improved, with the story and voice keeping the same high quality. The gameplay has no great improvements besides a few tweaks and the Riddler side missions took a hit. But all in all, the game is fun and deserves your money. 8/10
Batman Arkham Origins, the game many have anticipated since the day Arkham City release, is in many senses a flop/masterpiece. The gameplay is somewhat stale, but the bosses are greatly improved; the story is almost on par with Arkham City (and definately better than Arkham Asylum), but it's release was buggy. Therefore, I am going to review each part of the game seperately, then give you the final score (a weighted average with more important elements have greater weights). The scores are from 1-10 with a 1 being garbage, a 5 being average, and a 10 being spectacular.
1. The Gameplay - Both the greatest strength and weakness of this new endeavor in the Arkham series is it's gameplay. While WB Games Montreal was smart in not trying to rewrite a broken system, they also did not bring much new to the table in terms of gadgets and fighting mechanics. There are some cool new gadgets like Deathstroke's remote zipline, and these are implemented fairly well into the game. Others however, such as electrocutioner's gloves make the game to easy in some aspects by allowing you to bypass the difficulty of the shielded and armor wearing enemies. The puzzles in the campaign are fun and challenging (a couple stumped me for a little bit) but the riddler side of the game has been slightly downgraded (as of this review the Burneley tower bug has been fixed so 100% is now possible).
Gameplay - 7/10
2. The Boss Fights - The boss fights in Arkham Origins are easily the greatest improvement over Arkham City. With all of them being intuitive, imaginative, and creative, they are a joy to play. Most take something from an Arkham City boss and upgrade it e.g. taking the quick countering of Ra's al Ghul and then adding timing, variations, and a higher level of control for the Deathstroke fight (which is tied with the three part masterpiece of Bane's boss fight for best fight). This part is great, and I hope Rocksteady takes notes for the upcoming Arkham game they have been hinting at. The only dissapointing fight was the Electrocutioner, but it more served as comic relief than an actual flaw.
Boss Fights - 10/10
3. The Story - The story of Arkham Origins has its ups and downs, but for the most part is solid. While I would have liked all eight of the Assassins to have gotten their own boss fight each, they are each implemented well in the story (with the exception of Electrocutioner). The game has its share of twists of turns that attempt to reach the glory of the now infamous ending to Arkham City (which I will not spoil, but if you have not played that game, fix that now, before you even think of playing this game. Arkham Asylum is also fun, but in my opinion is not critical to play before Origins. But you should.), but that in the end cannot due to the incredibly high bar. The story at some points feel slightly disjointed and confusing, but does wrap up quite nicely with a solid, though not incredible ending.
Story - 8/10
4. Visuals - Arkham Origins has some slight improvements in the visuals, but overall not too much too offer in terms of newness. The cutscenes however, are beautiful and incredibly fun to watch, but the ingame graphics are only slightly better than Arkham City (which was as a side note, a beautiful game, don't get me wrong). Batman does move a bit smoother, but in the end it feels somewhat stale and halfhearted.
Visuals - 7/10
5. New Features - This is kind of a grab bag of features that caught my attention, for better or for worse. One of the coolest things they added was an amazing new Crime Scene mode. You can recreate what happened during a crime and then look for clues based on where they were and following their trajectory. Another new feature is the Fast Travel System. I'm sure many liked this system, but for me it took away from the experiance. I love the feeling of flying around the city, looking for and stopping crime, and just feeling like an all around beast. But, since the Fast Travel is optional, there is really no fault in it, just personal preferance on whether it should be used or not.
New Features - 7/10
6. Gotham City - While Gotham itself is not as big is many including myself thought it would be, it still is quite large, albeit that half of the city is a reskinned Arkham City with some new features. The other half however is as much a joy to explore as the Arkham City was in in its namesake of a game, the highlight being the ability to sneak in and take out corrupt GCPD officers in their own building. Perfect? No. Fun? Yes.
Gotham City - 7.5/10
7. Online Play - Online Play is a variation of the regular team deathmatch mode with a twist. There are two teams of three henchman, either Bane's or Joker's, fighting each other, and one team of two, Batman and Robin, trying to stop them both. It's fun for a short while, and though I haven't gotten tired of it yet I have not played very much of it yet and could see one getting tired of it quickly down the road. What we really all want (Rocksteady take notes) is the ability to do a co-op campaign. But that isn't what we got and the multiplayer itself isn't bad. Just don't expect this to be the next big third person shooter.
Online Play - 7/10
8. Voice Acting - Another major strength of the game is the voice acting. Many were scared to have Mark Hamill and Kevin Conroy relinquishing their respecive roles as the Joker and Batman, but fear no more. Troy Baker as a younger Joker nailed it perfectly and while there are slight differences, none are bad, and I am perfectly ok with him taking up the mantle as the Joker. His pauses, his laugh, his switch from soft to screaming in an instant, it's all perfect and I loved it. Roger Craig Smith took over Batman, and while I still stick with Kevin Conroy as the best, Roger does a good job showing what a younger Batman might have sounded like, not perfect, but still admirable and enjoyable. Other characters are voiced by the same actors as those from Arkham City, such as Tara Strong as the loveable but ever annoying (in a good way) Harley Quinn. The voice acting keeps it's high quality and it is always fun to just sit on a roof and listen to some annoying crook rant about the cold or missing Christmas Dinner
Voice Acting - 9/10
9. Side Missions - Side missions have always been a fun part of the Arkham series, looking around to find as many villians as you can, and this holds true, for the most part, here. All of the side missions are fun and interesting in their own way, whether it be gameplay, puzzles, wierdness (see Mad Hatter), or the conversations that go on while do them. The one exception to this rule, and one of the biggest dissapointments of the game so far has been the Riddler puzzles. These have been made much easier, and there are so many of these "datapacks it becomes a chore. The radio towers add a little variety, but in the end the Riddler is a flop.
Side Missions - 8/10
With all that said, what is the game's final score? Arkham Origins is a hard game to review, because it's hard to pinpoint exactly what is wrong with it. In the end though, it falls short of its lofty expectations without being a bad game by itself. Batman: Arkham Origins earns a 7/10 on release (due to bugs) and an 8/10 with patches, but I am going to blame the bugs on WB pushing the game out the Door and give it a Final Score of 8/10. It isn't perfect, but it is well worth your purchase, though I highly recommend picking up the first two, Arkham Asylum and Arkham City first.
Have Fun!
-Daniel

First off ignore my play time. I do most of my gaming at work and dont have an internet connection. Unfortunately Steam doesnt keep track of play time while in offline mode. As of writing this I have around 24 hours of gameplay in.
In short this game is excellent and well worth the money.
The universe is huge. And it would take a long while to fly from one side to the other. The ships are awesome. There is a lot to do.. You can be a trader, a pirate, a bounty hunter... The list goes on. It takes a lot of work to acquire new ships and level up. Not in a bad way.  I actually love it.. In my 24 hours of playtime I've only recently just captured a ship worth keeping and transferring to. Its not really grindy in my opinion as there is so much to do it seems you're all the time doing something different or new. I see that as a really good value for my money. I have only done 3 main/campaign quests at this point as you have to take time to level up and gear up for them. So its not a game you're going to beat within a few hours. Capturing ships better than yours is a real challenge and its very rewarding when you finally get one. So far Ive found capturing ships to be the funnest and most profitable thing to do. And when you finally get out of the starting gunship into something better it gets a little easier and much more profitable.
The learning curve is easy. Not like learning X3 or anything. You can pick it up fairly quick.
The game doesnt baby you.. You can run into a battleship that will destroy within minutes of starting the game so you always have to be careful and keep an eye out. There's always a challenge..It's not a game that will allow you to feel like a god that just steam rolls everything that comes along. I like that as it gives you something to strive for. However I will say now that I've gotten a better ship (Its a corvette btw) i come across a lot more ships that are weak or trivial. Its extremely cool when you come into an area with a bunch of them.. I just turn on Auto fire and watch my ship just destroy 5 or 6 ships within minutes.. It's awesome.
So far the only things that Ive found to be less than great are the voice acting and traveling..
The voice acting is far from good. Its not so bad that it destroys the campaign for you.. But its not good either lol. Your ships computer voice is great though and thats the one you'll hear 90% of the time.
The traveling.. When you first start you dont really have a choice but to fly all the way to each location. As warp gates are expensive and not really an option at first. Worm holes do damage and really dont have enough of them to justify them as a good way to travel. Rifts help but they are kind of hard to stay in. So at first the traveling gets kind of old as the map is just so hufmge it can really take a long while to get from one point to another. But after you get a decent income going and you can afford the warp gates its not bad.
All in all the game has been an excellent experience. And I feel the user rating should be quite a bit better than it is now. It's a game that I've quickly became addicted to and I already know I'll have hundreds of hours into before I get tired of it.

Batman Origins is not the most refreshing addition to the franchise, but it is certainly a valuable addition. Having recently also played the other versions of the franchise (again). It really showed some advances in gameplay over the previous version City. However the difference was less obvious as between City and the 1st installment of the franchise Asylum.
When the game was released at the end of October, the game was ok but still rough around the edges due to bugs negatively influencing the gameplay. One of the most prominent bugs was the Burley comss tower bug. Since then the developer has been releasing patches to fix the majority of the issues with the game. At the moment bugs mays still exist but wont be as blatantly visible as before.
The gameplay remains the same as the other Arkham chapters for the majority of the game. Off course there will be some new gadgets available to the dark knight, but the majority will be familiar from the earlier releases. The fighting system as implemented in the Batman games is one of the most entertaining systems I've come accross in action fighting games. This is still one of the strong points of the game and it remains one of the most attractive elements. Another strong point of the game are the predator rooms. The variaty of takedowns of the dark knight in a stealth environment remains entertaining. It has certainly not gotten worse.
As for the story. The basis of the story with the 8 assasins was already known before the release of the game. Getting rid of the assasins during gameplay is no surprise. The story as a whole however does contain some surprises (at least to me). The story is more engaging as the previous versions I found as in the previous releases I was less drawn into the story as wiht Origins.
Besides the story you will find some side quests as well as the famous riddler challenges. These challenges are easier than in the City game which I found good. Some of the challenges in City required to much training to master while in this version the majority of these are simple puzzles. Also the amount of riddles is less as in City it became too much of a grind fest to get all the trophies and riddles done.
The majority of what made the previous games fun is similar or better but then with a new story.
Is the game innovative? No. Is the game fun? Yes.

Arkham Asylum was a revolutionary game. Arkham City was as well. By contrast, Arkham Origins is viewed as an evolutionary game, and between that and the fact that the principal actors and development studio have been replaced a lot of people figured "eh, I don't need to play this for a year." Technically speaking, Arkham Origins does feature revolutionary additions over the previous games, but it's in an area that nobody particularly asked for in the first place: online competitive multiplayer. I myself have yet to even launch it, but given that it's developed by Splash Damage I'm sure it's not slapped together. They did after all make the Return to Castle Wolfenstein multiplayer (which got carried over into Enemy Territory, and then Quake Wars, etc).
The thing about the single-player is that while it's good, you literally cannot help but compare it against Arkham City the entire time. The combat system and animations are completely carried over, with some additions. You have some new gadgets (one is allegedly "new" but in reality is functionally identical to something else from Arkham City) and face a few new common foes. Luckily, one of the gadgets is straight out of Super Inframan and makes combat even more satisfying since you trounce everyone with it, and the others give you more options during the Predator encounters. The enemy AI is altered since the rate at which you counter rather than strike has gone way, way up. Boss battles are VASTLY improved over the previous games, as each one emphasizes that you do different things. At no point do you feel "well, this is the same thing I did for the last boss."
But even with that said, at most points you DO feel "well, I've done this before." Aside from the combat, the sidequests have you doing the same gameplay mechanic as 2 years ago (and 4 years ago) albeit for a different cosmetic reason. Example: in Arkham City you have to quickly travel across the city to answer phones in time to stop a killer. Here, you have to do the same to defuse bombs. It's the same map as Arkham City, albeit with some new zones. It helps a little that you can now fast travel. But there must be fewer grapple points because getting from place to place is a little trickier than it used to be.
You'll be fighting and fighting, and with the random "crimes in progress" that spawn, you'll fight more. You're rarely going to be scanning the environment unless you're prompted to do so. Crime scene investigations are a new addition, but much like the show CSI you aren't really doing anything yourself. The computer is magically reconstructing a series of events based on your having scanned a body and a spot of blood (which they can't show as red). Then you go beat up a guy. You can't inadvertently defeat the person you meant to interrogate either, so there's no "save this guy for last" aspect to combat. But you are now given grades for each encounter, such that higher grades yield XP bonuses. Winning is largely a foregone conclusion given that you're Batman, but winning with an A or S rank is the tough part. In fact, I still haven't gotten the last one because it doesn't always play the *wham* sound effect to denote you KO'ed someone with a hit (I call this the "BATMAAAAAN!" since if I could mod this game I would replace that sound with the screaming pug). The game offers various challenges for additional bonuses and upgrades, but it's buggy about deciding whether or not some of them "count." I busted my♥♥♥♥♥doing the "do 4 exotic takedowns in a Predator section" and then it didn't count it. And then it turned out there were no more Predator sections in the game. AND it won't let you complete those challenges on the challenge maps, so if you don't do it during the story you're screwed...unless you replay it on the much harder New Game+ mode...
The reduced architecture grapples and increased enemy attack rates are somewhat minor, but if there's a major "step backwards" here it's one of atmosphere. This Gotham City isn't yet overrun with supervillains who've marked their territory and themed their gangs. The incentive to see the world isn't really as strong. The Riddler's challenges were designed to direct you to all the cool little references, but at this point there is no "Riddler" etc so you're basically completing the challenges for the sake of hearing the "extortion data that's going to harm innocent people" recordings. Except pretty much all of them pertain to supervillains and corrupt civil servants whom you take down anyway. It feels more like a task since there's less "reward" for doing it. Why oppose this so strongly? That's the REAL enigma.
The strong negative online backlash to Arkham City's criminal dialogue means that EVERYTHING pertaining to threats or abusive language is long gone (that already got walked back since the Arkham City DLC) so pat yourselves on the back, Team "Woke" Gaming. Between that and the fact that Batman is less infallible at this stage of his career, the writing has gotten a lot more praise compared to Arkham City. But for me, it feels less satisfying to beat people up because I overheard them saying they're cold and hungry, or that they're resorting to crime because they lost their job and now they have to not be home on Christmas Eve. This definitely plays into the "Batman as fascist authoritarian conservative" reading of the character. I kind of wonder if the writers just hate Batman as a concept, since the villains all expose the flaws in his approach and morality and Batman has no answer because he can't admit "the reason I can't kill you is because you're all too profitable as IP."
Also, the game takes place over a few hours on Christmas Eve into Christmas Day, yet the amount that happens is absurd. True, a lot happened during Arkham City, but there was planning leading up to it. How can these locations be THIS devastated and re-renovated in just a few hours? And it's not even accidental; the game points out "yeah, it's been 3 hours." On the other hand, James Gordon isn't Commissioner yet, so the cops are pretty much all dirty. In this game you get to beat up SWAT team guys, which is the part of "Year One" that is the most important.
The Assassin's Creed guy as Batman has his highs and mids since he's mostly forced to imitate Kevin Conroy, but with a name like "Roger Smith" you'd think he was BORN to impersonate Kevin Conroy's Batman! Troy Baker (who already nailed his Richard Moll Two-Face impersonation in Arkham City) is about as dead-on a mimicry of Mark Hamill's Joker as one could hope, given that Mark can no longer really do that voice anymore. Richard Epcar (voice of the Joker in the fighting games) has a few background lines that jump out to me, but I guess he also directed a lot of the secondary dialogue recordings.
I enjoyed Arkham Origins, but I'd still say to hold off on getting it. Not so much because of the issues described above so much as the fact that there's a ton of DLC and all of it's spread out across platforms and retailers due to exclusivity (Challenge maps where you're Bruce Wayne in training, etc). There's a Season Pass which includes that stuff, but it costs another $20 and for now is almost entirely cosmetic. They say there'll be at least one story DLC, but what'll it be about? Maybe something inspired by The Long Halloween? I don't know, so I don't know if that, a few challenge maps, and some cosmetic skins are really worth the money. For now I'd say to pick this up once a "complete edition" is available unless you happen to buy a new video card that bundles it.

The scenery slowly fades into the background and hides until it can truly surprise you, like those dam cougars in Red Dead Redemption, except it’s not some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of an animal, but a majestic view or the depths of human madness. The games has a lot of flaws in both lighting and enemies pallets, making it hard for you to see the enemies some of the time. This would be inexcusable if the story was over the top like a Call of Duty. As it is, it seems like the game uses the graphical similarities with COD, even being lower than its year’s instalment, to show how a military shooter can still be good even with the mediocre graphics that others try to run from.
The graphics and character design change as you progress through the game, slow enough that you don’t even notice until it is too late. The overall graphics do add to the game play with only a few invisible walls or weird character movements.
Story: 3/3
You are a gruff military commander sent to find the best agent of the government gone rogue beyond the vail. You command a team of 3 into the depths of human pain, seeing them become some kind of machine-like husk. In the end the hero must fight the indoctrination of the villain and wonder if you were in his place, would anything be different? Wait, no, that’s Mass Effect. No, in this game you are only a captain.
The main difference between this captain and Commander Shepard is that your charature has self-doubt. This one aspect makes it all the more relatable and creates a deeper gaming experience. This is not a Greek tragedy where the hero is brought low by his own hubris. He does not fail his team because of a lack of skill or drive. He is just a man who was thrown into an impossible situation, and is affected by it.

The games does throw some nice small gaming moments that were new and unique to this. The gameplay was the weakest form of this game, but it was still better than most.
Re-Playability: .5/1

Borderlands 2 is an action role playing first person shooter, developed by Gearbox Software and published by 2k Games in September 2012. It is the second game in the Borderlands series and the sequel to the popular 2009 hit Borderlands 1.
As with the first game, you are able to complete a campaign with the main story quest and optional side missions as one of the four Vault hunters.  All of the key gameplay features are all present, such as online co-op, randomly generated loot and character building elements such as talent trees are all found in Borderlands 2. There has been a game of the year edition released last year which includes all the DLC apart from one.
The gameplay at it's core is the same as Borderlands 1. The focus on randomly generated loot plays a huge part. Each of the characters you have the option to play as have their own specialty, and will bring a feel of originality to each playthrough on either of them.  We also see a new elemental effect in BL2, Slag, this is a substance that increases the damage a target takes if they are covered in it. You will also find Eridium bars as you play the game, these can be used to purchase storage upgrades and increase the amount of ammo you can carry.
We also see an element of customizing how your character looks as well, you can unlock different skins, head designs, colour schemes and vehicle paint jobs.  Another major addition to BL2 is the "Badd@ss rank" system; points are awarded for completing certain in-game challenges, that in turn award tokens that will allow you to increase your base stats. These stat increases also take effect on all of your other single player characters too.  Also similar to the the original, we also see the return of a New Game Plus mode, in the form of "True Vault Hunter Mode", which increases the difficulty, and gives you a higher chance at even better loot drops. You are also able to level up to 50 in this mode too.
The graphics in Borderlands 2 are virtually the same as the original, but with just a more enhanced look to them. We see the vibrant colour schemes in each zone come to life. Along with better quality textures too.  The style of graphics in Borderlands has always been a huge drawing point for me as there are hardly any other games which pull this style off as well as this.
Your first playthrough Borderlands 2 will have a number of difficult encounters, but these can easily be overpowered by returning to the same bad guy, mission or zone after leveling up one or two more times, or getting a bigger better gun. If you stay on top of all of the side missions as you progress through the story mission, you will stay at the right level so that you won't just hit a brick wall of impossible monsters/enemies. To make matters easier when it comes to deciding how tough a mission will be, each one also has a recommended level - so you can easily see how hard a single mission will be without actually having to test the waters first.
A full playthrough on single player of Borderlands 2 took me just under thirty hours. That is a pretty decent amount of content on offer, with the side missions and a decent amount of loot farming involved too. I have put almost 140 hours into Borderlands 2, as I have played various different characters through the story a number of times. This is a game where you can easily spend 300 hours and still be having the same amount of fun.
I had zero amount of technical issues throughout BL2; the game is perfectly optimized, will run at 60 fps, and the cloud save feature makes it even better technically.
Borderlands 2 is easily in my top 5 favorite games of all time. Just like the original, Borderlands 2 is a perfect game with no flaws in it at all. I cannot recommend this game enough. Most people will already have it since it goes on sale so much, but PLEASE play it. You will NOT be disappointed.

Hey guys, thanks for reading my reviews. Let me make this as plain as possible. If you like pool and can find this cheap, check it out. It's not bad at all. I think the controls are better here in many ways than I've seen in previous PC pool games, but what's the game really like? You get nine ball, eight ball, and a few mini-games. There is a trick mode that hasn't been put into the game yet apparently. The humor is painful mostly, but not always bad. Just never very clever or subtle.
As for the negative stuff: I think it gets repetitious. It's also buggy. I don't like the AI at all, as it sometimes seems too transparent what's happening in the game. Some of the rounds a really good AI player will goof several times in a row to give me a chance to beat it. Other times it feels like it's cheating to win.  Sometimes the match challenges don't appear to count properly or are too literally applied, and it seems inconsistant with its application of what meets the requirements of a given challenge. For example, I played a match that wanted me to get a 3 ball streak with a jump shot. I got a 4 ball streak with a jump at the end and it didn't count it. The next time I played, it seemed to count it. So I just don't trust the AI at all. Also, some of the designer ball sets that you can unlock confuse me visually because the stripes and solids look too similar to me from a distance. The settings are very colorful, which isn't necessarily bad, but can be VERY loud.
Anyway, even though this seems a negative review, it's not meant to be. The devs say they are working to improve it, and if they do I think it has a lot of potential. As it is, if you can get it for a very low price and you like pool, try it. I've enjoyed playing it, but it can be frustrating at times.

I think if you enjoyed the BanjoKazooie games then you'll enjoy this one. The only "big" issues I see right now are:
blury looking textures,
when moving the background is out of focus (like depth of field I guess), but this makes it very hard on the eyes,
And the camera can be buggy or bothersome sometimes

For the record, I have played Banjo-Kazooie in the past but was not a huge fan.
If there was an option to have a middle opinion, I'd be choosing it, but for now, it's a no. Yooka-Laylee was meant to be the so-called "spiritual successor" to Banjo-Kazooie. I honestly think it could be like that. The game overall is great, the soundtrack, the graphics, but there's just a few quibbles that make it go from great to good.
The camera doesn't work very well and definitely with the Rampo boss fight, is incredibly infuriating. It occassionally lags for no reason whatsoever and my specs are perfectly fine to run the game. The world three boss (the tentacle dude) he constantly clips into my player model and makes me lose help unnessessarily. Sometimes the puzzles are vague and don't tell you that you need an ability to be able to do a certain part, which makes you waste a lot of time. World 3 in general is just designed pretty bad honestly. Everything is scattered around and not in a easy to reach path, like Tribalstack Tropics, which makes it annoying to play.
After a while, Capital Cashino gets boring as all hell. Some of the games are purely luck based and it's really dull considering how much space there is, oh and the boss fight is pretty confusing for that world. My favourite worlds are Tribalstack Tropics and Galleon Galaxy because to me, it brings back that 'feel' of 3D platforming, They are spread out well and are enjoyable to play for the most part.
I know some people who loved Banjo-Kazooie hated this game, and some who loved Banjo-Kazooie and loved this game. Just remember that it's your popinion on what you think of the game and don't feel influenced by other peoples ideas, because I saw the negative reviews (which were really bashing the game) and I thought "it's not that bad, it just has some problems)
I think the game in general was worth the 2 year wait and is a great game that is trying to revive the genre. It's not meant to be the best game in the genre because Playtonic know it won't be that. It's just giving an example of what can be done to make a collect-a-thon game genre be brought back to life.
Overall, the game is great and is definitely worth playing, But there are some minor issues that are pestering the flow of the gameplay which sometimes ruins the experience for me.

Super fun, a true successor to Banjo-Kazooie and Banjo-Tooie games.

Tried to capture the nostalgia of Banjo Kazooie but falls short in every aspect.  Level design, writing, and game mechanics all fall short.  I wasn't too certain about this ever since they disrespected a fan whom provided a voice for the game but decided it wasn't worth not playing something in Ode to my fave video game.   However what I got was a load of tripe.
The game and the people that make it don't seem to understand why Banjo Kazooie was so good at a fundamental level.  Perhaps that is a symptom of the times but I really don't think that is the case.  In every form it is a copy and paste job from Banjo Kazooie but without any of the depth.  The only thing about the game that is spot on is the music and soundtrack.
Here is the thing though.  Banjo Kazooie gives you a motive for doing what you are doing.  You are trying to save your little sister from an evil witch.  Yooka Leylee has you going after Capital B because he took a book you found.  There is no attachment, no real sentiment, and nothing personal or relatable going on here.  It is a poor imitation of greatness.  Level design is poor.  The quirkiness seems forced and unnatural.  The characters seem like they were brainstormed with genericness in mind.  The characters have no depth and those with development are boring generic husks that tire you after reading one line of dialogue.
Poor show.

BIOGRAPHICAL NOTE
LEO TOLSTOY, 18281910
COUNT LEO NIKOLAYEVICH TOLSTOY was born
August 28, 1828, at the family estate of Yasna-
ya Polyana, in the province of Tula. His moth-
er died when he was three and his father six
years later. Placed in the care of his aunts, he
passed many of his early years at Kazan, where,
in 1844, after a preliminary training by French
tutors, he entered the university. He cared lit-
tle for the university and in 1847 withdrew be-
cause of "ill-health and domestic circum-
stances." He had, however, done a great deal
of reading, of French, English, and Russian
novels, the New Testament, Voltaire, and
Hegel. The author exercising the greatest in-
fluence upon him at this time was Rousseau;
he read his complete works and for sometime
wore about his neck a medallion of Rousseau.
Immediately upon leaving the university,
Tolstoy returned to his estate and, perhaps inr
spired by his enthusiasm for Rousseau, pre-
pared to devote himself to agriculture and to
improving the condition of his serfs. His first
attempt at social reform proved disappointing,
and after six months he withdrew to Moscow
and St. Petersburg, where he gave himself over
to the irregular life characteristic of his class
and time. In 1851, determined to "escape my
debts and, more than anything else, my hab-
its," he enlisted in the Army as a gentleman-
volunteer, and went to the Caucasus. While at
Tiflis, preparing for his examinations as a
cadet, he wrote the first portion of the trilogy,
Childhood, Boyhood, and Youth, in which he
celebrated the happiness of "being with Na-
ture, seeing her, communing with her." He al-
so began The Cossacks with the intention of
showing that culture is the enemy of happi-
ness. Although continuing his army life, he
gradually came to realize that "a military ca-
reer is not for me, and the sooner I get out of
it and devote myself entirely to literature the
better." His Sevastopol Sketches (1855) were
so successful that Czar Nicholas issued special
orders that he should be removed from a post
of danger.
Returning to St. Petersburg, Tolstoy was re-
ceived with great favor in both the official and
literary circles of the capital. He soon became
interested in the popular progressive move-
ment of the time, and in 1857 he decided to go
abroad and study the educational and munici-
pal systems of other countries. That year, and
again in 1860, he traveled in Europe. At Yas-
naya Polyana in 1861 he liberated his serfs and
opened a school, established on the principle
that "everything which savours of compulsion
is harmful." He started a magazine to promote
his notions on education and at the same time
served as an official arbitrator for grievances
between the nobles and the recently emanci-
pated serfs. By the end of 1863 he was so ex-
hausted that he discontinued his activities and
retired to the steppes to drink koumis for his
health.
Tolstoy had been contemplating marriage
for some time, and in 1862 he married Sophie
Behrs, sixteen years his junior, and the daugh-
ter of a fashionable Moscow doctor. Their
early married life at Yasnaya Polyana was
tranquil. Family cares occupied the Countess,
and in the course of her life she bore thirteen
children, nine of whom survived infancy. Yet
she also acted as a copyist for her husband,
who after their marriage turned again to writ-
ing. He was soon at work upon "a novel of
the i8io's and *2o's" which absorbed all his
time and effort. He went frequently to Mos-
cow, "studying letters, diaries, and traditions"
and "accumulated a whole library" of histori-
cal material on the period. He interviewed
survivors of the battles of that time and trav-
eled to Borodino to draw up a map of the
battleground. Finally, in 1869, after his work
had undergone several changes in conception
and he had "spent five years of uninterrupted
andjgxceptionally strenuous labor Tnnierthe

Peace. Its appearance immediately established
Tolstoy's reputation, and in the judgment of
Turgenev, the acknowledged dean of Russian
letters, gave him "first place among all our
contemporary writers."

Arkham Asylum was a revolutionary game. Arkham City was as well. By contrast, Arkham Origins is viewed as an evolutionary game, and between that and the fact that the principal actors and development studio have been replaced a lot of people figured "eh, I don't need to play this for a year." Technically speaking, Arkham Origins does feature revolutionary additions over the previous games, but it's in an area that nobody particularly asked for in the first place: online competitive multiplayer. I myself have yet to even launch it, but given that it's developed by Splash Damage I'm sure it's not slapped together. They did after all make the Return to Castle Wolfenstein multiplayer (which got carried over into Enemy Territory, and then Quake Wars, etc).
The thing about the single-player is that while it's good, you literally cannot help but compare it against Arkham City the entire time. The combat system and animations are completely carried over, with some additions. You have some new gadgets (one is allegedly "new" but in reality is functionally identical to something else from Arkham City) and face a few new common foes. Luckily, one of the gadgets is straight out of Super Inframan and makes combat even more satisfying since you trounce everyone with it, and the others give you more options during the Predator encounters. The enemy AI is altered since the rate at which you counter rather than strike has gone way, way up. Boss battles are VASTLY improved over the previous games, as each one emphasizes that you do different things. At no point do you feel "well, this is the same thing I did for the last boss."
But even with that said, at most points you DO feel "well, I've done this before." Aside from the combat, the sidequests have you doing the same gameplay mechanic as 2 years ago (and 4 years ago) albeit for a different cosmetic reason. Example: in Arkham City you have to quickly travel across the city to answer phones in time to stop a killer. Here, you have to do the same to defuse bombs. It's the same map as Arkham City, albeit with some new zones. It helps a little that you can now fast travel. But there must be fewer grapple points because getting from place to place is a little trickier than it used to be.
You'll be fighting and fighting, and with the random "crimes in progress" that spawn, you'll fight more. You're rarely going to be scanning the environment unless you're prompted to do so. Crime scene investigations are a new addition, but much like the show CSI you aren't really doing anything yourself. The computer is magically reconstructing a series of events based on your having scanned a body and a spot of blood (which they can't show as red). Then you go beat up a guy. You can't inadvertently defeat the person you meant to interrogate either, so there's no "save this guy for last" aspect to combat. But you are now given grades for each encounter, such that higher grades yield XP bonuses. Winning is largely a foregone conclusion given that you're Batman, but winning with an A or S rank is the tough part. In fact, I still haven't gotten the last one because it doesn't always play the *wham* sound effect to denote you KO'ed someone with a hit (I call this the "BATMAAAAAN!" since if I could mod this game I would replace that sound with the screaming pug). The game offers various challenges for additional bonuses and upgrades, but it's buggy about deciding whether or not some of them "count." I busted my♥♥♥♥♥doing the "do 4 exotic takedowns in a Predator section" and then it didn't count it. And then it turned out there were no more Predator sections in the game. AND it won't let you complete those challenges on the challenge maps, so if you don't do it during the story you're screwed...unless you replay it on the much harder New Game+ mode...
The reduced architecture grapples and increased enemy attack rates are somewhat minor, but if there's a major "step backwards" here it's one of atmosphere. This Gotham City isn't yet overrun with supervillains who've marked their territory and themed their gangs. The incentive to see the world isn't really as strong. The Riddler's challenges were designed to direct you to all the cool little references, but at this point there is no "Riddler" etc so you're basically completing the challenges for the sake of hearing the "extortion data that's going to harm innocent people" recordings. Except pretty much all of them pertain to supervillains and corrupt civil servants whom you take down anyway. It feels more like a task since there's less "reward" for doing it. Why oppose this so strongly? That's the REAL enigma.
The strong negative online backlash to Arkham City's criminal dialogue means that EVERYTHING pertaining to threats or abusive language is long gone (that already got walked back since the Arkham City DLC) so pat yourselves on the back, Team "Woke" Gaming. Between that and the fact that Batman is less infallible at this stage of his career, the writing has gotten a lot more praise compared to Arkham City. But for me, it feels less satisfying to beat people up because I overheard them saying they're cold and hungry, or that they're resorting to crime because they lost their job and now they have to not be home on Christmas Eve. This definitely plays into the "Batman as fascist authoritarian conservative" reading of the character. I kind of wonder if the writers just hate Batman as a concept, since the villains all expose the flaws in his approach and morality and Batman has no answer because he can't admit "the reason I can't kill you is because you're all too profitable as IP."
Also, the game takes place over a few hours on Christmas Eve into Christmas Day, yet the amount that happens is absurd. True, a lot happened during Arkham City, but there was planning leading up to it. How can these locations be THIS devastated and re-renovated in just a few hours? And it's not even accidental; the game points out "yeah, it's been 3 hours." On the other hand, James Gordon isn't Commissioner yet, so the cops are pretty much all dirty. In this game you get to beat up SWAT team guys, which is the part of "Year One" that is the most important.
The Assassin's Creed guy as Batman has his highs and mids since he's mostly forced to imitate Kevin Conroy, but with a name like "Roger Smith" you'd think he was BORN to impersonate Kevin Conroy's Batman! Troy Baker (who already nailed his Richard Moll Two-Face impersonation in Arkham City) is about as dead-on a mimicry of Mark Hamill's Joker as one could hope, given that Mark can no longer really do that voice anymore. Richard Epcar (voice of the Joker in the fighting games) has a few background lines that jump out to me, but I guess he also directed a lot of the secondary dialogue recordings.
I enjoyed Arkham Origins, but I'd still say to hold off on getting it. Not so much because of the issues described above so much as the fact that there's a ton of DLC and all of it's spread out across platforms and retailers due to exclusivity (Challenge maps where you're Bruce Wayne in training, etc). There's a Season Pass which includes that stuff, but it costs another $20 and for now is almost entirely cosmetic. They say there'll be at least one story DLC, but what'll it be about? Maybe something inspired by The Long Halloween? I don't know, so I don't know if that, a few challenge maps, and some cosmetic skins are really worth the money. For now I'd say to pick this up once a "complete edition" is available unless you happen to buy a new video card that bundles it.

Do I recommend this game? That all depends on one simple question.
Did you absolutely and unquestionably love Batman: Arkham City?
If yes, then you will undoubtably enjoy Batman: Arkham Oranges. It is essentially more of the same; the beating on goons, the Riddler puzzles and slick gadgets with some Far Cry 3♥♥♥♥♥Creed style "sort the towers to reveal the map" mechanics thrown in.
If you answered No to my previous question, even if you just "liked" B: AC, then I would approach Arkham Oranges with caution.
Whilst the premise of an earlier, "rookie" version of Batman is rather interesting; this is oddly perforated by a couple of niggling plot holes. "If this is a prequel, why does Batman have all the gear I had at the end of City?".
Sure, for most players who just want to enjoy "being" Batman, such things won't matter. However, issues with the much lauded FreeFlow combat system will. For some unknown reason, WB Montreal have slightly "altered" the flow and timing of the combo system from the one used in the previous games. This results in you often messing up combos, usually leading to a thwack in the back of the head.
All in all, I can't be too negative on the game as it is very well polished and runs much better than it's predecessor (although that might be down to the joyful omission of GamesForWindowsLive).
Warner Bros. Montreal have crafted a nice looking and, for fans of the series, enjoyable game, however there's no escaping the "tribute album" feeling.

Typical Klei: an insanely addictive game.
A pretty difficult game until you get the hang of it. I was growing very frustrated at some point because my troops were seemingly doing absolutely nothing of value when I reached a certain progression. The duplicants would just run around like headless chickens, forgetting to power the oxygen generator, food machine, and generally just puking their guts out and breaking stuff.
So here are the main two pro tips:
- duplicants need a lot of oxygen. Don't grow your colony too much until you're 100% positive you can generate enough in a short amount of time.
- duplicants are not good at deciding what to do. Assign them to very specific tasks, e.g.: one builder, one cook, one delivery guy.
Once you have the tasks balanced out, the game is actually very rewarding. You'll make slow progress, but everything will run smoothly. The game systems really do work once you've figured them out.

The game is a survival simulation, and it executes that well even in the 'early access' state. The updates thus far have been meaningful changes that add additional gameplay depth, and expand the potential challenges of the game. Perhaps the cartoonish artwork and lighthearted style is why some people have commented on the game not having a purpose. It is an uncomplicated simulation game at its core; survival is the point. Admittedly simulation games can be sterile, where the focus on the accuracy of the simulation often takes focus over graphics and tone. Oxygen Not Included makes the genre more palatable, without obstructing the challenge and enjoyment of managing a colony of genetically printed rejects and the sometimes idiotic things they do.
Terrific game, and terrific devs.

I played Banjo Kazooie last year, relishing in each level and collecting every note and jiggy. It is a masterpiece, a delight from start to finish. This tribute to Rareware collectathons harbors only a shell of that, YL is riddled with shortcomings in every aspect. To the apologists who claim you'll like this if you enjoyed BK, you are wrong.
The game falls apart at the most basic level. Your talon-trot knockoff (for scaling steep slopes) controls like a fat man on a unicycle, slippery and imprecise. Bonus gift: now there's a stamina bar so you can't even move quickly across the game's pointlessly massive levels without taking a breath and slowing down.
Nearly every puzzle is an annoying game of where's waldo. You see a switch you have to press. In BK, Kazooie fires an egg at it. Simple and instant. In here you have to pause everything you're doing to find the annoying item (ice flower), eat it, run back and shoot it all on a very short timer.
The levels are too enormous, sprawling, and confusing without any regard for making them mesh into a solid unit. Each puzzle is just a glued on, interchangable setpiece pulled out at random. Finding the last
pagies in any world is a needle in a barn of haystacks. There is no greater pain than trying to solve a cryptic puzzle but not having the equipment you need to do it, then having to walk all the way back to it for 20 minutes once it's solvable.
Every level has a minecart and a retro arcade minigame. These are some of the most painfully shoehorned elements that fail to emulate the games that inspired them. The minecart controls like flaming garbage (suprise, there's a boss fight in one), while the arcade cabinet games are all uninspired tedium. Enjoy playing each arcade cabinet twice, because they lock TWO pagies behind each.
There isn't a shred of inspiration to be found in here, just a bunch of memories ripped wholesale from better games.
The levels themselves are bright and refreshingly colorful. However, the art direction leaves a bit to be desired. There are way too many recycled characters that don't mesh with any environemnt, plenty of bland open space, and annoyingly hidden destinations. They had to use neon purple arrows to highlight the recurring NPC who gives you new abilities. The most jarring and unnaturally cheap method of seizing your attention. No effort went into making your gaze naturally fall upon your next destination, and every world feels like it was just a bunch of random setpieces mashed together.
Grant Kirkhope makes his return, composing the musical score as he did for Rare's N64 collecathons. Many of the songs use the same soundfont as these classic titles, a stroke of genius that easily harkens back to those older days.
Sadly that's where the good decisions end. None of these songs hold even the slightest candle to the torch that is Treasure Trove Cove, let alone the myriad of other brilliant pieces in their older games. I walked away from this game unable to remember a single song in Yooka-Laylee.
Breaking the 4th wall isn't funny. Doing it again doesn't make it funnier. There's zero measure of suspense. No one's been kidnapped. There isn't a giant canon ready to destroy the island. There isn't even any proper resolution. Maybe the next game will provide some answers.
Looking down at any massive level from high in the sky really overwhelms you with the sheer mass of content. This becomes a detriment when you realize that you'll be painstakingly exploring every little nook to find the items that may or may not be hidden inside.
I died very many times in this game--luckily the game sets you with an infinite number of lives, and you lose almost zero progress when you screw up. Individual puzzles range from braindead easy to controller-breaking frustration when they refuse to follow your inputs. The difficulty just tanks to absolute zero once you can fly over all the obstacles and platforms. Finding your destination is still a frustrating mess though. Combat is broken with enemies that randomly don't take damage. You will run across many puzzles you can't solve until several hours later when you get the right abilities. The few ways in which it's hard are all for the wrong reasons.
These ex-Rareware developers really missed the mark. This game is only an emulation of a collecathon on paper, none of the qualities that made Banjo Kazooie a masterpiece can be found here. Here's one image to summarize this whole disaster.

I finally found my way to "Max Payne 3", and as preparation before the third installment, I decided to revisit the first two games to brush up on the story, get in the right mood, and simply to see if they still hold up as well as I remembered them. They do. In fact, they're even better, with me being a more mature gamer and properly appreciating the work of art that is the MP franchise.
MP was the game which introduced bullet time to gaming in a way that worked. Not only as a gimmick, but rather as a core gameplay element. Without it, and without using is smartly on top of that, you'd get nowhere. And be warned, MP doesn't pamper you and take you by the hand. It kicks you in the butt and shoves you right into the thick of it. That is to say, the game is H-A-R-D. Very, very hard. Even on the lowest (and default) difficulty setting bad guys ambush you all the times, they shoot very straight, and can mow you down in a couple of well placed hits. The quick save button will be your best friend (and occasionally you'll end up using it more than the 'shoot' button). MP is truly an unforgiving shooter, requiring a tactical approach to every gunfight: where you have to pick your targets carefully, when to roll, when to evade, where you'll land afterwards, who'll be remaining standing... otherwise - GAME OVER.
And then, there's the story - a hard-boiled noir crime drama told through comic book style panels, with superb voice acting and an amazingly well-written script. Even if the gameplay weren't so fun, MP would still have you in its grip solely because of the plot.
To conclude: an all-around amazing game, still incredibly fun even if its age does show. Despite that, it blows the majority of modern shooters out of the water. Needles to say, a must have title. I don't trust a gamer who doesn't like MP.

Game: Max Payne
Genre: Third Person Shooter
Developer: Remedy Entertainment
System: PC (Steam)
Total Score: 84/100
Value Score: 8.4/10
• Story: 10/10
o The story of Max Payne takes place in New York in the year 2001, however the story begins three years prior to the events of the current game. Max Payne is a police detective part of the NYPD, he had a great life going, a beautiful wife, a new baby girl and a good job. However everything comes at a price and his story is about to go down in a grim path. One day his wife and daughter were murdered in cold blood at his home in New Jersey, he quickly dispatched the murders however his family was slaughtered. A few years later in the year 2001 Max Payne's search for the real murders continues until he finally reaches a clue which will lead him to the right direction however what he might find will be far bigger than he had anticipated and will initiate his fall.
• Characters: 8/10
o Max Payne's characters are like from a usual Noire style film or a Mafia film better put as an example. All from the character designs towards the voice over, it feels like you are watching one of the great 1900s movies about gangs which is a pretty nice touch to the environment and the storyline. The best character of course is the main character, so much personality even through his narrator dialog that he speaks in majority of the game. The character designs for the enemies however may feel generic at first but the amount of different enemies is actually pretty big for a somewhat short game. The characters are best represented in the noire style film comic that is displayed throughout the entire game and that is how the storyline is shown to the player.
• GamePlay: 10/10
o Max Payne is your typical third person shooter, you play as Max Payne who can get access to all sorts of weapons and tools ranging from pistols, shotguns, rifles, grenade launchers, snipers, baseball bats, grenades and Molotov bottles. You also have a special ability called "Bullet Time" (which can be used with the right mouse button) which slows down the game enough for the player to do attacks against enemies with their weapon allowing you to do Matrix like moves in the process for precise aiming. You also get access to various amounts of Pain pills which can be used to heal your health. You'll be breaking through carts, boxes, cases and all sorts of instruments to get these items which will help you kill enemies. Enemies will usually pop up without warning, you can sneak up to them or even snipe them at different occasions. You'll also be prompted to start cutscenes showcasing the game's narration through a noire style film comic which you can replay with use of the F1 button. Pressing the F5 button saves the game F9 will load the game back to the previous state it was saved. You can press the number keys to switch weapons easily or roll the mouse wheel. Pressing space will let you jump and the usual WASD combo is used for walking in default mode. Pressing R will allow you reload ammo to your weapon and pressing E will allow you to search objects with exclamation points above them when you get near them or allow you to zoom in for sniping a enemy with a sniper rifle. You also have a arrange of difficulty modes which can only be accessed once you finish the default normal mode and have access to the credits automatically.
• Graphics: 7/10
o Max Payne's graphics at the time were in the mixture of N64/PSX and PS2/Dreamcast graphics. Although majority of the character sprites look like they were cardboard character cut outs from the WWF/WWE games, the environment, cutscenes and the narrator scenes were nicely done and matches with the story quite well. Adding a bleak color and setting to the storyline was well made and feels like you are in a movie. If you enjoyed games like GTA III you will not have any worries with this game.
• Sound: 10/10
o The voice acting in this game is simply amazing and you can tell they chose the best actors for the game. It really feels like you are watching a classic mafia/gang movie from the late 1900s. The sound effects from weapons, attacks, noises from the environment and characters were nicely made and was a rare thing back in its time.
• Music: 7/10
o The music may not be as good as other games but when it does play it brings up the mood and makes players feel like adrenaline rushing through their veins while fighting against enemies. Although majority of the game will not have any music unless you are fighting through a midway battle against the main enemies or against a "Boss" like character, the intro music plays during cutscenes giving a eerie feeling to the already gloomy and iconic movie like environment.
• Length: 6/10
o Max Payne 1 on PC is divided into three parts with about 7-9 chapters each with a prologue in the beginning as well to introduce the player to what the situation is. The main storyline should take you about 7 hours to complete and if you keep exploring through the terrain of the levels and areas within the game it could even take you up to 13 hours.
• Replay Value: 6/10
o Max Payne's replay value mostly comes from two extra levels which can be gained once you get to a higher difficulty. The game includes three additional difficulties which two of them can be unlocked at the end of the first playthrough and the third after a playthrough with one of the higher difficulty modes. The two extra levels adds extra challenge and little to no actual storyline however but it is great for replay value wise for players who want more hours squeezed out in this game.
• Player Value: 10/10
o Max Payne for the PC is an amazing experience. If you enjoyed noire type films, mafia style themed movies or action pack movies you will enjoy this game. To add to the amazing storyline and characters, you have an amazing gameplay system implemented that gives you more control to the game than most other shooters which also paves way towards future shooting games. Get this game on Steam now which is available with its sequel. You will not regret it.

I'm going to start this review by being negative. This is not to savage the work that Little Green Men did on this game, but rather to emphasize the positive bits later.
"Starpoint Gemini 2" has some pretty rough areas. The campaign, framed through (sometimes yawn-inducing) text boxes and uneven voice-acting, didn't connect with me very well. There's an interesting twist here and there, but I just couldn't manage to care that much about what was going on. The necessary "gloss-n-polish" doesn't exist, especially with the game dialogue writers having a strange aversion to using the word "the."
The game's difficulty curve is lumpy and strange, with the procedural mission generation apparently taking into account your level, but not what ship you have. This is also aggravated by a lack of mission information. Especially with the campaign, you don't know that much about what you're heading into. It's possible to get to a point where you just "hit a wall," and get thrown into an engagment that you simply can't win without (at least) having gotten into the next class of ship. There's nothing wrong with this if you have some sort of warning, but for it to happen suddenly and with no advance notice is a kind of "fake difficulty" that I dislike.
(I can appreciate a game that's not interested in hand-holding, but there's also a point where it all turns into sloppy experience design. "Freelancer" got this right by walling you off from taking the next campaign mission if you didn't have the prerequisites. "SG2" gets it wrong by basically telling you nothing aside from the story's flavortext. I simply don't equate legitimate game challenge with failing to communicate effectively.)
I finally got to the point where seeing what happened next in the story was insufficient incentive to work my way up to a more durable spacecraft.
But here's the thing - the above happened more than once. This is where things go positive; That I got pulled back into the experience is a testimony to just how well the basic gameplay loop was crafted.
What the developers really managed to do beautifully is to create an addicting "travel, do, upgrade, repeat" cycle that keeps dragging you back in. The space you fly through is nicely crafted, with a sense of scale that is large without having interminable length between interesting features. The combat is generally satisfying (as long as you're not in a situation where it's overwhelming), and the other game mechanics manage to be pretty deep without being clunky or hard to get your mind around. Other free-roaming space games give you all kinds of controls, and then those controls don't behave consistently (or at all) as you expect. This title, on the other hand, is very solid in terms of behaving intelligently when you give commands.
If Little Green Men Games built a sequel that was basically the same core mechanics, but with a far more refined mission (both campaign and procedural) experience, they would be in the same league as "Freelancer." The foundation is there - it just needs to be built upon.

Batman Arkham Origin: success or failure?
When we get a sequel to some successful game we can take either of the two approaches. The first one (and it is more common) claims any sequel should be better than the original. It must have some cool new features, it ought to be full of innovations, additional options and richer plot and /or gameplay.
The second approach is not so strict (though less common). It supposes if the original game was cool and tough the sequel must be also cool and tough and nothing more is needed.
But as I have already mentioned the first method of assessment is much more wide spread. For example Bioshock 1 was (and is) considered a masterpiece while Bioshock 2 was considered a rather weak sequel for the simple reason it did not have any expansion and development. Yet Bioshock infinite is again considered another masterpiece for it is actually is full of new and astonishing features (while the general story (shooting) line remains the same. But if you remember Indiana Jones set of three original movies (I can’t see anything but parody in the Crystal Skull Jones movie) you are unlikely to see any clear improving and development, and still it does not prevent the three Indiana movies to be excellent.
As for Batman Arkham series, the first game – Batman Arkham Asylum – was a breakthrough in the genre and it got (deservedly) the highest marks. Batman Arkham City in its turn met all the requirements that a sequel must meet according to the strict first approach. The game space got bigger, the story got richer and more sinister, Batman himself got new gadgets and skills. Also we got a lot of new characters and the sequel became even better than the original.
After I had played Batman Arkham City for several times I learnt there was another Batman on the way. I was glad and disappointed at the same time. I was glad to know I would return to Gotham City again and experience being a Dark Knight once more having another exciting adventure. Also I was worried as I learnt the new Batman Arkham game was being produced not by the original Rocksteady studio but by another group, Warner Brothers Montreal.
