Arkham Origins is slick and dark, but in terms of gameplay it's ultimately an imitation of its predecessors. It tells a story certainly worth telling, and it tells it wonderfully through great visuals, characterisations and performances, but all this wonderful work from the artists and writers and actors is framed within gameplay that is at best, a rung below its predecessors, and at worst, broken. I shall label my review using what I believe were WB's buzzwords during development.
SIZE: The city is enormous. This is both a blessing and a curse. For the impressive size of the landscape, there is not much to see but a whole mess of thugs and otherwise empty streets. Every single inhabitant is indoors, and there seems to be an overt amount of wasted space in the sprawling mass that is Gotham City. A testament to the fantastic design of Arkham City was the fact that every place had a secret to hide, whether within or without. Every building existed as either a functional location, important landmark, or simply to enhance the atmosphere. In AO this functionality is left behind to make way for SIZE.
DARK: The game is a darker, grittier portrayal of a younger, angrier Batman. As such, the game as a whole loses some of the sillier parts present in Arkham Asylum and AC - Bane is no teddy-cuddler, and the Joker has absolutely no qualms about killing many, many people in the blink of an eye. I praise the writer for his efforts, specifically in the sense that for every question I asked of the characters (e.g. Batman, ffs, why didn't you let him die?!) the story had an answer, or at least a demonstration of the toll that Batman's choices take on him.
VISUALS: AO is a slick game, in the sense that everything looks lovely. The character models are highly detailed, and the snow and water and ice and the lights of the city and the facades on the building are all rendered in glorious hi-definition. However, I feel that the focus on visual fidelity has left a number of gameplay issues wanting.
First of all - the E. Nigma quests. Because Edward isn't yet The Riddler, he hardly can be strutting around telling riddles, can he? Unfortunately, this means that you spend most of your time tediously checking off the dozens of collectible and destructible items around the city. And gone are the many references to Batman lore that gave the previous games a 'lived in' feel and a deeper personality.
Secondly - the rules of the gameplay. Given that the game has been patched a number of times since launch, this has, in a way, cleared itself up to an extent, as some of the issues were bugs. But the more I played the more frustrating I found the fact that the rules of the gameplay would change depending on how the developers saw fit. The niggly 'invisible wall' factor  dictates much of your movement in the game. Whereas the other two games were designed smartly in the sense that there was nothing like this to break the suspension of disbelief, this game is littered with pipes you can't go over or under, walls you can't scale, and ledges you can't grapple to.
Ultimately, I recommend this game. It looks great, the writing and characterisations are fantastic, and the combat is mostly fluid, with the boss battles being a lot more varied and fun than in previous iterations. While I don't think it's strictly a 'step up' in terms of what the series delivers, it's perhaps more of a 'step sideways', or a 'diagonal left' (to confuse the metaphor more). In saying that, I felt myself often distracted by a lament for what was lost in the transition away from the studio that knew how to make a game for the player. Rocksteady had an eye for detail that meant they avoided the petty but frustrating issues that litter AO, and WB Montreal feel like they attempted to grasp beyond their reach and failed. Were this the only game in the series, I would be lauding it a masterpiece. However, the existence of the Rocksteady games perhaps means not that AO is exposed as a poorly made game, but that AA and AC are exposed as the brilliant intuitive pieces of work that they are.

Batman Arkham Origins review text version:
Batman Arkham Origins is a worthy game to add to the series, although does feel like the stamp  Warner Bros. development studio have left on the game leans on the side of  subtlety rather than being overtly obvious. In a way, the game feels like an expansion of Arkham City, and tends not to stray too far from the tried and trusted formula - which can be considered a good or bad thing depending on how you view things. That said, there's really  little to fault here other than the sheer amount of hand holding, and perhaps lack of ambition with the franchise that leaves a somewhat by-the-numbers and over familiar experience. Fans will love the game, although might disagree with some of the villain choices used. Action gamers can once again take to the skies with ease and become the Dark Knight  again with fresh things to do, and that's what really counts.

This is a game that completely shocked me. I knew nothing about Borderlands during it's release. Being honest, I thought, "oh great, another shooter... I bet it's some cliche post apocalyptic first preson shooter where the player is the game's only last hope. Just another Call of Duty. GUNS?! Ughh. Boringgggggg!"
HOWEVER, I ended up recieving it as a gift thanks to a good friend, and I was completely wrong.
Borderlands 2 is meant to be played CO-OP with friends. Everything is well done. The game provides a large variety of guns with different abilities and elements.  You have to plan and think which gun is good for what situation and some are just straight out flashy and worth keeping just for personal preference. There is also a detailed skill tree system that allows the player to create the most BADASS character where the player can focus on what they want the most on. Best of all, there no pressure because everything is straight out obvious and there no PVP, so you never feel overwhelmed by tryign to make a perfect character to compete with others. I choose the cheap way and just max out my Turrent on the Commendo class. While the good character creation and a variety of guns are great, the gameplay can vary. At times, it can get really intense, ostentatious, BADASS! Hordes of enemies left to right, explosions everywhere, your PC probably screaming and explosing inside by the amount of particles  and graphical effects happenning in your screen. But, if you aren't a fan of shooters, you may at times find it repetitive as there are certain moments that feel the same. Some can argue it's just player heads to objective and kill a horde of enemies every time. I can't blame you if you feel like that, but...
Borderlands 2 is the epitone for story games that prove that a fantastic story makes a game better even if it feels like a fetch and grind MMO style game. It took a game that barely had a story and  used all the characters and story plot to create this  shockly interesting story. It's like if you took coal and turn it into gold, but this is gold writing!  In addition, Handsome Jack, a new character, is pretty much the main star of the game as he guides the player throughout the game and introduces the history of Paradora. The humor in some way is very immature, childish, and goofy that you'd think it would have been written by a 12 year old. However, in my opinion everything is soo balance and even immature cussing jokes are actually funny and never feel overuesd. Being a child I am, I always get a laugh when I hear the word "Badass". (However, I know some people would disagree, so read about it with caution when buying). Reguardless, it's soo well done that you end up wanting to know more about the game, so you end up doing every single side quest just to know what exactly happen. Almost no quest feels like a chore because the story is what motivates you to keep playing. During your progression, he does so many bad thing in such a sarcastic and sinster way that you can't wait to have the opporunity to punch him right in his freaken handsome face. but at the same time, you begin to hate him in a way that you're actually interested in knowing more about him if that makes sense. Who exactly is he, how did he take over Hyperion corporation, why does he hate you and the vault hunters so much, why is he so freaken handsome?!?!!
Buy the GOTY during a sale! Some of the season pass and level packs expansion are essential for the true experience! Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragon Keep expansion DLC is the minimum you need if you are just interested in the story because it is the conclusion of the story of Borderlands 2. This is no Mass Effect 3, I promise you that! The ending on Borderlands 2 is satisfying, but Tiny Tina concludes the game in a surpising way. Not to mention, who doesn't love dungeons and dragons?
Overall, I absolutely recommend this game to anyone as long as you have friends to play with. It can be played alone. If you do, I recommend Commando or Mechromancer class because they have the ability to spawn a turrent or mech-robot that aids the player in tough situations.

First off, let me be clear - this game is great, and I do feel like I got my money's worth. However, it's only by a fine margin that I can honestly recommend it.
I'll explain by getting the negatives out the way first, then I can get onto the good stuff - the total time I've spent playing is entirely solo. Now, granted, that might lead to bias in this review, but do stick with me. It's a brilliant game on the first two playthroughs, with a great selection of characters and a gorgeous overworld, both of which I'll get to later. The problems started setting in on my third playthrough, on Ultimate Vault Hunter Mode.
To newcomers (to whom I recommend playing the first game first), I'll explain some of the mechanics - there are various "elementals" that can be used to inflict damage on enemies, slag being one, and it simply increases damage dealt by non-slag weapons. Also, when you die, you pay a proportionate sum of your total money to respawn. Finally, in Ultimate Vault Hunter mode, enemies spawn with 2x health than in True Vault Hunter mode, where the enemies in turn have 2x more health than in Normal mode. They also now have regenerating health. These mechanics become important to explain my frustrations.
Since this review is based on my experience, I'll try not to turn it into a rant as much as I can.
Before starting this playthrough I found that I'd be capped at level 50, which happened towards the end of True Vault Hunter Mode (playthrough 2). I also found out about the two extra level DLCs which would take me up to level 72 if bought. As I began UVHM I actually felt pressured to buy them. £7.98 out of pocket, misery then ensued for the next thirty or so hours, consisting of switching between my slag weapon and my infinity pistol (a pistol that never needs to reload - without which, I honestly believe I couldn't finish the game), and dying - quite literally - twenty or so seconds into my latest respawn. During my playthrough of the Tiny Tina DLC, I was left with $200,000 after accumulating about $2.5m because I was continuously at the mercy of the Handsome Dragon's fire breath, and it must have taken me the best part of 90 minutes of slag-shoot-die-repeat to finally *just* manage to beat it. In the end, I wasn't gratified or happy. I was downright frustrated, because what should have been a straightforward boss was simply a bullet-sponge - an artificial difficulty mechanic, if you will. And I'm not exaggerating when I say that unless you go farming for unique or legendary weapons - which I won't, and shouldn't have to - this is all Ultimate Vault Hunter Mode consists of. The feeling of progression is also gone since the enemies level up alongside you now. I want to feel gratified plowing through hordes of crazed bandits and robots, not playing in fear of my next step triggering an encounter of thirty enemies made of lead. The best part? There are even "Overpower levels" after Ultimate Vault Hunter mode, where you remain on your own level whilst enemies level up even further. That isn't gratifying gameplay. That is simply punishing.
This leads me on to the solo experience on this difficulty, which is dire. I can definitely see it being more fun with three other players, that is if your idea of fun involves what would probably be reviving each other every minute or so. I could be wrong, but this scenario seems highly likely. Another problem of not playing with others is that all the raid bosses - yes, all of them - are completely out of your league alone. I mean, the regular bosses that are supposed to be designed for solo players are enough of bullet-sponges as they are, but making the raid bosses unbeatable simply because I choose to play alone? Really?
Finally - and I think this is an issue right across the board, and not just with Ultimate Vault Hunter mode - the way the guns are balanced is downright miserable. In the first game, three things stood out to me as great: the abundance of chests filled with satisfying and usable loot, how you could keep, say, a level 12 gun and it'd be completely fine against enemies even up to say, level 18 and how guns were truly randomised, with the possibility of getting shotguns shooting rockets, and pistols shooting shotgun shells. Borderlands 2 does carry this on, but to a foul, foul limit. Chests are scarce with a far lower chance of getting a decent gun. You can keep a blue/purple rarity (moderate rarity) gun for say, one or two levels before it becomes obsolete. The most varied gun I found was a scripted reward drop consisting of a shotgun that shot exploding swords, which is great out of context, but in a game where there are more rules to the randomisation, it's more of a moment of relief. Then, you level up, and your exploding-sword-shooting shotgun is now completely useless and you'll have to sell it. Aw.
Now, despite my actual seething anger at these parts of the gameplay, the good stuff does outweigh it, and explains why I continued grinding through UVHM for thirty-plus hours. The characters, both new and returning faces, are fun and fleshed-out, all with quirks that make them unique. The player-characters from the first game serve as core NPCs in this game which is a nice touch, and brings familiarity and life to the once seldom talking characters you played as before. The antagonist, Handsome Jack, taunts you relentlessly throughout the entire game, flaunting his power and wealth, and making below-the-belt jokes about you and other characters whenever he can. I won't spoil his character development but it really is worth the playthrough to watch him change. Plot twists come across as genuinely surprising, and the story in general retains the comedy value from the first game, although it does have far more fluidity and substance this time around. The planet of Pandora is vast and worth exploring, and full of colourful characters and gorgeous scenery. I still find new places to explore even after three playthroughs and finishing the DLC. The cel-shading divides players, and personally I like them - it matches the light-heartedness of the game in general. Levelling up feels rewarding, with skill trees adding to player customisation and progression.
Since I bashed the third playthrough so much, I should probably recommend that you don't bother with it if you're more concerned with gameplay experience and overall enjoyment than level grinding. Play through the game on Normal difficulty, and again on True Vault Hunter mode. Then, if you get the DLC - which I highly recommend - play through that on True Vault Hunter mode too.
So, to summarise - the game, along with its DLC, is one to buy for the story and overall experience, but only if you aren't interested in repeatedly getting your goods handed to you on the hardest difficulty setting. Ultimate Vault Hunter Mode is literally "trigger enemy spawn-slag-shoot-die-repeat", and it is downright miserable, but if you outright don't bother with it, you're left with an otherwise great game, and at the very least a great solo experience. Having not played with others, I feel like I have to recommend doing so. It does get lonely on Pandora when you're on your own, so get your friends together and kick Handsome Jack in his handsome face.
TL;DR
Pros:
+ Great story, world, characters, et cetera
+ Graphics are appealing
+ Combines FPS and MMO-style gameplay well
+ Skill trees contribute to feeling of progression in first two playthroughs
Cons:
- Ultimate Vault Hunter Mode is 30+ hours of pure misery and self-loathing, with no feeling of progression
- Overpower levels are downright silly
- Guns aren't as well-balanced or as varied as in Borderlands 1
- Passively pressures you into buying £8 worth of extra levelling up
- Game is constantly skewed towards multiplayer, especially noticeable during boss fights
- Most boss fights are simply bullet-sponges

Thoroughly enjoying my time with Yooka-Laylee so far.
In terms of comparison to Banjo Kazooie I think Playtonic have sucessfully captured what made Banjo kazooie great and improved upon it in some cases. examples of this are Jinjo hunting (or the equivalent of) has been altered so for each critter a different task need to be used. The Pagies are sentient meaning you get some cool dialogue with the main currency you're collecting and the quills will never respawn once collected making it easy to know where to pick up ones you havent found before (something I found quite frustrating in Banjo Kazooie)
It's important to note that you can't complete one world to 100% before moving onto another meaning that you will constantly need to be travelling between worlds in order to obtain and unlock new moves and pagies. Even in spite of the fact that Playtonic have put emphasis on "choosing" how you play you will still end up with a bunch of worlds open in varying states of completion which can feel like you're getting lost under a huge pile of things to do.
Visual cohestion is great each world that I have visited so far has had a really interesting visual style and theme music. While they are quite large they do feel a little disjointed just based on the amount of doors you walk through making each world a series of smaller platforming sections it becomes easy to get a flow for where you're going and traversing these worlds can be a lot of fun.
Overall I would definitely reccomend Yooka-Laylee as a fan of Banjo Kazooie I think this is a truly worthy successor.

I think this game has been treated unfairly since it's release.  If all the JonTron drama wasn't there, this game would have received a lot of "nostalgia" positive reviews.  But this nostalgia is now considered "outdated".  This game is fun, really beautiful, it has a cast of fun characters, a huge world, tons of collectibles and a lot of rewards.  It really makes you want to explore every inch of this world, and that's great.  It's bigger than Banjo-Kazooie and Banjo-Tooie, and it's actually a great successor of the series.  I grew up playing 3 platformers: Banjo-Kazooie, Super Mario 64 and Spyro.  Spyro evolved into something really weird, focused in an "adult" audience.  Mario 64 evolved into Mario Sunshine and Mario Galaxy, which is great, but I feel like Banjo,DK64 and Conker never received a proper continuation.
Yooka-Laylee is a proper sequel to all those N64 games and it's great how fun it is.  I really expect more games like this in the future. Consider supporting this kind of games if you are feeling this kind of games should be back.
My only complain would be it's a little bit difficult to control the camera and sometimes it's awful.  Also, it has some minor performance problems.  But still, it's really enjoyable.

Starpoint Gemini 2 is extensive and packs in an incredible amount and variety of content, especially with the two current DLCs. The map itself is evident to this. I myself enjoy the  freeplay mode, as it allows for more customization of my character and allows for a more unique exploration of the world.
Not to mention the unique dynamics the game allows, including the combat mechanics, political affiliations, etc.
The main achievement of this game- its size- is also part of an issue that it has. This issue is the immersion level.
Apart from the storylines and cutscenes, the only way to interact with other ships is to either repair them or (more often) fight them. Such a big world with only limited interaction can begin to feel... empty.
In a universe potrayed by Starpoint Gemini, such an expansive space, the aspect of trade would be very important.
I suggest a new dynamic with other ships that would allow the player to trade with them. In essence, using the same model as that when docked in a space station but with friendly freighters, carriers, etc.
Another suggestion is to add randomized large scale battles between rivaling territories. It seems odd to me that a system in such turmoil has so little actual conflict after the storyline. Not to mention being part of large scale battles is a thrilling experience.
Finally (I am unsure if your system allows for this), a very nice addition would be visible upgrades or customizations to the player's ship. For instance, one could buy a new engine/thruster for a ship and visibly replace the one their ship has or armor upgrades that visibly cover the ship's hull.
These additions would add some much needed immersion and keep the gameplay fresh without the need for another DLC.

Starpoint Gemini 2 is a space trading and combat game, think Elite or EVE. You fly around a vast galaxy, smaller than in EVE or Elite though, doing missions, trading, mining, bounty hunting, etc. Captain your ship and level your captain in a RPG-like fashion.
I turned to SG2 for that EVE Online fix. I would call it a simplistic EVE, but it's still very good to scratch that EVE itch. You can forget about the RPG system, it's so simplistic, but the rest is a full fledged space game. The game's looks take a little getting used to, coming from sharp and shiny EVE or Elite gfx, but after a while it grows on you and flying around the galaxy is as fun as usual.
Getting through the story and all dlcs can take about 50 hrs, then there's some additional hrs if you want to replay SG story in SG2 engine, and then there is freeroam. Freeroam will not be so fun after completing everything as your ship will obliterate everything that the game throws at you, but still, 50-70hrs of game time looks quite amazing considering you can get this on sale.

What a fantastic Pool Game! It´s been a while since I played a real game of Pool and it´s been even longer since I played a Pool game on a PC.
I got Pool Nation in a Bundle and did not expect too much, but this Game (or should I call it a Simulation) is just brilliant.
The first thing one might notice are the visuals. The environments are beautifully crafted, as are the tables. The lighting is superb (although a little bit less bloom would have been nice), the textures (especially of the balls and the cloth) are very highly detailed. And you can even see the chalk coming off in the slow motions you get sometimes when you make a great shot.
And the balls have nice, realistic looking reflections which only adds to the atmosphere.
One might think that the background tune is repetetive, but I did not feel that yet. It fits perfectly to the environments and it really wants to make you step into your screen, right into that room and have a very nice, calm and relaxing game of Pool.
Now to the physics: When I played first, I played through the tutorial which was a good choice. I would not have expected that the cue / ball interaction is modeled that well. You can do whatever I can think of in real life with the cue and land all kind of Trick shots. It seems there´s even a (free?) DLC in the works which focuses on Trick shots, and I´m really looking forward to it.
You can attend several tournaments with different rules (there´s 8-ball, 9-ball and lots of other play styles you can choose from) and there´s Multiplayer which I did not try yet. I want to play through all the single player Tournaments first to get some practice.
And the difficulty? Well, it´s partly up to you. You can select between various levels of how the game helps you to visually see in which directions the balls will roll. This is also great to teach you what kind of effects a shot by aiming the cue in specific angles to the white ball will have before you even shoot.
I can only highly recommend Pool Nations and I don´t see anything another Pool game could make better.

When hearing we were getting a new Batman from a different studio I got a little nervous; in my opinion Arkham Asylum and Arkham City were both ground breaking and quite rightly very successful. During a number of discussions with friends over this game it has generally been; just how can you improve on a solid enough gaming engine in the first place? You could possibly only really add to what has been an almost perfect series so far.
The story itself is set ten years before the story of Arkham Asylum and you run into all the familiars, joker riddles, other things to scan and collect to get the achievement, xp and upgrade etc.Having played the first two you knew that these things were going to be included again at the very least. So I won't rant about "same old the other two" because quite honestly if I was expecting anything different on that part I’d have been expecting a completely different and revamped game altogether. If you love the first two games then this shouldn't really be an issue nor a surprise.
Graphics:
Graphics are pretty solid, you get some nice camera angle action shots as before. I wouldn't say there is an amazing improvement but you should know what you’re paying for anyway. If you have a half decent graphics card (I only run mine on a gtx 670) then you'll have the same enjoyment as you did on the previous two. For me nothing really stood out unless I was being really really picky.
Gameplay:
I personally think the gameplay is a little stiffer than it was in the previous two. Before it came out I went through them to catch up and to generally be wiser to enjoy Origins more and I just cannot put my finger on it. It's nothing big, it's exactly the same controls as before. It might just be me being picky unless anyone else can vouch.
Repayable?:
Yes, you have multiple modes to unlock, riddler trophies and avatars to scan. There is plenty to do in Arkham Origins and plenty of achievements to get.
Multiplayer?:
Probably not going to take off, I don't think people buy Batman Arkham series because of the multiplayer in the way people buy Call of Duty and Battlefield games. Although a decent attempt and it's always nice to see a multiplayer mode i'd rather them focus more on perhaps putting out little bits of extra dlc instead or even better a co-op mode. But bottom line, Batman Arkham is all about the lore in my books.
Total: 7/10

The worse part of the game by far is the obvious console port aspects. There is mouse accelereation/smoothing present, and no way to disable it from in-game. I should't have to edit config files to enable/disable such a vital feature in a FPS game. The video options are also very barren.
Overall, I would not recommend this game if you have to pay over $10 for it. Could have been a decent game, but the lazy console port and linear level design make it nothing special.

So much potential!
First you take a scoop of base-building then you add a pinch of ressource management.
You sprinkle a healthy dose of tragedy and let it macerate overnight.
Then once morning comes, you take all your work, throw it in the trash and start over because you finally understood one more crucial detail that escaped you the day before.
Or you just feel crazy and wanna try something else that time...
So many systems!
Well they got a mood system for the Duplicants (the little souls you feverishly try to save from drowning in their own secretions half of the time), each of them have basic needs like food & sleep along with being suceptible to disease if you  subject them to filth & germ-filled areas without any way for them to clean themselves up.
Each Duplicant has a different response to stress ; some will empty their bowels incessantly, others will projectile vomit, the worst will outright go rampage and break your precious base.
Which is kind of the only real flaw of this game for now ; all your bases are required to be filled to the brim with endless "paintings" or statues to counteract the stress, there is no other way other than building massage tables that turn your colony into a fricking spa.
And everything stresses them : electric wires are stressful, plumbing pipes are stressful, toilets are stressful, ev-e-ry-thing. Unless an object is designed to lower stress like the massage table or statues/paintings, you can expect it will add more stress.
Which wouldn't be so bad in itself if the Duplicants didn't start expecting better conditions of life as they level up.
Any activity they do, from mining to building, has a level and the Duplicant also gains level, which makes his demands rise or else, you guessed it : more stress.
It's obviously done to keep some level of difficulty going as you progress, but it also means that arbitrarily for some reason at an early  point in time you will notice everybody is stressed out for no reason and if you have not researched the stress-reducing items at that point, your colony is in for a rough ride.
Maybe this is starting to sound like a drag and you're probably wondering why the hell am I writing such a long review if I don't like the game but that's where you're wrong.
They have gasses in the game.
Each gas has its own weigth. Heavy gasses go down and lighter gasses go up.
Same with liquids.
They have a working temperature transfer system in a base-building game.
They have working states of matter.
You can take a solid and let it freeze out if the area around it is cold enough.
Or you can heat it until it turns to steam
In a base-building game.....
It all becomes a complex game of gathering enough input and dealing with the waste output to get what you want.
If you take on too many Duplicants at once in the begining they will just breathe all your precious oxygen at once, eat all of your grub and die spectacularly very fast.
Sometimes the entire survival of your colony can be compromised by forgetting you lowered your task priority for making food or harvesting crops two weeks ago in order to deal with some catastrophy. And now they're starving, like right now.
Sometimes you'll forget to close an airlock and come back from the bathroom only to see your entire base swarmed with poisonous gas and your Duplicants trapped in some final pocket of oxygen...
It's a very rewarding game as far as problem-solving and crisis-management goes because in the begining you don't know anything.
They update the game on a regular basis every month, and the updates are always meaningful, they do bugfixes in between and have a preview branch to download for the next upgrade as they work on it. We've had disease update, oil update and automation update to name the last three.
I really hope they keep on expanding it into an even more complete game, so far there is no "end-game" to speak of, no getting out of the asteroid or anything. It is however a fascinating collection of interwoven systems that give you the opportunity to spend hours figuring out the perfect way to position machines and rooms so that you eliminate problems altogether (like temperature creeping up constantly until your base cooks if you're not careful).
Maybe I'm weird and this doesn't sound much fun for most people, but here's my thumbs up for the game that does it anyway!

The singleplayer is solid for a game that was released in 2003 but it's the multiplayer you should invest some time in. There are limited servers to choose from with active players, yet, the community is still somewhat active. This is a great game if you want to hone your lightsaber skills. As a Kickstarted backer, I was really hopeful this game would be the project that could rekindle the same joyous feelings and fun gameplay that games back in the day used to deliver.
It did not.
Instead what we got with this game was a rather large mess of poor controls, camera combating, and a plot so utterly torn from Banjo-Tooie you can easily spot where the writers took lines of dialogue from.
Granted, the game looks very pleasing and the sound and music direction is astounding, but I put the most points in story and gameplay and let me tell you: Even the game characters lean so heavily on the fourth wall that they themselves dont believe the world they live in is real.  Instead of a lush, fresh, vibrant story and plot filled to the brim with unique ideas and challenges, we get constant, CONSTANT reminders, satire, and jokes about the game series this was all based on (and games from the 64 bit era in general).
As I sat in this chair, giddy to open this game for the first time and explore this promise of a wonderful game, I thought back fondly on the hours I whiled away in my youth on my N64 with Banjo, Kazooie, and the rest of the cast and the joy it brought me.  As I played THIS game, I felt the joy drain from every fiber of my being as the minutes passed and I became increasingly uninterested in what the rest of the game had in store.
As much as I hate to say it, but L.O.G. from Banjo-Kazooie: Nuts & Bolts was RIGHT about one thing: "People these days just aren't interested in collectathons anymore..."  I found those haunting words to ring true to me.
All in all I give the game a score of 4/10 and thats putting things generously.  But who knows, if the devs decide to fix some of the biggest issues, then I might re-rate the game in a more favorable light.
In the mean time my lovelies, go find something else to play, if you have the original Banjo-Kazooie games, then go back and play those one more time, I know I will!

Of course, not everyone will like it, and that's totally okay. It's going to be too slow, too open/empty for some people, but for others (mainly who enjoy Banjo-Tooie) it will be perfect. I haven't really experienced any camera issues that a lot of people have taken issue with, but I'm playing with a mouse/keyboard so maybe that has something to do with it.

Disappointment: yes, for all the reasons previously stated about it in other reviews. It's bad; don't believe the hype. Average at best for $20, a disgrace for $40.
What's really interesting, however, is that it manages to have the worst script in gaming history, especially when compared to Banjo Kazooie. (EDIT: One of the worst. The worst is hyperbolic, and that prize probably goes to some David Cage game I never played.)
Yooka and Laylee as a double act falls completely flat because Yooka's a complete cipher and Laylee's a negative snark. With no one like Banjo for Laylee to bounce off, she ends up just being snarky to anyone and everyone in earshot, appearing needlessly hateful and unpleasant.
The stakes are laughably contrived, even for a game like this.
The game keeps pointing out its own flaws and laughing at them (like the long loading times and the time-wasting quiz game) while doing nothing to remedy them.
None of the lines are funny, in fact they're anti-funny, they steal laughter rather than passing by fruitlessly. What's more is that they're repeated in subtle and obnoxious ways. Example:
A Knight Pig from Hamalot. That's a joke in itself (a visual pun). It's not particularly funny but it doesn't waste a lot of time. Laylee, however, begins with "Let me guess, it's something weight/pig related." Which is one form of telling the joke. Then the Pig reveals he's from Hamalot. Joke told twice now. To which Laylee replies "I should have guessed."
The same unfunny joke that was already too dumb for an actual line of focused dialogue has now been told three times and it REALLY didn't get any funnier.
None of the characters have any chemistry because they weren't written to have chemistry, they were written to be walking jokes. A walking joke can't make jokes of their own, they can only exist as insular jokes; making chemistry impossible (see: the Meta Gag of 'Mo-Ron' from Freakazoid/ satirized by the Mexican Bee from Simpsons or the Chicken from Family Guy)
All character, personality, charm and wit have been tossed aside in the service of jokes that aren't even funny enough for a single line of dialogue, much less five or more.
The writing in this game is as bad as the writing in Gunpoint was good and that's saying something.

Just a quick note so you know where I'm coming from. I have played Borderlands (this game) plus the DLCs, as well as Borderlands 2. I have not played the pre-sequel thingy, so I have no opinion on that one.
As the 2nd game in the Borderlands series, this thing is far more technically polished than the first one. There are plenty of options for graphics, UI and so on, which makes it far more enjoyable from that perspective than the first game. The screens for inventory, skills and such are still pretty clunky, like in the first game, but I guess they do the job.
There is also a more or less constant main villain who stays with you through the story and he's one of those well written characters one simply loves to dislike.
Sadly, they also push Claptrap heavily. I liked how he was there for the short tutorial section in the first game, but here, they push him on you for way, way too long and he is just horribly annoying. There is also, too much focus on the various player characters from the first game in my opinion.
Other than that, I think the first game was more interesting in terms of classes, loot drops and environments. Still, this is not a bad game, and can be enjoyable with friends.

Batman Arkham origins is an excellent if tragically short game that's a worthy stopgap between The next Rocksteady Batman outing, An excellent title,with a few modest flaws that prevent it from being great. It once again perfectly encapsulates the feeling of being The Batman and it is gotham in all it's beauty.
Arkham Origins takes place before the previous arkham games when Batman was first starting out and was new at the whole crimefighter thing and hadnt even befriended Jim gordon as an ally yet. Man of his foes are new to him, and he's using a more armor like suit and makes more mistakes.
The game is not without it's flaws. it's story is too short and there's simply not enough to do outside of it. The "Enigma" challenges dont feel nearly as good as the previous game and is tedious, the complete removal of riddles is dissapointing as it was a source for numerous easter eggs. The combat is identical to the last game with one new item. Batman's foes aren't nearly as fleshed out and the twist midway through leaves me feeling cheated by the advertisement as (MAJOR SPOILER BETWEEN HERE AND THE NEXT LINE)
It once again is Hijacked by a certain villain despite advertising another. Sound familiar? Unfortunatedly so, however the game does an outstanding job of making it believable and being a good story and the voice acting and writing are superb more than making up for it
(SPOILERS END HERE)
The bossfights while having potential seem squandered, underwhelm in some cases and just amount to in a few instances more of the same. The combat isnt nearly as satisfying feeling, the sounds, the crunch the sense of impact isnt quite there like it was in the last game so it feels far less satisfying. And it's buggy, OH IS IT BUGGY. On launch the enigma side mission was uncompletable without an exploit to get past a vent that caused a particular hang up. Hopefully by the time of this writing it will be patched but it screws those who pre-order the game.
Finally, the one thing about Arkham Origins that is most dissapointing is how terrible the multiplayer is. At first I thought it would be great, dynamic duo co-op! awesome! Robin is my favorite character so I was so down, but not only is Robin not even available in challenge maps, it's randomly selected, and the Simply put, it's boring, it's laggy, it's cheap and flighty and half the time your shots dont even connect. I cannot tell the number of times I've dumped an entire magazine into someone's chest as a joker thug only to see them walk up and shoot me once. And then, it happens to them, and it's not just a problem when playing as thugs, oh no, it's like that as the heroes. the levels are far too cramped and small feeling, and really the entire thing just feels tacked on. The multiplayer was clearly just tacked on because every game has it now a days and it's tragic.
Now that I'm done with the bad, lets talka bout the good. The story is great, the gameplay feels wonderful, everything flows nicely and the voice acting is top notch. Once again, the story details Batman free roaming about a city under a blizzard so there is of course, a police lock downm,but you have a far larger map to play with. Sadly all this is , is a retooled, and slightly bigger arkham city map, but it works. Troy Baker has proven to be a worthy successor to Hamil in every sense of the word. an d if not for it's few but dissapointing flaws, this good game would be a great one.
Is it 60 dollars good? maybe not,

The Batman Arkham series has been critically aclaimed for it's fast paced action, fluid combat and above all because "you're Batman". Batman Arkham Origins is a prequel to the series and although it is not as revolutionary as the other two games I would say it is still a great addition to the series. This game features Batman meeting some of the Gotham super-villains for the first time such as The Joker, Bane, Deadshot and Black Mask. The graphics in this game are a step up from Arkham City and Batman has a new batsuit that looks more armoured. The combat remains the same with a few new gadgets such as the concussion detonator. The story is great, it starts with Black Mask putting a bounty of 50 million dollars on the death of Batman. Eight assassins take up the offer Bane, Deadshot, Firefly, Deathstroke, Shiva, copperhead, Electrocutioner and Killer Croc. I will not tell you more about the story for spoiler reasons but I can reveal that there is a massive twist. There are many bossfights and I must say they were all very good and polished compared to the Arkham City ones that were stun, beatdown,stun beatdown,stun beatdown, knockout. The one I enjoyed most was the copperhead bossfight when she drugged you and she made you see lots of her and you have to beat all the clones to harm the actual copperhead. This was reminiscent of the arkham asylum scarecrow fear gas hallucinations. There was a few bugs and glithches the first time I played through, one made me not able to complete the game, but these have been generally fixed with patches so it should be fine play right now. The multiplayer is a new addition to the series , which I did not have very high hopes for but it surprised me and I found I loved it. There are 3 teams 2v3v3 You are either Batman or Robin on one side and the other 2 teams are Joker's goons or Bane's goons. As batman or Robin you fly around, sorry glide around taking out thugs stealthily because only a few bullets can kill you, while you do this a meter is filling up for every takedown and if this meter is full then Btman and Robin win however this is very hard to do although it is fun silent takedowning (is that a word?) real people for once, not that I'd do it in real life(I've triedmit didn't work but I got a sharp slap from one of my brothers).The Gang's job is to capture posts and kill off the other team's reinforcement counter. If one of the gang's are killed off then the other gang wins.Once per game one person in the gang's will have a chance to play as Bane or The Joker which is also an enjoyable experience. Overall Batman Arkham Origins is very good. The game felt new at the beginning but then it just felt like a bigger Arkham city until you meet The Joker then it feels like a unique game again. WB Montreal has done enough taking over Rocksteady for this game to make it an enjoyable experience but some of the game just felt like the same S**t put into a new title but thankfully there was enough variation to make this game feel like it's own game although it is not revolutionary. If you liked the last 2 games you will love this game because it is more of what you love and then some. I give this game 7.4 out of 10. Thanks for reading and remember "your batman".

Batman: Arkham Origins - a concise review:
Rocksteady reclaimed Batman's significance in the gaming world with 2009's excellent Batman: Arkham Asylum.  Its sequel, Arkham City, took what was good about Asylum and made it better, while simultaneously fixing everything that was subpar.  Arkham City was a true sequel; Arkham Origins is an expansion pack at best.  It takes everything that was good about Arkham City and puts it in another package, a box that lacks the soul, inspiration, homage, and creativity of its predecessor.  Mechanically and functionally, Arkham Origins and Arkham City are virtually identical, but Origins lacks the narrative and obvious love for the franchise that went into City.
If you have loved the Arkham franchise up to this point, chances are you will love Origins, even if less so than its siblings.  If you have played City and found it "fun, but not great", you will likely feel like you wasted your money if you buy this game.

I am writing this review the reviews on this game are just a load of whiny b.s. and people dont realize that their dumb opinions can make or break a game but anyways now Ill begin.  Alright this game is good and has a lot of potential there are some minor gripes I have with it but overall I am pleased with my purchase and how the Hitman franchise is returning to its roots.  Gone is the linear mission structure of absolution and now we are given a very sizable playground filled with inumerable options of completing our objectives.
+ Graphics -the game is gorgeous on Ultra (you cant run this on a crap computer though, I run smooth as ice on Ultra     with an i7-4790  with a GTX 970 )
+ Open Maps with many ways of completing objectives - Replayibility
+ They kept the fluidity of Absolution and mixed it with the sandbox style of Blood Money
+ Contracts mode has finally been implemented in a way that makes sense
+ Smarter Disguise system some what like Absolution except not as irratating- enforcer system
+ The AI is improved from past games and more observant- but still easily fooled with coins
- Im not personally a huge fan of the episodic layout ( I do feel like that is going to hurt sales)
- Always online is always a terrible idea it's annoying when you lose connection and progress relying on servers to play a single-player game is a dumb idea and hopefully they patch it to where this will be implemented a little better
- I was annoyed the beta was the same as the tutorial for this game I really didn't wanna play through it all over again
- There are those occasional moments when the AI is completly stupid and can be easily exploited-
**I find no validity in people who have issues with running the game because their computer isn't up to snuff this is a big game with a lot going on all at once. Meeting minimum requirement means you will have to run the game on the lower settings there's a lot that factors into how the game will run your cpu, gpu, ram and what kind of hard drive you are using its not the devolopers issue its yours.

So as shown here theres way more pros than cons if you like the Hitman series and you have a fairly alright rig then this is a buy it's just the waiting thats gonna kill me.

Utter disbelieve at having purchased this lemon of a game.  No, I wasn't following development so I completely missed out on the incredibly inane design decision to make this an "episodic" release game (similar to Telltale Game business strategy) where a single chapter is released per month.  The DRM is no big deal but I think destroying a great single player game by forcing it into some kind of deluded multi player mode is utterly ridiculous.  They suckered me this time, but never again.

I really liked the idea of an open universe and custom contracts, so far I have submitted two of those.
I think playability and graphics are awesome and I'm looking forward to move beyond Paris.
However the PS4 exclusivity for the Sarajevo missions is something I cannot accept as a potential buyer, also the requirement to be online in a single-player game is extremely dissatisfying, I have lost already a few missions because the server temporarily disconnected. Not to mention that it's redundant when the piracy protection is already Denuvo.
Another great dissatisfaction is that I cannot set texture resolution beyond medium, I have maxed out all other settings and the game is running smoothly, to me resolution is more important than anti-aliasing and the like because the difference is much more noticeable when I'm in close range, I think it's fair that the player should be allowed to use the settings one wishes for his own machine, without limitations.
Despite all those reasons, because I see the potential of a great game nonetheless, I'm rating it positive temporarily until further developments, I hope your consumers can talk some sense into the developers so they can make the appropriate changes, that way everyone gets to enjoy the game they now own, and continue buying into your system.
P.S. What's up with the completely random crashes? I've had 3 of those in 17 hours but it's still a nuisance since some of the contract missions I was setting up, I don't get to save at all.

Borderlands 2 is an action role playing first person shooter, developed by Gearbox Software and published by 2k Games in September 2012. It is the second game in the Borderlands series and the sequel to the popular 2009 hit Borderlands 1.
As with the first game, you are able to complete a campaign with the main story quest and optional side missions as one of the four Vault hunters.  All of the key gameplay features are all present, such as online co-op, randomly generated loot and character building elements such as talent trees are all found in Borderlands 2. There has been a game of the year edition released last year which includes all the DLC apart from one.
The gameplay at it's core is the same as Borderlands 1. The focus on randomly generated loot plays a huge part. Each of the characters you have the option to play as have their own specialty, and will bring a feel of originality to each playthrough on either of them.  We also see a new elemental effect in BL2, Slag, this is a substance that increases the damage a target takes if they are covered in it. You will also find Eridium bars as you play the game, these can be used to purchase storage upgrades and increase the amount of ammo you can carry.
We also see an element of customizing how your character looks as well, you can unlock different skins, head designs, colour schemes and vehicle paint jobs.  Another major addition to BL2 is the "Badd@ss rank" system; points are awarded for completing certain in-game challenges, that in turn award tokens that will allow you to increase your base stats. These stat increases also take effect on all of your other single player characters too.  Also similar to the the original, we also see the return of a New Game Plus mode, in the form of "True Vault Hunter Mode", which increases the difficulty, and gives you a higher chance at even better loot drops. You are also able to level up to 50 in this mode too.
The graphics in Borderlands 2 are virtually the same as the original, but with just a more enhanced look to them. We see the vibrant colour schemes in each zone come to life. Along with better quality textures too.  The style of graphics in Borderlands has always been a huge drawing point for me as there are hardly any other games which pull this style off as well as this.
Your first playthrough Borderlands 2 will have a number of difficult encounters, but these can easily be overpowered by returning to the same bad guy, mission or zone after leveling up one or two more times, or getting a bigger better gun. If you stay on top of all of the side missions as you progress through the story mission, you will stay at the right level so that you won't just hit a brick wall of impossible monsters/enemies. To make matters easier when it comes to deciding how tough a mission will be, each one also has a recommended level - so you can easily see how hard a single mission will be without actually having to test the waters first.
A full playthrough on single player of Borderlands 2 took me just under thirty hours. That is a pretty decent amount of content on offer, with the side missions and a decent amount of loot farming involved too. I have put almost 140 hours into Borderlands 2, as I have played various different characters through the story a number of times. This is a game where you can easily spend 300 hours and still be having the same amount of fun.
I had zero amount of technical issues throughout BL2; the game is perfectly optimized, will run at 60 fps, and the cloud save feature makes it even better technically.
Borderlands 2 is easily in my top 5 favorite games of all time. Just like the original, Borderlands 2 is a perfect game with no flaws in it at all. I cannot recommend this game enough. Most people will already have it since it goes on sale so much, but PLEASE play it. You will NOT be disappointed.

It's games like this that make me wish for a third option for recommendations.
Let me start by saying that I'm thoroughly enjoying this game.
I grew up with titles like Banjo Kazooie, Gex, and various other collectathon styles of game. so this, in a lot of cases is a pure nostalgia trip.
That said, it's not the revitalization of the genre that people were hoping for. The title is.... okay. it has its neat little quirks, but it also has its nagging problems (like the camera. the Rextro minigames aren't all that fun, stages can feel a tad on the empty side, etc.)
The reason why this type of game design died out is sort of put on full display here. Large environments with not lots to do. Each stage is designed like its own playground, with puzzles and challenges scattered about. But while Banjo Kazooie kept things relatively tight in level design, I feel that Yooka Laylee opens things up a bit too much in the two stages that I've seen thus far.
Lots of space... not much done with it.
I enjoy this game. and I want to recommend it. But unless you grew up with this specific genre of gaming, it's kind of a hard sell.

Yooka-Laylee is fun. The graphics are bright and colorful, the music rocks, and the character progression feels right. The controls felt totally fine to me, playing with a controller, and the camera feels the same way it did back in the day. They pitched a game that was supposed to be a return to form from Collect-a-thons of the 90’s, and they delivered it.
Something got left in the 90’s however, and it was the charm. While the game DOES have charm, it simply doesn't have as much as its predecessors. The fourth-wall breaking humor that should be large part of the game is a 50/50 point for me. They break the fourth wall a lot in Yooka- Laylee and it doesn’t really work as well as it should. It worked very well in Banjo-Tooie, in my opinion, because it paid its dues for it. The jokes played off of points it set up in the first game. It got to be self-deprecating because it knew what it was. Being the first Yooka-Laylee game, I feel like it hasn't had enough build up for those jokes to really hit home
While I dont have any complaints with the worlds main worlds themselves, The hub world is kind of just thrown together, which I read about in a review before I bought the game, and I didn't think it would be that big of a deal. A hub world is just an intermediary between the actual gameplay worlds, right? Well I found myself actually missing the exploration and the build up that earlier Rare games had leading up to the worlds from the hub, the slight change in scenery, the shift in music, that sort of thing.
Overall, its slightly disappointing. It sort of feels like its a game that would be released before Banjo-Kazooie, and then they released Banjo-Kazooie which improved upon the formula. All that negative being said, I still recommend it. I haven’t fully beaten it, but I’ve still been enjoying it.

Batman: Arkham Origins - a concise review:
Rocksteady reclaimed Batman's significance in the gaming world with 2009's excellent Batman: Arkham Asylum.  Its sequel, Arkham City, took what was good about Asylum and made it better, while simultaneously fixing everything that was subpar.  Arkham City was a true sequel; Arkham Origins is an expansion pack at best.  It takes everything that was good about Arkham City and puts it in another package, a box that lacks the soul, inspiration, homage, and creativity of its predecessor.  Mechanically and functionally, Arkham Origins and Arkham City are virtually identical, but Origins lacks the narrative and obvious love for the franchise that went into City.
If you have loved the Arkham franchise up to this point, chances are you will love Origins, even if less so than its siblings.  If you have played City and found it "fun, but not great", you will likely feel like you wasted your money if you buy this game.
Its Batman.

Ah Batman Arkham Origins the game I waited for sense febuary when they gave clues for it. The game that I played right after preloading it. First of all the game is very alike to arkham city with I am completely fine with. But the changes I found in the free-flow combat and predator missions were bad. With predator moving to gargoyle to gargoyle is not as smooth as the previous games and silent takedowns sort of glich out with their knockout smash's. I found it very enjoyable to play with batman in predator maps with real players. There are two modes from the time of making this review: Invisible Predator Online and Hunter, Hunted. I must say that I enjoyed my Mad Max experience. I was hooked from the start by a pretty good story. I'm one of those who gets distracted quickly by "shiny new" things, so I quickly found myself leaving no stone unturned. I wanted the money to upgrade and upgrade, I wanted to complete side quests, so that I could upgrade, UPgrade and UPGRADE! I won't ramble on, so here's my list of Pros and cons...
Pros:
Good gameplay - simple yet effective - though the jump mechanic left thinking...how much does his gear weigh?
Upgrade system - not too shabby - "Guess I'll have to go kill some more things"
Graphics - as expected - love flinging enemies over the car's roof..."A whale! Harpoon away!"
The ending and main story line - no spoilers...grrrr
Cons:
Side mission - They tend to be a bit down the same line "Oh look another..."
AI - maybe a bit too easy for some - Didn't die much, mostly when I slid off cliffs thinking I could jump
Environment - Well, sometimes I thought..."If only Max wasn't carrying this heavy bitter soul, I could make this jump...and I failed"
All jokes aside, it had been a while since the last time I felt so raw near the end of a game that my leg was shaking and actually shouting stuff at my computer screen (things usually found in online gaming). After some time after finishing it, I came to the conclusion that they did well at capturing nostalgia and then having it run parallel with the harsh wasteland the Max wanders. What do we do when we no longer have hope?

I am writing this review the reviews on this game are just a load of whiny b.s. and people dont realize that their dumb opinions can make or break a game but anyways now Ill begin.  Alright this game is good and has a lot of potential there are some minor gripes I have with it but overall I am pleased with my purchase and how the Hitman franchise is returning to its roots.  Gone is the linear mission structure of absolution and now we are given a very sizable playground filled with inumerable options of completing our objectives.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

In almost every modern military shooter you play as a soldier who is just doing his job, saving the world and all that. In reality you are playing as a psychopathic mass-murderer who never questions his actions or thinks of the consequences of what he is doing.
In any other game you kill hundreds or thousands of people in an attempt to kill the leader of the enemy army or to stop something supposadly bad from happening, breaking every Geneva convention in existance as you go. The usual reaction of the player is; 'Who cares? This is fun!'
Spec Ops: The Line doesn't let you escape from your actions with a shrug of your shoulders. This game is not about the gameplay (very average 3ps stuff - possibly intentionally so). The whole game is designed to make you face your actions and the terrifying consequences that result. This things this game makes you do... it's dark. But it's a video game, so you continue foreward. Everything gets worse and worse, and yet you keep going to the next objective marker and then the next.
By the end of the game you will come to see what a monster the main character is and you will hate yourself. This game holds up a mirror to the modern military shooters that are so popular today and it's genius.

Many reviews critique the "meh" gameplay but it is important to realize that the "meh" is just using the same over used mechanics to highlight just how much of a monster a person in any modern war shooter really is.  So when purchasing this game don't do it for the gameplay but for the expierence.

Yooka-Laylee is fun. The graphics are bright and colorful, the music rocks, and the character progression feels right. The controls felt totally fine to me, playing with a controller, and the camera feels the same way it did back in the day. They pitched a game that was supposed to be a return to form from Collect-a-thons of the 90’s, and they delivered it.
Something got left in the 90’s however, and it was the charm. While the game DOES have charm, it simply doesn't have as much as its predecessors. The fourth-wall breaking humor that should be large part of the game is a 50/50 point for me. They break the fourth wall a lot in Yooka- Laylee and it doesn’t really work as well as it should. It worked very well in Banjo-Tooie, in my opinion, because it paid its dues for it. The jokes played off of points it set up in the first game. It got to be self-deprecating because it knew what it was. Being the first Yooka-Laylee game, I feel like it hasn't had enough build up for those jokes to really hit home
While I dont have any complaints with the worlds main worlds themselves, The hub world is kind of just thrown together, which I read about in a review before I bought the game, and I didn't think it would be that big of a deal. A hub world is just an intermediary between the actual gameplay worlds, right? Well I found myself actually missing the exploration and the build up that earlier Rare games had leading up to the worlds from the hub, the slight change in scenery, the shift in music, that sort of thing.
Overall, its slightly disappointing. It sort of feels like its a game that would be released before Banjo-Kazooie, and then they released Banjo-Kazooie which improved upon the formula. All that negative being said, I still recommend it. I haven’t fully beaten it, but I’ve still been enjoying it.
TL,DR:
Pros:
Fun
Controlls Well
No preformance issues
Banging soundtrack
Cons:
Severe lack of charm
Messy hub world
Not perfect, but amazingly well done and met the expéditions to enjoy this classic style "golden era" game.

Rating: good (7/10) Introduction Counter-Strike: Global Offensive is a First Person Shooter set in a comptetetive scene where two teams battle for an objective. It is a stand-alone follow-up to the famous Counter-Strike mod from Half-Life where terrorists battle the Counter-Terrorists on different locations. Gameplay & Story: 6/10 The gameplay consists of buying weapons and shooting your opponents. Easier said than done actually, since your opponents are either human players sitting on the other side of the world wide web or some AI programmed to shoot you first. CS:GO is for a reason the biggest competetive shooter on the market for years, since it offers great weapon balance, tactical possibilities for teams to approach and a large player base that keeps growning each day. The story behind the game is based on the oldschool Counter-Strike game, where one side takes the approach as terrorists either trying to plant a bomb or protect the hostages and other being Counter-Terrorists either try to protect a bomb site or trying to rescue the hostages held at Terrorist base. Combat & Challenge : 8/10 The combat is absolutely fluid in CS:GO and there are barely any moments, that you could the broken hitboxes or the bad netcode for dying. People tend to rage and blame the bad balance on maps, weapons or programming of the game, however the success of this title proves that it is the best competetive shooter on the market. The challenge in this game is definetely to be able to rise through the ranks in competetive matches, playing against hackers on opposite team or some players on your team that want to teach you some bad words in russian or french. I am always thankful for such opportunities to improve my language skills and consider it just a chance of becoming even better if I did not win the match no matter the team stacks. Reaching Global Elite rank after around 200 hours, I can safely say that it is possible to rise to the top even when the odds are stacking against you. Graphic & Interface : 7/10 The graphic when set to higher settings is actually pretty good, sadly the competetive scene barely allows it since there are certain tricks like setting your resolution lower on purpose to be able to aim better, that crash the feeling of this game in graphical matters. Most of the maps contain some details that make them distinguishable, like certain grapphiti on some maps. The interface is kept simple and almost transparent so that it does not disturb the concentration. Progress & Mini-Games : 8/10 It is possible to consider progress by rising up the account level that comes from simply playing CS:GO in any form, there are forms of rising up your ranking by playing competetive or gathering skins for the weapons you are using or want to sell. Some people actually make money by playing this game and selling the skins on the steam market, so different ways to progress in and outside of the game. The biggest progress for me was improving my hand-to-eye coordination by playing it competetively. Audio & Immersion : 8/10 Each weapon sound is unique for itself, and since the sound plays a great role in this game it is really important to get to know the sounds and be able to distinguish where the shooting is coming from. CS:GO fulfills its task really well. The music is played only in menues and during the highlights. The game music is nothing special, but since you can get/buy music kits to fit your music taste, Valve found a good workaround for not creating amazing music by themselves. Side-Notes This game offers single player, multiplayer and co-op modes that can be played either against other players or AI. This game offers different modes, some of that are just for fun, for example gun mode, while others are played in E-Sports. This game contains steam achievements. This game offers great optimization and updates to technology with time (updating their network code, updating the hit boxes, balancing the weapons). Summary CS:GO has its reasons to be the Number One FPS in the ESL Scene and its popularity is currently only rising. It is great to see that it has not been abandoned by the developers after reaching its peak state, but still keeps getting updated. I would recommend trying CS:GO to every game, just to know what this game is that defines the global FPS market so much and while FPS fans might love it, some might well get turned off by the hardcore players or the cursing and spitting wanna-bes. I hope this review helps you making the decision if its worth buying and installing this game. Rate and leave a comment if you enjoyed reading it. ~sensei

This is a sandbox-style game with some science/thermodynamics aspects. You dig and build your way through an asteroid (freshly randomized each session) in order to survive.
My opinion:
With 70+ hours of playtime I'd say I have had my share of the content by now.
20€ for 70 hours of fun is a very good deal in my opinion - and the game is not finished yet.
Gameplay:
Your duplicants (dupes) need food, oxygen, and somewhat comfortable surroundings.
In order to provide that, you hollow out an asteroid, composed of different (unin)habitable zones, and build your first machines of the mined resources. These first devices give you access to basic electrical energy, preparation of food, sanitation, and research. To sustain your colony, however, you need to unlock higher tech by conducting research. Which stretches your prime resource: dupes.
All the building, delivering and digging has to be done by your dupes. The AI is performing reasonably well so far, but some priorization of several tasks is required to ensure a proper workflow.
Your dupes differ in their skills (for handling machines, digging, cooking...) as well as in their positive and "negative" traits. Thereby it makes sense to assign dupes to some special tasks and relieve them from others (combat, building etc). Every few cycles (days) you can choose one additional dupe to reinforce your team (you start with 3).
In the beginning, your main concern will be the generation of sufficient amounts of oxygen and getting rid of the carbon dioxide. Then, providing enough electrical energy and food for your growing colony and thereby keeping your dupes happy. If you push them too hard and they build up to much stress they will start to freak out and the sh*** hits the fan.
Most of your machines require electrical energy and need to be connected to a power grid without overloading the circuits. Power is generated from coal, petrol, hydrogen or "gas". Aside the power grid you will also design a mad network of liquid and gas pipes/pumps connecting all the devices.
Finally, the electrical devices emit heat which will be one of your late game tasks (heat management). However, until you progress that far you will probably have restarted a couple of times, also to improve the layout of your base or simply to try something new. Once you got a stable colony, there is nothing left to do --> aside optimize or pursue self-set tasks --> sandbox mode. But until then its good fun.
Some cons:
The entire food / nutrition system as well as the clothing system feel unfinished. Yes I know, early access - just saying.
The production stops if one product lacks a specific resource, although a different product (later in the production queue and queued in the same device) could readily be produced.
All the build menus show too few icons and thereby constantly require tedious scrolling.
You get little feedback what stresses your dupes.
The game uses some aspects of thermodynamics and conductivity but a couple of processes and mechanics are, for the sake of gameplay balancing (I assume), distorted or scientifically incorrect. As the electrolyzer produces way more oxygen than hydrogen although consuming water. The gas and liquid flow appears pretty slow. Works for me though.
If you like base building and planning you get good value for your money here.

** A gorgeous space game marred by painful lore elements.**
[[Recommendation comes with strong suggestion to play in sandbox mode only]]
This game was an odd experience.  The longer I played it, the less I liked it.
When it started, it took me back to the wonder of games like Privateer.  Sandbox, big galaxy, lots of options.  And it's really gorgeous, from the ships to the planets to the nebulous backgrounds.  Some of space stations look oddly low-res compared to everything else, but that's minor.
However, things went downhill when I started to follow the main story campaign.  The voice acting is truly atrocious, and the writing isn't much better, from the minor (bad grammar) to the median (dialogue) to the major (an incoherent plot with characters whose motives don't seem to correspond to events).  And when you get to a more difficult mission that you have to try several times, the lack of any button to skip the dialogue becomes truly unforgivable.
Speaking of retrying, there are several design decisions that make sense on their own, but quickly become annoying when you have to replay a mission because it's difficult or bugged (like the infamous mothership mission).  First, you can save only at stations or planets.  OK, there's a sort of 'realism' sense to that.  Second, there's a lot of empty space between points of interest.  That actually worked for me at first, because it added to the sense of scale and exploration.  But when you have to retry a mission and reload to find you are about a 5 minute cruise from the action -- and then remember that you'll have to sit through 3 more minutes of unskippable community theatre auditions when you get there -- it gets really difficult to stick with it for the next attempt.
There were also a number of minor annoyances, like the fact that missions seem to get reset when you load a game (so if you pick up someone or something to deliver, you must do it before you end your current session or forever have that passenger or item in your non-cargo inventory), some inscrutable elements, several mechanics that seemed incomplete, and a handful of crash bugs.
I think there are the ingredients of a good game here, with a good core and beautiful graphics, but the lore side of things really lets those elements down.  Perhaps the best strategy would be to ignore the story and play only in sandbox mode.

That's this game. A turd with some slick packaging.
It presents itself as a space exploration/trading/combat game, and while I suppose it can claim all of those things, it does them about as well as the Chicago Cubs do at  winning the World Series.
Every aspect of this game feels underwhelming, if not painfully lacking. The game provides little information about how the various systems work, despite pushing many tutorial screens on you, that only server to annoy you with how much they leave out.
Add to that all of the almost could have been's with the combat, UI, graphics, sounds design, and trading system, the travel system feels like it's there to punish you for playing. The travel time it takes to get between the mission is insanely boring. It's not just the time it takes, but they did a great job of making a horrible star field to torture you with.
My greatest regret is that I gave this game a chance thinking it might get better and went over the two hours of play time and can't get a refund.
The developers of this game should be ashamed of the final product they made, especially if you want to charge people what you're asking. My life would have been better served buying burritos and making use of my life time supply of Chipotlaway.
