After a few hours in freeroam I feel like I've experience enough of Starpoint Gemini 2 to review it.
First of all, this is mostly a classic space sim when playing in freeroam. It's mining/trading/mercenary grind to get better equipment and ships but it has some differences - there's skill points and experience levels, which is nice if you enjoy playing RPG's (I do)
You don't start in fighter class ships. In fact - you can't fly the fighter class ships. You start in a Gunship class ship (or above if you have the DLC's). Your crew can man the turret hardpoints for you, and you will want them to. They are perfect shots every time. The turret AI is *very* good. You don't need to concentrate on weapons except to line up for heavy weapon shots, which are ammo limited but deal more damage per shot than your turrets. But....you probably won't even have to use them.
Starpoint Gemini 2 has a problem if you're a pilot who knows basic concepts of space sim combat. If you can assess firing arcs, manage shield energy and experience in MMO type skill buffs, normal difficulty is a relaxing grind even if you take assassination missions 6 to 10 levels above your level. Most enemy ships don't have cloak scanners, so you can drop out and unleash hell with an undetected approach and take down "Deadly" and even with a little luck "Impossible" targets.
This is a bit of a shame as this game wants to force you to fly combat role ships. I haven't seen ore freighters or transports. You can seemingly only buy Gunships and above with military kitting. Mining/Trading is viable but the cargo holds are disgustingly small and the mods that increase them in the workshop do not work with the DLC. You can not upgrade cargo capacity. If you're a frieghter captain your best bet is to get something with the biggest hold in the class which is marginally bigger than the rest and prepare to make MANY trips to and from asteroids and debris fields. Which is also a bit strange - asteroid and debris fields are EVERYWHERE, and you can't take advantage of it.
Unfortunately most of the modders seem intent on putting in ridiculous godships instead of addressing the lack of civilian vessels. I usually like to play as a frieghter captain, in my game now I'm just a mercenary taking contracts well above my level for the massive increase in EXP and Credits.
Overall I'm very pleased with this game. It's very underrated. I can expect I'll be putting many many more hours into it, as I have with X. This isn't Starpoint Gemini 1 for sure, and it's not the mess that is Star Wolves. It's not X either, but it's a better game than say Tachyon or Darkstar One and a nice alternative.
Haven't played story yet. Not sure I will.

The random, permanent gender/race assignment was a fascinating social experiment, but in the end I was unable to associate with my own avatar in a way that would allow me to become invested in this fantasy world. I understand that was the point, but I've had enough of it. If it had been done for a month or two, sure, it made its point. But as it stands now, removing agency and choice from players is not something I will encourage game developers to do, no matter how noble their cause. Tolerate it from Gary and then we'll have it from bigger developers and I'm not okay with that kind of dystopia unless I get a suit of power armor and a chance to fight against it.
Don't take away any more of our choices in our fantasies. Gaming is a way to escape the harsh realities of the real world. We live in a terrible place where people are increasingly unhappier all the time. I don't want to be reminded of that in my video games when I'm trying to unwind. I'll be going back to ARK, Conan Exiles, and 7 Days to Die where I can make my own choices and have control over my own safe space. I applaud the effort, but I reject the execution.

Picked this little gem up for $10 bucks the last time it was on sale. Knowing what I know now, I would have gladly paid more. I ignored it for a long time even though it seemed like it would be fun, because I haven't had the best luck in games lately. To make my point on how much I love this game consider this! I haven't even played another game since I started playing this, with the exeption of maybe some BL2 with friends. And I just finished it today. It was so surprisingly fun, kind of like a good book that I just couldn't put down. Very few games I've played have been able to captivate me this way. The graphics are top notch. Not the best I've seen (and I've seen many), but very nice indeed. Anamations are smooth, Sky textures are great. The dust storms effects are amazing. You really feel like you are in danger. And sometimes you die! The moon sometimes looks haunting above the sandunes at night. The fighting is fluid and although much like all the Batman games, (which I like), combat was satisfying. The car customization is awesome and it actually feels like like your car is getting better, faster, and more deadly as the game progresses. The same goes for Max himself. He upgrades as you go along too. You have full contorl over this process as well. It isn't dumbed down for you like in some games. You can choose. There may be prerequisites to certian skill, or things that you unlock later in the game so as to become overpowered too quickly. You do get a feeling of being pretty kick♥♥♥♥♥toward the end which I personally like. I enjoy feeling the time I've put into the game has paid off. The storyline was okay. I didn't love it, but then again I'm kind of a happy ending kind of guy. I want to kill the bad guy, save the innocents, and ride of into the sunset with the girl. That doesn't always happen in good stories. Do youself a favor. If you've been eyeballing this game for a while like I did, just buy it. Buy it now, buy it when it comes on sale again for 10 bucks like I did. It doesn't matter how or when, just do it. You won't regret it!

I bought the game in early alpha but didn't touch it until the Titans DLC came out. Why ? Dunno, really. Every time I booted it and flew around for a bit it seemed slow and dull, with small dinky ships and a dirty-looking skybox. Recently, I bought and played Rebel Galaxy and, while it was a lot of fun for a while, I quickly grew bored by the simplistic structure and extremely straightforward combat. But I was in a "space" mood and decided to give SG2 a solid try.
Boy, am I ever glad I did. After a short but steep learning curve, the game opens up like a pinata, pouring out quests, ships, modules, weapons, skills, perks, etc. I fired up the campaign mode because (just a personal preference) I like to have a meta-story to hover around. I found the campaign to be serviceable. Not great but perfectly adequate as a background for your adventures. The game really shines in its many, many choices of ships and one look at some discussions in the forums will convince you that there's no single "I win" build. Many ships and many configurations are viable. Gameplay is varied enough to keep me entertained and can give rise to some situations worthy of an action movie. One time I was returning to a station with a captured ship worth about 2.5 million credits in tow. I was out of boosters and had taken serious hull damage, with no way to repair it. As I approached the station, I saw to my horror that it was surrounded by a cloud of enemy ships. My first instinct was let go of my prize and beeline it to another station. But then I thought "♥♥♥♥ them. I've earned this ship. I'm not abandoning it to a bunch of jackals". I let go of the grapple some distance from the station and fired up the superdrive in order to evade enemy fire. By flying close to the group, I was able to detach individual ships from their group one by one, slowly reducing their numbers. On occasion, my shields went down to almost nothing, and I had to hightail it out of Dodge to let them recharge. Eventually, I killed them all and went back to reclaim my captured ship. That was the sweetest money I ever made in the game and I was replaying the fight all day in my mind while my wife was wondering why I was grinning like an idiot.

When Max Payne was released in 2001, it was one of the first shooters to have an in-depth, stylized story. To this day, Max Payne still holds up as a grade A product.

TL; DR version: classic game, great story, PC = definitive version, <3
One of my favorite games of all time!
This isn't remastered in any way, this is the original PC version, so if you're playing it for the first time... this is a 2001 title! If you're here feeling nostalgic, skip reading reviews and just buy it :) If you haven't played Max Payne previously, please keep its age in mind when judging it for the first time.
Though the graphics may not, the story, however, will always stand the test of time. Your wife and daughter are murdered within the first ten minutes, which is the basis of the mystery you must now unravel. Meanwhile, outside, the worst blizzard in years envelops New York City. The atmosphere matches Max's desperation, breathing life into otherwise usual settings like rooftops, or the docks, as you mow down foes in winter coats huddling around a trashcan fire. There isn't a dull moment in the game, whether Max is fighting armies of baddies, interacting with memorable villains (and allies) or losing himself in his own nightmares. The story gets an A+ in my book and an A+++ when compared to the trash passed off as game plots nowadays.
The dialogue can be both fantastic and cheesy. Fantastically cheesy? Whatever you think of it, it is fitting to Max Payne's comic book style. There are cutscenes, but more often there are panels with speech bubbles and illustrations. I'm not sure if this was a budget or style decision, but it quickly became the series' trademark. There are lines, both funny and serious, which my friends and I quote to this day ("As in... you cry a lot?").
The shooting mechanics are fine. At the very least it has aged MUCH more gracefully than other old shooters. You don't have to aim precisely, just point in an enemy's general direction and shoot. It's not realistic. You can snipe people with dual submachine guns from across a rooftop, and carry 10 guns, 5 Molotov cocktails, 5 grenades and a grenade launcher all at once. You get a great arsenal by the way, and new weapons are steadily introduced throughout. Ammo is abundant. Painkillers are plentiful. I truly believe Max Payne was designed in a way to let you enjoy its story without getting stuck on this or that.
I've also played Max Payne on several platforms: first on PS2, then original Xbox and finally PC. I play it every few years. PC is the definitive version. In addition to not having to dust off your questionable old system, which is stuffed in a closet somewhere (or at least in my case it is), it runs smoothest on PC, and there are little things you will notice (for example, the cool, comic book font used in the PC version was converted to a generic font in the console versions).
It's worth the $9.99 Steam is asking, and it's on sale all the darn time so there's no reason not to revisit Noir York City, as Max calls it.
Also note: there's a slight compatibility issue, and the audio won't work with Windows 7 initially. Check the workshop for a simple sound patch that takes moments to install and works flawlessly. Just follow the instructions exactly and you're good to go! Happy gaming!

Spec Ops: The Line is a game where everything but the gameplay is top notch. What it does well is the setting which is the beautiful Dubai and the time they put into the detail made me really believe I was there. I especially liked the fish tanks. The amazing soundtrack which features Deep Purple and Jimi Hendrix and the absolutely excellent voice acting surpised me and there was a great plot with a tweeeest.
It's just a shame that despite all this, the gameplay is just bog standard third person shooting you've seen in a million and one games already. It's all go into next room, suspiciously also full of chest high objects to take cover behind (!) and kill them nasty americans before moving on which has been done to death. There are some neat little things they've added though such as shooting windows with sand behind will crush the enemies dumb enough to stand next to them.
Moving on, there are some powerful scenes in this game. My personal favourite is the
scene, it just hits you hard once you've realised what you've done. It's clear the game wants to think about what you're being ordered to do and in the finale basically tells you that you're far from the hero you think you are. It's a rather hamfisted way to get you to think about what you're doing in other games but I admire the devs for doing this.
The voice acting changes throughout the game, as the missions and the plot progresses you and your men go from calmly talking and ordering around to full on shouting. I really like this as it does help the plot convey how far gone the main character is. Another part of the audio is the soundtrack, it matches the tone of every situation you're in and the radio man really knows how to set the mood when he deploys songs like
.
In conclusion, Spec Ops: The Line is a great game to pick up. It's an enjoyable experience which could've been amazing if not for the typical whack-a-mole third person gameplay. Pick it up for £10 or less if you can.

Spec Ops: The Line is your typical cover based TPS (Third-Person Shooter). It features your average modern weapons that you can see in other shooters that take place in a modern day setting: Call of Duty, Battlefield etc.
There is also the two gun limit like in many other modern shooters: Primary weapon / Secondary weapon.
The gameplay itself is not innovative at all. It doesn't add anything new to the genre: Shoot, take cover, shoot, run to the next cover, shoot - repeat
You can assign different tasks to your two squadmates but you don't need to use them THAT much...or you barely use 'em at all. The tasks themselves are quite basic: "Mark and attack that target" "Shoot that thingy over there" etc.
I have to say, though, that the gameplay in The Line is very smooth and the cover mechanics are one of the best i've seen. Sprinting to cover and vaulting over cover is very smooth. The gameplay is good, fast and smooth...very well done. It's just that it doesn't add anything new.
Spec Ops: The Line may seem like your average military shooter at first but make no mistake! It is quite the opposite.
The game doesn't glorify war. You may play the game for 30-40 minutes and think that it's another one of these "murika fu'k yeh" games but it's not.
The story will change soon and it keeps coming up with surprises till the very end of the game. I can't say much about the story without giving away spoilers but all you need to know is this:

Summary:
Everything I loved about playing Banjo Kazooie and other GREAT 3D platformers, this game manages to combine old school fun with more modern visuals (and yet somehow still "look and feel" nostalgic!), a fantastic sense of humor, and throws in some new surprises to draw and keep the attention of anyone and everyone with even a slight interest in the genre. My new "must have" recommendation game, one of my first of 2017.
Not just a Kickstarter success, largely because it made a promise and kept it (and then some!), but an epic win for all gamers because the result is a ton of fun!
Pros:
+ Excellent art style that is a pleasure to see, colorful yet clean, and combines nostalgia and new techniques in a beautiful way
+ Tight controls when using controllers (which are highly recommended on the store page and I agree)
+ Excellent sense of humor
+ Hits every target for a top-tier, among the best of its kind, 3D platformer: Excellent level design, characters, collection items and puzzles/challenges, creative but fair boss battles
+ In every way (look, feel, the controls, game design and even the humor) a wonderful, spot-on spiritual successor to N64's Banjo-Kazooie (one of the all-time greats for 3D Platforming, and a contender for top 3 of all time!)
+ Local Co-op play in the regular campaign (see note below for more on what co-op campaign plays like)
+ Up to 4 player local co-op in its mini-games: a great mix of games, from beat 'em ups, to racing, to target shooting and more
+ Steam Link certified: Excellent controller support, works GREAT played on the couch with Steam Link
Cons:
- Not much, though I will say it's difficult to grab a screenshot of the game using a controller, at least the XBOX controller. Pressing the home button brings up the pause menu (as does start, strangely) so every screenshot I take is of the pause menu. Super sad, as I want to share so many great things about this game!
- Some of the hints during the tutorial very early in the game can be triggered entirely out of context which can lead to some annoyance. As an example, if you get to the first encounter with swimming, but then back track away from it, you will get periodic messages on how to swim until you actually go back and finish swimming. That's very picky, I know, but I'm struggling to think of any flaws here!
A NOTE ON CO-OP CAMPAIGN GAMEPLAY:
Yooka-Laylee does technically have a co-operative campaign, but you should know more about it if that's what's drawing you toward a purchase, just so you're fully informed.
This game has a local co-op campaign mode, but it's local co-op in a similar way as Super Mario Galaxy was. The second player controls a cursor, a small reticle shaped like a honey comb surrounded by a swarm of bees, that operates independently from Yooka and Laylee, and can collect items and interact with certain hazards (traps).
This can be IMMENSELY helpful in overcoming some of the game's challenges, but it's not usually an active role. It's interesting in its own right insofar as it gives a passive audience an option for an (albeit limited) active role should they choose.
Given the nature of the game, I'm personally okay with this. Please know that normally I LOVE co-op and want it in almost all games I play. However, co-op options that I've seen in other games, or others have asked for here, seem like a poor fit here. Some of those include...
- Tag in with swaps between characters (odd because the characters are a team and don't operate separately in any functional way)
- Take turns at certain points (just as easily accomplished by handing over the controller after X has happened, which is what I've been doing with "X" meaning a Paigie retrieval or character death)
- Split-screen with multiple Yookas and Laylees (especially odd, but maybe a fit for some)
- Competitive play swapping (not co-op, but a decent local multiplayer option similar to Super Mario Bros. 3, where a successful completion of a mission or a death triggers a swap to the other player for an attempt to tackle the challenge and improve upon the performance of the other player)
Anyway, just my opinions. I hope they help you make an informed decision.

I grew up with Banjo-Kazooie, speed run it, backed this project two years ago. And finally got my hands on it. I'm going to keep this as unbiased as possible. So let's first look at one of the most important aspects to any game, the controls.
A controller is needed if you want to enjoy the game. Sure, you can play with a keyboard, but it's going to be one hell of an unplesant time. I recommend an x-box one controller.
The controls are so responsive, as a speed runner, fighting with the controls is sometimes something you have to wrestle with, however it feels so natural, especially if you played Banjo-Kazooie right before this.
When you make a jump you know exactly where you're going to land, there's no fighting with the controls, I'm very picky with how my platfrormers handle, and this is honestly even better than Super Mario Galaxy with precise jumping.
The graphics are phenominal, take everything you loved about a N64 era platformer and make it HD with a beautiful color pallet and you get Yooka-Laylee.
I have yet to experience any texture issues, I have a higher end computer (Gtx 1080 OC Edition, Intel i7 Kaby Lake 7700k, 32GB of Ram, SSD) and it runs without any frame drops ever, runing at a solid 60FPS never studdering and I'm already to the last world.
Just food for thought, if you've never played Banjo-Kazooie, I would highly recommend playing that before playing this, it's not required obviously, but it'll give you a spot on idea of what this game is going to be like.
Keep in mind negative reviews that I've seen have mostly complained about the poor performance of the game on console, but if you have a half-way decent computer, you won't have any of the issues menitoned.
There are 5 worlds total, with an over world, each world can be expanded once, adding more to the already masisve level. As childish as the game may appear, it is highly challenging in parts, almost rage quit enducing.
As a long time Banjo-Kazooie fan, it's hard to come across as un-biased when writing a review about this game, but I found myself acciedntly refering to pagies as jiggies and quills as notes, it felt that much like a Banjo-Kazooie game. So if you came here looking for a true Banjo-Kazooie sequel, you found it, I see myself playing this for years to come. It's well worth the $40.

Now I haven't completed the entire game, I'm not even close, but I've played enough on a few worlds to know it's a great game for the genre and holds true to the original Banjo-Kazooie. If you've been looking for a 3D platformer on the PC for a long time like I have, then this game is for you all day long. Otherwise, you're just missing out if you're not into this kinda stuff :p

Boss fights are frustrating, even on normal.  I pretty much had to do each of them twice to get the rhythm.  You don't regain health during encounters so the learning curve is kind of steep.  I do believe if I one-shot every boss the game would be about 7-8 hours in length.
If you're a completionist there's a lot here.  However if you're here for a story you can do it in a sitting or two.  I think this would be great at $20.

I will say it was better than City but not as good as Asylum.  The voice actor for Batman did a decent job, less so I can say for Joker.  I also didn't like the way the team at WB made the joker look.  He didn't look right, like what I think a younger joker would look like, and lets face it, nobody can hold a candle to Mark Hamill.  Overall I rate it better than City.  The gadgets were fun, combat was tight with a few new tricks.

Arkham Oranges is not a terrible game, but it's not the best in the series. They touched up on the Arkham City world by reconstructing many parts of the city that were seen as already destroyed in the Arkham City game and considering this is a prequel, you will see radical differences. While the game world has been expanded upon, it's mostly surface and not enough explorable interior that even after the story is interesting to walk around. I'm hoping that the DLC will expand on the gameplay as I felt the main game was too short.
The story did make a lot of references that long time Batman fans will recognize and they did it well.
The multiplayer is actually fun once you get the hang of it. Even though being able to play as Batman and Robin may sound over powered, the game implies that the thugs are really skilled and finally answers that question "if I was a thug in this game, would I have already spotted Batman?". Though the multiplayer makes this question meta, you can in fact take down Batman and Robin with your highly tacticaly advanced thug skills. Apart from Batman and Robin, you can get access to Bane and the Joker if you are the first to gain access to them.
My advice is that you wait for the full collection to come out if you are only interest in the main story. But if you are too hungry for another Batman game, then I guess you can go for it now, especially now that the multiplayer is hot.

Not necessary on this game).
Unfortunately, the game is a bit too conservative on both combat and stealth systems, and may feel "more of the same" to fans of the series.
It also has a very interesting and original online mode where you can play as Batman, Robin, or thugs in a power war. It's difficult to summarize, but it surely is a very interesting addition.
In case you didn't know previous Batman Arkham, just to mention they are some of the best game series this gen, with a fantastic and easy to grasp combat system, all the possible charismatic enemies and characters from the Batman comics, a very nice concept of adventure with fantastic side-quests, and a very good (though not exceptionally deep) combination of combat and stealth gaming.
A very honest recommendation, I was going to ignore it for looking "too similar" to the previous games (which I loved) but I'm happy I didn't. Good job from Eidos Montreal.

It's hard to decide if this is a good or bad game, but its certainly different from most shooters.
Pros:
The building is decent
Combat is heart pounding
Game looks nice
There are lots of updates quite often, the game strategy changes often to accomodate them.
Workshop system benefits both content creators and game devs more than the market.
Lots of servers to choose from, with plenty of modded ones.
Cons:
Performance is a big issue, especially on modded servers or servers that don't wipe often/have decay.
Most players talk ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ly or are edgy kids.
The text chat is server-wide, but voice chat is based on proximity, which makes it awkward when one person has a mic and another doesnt. Which leads to...
There isn't any in-game way to tell friend from foe other than asking in a text or voice chat if thats them running, or by wearing an agreed uniform. Note that at a longer distance, hats dont render either.
Building a decent structure on a hillside is a challenge unless its practically flat with no variation, which defeats the purpose of trying to keep it out of sight early on.
Game is not really balanced, but a lot could be changed:
Anyone can use twig to build to the top of your base or a tower to hop on it, which makes building big a priority
Components are nearly impossible to get since you have to follow roads, which offer a clear line of sight to shooters, or go to monument/landmarks, of which half the worthwhile ones have radiation and the other half are swarmed with people around them.
The node update makes finding stone a giant pain early on, which meants youre stuck with a rock for a long time for harvesting until you do find a stone node to make tools.
Big groups will dominate servers they're on until a wipe, nothing can be done if you dont have many friends.
In short, the game devs say they dont want to influence how players play the game, but theres a clear bias towards raiding. Meanwhile, a vending machine for trading costs twice as much high quality metal as an armored door but has less than a third of the hp.
TL;DR If you have friends and the time to play this game, its well worth $5 or even $10 since the game hopefully gets better over time when devs focus on balance instead of high quality wavy grass.

This is a stellar game with amazing gameplay and a phenomonal story. The gameplay consists of mostly running-and-gunning, although there's one mission where you should use stealth to your advantage. The difficulty is high enough to give you a real challenge, and you must conserve painkillers to survive, and there's no cover system either. However, you can dive around in slow-motion gunfights and dodge bullets.
The story centers around a man, Max Payne who has lost his meaning of life after his family was killed in a mysterious home invasion. 3 years after the incedent, Payne is framed for murdering his best friend. Now on the run, to prove his innocence Payne must find the perpetrator, all the while uncovering a government conspiracy in a world of darkness. The story is told through various comic strips, Max's internal monologues and surreal nightmares.
The only two bad things about the game? A lack of an autosave feature and the game's audio is broken when you download it, but there should be a fix somewhere on the Steam forums, just look up "Max Payne audio fix" or something. Other than that it's easily the best third-person shooter I've ever played.

A seminal shooter but one that doesn't quite stand up to modern scrutiny. A few genuinely awful dream sequences and a some serious compatibility issues with Windows 7 and 8 make this a hard sell to someone who doesn't already have an appreciation for Remedy's work, but if you have even a passing interest in Max Payne or the slow-mo heavy Hong Kong action flicks that inspired, then it's worth wading through this steadily decaying classic.

The original Max Payne, simply is superb.
If you enjoy a good story, and can see past some blocky graphics, this is worth a shot at a couple of $/£'s. The gameplay holds up, has the old school bullet time feature, and really hasn't dated too badly. The game is storyboard led, which means you don't have to deal with out of date facial animations!
You should be aware straight off the bat that the game is playable but has issues. You will need to download a patch which can be found in the Community Hub which changes a few audio files in to recognisable files - takes less than 2 minutes and makes the game work smoothly.
My Suggested purchase price = $3 -> $5

Excelent story telling and gameplay. Everything is spot on, save for a couple large issues.
1.) Cover is everywhere and reliable almost all the time. I say almost, sometimes you'll take cover against the wrong side of a wall and you'll end up dead because of it. Sometimes the cover doesn't work at all. Some things that look like they should be cover aren't, which can get you killed very easily. But as I said, it's very uncommon for this to occur.
2.) The Checkpoint placement is absolutely H O R R E N D O U S, forcing you to redo large battles over and over, considering the game is relatively difficulty. This is a major problem, especially near the end of the game when you lose a squad mate (not permanantly) and are forced to take on droves of enemies on your own. Many battles seem to occur in waves, it would have been nice to overcome one wave of enemies, then get a save, then continue. It has caused me on multiple occasions to quit the game because I just don't have the mental capacity to deal with this kind of rage. This is coming from someone with hundreds of hours clocked in Dark Souls. I know that there's nothing worse than getting far in a tough situation, only to die and have to redo the entire fight. At least in Dark Souls it  makes sense though.
Other than that I only have praise for the game The story is powerful, I like the clashing characters (I don't /like/ their clashing, I just find it realistic and a great way to cause tension), the gunplay is top notch. The enemy chatter when not engaged is realistic and immersive, reminds me of the guys in Battlefield Bad Company 2 who talk about the movie "Predator" before you have to kill them. It makes you think that these are real humans, it makes you think about your actions and everything you do. Which is, in the end, the entire point of the game.

GangBeasts is an amazing little physics brawler. With friends, family, or even drunk friends and family, this game can provide hours of non-stop, action-packed entertainment. The charm of the game is the fact that it is competitive, but losing doesn't necessarily feel like losing. I mean, it is hard to kind of keep a straight face when your character gets smacked off the top of a semi-truck by a Highway Sign.
The only gripe that I have against GangBeasts is how the game is constantly changing, but not in a good way. One instance of the game will have amazing features that make it feel fleshed out or make it easier to set up for prolonged play, while the next update will toss a few of these game mechanics away, replace them with a few more new mechanics, but the game will once again feel very "Beta". The game is still a ton of fun to toy with, regardless the state that it is in.
Hopefully, with the annouced console releases, GangBeasts will find itself in a more solid version of itself, and the only things the future updates will do is expand on the game itself, rather than being an endless game of tug-of-war deciding what kind of game it wants to be.

I think Pool Nation is one of those games that knows exactly what it is, and doesn't try to be anything it's not. Pool Nation is a billiards game, that's it. It's a slick-looking multiplayer/singleplayer campain billiards game.
And it's fun as hell.
Weirdly enough, I'm comparing this to Sniper Elite V2. While the two games' topics are in no way similar, both play out in coincidentaly similar ways. For example, both Pool Nation and Sniper Elite V2 hav slick, shiny graphics that look AMAZING. The graphics on both games look professionally made and I just love it. Graphics haven't been a huge thing for me, but wow, Pool Nation's graphics are actually better that Call of Duty Ghosts, and to top it off, my computer can run it.
Another weird similarity is the "killcams". In Sniper Elite V2, if you hit the enemy in a certain place, the camera pans out to the bullet or the enemy, and you get to watch the enemy get shot up close. In Pool Nation, if you make a Skill Shot or just a nice looking shot, the camera sets up on the hole, and you watch the ball fly in. The only difference is, Pool Nation does this less. For me, almost every shot in Sniper Elite was a killcam, and it got annoying as hell (except the ball shots). But the killcams only happen periodically in Pool Nation, and THANK YOU SO MUCH for doing so.
And the last thing, if you think about it just a tad, playing pool is almost like sniping. You have to aim carefully at a specifis target (and in some cases many targets) and shoot. Not only to you target all if the solid or striped balls in pool, but you also aim at a certain hole and shoot! How weird is that?
So now you know why I compared Pool Nation and Sniper Elite V2. Pretty good comparision if you ask me, but overall I think Pool Nation is worth your money. It's an amazing pool game, but its not Steam's only pool game.Buy it and hit me up.

Hands down the best pool game I've played. Graphically, it borders on being a tech demo for high end lighting and reflection effects. It's ridiculously shiny. The felt looks like felt. (I would not be surprised to see this game come bundled with every graphics card released in the next five years. It makes your GPU look like a hero.) The physics are just as good: crisp and consistent. Lots of game modes. Lots of cue sticks, balls, table decals, and pool halls to unlock. (I've played for 9 hours, I'm reasonably good at pool, and I've only opened up the easiest fourth of the unlockables.) Thanks to the quirky descriptions of your opponents before the matches, the game ends up having a ton of personality, considering it doesn't render the players at all, only their ghostly, floating sticks. It's got solid multiplayer, at least for two people. By people I mean friends. You can play big tournaments, in theory, with larger groups of strangers.
Perhaps most importantly in the context of 2014 gaming, Pool Nation is getting continued love and support from its devs. Snooker and "Box of Tricks" are both coming soon as free updates, and the devs are active in the forums.
As I write this, the game is on sale for $1.50. It's correctly priced at $10, so $1.50 is a steal.

When I first heard Rocksteady wasn't doing Arkham Origins I cried like Vader.  NOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOO.  My cries seemed justified at launch, as this game was riddled with game breaking bugs and glitches.
However, a series of patches have resolved all my issues and since then I'm loving this newest Batman game the most.  It's essentially Batman Arkham City (BAC) again with a few new gadgets, a revamped crime investigation feature, and a multiplayer mode.
Here's the new stuff you can look forward to:
Gadgets - Shock gloves replace the electron gun from BAC, and they are amazingly fun to use in combat once you upgrade them.  They'll allow you to punch through armored and shielded guards without the need to cape stun.
Glue grenades replace freeze nades.  Same functionality, but now it is glue!
Stun grenades temporarily confuse and blind enemies causing them to swing blindly.
Improved line launcher can now be used offensively by attaching it to enemies and environmental items causing collisions which disorient and take down enemies.
The new crime scene investigation allows deeper exploration in Detective Vision.  You can now scan evidence and scrub the scene by rewinding the events to unlock more clues to scan.
If you enjoyed Arkham City you'll also love Orgins, but don't expect anything too much different.

I think a large part of how you'll like this game is predicated upon whether or not you think games have gotten better in the last twenty years. I, myself, do not. Yooka-Laylee consists of many older mechanics and platforming ideas. The controls are good, but definitely leave something to be desired at times. It's what you'd expet from an N64 era, platforming adventure.
I like this game a lot because it puts almost everything on the player. It definitely reverts to an older mentality of being needlessly cryptic and purposefully obtuse. But, in a world full of highlighted objects and NPCs constantly telling you what to do, for me, that is a very welcome thing. I like the opaque nature of the puzzles, they require genuine interaction at times, and feel rewarding when they're resolved.
The powers, so far are pretty diverse, I like a lot of the mechanics they have you combine to solve new problems. This game has quite a bit of variety. You'll be doing tasks that are framed within similar concepts, but require new problem-solving. And, I think they've done a very good job in keeping things mildly familiar, while also making you constantly think in new ways.
I think they should be applauded for going against the grain and offering something vastly different than any game that takes place in a dungeon with swords. They've stricken those records from their videogame history, and instead are pretending the year is 1999. That loss of fat and pretension is a very powerful thing, and it's a tremendous benefit to the fun you'll have.
Yooka-Laylee exists inside a vacuum, where the world hasn't aged past Jak and Daxter. The innovations are limited because they don't have the same pallette of progression to draw from as FPS or RPGs do. But, what they've done with what they have, in my mind, has been deeply rewarding.
So, depending on your opinion of the state of games. The nature of hand-holding and cinematography versus gameplay. That should be a large factor in your decision. I played Banjo-Kazooie when I was a kid, and yada yada yada. That doesn't lend any credibility to my opinion of this game. I think developing from a place where there hasn't been progression in twenty years, they've done quite while. They've given an old genre new wings, bat wings...
Is it perfect? No. Are there numerous flaws that are there? Absolutely. But, in my opinion, they don't detract from the whole. Which is a maverick relic, shining in the face of more popular culture. And, at least from what I understand, that's exactly what the kickstarter was about.
It's not Banjo Kazooie but it surely manages to revive the old classic feeling.

*I'm a KS Backer, so my opinion is more important*
A fun game, if a little indicative that perhaps former Rare devs are a bit rusty.
I feel most of my criticisms come from this game taking too much from Banjo Kazooie, rather than Banjo Tooie.
Characters handle well enough, and I love how expansive the worlds are. The game also isn't very strict about out of bounds areas - being free to run around on the perimeter walls is actually really neat.
The soundtrack is nice, but not nearly as memorable as Grant Kirkhopes other works. Mumbos Mountain, Mayahem Temple, Jungle Japes all feel full of energy and really fit their settings, Tribalstack Tropics just feels meh and could apply to any number of settings.
Cutscenes could do with more character. It might have been easier to get away with just using character idle animations years ago, but not now. Even just having a handful of different character emotes play during dialogue would give the cutscenes more personality.

I really enjoy this game. I wrote a whole review on it - which you can read here:

Absolutely unique, beautiful, and a blast to play. Yooka Laylee's gameplay is centered around one simple concept: fun. You'll spend the roughly 30-40 hour quest playfully exploring giant colorful dreamscapes filled with a surprising amount of challenges and a plethora of quirky (and quite needy) characters.
Yooka-Laylee doesn't hold your hand while forcing you along a linear path--instead, it trusts you to play the game at your own pace. This freedom not only provides a fantastic and epic adventure but also a great sense of accomplishment as you see your collectable list fill up with tokens marking your achievements.
This game is a stunning creation by a very passionate team of developers and deserves a place in gamer's hearts. An instant classic!

This was the game I wanted when I wanted to be a space captain/pirate.  There are ships.  The ships come in different sizes and configurations.  You start in a tin can with a couple of turrets and work your way up to space battleships.  Some of them can be challenging to get your hands on, if a faction you've♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off is the only one that makes it.  There are different weapon systems, each with strengths and weaknesses.  There can be a story/plot if you want it to be the driving reason behind your space-captaining/piracy.  The game punishes you for thinking you are a main character with plot armor and can charge at whatever your quest is without strategy.  It rewards you for doing a bit of grinding on the side for money and xp, be that with asteroid mining, quasi-legal trading, playing space police, or space piracy.
Being a space game, there are a lot of different controls and interface options.  There are less than other space games I've tried.  Navigation is relatively simple, and wormholes, ion storms and radiation clouds make that more interesting than the vastness of space probably is.  You need captain 'levels' to fly bigger ships, but xp can be earned from basically doing anything.  Aiming is done via turrets.  Pick a view mode you like, aim the turrets yourself or let the computer do it for you, find a ship you like, and fly around space.  That's what you're here for right?
It took me 40 to 50 hours to finish each story line, taking my time and taking advantage of the vast numbers of pirates just waiting to be boarded and salvaged.  Ultimately this was the first 3d space game I've tried that gave me some complexity while still making 'fly a ship through space' enjoyably easy.  I enjoy leveling, working my way up from the bottom and becoming an unstoppable juggernaut.  I enjoy flying a ship through space and shooting things with lasers, or guns, or plasma cannons.  I enjoy some odd challenges and impossible odds.  I enjoy exploring.  I felt accomplished when I finished the plot in my decked out dreadnought.  I enjoyed this game.  And the free DLC.

There's no school like old school, and this game definitely fits in that category. There is only one selection for the difficulty until you have beaten the game, and that default sets the bar pretty high. This is by no means an easy game once you get into the harder levels, but you get a feeling of accomplishment once the credits roll.
This game also introduced a lot of new mechanics into the mainstream gaming world, such as bullet time and a 3rd person camera. It also made use of a few things that either haven't been done since or have not been pulled off as good since then. One of these being that the game, instead of using in engine cutscenes for most of the story, used something akin to a comic book or graphic novel to tell the story.
The story of this game is also amazing. It captures the feelings of a man that has nothing left to loose and sets out to get his revenge on the people that took away his former life. It also dives into his mind by literally letting you run around in Max's dreams every once in a while, trying to stay alive from the darkness that is eating at his mind.
Verdict: 9.9/10 Because that last area in the game was really hard (at least for me) [-0.1], but there is nothing bad I can say about pretty much anything else in the game.

I'm not usually a player of simulation games, but this game is very enjoyable. Potting is so satisfying and once you start completing skillshots, it's enough to make a grown man make girlish squeals of pleasure.
Pros
- Very easy to "pick up & play" the tutorials are well done, but are OPTIONAL, so you can do them whenever you feel like, if at all and repeatable, so you can brush up on certain types of shots if you are having difficulty.
- All of the things that make this more game than simulation can be turned off or not used. Those who want a challenge don't have to have aiming lines or use flashbacks.
- Loads of unlockable customisation options, unlike certain simulators where to get a new table or cues (or trains or pinballs) you have to get your wallet out, 95+% of the customisation options are unlockable by beating different challenges or tours.
- Each match in a tour comes with 2 challenges that require you to win the match in certain ways, such as using a particular shot or getting a high score, etc, giving completionists more to achieve.
- Scrolling the mouse back & forth to control the cue is enjoyable
- The graphics are amazing. Bearing in mind i'm playing this on a laptop, it looks beautiful. I would go as far as saying this is the best looking game i've run on this, with no framerate drops.
Cons
- The menu can occasionally get fiddly.

- Sometimes, when trying to aim the cue with the middle-mouse-button, the camera pans up instead.
- Extremely rare crashes. Had 2 so far, but i'm unsure if that's something to do with my hardware to be honest.
Seriously, just look through the rest of the reviews. There are HUNDREDS of reviews, all positive, some are casual players, some are hardcore simulation players, all of them love it. Even when this game isn't on sale, it is totally worth the full asking price. If you're even slightly interested in this game, pick it up, you won't be disappointed.

LOOOOT!! Although shallow at times, B2 still manages to hold its own as a single play RPG. Its real strength is the multiplayer system - it is about 1023 times better playing with friends, fragging away at all those enemies in search of new loot. Seriously - all about the loot. All gear is leveled to the character, but a big upgrade feels satisfysing as you spray bullets into the face of all those enemies. The talent system is reasonable, and gives a bit more flexibility in the game play, pending on how you enjoy playing. The humor is at times witty and enjoyable - sometimes it is a bit to pervasive and the "story" gets in the way at times; speed and combat being the main points of interest for the game.
The bonus system (for reaching specific acheivement milestones, like 100 head shots with a pistol for example) allows you to pick which attributes to upgrade: a novel system which provides a sense of customisation as you improve your character and get a feel for how you would best like to play/what weapons you would like the best.
I have logged quite a few hours playing with friends and still ocassionally go back to feel that sense of satisfaction mashing faces with critical hits from my OP weapons.

What a fantastic game. I had no idea about this game's existence until literally yesterday when it came out and I saw it in steam, and oh wow, was it a pleasant surprise. As a big fan of the old golden era Rare platformers like DK64 and banjo&kazooie, I'm amazed.
The only "gripe" I have with this game is the level design, worlds are huge and a bit chaotic, everything seems to be all over the place instead of fitting into the worlds enviroments in a natural way. The hub world, Hivory Towers, is really well designed though, I got no problems with that, I'm talking about the main levels. It's not a major thing for me, but I wish levels were more like how they were in Banjo&Kazooie, smaller and themed around a specific thing, like: desert, ice, fire, spooky, western, factory and such, to make them more memorable.
Aside from this, everything else feels like, sounds like and plays like Banjo&Kazooie/Tooie, so if you loved these, you WILL love Yooka-Laylee.

(A good friend gifted me a pre-order, so I guess it was free?) When you try to recreate an experience from about 20 years ago, you risk angering a lot of people wearing rose-tinted glasses. The vidya garm scene has shifted away from this genre, instead being replaced by endless CoD sequels and perverted anime RPGs. Going back to a simpler time, Yooka-Laylee is a big box of "Your mileage may vary". Some people will complain about not being able to play it on keyboard or the jibber-jabber voices being annoying. Some people will talk about the camera being bad at times. Others still, like myself, will note the slippery controls and energy meter which can get a bit taxing after a while. It's a title that relies on nostalgia, and for better or worse, it accurately revives the classic 90s era platformer.
As someone who grew up with Spyro and Crash instead of Nintendo 64 games, I'm not quite feeling the nostalgia but I will say they captured the originals quite well. It's certainly challenging at times, sometimes in a good way, others bad. It's a pure-hearted title, something I personally value quite high. Bright vibrant colors, cheeky humor that lends bonus points to adults that get the joke, a lot of exploring and stuff to get. A true "K-A" game, it requires patience and a relaxed, casual attitude. Like Final Fantasy XV, if you try to rush this game, you will not enjoy it. As someone who earns 100% (120%?) on the original Crash and Spyro trilogies, I found a lot of enjoyment to be had here.
TL;DR
-If you like Banjo-Kazooie or other 90-2000s platformers, you will probably like this. I like it, but it's flawed. Then again, I also like Deadly Premonition, so I'm probably not qualified professionally? 4/5 "Good, but not perfect"

Note before reading the review
--------------------------------------------
Keep in mind, the recommendation/non-recommendation of the game is NOT an indication of the game being good or not (it's a great game). I just can't recommend it because, in its current state, the game is a bug-riddled mess. I myself did manage to beat the game, and I enjoyed (almost) every minute of it. Fantastic game. When it works, it is definitely the best Arkham game out there, but I can't, in good conscience, recommend a triple A, 50 dollar title that doesn't work for a major portion of the playerbase. If these bugs are fixed, the game's an easy recommendation. 9/10 game. Phenomenal. Incredible atmosphere, incredible gameplay, and the best writing in an Arkham game (sorry Paul Dini). But right now, this game, in its current state, simply cannot be recommended.
-------------------------------------------
Batman: Arkham Origins is one of the best examples of a fantastic game riddled by bugs. Great story (probably the best in an Arkham game), and great gameplay marred by atrocious problems. Bugs so far include a bug that prevents people from launching the game, game crashes (preventing the game from being completed), and keyboard/mouse control problems (where you can't land critical hits). There are even reports of people being unable to attack! Some bugs are minor, like Batman jerking up and down while gliding (kind of funny, actually). Overall, I can't recommend the game, in particular because of the gamebreaking bugs that can occur.
Gameplay-wise, the game is great. It's not as good as Arkham City, because of major balancing issues with certain gadgets. For example, the Remote Claw is incredibly overpowered in Predator missions. Painfully overpowered, because of the Remote Claw Takedown, for example. It's basically a ranged, silent, inverted takedown. The Electrocutioner Gloves, in combat, grant you 2x per punch (3x per crit) on your Combo Counter, and can punch through shields/armor/stun batons, allow you to counter any enemy attacks. The gameplay is fun overall though. The new Crime Scene feature is cool, even if it holds your hand. The new gadgets do prove for interesting gameplay.
If you're gonna drop $50 on a game, it better damn well work, and right now, WB Games can't guarantee even that. If you can run it, I promise you that you're in for a damn treat, but there's a relatively high chance that you can't.
UPDATE: There are reports with people having issues booting the game still, a whole month after release. Sadly, this is unacceptable. I can't comment on the multiplayer for the game, as I've only played 3 or 4 matches. In terms of multiplayer problems, I've heard that after the recent update, player levels got reset without warning. Also, I was able to beat the game without encountering anything gamebreaking, but I also know that some of my friends can't even launch the game in its current state -- some FATAL ERROR OZZY thing. It's quite saddening, really.
UPDATE 2: I want to expand a bit on the graphics and sound design of the game, since I barely touched on it. The game runs rather well on max settings (apart from PhysX), using DX11 features at 1920x1080 on my setup -- with an i5-3470, and an AMD Radeon HD 7950 -- specifically between 40 and 80 frames per second depending on the area, it's perfectly playable, and it looks good for a game working around the limitations of Unreal Engine 3. The visual and sound design in the game together is absolutely amazing. It was good enough to make me believe it was Christmas, if not just for a moment in October. Roger Craig Smith, and Troy Baker are absolutely fantastic at reprising their roles as Batman and the Joker respectively. Brilliant stuff.
UPDATE 3: Aaaand Warner Bros has no plans to fix Arkham Origins bugs, apart from some keyboard/mouse functionality with Deathstroke challenge missions. ...Maybe.
UPDATE 4: Critical Hit on KBM bug was fixed some time ago, not sure when.

The Jedi Knight series moves onto this part where you no longer play as Kyle Katarn but get to create your own character. The game is much more lightsaber oriented as is shown by giving you one right at the beginning. And that is what the game excels at - lightsaber combat. Oh, and how much fun it is! With the dismemberment option on it feels like really having a powerful weapon you can cut every opponent with. On top of that you of course get Force powers. The story is not bad but lacks focus because you play as an unknown character without any background. Instead of looking over some plot events it instead rotates around your decisions to either become a Jedi or a Sith. This also effects the level design a bit. However it remains fun and enjoyable. Noteworthy are also two other things - multiplayer and mods. The community of players who play online is still strong and even some mods have a big following of players. The mods especially use most of the potential. like when some mods are letting you play ALL Star Wars lightsaber duels (movie ones and also others). This is definitely a game for anyone who likes Star Wars and lightsaber combat. Recommended!

This game a is a tough one to decide. It really isn't a game that I can sit and dump 8 hours into daily like some of the other games I've played, but it is fun to come back to it every once in a while and get my "freelancer" fix for the week. I personally found this game to be pretty fun when in sandbox/exploration mode. Story mode on the other hand.. was poorly completed, I believe I spent about 20 minutes in, and dumped it due to the appalling voice acting and poorly scripted story.
Now for sandbox I loved flying around blasting and capturing ships to sell at the local stations. I loved upgrading my ship from the inventories of captured  ships. I'm always looking for the shield or weapon improvment. I loved exploring the map and seeing all the cool spacial anomalies. UnfortunateIy, though I did find some general weaknesses in the way content is utilized in the game, there are only a handful of side mission types such as capture ship A, Destroy ship B, or Haul element C these side missions do get old pretty quickly and is a main reason why I cannot dump countless hours into the game in one sitting. Overall, I find the game to be pretty engaging when played casually, but any longer than a couple of hours and I'm ready for something else. To the developer: I really hope you guys haven't given up on this game now that it's considered "Complete" there is still a tremendous amount of possibilities with it, and I would love to see more content(More engaging space stations, etc.) Thanks a ton for creating a game that allows me to get my space sim fix when I feel the urge.

This game is unbalanced. Apart from an unengaging story line with bare-bones, tired story missions, the free roam (the idea of which I love) becomes stalled and unsatisfying because of the unbalanced gameplay. Your rank quickly surpasses your ability to upgrade to better ships. This means the missions generated for your rank level are mostly impossible - as noted by the threat lvl attached to your target's info display IMPOSSIBLE - because you're still flying around in a pea shooter. Impossible engagements for missions of my level? That's absurd! I quickly realized that at around lvl 10, the only time I was actually completing those missions was when heavy allied ships were there to do the brunt of the damage. I realized I was doing next to nothing, very unsatifying, and only survived because the target's fire was directed elsewhere.
So you spend your time wandering aimlessly trying to find easier missions which are few and far between. Also maddening is capturing ships - far and away the best means for generating credits - but which is nearly always hampered by allied ships blowing your target away before you can either commence or complete a capture attempt
So, if you like withering fire directed at your ship (who's shields are about as strong as plastic wrap), love constantly wrangling with camera controls, love grinding hour after hour after hour for little gain, and you absolutely adore constantly reloading save games, go get this thing. PROS:
++ Best community on Steam. I own a lot of games and visit nearly all the forums - but this one is the best. Devs are active, the community is friendly and helpful, and some of it is satisfyingly weird (meep...) meep. MEEP.
++ It's not overly complex. Which doesn't mean it's simple or dumbed down - it just means that you can jump right in and have a great time exploring space.
++ Combat sequences can be exhilarating! I've been in many skirmishes that could have gone either way, frantically deploying sinks and coming around to line turrets up to open fire. Enemies coming in at all angles and PTE disrupted...
++ With just a couple of mods (skyboxes and nebulas) the game can be breathtaking visually. I play with the lights off and the surround on and it is very easy to get lost in the moment.
++ It's just fun. You can do a lot of different things with it and have a great time doing them. The voice acting is infamously fun bad, and the story is a kind of canned - but who cares, it's fun running through it all.
++ Ultrawide!!! 3440x1440 - no problem and gorgeous!
CONS:
++ The economy is kind of not really there at all. I wanted to be a trader but the derelict mechanic made it more profitable and efficient to be a bad♥♥♥♥♥with scavenger bots. Which is kind of too bad, but it is what it is.
++ Playing the campaign like it is freeplay means you will be so OP that every enemy the campaign throws at you will be trivial to weak. Wish there was more scaling here, but it's not so bad to destroy waves of ships with out much thought because you outclass them by a mile.
++ The UI is kind of crap and it's all raster so you can't mod it out to be better.
++ Once you've played for a while, you start to realize that there isn't enough ship variance to keep it interesting. Some ships are clearly better than others, and you just sort of play the game out with that ship until the next tier - and its obvious captain, become available to you.

I purchased this game almost immediately during early access because I had been wanting to play a good space sim for quite a long time. It is a vast improvement over the previous title in the series and successfully creates a fun space sim experience with some rpg progression for your character.
Initially after release the game was somewhat buggy, but the developers have ironed out the rough edges and even successfully adapted most of the user interface for gamepad control. Thus far I have spent most of my time in the sandbox mode, but I have recently begun the story playthrough. Both modes are fun to play with the story mode featuring a rather standard, but competently-executed space sim plot. Best of all is that steam workshop is available for the game and there have been many great mods that improve aspects of the gameplay as well as those that create custom content.
There is a good diversity of ships and weaponry in the game, with ship types ranging from small gunships and shuttle craft up to battleship size vessels available to be purchased. You can also hire officers who confer stat bonuses and other ships piloted by mercenaries to join you. There are numerous ways to make money including a robust trading economy, asteroids to mine, spatial phenomena to explore, odd jobs to be done, transport/taxi missions, and of course bounty hunter missions.
Combat is satisfying, though you certainly feel like more of a ship commander than a pilot. This is probably due to the game's third person perspective which suits the game well because most of the ships you will use are more like capital ships than fighters.
To sum it up, this is one of the best single player space sim/rpg's to come out in a very long time. In some ways I enjoy this game more than Elite: Dangerous.

This game is getting a lot of hate from everyone, and I can't see why! If you are a batman fan, you must play this game. The story in my opinion is leagues ahead of the other two games. Sure the ending of Arkham City was shocking, but the rest was a long drawn out fetch quest. This game has a consistantly engaging story with character development for many characters like Alfred, Barbara, and Jim which creates much more interesting relationships between Batman and his allies. It is on the same level as the writing of Scott Snyder, Frank Miller, and Jeph Loeb. The new developers kept the combat system the same for the most part, with only minor tweaks. I don't understand everyones dislike of this decision. If they would have changed it, they would have gotten just as much hate. If it ain't broke don't fix it, and that method holds up in this game.They did however, greatly improve the boss fights. You feel like Batman fighting famous DC rougues. They are honestly some of the best boss fights I have played in a long time. With the industry moving away from boss fights, it was very refreshing to have such exceptionally epic battles with the assassin's. The city is a little bland, but it's no different than Arkham City. It's just empty streets filled with thugs to fight. The side quests aren't exceptional, but they are fun and make this game well worth the price. In my personal opinion, this is the best game in the arkham series. It may not have completely reinvented the series, but it improves on the previous iterations. If you are a Batman fan, or never have played the arkaham series before, this is a must-play. Don't believe the hate. The improvements the new developers made (fantastic story and epic boss fights) are massive improvements to the series.

As 2003's follow-up to Jedi Knight II: Jedi Outcast, Jedi Academy diverts from the largely-linear narrative of Jedi Knight to bring forth an open-ended, player-controlled experience to the Jedi Knight simulation genre. Rather than playing as the series' main character, the saboteur-turned-Jedi Kyle Katarn, you are his student, Jaden Korr, sent out from Luke Skywalker's Jedi Academy to save the galaxy once more from the dark side of the Force. Featuring a fully customizable main character and a story with two separate endings, Jedi Academy expands upon its predecessor's excellent combat, while at the same time preserving, for the most part, the quality we've come to expect from the Jedi Knight series.
If I had to point out my complaints towards this title, I would say that the narrative, while more open to player input, is ultimately slightly trivialized by the departure from series protagonist Kyle Katarn, and, though not nearly as awful as The Force Unleashed, is still a mild letdown after its prequel. In addition, ranged weapons seem to have been downgraded from an alternative form of assault to nigh-useless in this edition, limiting the player effectively to lightsabers, Force Powers, and a variety of combos. Neat? Yes. Ultimately more engaging and fun? Not really. At least give us a buffer between normalcy and Jedihood!
Still, if you're at all interested in Star Wars, or you've been playing the Jedi Knight series, or you're even looking for a good action game, there's not much I'd recommend more than Jedi Academy. It's a great ride, and it's a wonderful dose of that galaxy far, far away.

I played Elite: Dangerous, then X3AP, then X:Rebirth, went back to X3AP and finally I stumbled on Starpoint Gemini 2. How I came to this game? In elite, I was fascinated by the cool-looking fighters, the dog-fighting with HOTAS controller and hype of Horizon. I soon realised the game was time-consuming and i was unable to accomplish as much as I would expected. I loaded up X3 (I bought during a steam sale) and started playing. This game also had dog-fighting, tons of ship classes but the main draw was the scope and depth of the game. At the midpoint, I coud lead a wing of fighters, setup space stations and managed a fleet of trading freighters. It was really cool but I spent way too much time and the graphics were not as cool. I hopped over to X: Rebirth and got a headache navigating in the engine. I hopped back to X3 for a short while and finally got to SPG2.
SPG2 is a Space-Theme ARPG. In free-roam, you control a ship and navigate through a gigantic starchart map. You can pick up alot space-thremed missions, mine asteroids, trade between space stations and planets, be a pirate or police. It cover much of everything you can think of in a space sim game but to a limited depth. I won't not say it is a shallow game because you have a pretty good idea of what a space sim would be like after playing this game.
+ Tons of playable ships
+ Beautiful ship designs
+ Space combat is flashy and exciting.
+ Tons of things to do, you won't get bored of things to do
- Limited functionality in several aspect of a typical space sim game
- Reputation system, licences and bulletin news interface seems like a mere after-thought
- Shield system is surprisingly 2 dimensional
- No real space dogfighting

I bought Starpoint Gemini a couple of years back and just could not get into it.  I had put Starpoint Gemini 2 on my wishlist, hoping for a sale.  So I recently bought it on sale and I am find the freeroam mode very satisfying.
I started out mining asteroids, then doing missions and all the while figuring out the different mechanisms for the game.  I had googled some "Getting started" guides and found out that boarding and selling ships was where most money could be made.  I had changed the game mode to easy, I wanted to check out all the different ships the game has to offer without too much of a struggle.   There is a clear progression with the choice of ships and going from your beginner Gunship and ending up with a Dreadnought is very satisfying.   The controls are a lot like Freelancer.
Selling ships and taking out the most wanted from the Bounty board is a sure way to get rich fast.  There are different "zones" near friendly space stations that offer baddies from the different factions that are ideal for getting xp and capturing ships and dragging them to the spacestation.   Troopers are the currency that allow you to capture ships, space stations run out of them and then you have to go look for them somewhere else or wait until the space station has a new shipment of them.  I love the map with all the different factions and things to discover, there are structures called artefact vaults where you can collect an artefact, the objective is to collect all 50.  Some special kills (usually baddies from the most wanted board) yield unique weapons with better than average stats and some missions/kills yield   blueprint for unique equipment.  Most subsystems of  your ship can changed with upgrades that give bonuses.  You also can hire different officers that give bonuses. Furthermore once you reach a certain level,  you can hire mercs that join you so you end up with a little fleet.
The combination of different ships (70 apparently), different officers, skills, perks, mercs and equipment and the huge map makes this game a great experience for me. I enjoy the grind of doing missions and capturing ships.   Overall a great Elite clone.  The story is a little thin and the game could use some world-lore detailing the history of the various factions beyond the news bulletins, something like the books in the Elder Scroll games would be nice. Also, the capture/trooper mechanic could be reworked a little, I never understand why some of my troopers still have to die when they are capturing an empty enemy ship.

Starpoint Gemini 2 is surprisingly easy to handle quickly, it offers a variety of piloting styles through a few shortcuts (i.e. space bar, or v for turret mode). It is indeed a versatile game where you can choose from 3 classes which can evolve in a RPG-lite fashion. Each class has 4 base skills and in each 5 facets you can improve when you activate the former, and classes share perks which can enhance some facets of your character (i.e. you like boarding? enhance your troops efficiency, you like trading? enhance your mercantile skills, you like piloting destroyers? enhance your skill with that class of ships).
Several RPG aspects are simplified yet overall the existence of each feature serve a justified purpose. Depending on your actions, you will gain positive or negative reputation which in turn will make you hostile or friendly towards this or that faction. Once you are friendly with a faction, you may be offered to buy some "licences" which may provide diverse advantages like extra coin for destroying some other factions' ships or get free repairs at friendly starbases.
All-in all, the sandbox space opera SG2 is pretty vast both in terms of maps, weapon choices (while there are only 3 types of light weaponry: beam, guns and plasma and 3 types of heavy weaponry: torpedoes, missiles and shockwave, there is a vast arsenal to choose from in each types and categories) and ships. The latter comes into no less than 10 types, 8 of the standard military classes and 2 in the more civil transporters, and each major faction provides its own versions of each class (with different hardpoint layouts, cargo and trooper capacity, etc.) so at the end there are plenty of ships to choose from and you can perfectly go through the game flying a corvette (the starting class) if you like to and still be some kind of challenge for heavier classes. You can also deploy fighters and get mercenary ships (of any class) to escort you (one of the player character class, the commander, may enhance those drastically).
The combination of RPG and sandbox space opera inevitably means you have to grind (twice here since you need both money and xp), you'll be given the opportunity to peacefully mine ore, ice and much more (various type of asteroid fields, with more stones than you can dream of), you can attack any ship you like or you can do some mission from a panel of several ones (repair stuff, scan stuff, kill stuff, protect stuff from being killed, transport stuff) and while there is some diversity there it is of course very likely you'll do the same missions several times. In addition to the storyline (which is secondary in this game - you are even offered to skip it at the very beginning) you will unlock also some side missions (while some are custom scripted versions of the normal freelance missions, some are totally unique as well). So there is plenty of things to do, and the difficulity of the missions also scales up depending from where you are in the galaxy and your level. As a sandbox (freeroam) game, it is also possible for you to go to hostile territory and try to shoot down and loot anything you can, although this may be pretty difficult to do and you're more likely to die if you are not prepared for a proper war. If you are reasonable at start, you will do missions in neutral/friendly territory, watch enemies get shot by friendlies and scavenge the spoils of war (good thing being you still get exp).
Sadly, SG2 is not exempt of flaws and one of the major one I've noticed is the IA in the battles. Sometimes (emphasis on "sometimes") enemy ships stop there and don't do anything until you shoot them. While I am not sure what causes this, my guess would be that the IA is programmed to have the same behavior regardless of having guns on the side or back of the ship or not. While sometimes the IA manoeuvers around you, many times it also just stop there and shoots you at full stop. In fact and especially if you pilot even heavy ships like if it was a fighter, you will find yourself having to reduce speed drastically in order to catch anything (unless you have several manoeuvrability enhancement like officers and equipement). While this is something you can surely get along with, it is still one aspect of the game that can be considered a critical shortcoming as it does not give you a intuitive feeling of piloting and the latter does not have so much impact on the fight (beside getting your enemy in your firing arcs). So if you expect a simulation of space battle, you won't find it here yet there is still enough complexity and customisation options in SG2 to actually make up for that in some way.
A few other things kind of annoyed me like few specific types of ship seemed to always disconnect from my grappler when I set engines on overdrive while towing them. It only happened with those specific ships so far for some reason, so at some point, if I was too far from a station I would be discouraged to attempt to capture them. Some part of the UI are a bit clunky, manageable but lacking ergonomy like the contextual menu which you typically use for repairing or scanning which obscure the view. As I said a bit of a detail and easy to work around but still its one amongst several design calls that leave this "meh" impression instead of a "wow" one. Fortunately, there are a lot of well thought features that actually balance such little things in my opinion.
Also, be prepared to stare at your screen for sometime while your autopilot is active, there is no time-acceleration feature in SG2. You can of course set the "power to engine" which greatly accelerate travelling and you have several ways of enhancing your ship's speed even further. There are also space highways (wormholes, gates - this one being expensive to use) that you can use, but most of the time you will have to travel through the void (not so empty at all actually) just looking at the distance counter shrinking for a few seconds/minutes till you reach destination. Of course a lot can happen when you do so, an asteroid or structure can be in the way (autopilot may not always detect it), a cloaked raider may attack you from nowhere or good old pirates may invite themselves to your party. Also you may want to keep an eye on some space anomalies like those space streams that may actually send you to hostile territories without your consent. A big part of your gaming time will be just that, travelling and making sure you reach the intended destination (although I find it quite bearable myself, it may be a matter of personality/taste).
Overall, SG2 offers a decent space sandbox experience, with enough content, RPG elements and customisation options (character development, variety of space ships and equipements, additional bonuses with officers).  With the 3 character classes, there is of course a bit of replayability along with the 2 aligements (positive or negative reputation) nevertheless you will have to go through the grinding again (with a bit of experience though, you'll know how to progress faster on subsequent playthroughs). Economy is pretty balanced and merchant, mining, pirate, bounty hunter, military, scavenger etc. are all viable options to progress at similar paces (some are just more appealing to some types of players. some are more efficient for credits or xp's) and it is easy to switch from one career to the other" just by changing ship (you can store several in a garage accessible from all stations) and playstyle (for a cost you can even reset your abilities and perks).
If you like the genre (sandbox, not story driven) and do not mind the inherent features of it (grind) SG2 offers a fresh take on the open-world space opera. It is not as deep as the X series, yet it is much deeper in terms of game mechanics than many venerable predecessors like privateer or the earlier elite series to name but a few.
