I wouldn't reccomend this game for a few reasons. First being that it does not have the content I'd expect for the pre-order price. Having one non-training level at launch is just down right unacceptable. I thought there would be significantly more content at release. This alone warrants a non-buy if I had another chance. It's likely I will not play this game until I see that Steam has updated it so I know a new level/area has been downloaded. This is pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥ though, considering they already have my $60 or whatever. We all just LOVE spending money for nothing.
Second - as many other reviews mention - this game requires you to be connected all the time. While I have no issue with that, there are still a lot of people who get screwed over by this and are unable to reliably play the game and experience it's features without being interrupted. This isn't good by any stretch, and it should be corrected (aka feature removed). I understand why a game would require an internet connection to play all the time, but Hitman (and the entire series) has never been something that required instaneous online-only data to be drawn into the world in any way shape or form. That alone renders the feature useless and expendable.
Third, the menus are pretty bad. Windows 8 on a non-touchscreen laptop bad. They look cool as long as you don't try and do anything. Editing my loadout was awkward the first few times I attempted it, and I frequently ended up starting the level with incorrect and/or missing items (my mistake, but still).
I also haven't seen any customization. If this game is supposed to be with 47 being a part of the agency, he needs to be able to upgrade his weapons as he did in Blood Money. Again, that game set a tone that has yet to be touched. Now this isn't COD/BF/CS, and you don't need to go overboard with skins and accessories, but the simple mods (magazine size, silencer types) or even different model guns would be a fantastic change of pace. This also would significantly increase replay value. You could easily copy/paste the Blood Money weapon customization aspect into this game and have a perfect solution.
That said, I do enjoy controlling 47 again and it does feel pretty fluid for me once I got the controls down. The environment on the first level (at least) is very much a sandbox build that is enjoyable. The replay value on it would be higher IF it wasn't the only level in the game. I expect replay value overall to be very high once they (finished and) release more content.
The visuals and music are great from what I've seen. I don't have a 4K rig so I can't comment on what really is "Next Gen" about this game. To my eyes (and my PC), it's a high quality game but I wouldn't say it's blown my mind yet. I haven't experienced any lag in the game itself, and I could care less about the quality of the cut scenes.
TLDR: This game isn't finished (no content). They tried to recreate Blood Money and so far it hasn't worked out at all. Buy if you would enjoy replaying one level. Have your internet primed and online.

I'm writing this review while waiting for this single-player game to reconnect to its servers so I can continue playing from my latest savepoint because the game kicked me out of a mission due to a lost internet connection. In fact, just now the game threw the following message at me: "Unable to connect to the HITMAN service. Failed to authorize your account with the HITMAN server. For more information, contact HITMAN support."
My options at this point are to "Retry" or to "Go Offline". Retrying does nothing, going offline will let me start the mission again from scratch, but won't let me load any saves I made while I was online (even though I'm 99,9% sure that saves are stored locally and not in some cloud).
All the time while I'm writing this review the game is "trying" to reconnect to the servers (It has to be mentioned that my internet connection is fully functional at this point).
So here's what I'm asking myself right now: why is this even a thing? Why do I have to be online for a ♥♥♥♥ing single-player experience. I am not interested in making it to some leaderboards or something. Why does the game kick me out of a mission if I lose the connection? Dark Souls lets me play offline even though it's a much more internet-reliant game. This joke of a product doesn't.
I am sad because if you look past the always-online nonsense, the poor optimization and the fact that the game so far consists of just one mission (and two tutorial missions) you will see that the devs finally understood what the playerbase expects and wants from a HITMAN game and I won't lie, they actually tried to deliver.
However I can't look past those issues because at this point I am STILL not connected to the servers. In the end I am glad that I went with the intro pack rather than the "full experience" (which at this point is more of a "fool experience"). I'm glad I didn't spend more than 13 euros on it and I am positive that I will not purchase future episodes.

As someone who only marginally cares for Call of Duty, this one is probably the best CoD I have played.
The multiplayer is much easier to get the hang of than any other CoD, and remains fair no matter what level you are. It's much more reliant on skill than on getting to a high level. It just feels almost perfectly balanced. Unfortunately, the population is low nowadays and the use of an aimbot is relatively common. There are legitimately skilled players, though.
Zombies is not quite the same. It feels very different, but not overly so. It's not really as good as Black Ops zombies, but it's not that bad, either. It's a worthy successor. I feel like you won't enjoy the game without a map pack at the very least, though. Hence why I bought Die Rise (one of my favorite zombies maps on this game), as well as Nuketown Zombies (Thank you, digital deluxe edition sale). Overall, if you want to buy this game for zombies, consider Black Ops 1 first.
Now for the campaign. I owned this at launch for Xbox 360, and played the campaign through once. I didn't think too much of it. However, playing it again, I'm loving it. I've played quite a few campaigns for games, including the legendary Halo campaigns. From a story-telling perspective, I hold Black Ops 2 up there with Halo games. I can't recommend it enough. The campaign is probably the reason you should get this game.
Overall, it's not perfect, but it certainly is a league above the Call of Duty games of new (*cough*GHOSTS*cough*), and it packs a lot of fun and fair gameplay, which is strange for Call of Duty. I recommend this or Black Ops as a starter Call of Duty game.
Pros:
+Fantastic campaign
+Balanced multiplayer
+Zombies is enjoyable
+Gameplay is refreshing and enjoyable for a CoD
Cons:
-Low multiplayer population
-Zombies is less enjoyable than first Black Ops
-Many hackers
Mids:
~Most of the zombies maps are massive. This is both great and bad, because reviving becomes difficult, but the variety of locations makes it enjoyable.
~The default game just seems not as good as it could be, and map packs are really the only fix here.

Long ago I played the demo for Jedi Academy and wrote it off as a cheap cash-in in the wake of Jedi Knight 2, a game I enjoyed but didn't really want more of the same from. Boy was I wrong.
Years later I finally get round to playing Jedi Academy and it's surprisingly good fun. A steady supply of varied missions, fun lightsaber combat, and a force powers system that got a satisfying rebalance from JK2: they now recharge faster, upgrade in interesting ways, and are a complete joy to use. Force Lighning in particular is hugely satisfying to use at it's max level: it blasts everything in a forward arc with such intensity it sends people flying off platforms, crashing against walls, and slamming against ceilings. A bit overpowered, but christ is it hilarious.
Another interesting quirk of note: this game was made just before the advent of ragdoll physics. Keen to provide some sort of feedback as you slam people around, though, the developers developed a sort of pseudo-ragdoll system that blends animations programmatically to make characters bend (as best they could) with the environment. This makes various storm trooper corpses bend over ledges and objects in an entirely comical way. It's great.

I wouldn't reccomend this game for a few reasons. First being that it does not have the content I'd expect for the pre-order price. Having one non-training level at launch is just down right unacceptable. I thought there would be significantly more content at release. This alone warrants a non-buy if I had another chance. It's likely I will not play this game until I see that Steam has updated it so I know a new level/area has been downloaded. This is pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥ though, considering they already have my $60 or whatever. We all just LOVE spending money for nothing.
Second - as many other reviews mention - this game requires you to be connected all the time. While I have no issue with that, there are still a lot of people who get screwed over by this and are unable to reliably play the game and experience it's features without being interrupted. This isn't good by any stretch, and it should be corrected (aka feature removed). I understand why a game would require an internet connection to play all the time, but Hitman (and the entire series) has never been something that required instaneous online-only data to be drawn into the world in any way shape or form. That alone renders the feature useless and expendable.
Third, the menus are pretty bad. Windows 8 on a non-touchscreen laptop bad. They look cool as long as you don't try and do anything. Editing my loadout was awkward the first few times I attempted it, and I frequently ended up starting the level with incorrect and/or missing items (my mistake, but still).
I also haven't seen any customization. If this game is supposed to be with 47 being a part of the agency, he needs to be able to upgrade his weapons as he did in Blood Money. Again, that game set a tone that has yet to be touched. Now this isn't COD/BF/CS, and you don't need to go overboard with skins and accessories, but the simple mods (magazine size, silencer types) or even different model guns would be a fantastic change of pace. This also would significantly increase replay value. You could easily copy/paste the Blood Money weapon customization aspect into this game and have a perfect solution.
That said, I do enjoy controlling 47 again and it does feel pretty fluid for me once I got the controls down. The environment on the first level (at least) is very much a sandbox build that is enjoyable. The replay value on it would be higher IF it wasn't the only level in the game. I expect replay value overall to be very high once they (finished and) release more content.
The visuals and music are great from what I've seen. I don't have a 4K rig so I can't comment on what really is "Next Gen" about this game. To my eyes (and my PC), it's a high quality game but I wouldn't say it's blown my mind yet. I haven't experienced any lag in the game itself, and I could care less about the quality of the cut scenes.
TLDR: This game isn't finished (no content). They tried to recreate Blood Money and so far it hasn't worked out at all. Buy if you would enjoy replaying one level. Have your internet primed and online.

I'm writing this review while waiting for this single-player game to reconnect to its servers so I can continue playing from my latest savepoint because the game kicked me out of a mission due to a lost internet connection. In fact, just now the game threw the following message at me: "Unable to connect to the HITMAN service. Failed to authorize your account with the HITMAN server. For more information, contact HITMAN support."
My options at this point are to "Retry" or to "Go Offline". Retrying does nothing, going offline will let me start the mission again from scratch, but won't let me load any saves I made while I was online (even though I'm 99,9% sure that saves are stored locally and not in some cloud).
All the time while I'm writing this review the game is "trying" to reconnect to the servers (It has to be mentioned that my internet connection is fully functional at this point).
So here's what I'm asking myself right now: why is this even a thing? Why do I have to be online for a ♥♥♥♥ing single-player experience. I am not interested in making it to some leaderboards or something. Why does the game kick me out of a mission if I lose the connection? Dark Souls lets me play offline even though it's a much more internet-reliant game. This joke of a product doesn't.
I am sad because if you look past the always-online nonsense, the poor optimization and the fact that the game so far consists of just one mission (and two tutorial missions) you will see that the devs finally understood what the playerbase expects and wants from a HITMAN game and I won't lie, they actually tried to deliver.
However I can't look past those issues because at this point I am STILL not connected to the servers. In the end I am glad that I went with the intro pack rather than the "full experience" (which at this point is more of a "fool experience"). I'm glad I didn't spend more than 13 euros on it and I am positive that I will not purchase future episodes.

A valiant effort by WB Montreal, but ultimately too many things wrong with it for me to recommend. Rocksteady perfected the combat with Arkham City, but for some reason WB Montreal decided it would be a good idea to tweak things that would create a "no step forward, two steps back" sort of situation. At least on the PC, interrupting attacks to counter foes has been removed. Batman's attack animations are needlessly lengthy and sluggish, creating a situation where trying to attack an attacker head-on will result in Batman being beaten to the punch, 10 times out of 10. There are two problems with this: your default attack button now becomes Counter, and Batman is reduced to lower in skill than a common street thug.
The changes to the combat compared to Arkham City remove the power fantasy of being Batman. The game was incredibly buggy on release, as well. There are nitpicks, too, like the leveling design being completely linear, or the electric gauntlets basically invalidating any strategy the original two games required for dealing with special foes, but those are minor things. The real issues are in the combat, and when that's most of what this game is, you've got a problem.
Play Arkham City instead, or wait for Rocksteady's next installment. I can't recommend this one.

A Very Decent Action Game! (4/5)
Story & Setting:
Batman Arkham Origins takes player to a time before Batman Arkham Asylum and Batman Arkham City. Game takes place in Gotham City which will turn to Arkham City in near future. In this game, you will witness Batman's first time acting as a vigilante and where the characters from other Batman games are coming from.
Gameplay & Mechanics:
Gameplay is very familiar from first two Batman games. Almost everything is identical. You can wonder around Gotham City and attend to occasional petty crime. You can solve case files, go on a treasure hunt or progress through main story. Some of the equipment will be available after completing in-game challenges.
Fights however, are a bit frustrating due to constant need for blocking. You have to keep an aye for danger signs from enemies and use block all the time (yes all the time). If you try to free flow, ignoring attackers or simply thinking you are faster, you won’t make it. They will hit you all the time, interrupting your combos. So fighting is pretty much equal to blocking in Batman Arkham Asylum.
Rest of the stuff:
There is a lot of stuff to keep you occupied in Batman Arkham Origins.
There are several challenge modes. You can sharpen your fighting skills or work on your predatory skills. Completing challenges also unlocks artworks.
After completing main story, hard mode will be available for play. You can replay the story with all the equipment and techniques you previously unlocked but against a tougher opposition this time.
There is also multiplayer this time. You can change your game mode into multiplayer and clash with other players in 3rd person view. Several game modes are available in multiplayer along with in-game tutorials.
Bugs / Playability:
Game said to have a lot of bugs. Forums are floating with messages. WB is seemingly working on the issues. Most may be solved by now. Only major problem I can write about is, game kicks you to title screen if you lost internet connection during single player. This can by no means have any sensible explanation.
Verdict: If you are looking for a very decent action game, go for Batman Arkham Origins. If you already played and enjoyed first two Batman games, then you will like this too for sure. It has its problems alright, but it is a very much enjoyable game.

Here's My Say: Batman Arkham Origins
I thought that this game at the very start felt exactly like the previous games in the series. It started off nicely, I was slowly getting into it while being slightly disappointed with the lack of new "features" in the game. However... The more I played it the more addicted I became to it, I started enjoying it a lot more when I had time for a nice long session of around 2-3 hours (that for me.. is a long session, funny right? I'm a busy guy) so when I had time I had a great time playing it, I then realised it was more of what the Arkham games are which is by no means bad, but the game in general does indeed fail to bring anything strikingly new to the table in terms of gameplay mechanics and also the world itself just feels.. very empty. Too empty in-fact. Especially at the start when you are free to roam around Gotham City.
The game does look pretty though! There's some great PhysX details in this one which is always great to see which Nvidia users will appreciate, the paper on the ground doesn't move around as much as it did in Arkham Asylum which is a little odd, it's a bit more still even though it is interactive, heck I'm being way too picky now.
A friend of mine, Dan mentioned something to me about the combat in the game.. which made me think.. In Arkham Origins the combat doesn't feel as.. tight? as it did in the previous games, I found myself getting hit a lot more losing my streak bonus multiplier. Dan pitched the idea that it may be a purposely implemented disadvantage for Batman and the player because he is younger and less experienced as a vigilante which makes perfect sense... but then I couldn't help but also consider that it was just generally not as polished as Rocksteady's titles. Either way, it feels like an Arkham game, looks like an Arkham game and I haven't mentioned the story yet.. but it is very impressive. There's a HUGE twist that completely throws you off though but apart from that, that's all I'll say.

This is a good, solid game, and I find that it has three major strong points.
The first is a very, -very- large map to enjoy, with many different features and enviornments.  This is saying something, considering it is set in a barren wasteland.
The second is the amount of customization and upgrades that both your character, and your car, can go through.  Max has both a leveling system (which you then use scrap to buy upgrades for), and a token system (which allows you to buy additional upgrades).  All of these are unlocked through deeds and actions in the wasteland, which gives it a nice twist, rather than just using generic XP leveling system.  Your car can also be upgraded with scrap, and customized in many different ways, but only when you clear large swathes of the map of enemies, and bring the threat rating down for the different territories.
Finally, the third thing going for this game is enjoyable driving and combat mechanics.  The time slowing effect when using the different car weapons is fun, and allows you to enjoy your vehicular destruction.  The  ground combat is also enjoyable, but a little bit less so, made up of light and heavy attacks, counters, and melee weapons.  However, this starts to get annoying when enemies go behind you so that you can no longer see the parry/counter symbols above their heads, and they get cheap shots in.
After a while the game can become a bit tiresome, as the missions, bases, scavenging sites, etc, all start to blend together and become a bit boring.  A little bit more variety could have been added here, but it is still decent.  This sort of thing would skew my review more towards the negative side, as the most damning sin a game can commit is becoming boring, but like I said above, the gameplay is fun, so these things still remain somewhat enjoyable.

No game should rely on autosaving only anymore, unless it is a roguelike, but then the point of the game has changed.  This is an open world game.  If I want to save and exit where I am, I should be able to.  I don't want to have to go back to a base, or find a way to trigger the autosave.  The only reason I bring up jumping is the fact that I keep getting stuck!  I don't want to have to fast travel back to a base, and go all the way back to where I was, or exit the game and load an autosave, all because I can't get myself up and out of a pit no taller than my knee.
But anyways, a very solid game, very fun to play, and a very positive review.

Now, I love Banjo-Kazooie. And it is appearent that this games tries to be a spiritual succesor to that game, or even entire genre. However, while playing this game, I felt like something was missing. It took me 4 hours to find out what. It was the fun. The fun was missing. Everything I did felt as a chore, not as something that I do for fun. The game feel like it's following a formula, without experimenting too much, the humour is dry and mostly based on references, the levels are few and feels like you've visited them in every other game, the camera fights you more than it helps you, and the game could overall need more polish. Losing a "power-up" or an ability because of a timer, and then having go back to regain it is not fun. Being one-shoted by spiked walls that you have to jump over is not fun. Fighting the camera that keeps changing on its own, or won't change at all, is not fun. Rolling around, and then stopping because you run out of energy is not fun. Answering a quiz to progress is not fun. There are too many limitations in what you can do, and too many things that are just... boring.
I feel like the entirety of this game is trying to belong to a genre so hard that it forgets to be its own thing.
Even the music, but it rocks, easily the best part of the game, so it's forgiven.
This was a good try at reviving a long gone genre, that didn't quite go all the way. If they ever make a sequel, it actually might succeed.
So, I wrote this review while gathering my thoughts on why I didn't like the game. Might revisit to rewrite, and might even change it so that I recommend it instead.

Right off the bat, one thing that will catch your attention is the variety of game types.  Most billiards games like to focus only on either 8- or 9-ball.  Those games are here, but they do not stop at that.  Along the game, other games like Rotation and Golf are in the mix.  With nine different ways currently available with Snooker and Trick coming soon, there are plenty of ways to play.
Another strong point about the game is the controls.  Like in any other pool game, being able to control the cue ball is important.  Most games simply allow you to aim the ball and adjust the power.  Even though most games stop at this, there are more options to offer.  By being able to adjust the angle of the cue stick as well as where on the cue ball to aim, it gives the option of doing jump and swerve shots, something most billiard games leave out.  Additionally, with a full tutorial teaching how to do all of these moves, it does not take long before they become second nature.
Beyond all the gameplay details, a nice touch about the game is the amount of customization available.  Even games that try to simulate pro billiards tend to stick to a single, sometimes sponsored look throughout the game.  This one goes beyond the basics.  As soon as you start a game, the highly detailed and moving locals make it feel like you are in what could be a real location.  As you keep progressing, at least a dozen locals, cue sticks, ball sets, and even table decals make it that regardless your taste, there is plenty to see even from a visual standpoint.
Once the single-player game is over, there is still more to play.  Through online multiplayer, it is possible to keep playing with others.  It is even possible to create tournaments to learn who the best player is.  However, the one drawback is that there is no local multiplayer mode available.  This means that in order to play with another person in the same room, the two of you must play through a network.  This feels like a major oversight.  A simple hot seat patch would have made that the game could be a great party game.  Even without local multiplayer, this is still a great package that any billiards fan can easily enjoy.

If you're looking for a pool game on Steam, look no further. This is the most graphically, physically, and stylistically impressive pool game I've ever played, and I've been playing them for almost my whole life (going all the way back to Side Pocket on the NES.) The balls, rails and pockets behave just as they would on a real pool table. And there are a bunch of different ways to play, thanks to many diverse mini-games. There's a great training mode too, so even anyone who has never played pool before can pull off trick shots like a master. There's nothing more satisfying than seeing your perfectly aimed jump shot in slow motion as it knocks the target ball in the pocket. It's fun, it's calming, it's everything a great pool game should be. And I recommend it.

A weird case of a game. It is the weakest entry in the Arkham trilogy, but it is nevertheless a good game in itself.
Pros
* Good story, maybe the best of the Arkham trilogy. The characters and their motivations are adapted to their situation. Beware that it is not Batman's origin story
* Non-inventive but entertaining gameplay, slightly faster than its predecessor. Each boss feels different
* Graphics are good and the crumbling snow is a welcome addition
Cons
* Gotham City as an environment is very video-gamey
* Bugs, some were game-breaking on launch and were fixed, others are still here and annoying
* Visible lack of polish compared to the two other games
Do as I did, and treat it as an expansion pack for Arkham City. Don't pay full-price for it, but WB Montreal showed some love in their youth enthusiasm and thus you should buy it on sale and enjoy it for what it is.

I was apprehensive before getting this game because I've had a few billiards video games over the years and to be frank they all seem to be lacking.  The control of the cue, the physics of the balls, and the plausibility of the shots either make me feel like I'm being guided through the game or is so uncomfortable playing that it's just not enjoyable.  Video billiards has always reminded my of video pinball in that there just isn't a video game that can capture the feel of playing.  While this game "Pool Nation" won't replace the actual feel of playing actual billiards... it's miles ahead of many billiards video game I've played that are out there.  The only comparable game is "Virtual Pool 4", which is a good simulation but "Pool Nation" graphics are a bit better and this game seems a little more reactive to your intent for playing.  In other words, this game "Pool Nation"seems to be a bit more user friendly when trying to do what you want on the table than VP4 is.
The game gives you excellent control of the cue that includes spin, english, angle, and power.  The controls are easy to learn but I highly recommend the tutorial in game to learn it.  It's short enough not to get boring and you need to learn the skills to play the game and the tutorial treats each lesson as a segment to complete and check off.  The ball physics are a good feel.  I can see myself lining up the shots and predicting the shots as I would on a regular billiard table.  Nothing's perfect of course but the devs did a good job here in my opinion.
There are billiard circuits to play for single player and multiplayer.  There's leaderboards, achievements, and trading cards.  Steam Workshop seems like a natural for this type of game where you should be able to customize locations, cues, tables, rooms, or even players etc.. A good pool game for a nice price... on sale of course.

Unique TPS with good gameplay mechanics, an apocalypse-now type story and an excellent setting.
Good♥♥♥♥♥♥
+The setting is one of my favourites so far in gaming. Think a creative, beautiful and post apocalyptic Dubai.
+Story is interesting and different than the norm with subtle clues and interesting decisions.
+Gameplay mechanics worked well for me, but not for some. It's mainly a cover based shooter.
+Style, sounds, weapons and music. The main title has (I think) Star Spangled Banner by Jimi Hendrix playing.
+Melee finishers on downed enemies work nicely. No instant takedowns.
+Multiplayer is actually pretty good. There's free co-op to but I havn't tried it yet.
+(MINOR SPOILER) As the story progresses your character's finishing moves and "taunts" get more brutal. Nice touch.
Don't feel right:
-The shooting can get somewhat repetetive as there is not a lot of variation in what you can do.
-Little replay value unless you want the story again from a more understanding perspective.
Conclusion:
The game is solid and of appropriate length for a shooter. I'm glad they didn't drag it out unecessarily and that the gameplay mechanics are of good quality. Nothing ruins immersion and good story like bad gameplay. Sadly the story didn't get a hold of me emotionally as it did for some, I really wish I could get into it but I just couldn't get real emotion from it as a whole. Certain parts got to me a little but not overwhelmingly. Still, it was a very satisfying take on one of my favourite tales: man goes into darkness and creates his own vision of society. Certain parts of the story/ending confused me a little but the whole thing is up to interpretation and certainly worth venturing into.
Games like Far Cry 3, The Last of Us (especially), Mass Effect series and MGS series are examples of what engaged me emotionally. It's unfortunate that this did not but I still loved the experience and was always eager to play on and uncover the story unfolding. Maybe I've played too many shooters and become a little detached, who knows? Throughout the story you will get to make a few moral decisions but I won't say any more on that.
Anyway, I'd give it a 9/10 easily, a full 10 if it had increased combat options/variation. I'm not gonna mark it down for failing to grab me as it did for others, however, as it deserves praise nonetheless.

I want to like this game. I want to like it so much, but I can't. For every right thing this game does there are three things done wrong.
Most glaringly, the game performs terribly on its higher settings. I have a GTX 770 with a 570 for PhysX, 16 GB RAM, and an i5 overclocked to 4 Ghz. It can't handle AgrarSim 2013 on anything higher than Medium. Know this before playing it.
Now on to the gameplay. Common to all the other farming simulations out there, the game's tutorial only cares about teaching you how to operate the machinery. The tutorial doesn't tell you anything about:
1. Making fields (you can just plow anywhere, it turns out, and marking them out on the map is only for the benefit of AI workers).
2. How and where to sell your harvest (the mill, the town, the agrarian centre).
3. How and where to buy the things you need, like animals, seeds, and fertilisers (seed bags from town, seed loads from the agrarian centre, animals from the stables).
4. How to buy new equipment (the O key).
5. The differences between scenarios (the two hardest scenarios for each map have the same descriptions, but the second one is easier because it gives you an extra $10,000 and some basic machinery).
6. Where things are on the map and how to use the map view.
7. How to advance to the next day (hold down Ctrl and click on the sun icon near the clock).
The game requires a LOT of micro-management. You need to drive your harvest to the sale point. You need to buy individual bags of seed to load the bottom-of-the-line ('historical') seeder, and you need to load those bags into the seeder yourself. There is a grain shower that you can use to load trailers with grain from your silo, but you can't use it to load the historical seeder. You need a gravity hopper to bag your grain so that you can load the seeder. You need to drive your machinery all the way to the agrarian centre to sell it, and in the early game your tractor does an average of 15 mph, so it takes about 10 minutes to travel anywhere.
AgrarSim 2013 is also legendary for its crazy physics and unintuitive behaviour. Attachments fall at awkward angles that prevent attachment, and there's no way to rescue or reset them. A several-ton combine harvester can do a backflip when driven over a furrow at 5 mph. The historical seeder can often go nuts and flip your tractor over. There's no way to nudge around an unhitched trailer on foot, so you need to keep adjusting your tractor. If you try to sprint while carrying a seed bag, its collider bumps up against you and slows you down. The on-foot FOV is the narrowest I've ever seen in a video game (45° horizontal), and you will be disoriented for a second or two every time you step off the tractor. The mill won't buy trailers full of grain from you, it only wants bags. A MILL, FOR GOD'S SAKE. And one time I loaded some bags of grain onto a trailer and brought it halfway home, then saved the game and played something else. When I reloaded, the grain bags were gone! Just disappeared into the aether, never to be seen again!
And yet for all its massive, unforgiveable problems and its numerous hair-tearing moments of frustration and confusion, AgrarSim offers something you can't get out of any other game right now. Because you see, when you drop a plow into the ground in AgrarSim, it actually digs out a furrow. It's a hole, an excavation, you can stand inside it. And when you drag a cultivator over that land, it smooths the furrows out. The simple act of working the soil is immediate and rewarding, and when you seed it and see your crops springing up there's a great sense of satisfaction and wonder.
I think as a gaming experience, this game is worth about $5. As a simulator it's worth about $0.50. The gameplay is just too unpredictable. But it sure is fun to work the land!

As someone who grew up on 3D open world platformers on the N64 (Mario 64, Donkey Kong 64, Banjo 1 & 2) I've been overjoyed to see how much tighter and enjoyable the genre was carried forward by the Mario Galaxy series. Having finished Yooka-Laylee, I can say it falls victim of retreading the flaws that are found in the classic 3D titles: too spacious and empty worlds, a camera that you will have to constantly wrestle with, and annoying unskippable cutscenes.
The game controls well, for the most part. Mini-games are present and most are awful. Thankfully getting around is quite fun, you have a number of abilities that need to be purchased to better explore the world, menaing you won't be able to see everything your first time through any of the 5 worlds. The presentation is solid: the music is great, the art style is very palatable, animations are well done, and textures are spotty.
Annoyances: unskippable cutscenes, camera visual tour when entering new rooms, not being able to quickly retry challenges when failing
TLDR: Yooka-Laylee retreads the tropes of the classic N64 platformers instead of honoring them and presenting something new or interesting. I'm glad the 3D platformer is being represented, but after the Galaxy series, this needed to be much more than what we already knew.

Well there's a lot to say about Batman: Arkham Origins. Five words describing it best would be "Disappointment even to Batman fans" because it's simply not as great as previous Asylum and City games. Firstly, there's the difference between Rocksteady studio (previous parts) and Warner Bros. (Origins). Whereas Rocksteady wanted to create perfect Batman games maybe just as good as the Nolan movies, Warner Bros wanted money in the first place. So they rushed the game resulting in hundreds of bugs appearing even months after release, the movement and gliding technique, which is frustrating, the platformer parts where Batman moves just weird, the freeflow system doesn't really respond to the buttons you press so even the fights are less fun, weird lip and other animation visible mostly on Alfred and so on and so on. If they tested it a bit and repaired all these frustrating bugs, the game would be just as good as the previous ones even despite a bit weaker story, which is still AAA and high above average.
As for some positives, the city itself looks just great and once again includes challenges from Riddler and other foes. The new detective vision looks just wonderful and is fun to use, just as the new gadgets. Last but not least, also the main characters and foes look really cool and badass, (maybe except Bane, which looks like a clever foe like Tom Hardy in the movie, but later in the game changes into the lame giant ball of muscles, which looks a bit ridiculous and doesn't correspond with the story at all). The voice acting is pretty decent too, though not with the good old cast. Finally, the multiplayer is a very pleasant surprise promissing hours of fun gameplay, editing your character and levelling up for new weapons and gadgets.
To sum up - pretty good story, wonderful graphics and hours of fun with another hours of frustration from various glitches and bugs. If they get repaired, Origins should be considered just as good as the rest of the Arkham series. But they are still there so this game is the weakest of the three and we can only hope for new Batman games comming back to Rocksteady instead.

Batman: Arkham Origins is a sequel that presents minor new tweaks and features over its predecessors. But it manages to be a good game and a worthy sequel nevertheless thanks to the still kicking Arkham formula and few good elements on its own.
Regarding the gameplay, Origins focuses mostly on direct combat encounters: the few new gadgets you will get are suited for direct confrontations and the game will throw new kinds of enemies at you, the majority of which are able to either retaliate from your attacks or be downright invincible till you'll perform the right "trick" to bring them down to normal. The stealth sequences, on the other hand, didn't recive any improvement or new gimmick whatsoever.
That said, two of the new gadgets tend to make the late game much easyer: the electric gloves can nullify every kind of enemy defense, effectively breaking down the main appeal of the fistfights, while the remote claw can connect an enemy to an explosive object from the environment or a vantage point for an easy takedown, without any ammo limit to prevent you from clearing up entire rooms.
The new expanded map features environments you already visited in Arkham City, albeit reskinned accordingly for a prequel, along with new areas of Gotham, including a long bridge that separates the two. The level design and the attention to the original sources are as polished as usual for an Arkham game.
The plot is the most praised aspect of Batman: Arkham Origins, since it feels original and makes an overall good use of the various characters. As a reader of the comic books, however, I would had handled the main antagonist a little better and crafted  the various assassins and criminals into the plot better, at the cost of reducing the importance of already enstablished Batman rogues.
The multiplayer mode is a novelty for the Arkham series, and is about a capture the control point kind of experience between two weapons-wielding gangs while a third team of two people, who control Batman and Robin, try to thwart them as much as possible via stealth gameplay. While controlling the elite forces of either the Joker or Bane (and sometime the bosses themselves) in a third person shooter fashion and customize them as you see fit when it comes to weapons, gadgets and gear is a new and interesting feature, Batman and Robin are so much less effective in this mode than in the main game, making playing them sometimes more an annoyance than a blast. Beside that, the multiplayer mode as a whole is a worthy addiction, all things considered.
The Initiation DLC is just another challenge campaign tided up by some unique cutscenes and an original setting, an eastern ninja training ground. While the change of scenary is surely a novelty, the various combat and predator challenges are nothing new, gameplay-wise.
The Cold, Cold Heart DLC is the only story-driven pack for Arkham Origins, which basically shows the first encounter between Batman and Mr. Freeze. The DLC itself is very short, with its main story being beatable in two or three hours, and the few side quests are just recycled from the main game. There isn't anything new even on the gameplay's front. The only highlight of Cold, Cold Heart is the final battle against Mr. Freeze, a challenging predator encounter.
Batman: Arkham Origins can be considered a fairly good attempted for an official prequel for the series, but really suffers from several not stellar development choices

The buggiest and worst multiplayer i've ever played... In a game about multiplayer.
For a game about beating up your friends as a jelly-baby avatar this game fails so spectacularly with such a simple and wonderful idea it's almost funny if it wasn't the price it was...
First off, the multiplayer in this game could be called almost non existent. It is the most barebones basic construct of multiplayer I have EVER seen in any game, even in free titles the multiplayer feels like it's years ahead of this game that's had YEARS TO IMPROVE ON IT'S FLAWS... From bugs to not being able to play with your friends, the multiplayer is some of the most flawed i've come across.
Secondly, the bugs in this game are seemingly endless. I realize a game with the physics this one has means that bugs are going to be an issue and a common one at that. This I could forgive, however the bugs I have seen have been absolutely game breaking, wether it being stuck in a wall or just kicked from a server after all of the players T-posing for a solid five minutes, I get the feeling the bugs this game has could be easily fixed as it didn't seem to have this issue earlier on in development, the fact that it exists in the "Full game" is flat out inexcusable. (This portion is from my own experience with the game, this may not apply to all players.)
Thirdly as I mentioned this game has had YEARS of development to expand and fix it's game... Not only has this barely happened, they've somehow managed to bring more issues to it than it had before, I feel as if the development team realized that they did have a good idea, that the game itself was infact a great basis for an entertaining videogame about punching people. And with that knowalge they took it too far, they kept adding onto the game in areas where addition not only wasn't necessary but it ended up harming the game. For isntance while clothing is a nice addition, I would have personally prefered a working multiplayer. And while the new options to the game modes are an interesting concept, I would have prefered more maps to play them on...
In short this game isn't a finished title as it's claimed to be, it feels more like playing a beta or a test version of a game that's had more than enough time to prepare itself. I'm not going to rate this game out of 10 or assign it some arbitrary number, rather i'm just going to say I had high hopes for this game, I enjoyed the concept and I thought it was genuinely a good one... But the development team has lost all of my respect by letting this game go out and calling it finished when infact... It's not.
If they make more improvements then this game may be worth the buy, but as of right now, don't waste your money...

This is actually a much better game than I ever thought it would be.
After the "It's an open world, if by open world you mean a corridor" release of Absolution, I was expecting to be disappointed by this release.
I wasn't.
Actually I'm pleasantly surprised!
Yes, I thought the "we're going to release the game in episodes" thing was a bit odd, but perhaps it'll make sense to us when the next episode is released. It's not really that far of. A few weeks.
So why do I like it?
Well, it's actually much more detailed and richer than any other Hitman out there. Sure there are people here who wil moan that they completed the mission in 30 minutes and they want their money back.
Well go back and play the mission again because there are so many, many, many ways of executing a contract. So many objects, traps, weapons, opportunities, disguises, approaches, rooms, conversations... it's immense!
You will however have to have a lot of patience. Like... I don't know... an Assassin maybe?
Now it's not all great... unfortunately...
There is the problem with the "always have to be connected to the internet or else" problem.
Play the game during the day here in the UK and you're fine. Come 4pm (16:00), and suddenly the servers seem to get overloaded. You get kicked off mid-game and lose all progress. Especially infuriating if you're trying to accomplish one of the more hard earned rewards in the game.
This is the biggest problem that IO and Square Enix needs to fix.
There are also people moaning that their game looks rubbish on full settings.
I'm sorry but what? I have a graphics card that isn't even supported by the game. A GTX 460Ti... with 1Gb memory... it runs the game beautifully. It really does! If you look at the amount of objects and NPC's there are in this game, the fact that my old graphics card can play this is fantastic!
So to sum things up... great game... great atmosphere... puzzling about episodic releases... please fix the Online Server issues.
Thanks IO and Square Enix. You've made a longtime Hitman fan happy again.

Hitman goes back to most of Blood Money's roots, while retaining the good parts of Absolution's movement and contextual actions. AI is not as paranoid as Absolution, which is always a good thing.
The Showstopper level, the first actual assassination mission in the game, is enormous in scale, and has a lot of replayability thanks to the numerous challenges added to the game. Excluding all the challenges, there are quite a few ways to kill the targets, all of which require careful planning and timing.
Now for the bad parts.
The game has an always-online requirement to play the game the way it was designed, making the offline mode pretty much useless, since your progression isn't saved, and challenges aren't available.
But the server crashes are not as bad as some of the other reviews make it out to be, I've had it disconnect on me only once in my entire play time, and that was quickly resolved with a retry a few minutes later.
If the always-online component is removed, then this does well as a Hitman game, coming pretty close to Blood Money.

In a world ravaged by man kind, a lone road warrior stands alone, as the final bastion for hope and peace. He goes only by one name. And that name... Is Max. The Warrior, Max.
-----------
While most people would say Mad Max is just another case of Hollywood cashgrabbery, it really isn't. Whereas most movie tie-in games are thrown together in a few months by the Budget Studio. Mad Max, on the other hand, grabbed the entire attention of Avalanche Studios, famous for the off-the-rails Just Cause series, while an affiliate studio was working on Just Cause 3. That's right - Avalanche's main franchise was handed to an affiliate, while Mad Max got the five star treatment. That's pretty friggin' cool, as it is.
For those expecting Grand Theft Auto: New South Wales, you aren't going to get it here, as you'll only really be driving one vehicle throughout the game: The Magnum Opus. If I were to make a top ten list of fictional vehicles, The Magnum Opus would rank higher than the V8 Interceptor, one of the most famous Wasteland Rollers. The Magnum Opus, unlike most video game cars, is completely and fully customizable, from the body, down to the side-mounted flamethrowers. That being said, the number of car bodies is... Lacking. There are six available, five if you don't possess one of the three DLC packs for the PC version. However, you can do just about anything with them. Want to have a double-stack supercharger married to a gold-plated Chevy Deuce Cupe? Go for it! Wanna have a nitro-boosted tank with the body of a Rolls-Royce? Mad Max has you, fam.
The gameplay, while not original, is very engaging for a game of this calibre, with an extreme emphasis on vehicular combat. It just wouldn't be Mad Max without being able to send a car into a triple barrel roll and then blow the ♥♥♥♥ up, would it? The controls are relatively simple, using mostly standard controls if one is using a controller, and the industry standard WASD + Mouse if one is not using a controller, though I would strongly recommend a controller. Included with the game is a rather intuitive photo editor, which is accessed by pushing both thumbsticks on a controller. Using weapons is simple, as well, with the standard aiming and firing controls as one would expect from a game with weapons, though the game's combat is primarily hand-to-hand, with ammunition exceedingly scarce.
And lastly, the graphics. This was easily one of the best looking games of 2015, and it is still very good looking, even in the face of games such as The Crew, Need For Speed 2015, and Doom 2016. While I personally don't think this game will remain one of the prettiest out there, it's still a welcome breath of fresh air, compared to most dark, drab and dreary post-apocalyptic games.
In short, while this isn't the greatest game out there, I highly recommend checking it out, even if just for a few short minutes.

Let me get this straight - the game is fantastic graphically. The cars, the amount of detail is astonishing, the scenery is breathtaking. However, as it often happens, the developers forgot to add one thing - gameplay. The whole territory really feels like sandbox, or, more precisely, a theme park, filled with evenly spaced stuff of the same dozen types - Enemy camp, tower, Friendly stronghold, Scarecrow (a sort of tower), Scavenging site, Encounter, etc. It just feels like you're doing the same thing all over again. You're constantly showered with upgrades, the amount of points to spend on skills is ridiculously high, the game becomes ridiculously easy and boring very fast. THERE'S NO DIFFICULTY SETTING. You got this right. I'll repeat - graphics and general athmosphere of this game is fantastic. But there's no challenge. So I would not recommend this game for people looking for challenge and true portrayal of the gritty survival world of Mad Max.

if you are interested in mad max's story and universe, id say this is a pretty good purchase. but aside from that, it aint anything to write home about.
I heard this is a port of a console game, well for a port, it sure runs a very crispy 60fps. so technical stuff which includes bugs , glitches and whatnot are almost non-existant unless you look reaaal hard. havent had any single problems from the first hour of playing it.
soundtrack is meh, not really memorable. but the voice acting are all well-acted and makes me feel like watching another mad max movie.
story-wise, its not much to think about either since basically its about max trying to get some place called plane of silence or something and he needs to find car parts plus kill a few people to get there. i havent run into any interesting plotlines or twists so far in the game and im pretty far from finished so i could be wrong here.
as for gameplay, its kind of bland for an open- world game. i mean yes theres a "ton" of stuff to do and find but most of it just feels like a chore. like the scavenging areas contain scraps , which you will need for upgrading your things except they only come in like 10-20 scraps at most where you will need a few hundred to thousands to upgrade your car and skills.
it kinda becomes redundant to scavenge for scraps so its way better to just steal a scrapulance and bring it back since it nets you tons of scraps. these scavenging areas also sometimes have history relics and parts to upgrade your respective stronghold in that area. the parts are fine to look for since you actually benefit from it, but the history relics BARELY tell any history of the universe and mostly just random notes lying around by people early post-fallout with some old pictures on it that sometimes remind max the world of old. aside, from that theres really no reason to look for these history relics.
combat in the game is okay but it will get boring at some point. thankfully its responsive and has impact enough to make you tolerate it. think of it like batman/ shadow of mordor but much less fun than those 2.
i wish they bothered to put at least new combos or special moves initated by a few button combination instead of your X button will now hit harder and maybe you can do some finishers while the enemy is pinned/stunned/grounded. its such a shame they decided to do a 1 button combat because this couldve been much more fun to play if they just developed the combat more. its not crappy by all means, just feels like a wasted opportunity.
but thats not saying they didnt do some of the gameplay nicely. The car combat for one, id say is quite fun even if theres too much auto-lock from the game at times. you can hook enemies, shoot spear-bombs, grind their tires, pull out armor ,etc. im personally not very good in racing or driving games like this, but i had a blast with the car combat, perhaps this is where all the attention is going, since mad max features tons of driving.
the side activites are pretty okay and standard for open-world games like this but you wouldnt miss anything if you dont do them entirely aside from a few tokens for griff to upgrade some arbitrary things like, how much water you can extract or how much extra scrap you can get from looting (this one is really useless as it only gives like 5 extra scrap and im at the 5th level.) griff tokens are quite easy to obtain and meeting him everytime gives a little insight on why max is like this and whats his real goal is which is pretty interesting to see despite the guy keeps changing locations making you drive and walk up to him everytime you want to upgrade your stats.
Overall gameplay is okay i suppose, playable and takes a while before it gets too boring to play. and if you are one of those OCD gamers that have to collect everything, this might be the game for you too. although i wouldnt buy it at full price since its rather mediocre for a full priced game, get it on sale i say.

Oxygen Not Included is a base building / simulation game from Klei Entertainment Inc.
If you're not familiar with them then you've been missing out. They're known mainly for Don't Starve/ Don't Starve Together on steam. They have a really healthy playerbase and are excellent about listening to their community and implementing updates. This game is similiar to Don't Starve, but isn't open world and is set in a space/sci-fi setting instead. You're stuck on an asteroid and are basically stuck there (there's no way to advance off the asteroid or actually "win" as of now). You have to mine/build/and manage your colonists (known as duplicates) and your base with a lot of intricate systems in place. Air Pressure and Gas levels such as Oxygen, Hydrogen, Carbon Dioxide as well as power, water and plumbing, HVAC, temperatures, lighting, food, and various other precious resources will have to be considered as you progress your research and understanding along the way.  If you like "learning curb" games like this where you can have a good laugh when something goes wrong and won't just get frustrated and give up, then it's well worth diving into.
A lot of people who are writing negative reviews about the game being frustrating or too complicated aren't exactly wrong, it can be a little annoying with some of the early stage bugs while they implement new updates. I was scratching my head on how a few items worked but with tinkering around I figured most of it out. Dismissing your lack of understanding as "bad game" or "bugged game" is just a hilarious and very immature way to conduct a review considering you know full and well that it's an early access game and the very first screen you load into warns you that you may experience a few annoyances along the way, I feel like if you still decide to get mad enough to write a negative review after considering this then you're probably a little kid or a very entitled idiot that expects everything to be perfect all of the time. Which doesn't surprise me with the toxic gaming era that we're currently in.
I feel like I had to address my opinion on the matter with the short-answer negative reviews that leave no good detail about why they hate it other than the fact they're mad they bought an early access and don't have the patience for it and I think I'm 100% right about them. Some people may just not like it and that's okay but for the people who understand how old-school early access practices are implemented (the way they should be) where a company grows their game with a community who are interested in it, will not be dissapointed in Klei Entertainment. I do know Klei Entertainment pretty well. I funded Don't Starve back when it was on Greenlight in early access. They're really good at utilizing early access to build upon their games and iron out their bugs. They're the kind of company that has a really good idea and perfects it over time and really listens to their community along the way. I've played too many Early Accesses where a company just completely rips me off and then goes in hiding, leaving you with a dead game. I can count 2 or 3 Fully released games from major companies that I bought this year that done that to me, if i'm being perfectly honest. If you had mixed feelings I hope my blunt honesty and loyalty for Klei helped sway you. Thank you for reading and I hope you enjoy as much as I do while they work towards full release!

Playtonic has indeed delivered what they promised; a spiritual successor to the beloved Banjo series, while updating the platformer genre so that it is not merely a Tooie-esque copy. Why then, are there a decent amount of people upset with this game? Because it went up against a Dream.
I was a child when Banjo-Kazooie released. B-K, like its sucessor, was a major building block in the fortress of my childhood. (As were most things read, played, or watched at the time.) Banjo-Tooie was met with thunderous applause, and after Gruntilda's second defeat, players went to bed that night dreaming of her promised "Banjo-Threeie".
But that is all Banjo-Threeie was: a dream; one that lasted nearly twenty years, growing and maturing as we all grew and matured. It had no story, no characters, and no gameplay, and yet players were more than ready to herald it as "the next greatest game". There is no possible way that any game, made now, then, or in the future, can compare to the unrivaled power that a dream holds.
Yooka-Laylee captures the spirit of the Banjo series; from the three character-based data files, to collectibles, to all those googly-eyed creatures. There is a glimmer of Gruntilda and her lair in Capital B and his coporate world, and I'm certain Moodymaze marsh is a glimpse at Fungus Forest in the dystopian future. The writing is clever, and I often find myself talking to characters again and again to see if they have anything else to say. The power gauge works similarly to feathers and eggs; their power was always depletable, and so are some of Yooka and Laylee's moves. I don't miss the large amount of collectibles in YL, beacuse those belong to Banjo and his games. After all, HE wears the backpack.
The idea of expandable worlds is an interesting update to the genre, although it's inclusion meant sacrificing more worlds. It's innovative, however I miss the days when games included more than five distinct world designs.
The transformations are unique and match each level, my personal favorite going to World Three's transformation because it's just so different to anything we've seen stylistically in the Banjo Series.
Perhaps one day players (and the creators) will get their chance to truly see a completed  and playable Banjo-Threeie, but until then it must stay relegated to the realm of dreams. All games have their flaws, but to me, Yooka-Laylee is just as entertaining and playable as re-playing Banjo-Tooie is now. I always liked the genre, and I'm glad to see it return.

It's hard to decide if this is a good or bad game, but its certainly different from most shooters.
Pros:
The building is decent
Combat is heart pounding
Game looks nice
There are lots of updates quite often, the game strategy changes often to accomodate them.
Workshop system benefits both content creators and game devs more than the market.
Lots of servers to choose from, with plenty of modded ones.
Cons:
Performance is a big issue, especially on modded servers or servers that don't wipe often/have decay.
Most players talk ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ly or are edgy kids.
The text chat is server-wide, but voice chat is based on proximity, which makes it awkward when one person has a mic and another doesnt. Which leads to...
There isn't any in-game way to tell friend from foe other than asking in a text or voice chat if thats them running, or by wearing an agreed uniform. Note that at a longer distance, hats dont render either.
Building a decent structure on a hillside is a challenge unless its practically flat with no variation, which defeats the purpose of trying to keep it out of sight early on.
Game is not really balanced, but a lot could be changed:
Anyone can use twig to build to the top of your base or a tower to hop on it, which makes building big a priority
Components are nearly impossible to get since you have to follow roads, which offer a clear line of sight to shooters, or go to monument/landmarks, of which half the worthwhile ones have radiation and the other half are swarmed with people around them.
The node update makes finding stone a giant pain early on, which meants youre stuck with a rock for a long time for harvesting until you do find a stone node to make tools.
Big groups will dominate servers they're on until a wipe, nothing can be done if you dont have many friends.
In short, the game devs say they dont want to influence how players play the game, but theres a clear bias towards raiding. Meanwhile, a vending machine for trading costs twice as much high quality metal as an armored door but has less than a third of the hp.
TL;DR If you have friends and the time to play this game, its well worth $5 or even $10 since the game hopefully gets better over time when devs focus on balance instead of high quality wavy grass.

Graphics: 8/10

Artstyle: 10/10
The sand is everywhere and it also works as a gameplay feature. Dubai and everything in it is very colorful, which could contrast with the story, but most importantly it's pleasant to watch. The darker areas are executed the way they should have been, if not better.

Sound: 10/10
The weapons' sounds probably aren't the most realistic, but were they ever supposed to in any game of this kind? Game's Original Soundtrack is great, you can check out "Spec Ops: The Line - Truth Revealed" on youtube - it's great. Music(that isn't made specifically for the game) plays here and there and it's also very climatic, being played by Radioman. This music being played by him works well with the story.
Controls: 9/10
There could be something to be desired with the cover mechanics to some people. It suffers from "Omni-key" of modern games that does almost everything whenever you click it, but it wasn't a problem to me. (Your opinion will vary)
Gameplay: 9/10
Gameplay's typical TPS, but it does what's it supposed to perfectly. It doesn't seem unfair, unless you play on FUBAR(the hardest difficulty), but I loved it. There's probably no replay value compared to other games, but if you like it, you can play it again, right?
Story: 10/10

Oh, and if you're going to play it, listen carefully to the antagonist(especially in the ending), as he's also talking directly to the player.
Overall: 10/10

The development of Gang Beasts has been something of a roller coaster.  It was always the fun little physics brawler that dreamed big, but updates could sometimes be head scratching.  Mechanics would change seemingly randomly, Something might be broken, and would remain through months of updates.  Stages would see repeated radical redesigns.  The game could be chaotic fun, but it always looked like it need more work.
Gang Beasts is now officially out of Early Access, and it feels like it should still be in Early Access.  The graphics might be a bit shinier, but it still doesn't feel like a polished finished product.
Making matters worse is the console nature of the game.  Gang Beasts leaving Early Access coincides with Gang Beasts launching on the PS4, and the "full release" is in some ways a downgrade over the previous version.  Resolution options have been removed, controller icons have been replaced with PS controller buttons, and some stages have been simplified.  It is hard to see these changes as just a coincidence.
Not that the "full release" is absent other issues.  Performance seems to have declined (despite seeing some simpler stages) and some new bugs have cropped up.  The often criticized camera system (though as often the issue was that stages were designed seemingly without concern for  the limitations of the camera system) was replaced with a new camera system that doesn't actually seem to be any better (but is now determined to zoom in really close).

The short version: a crunchy, violent, sometimes cheesy brawler-- vehicles, fists, and guns-- that succeeds in spite of itself. I'm not sure if it's supposed to be a parody but some bits sure seemed like it.
Blah blah blah, light spoilers ahead:
For a triple A title this game cheaps out a lot. You run into the same NPCs, the same voices (few Australian), and if you drive a car off a cliff, landing in a tire-blowing, frame bending smash, you get to watch the same old animation of your mechanic tightening a nut on the engine. I probably watched that motorsexual crank that bolt at least 100 times. Each region has the same stuff, camps, minefields, a friendly fortress (you can build the exact same upgrades in each), and a balloon that allows you to mark enemy locations and fast travel. Why not a really high hill in one region? Or a radio tower or something? Why didn't the baddies trash the balloons? Max don't know, Max don't care.
But the core of the game is solid. Driving, once you upgrade enough so that you don't feel like a blimp pilot in a windstorm, is pretty good. Car combat is really good. You ram, grind, shoot, harpoon, and eventually blow the snot out of any car on the road with a fully upgraded THUNDERPOON. It's stuff like that that makes me wonder if they're joking around.
Once you're done hooning around, you hop out and smash in the faces of a (limited) range of enemies. Melee is less clinical than I remember the Warner Bros. Batman games being, you mostly attack or heavy attack (same button, I played with a controller, which worked really well, except for the sniper rifle, which is attached to your car for some reason). As the game progresses you have to use counter more often and against bosses I dodged a lot. You can also use a shotgun (good as an ice breaker), a knife (useful for when grappled), or, when you can find one, a melee weapon. Why doesn't Max just carry a sword or mace instead of scrambling around a room full of rabid cannibals to pick one up? Because then you'd miss out on the fun of killing people with your hands. Which is super fun. The sound during melee is well done, growing in intensity as you chain together blows to fill a rage meter, whereupon you start snapping necks and breaking heads against walls. The sound track is the usual brass and percussion. If ever a game cried out for heavy metal, this is the one.
Aside from the core, there's problems. I found the level design lacking in cues to help me find my way, leading to a lot of running in circles and the occasional resort to walkthroughs. Max is a jerk who keeps saying he doesn't care about anybody but helps them anyway, and stupidly leaves people who helped him. You don't get a choice about that, other than to switch off the game and not start it again. His motivation is to cross the Plains of Silence, but I don't know why.
Speaking of plot, and to circle back to why I think this might be satire, at one stage you have to venture into an airport to fetch the dumbest quest item ever-- it's a creepy environment and the game does a good job of building tension, so long as you don't think about why you're there. Once I got out of the airport, I happened to talk to an NPC out in the wastes. Sometimes they have something useful, but after a while they mostly they talk pseudo Aussie gibberish or say you're great. This was one of those and said something like "Crikey! Yer a true blue prophet of the wastelands, surely you are!" at which point my hunchback idiot friend piped up with *his* usual gibberish, ending with "...and don't call him Shirley!" A line from Airplane!, of course. No idea if that was intentional.
Another bit that I won't be forgetting soon is the oddest hallucination scene I can remember in a game, featuring a talking dog, my idiot mechanic, and Max's dead wife telling him he should marry a hooker.
There's a good deal of grind required, although some of the content can be skipped. Unfortunately, some can't-- I didn't enjoy clearing minefields, but I had to do some in order to get an important upgrade for my car. I did leave a lot of camps only partially looted and several untouched, but it still took me over 50 hours to finish. And it was worth finishing, or nearly, if only to see the hallucination.
I found the end game uneven, with a race in Gas Town that I found frustrating (I died probably three times more in that one race than in the rest of the game combined) followed by some pretty easy fights. Then, as mentioned, Max has a wierd dream, saves somebody and acts real nice for 5 minutes, returns to jerk mode, and has a rather tedious penultimate battle with a truck (I took breaks for repairs), finally delivering his last beatdown, ending up basically exactly where he started. Roll credits. I'm still not sure if they were kidding or not, but I had fun.

First off, this is the best looking pool game I have ever played.  Period.
Beautiful pool tables, balls, and environments that are fully fleshed out and animated to give you a real sense of immersion.
The game is full of details that kept surprising me.  Some of them are so subtle that you can't even notice it unless you are watching the replay.  Here are a few things you will find:
* 3rd dimension: this isn't a simple pool game where balls stick to the table.  All pool balls can be knocked off, up in the air, and over other balls (given enough force).
* When hit certain ways, chalk will fall off stick and sprinkle on the table.
* Tiny woven texture on table material when you zoom in close
* Sides of table (bumpers) actually give and bend in when a ball hits them with force (very hard to notice without replay!)
For single player there is enough to keep you busy for awhile with tournaments in various game types against different AI.  One thing I found keeping my interest is bonuses you can try for on each game in a tournament.  For instance one might have a bonus for pulling off a jump shot during the match.  You can still win the game, but there will be a bonus for doing the jump shot.  Earning these stars while winning makes for a fun challenge.
There are also many ball styles, cue sticks, and locations to unlock through single player.  So far every ball set I have unlocked has been great looking and is a good incentive to keep playing and unlock more.
For multiplayer, it is fully functional in both same computer and online play.  Unsurprisingly you have to wait awhile for a game to show up, but that's less the fault of the game and more of the popularity of online pool :).
Last I should go over the physics.  This is a tough point to argue because so many factors go into pool physics and without a doubt there is no game out there that is 100% accurate.  If you have ever seen a ball hit another ball at high speed in close up slow motion you'll see what I mean.  Not to mention there are many different ball sizes/weight, table materials and cue sticks used in different areas that add to the difficulty in comparing this to the real world.
All I can say for sure is the physics seem real and have been really fun.  Added to the ability to hit the ball just where I want at power levels I never could in RL the game makes you feel like a pool master.
Game is on sale for $1.99 currently.  Sell a couple summer trading cards and pick it up!

*note: this is a review of episode one. will update review with the upcoming episodes*
After the linear and story driven absolution, Hitman 2016  returns to it's sandbox roots. Episode 1 sees the release of the paris showstopper level and the prologue from the beta which is three missions in all(4 if you count the first hand hold tutorial in the prologue). The prolgue does a great job in introducing the players to the changes in gameplay.
The disguises have been rehauled here. Think of it as the blood money disguise system but with a twist. On each level, there are certain people who can see through your disguise. They are marked with a bright white dot on the map and on top of thier heads(this can be turned off in the settings btw) so you'll have to stay clear of them. There is a right number of them in the paris level to make players think about thier routes but not too many to frustrate first time players.
When you select the showstopper mission, you see a screen where you can see your objectives and select how you want to enter a level, select your gear, and if you want to smuggle in any weapons or additional gear but you'll need mastery points which is xp points foe doing opprotunities and challenges.  Earning mastery points in a level unlocks more weapons, gear, and entry points. For example, get to a certain mastery level early on and you'll unlock the sniper rifle(but no case). After you are done setting up for the level, you just hit play.
Let me tell you, if you were dissappointed in absolution's mostly small levels then you'll love the showstopper. It's a huge place that you'll get lost in. I know I still do and I've played it for 9 hours! and there are plenty of ways to kill your targets.
You can discover them yourself or look at the opprotunities/feats section of the in game menu or track them in real time in the level(this can also be turned off). Unfortunately, event triggers from absolution have returned. certain npcs won't act unless you enter the same room as them. This is dissappointing but it's not game breaking. After you complete the level, you go to a results screen that shows you how many points you got and it also rates you with 1-5 de fleur's signs in which all 5 means you got silent assassin.
Let's move on to contracts mode which I must be honest is bare bones compared to absolution, at least at the time of this review. For one, you can't search for specific contracts. Accident kills aren't counted and are marked as "any weapon" on the results screen. No matter what melee weapon you choose to kill with, it will be marked as lethal melee(This doesn't personally bother me but it might others), and you can't buy weapons/disguises for contracts mode. Besides that, it's the same except you can choose 5 targets instead of three. I must note though, if you make a contract, you must complete it again as you won't even appear on the leaderboard after the first time.
There is also a mode called esculation contracts which have 5 levels of, you guessed it, esculation in performing hits. there's only one so far and that's in the ICA training facility. Level 1 requires you to kill a person wearing a disguise while level two has the same requirements in one but it wants you to steal the safe's contents and it keeps building up from there.
Finally, there are elusive contracts. You only have once chance and that's it. No restarts and no saves. The first contract hasn't been released yet but I can tell you if you do a number of these you'll gain rewards like suits. Five completed contracts will give you the absolution suit for example.
As for animations,some animations from absolution hae returned like the fiberwire kill. Not a bad thing though as absolution had some great animations. However, you can't strangle someone in a chair. There is an option but if you do, 47 strangles him as if the target is standing up. There are some new animations as well, try stabbing someone with a knife while standing in front of them and you'll get a pleasent surprise.
In short, while it does have flaws, it's still a great hitman game. If you loved any of the previous hitman game then you'll love this. Let's hope the rest of these levels will be as entertaining, if not more, as the showstopper was.

I'm going to play Devil's Advocate here. Yes, the release model is bad and undesirable. Yes, it's slimy and shady, and a nearly unethical business practice. However, if you're anything like me, and have been waiting for a worthy follow up to Blood Money since 2006, this game is what you've wanted.
Everything is there: The sprawling, open levels, seemingly infinite ways to approach your target, and plenty of ways to screw everything up. The only things missing for me are customizable weapons, though that's been somewhat replaced by a more advanced mission planning screen that allows you multiple ways to begin your hit. Also, it's a minor gripe, but I really liked the newspapers and notoriety system from Blood Money. Again, minor, but it was such a nice detail that I can't help but notice its absence.
No, I can't defend the business practices, but as a longtime fan of the series, I've had more fun with this game than anything I've played since perhaps The WItcher 3, and I am excited for the future of the game.
As such, I'm recommending it with something of an asterisk, only because of the release model.
EDIT: I glossed over the always onine DRM. I've only had a problem with it once in quite a lot of playtime, but once again, poor business model. If I could I would put my review somewhere between a yes/no recommendation as a result.
EDIT 2: At this point, I can absolutely recommend this game. Now that over half the episodes have been released and each one has been fantastic, I feel that the risk involved in buying this is gone. Only major con I can think of is the always online aspect.
