As of the Automation Upgrade I cannot recommend this game.  It suffers from a couple of major flaws that keep if from being really enjoyable.
1st: The UI for both duplicants and objects does a very poor job of highlighting the most important information. This makes it difficult to find even simple information like why is this guy really stressted, what do my people need that is not getting satisfied. Or what is in the box.  This information is available its just all text and I think they need to do another pass and prioritize information that is most commonly searched for.
2nd: Many of the games systems are poorly implemented.  For example, a game called Oxygen Not Included should model gas physics correctly.  You will have one room where half the room is a vacuum and the other half is full of oxygen.  This makes no sense in the real world and in the game it ruins what should be a fun system.  You can't circulate air because gas doesn't redistribute (or if it does it behaves like a really thick liquid).  Likewise its impossible to separate germy food from the clean stuff, or clean germy water.
The game has a strong style going for it, but its really held back by some almost working systems and crappy ui.

It’s hard to believe that it has only been four years since Batman: Arkham Asylum. The title that seemingly broke the curse of non-Spider related super-heroics in gaming has cast a shadow over so many games that have come since. Its masterful combination of Nolan’s dark vision of Gotham with the expanded rogues gallery afforded by decades of comics history brought even the most mainstream of Batman’s fans up to speed on everyone from Calendar Man to Victor Zsasz. Its narrow corridors and expansive tool-set created a tight, linear narrative where players nonetheless felt completely in control. Arkham City introduced open world mechanics to the formula that arguably opened up the world too much, taking away from that tightness that made Asylum such a breath of fresh air. Now, with Arkham Origins, new developer WB Montreal has struck a great balance between the levels of Asylum and the open world of City. It doesn’t quite eclipse the original, but Origins is a much more refined sequel than City was, and it’s one that is well worth your time.

Yooka-Laylee is a fun adventure collectathon game. Intended to be a spiritual successor to Banjo-Kazooie, which is a very praised game.  People are having very polarized opinions about the game at-the-time im writing this review. I think it would bee wissse to wait for the game to eventually get some sort of sale, if you're having second thoughts but,
If this price is right however I can definitely recommend yooka-laylee for someone looking to play a releaxing collectathon.
Even on my dated GTX 770  I run the game at its highest quality and have never noticed the framerate drop below 60 Fps
Tonics are a way to change up the players base stats or the gameplay itself they're some very useful tonics and ones that aren't very useful at all. While others have some very special effects!
It's a system that can be improved upon but is a great base.
Yooka-Laylee has a new mechanic on expanding a world. This will allow the player to explore new areas and puzzles to obtain more collectibales, in return for Pagies.
The game does a great job at capturing the cheeky and snarky remarks that its predecessor did so well. Fantastic writing overall
Like Banjo-Kazooie this game delivers on a fantastic selection of songs that you will find along your adventure. It also includes a lot of variations of specific songs.
The movement in Yooka-laylee feels very tight and fluid overall. Only very few select parts of the game will feel floaty and sloppy, thus contradicting  my point here.
Theressss a lot of movessssss....Really..
This is subjective but I think that the boss fights where really fun. Not exactly challenging but fun.
During some puzzles and some areas of the game you will find your camera holding too close to Yooka-Laylee and other objects. this will inturn mess up the movement of the game that is generally very good and because of this it will sometimes cause you to fail a certain puzzle or platforming section.
The game is a breeze quite-litereally at times the game features a whole staggering 3, maybe 4 ?varients of enemies in the entire game. They offer little to no challenge at all, a simple ground smash, or tail spin is enough to deal with most of them.
There is no such things as lives and punishing the player for dying making the game feel a little..boring at the very least. There's nothing ot worry about if you die. Some people may like this but I see it as holding the player's hand and it can be annoying to some.
Yooka-Laylee is a great game. It's by no means some sort of revolution for platform games but it is a fun and enjoyable experience. It does have issues, mostly subjective but they must hold some value as this game does have very polarized opinions. If Playtonic does want to continue to develop games and addresses some of the issues that I and many others have in future titles, I think we truly might have something to look forward too from this evolving company

Starpoint Gemini 2 is pretty interesting so far if you're played Freelancer, or any trade, explore, fight, pirate type of space game.

As someone who loves space games, including strategy, simulation, sandbox, RPG, and almost any genre in space, I love this game.  Im an avid fan of X3: Terran Conflict and the X series in general.  Starpoint Gemini 2 has so many things right and is fun, simple, and rather elegant.  I highly recommend it.
However, as with all games, it does have drawbacks and a few not so great things.
First off, Voice Acting-
You will likely notice it straight away when you start the campaign.  The voice acting is certainly better than that in the original, however it is still poor.  Most characters have strange accents or inflections, strange pronunciations which are inconsitent between characters (specifically the word "stasis") and no emotional connection.  The main character, Adrian Faulkner, is basically monotone with no depth nor feeling thruout. As a man who just lost his father and is out for revenge, he is VERY boring.   So do not expect the story to be compelling on that count.
Story/missions-
The story in SPG2 is better that is was in the original, and seems more streamlined, however it still remains quite boring after a short while.  I understand the game is mostly freeroam/sandbox, so take this as you will.  However, the missions are a bit more diverse than the original with some capture stuff added in as well as some scanning and transporting.  But it still remains the standard "Go Here, Kill/capture/scan/transport, Return, Listen to more dialogue"    So dont expect alot of diversity in missions.  Its pretty much the same with side missions and freelance.
Gameplay-
The gameplay is terrific. Its nice, simple, and easy to use.  Its easy to jump into the game and not have to learn 1000 controls or things to do.   However I personally miss some of the depth of controls and other minor things for the sake of immersion. (Thinking of X3)
Ship models / aesthetic -
The overall design, and texture of all ships and stations were fantastic and very intricate.  I might have to say they are some ofmy favorite ship designs in a long time.   Planets are ok, but lack proper scale.  Vigo at the start is almost the same size as planet trinity or at least pretty close.  Go look at planets in X3 and see proper scale.  However I understand such an accurate massive scale wouldnt work in an sandbox single system. Its something that many space games (mostly strategy games) do.
In the end I would definitely recommend this if you are looking for a nice, simple space sim with a bit of RPG elements thrown in.  You will get a good 40 or so hours out of it, then will lack anything to do. There are freelance missions that will repeat forever.

I just finished Mad Max, and think it was fantastic. It's been a long time since I played a game that made me actively want to play, rather than feel I had to.
The plot and action is well paced, and the upgrade system is a nice idea. It feels a little like there's a little too much to do and find, and that would most likely be because executives believe that a game only has value if you put a lot of stuff in it. Here's a hint to the devs - you don't need to swamp games with collectibles and artificially extend it. The end-game was a little disappointing - action packed, yes, but it did not leave me as satisfied as it should have.
While I enjoyed the game as a whole, there's some feedback I'd like to pass on:
- The storms and minefields are too immersion breaking. Having to stop what you're doing and wait for 10-15 minutes for a storm to pass, and having to drive the buggy around with Dog to get the minefields, just stops the action for too long and breaks down the immersion.
- There's too much stuff to do. Strongholds, upgrades, Archangels, lowering Scrotus' influence, scavenging locations, collectibles and bios, upgrading Max and the Opus, collecting cars, races, encounters - I'm sure there's more I missed. You don't need to add all that stuff in. Add in what you need to survive, some fun stuff, and spend the rest of the budget on actual plot and side missions.
- The upgrade system is broken. You have your Opus and Max almost totally upgraded almost by the end of clearing out the second region, and Griffa stops serving his purpose by about the same point. You can even upgrade parts of the Opus out of order, forcing you to upgrade lesser improvements as plot points. You need to ensure these things are all in order, and not exhausted too fast.
- For a game all about the cars, you really only have two modes on the Opus; no armour, no ramming grill, and everything else top gear for when you need to be fast and light, or heavy armour, heavy grill, and everything else top gear for when you need to survive.
Outside of those things, though, Mad Max was an excellent game. Though desperatly in need of some DLC!

FINALLY FINISHED.
Took me some time to actually finish this game 100%. Considering I paid only 21 Quid for it on release, I'd say just over 100 hours is good enough.
Mad Max is a good game, not what it could of quite been, based on the initial advertising of this game. But it was an enjoyable ride nonetheless. Story was engaging, characters were memorable. If you're a "I'm just here for the tale of the fabled road warrior and australian accents" kinda person, wait for a sale, game price regularly goes as low as 12£/15$ nowadays.
If you're a "Cocka-Lockin Shiny and Chrome Storm Chasin Leatherbound Motor Tamer" then strap in, because beyond the story is a world full of locations, side missions, conversations to be had and collectibles to find that offers a healthy dose of Lore and overall an immersive Mad Max experience that, whilst doesn't stray too far from what you'd expect in a Mad Max game narrative-wise, still manages to stay true to the films both new and old.
Either way, bring your Dinki-Di, get strapped in to your black on black and journey exit the big nothing, your time has come to face the ghosts of your past.
Pros +
+Story is really great, characters are pretty cool. Voice actors are excellent, my personal favorite being Griffa.
+Optimized for modern systems, If you've got a quad core, and a card with at least 2GB of memory and at least 8GB RAM. You're absolutely going to have no trouble getting 60FPS.
+Hours worth of content in Story and Side missions alone outweigh the cost of the product even when not on sale.
+Immersion and attention to detail both narratively and in the open world.
+Combat (Being from other Warner Brother titles, Batman Arkham Series, Shadow of Mordor etc) is tight, fluid and a joy to master. You truly feel immersed and feel the weight of your blows against the heads of your enemies and nothing really racks up your adrenaline like fighting 30 war boys and getting those perfect parries off to break the arm or leg of your attacker.
+The Magnum Opus. Driving is a huge part of Mad Max and there are a lot of cars to find out there and use, but the best car is your very own Magnum Opus. A fairly customizable, volatile motor beast of your own design. You unlock new items as you progress through the story, and you change it's parts out to fit your play and driving style. Speed, Defense, Strength. Are you a desert crawler, or an asphalt runner? Certain upgrades make some statistics better or worse. Your playstyle and choices can be complimented by this.
+Driving mechanics are quite realistic and fun to master. The previously mentioned choices of your Magnum Opus can also influence how "fun" it is to drive.
Cons -
-Story is quite short. If you're a completionist. My advice is do the game in bursts. The sheer amount of collectibles and challenges might seem like a plus to some, but to others it can be quite tedious. So personally what I did is complete a bunch of optional side content, then reward myself with a story mission when I got bored of the constant stream of collectible hunting and scrap looting.
-Early stages of car development can be quite frustrating. Having the worst available car parts can make driving a chore. Where turning too hard can cause it to steer out of control very easily, especially on a keyboard.
-ZERO Support. Sadly after Warner Brothers many stunts and trash ports to PC (Mortal Kombat and Batman Arkham Knight) they cancelled support plans for their other games already out. Meaning if there is a glitch or a bug that exists now, it's not getting fixed. No new patches are coming. Thankfully though. Our great community has found workarounds and fixes for some of the most irritating bugs. Chances are, if you get this, you'll probably encounter a bug in the story which requires you to construct a vehicle, but don't worry, visit the guides when that time comes. Workarounds to fix the issue exist, thanks to the community.
Con/Plus+-
-+Best played with a controller of your choice. The keyboard and mouse controls, in my own personal opinion did not have much thought put in to them, not enough thought or testing. The aim whilst on foot or in a car will sometimes just go insane like Max is having a epileptic seizure. Only lasts a second or two at most, but if it happens (And it did happen rarely, but often enough to make me switch to Controller fairly early on) it can happen at the worst of times. In a fight, or car chase. And unfortunately, being a Warner Brothers port. Controller is heavily focused on and most of the game revolves around controller orientated actions (Combat, Driving, etc) for some, who use both Controller and Mouse & Keyboard in games regularly it might be fine. But if you're a KB&M user (and likely have been for just about ever) you might dislike the keyboard and mouse controls in this game, I know I did.
-+Overall size and amount of content. I personally was happy with it. But as I previous explained. Some can find this horribly tedious. Especially since you're required to progress to unlock some items for your Magnum Opus.
7/10 is my final verdict.
It's better than average in many aspects. Although it's not perfect. They had more room with this game, to do something very much incredible. But Warner Brothers happily stopped that before it could be better than what we have here.
It was worth the price on release, and I'd say it's worth the price now even for just the story and unique experience it offers.
(P.S. if you're a completist, another hot tip. Load up a playlist of y7our favorite music, set to shuffle, and just drive. It really creates some cool moments when driving and fighting, another form of media to add to your experience is never a bad thing)

I am very tempted to give this game a positive review. If there was a neutral option, I'd take it.
My biggest problem with the game is that many of the tasks feel empty and hollow. Tearing down a scarecrow or a sniper's nest isn't really that much fun, but it's there to be done, and it stands between you and the upgrades you want.
The on-foot combat is easy to pick up, but has very little room to raise your skill in. You basically smash the left mouse button until everyone is dead, and occassionally block or evade. Weapons you temporarily aquire just dumb the combat down even more, as you now just have to smash the left mouse button. Shadow of Mordor, a game published by the same company with similar combat system, offers so much more variety in terms of skill, that it baffles me how they could make this so similar, yet fail so hard.
The vehicle combat is a lot better, but it has its own set of flaws - some of them critical. At first, it feels really satisfying to crash into enemies, pull them out of their car or shoot their tyres, but it gets somewhat boring soon. As soon as you aquire the Lv. 4 Harpoon, you just pull everyone's tyres off instantly, thus making you win every fight. Upgrades, on the other hand, seem to do very little in terms of combat. The improved ramming grills barely make you deal more damage, while the armor only seems to make your car go more sluggish, while offering no real incresed protection. After you get the thunderpoon upgraded, you can just one-shot every enemy you engage.
The story feels non-existant until you reach gastown (which was the majority of the game for me), and then turns somewhat nonsensical. The next part will discuss some characters, so it'll naturally contain spoilers:
All in all, this game might have done just as well without the story.
As for the good parts, the game does offer a lot of content, even if the content itself is rather dull. If you are looking for a game into which you can sink 20-40 hours, then I would recommend it. If you're looking for "the action version of New Vegas", then this isn't it.

After the linear and story driven absolution, Hitman 2016  returns to it's sandbox roots. Episode 1 sees the release of the paris showstopper level and the prologue from the beta which is three missions in all(4 if you count the first hand hold tutorial in the prologue). The prolgue does a great job in introducing the players to the changes in gameplay.
The disguises have been rehauled here. Think of it as the blood money disguise system but with a twist. On each level, there are certain people who can see through your disguise. They are marked with a bright white dot on the map and on top of thier heads(this can be turned off in the settings btw) so you'll have to stay clear of them. There is a right number of them in the paris level to make players think about thier routes but not too many to frustrate first time players.
When you select the showstopper mission, you see a screen where you can see your objectives and select how you want to enter a level, select your gear, and if you want to smuggle in any weapons or additional gear but you'll need mastery points which is xp points foe doing opprotunities and challenges.  Earning mastery points in a level unlocks more weapons, gear, and entry points. For example, get to a certain mastery level early on and you'll unlock the sniper rifle(but no case). After you are done setting up for the level, you just hit play.
Let me tell you, if you were dissappointed in absolution's mostly small levels then you'll love the showstopper. It's a huge place that you'll get lost in. I know I still do and I've played it for 9 hours! and there are plenty of ways to kill your targets.
You can discover them yourself or look at the opprotunities/feats section of the in game menu or track them in real time in the level(this can also be turned off). Unfortunately, event triggers from absolution have returned. certain npcs won't act unless you enter the same room as them. This is dissappointing but it's not game breaking. After you complete the level, you go to a results screen that shows you how many points you got and it also rates you with 1-5 de fleur's signs in which all 5 means you got silent assassin.
Let's move on to contracts mode which I must be honest is bare bones compared to absolution, at least at the time of this review. For one, you can't search for specific contracts. Accident kills aren't counted and are marked as "any weapon" on the results screen. No matter what melee weapon you choose to kill with, it will be marked as lethal melee(This doesn't personally bother me but it might others), and you can't buy weapons/disguises for contracts mode. Besides that, it's the same except you can choose 5 targets instead of three. I must note though, if you make a contract, you must complete it again as you won't even appear on the leaderboard after the first time.
There is also a mode called esculation contracts which have 5 levels of, you guessed it, esculation in performing hits. there's only one so far and that's in the ICA training facility. Level 1 requires you to kill a person wearing a disguise while level two has the same requirements in one but it wants you to steal the safe's contents and it keeps building up from there.
Finally, there are elusive contracts. You only have once chance and that's it. No restarts and no saves. The first contract hasn't been released yet but I can tell you if you do a number of these you'll gain rewards like suits. Five completed contracts will give you the absolution suit for example.
As for animations,some animations from absolution hae returned like the fiberwire kill. Not a bad thing though as absolution had some great animations. However, you can't strangle someone in a chair. There is an option but if you do, 47 strangles him as if the target is standing up. There are some new animations as well, try stabbing someone with a knife while standing in front of them and you'll get a pleasent surprise.
In short, while it does have flaws, it's still a great hitman game. If you loved any of the previous hitman game then you'll love this. Let's hope the rest of these levels will be as entertaining, if not more, as the showstopper was.

I'm going to play Devil's Advocate here. Yes, the release model is bad and undesirable. Yes, it's slimy and shady, and a nearly unethical business practice. However, if you're anything like me, and have been waiting for a worthy follow up to Blood Money since 2006, this game is what you've wanted.
Everything is there: The sprawling, open levels, seemingly infinite ways to approach your target, and plenty of ways to screw everything up. The only things missing for me are customizable weapons, though that's been somewhat replaced by a more advanced mission planning screen that allows you multiple ways to begin your hit. Also, it's a minor gripe, but I really liked the newspapers and notoriety system from Blood Money. Again, minor, but it was such a nice detail that I can't help but notice its absence.
No, I can't defend the business practices, but as a longtime fan of the series, I've had more fun with this game than anything I've played since perhaps The WItcher 3, and I am excited for the future of the game.
As such, I'm recommending it with something of an asterisk, only because of the release model.
EDIT: I glossed over the always onine DRM. I've only had a problem with it once in quite a lot of playtime, but once again, poor business model. If I could I would put my review somewhere between a yes/no recommendation as a result.
EDIT 2: At this point, I can absolutely recommend this game. Now that over half the episodes have been released and each one has been fantastic, I feel that the risk involved in buying this is gone. Only major con I can think of is the always online aspect.

Iv'e seen some other reviews make some significant complaints about minor things and here are my response to them:
"you don't get all of your basic abilities from the start" - Game works you in slowly as you are working with a new hero duo with entirely different moves
"levels are big and engery bar is too small, energy is hard to recover, butterflies are hard to find" - Energy bar refills itself after about 10 secs and can be expanded as you progress through the game, butterflies are everywhere
"guy that sells moves is hard to find and moves menu navigation is tedious" - If everything was in plain sight the game would have no challenge and this guys is in the middle of the first 2 levels in plain sight. Moves purchase menu - scroll up or down and selct move for purchase, not rocket science
"gathering every single item is plain annoying" - Then don't collect every single item! It's not required!
That was fun. As you can see there is a lot of nitpicking in the negative reviews. I understand that this game is not for everyone and is far from perfect but the gameplay so far has been fun and I have not experienced any game breaking bugs or issues.

I actually enjoy most of the quirks associated with the old Banjo games. My main issue with this one, really, is that the worlds are SO massive, bland and rather sparse for content that a majority of the gameplay, at least for me, is boredly wandering around trying to find something to actually do. And when I DO find something to do, it's either something small and very simple, or a horrendous task where the "challenge" is fighting with awful controls.
This is also coupled with the game not really having its own personality other than just trying and mostly failing to be Banjo-Kazooie again, as though they forgot what charm was and are entirely banking on references.
The worlds in Banjo-Kazooie were memorable and just condensed enough that you were never far away from something to do. The collectables were laid out in ways that led you to things or just added fun little platforming additions to your level exploring routine. They all also had distinctive landmarks so that you never really got lost after your first run-around. Yooka-Laylee's worlds are just... Huge, indistinct, and boring...
Those are my opinions, at least. I've played Banjo fairly recently and still enjoy the collect-a-thon playstyle when it actually gives you fun levels to explore and things to do and interact with. This game just didn't even really come close to even par with those experiences for me.﻿

It's hard to decide if this is a good or bad game, but its certainly different from most shooters.
Pros:
The building is decent
Combat is heart pounding
Game looks nice
There are lots of updates quite often, the game strategy changes often to accomodate them.
Workshop system benefits both content creators and game devs more than the market.
Lots of servers to choose from, with plenty of modded ones.
Cons:
Performance is a big issue, especially on modded servers or servers that don't wipe often/have decay.
Most players talk ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ly or are edgy kids.
The text chat is server-wide, but voice chat is based on proximity, which makes it awkward when one person has a mic and another doesnt. Which leads to...
There isn't any in-game way to tell friend from foe other than asking in a text or voice chat if thats them running, or by wearing an agreed uniform. Note that at a longer distance, hats dont render either.
Building a decent structure on a hillside is a challenge unless its practically flat with no variation, which defeats the purpose of trying to keep it out of sight early on.
Game is not really balanced, but a lot could be changed:
Anyone can use twig to build to the top of your base or a tower to hop on it, which makes building big a priority
Components are nearly impossible to get since you have to follow roads, which offer a clear line of sight to shooters, or go to monument/landmarks, of which half the worthwhile ones have radiation and the other half are swarmed with people around them.
The node update makes finding stone a giant pain early on, which meants youre stuck with a rock for a long time for harvesting until you do find a stone node to make tools.
Big groups will dominate servers they're on until a wipe, nothing can be done if you dont have many friends.
In short, the game devs say they dont want to influence how players play the game, but theres a clear bias towards raiding. Meanwhile, a vending machine for trading costs twice as much high quality metal as an armored door but has less than a third of the hp.
TL;DR If you have friends and the time to play this game, its well worth $5 or even $10 since the game hopefully gets better over time when devs focus on balance instead of high quality wavy grass.

This game is an amazing point in the star wars video game franchise. Since it came out in mid september, 2003, it easily surpassed Jedi Knight II: Jedi Outcast. The story revolves around a custom character named Jaden Korr. Jaden Korr is on his way to Luke Skywalkers Jedi Academy and meets a guy named Rosh Penin along the way. The two have differences but easily become friends. The story for this game is a little predictable and henceforth, not worth paying too much attention too. The real highlight of this game is the lightsaber combat. Players seem to dub this games lightsaber combat as the best in the franchise, but i'm inclined to dissagree. Look, i'm not saying it's bad by any means, but it's not as good as people seem to imply. In this game you get 3 choices of lightsaber: Single, Double, or Double Sided (Like Darth Maul) lightsabers. They all control differently and both Double and Double Sided sabers can retract to Single sabers. They all have different move sets and look flashy as hell. The actual combat is pretty good, but as i said before, has flaws. Lightsaber moves look flashy enough to look the part and control with ease. Force powers are where it becomes tricky. When in Jedi Vs Jedi combat, NPC's seem to just deflect forcepowers the first time, and react to them the second. When using the overpowered Force Lighting and Force Grip, this becomes a cake walk for a room with a lot of enemies in it. If a pit is nearby, the player can just grab them and toss them into the pit with little resistence. I kind of wish that this was not as common because I found myself just using this to avoid a risky battle with lightsabers. Lightsaber attacks drain huge chunks of heath with each landed attack. If you're really good with the combat, you can finish off both NPC and PVP Players with 2-3 hits. Although this is easier said than done, it is still an issue, but adds the realism to the lightsabers power. I give the Singleplayer game a 8/10. Multiplayer is also in this game and has a small, but loyal community. Back in the day when this game was popular, certain servers would ban players for not having proper Lightsaber combat etiquette. Most servers that support this type of etiquette are very clear on what must be done to conduct battle. Any interfierence with another players battle may land a ban. Force powers are usually dissabled along with blasters because of the overpowered dark side force powers. Multiplayer is also pretty fun and i give it a 6/10. Overall, Jedi Academy is the best game in the Jedi Knight series and is well worth the buy, especially on sale.

+ Nice gameplay /  Mix of Rpg and tactic space game ; if you play in high difficulty it can be very challenging.
+ A lot of things to do.
+ A lot of ships and weapons to suit all tastes.
+ A extremely nice and responsive Dev Team. Basically if you post anything ( interesting ) on the steam forum, there is good chances that a Dev will be the first to answer.
+ A perfect example of how a Early Access should be done and handled.
+ Mod support.
- Scenario not great.
- A little bit short. I know it is against my + on greate value, but the thing is  I think 35 hours to reach max level is a little bit to quick; of course if you want the best weapons you will have to spend a lot of times, but it lacks the motivation of leveling up.

So highly recommend this game made by a very nice and little team of passionate Dev.
Will by their next project without hesitation.

There are 4 things that I don't like about this game...
1.  After downloading the game, I discovered that the tactical display key would not function.  I had to do some extensisve remapping to finally get it to work properly.  Until this key was repaired, I lost every single combat that I was in.
2.  This game boasts of lots of locations that you can fly to.  This is somewhat true (to a limited extent) and I was quite pleased with all the different kind of space stations.  That said, this game has a huge & glariing problem.  After you dock at a space station, all you get is a rather sterile screen display (like a spreadsheet) THAT IS THE SAME FOR EVERY STARBASE IN THE GAME.  There are no people to meet, no places to see, no contacts to be made, simply nothing!  Other companies have solved this problem with procedural generation, but the Devs didn't seem to be up to it.  Since their game is primarily hard-coded, they will never be able to add the flexibility & expandability that a game like this would do best with. I'm trying to manage my preconceptions about this game. I backed it on Kickstarter, hoping for a worthy successor to Banjo-Kazooie. I don't think we got that, but I think I at least got my money's worth. I wouldn't pay $40 for this though. It faithfully follows the formula visible in the old BK games, but there are glaring flaws.
The levels are pretty to look at, but too large and sprawling. It's possible to get lost, and with nothing like a map or at least a compass, you could be stuck wandering aimlessly until you get your bearings, or until you give up and return to the hub world through the pause menu.
Speaking of the hub, it suffers from a similar problem. Lots of space with very little to fill it. This only gets worse after world 3, when the hub expands outdoors.
Like in BK, the villain will taunt you as you roam the hub, but unlike in BK, he has nothing clever or witty to say, and cycles through the same (very few) lines.
The enemies are quite possibly the most lazily designed part of this game. With (too) few exceptions, they are ALL reskins of the same enemy. Nearly all of them die in one hit, except the ones with hats. They require two hits. Riveting gameplay, this isn't.
I could go on, but I think I've made my feelings about this game fairly clear. To summarize... it's a disappointment. If it's trying to be a successor to Banjo-Kazooie, it falls short of both games in all areas (bar the obvious graphical upgrades). If it's trying to pull in new fans for the genre, it lacks too many basic convenience features to bear through the first world, maybe the second if you're really patient. The only thing this game accomplishes is that it makes me want to play Banjo-Kazooie and -Tooie again, to see all the things from those games which are missing from Yooka-Laylee.

I'll be covering the biggest negative aspects that people have brought up, but overall this is one of the most genuinely fun games I have played in years.
For reference, I have completed up to around 75% (very rough estimate including all collectibles and secrets) of the 1st expanded world.
Negative complaints:
"camera controls are bad"
- Yes, the camera is pretty much garbage. It gets stuck on terrain leaving you moving blindly, until it either snaps very jarringly or moves incredibly slowly to a more suitable position. Narrow "hallways", corners, and platforming adjacent to walls/cliffsides are affected by this.
- The FOV is also pretty bad, being unable to move the camera away from you or even look below you (even though you don't need to) is sometimes annoying.
"general controls are bad"
- Nowhere near as bad as the camera, but yes. Movement is a bit wonky as you turn in wider than expected arcs, but I quickly got used to this. The only trouble this gave me was trying to defeat static hovering bee robot enemies. They must be faced exactly before you can jump and attack otherwise you will miss pretty easily.
- Somebody forgot to map the "B" button properly! D'oh! Esc is the "B" button but every now and then decides not to work and just opens the pause menu instead. This means you can sometimes never refuse an offer from a character. I'm sure this will be patched soon because it's game-breaking.
- For some parts of the game you will have to stand still and aim the camera manually so you can fire at a secret switch hidden below or above etc. but this feels horrible. The camera for some reason shifts to one side of the character, the aiming has some kind of acceleration on it, and the cursor isn't actually lined up properly with your shots. Thankfully this aiming mode is only used for puzzles and not in combat or timed events.
- Steep slopes are pretty annoying. Stepping or landing on to one instantly puts you into slide animation that can't be cancelled out of by jumping as one would expect, but instead you must wait until you reach the bottom. These never appear on environmental buildings or terrain though, so are never encountered while exploring but only on what appears to be slopes that are programmed to do this specifically.
- Controls are unbindable, and for some reason all menus incorrectly display xBox controls while dialogue boxes disaplay actual controls.
- Collision is amazing. After playing a game like Overwatch (which has atrocious hit-boxes, environment collision, and nasty invisible walls) this game is a breath of fresh air. It's so refreshing being able to take a path or explore an area that was not intented to be optimum or accessible. The stone temples and pillars in the first level don't have set-straight bricks, meaning you can shimmy along the tiny jutting out edges to get around somewhere quicker or jump out, up to the next one and back in, like a ladder to the top. There are no invisible walls restricting you, only your own platforming ability to climb or jump places without falling to your doom. Hit-boxes are great, meaning you will have a few moments where you are surpised that your late attempt at hitting something attacking you or jumping to a precarious edge will actually succeed.
"graphics are blurry"
- The detail, models, and textures of this game are pretty amazing, but a lot of this is undone by the poor post-processing. Looking out into the far distance is painful because everything becomes a blurry mess. Especially annoying when the game would look miles better with a bit of anti-aliasing instead of the awful blur effect. Regular distances look fantastic though.
"voices are annoying/unskippable"
- Cutscenes seem to be completely unskippable, so text cannot be skipped during them either. Cutscenes mostly occur between gameplay to advance the story, or to highlight an outcome of an action that wouldn't otherwise be obvious.
- Dialogue can be sped up during regular gameplay interaction, but not skipped all at once. Similar to the earlier Pokemon games.
- I can't dispute whether the voices are annoying or not, but I can say they're not really voices but more like animal or ambient noises. Ex, A pig character oinks and snorts, a mine cart character creaks and clangs, etc.
- Dialogue is actually pretty funny and riddled with adult humour. I caught mention of a ship named "Bat Ship Crazy", a sentient vent complaining in graphic detail about his "job that blows", a cloud that needs help being relieved that requires "washing you hands after", and a snake salesman named "Trowzer", all during or before the first world.
"energy meter makes travelling a chore"
- An energy meter is present in the game that reduces as you use skills and refills after a few moments of not being used.  It can also be refilled instantly by collecting a single butterfly, which are absolutely everywhere.
- In my opinion, travelling around is nowhere near as big a chore as other large-world games such as Skyrim, Breath of the Wild, Grand Theft Auto V, Minecraft, Borderlands 2, etc. simply because not only can you travel around pretty fast using your roll skill, but the game is extremely dense and has secrets and things to find in many, many places. This means once your energy meter is depleted and you have to wait a few seconds before you can start rolling again, you can take an alternate route such as gliding across somewhere, climbing to a higher point to jump down etc. and you are very much likely to spot something you missed beforehand.
- That being said, you will never fully enjoy or 100% the game if getting to main objectives as quickly as possible is more important to you than slowing down to explore suspicious looking scenery for secrets. Collectibles and secrets should not be seen as a distraction from the main quest, bur rather the main objectives of the game should be seen as an excuse to go exploring in an unvisited area, or re-exploring somewhere with a new ability or knowledge of a mechanic.
"worlds are too big, characters are in strange locations, not enough info is given on character locations"
- The worlds certainly are big, but they are very dense and feel very cohesive. Unless you are on the edge of the map, then from any given point of interest there will be at least 3 "paths" to more nearby points of interest around you, and a secret or two hidden between.
- Characters are indeed in strange locations, and are even stranger themselves, but that's part of the charm of the game. Their locations are not meant to be shoved down your throat, instead leaving the player to discover them for theirselves. You might find a pig knight in a small clearing in a haunted forest that gives you a riddle based quest, or a sentient cloud hidden behind a mountain that can be fed elemental fruits to change the environment of the rest of the world.
-------------Conclusion-------------
At a core design level, the game is very well made. The voice acting, models, graphics, hidden locations, secrets, world layout etc. are very well done.  The comedy and dialogue is great, with many daft jokes that make older people groan but there's quite a bit of cleverly disguised adult humour. However, the worlds will feel about as sparse as most open-world games to players new to the genre (which hasn't seen much love in a long time), or players that like to get through quickly with clear goals. The real fun of this game comes from discovering a numerous amount of clerverly hidden secrets and working things out for yourself.
The polishing is also not too shabby. The freedom feels great, and movement very unrestrictive. The post-processing and camera, however, are just plain awful and really hold the game back.
Overall I would give this game a solid 7/10 until the camera, post-processing, and PC controls are fixed. I would give this game a solid 10/10 otherwise.
tl;dr:
Like treasurehunt genre: 7/10, 10/10 when patched
Dislike: 3/10 & 6/10

I've been an FPS player for upwards of 9 years now, and BO2 was my 6th or 7th game. After 7 years of playing COD4 straight, this game was a bit of a shock. The mechanic's are fairly smooth, comparable to the first of this series, but the draw graphics are cleaner and more elements refined. The common characteristics are carried through as per each call of duty, i.e: 3 overpowered guns everyone uses, (AN94, MSMC, Peacekeeper (pay2win..)). The micro-transactions are out of hand, with at least 50 skins available to buy, not including extra class slots, flag+playercard packs, etc. The maps are all quite small, making timing rather than skill an essential element. Even if you possess much higher gunskill than your opponent, you'll find yourself dying more than you'd like. However, this being said, I have had a lot of fun on this game over the past few years, and looking past the majority of the braindead community, I have made a few friends as well. This game is dying out, peaking at 6-8k players, so, it's a risk if you'll be able to play the gamemodes you're after.

Not really a review of the game as such, I remember coming across the game by mistake on the store page. When I browsed the discussion boards I was gobsmacked at how well and often the development team engaged with the community, for this reason I bought it and hopefully once I've done with the current games I'm playing I will sink my teeth into it.

Well...the game looks nice but is actually quite boring. Here is why:
1. Unengaging story
The story consists of a lot of text (white on color, not very legible) and really really atrocious voice acting (which sometimes just cuts out). There are so many factions with text descriptions I did not bother to read all of them. Honestly I did not understand half of it because I have not played the predecessor. The game did not present its universe in an engaging way.
2. Simple missions
The free missions are all randomly generated but they consist  of either go to A and kill / capture or go to A and scan / repair (same menu button) or go to A and transport to B.
The campaign missions are the same. Go to A and usually kill everything there...done. Sometimes you need to ferry stuff. But the whole involvement is detached. You arrive...the game cuts to sequence and some voice acting..suddenly to reappear with enemies around...you kill them...cut to the next short scene...done. There is no drama, no real action, no emotional involvment. I did not respond emotionally to the characters, who are just pictures with horrible accents.
Trading and mining is a horrible grind if you like it. It is certainly helpful in the beginning but not worth your time later on. Just take the "kill pirates" mission and blast everything to hell.
Once I got capturing ships down...I had so much money I could have bought ships that were not yet unlocked for my character level.
3. Simple combat
Usually you fly somewhere, click F for "Fire at will" and maneuver a bit around. There is not much strategy involved. Starfleet Command or Space Empires Starfury had more interesting combat. Manal aiming is cumbersome because you can't really see the ships at longer ranges and there is no help with aiming. Due to the turret placement your shots might not go where your reticle is...so automatic fire it is most of the time.
Also medium difficulty is way to easy. I had a destroyer that could easily defeat a dreadnought without breaking a sweat (loosing shields).
4. technical stuff
Although the combat is in 3D the star sector is actually in 2D. The map is in 2D. You can fly "up" and "down" but it feels like all planets and stations are on the same plane. It is not a globe but rather a "thick" square.
Flying around especially in the beginning is tedious because jumpdrives or jumpgates are way too expensive and when you have the money to buy jumps you can get a perk that allows you free use of the jump gate system.
After about 10 hours the game just felt like a grind to get better ships and more weapons and do all the story missions (usually just killing enemies). It simply got boring.

Steam turned me down for a refund ( I bought the game in 2014, when the game was in Early Access for about $14 ). Every hour after 2 hours, was me forcing myself to play the game.
This game is a huge disappointment:
- Combat is underwhelming. The game essentially plays itself. There's no lead targetting reticle, so you hit the F key, to order your gunner to target the ship ( auto aim, for the most part ). All you do is WASD, to manouvre your ship. At short range, the enemy ship will often be off the screen. Combat is as complex and interesting as using a toilet ( as Kenuty would say ).
- Missions consist of mind-numbingly boring: fetch quests; being taxi driving driver; assassinations ( see combat above ); scanning anomalies ( being close to a pretty space anomaly and hitting the scan button ); ferry quests ( smuggling some VIP ) which ( half the time ) are very dangerous and will often lead to your ship being insta-killed ( so why bother doing them ).
- Pathfinding ( asking the game to plot a course and fly to a mission waypoint ), next to large objects like space stations is sometimes so awful that the game will either have you flying loop de loops continuously, or pulling violent u-turns and trying to fly through solid objects like the actual space station or asteroids ( sometimes the station has solid collision detection, so you'll take damage... sometimes you can fly right through it, as if it was a ghost ).
- Flying through the automated space repair facility often does not repair your ship.
- Game froze after a couple of hours.
- Memory leaks ( which forced me to close the game, which is why I'm writing this ).
- I just got my second memory leak in 8 hours and uninstalled the game. This game obviously appeals to casual gamers who have low standards. I asked Steam once again, to refund the money that I spent, based on memory leaks - they turned me down, based on 8 hours played...
- The voiceovers are (B movie ) lacklustre.
- Crashing into planets is idiotic ( the fact that you can even do it in the game ).
- Nanobots that dissasemble derelict ships cost $5,000 yet the yield from a derelict ship is less than $5,000, so why bother even buying and using nanobots? Nice balance ( lack of ). The operating costs get even worst if the ship has contraband on them ( forcing you to flush the contents down the toilet ).
- Mining consists of firing your laser at the asteroids and clicking, "collect". I don't mind the mining but there are more interesting mining mechanics in games like Galaxy on Fire 2 ( where you have to try and centre the drill, because the drill bit keeps going askew ( like using a real drill in real life, that has low revolutions per minute ). Honestly, it's sad to say that Galaxy on Fire 2, on my android phone was more exciting than Starpoint Gemini 2 or Elite: Dangerous and a fraction of the cost *.
Pros:
+ The aesthetics are nice ( graphics, music, female ship command voiceovers ).
* It seems like the developers took a massive♥♥♥♥♥♥on "Galaxy on Fire 2", by destroying the economy:

This game could be so great. A real worthy successor for the likes of Freelancer and Privateer but it has so many flaws that it is very close to not being recommendable...
I still recommend it though for those in urgent need of a space sim who don’t like Elite: Dangerous and can’t wait for Star Citizen since chances are good that you still will get lost in the vicious circle of just one more mission to be one step closer to the next upgrade/weapon/ship.
Let’s start with the good things:
I really like the music…
ok… that’s not all, there is so much to see and do in this game, too. The galaxy is huge and there are many (unique) space stations and planets to visit, missions to do, artifacts/blueprints to track down and especially ships to destroy, buy or capture. Yes, you can capture enemy ships – in theory – that is one part where the design just doesn’t work out so well, more on that later. You also gain experience and level up which will give you skill points and every 5 level a point for perks. Skills feel rather cheap and bad for me. There are 4 active skills (temporary boosts) you can invest your points in, each skill for one of the available weapon systems (railgun, plasma, beam and heavy (missiles)). So you basically decide which is your favorite weapon system and put your skill points into that skill. Perks are passive but also don’t feel that well thought out. Again you can increase the effectiveness of your favorite weapon system up to 3 times and then there are a lot of semi useful perks to invest in. Additionally you get permanent bonuses by getting (steam) achievements (never seen that before in a game...)
The actual space simulation needs to get used to, too. I was expecting a feeling like in the old games and even bought a joystick to get the good old times back, but that just doesn’t work out (for me). The shooting is turret based (you have chase cam and no cockpit view anyway), meaning you can see around your ship and you just move the camera freely and aim with your mouse (depending on the turret placement on the ship). Furthermore the hit feedback is so bad that I quickly decided to switch to beam weapons that are instant hit so I know where I aim is what I hit. Railgun and plasma are projectiles flying somewhere in the direction of the enemy and unless you are not fighting a huge freighter close combat you barely see if you hit or not and especially if not why not (ok, it might just need to get used to but beam seems the better solution). Also you can just tell the system to auto fire (that's why there are acurracy stats you can influence, but I want to play the game as space shooter and not strategy game like star wolves so I don't want to use autoaim...)
What is really bad and I don’t understand how the design can fail so hard is that you can’t see your enemy information in the hud. Instead the hud is clustered with stupid, bad looking buttons I barely use (which I could easily access by keys). You only see the enemy information when the enemy is in sight and when he is close it is so fast moving that you can barely read it. So what is happening all the time is: There is a bunch of enemies closing in, you see them in the radar, you can target them (via hotkey) but you have either to start flying into their direction (which is a great idea when it turns out that they are deadly) or switch to turret and target mode and move your camera wildly to get them into focus and be able to identify their threat level. Both very inconvenient since you should be able to quickly cycle through all targets and identify them with one glance. Well perhaps I’m missing something, there even is an info hotkey but it won’t work for enemy ships, only for special objects.
The other really bad design issue is the character level system. You level up quite fast and the missions you can get (you don’t have to visit stations to get missions, you will get them while in space, which is good) show the suggested level you should have to take that mission. The problem is: the character level does tell♥♥♥♥♥♥about your actual strength. That only depends on your ship and weaponry. So this indicator is useless in the first place. Coincidentally it is also useless in the second place because there are types of missions that are just no brainers – regardless of which level they show. If you have maintenance or science missions you just fly to the target, repair or inspect it aaand… it’s done. On the other hand, good luck with rescue or capture missions, which are often impossible even on low level. So the balancing is very bad in general but luckily you can cheat your way out most of the time: Early game you just start your engine boosters and outrun every enemy, mid game they sometimes start blocking your boost mode but you can have a ship with cloaking device by then and just turn that on. Later this doesn't work and thats when you get in real trouble…
Talking about capturing… first you can’t capture 90% of the enemies because they have a larger crew than you have (capturing works this way: grapple the enemy with a tractor beam, send troops via teleporter to his ship, if you have more than him you possibly take over the ship). You can focus on capturing by searching for a cheap ship which allows a large army of troopers on board and you can get perks or officers (you can hire 3 officers for your ship, by the way, you can also hire merc ships that follow you and certain ships allow to take fighters on board you can launch during combat so you end up having your own fleet) that give a bonus on the capturing chances.
Second most of the time there are other ships around. So even when you manage to find a capturable ship chances are high that it will get blown apart by some other ship nearby. So it is a great feature in theory that just is no real fun most of the time but satisfying when it finally works.
Other weaknesses I like to mention:
The presentation is really bad. The main story has a ridiculous voice over most of the time, sometimes just dialog (not sure if it is a bug that voiceover is not playing because the music gets muted anyway) and sometimes just a text popup – atmosphere = 0.
The balancing of the main and some side missions is also a bad joke. You will be stuck for hours until you have enough money for a capable ship and after you finally progress you often get much easier missions afterwards.
The menus are confusing and tedious to use. E.g. you can either sell all cargo or one good at the merchant, but if you have more than 1 of a good you always have to go to the next screen to select how much of the good you want to sell (well everything!). And you will do that a lot because the screen shows if you are having good, mediocre or bad prices so you most likely don’t want to sell the goods with bad prices and rather fly to the next station. I think the ship loadout menu is simply bugged. edit: it is not bugged, turret handling is just another unintuive feature. Also when I unmount a rocket launcher I lose my missiles. The good thing is that I can store my ships with their loadout in my garage and can swap them easily depending on the situation (cargo space/troop count/gun power).
But the weapon/ship prices balancing could be much better. The next better systems are so expensive that it takes hours until you can afford something new that actually feels more powerful. The upgrade flow was much better/faster in Freelancer.
Last but not least there are that most annoying situations where a cutscene triggers in the middle of a fight, you can’t do anything but the fight continues in the background usually resulting in your death or at least a great headstart for your enemies.
So there are many occasions in the game where I ask myself: Did the developers actually play what they created?
And then I go back to the game desperately hunting for the next better ship…

Mad Max is a game you'll either love or hate, or maybe love and THEN hate.  It plays like mashup of other familiar titles.  It has open world driving like GTA or Saint's Row, but the exploration, tower, and "do all the things!" aspect of Far Cry 4, with melee combat like the Batman: Arkham titles.  I enjoy all those games, so I really enjoyed Mad Max for most of the time I played.  I tried to do EVERYTHING in the game for the majority of it, except for the races (called Death Runs) because racing in these types of games has never been fun.  The environments, graphics, sound and overall production was all great!
The longer I played the game, the more it dragged on me.  I reached a point where the story progression was moving along quickly, but there was still SO MUCH TO DO.  It feels like they tacked on too many locations and side objectives that really had little benefit.  But I worked hard and kept upgrading my car to the point where it was ALMOST fully upgraded!  After completing almost all of the side stuff, I wanted to just mainline the story and finish it up, but then it required you to complete a race using a much weaker version of your car, and I just was done at that point.
I got the game on sale, and I feel it was worth it, considering the amount of time played, but the later I got in the game, the more frustrated I would get with areas where they would just throw more and more enemies at you, which is never fun, so I had had enough.  I choose to recommend it because there is a lot of good to the game, but there are just some really dumb things too.  So of course, your mileage may vary.

Being the huge Batman fan that I am, I still knew that at some point I was going to try it out. And that I did on Halloween night. Ten hours later, my opinions on the game have changed drastically. This is the largest, most complete, most refined Arkham to date. Every single aspect of the game has been tuned to the point where it has reached its full potential.
It is true that regarding game play, this is Arkham City on a larger scale, with a larger map and plenty more skills, animations, gadgets and so on. But the story in Origins is fantastic and stands out as the best in the trilogy. Every major enemy is introduced with flair, and the fights are spectacular. The Deathstroke battle (which has caused many a lot of trouble, but I thoroughly enjoyed) in particular, was epically designed. The martial artistry displayed in this scene is jaw dropping. I cannot think of a more awesome and cinematic showdown in a comic book-inspired video game.
I must say I do find a major setback with regards to a particular decision in the art direction, and that is Batman´s character design. It makes no sense at all. An excessively armored Batman on his second professional year cannot be justified on any grounds, and the countless amount of gadgets, from the get, go, at times removed me from the context the story so passionately tries to portray.
The atmosphere is thick with immersion and somehow darker as well. I feel this visual interpretation more akin to the Batman world I know and grew up with. Similar to what Tim Burton did on his second Bats movie.
So to wrap things up, yes, Origins is very similar to Arkham City. Yet after spending some time with it, I´ve come to the conclusion that the Arkham formula is too much of a winning one, and polishing it rather than messing with it was perhaps, the safest and truest (to the franchise) course of action WB could have taken. Batman Arkham Origins´ biggest hurdle is its legacy, and the uncontrollable human tendency to compare.
As a gamer and Batman fan, I have given the game a chance and wholeheartedly recommend Arkham Origins. A truly memorable experience if measured on its own grounds.
Overall: I can only wish this was the first installment. Arkham City was pretty much a perfect game but it doesn't preclude Origins from being a great game.
Note: Don't skip the credits scene.

NOTE: I recently did a major edit because I last updated the review months ago and also didn't want a wall of text to put the Great Wall of China to shame.
People on the internet seem to hate this game and often for reasons I can understand. However, putting complaints about Denuvo and always-online aside, this game is actually quite good.
The second episode of Hitman might just be one of the best Hitman levels in the series (I should know, I've played every single one of them). The level has tons of nooks and crannies to explore and definitely feels more like a Hitman level than the Paris level did. It also seems to be more alive than the previous one, likely thanks to the absence of large crowds of mentally handicapped people that won't recognise danger until they're basically already dead. The more recent levels have also been great fun to complete and I've managed to get Silent Assassin, Suit Only on all but one of the levels.
The first two elusive targets were both a great way to shake things up, and might just be the best experience I've ever had with a Hitman game. I've been lucky enough to get both of them and even earned the Silent Assassin rating on the second one, mostly thanks to my trusty cans of expired spaghetti sauce. After this, however, the idea seemed to get a bit stale given the fact that they kept coming up with reasons to make each target special. Sadly these often fell flat with me. It's also a bit annoying that these targets aren't announced until not long before their appearance in the game, which has lead to me missing several of them. I will give them credit for making an app that alerts you when they are going to release a new elusive target into the world, but I really can't be bothered to install it on my phone.
Performance wise the game runs fine, a few drops here and there when you're looking at a particularly shiny set piece, but overall a solid 60 and over on my GTX 970. I do have to say that the DX12 version kept crashing on me back when there was only one episode, but I haven't tried running it with DX12 since then. I also want to point out that I've only gotten this solid 60 and over after upgrading my i5 3.2 GHZ to an i7 4.0 GHZ, so I'm going to assume that there's some AI things going on behind the scenes that make this go heavy on your CPU at times. There's also a few bugs that haven't bothered me personally and the worst ones like save game corruption, which is the only one that bothered me (exactly once), seem to have been fixed on release of EP2.
At this point I'm going to say yes and recommend the Full Experience to everyone. I've really had a lot of fun with the game and while there have been a few levels that I personally think aren't as good as others, I feel that IO has taken large steps in the right direction. This isn't the second coming of Hitman Jesus (or Blood Money as it's more widely known, though I'm more of a Hitman: Contracts fan myself), but it's a great game in its own right.

First off, the game is absolutely beautiful in every way; beautifully optimized, beautiful physics, beautiful graphics, etc.
I've always enjoyed playing pool ever since I was young, whether it be at the arcade, bowling alley, or pool hall, I always enjoyed it; and up until this game, I considered the
pool video game in existence is
, which I had owned for the Nintendo Gamecube and still have for pc. Pool Nation is a more modern version of Pool Paradise, doesn't have as many features as Pool Paradise
I feel Pool Nation doesn't really live up to Pool Paradise, but is a good pool game, nonetheless; less than five minutes into my first playthrough of Pool Nation, I was immediately addicted to it.
Without a doubt, for an indie game, the quality is amazing. The optimization, which is usually lacking in indie games, is perfect.
The physics engine is awesome, right up there with Pool Paradise. When I'd look at other pool games, other than Pool Paradise, the physics would be a disaster, either too stiff or too loose; Pool Nation's physics are as true to the real game as you can get. With precise cue control, you can curve, give spin, jump, etc, to your heart's content!
The textures are beautiful; from the detailed wood grain of the cues, to the fine threads of the pool table mat, everything's in stunning detail. With realtime ball reflections to stunning environments, Pool Nation is in a league all its own!
An awesome soundtrack is there to set the mood and keep you company while you play. From light piano music, to downright funky, it's got you set. With each location having its own custom music pieces, the variety is right up there.
As you progress and beat certain challenges, you can unlock new cues, ball sets, and mat decals; a vast array to accompany anyone's tastes and wants!
As a sound designer, this is my bread and butter. Pool Nation's sounds are top notch; everything from the cue hitting the cue ball, the balls hitting each other, hitting the cushions, going into the pockets, and to bouncing off the table and hitting the floor are superb. I was actually surprised when I heard the ball bouncing on the floor after it left the table, nice and lively with reverb!
Not my most favorite gamemode ever, but it certainly is one that'll keep you on the edge of your seat, your palms will sweat, your heart will race, and will truly test how good and quick you are.
The slow mo feature is a nice touch. Your last ball is going for the pocket, you're not sure if it'll make it, the slow mo kicks in showing the pocket, as the ball eases in in stunning, glossy, detail, it slowly reaches the end of the mat, you're on the edge of your seat...BOOM it tips off the edge and goes in, you win! It's also great for those action shots with the ball cruising into the pocket.
The replay is awesome. Just pulled off the most amazing shot ever and want to see it again in slow mo? No problem, the replay feature's got your back! Everything from chalk dust to cushion distension can be seen in replay, and features allow you to slow down and move the camera to get a nice look on all the action that took place! (UPDATE, read below)
Occasionally, the music will cut out and all you can hear is the ambience and regular sounds. Sometimes the music will come back, but sometimes it doesn't.
Random crashes. The game's full of them. Crashed on startup, crashed multiple times after beating and opponent. I think it's due to the saving. Trying to return to the game after Alt+Tabbing also causes the game to crash sometimes, other times you CAN'T get back in.
Chat. When typing in chat, sometimes a key will appear as though it was pressed more than once and sometimes not at all, causing
Your cue, balls, and mat decal will sometimes reset to default. It always resets after restarting the game.
Certain moves will not register, especially banks and kicks at certain times.
The chat can sometimes interfere with a shot.
Some hud/menu things can also interfere with gameplay.
Spin from the cue ball does not transfer to the object ball. A feature that takes away the realism. It's common physics, "for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction." The cue ball is spinning right, and when it hits the object ball, the object ball should spin left, therefore adding more control; even Pool Paradise had this feature.
Bag of Tricks REQUIRES purchasing dlc packs, without said dlc, you get a very small number of "Starter" objects, which don't help you create anything worth while.
The replay mechanic has been changed. You can no longer slow replays, it's either start off slow or build up to faster, or, reverse slow or build up. You can't start off normal speed and then do a dramatic slow down. The controls were changed, too and are, in my opinion, pretty condescending.
A new dlc has been put in the store that will unlock ALL unlockables (other than dlc unlocks) without the need of having to progress which is, in my opinion, the lazy man's dlc.
Other than that, this game is a must have for anybody who loves pool!

Spec Ops is a strange, yet very interesting beast.
It starts off like one of theses bombastic console shooters (Call of Duty, Gears of Wars 2, ...) both in terms of gameplay (lots of cutscenes and action set pieces), and story (Americans going at the opposite side of the world to kill baddies). But after the first mission, which is also the tutorial, it suddenly takes a more interesting turn.
On the gameplay side, the game is a third person, cover-based, shooter but is more interesting than others cover based titles. A rudimentary command system allows you to give some orders to your AI teammates. The level design is also well done, with more verticality than most shooters. Combining the command system with a clever use of the map allow for nice flanking positions. That feels very satisfying when you can dispatch a wave of ennemies by being actually clever rather than just rushing in. It's also a lot more dynamic and interesting than the extremely static "first guy to raise his head above his barricade is dead" gameplay of Gears of War 2.
On the story side, well...it's hard to talk about it without spoiling, but i will just say that it will soon take an unexpected turn. That story is interesting enough that i enjoyed playing the game twice (something i usually never do, even when i like a game). It allowed me to find some details that i didn't notice on my first playthrough (such as paintings on the walls, or references in the NPC dialogs) as well as better understand the story and its characters.
The game however is not perfect.
On the story side, it's not conveyed perfectly. It tries to be interesting with many stuff happening (again, i'm trying to not spoil), but it's sometimes more confusing than it should be due to some slightly wonky dialogs from time to tim (either too heavy-handed, or on the contrary not explaining enough). The second playthrough will of course help clear out any remaining doubt you may have on the story
On the gameplay side, the controls are clearly made for console, and are therefore annoying to use on PC (many buttons have 2 or 3 roles, which lead to confusion and stupid deaths while in battle). I would have wished to be able to rebind all actions separately. Another annoyance is that there are still some of theses set action pieces (such as defending with an infinite ammo turret) that you get in the bombastic shooters. The kind of stuff that are exhilarating the first time you encounter them in a game, but get annoying when all games have them. Finally, and probably the biggest issue, is that it shares some of the usual problems of cover-based shooters. If you're next to a ledge/barricade, but not actually in cover, you magically can't fire down the ledge and you take more damage even though the barricade should protect you. That's annoying, but well, it's part of the genre that you have to stay in cover every single time.
On the whole, Spec Ops feels like a game that has some slight issues, but is original and interesting enough to have its own charm, and i find it quite endearing. It will remain as an interesting experimentation, and i'm sad it didn't have more commercial success, as I'm sure a spiritual sequel would have fixed the small issues while keeping what makes it good. I still believe this game is the best Star Wars Jedi/Saber Fighting game out there, even 12 years after its release. The single-player story is only so-so, as some of the characters and dialogue are weak at times (much like the movies) and the story-mode itself is not very long or infinitely replayable.  However, this game really shines in the multi-player mode with plenty of active servers, a very helpful community and a large collection of amazing custom content that greatly enhances the game.  You can get custom skins and maps with characters/locations from the Star Wars Universe if you want to play as one of your favorite characters.  Saber-dueling is the primary interest of the online community with some other communities focusing on full-force combat, gun combat and even role-playing.  There are also a collection of mods that help improve the MP experience like JA+, Movie Battles II, Lugormod and more!
Even in 2015, this is still one of the greatest Star Wars games ever made and is truly the closest you will get to fighting like a Jedi in a video game.  If you prefer RPG games you would probably like KOTOR or KOTOR II more and if you enjoy Battlefield, Counter Strike or CoD then Battlefront and Battlefront II might be more your cup of tea.  Still, I highly urge you to check out this title; new players are what keep this game alive despite the good amount of long-time active communities that are still around.
TL;DR Buy this game if you want to be a Jedi!  :D

Max Payne a man that lost everything and has nothing but the truth to find, a truth he wants, but sometimes the truth hurts, this is not the case. Max comes home from his job as a NYPD officer to find his loving wife and his baby daughter Rose dead, the people who killed them still in the house. He kills them and starts on a downward spiral trying to find what happened to his family.
The game starts off straight forward enough, as far as a third person shooter goes it did two things 10 years ago when it came out, it set a standard for third person shooters, and it introduced bullet time. The only thing that sepreates you from the NPC's of Max's universe is the ability to heal and the ability to slow time, past that you are just as human, you will get frustrated. You will hate rounding a corner at full health and dying to a single bullet, but that is made up quickly with the ability to save anywhere, one tap of F5 and you save your state.
The game does a good job of telling Max's story, you play him through his quest to find answers and this leads you to many different places, the levels all vary heavily, they rarely feel samy unless it a particulary long level, and that only happened once to me. The weapons list is short, you could drag it out if you included the dual weild function on some of the guns, but even then it's only the same gun in each hand, so they built the game to be simple but delivery very well.
Most of Max Payne is focused on the narration that Max gives you and the story, it's different, enemies will talk to each other before you enter a room, some insight into thier lives or views, favorite movies and so on. The game is amazingly immersive and gives you alot to keep going, it's not afraid to break the fourth wall a couple of times to sell a few key points in the game, so it often adds to the immersion rather than taking it away.
If i had to say one thing to sell Max Payne to someone is, if you like third person shooters, and want a good story, this is it. If you want a good game to play that passes the time and will give you some awesome noir quotes then this is the game for you.

I'm gonna slap a big ol' nasty asterisk on here real quick:
THIS GAME IS A COLLECT-A-THON.
That means that the entire game is based around exploring levels and collecting stuff. If this does not appeal to you, just walk away.
Now that ninety percent of people who were only vaguely interested are gone, this is a quality spiritual successor to the 90's 3D Platformer Collect-a-thons of years gone by. In terms of quality, I'd say it's better than Banjo-Tooie, but not as good as Banjo-Kazooie. There's a lot to like here: a diverse moveset that the devs kept highly relevant throughout the game, great animations, great environments, and not a lot of hand holding. The controls are tight and on-point, and, despite how it may look on the outset, the game is not nearly as empty feeling as you may think it is. The levels are expertly crafted with a lot to do in every area, and the movement options you have accomadate the size well.
Currently, my biggest gripes with this game are the camera, which is not disimilar to trying to make a toddler stand still. It just wants to keep moving on you, and when you try and take it and put it back, it pulls on your arm and wriggles free to do what it was doing before. It usually isn't an issue, but when it is you will take notice. The other thing I have an issue with is enemy variety. Each world has two to four enemies, each of which are the same across each world. While fighting them feels fine and all, I'd prefer it if there were more types of enemies to deal with other than Grunt, Eyeballs that take over nearby objects, Jerk flies, and the occasional brute that isn't worth dealing with.
Overall, did this game live up to the hype? Hell no, but that was going to be an impossible feat anyway, considering that the hype was likening it to the second coming of Christ. But, did we get a quality game that does exactly what it said it would do? I'd argue, yes. Worth a purchase if you are into collect-a-thons.
