Thus far, this game is exactly what I wanted it to be. I won't say it's a perfect game, but I wanted a fun to explore, spiritual successor to those old N64 games, and that's this, no more, no less. If you loved those games, you'll have fun. If you didn't, you won't. It's a niche genre that fell because it wasn't super popular to begin with, so this is not a game for everyone as Yooka Laylee very faithfully captures that feel.
The first level is fairly easy, it's about getting used to the game flow and mechanics. But after that, there's a fairly significant difficulty spike and more intensive puzzles, some of which I still haven't figured out. The characters have fun to them, the script's good, and the gameplay feels quite quick and fluid. The music feels good on the ears, and even though there's only five worlds they are simply massive, with each having 25 Pagies to collect in the line of DK64 rather than 10 like Banjo. They aren't laying about entirely exposed either, you have to put in some work for each. Worry not if you are concerned that there are too many collectibles, as there are only Pagies and Quills in large numbers in each world. Beyond that, it's just four other items of which there are I believe only one each per world. It's actually lower in amount than even Banjo Kazooie.
Every so often there's some framerate hiccups, but it's not frequent enough to be bothering. Beyond that, I can't think of too many flaws other than that if you don't like collectathons, the game won't sway you. If you've been hungering for a game like this for the last decade, look no further.

Tl;dr - It's worth is not visible yet, and Square Enix has gone temporarily insane. Wait for a Steam sale or the complete game. You'll probably find the full review fairly funny, though.
------------------------------------------------------------------------
Square Enix, lets talk.
Kudos for making another Hitman game. I mean, the franchise is still profitable, so it's a bit of a no brainer to make one, amiright? But thanks for finally ending the wait.
Now, you've done some good work in the past, and some good work here. You've hit your stride making the levels feel "real" with background conversations, and the "immersiveness" factor of letting you interact with bystanders and steal tools for use elsewhere really gives a lot of flexibility. It makes possible the whole "do I shoot them? Poison them? Bomb them? Drown them?" smorgasbord of death thing you've got going on, which is honestly somewhat entertaining. The effect of having many different "right" (not going guns blazing at everyone at sight - you're an assassin, not a terminator) ways of killing your target reduces my frustration at trying to divine the subtlest way of killing the target. It makes it "easier" (less time consuming) to kill my target because if one method fails I can switch to another, keeing me from scum-saving to hit a security hole or get to my target in a 3 second window or the like. You've made the levels themselves things of beauty, and the work you've done in giving targets and bystanders extensive dialogue and real "lives" really pays off here. They're no longer faceless mooks, and because they DO have personalities, I almost feel a little bad about killing them. Congratulations, you've made a game, and a very polished one, too. *golf clap*
That being said, what were you thinking?
Okay, I get the temptation to try new things when making a game, and you've tried several new things here. Let’s take a look at your choice to make things “episodic”. The word means "an event or series of events considered in isolation", so I suppose it’s used appropriately. But in this episode, once you get past the training and “graduation” mission (NOT a mission) you have given me a grand total of… one mission. ONE. Yes, it's a mission with some of replay value as there are a thousand ways to die, but now I know how the level works from the first time, and my gameplay is now reduced to running around to unlock various triggers I know about to find one or two I don’t know about. One real map does not a “world of assassination” make, no matter how many different ways there are to complete it. You've provided "challenges" revolving around your 1000-ways-to-die level design model to unlock things like new guns, and I suppose that gives me an incentive to replay, no matter how contrived it is. You provide “escalation” contracts revolving around ascending difficulty levels to kill the same target again, in a previously played map, but in a harder setting this time, and you provide “featured” contracts which make me....oh. I replay the same level again and kill two different targets instead, sometimes wearing special clothing. I mean, I get some of these ideas – you HAVE to try new things, right? Otherwise how can you justify the $59.99 you ask? New is fun, right?
What were you thinking? Were drugs involved? You can TELL me!
I suppose I can understand why you did this – I mean, it’s pretty clear you’re looking to have me spend more time on fewer levels. By having users pick their own targets and trade “contracts”, it encourages playing with friends, which is the biggest single characteristic of the console crowd. I guess that makes sense, even if it seems kind of lazy, like someone has cut your art budget. But it’s not automatically bad! I mean, if people are happy replaying the same level killing…let’s see. I want….the construction worker on the third floor, and the escort on the patio. If they’re happy killing people like that, more power to them, right?
And I guess I see how it seems like having fewer missions (oh, I hope not) with greater replay value might work - but giving me these “challenges” doesn’t make a lot of sense in the world of Hitman. I mean, I have an agency backing me up, right? Why would killing the target with fireworks while dressed as a fashion model get me a new gun? In “Hitman: Blood Money”, I could buy intelligence on my target and pay to cover evidence. This provided a connection between missions – my success in the first carried through to later levels, and I couldn’t just load up on ammo and go Expendables on everyone in sight. Well, I could, but it would cost me a ton to get new fingerprints afterward.
What were you thinking? Were they blackmailing you? Did they have pictures? Is that why? You were young, and needed the money, right?
I suppose if I were more cynical, I’d say that forcing players to spend more time on fewer levels is supposed to make Square Enix more money by having them spend less money in development in the first place. I mean, players still play the game a lot, but you only have to make one-half to one-third as many levels. The first episode had one training mission, one “graduation” mission, and the first assassination. If every new episode had three maps, we’d be looking at 15 more maps overall, which is a respectable game. But if the first assassination is the first “episode”, then you’re only looking at five new maps and a few cinematics! Cake!  But it’s also a good game for DLC, selling new gear or “micro-missions” with less work on each one. Better yet, having users make their own missions means less need for new official missions, period.
What were you thinking? We can HELP you! They have support groups for what you’re going through!
None of this covers your insane paranoia of the “constant connection” online DRM. I genuinely can’t see the point of it, as I’m not noticing any gameplay benefit I receive from it. However,  I generally don’t play user-generated missions. Given that the game is on Steam, itself a DRM service, it may be that the constant connection requirement is designed to support user-generated missions, itself a bad sign for the length and quality of future episodes. To put it baldly, Square Enix may be hoping the user-generated content, only distributable through the constant connection, will be the game’s selling point, making the “official” levels, playable on pirated versions without an internet connection, an inadequate reason to pirate the game . Or, why pirate the game if you only get six or seven levels, when all the “good” content requires a legit copy? (This theory is supported by the low "intro pack" price)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------Despite a few flaws, the gameplay, ship options and open world win out.  I  give it   --   8.5/10

Starpoint Gemini 2 + Secrets of Aethera DLC:
Excellent sandbox space game, campaign missions are quite easy at first and then they aren't, you need a bigger ship. Which means credits.  Trading, pop-up missions, side missions, capturing ships and mining are your friends now.
Once you get you fingers trained on flying it's a lot more fun...fly in hard and fast and then slow down to stay on the tail pipe of your target, watch out for the explosive radius of your own missiles.
Trading/Mining could use some TLC. The small cargo space and low margins on items makes for a lot of trips for those playstyles to make a lot of credits.
A dedicated mining ship would be a good idea, with maybe a compressor item or mining laser enhancement or something so that you can fit more than 1 ore in 1 cargo slot.
The trading screens in the map could really use a mode to show best to/from, rather than a per-item best buy/sell, also remote buy/sell ala Eve would be great.
But trading and mining isn't what this game is about. The real fun comes with capturing ships and running the various types of missions.
Capturing takes a while to figure out, I suggest youtube and practise.  Basically, grapple, burn the hull down 2/3rds of the way, transport your troops and keep transporting them as long as you have troops. After you get the hang of it, you take every mission around your level just to try and capture another ship.
The pop-up missions are rather generic, about 10 or so different types that I've found and they differ only in the difficulty of the enemies. Some are out-right free credits and XP (science, repair).
The Side Missions are quite variable from the few I've done, more credits and XP and more difficult than the pop-ups.
The Campaign Missions are similar to the Side Missions in reward and difficulty but advance the story-line.
Exploring the map is a lot of fun, it's huge...also more areas to find capturable ships and missions.
One downside, when you play windowed, if you focus off the game, it will pause. This is non-condusive to setting a long waypoint, maxing your engine power and doing something else on the other monitor.
Very fast save/loads.
The fights can be quite intense, the AI seems to be aggressive, but not stupid, it'll gang-tackle you quite happily. The auto-firing works great, but I'm not a fan of the way it keeps shifting targets to closest enemy as opposed to the target you've selected. I guess I have to learn manual firing.
I suggest staying with the Tauris starter boat, pick a weapon type, level that type up  and stay with it for the first 20 levels or so. The gunboat is a paper-tiger, so you learn a lot about dodging, firing, and your equipment needs. Lot's of save and reloads figuring it out. ++Shield Boosters, Repair Nanobots, Hull Plates.
66hrs, 8.5/10 and am still playing. It's not solo-Eve, but darn close.

After playing through the first few missions you'd be forgiven for thinking this was a pre-release indi title, with awful voice acting of poorly written dialogue giving it a horribly unpolished feel, and a tutorial given in the form of a series of short descriptions you need to click through for each UI element but lacking in any practical examples of how they're used leaving you bewildered as to how you're meant to control your ship.
I got my first achievement purely by accident just by following the first waypoint . . . which turned out to be in the core of the planet I was trying to land on rather than, as I'd assumed, at some kind of space elevator docking station.  When I finally figured out how to land, visually it was much the same as crashing into it - I still flew to about the same range but instead of warning me to stop and then exploding, the ship stopped and I got the planet menu.
While the game claims to support joystick control it's very much designed for mouse and keyboard, with the mouse leaving the targeting reticle wherever you last clicked something.  I ended up awkwardly using the joystick in my left hand and trying to target with the mouse before giving up in disgust and returning the controls to their default joystickless configuration.
The starting spaceship flies like it's on rails regardless of the control method you choose and looking through the keybindings gives me no hope of more maneuverable craft later on - you can move forward, turn and roll.  No backward or lateral movement.  Your best bet in a firefight seems to be to leave the turrets on autofire and do your best to fly out of the way of your target's firing lanes.  High speed dodging just doesn't seem to be in the cards, contrary to what was shown in the trailer.

One of the best space simulation games I've seen to date. EVE Online was too complicated, BS Galactica too dated, ect.., but this game struck a special chord. It's devs are very active, taking player considerations seriously. The mods are pretty dang fun, it's cheaper than most other games of its type, you can fill a variety of roles in game, ect.. The only real con I can see with the game so far is it's single player exclusive. If multiplayer's eventually implemented, I can easily see this being the next big thing for online MMORPG space simulators.

Short Version: If you like space tactical combat, exploration, a bit of trading and if you're not just looking for another stupid space dogfighting simulator, this might just be the game for you.
At a decent price and with DLC at a very low price, this game is totally worth a shot.
It's not without it's flaws though.
The devs, apparently, take player input seriously and are constantly looking for ways to further improve the game, which is rare nowadays.
The long version:
The Good:
- You actually feel like you're in command of your ship. You're flying tripulated ships with several guns and missiles to fire on your enemies and sometimes even fighters and bombers to assist you! This is not another stupid "dogfighting style camera view". It's more tactical and I love the devs for making that choice.
- Combat is very interesting and you can decide how you want your engine/shields/weapons focus in the middle of the fight.
- Graphics are very good and the design is "colorful".
- You actually feel like you're evolving as you advance in the game and have access to new ships. There are many options to suit your playstyle.
- You can fly Capital ships (dreadnoughts and carriers) and they're not useless sitting ducks like they're in EVE online. In Starpoint Gemini 2, you can actually destroy smaller ships in the blink of an eye flying one of those, as it's supposed to be when you're flying a freaking Battlestar with fighters and tons of guns at your disposal.
- Devs are constantly looking from feedback from the playerbase and they're very active on forums, taking players advices and questions and participating on the debates in a polite and helpful manner.
- You can send your troops to board enemy ships and try to steal them in a very interesting and original mechanic. Nothing like trying different strategies and escaping with a nick of health from a battle after taking your former enemy's ship with you in tow back to a station.
- Capital ships!
- DLC at a very low price that offered some new content.
- Did I mention Capital ships?!
The Bad:
- Several things are not clear on the tooltips and there are no manuals inside the game. There is no "ship encyclopedia" as you'd expect on a title like this.
- The difference between weapon types, bombers, fighters and interceptors is not clear.
- There are not too many weapon types in the game. It seems like it lacks some variety.
- There is no clear DPS indication. There's an "average" indicator on weapons, but you have to calculate the firing rate manually to figure that out, apparently, so it's hard, at a glance, to know which weapon to use as an upgrade.
- The management of your shields could improve and be something more like Star Trek Online, where you have to define what side gets the bonuses.
- The way "Fire at will" works should be improved on. You could mark targets (as you do with fighters) and your tripulation would shoot them, instead of firing on everything and everyone around randomly as it is right now.
The Ugly:
- A few bugs still annoy me, such as not being able to launch the game if I have Teamviewer service running on the background or not being able to run the game in window mode simulating full screen. If I alt tab while in fullscreen, the game will switch to a window mode, and I have to close and reopen the game to load the fullscreen again. Another bug happens when you take a mission and you're unable to complete that, such as the missions that tell you to patrol and when you get to the place you're supposed to go, nothing happens.
- Voice acting is TERRIBLE.
- Missions get repetitive quickly, so you'll be unwilling to play after the grind for the big ships is over.
- Strongest ship unlocks at level 40, so nothing to look forward to after that level.
- Story is poor.

Thus far, this game is exactly what I wanted it to be. I won't say it's a perfect game, but I wanted a fun to explore, spiritual successor to those old N64 games, and that's this, no more, no less. If you loved those games, you'll have fun. If you didn't, you won't. It's a niche genre that fell because it wasn't super popular to begin with, so this is not a game for everyone as Yooka Laylee very faithfully captures that feel.
The first level is fairly easy, it's about getting used to the game flow and mechanics. But after that, there's a fairly significant difficulty spike and more intensive puzzles, some of which I still haven't figured out. The characters have fun to them, the script's good, and the gameplay feels quite quick and fluid. The music feels good on the ears, and even though there's only five worlds they are simply massive, with each having 25 Pagies to collect in the line of DK64 rather than 10 like Banjo. They aren't laying about entirely exposed either, you have to put in some work for each. Worry not if you are concerned that there are too many collectibles, as there are only Pagies and Quills in large numbers in each world. Beyond that, it's just four other items of which there are I believe only one each per world. It's actually lower in amount than even Banjo Kazooie.
Every so often there's some framerate hiccups, but it's not frequent enough to be bothering. Beyond that, I can't think of too many flaws other than that if you don't like collectathons, the game won't sway you. If you've been hungering for a game like this for the last decade, look no further.

I was born in 1986; Banjo Kazooie just came out as I turned 12 years old, and I instantly fell in love with it.
If you're old enough to have expierenced Banjo Kazooie and the magic that was Rare games back in the mid to late 90s, then this game is a love letter to that time in your life.
Yooka-Laylee doesn't try to be anything other than another Banjo Kazooie game for fans of the original; it has many of the same lead developers as well as the same composer for the soundtrack (Grant Kirkhope). The gameplay mechanics, sounds, shapes, colors, character designs, humor, and even the silly way they make voices are all a tribute to Banjo Kazooie.
If you have a childhood love for Banjo Kazooie and Rare games, don't read reviews; just buy Yooka-Laylee and feel the same happy feelings I've felt ever since I started this game.  The people who are giving Yooka-Laylee low reviews have expectations beyond what this game was trying to acomplish, and are likely too young and/or are taking this game out of context.
Yooka-Laylee gives me a feeling of magic that I haven't felt since I was a kid, and I'm so thankful that Playtonic has acomplished bringing this type of game back into my life all these years later.

This honestly gives more appeal to the adults who grew up playing these games.
It is full of game industry humor such as poking fun at marketing blurbs and tropes in games or specifically troops with the gaming industry such as DLC, cloud-based AI for racing games, and it's full of some pretty crude humor. The humor is like a middle ground between Banjo-Kazooie and Conker's Bad Fur Day. Which I honestly like because Conker's Bad Fur Day seem to be a little bit try hard with its humor. The game's humor is not dry at all, and anything that is slightly dirty or an innuendo I guarantee a child probably wouldn't be able to get it.
The game features some pretty new Innovations such as leaving the level and expanding it so that you get more content such as boss or like areas to walk to get all the Collectibles, this is done with the pages which are pages from the magic book that is lost at the beginning of the game. Beegees are like the Jiggies, quills are like the notes, health is restored by eating butterflies and stamina is restored by walking into them. Stamina is only used for special abilities that allow you to use sonar Rays or to go up the steep ramps. Even when I've expanded the first level once I'm still not able to find all the Collectables, it seems like even though this game only has five levels I might have to return to this level at a later point to expand it once I have a lot more pages to power up the book.
I honestly don't feel like the company was just trying to make a Banjo Kazooie cold, I feel like they were trying to make something new. And because a lot of us were wanting a new Banjo Kazooie game we might be a little bit disappointed. But I feel like there's potential with this new duo.

I wanted to like this game, I really did. But in the end it feels pretty meh overall. It is a fun game no doubt and I do think it is worth it. I'm a fan of 3D platformers, but Yooka-Laylee is lacking something. That lacking something is good level design.
There are a total of 5 worlds as well as the hub area. I have done worlds 1 and 2, and so far they are pretty generic and forgettable. World 1 is a tribal forest location while world 2 is a snowy location. The problem with these worlds so far is they lack the charm. Nothing about these worlds seem particularly unique. While they are certainly bright and colorful with great soundtrack, nothing else stands out about it. It is missing those iconic areas/landmarks to identify each world. In other 3D platformer games, there would usually be a unique mechanic tied to that specific world along with areas that feel like its own little playground. But here, each world doesn't seem to have anything special. It feels like it has a ton of ranodm architecture placed around the world. While it helps the world feel consistent theme-wise, it lacks the iconic locations. I found myself often confused on where I was because nothing stood out to me. The game could use a mini-map at the very least.
Another issue that ties with the level design is finding and collecting things. Yes this is a collect-athon but I feel that some of the NPC placement and other items feel a bit too random at times. They would often be located behind a small corner or in a rather odd space when there shouldn't be a reason to have it there. It feels like they place some things here and there just to fill in the empty space gaps.
The gameplay is fine, but I do find the combat portion a bit boring. There is a lack of enemy variety from what I seen so far and they don't put up much of a interesting challenge at all. They are mostly just in the way and are space too far from eachother. Again, it feels like they are placed just to fill in some empty spaces.
The writing and characters are alright, however I do find myself often annoyed by the constant blbber from characters to finish their sentence. I wish they would just blabber like 3 syllables instead of blabbering until their sentence is over. No reason to have it constantly do that as we get the point that they are talking. As for the writing, I like that it has alot of corny jokes and 4th-wall breaking, but I feel that it does it way too often and it wears itsself out quickly. Usually Laylee is the one cracking jokes, but it feels like every sentence he says have to insert a joke and it gets a little tiresome. Otherwise, the characters/writing is ok for the most part.
Music and soundtrack is great, no complaints there other than the voicework.
Graphically it gets the job done. However I do wish they spent a bit more time on the texture work as some areas look rather blurry and muddy at times. I also don't like the weird depth of field as I feel it ruins the game's atmosphere and there doesn't seem a way to turn it off.
Controls could use a little work. My main problem is the camera can be very janky at times which I'm sure other people have mentioned. The other issue I have is I wish the controls felt a bit tighter as right now they feel a little loose.
Overall the game is fun yes, but I think it could've been much better if it had maybe another year to iron out some issues and improve the level designs. I do think the game is worth buying, but its best to wait for a sale of maybe $25 or less.

Do you remember Rockstar Presents: Table Tennis? Yes, Rockstar, the people that make Grand Theft Auto and Max Payne 3, also made a table tennis (ping-pong to us plebians) game. And it was fantastic. Pool Nation very much riffs off of Rockstar's Table Tennis in the best of ways and presents an amazingly solid product.
The models are sparse, as one might expect in a billiards game, but extremely well presented. Textures are rich, colors are vibrant, and the lounges are all fully decked out. The game really does look beautiful. The soundtrack is fairly pedestrian but enjoyable; soft-beat electronic music with a touch of disco.
There are no models moving about, so the background does seem rather static. There are no human models at all, period. Floating poolsticks is the order. Your shot takes place behind your stick and the view can be easily manipulated by simply moving the mouse. Symbols will show you where your ball will ricochet, up to a distance, and show your line-of-path. (this can be turned off) Shooting is easily done on the mouse or joystick. It all feels very natural, responsive and the game runs very smoothly thanks to its low required specs.
There are unloackbale pool cues, ball sets and decals for the pool tables, but not a lot of visual customization. Workshop integration is in the works which will allow a lot more things to be added to your virtual pool halls.
There is a multiplayer for friends and even a searching feature to play with random players. Unfortunately, you can only do 1v1 pool matches. Multiplayer options let you set up frames, aiming helping ability, game type, etc.
If you like billiards games, you'll probably enjoy Pool Nation. It's a fast, fun, and easy to pick up game that looks great and is easy to run. I've run this on my Surface Pro 2 with a USB joystick and hooked up to a TV with no problem.

Tl;dr - It's worth is not visible yet, and Square Enix has gone temporarily insane. Wait for a Steam sale or the complete game. You'll probably find the full review fairly funny, though.
------------------------------------------------------------------------
Square Enix, lets talk.
Kudos for making another Hitman game. I mean, the franchise is still profitable, so it's a bit of a no brainer to make one, amiright? But thanks for finally ending the wait.
Now, you've done some good work in the past, and some good work here. You've hit your stride making the levels feel "real" with background conversations, and the "immersiveness" factor of letting you interact with bystanders and steal tools for use elsewhere really gives a lot of flexibility. It makes possible the whole "do I shoot them? Poison them? Bomb them? Drown them?" smorgasbord of death thing you've got going on, which is honestly somewhat entertaining. The effect of having many different "right" (not going guns blazing at everyone at sight - you're an assassin, not a terminator) ways of killing your target reduces my frustration at trying to divine the subtlest way of killing the target. It makes it "easier" (less time consuming) to kill my target because if one method fails I can switch to another, keeing me from scum-saving to hit a security hole or get to my target in a 3 second window or the like. You've made the levels themselves things of beauty, and the work you've done in giving targets and bystanders extensive dialogue and real "lives" really pays off here. They're no longer faceless mooks, and because they DO have personalities, I almost feel a little bad about killing them. Congratulations, you've made a game, and a very polished one, too. *golf clap*
That being said, what were you thinking?
Okay, I get the temptation to try new things when making a game, and you've tried several new things here. Let’s take a look at your choice to make things “episodic”. The word means "an event or series of events considered in isolation", so I suppose it’s used appropriately. But in this episode, once you get past the training and “graduation” mission (NOT a mission) you have given me a grand total of… one mission. ONE. Yes, it's a mission with some of replay value as there are a thousand ways to die, but now I know how the level works from the first time, and my gameplay is now reduced to running around to unlock various triggers I know about to find one or two I don’t know about. One real map does not a “world of assassination” make, no matter how many different ways there are to complete it. You've provided "challenges" revolving around your 1000-ways-to-die level design model to unlock things like new guns, and I suppose that gives me an incentive to replay, no matter how contrived it is. You provide “escalation” contracts revolving around ascending difficulty levels to kill the same target again, in a previously played map, but in a harder setting this time, and you provide “featured” contracts which make me....oh. I replay the same level again and kill two different targets instead, sometimes wearing special clothing. I mean, I get some of these ideas – you HAVE to try new things, right? Otherwise how can you justify the $59.99 you ask? New is fun, right?
What were you thinking? Were drugs involved? You can TELL me!
I suppose I can understand why you did this – I mean, it’s pretty clear you’re looking to have me spend more time on fewer levels. By having users pick their own targets and trade “contracts”, it encourages playing with friends, which is the biggest single characteristic of the console crowd. I guess that makes sense, even if it seems kind of lazy, like someone has cut your art budget. But it’s not automatically bad! I mean, if people are happy replaying the same level killing…let’s see. I want….the construction worker on the third floor, and the escort on the patio. If they’re happy killing people like that, more power to them, right?
And I guess I see how it seems like having fewer missions (oh, I hope not) with greater replay value might work - but giving me these “challenges” doesn’t make a lot of sense in the world of Hitman. I mean, I have an agency backing me up, right? Why would killing the target with fireworks while dressed as a fashion model get me a new gun? In “Hitman: Blood Money”, I could buy intelligence on my target and pay to cover evidence. This provided a connection between missions – my success in the first carried through to later levels, and I couldn’t just load up on ammo and go Expendables on everyone in sight. Well, I could, but it would cost me a ton to get new fingerprints afterward.
What were you thinking? Were they blackmailing you? Did they have pictures? Is that why? You were young, and needed the money, right?
I suppose if I were more cynical, I’d say that forcing players to spend more time on fewer levels is supposed to make Square Enix more money by having them spend less money in development in the first place. I mean, players still play the game a lot, but you only have to make one-half to one-third as many levels. The first episode had one training mission, one “graduation” mission, and the first assassination. If every new episode had three maps, we’d be looking at 15 more maps overall, which is a respectable game. But if the first assassination is the first “episode”, then you’re only looking at five new maps and a few cinematics! Cake!  But it’s also a good game for DLC, selling new gear or “micro-missions” with less work on each one. Better yet, having users make their own missions means less need for new official missions, period.
What were you thinking? We can HELP you! They have support groups for what you’re going through!
None of this covers your insane paranoia of the “constant connection” online DRM. I genuinely can’t see the point of it, as I’m not noticing any gameplay benefit I receive from it. However,  I generally don’t play user-generated missions. Given that the game is on Steam, itself a DRM service, it may be that the constant connection requirement is designed to support user-generated missions, itself a bad sign for the length and quality of future episodes. To put it baldly, Square Enix may be hoping the user-generated content, only distributable through the constant connection, will be the game’s selling point, making the “official” levels, playable on pirated versions without an internet connection, an inadequate reason to pirate the game . Or, why pirate the game if you only get six or seven levels, when all the “good” content requires a legit copy? (This theory is supported by the low "intro pack" price)

At a glance Starpoint Gemeni 2 is a sandbox space sim, nothing special and it has been done better before.
I could live with it if the game features an interesting story, which the game does. So the redemption from story doesn't apply. If anything it just makes me more frustrated.
Looking further into the game, you realize it is a single player MMORPG, ship upgrades are gated behind arbitrary level requirements. Ships handle basically the same except for the top speed, so your carrier is just as agile as the starting gunship.
Weapon upgrades follow a similar MMORPG route, some weapons are poor and you go through the game trying to find better weapons. Weapons that are described in awkward and sometimes even incorrect ways, such as "rate of fire" being the delay between each shot. Once you get over the initial hump of how weapons operate you realize you need a calculator to figure out which weapon to use.
Sure I can play this, but all the time doing so there is a thought in my head asking why I am playing this game when I have better games available.

I didn't enjoy the game. I played it till I got the controls down. But between a tutorial that dumps a bunch of dialog boxes on me. To a rather clunky space game control setting, I couldn't get myself enwraptured as much as I wanted to. I wanted something that would send me back to the days of Freelancer.
For those of you who like space games, it has some real meat, but it is a different veriety of meat, much like the difference between Beef and Chicken.
There was a lot of flying around doing nothing, the system travel gates required money and just dropped you into loading screens. And while the scale of the star system is right and the customizability is there. It lacked a certain charm. A polish.
Plus!
-Customizable Ships
-Huge in depth system
-Lots of ways to burn time
Minus!
-Boring Non-Customizable Campaign Protagonist (I wonder why the same guy gets used game to game, is it the same guy?!)
-Clunky combat controls
-Flat uninvolving ports and planets. (At least early game)
-The Tutorial
---
Notes to the Devs.
I honestly respect the work you put on this game, and I can give you a few pointers.
On a thread I read you spoke about how your hands on tutorial didn't please, and how other people complained about this tutorial. There is a middle ground, hear me out.
Rather than dump it all at once in a click through while the game is paused, simply in the opening acts give a small, non intrusive note that tells you how to do something, without pausing, or forcing you to do it.
For example when you start get a quick side note saying how to fly the ship. When you encounter your first enemy get a little side note without pause saying the right mouse button fires.
What you have currently is page after page of tutorial sheets, which, while not as long as EVE is thrown far more upfront. Sure EVE had a lot more tutorial text, but EVE didn't dump it on you the first ten seconds.
Secondly, the Protagonist. For a space RPG many people regard who's in the Cockpit as optional or make a character. In this case we have the typical inexperianced yet cocky caucasian male. But my question is, what if you made the protagonist for the actual game slightly more customizable. Give him titles instead of a direct name. Like his father saying 'son' while others call him by other things. Next, why not increase a few lines of dialog by adding gender options, a female voice actor and the ability to choose as many options as Freeroam? Really honestly give the illusion of choice to the player by letting them make the person they play as. Kind of like Bioware did with Shepard, Hawke or the Inquisitor. Sure you don't have to be that in depth about it with 3d renders. But a few portraits and the options would have been amazing.
On combat, a good thing that most space games do, is have a lead indicator and a smoother method of control. In this case I felt like I was trying to reign in a finicky second hand robot. And the lack of a lead indicator made dogfighting a pain. (Not impossible, but annoying. I still won, but it wasn't as pleasent.)
I think there really isn't much that can be done about the planets, except maybe adding a more visual docking procedure such as an orbital station or docking ring, or some sort of 'Decending/Ascending' animation. Secondly on the Travel Lines, instead of making it a loading screen jump pointer, make it a long thread that you can ride that steadily consumes money as you travel it, and you'll be booted from the stream when you run out or hit abort. Maybe add lane contols and make it work like a highway.
---
All and All I think this game does a lot right and a lot wrong, and I love the passion I see from the developers and can't wait to hear what Starpoint 3 might hold on the someday. If you come into this expecting the next Freelancer, you're probably not going to enjoy it. And the asking price for the features which are missing are pretty major.

One of the most unusual single-player first person shooters that I've played, Spec Ops: The Line takes a page out of Heart of Darkness with a strange and dark descent into THE FEELS. If you like going around slaughtering waves of baddies without remorse  or consequence, this probably isn't the best game for you. Mired in real moral dilemmas where you really don't have any good options; and yet have to live with the consequences, conveys a depth of emotion uncommon for a video game (and First-Person Shooters especially). This game is great at drawing the player in, and showing them the bad side of combat. That having been said... its slightly painful to play. Negative feelings like regret, remorse, fear, helplessness, anger, guilt... are usually the kinds of feelings people try to avoid, or at least take in small doses. This game gets pretty intense and immersive, as the player increasingly feels as the character feels. If I might sum it up in a phrase: Spec Ops: The Line is the best game that I never want to play again. But its definitely worth experiencing once.
Now, a quick breakdown of the game's qualities...
---- THE GOOD ----
* Departure from the standard FPS tropes
* Interesting characters
* Interesting storyline
* Amazing ability to make the player feel unnerved, especially towards the end
* Really great level design
* Great atmosphere
* Love the voice acting
---- THE BAD ----
* Short game. I think I finished it in about 11 hours
* Nothing really innovative with the gameplay. Everything amazing is in the story and setting. Outside of that its mostly a standard FPS
* The Feels can get a bit intense and make the player uncomfortable.
* Graphics seem really dated, even when it first came out. Not quite sure what I dislike about them....
* Controls could be tightened. Tends to feel a bit sluggish in a large firefight, but maybe with a newer PC it would be fine
Thats about it. I give this game a 7.5/10 . That might be lower than it deserves. I did enjoy it, but I wish it were longer and more gradual. I also kinda wanted it to end towards the end 'cuz it was getting very dark and very negative. Then there's the sub-par graphics and sluggishness, and that's what I felt 7.5 was a bit more appropriate.
Hope this review helped, thanks!

While Yooka-Laylee is bogged down by camera issues and some pretty annoying chunks of "Tell, don't show", it's ultimately a really addicting exploration platformer. Even background terrain has full collision checking and you have quite a bit more mobility than you need, so you can circumvent some obstacles completely and get collectibles in unintended ways if you master the mechanics. Apart from the obvious Banjo-Kazooie references, you'll see stuff based on other Rare classics like Goldeneye, RC Pro-Am, Cabal and Snake Rattle n' Roll. (Yeah, seriously.)
No matter whether you're looking for a cute high-quality game to keep your kids busy or some fanservice to relieve your childhood memories, you'll find them... but if you're looking for anything else, you won't find it.

First off, y'all are a bunch of hypocrites. Apparently, all the negative reviews that do nothing but go over the minor nitpicks about why they basically don't like this type of game anymore are "helpful", and all the positive reviews aren't. Honestly, I feel like all the people who bought this game either
A: expected banjo-kazooie that isn't banjo-kazooie but is banjo-kazooie without being banjo-kaooie (negative reviews)
B: Expected a 90's platformer made by an indie developer making a large 3D game with a rather small staff, a LOT of platforms to worry about and a slightly decent budget
Anyway, enough ranting. Here's my actual honest (biased)  review .
Con's (I'm sure many of you here are going to read this section to justify your own bias)
-The camera can be a TINY bit janky (im using keyboard and mouse, so if I find it only a TINY bit janky then I don't know what these controller people are complaining about)
-One or two of the voices are annoying. If you dislike this type of voicing, you won't like it. If you aren't bothered, it won't affect you
-The music has cut out on me for a second or two in some very specific places.
-The first transformation you have access to is a little off-putting, because its so slow and so annoyingly loud.
-The controls are a little floaty. It takes a good half of a second to stop moving sometimes
Neutral (These are things I don't find to be con's, but can be taken either way)
=You have a power bar for moves. Now, there are 'tonics', or unlockables, that make this bar less noticeable and honestly, its certainly less annoying than collecting eggs, feathers and golden feathers in banjo-kazooie.
This bar does automatically refill, and you can speed up the process by collecting butterflies, which are literally everwhere.
=There's backtracking. Some people love it, some people hate it.
Personally, it doesn't bother me. I LOVE seeing something, going "how the heck do I get there!!", then realising it 10 minutes later after getting a new move that unlocks a whole new portion of the game.
I guess if you are too used to "Quick travel", you won't like it. Otherwise, its not a bother and actually adds to the game.
=The worlds are large and sprawling. Sometimes large worlds can be overwhelming, and maybe a little empty, but I'm not gonna lie, many of the last centuries best praised games have been emptier than the fridges in Chernobyl.
Pro's (now we get into the REAL bias)
+The game constantly has something to offer.
This is the one complaint I had about Banjo-Kazooie and (off track but whatever) breath of the wild. In Banjo-Kazooie, you complete the first two worlds and BLAMO, you have all the abilities.
From that point on, everything is basically the same thing, but In a different format. In yooka-laylee, on the other hand, each world has something new to give you (at least 2 new abilities), so each world is quite different from the last.
+The camera is janky and gets stuck on walls, but the worlds are incredibly large and empty with few walls to actually get stuck on.
Now, this isn't ACTUALLY a pro. Its just a contradiction I've noticed in other reviews. The BIGGEST cons are the "empty worlds" and "janky camera", yet if the worlds are empty...shouldn't the camera have very little to be janky with? I feel like these people are just picking at straws, here.
+The music. Man oh MAN the music is good. Every world has some new, exciting music. From the quiet and serene to the booming and overpowering. Oh, and its catchy. Unless you are too used to the current day's format of either
A: No music except in specific areas
B: Background music, like the few notes played in BoTW when you walk around.
+The game is fun. I mean...Yeah. That's certainly a pro.
+The graphics, although not without its issues, are actually pretty damn good for a small indie team.
Maybe one or two parts of the game might seem "last gen", but people seem to forget that such well-praised games like shovel knight and terraria's graphics are...well...last 5 gens.
+There is so much to collect. This is what I expect in a COLLECT-a-thon.
You don't NEED to collect everything to finish the game. You don't NEED to do every puzzle to finish the game. And that's great. Anything extra you choose to do is for your own personal enjoyment. The game doesn't force you to go that extra mile.
+The swimming feels fantastic. Remember the days when to swim, you had to awkwardly hold down a button while holding the direction you want to go?
Nope. Now up, down, left ,right, forward and back all have their own controls. Some might love this, some might hate it.
I've just spent the past 40 hours dealing with Monster Hunter 3U's swimming, so this games swimming feels like bliss to me.
+The tutorial is just kind of...there. You get to it, you are given a few lines of text, you press a few buttons then boom, you are in the game.
+Each world has its own unique charm. Sure, one of them may not be your cup of tea (varying from person to person), but come on. Who REALLY liked Klankers Cavern in BK? That world was the opposite of what people are complaining about in yooka-laylee's world(s).
+The characters are memorable. A talking refrigerator? A high-class gremlin? An octopus lady wearing a fishbowl? A duck in a robot? A giant, talking, tycoon bee called Capital B? A pig knight?
+The game is fun.
+The ability to expand worlds is so unique and really adds to the game. It makes going back to worlds you've "finished" meaningful. Who ever really went back to the first 3 worlds in BK unless you missed a single jiggy or (♥♥♥♥ this mechanic) note?
Anyway, I could go on but then I would be a hypocrite, because I would just be nitpicking all the things I like about the game aka the opposite of most of the negative reviews.

Max Payne is GREAT, It has badass style, music and that overall gritty and cool feeling

There's few sections which involve some heavy 3D platforming, which play really bad, the floaty jumping and the TPS camera don't help at all, luckily there's just few of them in the game and they don't really break the flow of the game.
For the most part the game has great shooting and really good level design but there's one big flaw on the game, It forces you to quick save before and after every encounter because the enemy placement is something you just can't see coming.
There's many parts in the game where you will die cheaply if you haven't played the game before because there's simply no audio or visual cue to know something is coming, Be advised, if you want to play this get ready for many cheap deaths that you wont be able to avoid even with bullet time activated.

I finally played through this game. I remember playing the demo years ago when it was new, but I thought the theme was too dark and didn't play it.  I figured it would be easier to play now, but the beginning of the game is as dark and creepy as ever, although it does provide you with strong motivation.
The game makes liberal use of bullet-time from The Matrix.  Heck, it even steals the hotel lobby scene right out of the movie, which is a blast to play.  The effect is done masterfully.  At first, it seems like this may make the game too easy, but before long,  you realize you'll need it to survive.  There is no health regen, only a limited supply of pain pills you have to hunt for.
The game was released in 2001, so the graphics look dated now, but you can tell they were very good for the time.  The game supports widescreen resolutions, but it stretches out the picture.  You'll be better off picking a 4:3 resolution with the same height as your monitor.  If you have sound problems, setup the game with Alchemy (SoundBlaster only) or look for a user patch.  The game clocks in at "only 10 hours", which was short for back then. It makes you wonder if this started the trend towards shorter, but more action packed games.
All-in-all, a great game.  Better games may have been made since, but Max Payne raised the bar and left its mark.

Even at 2013's standards, Max Payne is an enjoyable romp. With a great story, fun gunplay accompanied with the awesome revolutionary matrix-esque gameplay mechanics, it's 10 hours game time is a joy to blast through.

MP has its flaws however. The frequent interactions of objects that initates a cut-scene can annoyingly break the adrenaline flow, and the saving system can be quite infurating, if you've forgotten to manually save the game by pressing a specific key.
Small flaws aside, Max Payne is still a great, fun game.
Recommended for newcomers to the series indeed. You may have sound issues during gameplay using current Windows operating systems, but thankfully there is a great fan patch that fixes the issue perfectly, so definitely grab that.

A classic., a big brother to the genre. And FRUSTRANTINGLY difficult towards the end, frankly. My reactions were usually "I STUCK A SHOTGUN IN HIS MOUTH AND PULLED THE TRIGGER, HE SHOULDN'T HAVE A HEAD ANYMORE" kind of thing. The mechanics are solid enough, but the game can be so unfair. The damage is realistic and a example of good difficult: a good headshot and you're down. But when the game has enemies that just.won't.die. Plus enemies that spawn out of thin air(and yes, I've seen it). A lot of situations in this game are hair-tearing. Think press-a-button-spawn-three-enemies-next-door kinda of thing. And then the walls disappear. Towards the end, most weapons you'll be using are the AR, the semi auto shotgun and the dual wielded SMGs... which I personally found a shame. Not that the weapons weren't good, but I just loved using Max's trademark dual Berettas. Neverthless, a great game, marked by some traits of its era. Some are flaws, like that half step lag before Max switches running directions which got me killed countless times, some are design decisions, like the punishing difficult, the unclear directions and the bland visuals(its 2001, to be fair). All part of its charm. Yes, even the unfairness. And while the Bullet time got refined in the next games(it just depletes way too fast for me to have any fun), this is where it started. And the story is...well, it's been copied numerous times by today's standards, but its superb. Max may overblow the drama, but the twists and turns are unexpected, always bringing something new into the table.
So, yes, I was frustrated. Yes, many times I wanted to say "♥♥♥♥ THIS". But I kept coming. Because I was being stingy with my items,playing at the edge of my life, and I knew I could get over it. I knew I could aim that next shotgun blast a little bit better and kill that guy faster, giving me time to pump lead on the guy who would walk through that door. Give it all or go home.

*UPDATE* Latest patch seemed to double my fps and I just found the escalation modes which are are more challenging experiance after just finishing the level which doesn't allow saves. So Aside from always online this Hitman is a fantastic game.
I see a lot of negative reviews that pertain to the issues of always online drm and poor performance.
While those issues are really unacceptable for a triple A game in this current age, the game itself is really great.
It’s clear that work went into this title and the asking price is well worth it if you understand what a hitman game is supposed to be like. If you enjoy an assassination sandbox then you will get a lot out of what’s here currently.
The intro pack comes with 3 levels, 2 of which are tutorial levels that are about the size of an absolution level, and the Paris level which is like the size of 5 absolution levels. It has like 72 unlockables alone. If you’re just planning on running through a level one or two times then maybe this game isn’t for you.
I have also seen negative reviews about the graphics being bad or ugly, which I would say is a ridiculous commit to make and I feel people are only saying that to try and add onto their frustrations with the issues they’re having.
I do though have a pretty powerful gaming pc and I had to set all my settings to the lowest settings to get a smooth 60+ fps at 1200 res. Not sure what the issues is, but I think it has something to do with the lighting tech, but even at the lowest the game looks great. I can understand though why people would be upset if the game doesn’t run well on their pc, but if lowering your settings work then just do that for now and hope a patch will let you increase your settings.
For what really matters though the only issues I have in the gameplay is the removal of difficulty levels and the ability to manually save. I can of course make it harder in the settings by turning off some help, but if the game gives me the help I’m going to use it. It’s actually hard to complain about the manual saves because of how large the levels are, but at the same time there are unlockable starting locations that let you skip some stuff when you unlock them so I really don’t see why saves are necessary.  It also makes challenges feel a bit too easy.
I like the changes and dislike others, but at the end of the day it’s Hitman.

If you lack strategical thinking, there are things called "Opportunites" to help you throughout the mission which explains the many different ways you can kill the targets (you can turn this off of course). My biggest complaint about this game though would probably be the story, for me it's extremely hard to follow. So I don't recommend picking this up if you're looking for a good story to delve into, it doesn't really offer much in that category. However if you're looking for a great stealth game with amazing gameplay and freedom to assassinate various targets I highly recommend picking this game up.

When I was a young adult (28) I bought an Amstrad CPC 8-bit computer and a cassette with the game "Elite" on it. I played that religiously at least a year and after that again every now and then. The graphics were underwhelming (green wire graphic), the plot practically non-existent. There were only 8 "missions" I knew of and the grind to get to Elite level was enormous.
I looked for such a game a long time after that. Freelancer was a good try. The direct Elite successors were overdone and technically underwhelming. After a while I gave up.
Then I stumbled over SPG2. And here it is again. Nearly. The freedom to do what I want, the grind to get to the top and a vast universe. For such a game it is important that the combat is interesting, and it is. If you are level 20+ you will encounter more than one enemy at a time, and then you will have your hands full.
Here a pro and con list:
+ Graphics are good. Not brillant, but good.
+ You are free! You may do what you want. You can safely ignore the main quest if you want.
+ You can capture ships. That is not only very profitable but also fun and later on you have to be quite skillful to pull that off (with battleships and the like).
+ The map is huge.
+ Fighting feels great.
+ Your character has levels, perks and skills. And they are surprisingly useful (I play an engineer). And fun.
+ You have to learn the UI but after the initial learning process it is very functional.
+ You can change all keys. And you should change at least some.
+ There is a nice levelling curve. It could be even slower, to be honest...
+ There are secrets in the game. A secret station I just discovered (named after an astronomer, won't spoil it too much), sectors with radioactivity, anomalies and so on.
+ If you don't know what to do you can do an automatically generated mission. They are endless.
+ You can save only on a station. I like that because it means you risk a bit if you venture outside. But only a bit. Just the right amount :)
+ The developers are very active and really trying to please their customers.
- Trading is not risk free (there are enemies out there) and not profitable. That is not well designed because either you avoid risk and gain or take risks and get profit, but the trading option means that you take the worst from both worlds.
- While there is a reputation system it is not individual to each of the factions. You are evil or good (or something in between). If you are "good" you are liked by all lawful factions. If you are evil you are liked by all evil factions. That could be more individualized.
- The main quest has quite a boring plot and is not written very well. The voiceovers are horrible. These accents!
- The map is not endless. That is not a big disadvantage because it is huge as it is. But it would be nice to have an option to generate a new "universe" procedurally.
- If you land at a station the graphics are disappointing. It is nothing more than a greyed-out picture of you in front of the station. You don't feel you are on the station, you feel you are in a system menu.
- The full screen mode does not work every time. On Windows 8.1, NVidia 760, full screen mode is only achieved after I start the game the second time. That is a bit unprofessional...
Graphics: 8/10
Gameplay: 9/10
Developers: 10/10
Main Quest: 3/10
Combat: 9/10
Feeling of Progress: 9/10
Overall: 9/10

Spec ops :The line is a massively underrated game in my opinion, brilliant graphics and great frame rates, no lag or stutter during even the heaviest firefights, the gameplay mechanics are solid, great 'gears of war' style cover shooter with a story thats absolutely fantastic- if you blast through the game without reading/listening to all the intel you find then you are missing out on a much darker experience, which is good as you actually look forward to finding intel and progressing the story how its supposed to be portrayed. Of course theres some instances of dumb AI and you can feel limited as to how youre squad can perform (simple stun/attack commands only, theres no movement issuing orders) but it doesnt retract from the gameplay at all as it helps youre character feel more human as opposed to an all seeing all powerful supersoldier. The way the game progresses and how you feel as you get further into the horrors start to genuinely make you think about the morality of your actions and any game that can make you seriously think about what you are doing is an achievement in my book. Worth buying and highly recommended.

Review is strictly just for the single-player campaign. I picked this up during a Steam sale for like $5 and boy, it's really worth it. It's highly engaging, exploring the true depths of the horrors and triumphs of war and all that it does to the people involved, and to the people not involved. The character progression is extremely well-done, and all the choices you'll have to make throughout the game blur what's right and what's wrong in a challenge to stay sane.
The gamrplay is pretty strong, although not too much different from other modern-day military games. You start with a group of three and you can command the other two guys to do stuff such as snipe long-distance targets, full-out attack a target, or throw a flashbang to stun the enemies. I rarely used this though as I was too busy just shooting the targets, but all-in-all, the AI is at least helpful in the battle and they don't get themselves killed too often. One thing I really liked was that they made ammo pretty scarce throughout the game, which I found to be realistic when engaged in a long-lasting firefight. I was constantly changing weapons just to have some extra bullets, and it added to the difficulty of the campaign.
Overall, if you enjoy military shooters and want to try a game that isn't just "GO AMERICA, WE RULE!" then you definitely want to give this a try.

This series, as most, if not everyone knows is based off of the Banjo-Kazooie series. While you might remember Mumbo's Mountain from the first game, this tends to get a lot of its tendancies from its sequel, Banjo Tooie.
Story: 8/10
Going into this story, I saw Yooka, a lizard whom was never clarified to be a chameleon until I felt stupid for looking it up on the wiki, and Laylee, the bat. Laylee really reminded me of Kazooie, and Yooka of Banjo, but their desires for adventure seemed to be reversed. Yooka seemed to be the energetic Kazooie, while Laylee seemed to be the type that would sleep through their sister's kidnapping. After progressing through the levels, I could see kind of a trend arising with how the characters acted. But more on that later. I felt for sure that Trowzers was going to be this uber-villain so I just couldn't help but doubt him. Hearing him talk about faulty washers and TVs really made me doubt the guy. And perhaps I should've. Going level to level and seeing all these characters really made me smile. However, the main problem this suffers is that none of the unique characters to the level are particularly memorable. There's Nimbo that I remember from the first level, and he's basically the main one because he controlled the weather. The snowmen from the second level kind of lacked that existence. The expansion of worlds was a really cool idea that I didn't figure out that I'd have to leave to do for a while. I was searching for buttons expecting for some sort of switch to trigger it. I found it best to expand the worlds before I even entered them as to avoid confusion later. The fact that I can't really remember what the names of the levels are doesn't exactly help, though. I would've liked an explanation as to what the beehives did when I used my tongue on them rather than having to figure it out myself, but I suppose figuring it out eventually was okay.
Art: 9/10.
This isn't even up for debate in my mind. This game has beautiful visuals, and just going into it made me feel in awe. Having to expand the first level after I entered it made me realize how much expanding the world actually does, which incredibly impressed me. The characters that actually mattered in this game were really cool, and the statue of Dr. Quack that remained behind was a nice touch. The library was pretty cool as well. I loved how each book had its own presence and the fact that you could climb every book reminded me mildly of The Legend of Zelda: The Minish Cap. Totally fun and definitely good to look at.
Sound: 10/10
Music is gorgeous, I haven't found a single track I don't like. The last time I was able to say this was about Nier: Automata's music, and both are amazing. I especially liked the music from the ice world, as such was really nice. The overworld map's music was nice, but probably the least memorable out of all of them.
Characters: 7/10
This is kind of where I felt the game started falling a little flat. Besides the main characters, there wasn't really any characters I really felt particularly interested in. Banjo Kazooie and Banjo Tooie had Clanker, Old King Coal, Boggy, Humba Wumba, and Mumbo, but I didn't really feel like I cared about Kartos (Who I couldn't stop thinking of as Kratos from Tales of Symphonia) or Nimbo from the first level. I can't even really remember the character's names. They just don't stick with me, and I really wish they could. Same goes for the bosses of the levels. They were annoyances to progression, not bosses I wanted to fight that were out of the way.
Controls: 7/10
The camera seemed to be a little wonky, but I feel like that's a recurring thing with games nowadays. The vehicle in the second level I couldn't control for my life, but I don't know if that's me or the game itself. Maybe a little bit of both, particularly leaning in the former's territory? Not quite sure. I sucked at Nuts and Bolts because of this exact reason, so there's that. I didn't really like how the butterflies were both for your power bar and your health. I can't count how many times I jumped into the butterflies expecting them to restore my health only for the controls to remind me AFTER I collected them that I needed to press a button to restore my health. Gosh!
Menu Design: 6/10
What keeps on confusing me is why my health bar isn't consistently displayed - as well as the bosses displayed at all while I'm fighting them - and why it gives you a total of the quills and pagies you have, rather than toward the world amount. Having to check the totals menu every time I was wondering that was REALLY annoying.
Level Design: 8/10
While everything is incredibly beautiful, I couldn't help but feel overwhelmed by how massive the levels were. In Banjo Kazooie and Tooie, every level had its particular landmark. The tent in Witchyworld, the house in Mad Monster Mansion, Clanker in Clanker's cavern, and so on. Needing to collect all the collectibles but not knowing where I've been before really kind of overwhelmed me. I didn't really like how there were so many "pits." I really got frustrated when I spent a decent amount of time progressing through a cave only to slip and fall into a pit and have to start from where I was at the entrance five minutes ago with the enemies respawned.
Enjoyment: 8/10
I enjoyed/am enjoying the game a fair bit, and I can't really say more than that. I've played the game and not even pondered the thought of requesting a refund. I really like the game, I've created the badge already (don't know if I'm going to do the level 5 badge, though.) I'm still playing it trying to go for the entire 100% toward the game, though I don't know how soon it will be until I get that done. I really liked the retro arcade games, for sure.
Overall: 8/10
The game is definitely worth playing in my opinion, especially if you've played the Banjo Kazooie and Banjo Tooie games. Don't worry if you haven't played Nuts 'n Bolts, because I don't think that really matters. In fact, I tend to pretend that game never existed even though it's still sitting on my shelf with a completion rate of "not even beat the second boss yet." I intend on getting the full 100% of the game, but don't really know exactly when that will be. It is a game I don't regret buying, and I definitely disagree with reviews in the past.
Would I recommend this game to you? Most definitely, unless you're a person who doesn't like platformers and never really liked Banjo Kazooie and Tooie. The main characters are fun, and who knows. Maybe you'll have more luck with the controls of vehicles than I do.
Final notes:
+ Beautiful level design
+ Fun characterization
+ Great music
+ The sequel I've been waiting for to Tooie so I can pretend Nuts 'n Bolts never existed.
+ Primary villains you can't help but hate
- Why were butterflies used for both power bar and health?
- Why does power bar exist, for that matter?
- Levels are too large.
- How do I kill those bee enemies?
- Please make the health bar visible at all times, and the quill/pagie count the amount of the world that I'm in, not the overall amount.
- Side characters are bland at best.

Don't be fooled: There's quite a few people out there who give this game a bad review due to the JonTron controversy. Those are usually the ones with playtime below 1h.
What to expect: This is an indie 3D platformer, and in my opinion it's worth every penny, even if 29.99 would have been a better price if you ask me, but just wait, it'll get there.
It's a slightly modernized callback to the late 1990ies platformers on consoles, primarily Nintendo. The camera has been fixed since pre-release and works loads better now. It relies heavily on collecting a cavalcade of categorized objects, so if you're not into "collectathons", then this game is really not for you - puzzles and collecting is basically all that you do. I personally like it and have been looking forward to it.
What to consider: I've put 4h into this game and I'm about in the middle, and so far, I couldn't find much to criticize. Controls are sharp, but I cannot emphasize enough that you'll need a controller to play this. Even the developer says so nearly everywhere, including the Steam store page. The biggest flaw with this game is that it lacks polish here or there, miniscule things like the lack of customized animations on the minions in the second world. You might notice it, but it doesn't really impact the experience.
Score: 8/10 - it's not the be-all-end-all of platformers, but it's good in what it does, and it gives you the platformer fix you've maybe been waiting for. There is definitely room for improvement for a second installment, and if there really will be a yooka-laylee 2, I personally hope it won't be on the Unity Engine.
If you're boycotting this game because of the Jontron thing then you're a fool. Great game.

The Game is great fun but I think people have jumped the gun with their expectations.
So these are something you should consider before purchasing.
*If you try and rush through the game your just going to get frustrated and give up
Your going to need to take your time to pass some challenges and getting frustrated after the first attempt will surely ruin it.
*There are some wonky camera changes so be careful.
Yes every review so far has mentioned the camera issues, but so far it's not as heinous of an offence that others make it seem. If the camera changes sudden you should slow down and try to get your bearings before proceeding.
* Your not going to 100% a world first try (and it's not expected of you)
Yes it is a collect-them-all game, so you should try to collect all you can get, but don't tunnel vision into not being able to get the last pagie or where the final 10 quills are. Your able to go on without them and maybe after working on a new level you'll be able to return and collect what was missing.
Additional minor issues:

*Some dialog is unskipable, however it is fairly predictable which ones you can skip and which ones you can't.
In conclusion: If your willing to take your time , explore, and take things in stride you will find a very satisfying and enjoyable experience. However if your going to approach the game with a very objective mindset and expecting everything to be over in a few hours you won't enjoy this game

I believe Yooka-Laylee has the potential to be a great game, but from what i have played so far, the controls and physics of the overall game have let me down and have kept Yooka-Laylee from its full potential. Now i dont want to rant or go too far into scrutiny as i have yet to complete the game, so i will simply list a selection of pros and cons for what i have seen of the game so far .
Pros:
- The game for the most part looks beautiful apart from some odd low quality textures in some areas.
-Yooka and Laylee look great and have fantastic animations for their abilities
- The game runs great, i have yet to come across the fps problems alot of other players have complained about
- Contains the wit and charm of previous Rare alumni games, such as Banjo Kazooie and Tooie
- Fantastic music as always from Grant Kirkhope, David Wise and Steve Burke
- Alot of the challenges and collectible trails kept me entertained
- This last point i am very hesitant to put on the list, which is based on nostalgia. If you played the Banjo kazooie games (or other N64 collectathon games) growing up i firmly believe you will enjoy this game more than those who have not, but a game should not be measured through its nostalgia factor and have its faults overlooked as a result.
Cons:
- The controls are complete garbage at times, leading to pure frustration, aiming when shooting projectiles without zooming in is just borderline impossible without spamming the shoot button. fluent controls are key to 3D Platforming. (I played with an Xbox controller)
- Alot of the sections of the game are very tedious to the point of it being straight up not fun, such as any section of the game which includes ramps (The very thought of Rampo from world 1 makes me want to curl up into a ball and cry)
-The hitboxes in the game can seem too close, there were many times when i was hit by an enemy or burnt by fire when i wasnt even close to the threat.
- It relies too much on certain aspects from Banjo which havent aged well, for example slow transitions between sections of the game, or the inability to skip certain parts of slow moving text or animations. All parts if in which were "Modernized" would allow to game to be much more enjoyable for the player.
- Some of the supporting characters (A handful of which are poorly designed) are reused for other sections, which could come off as lazy.
- The Rextro arcade games arent as good as they could be (Although the multiplayer segments do look like a laugh)
So all in all i do believe there is some good to Yooka-Laylee and that it is not the coming of the Anti christ like some have suggested and yes, i know, alot of the problems could be adressed in future patches (At least i hope they will be). So, should you buy it? i guess, if you want. Your money do what you please, just keep in mind the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ controls.

Excellent third person shooter. One of the best stories ever told in a game. Very dark and melancholy.  The same can be said for the game's atmosphere, although there isnt much detail and a lot of areas look alike. The voice acting and the well written dialogue brings max payne to life. This is a game where you don't want to skip the cutscenes because you'll miss one of things that truly shine. Combat is fast and frantic, making the slow motion ability not only nice looking but useful. Guns vary and each one excels in different situations. Enemies dont vary much but they always provide a challenge. Max Payne's health can deplete very quickly, so make sure you use pain killers wisely. Fun gunplay and an excellent story with plenty of depth for the main character makes this a favorite of mine. 8.0/10

Another child died today Garfield. He was terrified. In that moment I wished I could merge with his fear and slip into a saccharine foreverscream. But this is my duty Garfield, have you stopped eating my lasagna? Have you ever looked in that pan? When was the last time you tasted what you were chewing? You shuffling, bumbling, crusty, dumb ♥♥♥♥ cat Garfield. If I pelted you with rocks who would hear the dumb screams? If I set myself on fire and smothered you who would die first? You're a tumor Garfield, but God made cancer, just like he made lasagna, except I made the lasagna. Does that make me more than a man?
They call you a "bad cat" but they will never drink from the fat and rotten juices, they are unfit to be in the kingdom of Heaven and Hell Garfield. You are cut from the nape of the Earth, you little bitty cat. Don't kick Odie off the table!! Gaaarfiiieeeeld!!!!
You stumble home drunk and your bits are all cut away. Did you let someone get to them? Did you snip them off yourself? You won't tell me. Instead you sit in front of the telly, sagging and staring at a sitcom. Your bits are still bleeding. Chunks soak into the upholstery. You'll be fine tomorrow Garfield
You live here, Garfield. You are in between the walls and the beams but you live here. I breathe you in sometimes. It makes me remember innocence. I scream and shake outside of the shower. I try to step in but I slip on a wacky tie. I catch a glimpse of you on the way down just outside of the door frame. Your smile all pus and burn scars. Whose face will it be tomorrow? Garfield, I am your keeper. I just can't seem to get a date!
A thousand shifting fever dreams couldn't molest my love for you, Garfield. It runs through the wires and the cogs and the paper cuts and the plushies. It died twenty years ago. It's pumped up again from a black river bottom and vomited onto naked little bodies. Can I remove myself from its fate?
They pick at you like a great big feast. Garfield, your bulbous thoughts were always clear. I just didn't want to hear. But now it doesn't matter. Now you will see tomorrow. A thousand million living things melted for you. A hundred thousand writhing tongues coming from you. It's a wonderful world and this is all that there is. Tell me you're happy, you fatty cat. Tell me to sleep. Nermal comes to visit.
