I remember getting this game when it was still in its alpha/beta form with only a few things to do besides blowing up ships, blowing up asteroids, taking their goods, and then selling them at a market for a few dollars (which seemed weird back then because ships cost a ♥♥♥♥ TON and still do, but there are ways to get more money now.) So playing now, seeing that it is full release form, welllllll....it's still empty. I mean, there is absolutely almost nothing going on except for an occasional enemy ship flying in to a friendly territory that gets obliterated in a second. Other than that, nope, nothing. People that hate you, hate you and people that like you, like you, not much else. I thought it'd be awesome to be the revered space pirate captain who steals from all and gets in the way of people to scavenge as much money as possible, even between factions. Which is another huge problem, factions do not feel like they have bad ties between each other, it's as if they are both completely isolated with their borders set in place without anything in between. And there aren't even any huge battles as well, the closest one I got was between myself and 30 other enemy ships. So you might ask, "What is there to do?" Well, exactly what I explained at the beginning, you do missions, kill enemies, blow up debris and turn it into a station for some money, like, a little amount of money. And the most money you get is from ship debris -floating ship debris and destroyed ships- which on maximum with the stock ship which can only hold 45 units is about $30,000 maximum give or take. So how much does an upgraded ship minus weapons cost? Depending on your preference from the different types, a direct upgrade would be from 2-5 mil even though it can go higher to prices of 30 million. So with mining and missions ranging in price from 10-20 thousand, you're looking at doing this 66 times to afford a new ship and that's at the maximum you'll get from mining and missions just for a 2 mil ship. Yes, there are hero ships that give you about 5 mil if you destroy them, but so far I've found no real way to track them other than hearing the news saying they are in so-and-so region, and even if you do find them, they are at impossible difficulty and usually have other ships around them so good luck. Did I have fun though? Yes, I had fun in some parts when I tried to dodge enemy ships while firing, but after your first few things to do it gets incredibly boring.

This is a really good space game.
The game offers various control methods to let you fly your ship like a pilot/dogfighter or play more of a commander role using turret view. At first it takes a while to get used to the controls and fight effectively with a style you like but once you play out a few battles out you will find a control style that suits you and probably end up switching between them depending on the situation and the ship you are using.
The graphics and interface are really nice and the game runs very well on my medium system which is an AMD APU with integrated graphics.
The sound effects are good but some cool warp like sound effect for the t-drive would be nice. The music is very good although perhaps some more variety would be nice especially for the battle music.
The story and voice acting is probably the weakest part of the game but the game offers plenty of freedom to explore space and play how you want to. So you can play like a pirate or a trader, mine or do missions etc. There's plenty to do and it's all fun.
The game has a nice rpg element which means you can upgrade your skills for when you are in battle and upgrade perks for various different effects like trading bonuses or ship capture bonuses etc. You can customise your ships weapons and buy bigger and better guns and ships as you progress through the ranks and acquire more credits.
Overall I would recommend getting this game, especially if you are into space games.

(TLDR Below)
I got this game after being a long time RimWorld player with a few hundred hours of playtime. It is definitely appreciably different. As opposed to RimWorld where raids and random events are what ails you, the environment in Oxygen Not Included is your greatest threat. While the two games have a similar core aspect to them, colony building and management, they go about it in entirely different ways. The reason I bring up its core similarity to RimWorld first and foremost is that it's my humble opinion that if you like or love RimWorld you will probably enjoy Oxygen Not Included.
In Oxygen Not Included your colonists are basically stranded inside of an asteroid/planetoid or what have you. They are completely underground, in a totally closed loop system. This game is all about toeing the line and balancing a few core aspects: having food for your colonists, oxygen for them to breathe, eliminating waste products (think latrines and carbon dioxide), and producing the energy to facilitate the previous. Careful resource management is the name of the game here.
If you let any of the previous aspects get way too far out of balance, your colony is likely to start losing members and/or the colony will break down into a death spiral. Don't produce enough oxygen, and people start suffocating and become unable to reach far out sections of the base. Don't produce enough food and colonists will pretty quickly break down into high stress states, and eventually starve. Manage the colony's waste products poorly and before you know it you're unable to produce more oxygen, running out of water to use for other processes, and having stress breakdowns. Don't produce enough energy and food, oxygen and waste management aren't happening at all.
One of the game's biggest challenges, and likely one of its greatest selling points, is in the way it simulates thermodynamics and fluid mechanics. Heat is a big factor in Oxygen Not Included. Trying to grow temperature sensitive plants directly above a hot power production/storage area is almost guaranteed to fail without gratuitous insulation. Different substances can be heated or cooled to solid, liquid, and gaseous states. Heavy gases like carbon dioxide will pool in sumps at the lowest points in your colony, potentially rendering them inaccessible. Lighter gases like hydrogen will float to the top of an area and displace oxygen. Clean water and waste water will need to be pumped around the base for different purposes and allowing them to mix can lead to damaged equipment or contaminated water sources. Managing all of these physical aspects can be challenging, frustrating, and rewarding all at the same time.
This game looks very good, and runs very well. The game is set in a 2D side-view perspective. It has an entertaining art style, reminiscent of Don't Starve, but more cute than creepy. The environments are very pretty to look at: different gases give a subtle background to the open areas in the colony, liquids move and swirl around, ore deposits in the rock shimmer as you move the camera around. The game seems to perform perfectly on my rig with a reasonably large base and over a dozen colonists. I cannot say, however, where the threshold is where performance will start to degrade. I have experienced zero game breaking bugs or CTDs.
The game's first major shortcoming at the time of writing this review is its lack of end game content and goals. The main idea of Oxygen Not Included as of right now is to basically have as many colonists survive for as long as you can manage. Once you realize that it's in your best interest not to always take a colonist every three days when you're offered one, and once you can create a sustainable system when you are recycling waste and making your own power in house; you can get to a sort of stagnation where an established colony isn't as fun to play as a struggling one.
The game's second major shortcoming is its colonist AI. Ensuring colonists are getting things done in a timely manner, and avoiding every colony sim player's worst nightmare,
, can be a huge matter of micromanagement. This is because getting more important things done is a matter of manually setting the tasks themselves to a higher priority, between 1 (lowest) and 9 (highest). Colonists can also have certain tasks such as digging or delivering enabled or disabled. When things are going right and you're not in a hurry to get something done, the AI and work priority system works well enough. The problem comes when you queue multiple things up and colonists attempt to get them done. They do not organize their work/time very well when faced with a great number of tasks rated at the same priority. I've become a little frustrated more than once when a colonist runs far out from the established base to mine something, mines one piece of material, then turns around and runs all the way back into base to do some arbitrary task back there. This game would greatly benefit from a work type priority system at the colonist level, in the same fashion as how RimWorld manages work priorities. It's sad seeing how inefficient these colonists can be; especially when their survival is riding on how quickly they can get some resource back to base, or how fast they can break into a new area to pump waste into to prevent the colony's first cistern from overflowing into the ground floor. The only way to avert these issues is through the excessive micromanagement of individual task priorities.
I am not trying to bash the game or the developers with the above negatives, as it is an Early Access. Despite these two major flaws the game is still quite entertaining and promising. Klei has been pushing updates for this game on a regular schedule, full of content and improvements. This company is pretty well known for seeing their Early Access titles through, and I don't think I see it getting abandoned/stagnating for some large amount of time like games such as Cube World or Starbound did. I think for the price they're asking to get into the Early Access this game is most definitely worth it. If you like colony building games and management sims this will definitely do the trick for you. It looks like it should get refined and expanded upon more into the future. If you want something that is much more fleshed out and fully realized, it might be worth waiting on this one, but as of right now it's quite a bit of fun and definitely entertaining.
TLDR: A very good looking, interesting and entertaining game if you're into colony building and survival. A bit rough around the edges with end game/goal content and colonist AI. Makes very interesting use of some light physics to make the environment and resources the primary thing that kills you. Worth it for its current price point as of right now, but might be worth a wait if you want something more fleshed out.

Spec ops :The line is a massively underrated game in my opinion, brilliant graphics and great frame rates, no lag or stutter during even the heaviest firefights, the gameplay mechanics are solid, great 'gears of war' style cover shooter with a story thats absolutely fantastic- if you blast through the game without reading/listening to all the intel you find then you are missing out on a much darker experience, which is good as you actually look forward to finding intel and progressing the story how its supposed to be portrayed. Of course theres some instances of dumb AI and you can feel limited as to how youre squad can perform (simple stun/attack commands only, theres no movement issuing orders) but it doesnt retract from the gameplay at all as it helps youre character feel more human as opposed to an all seeing all powerful supersoldier. The way the game progresses and how you feel as you get further into the horrors start to genuinely make you think about the morality of your actions and any game that can make you seriously think about what you are doing is an achievement in my book. Worth buying and highly recommended.

Review is strictly just for the single-player campaign. I picked this up during a Steam sale for like $5 and boy, it's really worth it. This is one of the few military games recently that actually had me hooked not just because of gameplay but also because of the story. It's highly engaging, exploring the true depths of the horrors and triumphs of war and all that it does to the people involved, and to the people not involved. The character progression is extremely well-done, and all the choices you'll have to make throughout the game blur what's right and what's wrong in a challenge to stay sane.
The gamrplay is pretty strong, although not too much different from other modern-day military games. You start with a group of three and you can command the other two guys to do stuff such as snipe long-distance targets, full-out attack a target, or throw a flashbang to stun the enemies. I rarely used this though as I was too busy just shooting the targets, but all-in-all, the AI is at least helpful in the battle and they don't get themselves killed too often. One thing I really liked was that they made ammo pretty scarce throughout the game, which I found to be realistic when engaged in a long-lasting firefight. I was constantly changing weapons just to have some extra bullets, and it added to the difficulty of the campaign.
Overall, if you enjoy military shooters and want to try a game that isn't just "GO AMERICA, WE RULE!" then you definitely want to give this a try.

"Do you feel like a hero yet?"
Spec Ops: The Line is truly one of the most underrated game, modern millitary shooter EVER, and its sickening in every way imagineable. While games like CoD and BF rule the millitary game market, a game that only view the "badass" part of war, that "glorifies" war. A more honest and factual game about war, that tells war as a one of the most horrible act that humans have ever done, a game that tells you the reality of war, especially from psychological, morality, and phillospical standpoint is heartbreakingly pretty much unknown.
Spec Ops: The Line, despite its not that impressive name (oh, that "Spec Ops" give me an impression of a cliche'd and poorly made U.S soldier heroism-themed game, could've been better if they just named it "The Line") turns out to be a very emotional, memorable, and fantastic game of 2012, and the last 5 years, probably even for the next coming years. It's a rare game, especially in this oversaturated modern millitary game, that it so AWESOME it doesn't even need a sequel, and I'm not even being sarcastic.
Story (10/10)
The Line (to shortened it, and because I like the name better) takes you to a story of Captain Walker and his Delta squad in a mission to Dubai to rescue and evacuate survivors and to search Walker's most honored comrade, John Konrad. Seems like just another day of run and gun mililtary game, right? Nope, not at all. It do have the basic premise, it do have a so-so, and even slow start (which actually help up to build the general feeling and atmosphere), but fortunately that slow start really pay off and feel like its necessary for the story progression. And that's all what you need to know.
The story is the ultimate driving force of this game, inspired by "Heart of Darkness", which is I don't read it myself yet (that's my longtime homework), that inspired a movie called "Apocalypse Now", having watched the Redux version of Apocalpse Now (and love it wholeheartedly) I know what to expect from this game, its not your typical modern millitary game, rather than pure soldier heroism, The Line tackle themes like morality of war, PTSD, and the darkest side of both war and human's nature. When morality and humnism collides with duty, obsession, and the will to survive, a man's  rational and sanity can be pushed to the very edge of madness and depression.
"I thought we're here to rescue people"
The Line is a beautifully horrible experience, its like a surrealistic painting, it looks well...surreal and full of unexplained mind♥♥♥♥, but somehow it has magical spell that make you appreciate the art as something meaningful and beautiful depite its sometimes disturbing look. So does The Line, its surreal, full of twist and mind♥♥♥♥, disturbing, and even disgusting in a point, Yet, its still a brilliant and one of the most beautifully written game that will make you stop and think, about the consequences of war, consequences of every choices you made, and will raise a lot of question and interpretaion as you move along.
The Line is a game with extreme detail of storytelling, making sure there's no plot holes and illogical plot progression yet it still retain its surrelistic aspect and able to  raise a good amount of question and interpretaion for the players to evaluate and speculate. And the character, both cast and development is OUTSTANDING. They feel so alive, very emotional, much human. Wow. Well, yeah, I mean it. And once again, the subtle things is the greatest aspect of the game, and it applicable to the character.
"I've saved so many lives Captain, but I've killed so much more".
Gameplay (8.7/10)
The weakest part of the game, but still the gameplay is incredibly tight, intense, and solid. It's just that, the control and default key binding is not the most confortable I've experienced so far. There's nothing really innovative or noteworthy about the gameplay, but it does the job very well. The Line is a third person, cover-based millitary game. Oh yea, firstly, the gameplay section, and even sound and graphic section will be filled with the element that could've belong to the Story section, because once again its the ULTIMATE driving force of The Line.
"There must be another option, THERE IS another option"
" No, there really isn't"
The "choice" system is the most unique and the probably the best I've ever seen in a game. One thing I can say, its war, when you faced by two (or more) chocies, the latter doesn't make the former any better, vice versa. Every action has its consequences, and I must say it again..this is war, the conseuquences are unsatisfactory and bitter, and will always be. Sometimes the choice do matter, sometimes doesn't. Sometimes we have to choose to sacrifice between yourself or the other, sometimes we faced an inevitable chocies, sometimes we don't really have any other choice.
The subtlety and the "smaller, more detailed" things in The Line is the more interesting part of the game, This is surprisngly where The Line shines through. As I said, this game is about extreme detail of storytelling, that affect the other aspect of the game like gameplay, sound and in a way, graphic. As for the gameplay, I can't really tell the "little detail", since I can't seem to word it out, and I might be spoiling something along the way. But, then again, The Line is a simple, action-packed, third person game, with enough intensity to keep you hooked to the game, with enough variety of weapons and enemies, and also a simple yet effective tactical commands.
And for the A.I, they're  competent and smart enough to give me a good deal of challenge, and I must say that I get the "Max Payne 3" feeling, simple, action-packed run and gun with heavy emphasis of storytelling, a bit repetitive but.. (continues to graphic section)
Graphic (9.2 / 10)
...the level design and set pieces is  pretty amazing and well thought of, that it retain a sense of vairety and familliarity in the same time. It is varied, but you won't feel like you're moving to another place that is in another continent, you're still in Dubai from start to finsih, but you won't feel bored. The use of Unreal Engine 3 give me the "Bioshock Infinite" feel (which is another example of great storytelling in a game), no,no, not that UE3 games looks like BioShock Infinite, but its more like the atmosphere, the presentation of the game. While BioShock Infinite is a mixture of cinematic-fantasy, The Line is cinematic-reality. And the use of UE3 is the best choice, I like the rough look of UE3 (Rainbow Six Vegas is one example) gives you a sense of reality and believable atmosphere at the course of the game. The effects is done right, not underused nor overused, giving both realistic and dramatic feel in the same time. The animation is fluid and well done overall. I have nothing bad to say really
Sound (9.6/10)
AMAZING, again.. this game fascinated me on how they blend in cinematic and realism. The gun sounds so intense, the voice acting easily put most games to shame, they're just lfielike. Not to mention the brilliantly written dialogue. One thing that caught me off guard is the dialogue between the enemy soldier, even the enemy soldier is very much human, at many occassion, I feel really bad for killing those soldiers who talks about gum, peace, and family. They're just group of soldiers that fights for their life, their people, their family. And I question myself, Do I really that of a monster to kill those people?
Overall (9.8/10)
There's nothing call as perfection, but near pefect, there certainly is, and this is the game. The Line is a game that everyone has to experience, It's a game that ask us a serious question to reflect, a series of phillosophy worth noting, and it tell us the cause and effect, action and consequences of war in a 'disturbing' way.

A great Star Wars combat game where you can play from the perspective of a Jedi.
Multi-player wise, this game is superior to Jedi Knight 2: Jedi Outcast, however, since multi-player is now rare, the single player although good, was not better than Jedi Outcast (which had better pacing, and a better plot -- it felt more like the original films, whereas this game feels more like the prequels in tone). This game allows you to have a double saber, or hold 2 light-sabers, and there are a few more force powers (nothing significant). However, for some reason, the saber combat in Jedi Outcast felt tighter; in Jedi Academy, each of the saber styles have new "special moves" but they are more acrobatic than useful, they look cool, but end up being sluggish and will get you insta killed on the highest difficulty.
Jedi Outcast's campaign is more like a movie (intro, rising action, climax, etc), whereas this game opts to give you more freedom -- not only in creating a character and saber choice, but in the missions you take on. Of course, this freedom comes at the cost of sacrificing a story in favour of just throwing random missions at you. After a set of missions, you're forced to take on a 'main' mission which will propel the story forward... there is SOME semblence of story, but again, nowhere near the pacing of Jedi Outcast.  However, this game does have some interesting choices that you can make (minor spoiler, light side/dark side) which will change the last set of missions/final battle/ending scene (each with their own pros and cons...)
Regardless, this is a great game that holds up despite being a bit aged. You'll feel like a Jedi badass and that's all it needs to do.
If you want a game with a lot of choices where you can role play as a Jedi, taking on various missions, etc, then this game is great.
If you want a well paced and tight story, with simpler but tighter gameplay, Jedi Knight 2: Jedi Outcast is the game for that.
I would recommend both for any fan of the Star Wars mythos. These games do a good job of taking care of the "Jedi Knight, light-saber, blasters etc, force powers combat niche).

Most of the time, you are driving a truck, either yours or you borrowed one. The scenery is brilliant with beautiful fields and mountains but cities are quite dull, featuring only a few roads and little 3D buildings with landmarks in the skybox and are inaccessible. Driving is quite normal but more challenging as you are not driving a regular car but a 300-500hp engine truck.
There is only a career mode in the stock game but it is very fun and quite challenging. You must be a responsible driver in the game and not damage your and other vehicles in the game as that will result in fines. The career mode is also endless and your goal is to make your truck company thrive.
The game features many significant cities in europe and you'll have a great time exploring them. You also need to find truck dealers and recruitment agencies in-order to find good truck brands and find good workers. When you do buy a truck, you have quite a lot to choose from depending on your in-game experience. Yes, when you complete jobs you get in-game experience and level up to unlock great things and more trucks.
To conclude, the graphics and scenery are fantastic, the gameplay and mechanics are great and the customisability this game gives you is mind-blowing. If you like playing an open-world, 'educational', driving simulator type of game which requires you to take good decisions to better achieve your goals, this game is for you!

So what would i rate it? Thats a tough one, i want to rate it 10/10 because i really enjoyed it, but some of the repetitive missions, some of the bosses and sometimes just getting lost because of misleading directions frustrated me, so ill rate it 9/10, a close 10/10.

I am loving this game - it feels like a mashup of X3, Elite and  a couple of other games.
Your starter ship is good mix of everything, good size cargo bay, two weapon points (light - railguns, heavy missiles).  upgrading it is expensive so take care of it.
You earn money by trading, completing missions, mining.  You can also try pirating, though this doesn't suit my game play.
The universe is a series of hex's that you fly across normally.  Alternatively, their are gateways between locations that require jump drives, worm holes that require increased health (haven't managed to get through one yet) and rift lines, which accelerate your speed whilst you are in the rift.  The subtle difference between worm hole and rift - I think - is that you are exposed to enemy fire in the rift, but not in the wormhole.
There is a story (and with the DLC, a second one), but often you will find yourself doing "things".  I targeted a level 2 pirate and thought it would be easy, but he called for help, deciding to avoid the agro, I pushed the engines to max, turned and flew through a rift and ended up in the middle of an uncharted system, alive, but with a battered ship.
It is a slow paced game - so far at least - but you have to learn that your ship is NOT a fighter, but a small frigate with a crew and gimballed turrets which you can either fire, or have the crew fire.  Later you can buy carrier vessels or cloaked vessels.  You can also command some sort of fleet (hiring mercenaries to accompany you).
Like I say, I am loving this.

This game is super fun; I like Star Trek, Firefly, Cowboy Bebop, etc. and when I'm in that mood SG2 in perfect. Every time I resume my game the first thought I have is that this is a great, immersive game. It's really frustrating to see negative reviews because I love this game so much. The developers continue working on it and it keeps getting better which is really saying something since I loved it at early access. recommend for any sci-fi fan that wants a single player open world experience with a ton of ways to play. It's viable to be a miner and buy ships and outfit them just for that. I personally spent several fun hours just doing that, it was great. You can buy and upgrade ships just for smuggle or escort or freelancing. People complain about the expense of ships versus reward of missions; these people simply don't get it. There are lots of ways to build your bank roll and the time and effort it takes make the game more rewarding and immersive. The balance makes it so much better as you progress, you can't just jump from the first ship to the most powerful ship or even the most powerful weapons right away, and that is good. You actually get to enjoy and explore each level of progress , as you get a new ship, or a new upgrade and you slowly work toward that next purchase. All the while playing however you want, avoiding combat in favor of mining and trade which is super fun, figuring out how to avoid destruction or detection while making the kesel run in under 3 parsecs. Or you can be a pirate, good or bad, hijacking ships with a ship optimized just for that sort of activity. So good. So highly recommended.

I am a SUCKER for space exploration games (I even played Darkstar One, and it was mediocre at best). An yet I did not like this one. This has mainly three reasons:
* The story (what little I have played before giving up on the game) is not riveting and seems to follow already trodden paths (trodden by games far superior). The whole "The system is riven with conflict and there is some hidden threat only YOU can uncover" is nice and dandy, but again, done better by previous games. The voice acting is .. unethusiastic. I know, I have been spoiled by world-class actin as in Mass Effect, but still...
There is a lot of grinding - trading, mining, doing freelance missions, to get a ship that you need to NOT be blasted to smithereens by the next main mission,. There ALWAYS is. It is a core principle of the game, and usually, one that I like. In this game, it feels like a chore. This has again to do with the story, which just does nothing to make me want to reach the next mission.
* The steering. This is a MAYOR point. I did not think one could botch follow-the-mouse-steering. Sadly, one can. The point you fly to is somewhere in the upper third of the monitor. Which KINDA makes sense given the perspective and the axis of the ship and all. BUT the neutral zone of the mouse-steering is in the center of the screen. Which means that when you point at an object an try to fly towards it, you will pass OVER it (for given values of "OVER" in 3D space).
This is annoying, to say the least. It is also unintuitive. I remember when Freelancer made me use the mouse (for me, it was the first time then) to steer the ship. I took to it in seconds, because it was so intuitive. Well, this one is NOT.
* The mission system is bugged, if not broken. "Yes, you can take this mission with level 6" Great. They WHY is there a friggin' CRUISER waiting for my gunship at the mission point, blasting the living hell out of me? This happens regularly, and it is annoying. "Nooo, THIS science mission is WAY to dangerous, it requires you to be level 11." Ah-ha. So floating in space, with NO enemies to pop up (I have yet to meet one on science missions) and waiting for the scanner is something only my higher-level self can handle..
All those points make me kinda regret the purchase. Oh, and one final note: it may be okay with copyright law to use the theme from the mining minigame of Mass Effect 2 and use in the score, for me, it was just an INSULT to the ME franchise, because this game is not even doing the same sport, not not mention playing in the same league.

TL;DR - I'd rate the game a 7-8/10. It has many of the elements veteran platformers love about the past with modern polish. Great, cartoony-style graphics combined with nostalgia inducing music, smooth controls (on controller), and plenty of funny moments.
Having played multiple hours but only seen a few levels, I think I can give the game a mostly fair review. Overall, I'm extremely happy with it. Going into the game I had a sense of nostalgia for the 90's platformers. It's definitely a spiritual successor to the old Banjo-Kazooie games, and it follows the exact same trend from the "dialog" to the interface, and even the music. In many ways, it's like Banjo-Kazooie in a new coat of paint.
Starting with the positives,
+ Gorgeous graphics. Of course it's a very vibrant and cartoony art style, but that is very much the point.
+ Diverse cast of characters. Anything you can imagine, they probably attached googly-eyes and grunty voices to it.
+ LOTS of things to collect. Being a collectathon platformer, this is important. You'll be running into things to find left and right, although it does start to make it difficult to locate the handful of things you're missing later on.
+ Massive worlds! There's a lot to explore.
+ Nostalgic elements for those of us that played the old Rare platformers.
+ Decent variety in humor, ranging from moments of "breaking the fourth wall" to not-so-subtle sex jokes. This might be a con for some people, though.
+ Smooth controls (sans camera) on a controller.
Negatives,
- Keyboard controls are horrible. Get the game on console or hook your controller to your PC. I'm serious, don't buy this game if you can't play with a controller. You'll hate it. I specifically bought a receiver for my PC for this game after I  played the demo. It's that bad.
- Though the worlds are big, there's only 5 (not counting the overworld, minigames, etc). There seems to be a big variety of environments, but I personally would rather have smaller worlrds if it meant even more unique locations and stories.
- The camera controls are a semi-polished version of what we dealt with 20 years ago. Trying to get creative in some places might have you suddenly running off the edge, or your camera might get stuck on the lower floor staring at the ceiling. Overall this doesn't occur too often, but it probably could do with some improvements.
- Level design feels stale. There's a lot to explore and a few interesting easter-eggs, but to me, it felt like the platformer elements were constructed first and scenery arbitrarily built up around it. Worlds don't feel natural to look at or navigate, and major landmarks lack personality. There's also VERY little in the way of subtle hints or guidance beyond the "where to go". Very obvious puzzles might prove unnecessarily difficult because of uncertainty as to HOW to complete them.
- There's a LOT of black-door teleporting, which can make it difficult to keep track of where you are/are going if you're directionally challenged.
- The game feels too small for its price tag, time in development, and experience of the developers in this genre.
One last point that I personally would tack under 'negative', but many people are likely to disagree.
- Unlike other games, you have a lot of freedom as to the order in which you unlock your abilities, but I feel like this freedom came with unfortunate design consequences. The cost to unlock them so far has been surprisingly small however, so the decision making  behind it feels very minimal. A substantial portion of the worlds I've visited so far feel like they're designed with a "worst moveset possible" combination in mind (so you don't make a choice that leads you to a bad end). Ideally, this design would allow for more interesting ways to reach objectives and complete puzzles, but it ultimately just contributes to confusion every time you run into something that you can't properly interact with yet and most collectibles are simply gated behind the path of least resistance. I'm going to hope this becomes less obvious in later worlds when you have most (all?) of your core moves.
Some degree of linearity is important in a game like this, so that worlds can be designed from the ground up with certain abilities in mind and players can more intuitively progress through the game. From a design perspective, I find this choice to be one of the worst elements about it.

Exceptional game. It really has that 90's nostalgia vibe about it. From what I've played so far, it has been pretty amazing.
Yooka-Laylee feeds off the old nostalgia of the 90's back when Banjo-Kazooie was out on the Nintendo 64 home console. It was pretty amazing game for its time back then, and followed predicessor Banjo-Tooie which later came after it brought even more stuff to the Banjo-Kazooie world. -- Long gone are the old days of Rareware, many fans of BK series never saw the day of light of a Banjo-Threeie
. Yooka-Laylee tries to give us what we never had, which was that third BK sequel. Only this time we have a Chameleon and a Bat duo.
Yooka-Laylee brings back that long lost formula of a genuine platformer adventure-type videogame, where the gaming world is saturated heavily with FPS, TPS, and Horror style of videogames. Yooka-Laylee has a massive expensive sandbox worlds that slowly expand as you progress the game by collecting items called Pagies, and these open up new areas in the game and have additional task missions to do. You learn new moves and abilities as you progress throughout the game which you learn from a character within the game called Trowzer Snake, by trading off Golden Quils that you collect throughout each of the worlds you go to. -- The game somewhat feels pretty linear and closed, and I have to compare it with the likes of Banjo-Kazooie/Banjo-Tooie where you had a hub world like Spirale Mountain, Jinjo Village and so on,  in Yooka-Laylee however there doesn't feel that much of expansiveness in the hub worlds, but I guess that's kept like that intentionally for now just for this game to get players use to the new world that they are in before later expanding it further in later games.
For a Unity game this is pretty amazing quality game to come out of it, and yes, there are many Unity games where people don't put much effort of quality into it to make their games look good, yet people still get so surprised when a really good quality game is made in Unity. -- At the time of writing this review the game does have performance and stability issues, most so with issues on Linux where the game will crash almost constantly with mono runtime libraries being the cause of the crashes, which I hope will be fixed in due time, and will update my review later when that happens.

WAIT TO BUY THIS GAME OR DON'T BUY THE FULL EXPERIENCE. Yes, I used caps because I'm trying to help some people that will be frustrated like I am.
I'm rewriting this review after spending more time with the game. I like the game, but they shouldn't have released it in March. Their September announcement said six campaign, three locations, forty signature kills, contracts mode with 800 targets and weekly live hits and events. That's the bit I saw and thought wow this game sounds awesome. I never saw the January announcement that said we're getting what I have now. After seeing the September announcement I fully planned on buying the full experience. I completely screwed up for not paying more attention but in all fairness to me, who would expect they would need to keep an eye out for this kind of change? Now all I have is one location, some occasiona escalation contracts, and the normal user contracts. Elusive targets have been pushed back until April. On top of that the game does have problems. People and items fall through the floor a lot. I've had weird graphics issues at times too. Don't get me wrong I do enjoy the game at least as far as the one story mission goes. The escalation contracts just aren't my thing.
I don't recommend buying this game yet... or at least not yet. Some will love it and defend it to the end and blame the people who expected to get what was announced in September for not paying enough attention to the later announcements about changing how this release worked. Again, who would expect such a drastic change to happen mid January when the game is due out mid March? I don't game a lot, but I figured the last three months would just be for polishing the first three locations up. Then the next three locations would be polished up in the month to come before they are released. There was all this promised live content but all there is are a few escalation contracts every week and a half or so. Basically for those you're killing one of the NPCs in increasingly "difficult" ways; more like odd ways. I mean seriously, why would any hitman where a vampire magician outfit to carry out a hit on anyone?
The little bit of the game we have is good. Trust me when I say you should wait or at least don't buy the full experience like my idiot self did. I remember what was announced in September went on steam pressed purchase for the full experience because I was all in since September and was confused as hell where the rest of the game was. Go back and do some internet searching and felt both lied to and like and idiot for noy paying more attention.
It boils down to this. You buy the full experience now and you'll be frustrated with the constant deplays for content and patches to fix problems with the game. I've noticed on forums the people using consoles are having a really bad go of it. If you buy the intro and decide you want to go all in for the rest of the game or take it episode by episode then you'll end up spending more money for a game that may not have nearly as much content as they promised.

At first I though that this game was too complicated. But after a couple of doomed colonies, I got used to basic mechanics and my third base started well. Really well... At some point I even though that now I got it and the game is too easy. But I was wrong... Dead wrong. Damn bacteria took over my bunker. Great sickness stroke it's habitants and soon everything was contaminated. The air, the food, the water and I didn't even see it coming. That colony died as well.
"I got it... I got it now", I though for a forth time. Got myself a slick well-planned habitat. Tons of oxigen, flitration sistems, kitchen, crops. All the package. Completelly sustainable, expcept for one small detail. The hidrogen, then my pump used to send to the generator that was making the juice for all the air sistems, eventuall run out... And the pump started to feed it poisonous gas. Generator died... And with it, all of my sistems. On which I relied so heavily.
Sooo... Here I go again. Another day, another colony to build. I hope that some day I can take everything in consideration and make an asteroid paradaise... But for now, it's all about trying again and learning from my mistakes.
And to put it in less words: Game core mechanics are simple. You can surive on basic tech with a low population without any problem, but it get's more complicated with more dwellers and that is where you need to think about how can you improve your bunker.
So...If you like games like "Dwarf Fortress", "Don't Starve" and "Rimworld", this one is a must-have. It adds a lot of new aspects of colony to consider, such as air, water managment, energy managment and desinfection. And it's only the tip of the iceberg in here, I keep discovering new features with each gameplay, so replayability is good too. You can play this as long as you like and you won't get bored. And if you do eventually... Devs added a counter right in the main menu to tell everyone when the next patch is done. So, new content comes out quite frequently and adds more chalenges to already complex game mechanics.
So, with that, I finish my review and I give it 10/10. Great sandbox survival game.

This is a game with much promise, but little to recommend it. It has a massive universe, but it is mostly a boring, empty grindfest.
The main issue is that the designers simply haven't bothered to balance out the various elements of the game. While missions are on offer, they don't actually provide anywhere near the sort of money that you will need in order to upgrade to newer vessels. And you do need to upgrade, because the game difficulty assumes that, so let go any dreams you might have of having any real choice over the sort of ships that you choose to play.
Because of this, players are forced into the incredibly boring and highly yawnworthy process of capturing ships for sale, just so that they can earn decent income. What this means in practice is that rather than wandering around the universe engaging in exciting dogfights (Freelancer did this well), you are forced to try to capture the first ship you come across (although it might just be destroyed by "friendlies", who don't care that your marines are aboard).
From there, you grapple and ferry the thing back to the nearest starport. Rinse and repeat ad nauseum. Of course, you could trade, or you could mine, but these are equally boring activities and if you wanted to be an accountant, you could easily do that in real life.
Thus far, the designers have shown absolutely no interest in addressing these issues. which is surprising, because they are a widespread criticism and would be easy to fix, simply by upping the cash rewards for missions, while significantly reducing the amount that players earnt from selling captured ships.
By comparison, at level five I might earn 12,000 credits for a mission, but over ten times that from the sale of a captured ship. Why not just make it the other way around? Afterall, how much is a ship full of holes really worth anyway?
As one other reviewer said, this is a game that doesn't get fun until you have at least ten million credits. Sure, if you are the sort of person who loves highly repetitive, routine actions, then you will probably be in your element. But then again, you are probably already an IRL accountant anyway... ;-)
The other really crappy thing is that there isn't really much out there to explain the "classes" and what all of those skills and perks really do in the game.
All in all, this is a very bland and uninteresting game and if you are looking for lots of boredom, or need something to keep you occupied while you read your book, in between overly long flight from one boring location to another, then it might just be your cup of tea.
Personally, I don't want to have to grind for hours just to get to some decent content. At which point the grinding recommences.
Even after more than ten years, Freelancer (especially modded)  is easily the better game.

This game was absolutely amazing when I first played it over a year ago. I really feel like the blend of glitchy physics and simplistic gameplay on levels breakable in ways that shouldn't have been possible absolutely captured lightning in a bottle.
Since then, however, I feel every update has been loosening the lid and letting a little bit of that magic slip out to the point where the remaining charm exists solely in the mild amusement from watching increasingly Raving Rabbids / Minions-esque characters slap each other a little bit.
It makes me feel as though Boneloaf had a very specific vision for this game - one that is unfortunately wildly superceded by the earlier releases. Trying to reign in the out of control physics and removing things like Waves and Race mode - tweaking the climbing system and dumbing down the options available to you for game customisation (off the top of my head, infinite grip) has truly killed the fun I had in this game.
This, in combination with wildly simplifying the levels has turned this game into nothing but a reminder of the great fun it used to be. Back in the day, it wasn't uncommon to uppercut someone onto an airvent attached to the ceiling before knocking it down in an attempt to climb up there with them, or dropkick someone across the room into a well-timed sausage-hole. Now, it's unlikely that anything will happen other than two characters wildly flailing until one falls over followed by the survivor dumping the fallen off an edge.
TL;DR: What was once up in the pinnacle of couch competitive games has unfortunately slipped into disappointment.
Would no longer recommend, but it was fun while it lasted.

Max Payne is now an old game and this is more a recommendation for retro-gamers than anyone else since this game is quite dated in many areas. If you never looked into that title before and you love full-action-third-person-shooters, then you should give it a try because it does it quite well even compared to modern standards. The story has a good atmosphere despite being a classic « lone man seeks revenge » and it has the advantage of begin quite short (7-9hrs) which makes the retro-experience more bearable, especially if you plan to get into the series before or after Max Payne 3. The shooting is very satisfying for game of its age, since its a forerunner of the slow-motion matrix like « bullet time » that will later appear in F.E.A.R and other games. The games difficulty scales well as you progress and requires a good use and management of the bullet time mechanic which is extremely satisfying to play with. I'd recommend you pick it on sale, and that you look on steam forums for the sound patch to make it run on modern systems without issues.

Spec Ops: The Line may seem like a typical military shooter at first, but it isn’t... not at all.
Its strongest point, the story, makes up for every flaw that this game has. I won’t give you any other detail about it, with the exception that it is one of the most intense stories I’ve heard from a game and you just have to trust me and play through it. I don’t believe that there is any other game with such an unique plot and, in terms of how good the narrative is, it can be easily placed at the same level with other good story-driven games like The Last of Us and Alan Wake, which I highly recommend if you are interested in intriguing stories. Also, it is filled with lots of action, which makes it a good choice, even if you want to play something just killing some people, but, in my opinion, if you choose to play this game without paying attention to the story, you are simply wasting your time, as probably there are other mindless shooters out there which excel at this category.
The cover system is pretty well done, even though your character will sometimes get into the wrong cover, which can instantly lead to your death if you are already being shot, especially on harder difficulties.  The AI of the squad mates sometimes made my enemies' lives easier, by going out of cover in critical situations and dying, which, combined with a hard difficulty, made it impossible for me to get my squad mate revived. Neither of the above is game breaking and, fortunately, these things rarely happen, so I can say that the gameplay itself is well polished. One thing I want to point out is that the enemy AI is pretty challenging, forcing you to take tactical approaches instead of getting out of cover and shooting everyone. Also, I feel that the sand mechanics were not used at their maximum potential and the developer could do much more with the idea.
The sound is another aspect of the game where it can be seen that the developer put a lot of effort.  The voice actors did a tremendous job, succeeding in making players easily cope with the characters. Fun fact: every single line of the script was recorded in just one day. You’ll probably think that the actors didn’t manage to do this without getting tired. Firstly, that’s the point: the developers wanted the voice acting to closely follow the game, which, with the help of the actors, they did. Secondly: you are talking about professionals. Should I mention that the main character is voiced by Nolan North, the one who was featured in games like the Uncharted series and The Last of Us? Also, the OST fits the game perfectly, giving you an adrenaline shot every time you find yourself in front of many enemies. (I have to admit that I’m into rock/metal music, but in my opinion, the music you’ll find in the game is best suited for this genre.)
The graphics are pretty amazing! Everything takes place in a post-sandstorm Dubai, which was very well represented by the developers. You get the opportunity to see a beautiful sight of the ruins of Dubai from one of its tallest buildings. Also, the great lightning effects and the attention to details makes up for some minor texture loading issues. There isn’t really anything else to complain about the graphics! I didn't experience any FPS drops, graphical artifacts or any other technical problems throughout the whole campaign.
I was looking for a game with a good story and I gave this one a chance when I caught it on sale. I have to admit that I don’t regret a single penny I spent on this game and even if I had to pay the full price, I would not complain, because it is one of the few games that sent chills down my spine. So, if you are wondering whether to buy this game or not and it happens to be on sale, do yourself a favor… buy this game. I can assure you that you won’t regret it at all.

I'm amazed at the stupidity I'm seeing in these negative reviews. Most of them boil down to either
1.  "I don't understand this game, therefore it's not fun." or
2. "This early access game isn't finished yet, therefore thumbs down."
This game is one of a kind and in my not-at-all-humble opinion it's brilliant. It's the only game I've seen that tackles gas and temperature physics and really REALLY rewards you for careful planning.
It's impressively deep, even in it's EA state. You can actually do things that you would think you could in this situation, such as
1. Cooling down an insulated room to the point that the oxygen in it turns into liquid, or even solid.
2. Bottle that oxygen up and carry to a new room where you heat it up and turn it back into breathable gas.
3. Pump a room full of chlorine gas and use that space to disinfect objects that are covered in germs.
4. Fill boxes up with ice to cool down a space, until it melts and floods your base with water.
5. Sprinkle water over your machines to cool them down, and have a pump at the bottom that sends it back up for re-sprinkling.
6. Throw a bunch of copper into the magma biome and watch it turn into liquid.
Too many to list really. It's a one-of-a-kind sandbox that becomes extremely fun once you figure out how to survive effectively. I highly recommend. Plus it's adorable.

Ever wanted to summon a hundred sith and 20 Luke Skywalkers to see how they fare against each other? You can do it in this game! (with cheats though). Also, this game has a rather interesting single player story mode I played through multiple times and sank approximately 40 hours into.
Pros:
1. You can be a Jedi! Also, it has Kyle Katarn and Luke Skywalker in it!
2. A plethora of mods!
3. Although the story is linear, the levels offer a variety of experiences (crashlanding on a planet and repairing your ship, while trying to escape a sand worm; fighting Boba Fett; disarming a bomb-rigged train; speeder chase, and many other routine adventures a Jedi Padawan/Knight goes through)
4. Awesome acrobatics, swordsplay and Force powers, which feel way more fluid and natural to the game than the guns.
5. Great sandboxing potential of both SP and MP. You think this plain on Tatooine would make a great battlefield? Spawn in Boba Fett and 3 Kyle Katarns and see who wins, then spawn in 20 Boba Fetts and 60 Kyles. (spoiler: Boba Fett wins every time, since he's immortal). Would you make this roof to roof jump on the moving train if you had a speeder with you? Spawn in a speeder and try it out!
6. There is an active multiplayer community and the sandbox is real on the servers (there are banks, quests and other different RPG-ish kinds of stuff). There are some classic FFA, TDM or CTF servers too. While the sandbox is something very interesting and unique to this game, I can't really say it was that big of a deal for me.
Cons:
1. Dated graphics and cinematics.
2. Very predictable and linear story.
3. Gunplay is pretty subpar, compared to lightsaber combat and Force powers.
4. Possible compatibility problems with Windows 7/8. Also, some tinkering is required before you can set it to 16:9.
This is one of the games, that aged really well, considering it's over 10 years old. If older graphics are a problem for you, there are mods partially fixing them, as well as adding a bunch of new things to the game.
The most fun I've had with this game was either by spawning in enemies and allies and organising battles royale, or trying to get speeder jumps in original places (for example a roof to roof jump on the moving train level).
I return to this game every now and then for the great lightsaberplay and to have some fun cheating in enemies and vehicles.
You might encounter compatibility problems, so purchase at your own risk!
Verdict: 9/10 - Would get choked by Kyle Katarn again (no homo).

I bought this game mainly because I've always liked all things Garfield, and besides that, I somewhat also like kart racing games the likes of Mario Kart, but despite my love for this fluffy cat, I strongly regret my purchase.
Somehow you may think that this game is child-oriented because of the style, graphics and theme, but as soon as you open it, you'll see that the menus and options are not that user friendly to the point that even an adult can have a rough time figuring out how this works.
Before the game actually fires, you'll face a small configuration window with two tabs, "Graphics" and "Input", pretty self explanatory. The problems begin when you try to configure your own keys (or controller) since the assignations are not intuitive; for instance, this are the first options you can choose from when setting up your keyboard:
- Turn right (Digital) (+)
- Turn right (Digital) (-)
- Turn left (Digital) (+)
- Turn left (Digital) (-)
- Turn right (Analog)
- Turn left (Analog)
...and so on.
The options for the graphical configuration are merely "Screen resolution" and "Graphics quality", which you can change from "Very low" to "Very high" with five steps, but I don't have any complains in those since this is a pretty basic game and that will suffice, I bet this can even be played on any recent iGPU.
Then, after you're done with te settings window, you'll find out that no matter what keys you entered in the config, the game will act completely different: in my case, after setting up the keys, I have to press Left in order for the cart to go Right, I have to press Down for the cart to accelerate, etc.
I think the only "positive" point of the game, is that it looks nice, it's only visually attractive, no more. You'll have to deal with key mapping problems, config issues and even, maybe, optimisation issues since the game suffers from frame dropping even with its simple and undemanding graphics.
The only reason I'm keeping the game it's because of the cat and because it will be an extra number in my Steam library, but I'm sure I will never install it nor "play" it again.

Let's get this out of the way: if you have a shoddy connection, getting booted out constantly would make this game unplayable. Strict online requirement was probably the awful idea of some stiff-necked higher-up.
THAT BEING SAID:
My defense of episodic release- It gives the freedom of choice.
Don't want it till later? Don't buy it till later brah.
Want it now? Buy it now.
Not sure about it? Just pay $15 instead of $60 to try E1.
Pros
+Sandbox? You betcha. Tons of stuff to do. Just walking around and screwing with everyone's stuff is pretty fun.
+Living, breathing world where all NPC's have names and many have funny conversations
+Paris level is big. Like, "YUGE" for a Hitman map.
+Great sense of aesthetic in-game and in-menu
+Did I mention it really is a sandbox?
+AI is in many ways MUCH BETTER than previous games, where NPC's would spontaneously turn on and murder you or act like a hive mind. Seriously, I've heard the complaints that these guards are too lax but go back and play any other Hitman game and see how much more sense this makes.
+Escalation is a great idea. Elusive Targets is super promising.
+Contracts mode basically legitimizes how my friends and I used to make up challenges in Blood Money. May ultimately be a huge source of replay value.
Cons
-Handholding. But you can (and should, for sake of discovery) turn off minimap and opportunities at least.
-Textures could have been better, but overall art is great and game still looks very pretty.
-I miss Jesper Kyd
-Online requirement BS. I have not been booted from a game though so I can't complain.

This reviews contains no major spoilers. Everything mentioned in this review is encountered in the first level of the game.
This game was launched on Kickstarter in 2015 as a spiritual successor to the original Banjo Kazooie and Banjo Tooie, with key persons of the same development team behind it. They promised a game that would basically be what a "Banjo Threeie" could have been. A lot of negative reviews rely on the opinion that the 3D platfromer and collect-a-thon is an outdated format. I supported the kickstarter personally back in 2015.
You control a lizard named Yooka and a bat, Laylee, on an adventure to retrieve the golden pages of a special book that was stolen from you. A corporate bee named Capital B has stolen all the books in the world in order to monopolize the market and maximize profits. To find all of the golden "Pagies", you have to enter the worlds inside the Grand Tomes laying around Capital B's hive.
If you are expecting an alternative to Mario Galaxy or Sonic with a definite start point and end goal for each mission, this is not the game. This is an open-ended 3D platformer. You can jump into a world and go anywhere your moveset will allow you. There are areas you can't reach until you've unlocked new moves, which can be purchased with Quills that are all strewn over the various worlds. You are also restricted by needing golden Pagies to unlock new worlds, but there is never just an invisible wall keeping you from advancing further into the game.
There are five worlds in total, along with an overworld that also contains a few collectibles. The five worlds can be further expanded after opening, which means that when you first open them up they are missing some segments, and you need to spend more Pagies to expand them to their full size. This mechanic works great, because it allows you to advance through parts of the game without completing the more advanced segments of the world, hoping to uncover new movesets along the way. On the other hand, you can choose to spend all your Pagies to expand the worlds quickly and complete more of them immediately with the moveset you already have.
Being a collect-a-thon with much of the gameplay revolving around collecting items, there are certainly a lot of items to collect. All of the items, even the 1010 Quills, are cleverly placed and not just put randomly across the map. While the Quills often guide you to new areas, some are placed on some hard-to-reach platforms or used as decorations on larger objects. Pagies, which are needed to progress the game's story, usually require you to complete challenges or puzzles to get, and while many of them are outright easy the latter pages can be a real challenge to earn. There is also an arcade game inside each world that may be played from the main menu and with up to 3 friends in multiplayer.
All in all, Yooka-Laylee is a great game that seems to have accomplished exactly what the devs set out to do! It is a true successor to Banjo Tooie in all but its name.
Reviewed with a Xbox 360 game pad.
Controls are often what makes or breaks any platformer, 2D or 3D. Luckily, the controls work great on a gamepad. Yooka-Laylee's movements are crisp and responsive and it doesn't ever feel slow in any aspect. From accelerating, to decelerating, to turning around and suddenly switching direction. You start out with a simple double jump which gives you great control of your jumps, and the game also features rolling jumps (roll of an edge before jumping) and jump attacks (roll in air to perform a forward jolt). As the game progresses you also unlock moves that enable you to high jump and glide, to name a few.
In some parts of the game you control other characters than the usual Yooka-Laylee. Their controls might be a bit slow, floaty or clunky, but it seems like that is what was intended by the devs for these characters.
Some people are complaining about the camera being terrible, but I can't say I share their sentiment. I seem to have great control over the camera while running around, and the axes are invertible via the game options. There are a couple of very specific locations which enforce a side view making the game almost 2.5D, but I find it appropriate in those locations. The only issue is that the camera will sometimes jolt into another position when it has been restricted by the environment, making you suddenly run in another direction.
Perception of depth may also be an issue in 3D platformers, but with Yooka-Laylee's shadow to guide and moveset to assist you it never really feels like the game itself makes you miss a platform. And don't worry if you do! Dying in this game doesn't really have any repercussions at all.
Great game for any old school platformer and collect-a-thon fan. The platforming is never too hard, but sometimes a bit challenging. The story is nothing more than a simple children's cartoon plot. The puzzles are varied and the not-so-subtle humour keeps the game fresh and fun, even though you don't care about the story. The enjoyment all lies in the gameplay and sheer enjoyment of exploring a diverse world of challenges and secrets. Within the general direction of the game's progression, you have full control over what you want to do first and last.

I'm going to be honest. Spec Ops the line is one of the most amazingly polarising experiences I've had.
On one hand, the gameplay is mostly generic and has your conventional third person shooter mechanics with occasional turret sections and the usual hoo-rah military gun porn one would expect of the genre.
On the other hand though, Spec Ops the line has a BRILLIANT and wholly original plot which not only seperates it from the endless stream of generic brown FPS games nowadays, but also had (or at least in my opinion) one of the best and most truly thought provoking plot twists I've encountered in recent memory. I dont want to spoil it obviously but what I will say is no matter what ending you get, much like Fallout New Vegas, you will feel like a terrible person.
This is a game where there is no clear cut line on morality and doesnt approach storytelling in the usual black and white way, where characters cant be labeled as simply good or evil. The great thing about the plot is that it makes you question the moralality of each character, including the protagonist and makes the plot almost imperative to reflect on.
It's just too bad the gameplay is just so uninspired and considering the games length it begins to feel long in the tooth really fast. I actually found myself bum rushing the last parts of the game after doing posisbly the 20th sniping section because I wanted to get answers so damn badly. Also the checkpoints near the end are f**king brutal to the point of frustration and many moments suffer from seeminly endless spawns of enemies (much akin to Modern Warfare). It's nasty.
At the very least I will give points to the game not skimping out on gore, to the point of nightmare fuel and it's use of sand as a major mechanic. Speaking of visuals, the game's art design is also VERY well done. The game leaves alot of very subtle hints about the narative through visual ques and colour filters, Once again I dont want to spoil too much but if your familiar with films like 'Synecdoche new york' you will notice what I mean.
In short, this is a game that despite it's frankly mediocre gameplay, has a plot and design execution worth discussing and reflecting on.
If you want to get past the gameplay, a lets-play is a worthwhile venture. Either way, check it out.

Having said that however, the gameplay is only meant to connect you to the story which is the heart and soul of the game. Burrowing cues from the book "Heart of Darkness' and the movie "Apocolypse Now", the narrative explores the 'Morality' of war and invites the player to question whether their actions really make them the good guys. You experience a wide range of emotions including fear, doubt and regret...
Play this game if you really want to find out the 'other side' of the FPS genre. The side that FPS companies like Activision and EA  don't want you to experience. The truth...

Probably one of the best games from the RPG Genre I've played!

Positives
+Classic RPG style turn based combat with a few twists. You have the option to FIGHT or show MERCY and whichever method you choose overall throughout the game affects the story.
+Charming and memorable characters. That includes the random mobs in the game as their personality is used to decipher how best to pacify them if you want to show them mercy.
+With most RPGs you are expected to grind to increase your strength, this one is different as the developer decided to minimise the need to do this. The lack of heavy grinding being necassary is great and if you decide to show mercy to literally everything you see don't worry. You can make it all the way to end without killing a single thing and still beat the game. Trust me.
+The boss encounters have the perfect amount of difficulty in that they're tough to beat but not so tough that it's not even satisfying when you win.
+Replayability. Your first playthrough will likely take between 5-6 hours to complete but chances are you're likely going to playthrough the game at least one more time to experience the different effects your actions have on the story.
+A surprisingly layered and touching story.
+The music.
+MY GOD THE MUSIC.
Misc points
/The visual style might put some people off. It's presented in a very 8 bit style similar to games like Earthbound or Chrono Trigger. I personally like it as the character designs are brilliantly done, especially during combat.
/There's one section of the game where one of the characters calls you on the phone to help you with certain obstacles. They call you A LOT. This was going to be a negative but it's actually in line with the character and pretty funny because of it but some will find this part a little annoying.
/Lack of voice acting as it's all text based, each character does come with unique sounds when talking in a similar fashion to The Sims but not as annoying.
Negatives
-The character you play as doesn't have the greatest design, your character looks like the grumpiest little kid I've ever seen. This is admittedly a nitpick but i can't really think of much objectively wrong or lacking with the game. For what it sets out to do it does it really well.
Overall
The hype for the game might have it set up on some sort of pedestal as one of the greatest game EVAR but if you come into it with an open mind and no prior knowledge of the story then by the end you will see why it has built such a big following. It might not match the production values of a triple A game but it manages to do what most of those games wish they could because Undertale will stick with you long after you're done with it.

Incredibally fun with lots of gasoline and explosions. The driving mechanics and car combat are very on point and never feel like they become stale or unfair. The hand to hand combat is about on the level of Batman Arkham Asylum, but becomes too easy a little too fast as enemies don't feel like they improve to match your newly gained abilities and there aren't a very wide variety of enemies. The biggest drawbacks to the game as a whole come in the form of Minesweeping and the final act of the game. The minesweeping is very boring and feels like it was just thrown in. It will take up a few (at least 2) hours of your playthrough and feels like the biggest chore of the entire game. The final act of the game feels VERY rushed and poorly thought out as far as writing and story telling goes. For example, there's a certain character you're supposed to feel bad for, but you are only given about 15 minutes to get to know them. The final boss is a joke and lacked any sort of impact (the fight leading up to him was pretty fun at least) and it felt like the player was supposed to have some sort of choice, but instead you are forced into doing something incredibally stupid when the tools you have on hand would solve the problem with the simple click of a button. Seriously, it's like you're forced to hammer a nail in with your forehead instead of using the hammer in your very hand.
All in all, 41 of my 44 hours were very enjoyable so it's safe to say that the good vastly outway the bad. I will admit that I got the game on sale for $10 which may sway my opinion a bit, but if you're a fan of the Mad Max universe and love all the fire, cars, and death then I wouldn't hesitate to buy at the full $30 price.

Mad max is one of those rare movie licensed triple A games that actually stays true to the movie's universe which I found very surprising. I felt the need to talk about this title simply because of how fun, tense and gripping the gameplay actually was both with the car combat and ground combat, as well as its gritty survival mechanics which made me actually feel like I was a wasteland brawler trying to survive without a care in the world.
Lets start with the pros of the game:
- There are side activities galore to be had here, this is a sandbox open world exploration game that feels like they are trying to tick off boxes for everything a sandbox game should have. I see this as a good thing because the gameplay itself makes up for this, plus if your a completionist like me you will want to find all the collectibles, take out all the threats and upgrade max, the car and the fortresses completely which can be very rewarding at the end.
- Scrap metal is the main resource in the game which can be collected from literally anywhere, it can be used to improve Max's fighting skills, his car known as the Magnum Opus and all 3 fortresses in the game. Improving these 3 fortresses will give the player bonuses when returning to them like replenishing their ammo, health and car fuel for example. Unfortunatly to collect scrap you will have to get out of the car a lot more which I find irritating as it breaks the immersion a bit, but that doesn't mean the car combat is not there, its just spilt 50/50.
- The upgrades for Max and the car are actually really useful, melee combat stays the same most of the time sadly using a combat system similar to Arkham origins by pressing Y on the controller to block and X to attack and RB to roll out of the way which is pretty much it. Car combat allows you to change your gameplay stlye all the time however, using the harpoon to pull off enemy camp doors, car doors and tyres. The thunderpoon can be used to destroy enemy armour, while Max has his trusty sawed off shotgun that can be used in both melee and car combat. Things like border spikes can be upgraded to prevent enemies from bording, in other words car combat is the best here.
- The side activities actually have a wide variety in them, theres just a bit too much to do for them. Old world history relics are an interesting read for collectibles. Project parts can be found all over the place to upgrade fortresses. Eliminating threats in all 3 regions like scarecrows, camps, top dog camps (harder camps with a boss at the end) Convoys and snipers are a great way to earn more bonuses from your fortress upgrades.
- Convoys once eliminated will earn you a new hood ornament to customise the car with, while taking out top dog camps will earn more paint jobs for both the car and max.
- The game runs smoothly at 1080p 60fps and is an amazing good looking desert, with things like rusty old ships buried in the sand, swamps and camps all over the place so hats off to Avalanche for making a desert look nice which can be tough to do from scratch.
- Death runs can provide another nice side activity which include things like death races to compete with friends in an online leaderboard.
Unfortunatly this brings me to some of the major cons of the game, but dont let these put you off from buying it
- The side activities can become a bore to a lot of players because there are simply too many things to do. They dont have to be completed but it still feels a bit irritating, there could have been a wider variety here.
-  The character development in this story is unfortunatly lacking, while the characters are all interesting they felt very short lived, there wasnt much tension in this story at all sadly, luckily the gameplay made up for that.
- The story itself wasnt very gripping, you basically have to upgrade the magnum opus so max can reach a certain area, basically point A to point B with a lot of enemies inbetween, most open world triple A games have been made this way nowadays so its something to expect but still its gameplay was fun at least.
Summary
If your a completionist, want a game thats different from most, is post apocalyptic with a combination of exploration, car and melee combat and basic storytelling this title is completely for you.

I really wanted to love this game. Honest. But, it is just okay. It is not a space sim, it is more of a tactical space game with RPG elements. There is a badly voice-acted plot that is really not engaging. You advance the plot by playing the missions - you are not forced to play them. There are additional "side missions" that have a very rough plot - these are single missions, and again optional. There there are tons of jobs available, varying from scientific reseach, repair, assassination, convoy defense, etc.
Graphically, the game is just okay. I have a powerful gaming PC with wicked powerful GPU (GTX 980), and the game was very smooth until one mission where I had to attack a space station. Lots of ships arrived, and the game stuttered quite a bit. This, along with just decent visual graphics, means it is not very impressive graphically.
Sound-wise, the game is just okay. Music score gets redundant real fast. Voice acting is HORRIBLE. Seriously, you and your high school friends could do better. Sound effects are decent.
All of this would have gotten the game maybe a 4 out of 5, but the game is buggy. Seriously buggy. About 10% of the time the game will just lock up - alt-F4 to kill it, re-open it, and lose your progress for the however long since the last time you docked at a planet/station (which creates a save). On top of this the game has serious playability bugs. I reached the Shinova mission in the plot, and encountered the same bug that litters forum posts all over - the enemy go blue (friendly) right after the dialog, the ship I need to rescue is waiting for me to kill everything, and there is nothing to kill. So the game sits there. Forever.
This bug has existed for a while, and forum posts from the developers say that they have "fixed" it at least once. But over and over again people run into the bug, and it totally halts game progress. All you can do is finish up side missions, then you can wander around for contract missions (which are VERY repetitive). I contacted support, sending them my savegame, and they NEVER replied.
It is not a bad game - it is decent. No great, nor good, but decent. Buy it if this type of game interests you, and hope you avoid the Shinova mission bug. I found a workaround for the Shinova bug - use a t-drive to appear directly on top of the map point. The mission starts immediately because you did not kill anyone on the way in.
Again, if the game were less buggy, if the developers responded to emails, etc., I would give this game 4/5. But I can't.
