Super Meat Boy is an incredibly difficult 2D platformer. The objective of the game is simple, reach the end of each level in the shortest time possible to get to Bandage Girl. Whereupon Dr. Fetus, who hates Meat Boy, will teleport in, and whisk Bandage Girl off to the next level.
I was going to write a long review here, but the word limit stopped me. Instead I will list the positive and negative points of SMB.
Positives -
- Precise, simple control scheme
- Incredibly challenging
- 300+ levels
- Bosses
- Secrets (100 Bandages to collect, secret characters, hidden warp zones)
- Excellent music (The darkworld remixes the lightworld music to make it sound more... evil. Very cool effect)
Negatives -
- Incredibly challenging. (To see why this is a negative as well as a positive, play the warpzone titled "The Kid". Go on I dare you...).
In conclusion I would recommend this game to anyone that enjoys 2D platforming games, especially if they like a challenge.

Spec Ops: The Line is a hidden gem in the shooter genre. In the wake of other AAA titles like the Call of Duty, Battlefield, Gears of War, Just Cause, Resident Evil and countless other shooter based franchises, Spec Ops: The Line truly captures the essence of great gaming that is usually missed by other tripple A titles. A heart felt story with likable characters who go from clean-cut delta operators to rugged murderers with heavy conciouses. The story is truly beautiful with severeal different endings all of which prove to give the feeling of sorrow as you see how far Capitan Walker has fallen into darkness. Stellar voice acting that progresses as you move through the campaign and reacts to situations. Spec Ops: The Line take away the romanticised views of war that most war games have and open the player's eyes that in war you're going to make choices between outcomes that are wrong and wronger, there is no right in war. With beautiful writing and an action pack campaign Spec Ops delivers 110%.
Some people complain that many of the choices you make don't have too much effect on the story but personally i belive the devs made it this way to show that in times of crisis a lot of the decisions you make are insignificant because in the end everyone dies in a blaze of glory and only the lucky can make it out alive and even then, they leave part of themselves behind.
The only things I can find wrong with the game are the♥♥♥♥♥♥multiplayer (so close to having the perfect game but sorry), and slightly wonky controls, however you get used to judging distance before hitting certian buttons (example: accidentally meleeing a car instead of going into cover because you were too far away when you hit the cover/melee key)
Don't get me wrong, the game doesn't bring anything new to the shooter genre, some could even say it starts off as a generic shooter game but, it quickly shows that it did so deliberatly in order to show the true horrors of war. What it does is use everything the shooter genre does right and fix the one thing it does wrong: leave out the results of your actions and the true horrors of war.
I would highly recommend this game to all fans of the shooter genre and those who are casual players of shooter games because this game is truly an experience that everyone need to experience once in their life.

First off: If you are expecting a fresh and new game that has never been done before: This is the wrong game.
This is a very niche game – it caters to people that want another classic collectathon adventure platformer. It has dialogue like the old games, it plays like the old ones aswell. They didn’t make them new, they just made another one in the series. So, if you loved these old collectathon and want to play another one with pimped graphics: This is the game for you.
+ Beautiful, consistent artstyle
+ Absolutely amazing soundtrack
+ Controller controls feel nice and responsive
+ World feel fresh, different and very large without feeling empty
+ Invisible walls are rare, allows you to take all the jumps and paths you wish (Also allows you to sequence break)
+ Very nostalgic experience, they captured the old style very well
Of course, this game isn’t perfect, it comes with a few annoyances and downsides:
- Camera feels very wonky at times, especially underwater
- Camera snaps into fixed angles in a few areas, usually without a transition, feels very unclean
- Slow text speed paired with unskippable text during choices makes dialogue feel sluggish sometimes
- Weird design choices – You clear a Puzzle you can figure out to get to another Puzzle you can’t clear yet
Overall this game is exactly what I expected, and very good at that. I can only recommend it, even more so if they tweak the camera a little more.

I backed this game what feels like years ago,and lemme tell ya it was well worth the wait. I had exremely high hopes for this game, and it absolutely blew past my expectations by miles and then some. I absolutely love every bit that I've played so far, it's incredibly detailed, the dialogue is funny in its own charming way. Honestly, this was supposed to be a spiritual successor to Banjo-Kazooie, and in my humble opinion BK couldn't hold a candle to this game.
So how does it run? Well my computer is a four year old laptop/potato with a few wires poked in, and I had to mess with the resolution a bit and set the grapics down to the "Fastest" setting but it still runs good. It's a bit jittery in places, but *that is entirely my computer's fault* not the game.
What about the controls? First off use a controller, it's designed for it. The controls are super responsive, Every movement feels good, every attack does exactly what it's supposed to and it feels good doing it, every screw-up I made has been entirely my own fault and the controls reflect that. You won't miss a jump because the controls are bad, you'll miss it because you're terrible at jumping, is what I'm saying.
Okay, well how about the Graphics then? Beautiful. It's spit-polished to a shine. Shame my own computer can't run it at much higher than 1280x720 but it looks absolutely beautiful even at that low setting. The amount of detail in every rock, every enemy, every little thing is just sublime. It's easily the most beautifully designed game I've seen in a long while and I can't even play it at its full potential.
Grant Kirkhope did the music. If you don't know who this gentleman is, I invite you to play Banjo-Kazooie, -Tooie, and Donkey Kong 64. It is so reminiscent of BK it had me humming along in no time. The songs are very catchy, and memorable and very fitting to the Worlds they're matched to.
The characters are all very charming and the humor is a bit British at times, so if you're an uncultured American swine like myself you might miss a couple of the jokes but that doesn't take anything away from it. The dialogue between Yooka and Laylee really bring them to life and they have their some serious charm and they're just absolutely adorable in their own right.
All of this, and I haven't yet found the World 2. I promise you, if you liked BK and other "collectathon" games like it, you'll be hard pressed to find another game this well polished and well done. I can't recommend this game enough.
TL;DR Beautifully polished, fantastic music, Awesome Gameplay and controls, charming characters. Buy this game.

Edit / Continuation
So now that's I've essentially completed the game I figured I could add more to my review.
First I still enjoy the game, all the worlds were really good except Moody Marsh, it was a bit dry/bland to me and didn't really feel like it fit the game. Especially considering of all the characters you encounter in other worlds for challenges, almost none of them are used in this world besides the requisite Rextro, Kartos and Dr. Puzz. There's four shopping cart characters, which I don't understand... it's a swamp and here are shopping carts, why shopping carts? Why not use other characters you encounter in the game or swamp specific characters. Also quite a few challenges in this world are really lacking compared to the other worlds'. And unlike the rest the Rextro coin is not near Rextro... at all.
The Casino world reminds me completely of Sonic Adventure, it gave me nostalgia for a completely different game, which I thought was cool, and almost none of the challenges are luck based, but even those that were just took a few tries i.e. the Plinko type challenges. I will say though this probably had the most difficult Kartos challenge, you pretty much can't hit anything and seems a bit bugged. The boss is also incredibly difficult and can on occasion get into a loop of not allowing you to attack it.
Probably the worst thing in this game are the mini games, most don't seem to be well thought out at all in what the high score is you have to beat and two, Hurdle Hijinx and Up 'n Nova are very long and really hard to beat just regularly without the high score portion. None of these should have lives, and the quill loss from getting hit needs to be changed because currently it's proportional to how many you have which requires a near perfect run it seems.
I do like the idea of expanding worlds, it does give more to explore. I can understand them going this route as they could focus on really developing each World. The visual interest is really good in all, except Moody Marsh, I enjoyed exploring them to find everything, though in a few cases some quills won't be in areas you can explore before the expansion, but will be there after (World 5 the initial transformation challenge area).

For years I wanted a new game in the Banjo Kazooie line up. It has been 17 years since the last proper installment in the series and the idea of a new entry seemed less and less likely every day.
Well here we are in 2017 and it finally happened.
It's not quite Banjo Kazooie, not quite Banjo Tooie and not quite any of the other Rareware games it's taking inspiration from. It's an amalgamation of them all with new ideas thrown in. It's hard to see why people don't like it. There are certainly areas where it doesn't quite hit the marks in comparison to the predessors and I know that shaking off 20 years of nostalgia is hard to do when looking at a new hyped entry. But even Yooka Laylee certainly is a welcome addition to the series.
One of my favourite additions to the game is the new protagonists and the abilities unique to them. While they look like a reskinned Banjo and Kazooie they actually do feel quite different in the best possible ways. Yooka being a chameleon now allows him to do actions entirely unique to his species; you can't imagine Banjo turning invisible or copying attributes from specific items, can you? The same goes for Laylee to a lesser extent. This time instead of just being wings and a way to move faster she also has her sonar which not only differentiates her from the obvious comparison but it leads to nice gameplay both in and out of combat.
The rest of the characters don't disappoint either. A lot has been said for a particular snake but only focusing on him undersells the comedic roles of the other characters. At their best they're amazing and highlights for the entire Banjo series and at worst they're just alright.
Oh and the music for the game is phenominal. It's certainly a different direction but I can safely say I love all of it. In fact the Minecart music for World 3 has been stuck in my head since I first heard it, and I love that it's still playing for me.
I don't get the hatred for Yooka Laylee at all. It's a fantastic game and while it may not live up to some people's hype I don't see any reason for it to be treated the way it is. Yooka Laylee isn't perfect but neither were Banjo Kazooie and Banjo Tooie. That doesn't stop any of these 3 games being amazing titles worthy of anyone's attention.

"On release players have access to the Intro Pack content - Prologue Mission, the Paris Sanguine Fashion Show, full access to Contracts Mode, Escalation Mode, elusive targets and other live content. The way I read this was that you had different contracts and different modes and they would be releasing content throughout the year, like DLC.   I thought contracts were more like side missions.  In reality, all contracts really do is allow you to kill someone else in the same missions you get on release.  No going to California and killing some movie star. This is the most overhyped game I can ever remember playing.  It's not only a step back from the first Borderlands, it's uninteresting, frustrating, and tedious.  There is a large amount of content in the game, but overall the experience isn't worth more than $5, in my opinion.  The enemies are cheap, overpowered, and unintelligent.  If you're not fighting monsters that can destroy 90% of your HP/Shield in 1-2 hits, you're fighting invisible teleporting monsters that move faster than your bullets.  Seriously, the speed of bullets in this game will make you feel like a monster 100 feet away is actually a mile away.
I'll sum up the story in one word:  boring.  Every single story mission sounds straight forward to begin with, but when you reach your objective, 100% of the time something will go wrong and you'll end up backtracking and doing a whole bunch of other stuff to accomplish what seem like simple goals.  Menial tasks is story missions.  Unbelievable.  There were three times in the course of hundreds of lines of dialogue that made me laugh.  90% of the dialogue was written with the intent of being funny, but it's not.  The "comedy" feels forced and unnatural.  The game tries way too hard to be comedic and the whole effort just seems like the writers were trying to manufacture memes.  The most memorable character from the first borderlands is barely even featured in this game and has become just another uninteresting NPC.
This is not an RPG (it has quests but you might as well call every game where you fetch a key an RPG), it's an FPS where there is no strategy in taking down your opponents.  More importantly, it's a loot-grinding game much like Diablo 3.  I hope you like Twitter, because if you want weapons that will actually let you progress through the story without doing dozens of side-quests, you'll need to watch their Twitter account so you can get good loot.  In the course of this game, I saw two purple rarity weapons.  Follow them on Twitter and you can get a key that will give you more than that.  Don't want to do that?  Hope you like side quests.
Let's talk again about the enemies.  Invisible, teleporting enemies that can also run faster than your bullets do not make good enemies.  They are annoying ones.  There are probably a dozen, maybe as many as 18 different enemy types (not counting bosses).  Many of the enemies will simply spawn all around you when you enter an area.  That makes the game challenging, but not in a fun "I can do this!" kind of way.  It's more like, "Why the hell did all of these dudes emerge from huts once they had me surrounded?  Why can't I enter or blow up the huts and approach areas like I don't want to be killed?  Why did anyone think this would be fun?"  The vast majority of the encounters you will face are difficult because the enemies are so much more deadly than the player.  It can take hundreds of bullets to kill a single enemy, but that same enemy may only need to hit the player twice to kill them.
The AI is almost nonexistant.  Enemies spawn all around you, occasionally take cover, and usually just walk towards the player without any regard for their own safety.  Enemies do not flank the player except by accident.  There are TONS of kamikaze enemies, but even the ones that aren't kamikazes prefer to be right in the player's face, shooting the hell out of you.  This is a good strategy for them because they are ridiculously bullet resistant, but it's cheap.  In short, the enemies are cheap and annoying in almost every instance.
The heart of this game is about loot.  99% of the loot you will see will not be an upgrade and will be sold.  In the first Borderlands, I felt like I was getting upgrades all the time.  In this game, even the big upgrades feel weak.  Elemental damage weapons are more prevalant in this sequel, but interesting weapons have been removed.  There are no shotguns (at least that I ever saw) that shoot bouncy projectiles, but there are weapons that explode when you reload them.  After the first few hours of the game, it will feel like no weapon upgrade is enough to deal with the cheapness of the enemies you will face.  You will look at the stats, you will say to yourself "Now this is what I needed!" and after 15 minutes, the weapon will feel weak again.  The guns do look VERY cool.  Too bad they're not.
The classes are just tweaks of the first game's classes.  Pathetic.  I tried really hard to like this game and was excited because I enjoyed the first Borderlands quite a lot, but I was very disappointed.
3/10 - Too much hype, cheap enemies, boring characters/story, social media is part of game design, and bad loot.  HOPE YOU LIKE TWITTER.

A classic game set in the classic universe. This is a must play not only for the Star Wars fans.
+ Magnificent and balanced combat system
+ Choose your style: single, dual, or a sabrestaff
+ Variety of guns
+ Use the Force, Jaden!
+ The protagonist doesn't have to be a human :)
+ Option of choosing between the light and the dark side
+ Soundtrack
+ MULTIPLAYER
+ Tons of player-created content
- Plot isn't an A+ material (but it's not bad by any means)
It's a blast from the past – still fun after all these years. The game tells us the story of the Jedi struggling to prevent the Cultists from resurrecting Marka Ragnos – an ancient Dark Lord of the Sith.
The protagonist, unlike in most of the games in the Jedi Knight series, is one of the Luke Skywalker's students named Jaden. One can choose race, gender, and appearance of the main character. What is more, the hero's lightsabre can be customised as well. Later on, there is also a possibility to choose either a single blade, dual blade, or a sabrestaff. Each of the weapons feature a different playstyle, animations, and moves. In addition to the elegant weapon(s) for a more civilised age, there are a few guns and explosives available.
The lightsabre combat system is truly unique and works like charm. It is easy to learn and hard to master. It punishes the weak and empowers the strong, so to speak: it rewards well-timed blows and dodges as opposed to mindless mashing the buttons as fast as possible. Moreover, it is well-balanced: every playstyle is viable. Apart from fencing, a player can use a variety of Force powers which are divided into three categories: Neutral (e.g. Push), Light (e.g. Heal), and Dark (e.g. Lightning). In single player, a player can assign points to the Light and the Dark side powers (the Neutral ones grow as the story progresses).
While single player is decent, the clue of the game is its multiplayer. I have put around 200 hours in the multiplayer alone and I definitely am looking forward for more. Despite the game being past its prime, it still has a small but devoted community. There also are myriads of mods, characters, maps, and other types of player-created content which further improve longevity of the game.
Concluding, Jedi Academy still is one of the best Star Wars games in my opinion. I have yet to play a game with a more enjoyable and balanced combat system and I strongly recommend trying it out even today: it may look dated, but the core mechanics are timeless.

Garfield Kart is a racing game developed by Gravity Europe releasing on PC in November 2013. The game has also been released on Nintendo 3DS previously as well.
We have all come to know what to expect from kart racing games from the likes of Mario Kart in the past. Most kart games that have come out to try and rival Mario Kart have often fallen flat on their face. Prior to playing Garfield, I had played another kart racing game on Steam, Coffin Dodgers and sadly that didn’t live up to the mark. Garfield Kart is almost an identical game to that of Coffin Dodgers.
Gameplay is going to be simple when it comes to kart racing, simply beat your opponents in the race around a circuit. There are 16 different courses to race around with 8 different powerups to collect around the circuits too. The game’s tutorial is back to front when it comes to explaining the controls; whether they did it with a different controller in mind I am not sure, but the controls on an Xbox controller were the complete opposite to shown on the screen. Garfield Kart has three different game modes to play, Grand Prix, Single Race and Time Trial. Grand Prix is the more structured part of the game, where you take part in 4 or 5 races at a time in a league, depending on where you finish in the races will determine how many points you get. Single Race is more like the “free mode”, whilst you can gain money from competing in races here; there aren’t any huge rewards for winning. Time Trial is what you would expect from a Kart Racing game; nothing too exciting and certainly the least interesting of the three modes.
There is one final game mode which is where Garfield does something a little different to the rest of the Kart Games on Steam. A daily challenge mode is included, complete the set task and you will get a reward at the end of it. This is a really easy way to gather better upgrades for your car without having the need to grind out money by replaying previous tournaments.
Graphically, Garfield Karts looks really nice. It looks like one of the cartoons, with some really nice modelling, textures and animations on show. The game’s environments are all very nicely designed as well. The sound effects do let the game down a little bit; it can sometimes seem too quiet at times. Your engine noise can almost seem too quiet for it to seem realistic which something which felt really odd when playing is. The sound track is really catchy though.
Garfield Kart has three levels of difficulties. Whilst you are not able to choose the difficulties per race, you choose which bracket of difficulty race to take part in; 50cc, 100cc and 150cc.  Obviously the higher the number the more powerful the rest of your opponents cars will be. In order to even be competitive in the 100cc and 150cc bracket, you will have to completely upgrade your car using the upgrade system; you are able to purchase items for your car which will improve three criteria of performance, speed, handling and power. You will also be able to choose from a selection of helmets which will also grant you a specific bonus for individual power ups which you can collect. Whilst I really liked the upgrade system, it does feel very much like a grind to unlock items as you have to replay previously won competitions in order to get anywhere close to being able to buy anything. I would have personally liked to have seen a reduction in the price set on the items so you aren’t forced to replay already played content if you don’t want to.  The daily challenge mode helps with this, but only if you play the game in small doses.
I have been playing for over an hour so far and I have just completed the first bracket of races whilst also taking part in the daily challenge and a couple of time trials. There is easily another 3 or 4 hours of content from this game. Sadly the game will have very little staying power and I will more than likely not play the game again after completing the three stages of difficulty. With the lack of any multiplayer mode, the developers have really shot themselves in the foot of making game out of a genre which is so perfectly crafted for any type of multiplayer action.
As the Steam page says for this game, there is only partial controller support for this game. The gameplay itself works well with a control, however you have to navigate menus with your mouse, making a bit awkward to play on a couch setup.  There is a wide selection of resolutions to play on, right the way up to 4k, with minimal graphic options to change.
To sum up, Garfield Kart is purely an OK game. There aren’t any glaringly obvious negative points; it’s just not going to blow your socks off with exciting game play moments and hilarious local multiplayer. The only thing that resembles Garfield in this game is the character models; there is no story, no voice acting, and nothing else that makes this game any different to a generic kart racer. Luckily the game is priced low at £5, 59, and for that price you will get some enjoyment out of it, just don’t go into it expecting all the bells and whistles of Mario Kart.  I’ve marked it down as a 3 on my scale, it’s not the best game, but it certainly isn’t a bad game either. If you can get it less than the sale price, you will want to consider checking it out for an hour or two of action.

Garfield Kart is the third title in the massively popular Garfield series, following 2008's Garfield: Devasta Coastline and 2011's Garfield: Tides of Darkness. Garfield Kart follows the titular character 'Garfield' and his crew of ragtag mercenaries as they continue their search for the buried treasure of the legendary pirate captain Orion Baskerville. The sound design is absoloutely top-notch, from the report of gun, rev of an engine or blood curdling squeal of an undead aboriginal pirate. Guest voice actors include Michael Rosen, Johan Hegg and Alexis Texas.

My only criticism is that the controller support is a bit dodgy, the only button prompts i could get to show up on screen appeared to be from a Neo-Geo pocket X.
Overall, 9.75/10 would definetly play for 104 hours  again

The basis of this game is, you are thrown into a strange but amusing scenerio that you have to climb or crawl your way out of, with only your two hands being controlable, And then being thrown into a slighty harder/longer level then before. Your two hands are constantly getting stuck on various objects and even inside yourself and due to the lack of camera controls this makes it very hard to get unstuck.
The grabbing system is also rather dodgy. There have been multiple times where I have went to grab something and at the last second it changes, therefore making me fail or have to climb again. The mouse controls are very strange aswell. It's not that they are

I should also mention this was solely on solo. I was planning on playing co-op but I decided against it after my initail experience.
Firstly I would like to thank the developer for being mature and listening to the feedback given. This is rare with indie developers. Secondly I must apologize as I didn't mention you could lower the music and sound effects, but I do still think that by default it is too loud.

Once again I would like to applaud this developer as even though I didn't enjoy the game, he is listening to feedback

A title that deserves much more recognition than it has. I'd categorize Spec Ops: The Line as one of those games that everyone should play before they die. As many fans of the game will tell you, however, it's hard to explain my recommendation without spoiling the beauty of the game itself.
Gameplay-wise, there's nothing remarkable to write home about. The game is played from a third-person perspective, and unlike other shooters I've played, the controls feel awkward and clunky at times. The gunplay isn't terribly exciting and some confrontations tend to drag on for long periods of time, so I did find a lot of the fighting to be repetitive. The developers do throw some interesting dynamics into the mix that help keep things fresh, such as semi-destructible environments and the ability to issue minor squad commands. However, I could never recommend Spec Ops on its gameplay alone.
And I'm not. The main attraction--by far--is the plot, and it's why everyone should give this game a shot. Spec Ops delves deep into the questioning of morality and good intentions. It makes us question if we can define a side as "good" or "bad" in a given conflict, and it warns us of the potential repurcussions of acting on half-truths and speculation. At its surface, and for the first hour or two of the game, Spec Ops masquerades as a typical, generic military shooter. But by its end, it leaves us uncertain of even ourselves.

Jedi Academy is the latest and greatest (2003) of the Kyle Katarn/Dark Forces Star Wars series and the only one that I was able to play recently, due to the older games’ incompatibility with more modern Windows versions. I was unfortunately unable to get the game to run at higher resolutions than the default 800 x 600, but since I’ve played the game before, I was able to go through pretty fast and just ignore the poor graphics. The game is more than a decade old after all.
The game’s story follows a new Jedi recruit named Jaden as he tries to work his way up to Jedi knight status. He has to hit the ground running though, since his very first day arriving at the academy there’s an attack by a mysterious Sith cult called the Disciples of Ragnos. This cult of dark force users is led by Tavion, one of the minor villains from a previous Jedi Knight game, who has now acquired some ancient Sith tech and is able to power up herself and her followers with it. With some help from your master Kyle Katarn, you have to stop Tavion and her followers from their grand plan of resurrecting a long dead Sith lord.
Like the preceding Dark Forces Jedi Knight games, Jedi Academy is a first person shooter except when you pop out your lightsabre, then it switches to a third person perspective. Honestly though, you should probably have your lightsabre out all the time, so really it’s a third person sword game where you can use guns if you want. Right from the start you have a few force powers to choose from, such as push, pull, speed, and sight. These powers improve naturally as you go through the game and you can also choose between light/dark powers such as heal, lightning, protect, etc. I’ve played through the game about half a dozen times and I almost always get the same powers (heal, lightning, dark rage). They’re just too good to skip. You won’t be able to max all of the available skills, but you do have some room to experiment.
The guns in the game, while good, just can’t match the effectiveness of a lightsabre. The lightsabre not only kills most enemies in one hit, it also deflects enemy lasers. As you progress, your ability to deflect/reflect enemy shots improves, and by the end you probably won’t be taking much damage from stormtroopers. The true obstacles in your path will be the cultist warriors who use lightsabres and force powers of their own. Lightsabre combat is a huge part of the game and if you suck at it, you’ll be stomped many times over. Fortunately (or not) there seems to be a tremendous element of luck when it comes to sword fighting, and if you swing wildly, there’s a good chance you’ll chop down the weaker enemies easily. Just remember that the game doesn’t autosave very often, so if you don’t manually save before sword fights, you might end up replaying large sections of the game. Remember how I said there was a lot of luck involved? Yeah, a weak enemy can slice you down in one shot very easily.
Pros:
+Right from the start you have force powers and a lightsabre, unlike the previous Dark Forces games I played. The sword fighting can make you feel like a badass with the slow-mo kills and katas (flashy sword moves) that you can use.
+The story is intriguing and you get to try out a bunch of Star Wars weaponry. Most of them suck, but the concussion rifle is pretty cool. Watch out for the splash damage though, it’s huge. Remember though, that guns do not work on enemy force users. They either reflect the shot at you or just dodge it like Neo.
Cons:
-The game is very old, and with that comes poor graphics and incompatibility with Windows 7 & 8. You can get the game to run, but the screen resolution thing is very annoying. I tried everything from using compatibility mode to manually setting custom resolutions and restarting, but it just never changed.
-It is possible to just run through most of the game not fighting anyone, especially in the last few levels. The vast majority of enemies will stop chasing you if you get more than one room away. This includes the more powerful cultist sword masters as well (the real threats). Also, if you’re looking for an overpowered force ability, the force lightning can get you through most of the game, clearing out entire rooms of baddies in one shot.
Overall, the game is fun to play, and if you have it from the recent Star Wars bundle, this is probably the oldest game on there that I would still replay. The other Dark Forces/Jedi Knight games have aged poorly and may not be worth it, despite how good they were back in the day.

Ok, time to write my first initial expressions. I backed this game when it was on kickstarter when it stated it would be a spiritual successor to Banjo Kazooie.
This review contains some mechanics-related spoilers. I marked them whenever appropriate.
Summary/important things:
- Game has backtracking
- Camera is a bit janky, but is usable (for me), sensitivity two notches down
- Jiggies seem to have quests/challenges attached to them, so no "finding them in the wild" -> I may be wrong on that since I haven't played the entire game (yet!)
- Typical BK humour
- Typical BK voices, if you are getting annoyed by them, try skipping it with 'jump'
- With a controller the controls feel tight
Expectations:
- Specific kind of humor, dad joke like
- A lot of collectibles
- A lot of things to explore
- Difficulty ranging from easy to medium (to be fair, most of the jiggy's weren't hard to get; end boss of BK was quite hard)
What I got was :
- The kind of humor clicked for me
- A ton of collectibles
- A lot of things to explore (may be too much for some people because levels get  quite large)
- Difficulty so far is easy to hard (but that may be me getting used to controls).
Controls:
- I played this on an Xbox 360 controller
- Controls felt quite tight, especially if you don't press the stick forward like a neanderthal when doing precision stuff like rolling.
- Jumping, turning in the air on a dime is quite nice for me at least. I didn't have too many issues overshooting jumps.
Camera:
- It felt a bit trigger happy at the start so I turned down the sensitivity (2 notches to the left).
- I feel like the camera snaps back to the default position a bit too quickly, a bit of an elastical feeling.
- Some spots have a fixed camera, which I generally am ok with, the camera tends to snap abrubtly to those spots. I can live with that but it is something to take into account.
- Snappiness of the camera, I made this  a specific point since I feel like this can be tweaked (maybe smoothly move the camera instead of snapping it into place).
Gameplay:
- 2 worlds in, a few moves are like the classic ones
, some are new and refreshing
- Worlds could have used teleporter pads since they start to get quite big, especially
- Some
paigies are easy to get since some challenges have no time limit and you can take as much time as you want. I will call them jiggies from now on :D.
- Other paigies are challenging (or I suck at the game ;)), like a certain race at the start, certain arcade mini games and a mini boss in level one took a bit of time to get used to. I liked that.
- It seems that (most of) the jiggies have a "quest" for them. I am ok with that but some people would like to find them like in BK, so keep that in mind.
Performance:
- Runs fine, no noticed framedrops.
- Music was popping a few times during screen transactions at the beginning, not noticed that later on. Odd. Let's hope it stays away.
- Advanced graphical options are lacking in the menu's. Maybe some .ini edits are possible.
- Loading times are good, on a 7200RPM hdd, it loads levels in like 10 seconds.
If I have anything more to add, I will let you all know. So far I am enjoying it. Recommended.

As a lot of people have stated, if you were a fan of Banjo-Kazooie and other Rare games like Donkey Kong 64, then you will absolutely enjoy this.

Approximately 6 hours long, it's what you'd expect from a CoD Campaign. It's pretty much a non-stop interactive action movie with a good variety of guns (of which you can choose in your loadout before a mission) and, you guessed it, quick time events. The story is decent but I felt that the Strikeforce missions were subpar. I would describe them as RTS x FPS x Wave-based shooter missions that had objectives to complete, but I just felt like they were a fill-in for the (in my opinion) short single-player campaign. I enjoyed the futuristic setting, but I just felt like the overall presentation was slightly lacking. Having said all of this, I have to say that I did enjoy the singleplayer but, if that's what you're wanting to pay $90 for, then I'd suggest you give it a miss.
Unless you've been living under a rock for the past number of years, you're most likely interested in CoD because of the multiplayer (or Zombies...). I put a tad over 40 hours into it (because I joined the party late... 2 years late, that is) and, I have to say, it was enjoyable. Frustrating at times with connection issues but, for the most part, it was fun. 2 CoDs have been released since this one, though, so you may find that the playerbase is lacking. I live in Australia, and I had no troubles finding people to play with on 50ms ping, which is good considering the age of this game now (in terms of CoD's lifespan...). A good variety of weapons and maps and, again, the futuristic settings was a nice change to the semi-bland modern settings we've seen in the past. It isn't worth the $90 asking price it is now, so I'd say get it on sale (or somewhere cheaper...).
I have to say, I was a fan of the zombies mode that appeared in the original Black Ops, but unfortunately (mainly due to a lack in playerbase) the zombies mode in this game did nothing for me. I'm sure it would be a lot of fun with friends, but unfortunately because I got this 2 years after release, I had to go solo, which I found kinda lame... I did only play this for about an hour, so be sure to check out other reviews instead of relying on me!
- Fun game, especially with the variety of Singleplayer, Multiplayer and Zombies
- The futuristic setting is a welcome change to the CoD formula
- Unfortunately due to it's age (now), it's lacking in a Zombies playerbase, but it currently maintains a decent Multiplayer population
This over-the-top action first-person shooter is worth playing but I can't recommend it for it's price, so get it when it's on sale (if you're interested)! Enjoy :D

Yooka-Laylee is finally here and I have things to say about it.
First off, if you are a big fan of Banjo-Kazooie... then you will probably love this game. Despite what I've read in reviews, the puzzles, and controls and music are actually pretty spot on in recreating the feel, the tone, the atmosphere. From the minute you see the logo, the characters garbled speak, you will be in nostolgia heaven.
That said, if you are specifically nastolgic for bear and bird, and possibly a skull wearing shaman and nothing else, then you may be disappointed by the classic feel with out your fave cult hit characters. Likening it to an imitator or just seeing it as a game living in that legendary series shadow.
Personally I think it's better than the original Banjo-Kazooie (speaking from a level design stand point specifically), but not quite as refined and as well thought out as the very intertwining worlds of Banjo-Tooie. Some things will also never be replaced... like picking up puzzle pieces as opposed to magical gold pages.
Putting all the nostolgia aside though, the real issue with the game is in fact it's performance. It's simply not optimized very well. I've tried various settings and frequently still see slow down, doesn't matter the level of detail. Hasn't been enough to outright frustrate me, but I can see random frame rate dips here and there affecting people as they are trying to control the camera and make tight platforming jumps. This is where the original games antiquated controls and feel would actually be seen as a negative. The games traditional 3D patformer controls work great.. but that's when you aren't wrestling with the performance issues.
Either way, I went in expecting the worst based on what people were saying about the game, and honestly from an art style side, and level design side the game is actually great at replicating the feel of the original B-K games.
One recommendation though... if you didn't already know, worlds start off small and then can be expanded later with pages you've collected. Expand as soon as you are able. Don't bother exploring a world in it's base form if you have the option to expand it immediately. Simply put the worlds are incomplete until you do, and you will awkwardly find yourself running into curious areas that turn out to be dead ends... and only become something worth discovering after you've expanded the world. It's really the only game design flaw I can honestly say was not worth trying.
_____________________________
So should you buy it? If you are a fan of the B-K series, then definitely.
If you are a fan, but are still on the fence because of performance, well it never hurts to wait either. It needs more polish in that respect and I can't blame anyone who waits till they've made some tweaks to the game.
If you aren't a fan of the series it's based on... it will probably be harder to get into, but if you like quirky adventure games with a great sense of humor give it a shot.

Just note that my recommendation on this game comes with a condition attached to it. Don't just look at the thumbs up and think that that's it. Also, this review is only taking place as Episode 1 is out. If you're reading this for anything more than that, then this review is probably outdated.
PROS
- A return to the classic Hitman feel. The Blood Money roots are absolutely in this game. For previous fans of the series were were scorned by Absolution, don't worry about this being a repeat of that. In my opinion, this game takes the best bits of Blood Money AND Absolution, then expands on them. It should be noted that for the main Absolution features (Instinct, markers, etc.), there is an option to turn that off for a more purist feel to the game.
- Graphically, it looks very good. Screenshots really do not do this game justice. It looks beautiful in terms of design and aesthetic. While it isn't something that you would showcase maybe, it's leagues ahead many.

- Gameplay flows VERY well. I can't say that there was ever a moment where I got frustrated with the controls of the game or anything like that. If there is something that I want to do, then I can do it very easily. Plans can be carried out almost flawlessly. Though note that I do say 'almost' here. The one thing that comes to mind is maybe climbing buildings can be a little faster. But it's something that you'd be rarely ever doing.
- A living, breathing atmosphere that is very easy to get immersed into. As of Episode One, the main level is The Showstopper, a fashion show taking place within a very large mansion. When I say that I could easily believe myself to be there, I mean it. NPC conversations are plentiful, and nearly everyone is given a personality of their own. Every nook and cranny of the place is very high detailed as well. to the point that I am still (After 13 hours in) finding new things to do on this level. Of all, I hope that this is something that continues on into future episodes.
-Amazing replayability. Challenges, contracts, new things to discover, different plans to test out, this game has it all. You're not going go into this level, kill your targets and suuddenly have no other reason to play. For each target, there are literally dozens of ways to kill them.
Cons
-Always online DRM. So this is a pretty big one. I'm starting here because above all else, this is the thing that I hate the most. Players were never told that there would be always online DRM. And much more, if you suddenly disconnect from the servers, you're kicked out of the game. I'm just going to put it lightly and say that this is absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Hitman is a single player game. The only online feature that would warrant this are the Leaderboards- which even those are absolutely worthless. Want to see 50 people who scored 210,000 on a level? Check the leaderboards.
Oh, and then we have the fact that modes like Contracts, escalation, your end screen and all are cut from the game when you're offline as well- thus stripping any replayability from this game if you don't have a stable internet connection. This is NOT cool.
-Bad AI. AI is pretty weird. Not sure how to explain it more than that. But you know what I can explain? How much ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t Always Online DRM is. Hitman is a series that, in itself has a lot of replayability. If I wanted to, I could pop in Blood Money and have a GREAT time.  And that game is 10 years old.  Do you think that Square Enix is going to be still supporting this game 10 years on? No. So basically, this game is going to tank. It's not a question of /if/ but rather /when/.
-Lacking weapon variety.   And you know the worst part about that too? I love this series. I always have and I always will. So to see such a beautiful game go to waste because of the DRM is just heartbreaking. Oh yeah, and there aren't many weapons in this game, most notably a sniper case.
-Poor optimization for some users. I'm using an Nvidia card and at launch, there are reports of AMD users once again getting the♥♥♥♥♥end of performance.  Meanwhile, the rest of the fanbase gets the assend of this industry. Always online DRM.
Would I recommend this game? Yes. If you're a fan of the series, then definitely check this game out. Currently, the intro pack is 15 USD. If you can get it for cheaper, then have fun. You'll get a lot of replayability and have a pretty fun time
However, if you're new to the series, first check out Blood Money. See if you like the premise of the game because some very well don't, and that's understandable. Then when you're finish with Blood Money, seriously ask yourself if you're willing to deal with always online DRM. Like, sit yourself down and start questioning your life choices. Think of everything that led you up to this point. Think about growing up, the experiences you had. How there used to be a time where you bought a game, went home and played it with no questions asked. Think about how much fun you had.
Now imagine a rich Japanese man coming over and snapping your disk in half because some people over in Russia played the game for free that one time. Do you want to give this man money? What's that? No? Okay then pop Blood Money back in and have fun.

Let's just get right into it.
This new installment brings a very interesting concept to the Hitman Series. It's episodic, which you will either love or hate (personally I think it's a neat concept, as it allows for players to explore many different ways to eliminate their taget or targets before proceeding to the next level). The first real level is absolutely huge. I have played a little over an hour of the level, and I'm pretty sure there are MANY more ways to kill that I have yet to discover. So A+ in terms of creativity and map design/size.
Most of the mechanics present in this installment have been adopted from Absolution, which is a good thing.
The graphics, most noteably in cutscenes, has durastically improved from the blotchy-ness that Absolution had to offer. It's as if they got rid of the artsy look they were going for in Absolution and went for a more Blood Money look; again not a bad thing.
Now to the only real complaint I have so far; framerate. I constantly get drops in framerate and it can't possibly be a hardware related issue. This is more than likely something that will be fixed in an upcoming patch, or at least I hope so.
Overall, I like this 're-imagined' version of Hitman. But due to performance Issues, I'll give it a strong 7-8/10.

The TL;DR: Amazing Pool game for both veterans and beginners. With many game modes(rule sets) and Free Play, local and online multiplayer, and several things to aid beginners, such as aim assist, an interactive tutorial to teach trick shots, and to always have the controls listed on the side of the screen. This, of course, can all be turned off.
Great pool game! The main game modes in single player seem to be 8 and 9 Ball Tour Modes, where you play that ruleset against increasingly difficult AI opponents, who have humorous Bios. However they have other game modes/rule sets as Bonus Matches in the tour. Each opponent has 3 Stars you can collect as an added challenge, which can be completed for extra replayability. You get the first star simply by beating the opponent, which will also unlock the next opponent. The other 2 stars are gained by completing the objectives which are different for each opponent, then winning, since even if you complete the objectives, they won't count unless you win the match too. These Challenges range from doing specific trick shots, reaching a certain score, using no flashbacks(feature where you can redo a shot twice per match), etc. There is only one use for stars. Each of the Bonuses Matches are 'linked' to an opponent. When you beat that opponent, therefore getting 1 star, the next opponent is unlocked. However, to unlock the Bonuses Match linked to that opponent, you must have at least 2 stars, which includes the one you get for beating him.
There are 2 Tour modes, each containing the same 4 competitions, each divided into 3 Rounds. Each competition is increasingly more difficult. In order of easiest to hardest: Sky Lounge Cup, Exchange Square Cup, West Coast Trophy, and Valley Lodge Masters. Initially you only have access to the Sky Lounge and Exchange Square Cup, but you can unlock them in order, starting from the Exchange Square Cup if you wish.
Each Competition features a new area, and each Round features a version of that area at a different time of day. So Round 1 for the Sky Lounge During the Day, Round 2 for Evening, and Round 3 for night. Each time of day alters the look of the area to varying degrees, all of which look great. Beating a round will unlock that location/time to choose when creating a Versus or Online game.
Now for the Bonus Matches I mentioned. In each Tour mode, there are various 'Bonus Matches' which deviate from the 8/9 Ball ruleset, which are Straight, Rotation, Killer, 3 Ball, etc. Completing the bonus match will award you a star, and also unlock a new graphic for either your Cue Stick, Table Decal, or Pool Ball skin. Bonus Matches are not necessary for advancing in the Tour.
There is also a Versus game mode, which can be against a human player or against the AI. You start with one AI opponent on the easiest difficulty, and you unlock more by defeating them in the 8 and/or 9 Ball Tour. For a Human vs Human Versus game, it's a local multiplayer game, where you either share the keyboard and mouse, or 1 person uses the keyboard/mouse and the other uses a Controller. Theres many ways you can set up a Versus game: You can change the look of the Cue Stick, Pool Balls, and the Table Decal with skins/textures you've unlocked during the Tours Bonus Matches. You can change the ruleset, ranging from the classic 8 Ball and 9 Ball, to Straight Ball, Speed, Killer, Golf, 3 Ball, and Rotation rulesets. Online mode is basically the same, but with added ranked/unranked/custom options.
In the main menu there's also "Free Play" mode. This give you the 9 Ball set up, but you can do anything you like. There's no human opponent, and you can consider it a practice mode, especially for practicing your trick shots. You can pick up the cue ball whenever you like and place it wherever you like. Once you pocket all the balls, it simply resets the table. I like to use this mode when I want to relax, practice trick shots, or just goof around and see how many balls I can send flying off the table in one shot. Pity you can't send it through a window. :p
Also in the main menu is Endurance mode. In this mode you need to make shots(also called 'potting' or 'pot') as fast as you can. New balls will constantly spawn, and when the active ball count on the table reaches 24, you lose, so you need to keep potting. After potting enough shots, you'll earn a brief period will the spawn rate will completely stop, giving you some breathing room.
One thing that should definitely be mentioned, is the Aim System. There's various aim modes which will project not only where the Cue Ball will go, but the direction of the ball you're hitting. This is great for making not only regular shots, but making trick shots easy too. There's multiple levels of Aim projection, which will gradually decrease how far it will project the shot, then only show the cue ball's path, and finally no aim mode, where it won't even show the Cue Ball's path. This, combined Free Play, will help you become better and better.
While we're on the subject of practicing, there's a Tutorial mode in the Single Player menu. This will teach you how to do various shots. From simple straight shots, to Jumping, Curving, Knife, Kick, Bank, etc shots. It's great for learning the various moves. There is an odd graphic bug/oversight. While the tutorial plays, it will always show the keyboard/mouse bindings at the top, but when it's your turn to try the shot, it'll show whatever control method you're using. It's not a big deal, since the controls are simple and there's even an option in the settings that will let you push the Help button, which is 'X' for controllers and 'K' for Keyboard, and will show all the controls at anytime and any game mode, so this game does great for helping beginners, but has the option of turning them off.
You can save replays of your matches too, so you can view them again. Also works in Free Play mode. The replay feature isn't as fleshed out as it could have been, but it's okay.
People have complained about controls, so I'll throw in my opinion: After playing it for a few hours with both the Xbox Controller and Keyboard, it does feel like it was intended to be played with the controller. HOWEVER, the keyboard and mouse controls are still great and nowhere near as bad as some have complained, and feel almost completely natural. I say 'almost' because I'm the type to keep my hand in a single position and dislike moving it too far. However, it's very easy to remap the keys closer, and honestly, only 2 or 3 keys I needed to move closer, and they weren't even necessary really. And in the Straight ruleset, the shot calling function was very awkward and overly sensitive for the keyboard/mouse. The replay modes keyboard/mouse controls are also awkward to use no matter how you map it.
Anyway, to summarize: Great pool game, many game modes, online multiplayer, and great controls for BOTH the keyboard+mouse and controller. Most of the complaints on the keyboard controls are over exaggerated.

Pool Nation has a very realistic physics engine, with very nice graphics. There is a ton of achievements to be unlocked and replayability is great.
There are, however, a few problems with this game:
a) If you simply want a quick game, it isn't so quick, because there are lots of menus to go through, and the cutscenes before the game starts are painfully long.
b) the graphics are great, beautiful, but some of them very unrealistic when it comes to pool tables. The developers did a great job exploring the rendering engine they had in hand, but I believe there was no need for so many fancy and colored pool tables and balls. IMHO, a pool table has to be green. Forget about everything else, because it just gets in the way of the game.
Neverthless, Pool Nation is a great game, worth every penny. I am not afraid to say it is possibly the best pool game ever made, and the closest thing to a pool/billiard/snooker simulator.
If the developers ever read this, I have a suggestion: make it possible to create custom game rules, like we do in real life.

TLDR; CAVEAT EMPTOR, BUYER BEWARE
So, the third outing of Rocksteady Games' Batman: Arkham franchise is upon us. Rather than Rocksteady Games however, new developer Warner Bros. Montreal are at the helm this time, and it shows. Based on an Xbox playthrough, I can safely say WB:M were very wise to make no radical departures from the existing Arkham format, characters and locations feel very familiar, the near legendary combat engine is present in full with only minor adjustments (parry leniency, strike range, shock gloves). Everything feels pretty good, barring the odd input quirk here and there (Silent Takedown? Why not walk the dinosaur instead?). The actual game itself is really good.
But there's a problem. There's a laundry list of problems. We are pretty used to half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥PC ports by now, but throw in core system problems including save corruption on consoles next to a staggering list of PC issues (see
to get started) and you have a highly questionable release on your hands. While WB:M assure they are "working on it", things are looking chilly.
I've been unable to complete the game on PC, only on Xbox, due to ranging issues including startup and exit hard system freezes, and ultimately save file corruption 10 hours into the campaign. Given the sheer number of issues the game is having on various platforms, and the lack of resolution to these problems from the recent fixer patch, I probably won't keep trying.
All said and done, I am unable to recommend Arkham Origins in any way shape or form at this time. A potentially great game worthy of the Arkham name has been rendered unplayable by a seemingly untested, thoroughly buggy release.
Wait for a later edition (GOTY seems unlikely, hurr hurr hurr), or revisit either of the earlier Arkham titles instead.
Unless, like me, you're a giant bat-nerd, go get arkham city instead.

A negligible addition to such an astronomical series.
Arkham Asylum was easily one of the best action games of its time.
Arkham City took most of the best features of Arkham Asylum, and added significantly more content and a free roam, sandboxy style of gameplay. Arkham Cities huge list of additions and improvements give extremely high expectations to any sequel.
Arkham Origins on the other hand does very little, if anything, to build upon Arkham City's accomplishments. If anything, it is a disappointing failure, bluntly put.
Origins is simply too much of the same as Arkham City. While some people might not understand the significance of that criticism, hopefully the following context helps. Arkham Origins feels like Arkham City but with a 5 dollar DLC that adds 4-5, maybe 6 gadgets, and a 15 dollar DLC that adds a different story mode. At no point in this game will you truly feel like you're playing something that ISN'T Arkham City. This game is maybe only 5-10% different from its predecessor.
Please understand, Arkham Origins is by no means a BAD game, it simply isn't an excellent one given its high expectations. This game is only for people who are interested in Batman's story, and aren't necessarily looking for a gaming experience that is any better or different from Arkham City.
On the plus side, Arkham Origins features the best boss fights out of all three Arkham games, and has some of the best story telling as well.
The game is indeed a let down, but is still moderately enjoyable for die hard Arkham fans, or for people who have never played Arkham City to be entranced by the high expectations it sets. To everyone else interested, it is best to wait for the game to drop in price or wait for a sale. Arkham Origins, while it does a great job at telling the story of a younger and more reckless Batman and sets up the events of Arkham Asylum and Arkham City nicely, remains the overall weakest chapter of Arkham's Trilogy.

In some ways, this feeling while playing this game is very much like Don't Starve, even if gameplay is entirely different. The constant feeling of "oh♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; when you realize you've run into yet another problem encourages me to make new plans and upgrade older systems. I'll give an example:
In the beginning, some oxygen and food is given, but you need to make more. The first easy choice for oxygen requires the use of algea and electricity or algea and water. Eventually, you'll run out of algea, causing you to advance your methods either into making algea from slime, or converting water into oxygen and hydrogen.
While there isn't a feeling of 'congrats, you solved the problem!' as much as "oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ I'm running out of water, now what do I do to fix it?" where you figure out your next problem just as soon as you fixed your last one. That kind of game play is similar to Don't Starve in that you never feel like "Well now what should I do?" as much as "Now I have to do this".
Obviously this game is different in many ways from Don't Starve, as it is more of a management simulation with it being hard enough to never be boring, which for some people results in "too hard to enjoy". I enjoyed this game way too much, as I have spent many nights staying up to 'fix this one last thing'.
In earlier versions of this game, there weren't sustainable colonys-- eventually you'd run out of Something (e.g. water) that you couldn't get any more of. Those things have been changed, and we continue to see massive modifications and additions to the game. Remember this game is in Alpha, so if you don't enjoy the challenge or you have difficulty dealing with the issues as the game is developed, wait until later to buy it.

Oxygen Not Included is a wonderful little colony management game, with a soundtrack and graphical style that Klei mesh beautifully. The UI is responsive and intuitive while in-game actions are fluidly animated. I really dig the art direction taken in Don't Starve and Oxygen Not Included, it's crisp and colorful and bouncy and just fantastic. The wacky characters look unique and the procedural worlds are rife with diversity and content.
The main objective of this game is to corral an ever-growing number of settlers--around the guts of what seems to be a giant meteor--into a safe habitat of your own creation, and hopefully guide them to utopia. They each have individual thoughts, traits, and skills to manage as your stronghold expands, but ignoring your colonists' needs and desires will lead to a stressed colony. That's bad.
There's research, crafting, cooking, fighting, tinkering, building, micromanaging and a lot of exploring to be had in this game. I'm only about 50 hours in at the time of writing this review, but it's definitely something that I'll keep coming back to. ESPECIALLY with the continued free content updates like the recent Oil Upgrade and upcoming Automation Upgrade. Yay, Klei!
ONI is definitely worth it at its $24.99 price point. You're getting a deeply replayable, enjoyable simulation game. Have fun :D

If you loved Banjo-Kazooie, Donkey Kong 64, Super Mario 64 (or even Super Mario Galaxy), then you alreay know two things; what you're getting yourself into, and that you're going to love this game too. If you grew up in the 90's, you'll wear a grin ear to ear. From the atmosphere of the fairy-tale-esque storyline, to the silly 4th wall-ing of side characters who speak in gobbly-grunts; it's all here.
The two all-new mascotts are uniquely their own characters while still offering the parts of Banjo and Kazooie's personalities that really made
stand out. Yooka is a straight forward fellow, always willing to help for free, while Laylee very much reminds me of Kazooie; constantly cracking wise and seeking compensation. The basic move-set handles almost identically to Banjo-Kazooie or Super Mario 64, and it took me only seconds to memorize the controls (NOTE: I play this with a PS4 Controller). If anything, I nominate Yooka and Laylee as Super Smash Bros. Guest Stars in the next entry. Instant classics, enough said.
The music is superb and I found myself humming the main theme after hearing it only twice. Certain early areas of the game very much remind me Banjo-Tooie. Specifically worlds like "Mayahem Tample", "Terrydactyl Land", and "Gruntilda Industries". And that's no bad thing either. I was immediately happy with my decision to get the Digital Deluxe Edition just for the Soundtrack.
The graphics are like a modern version of the N64 Era. Things are purposefully designed to look kind of blocky, but with the edges and corners smoothed out in a way that just wouldn't have been possible back then. The colors a bright, and the lighting creates very nice shadows that caught my eye immediately upon entering the first world. In other words; it looks like you
the N64, not the way the N64
looks. I run the game in its highest settings just fine on an nVidia GTX 750Ti with only a single frame dropped
or maybe
. To sum it all up; it looks beautiful without being too hardware-demanding.
If you were a 90's kid like me, you simply can't afford
to buy this game. Your sense of nostalgia demands it.

I totally get the dynamic stuff would be hard to implement, but then perhaps an easier way to liven things up is to throw in some random stuff like starports getting blown up (then coming back online after repairs), or certain races getting push back into the fringes or something. You can basically just settle into trading and fighting between two starports and essentially, aside from the background visuals not being different than another area... that.. is all the game becomes. Easy to learn and hard to master. You start out with 3 people and a portal. You won't know what to do! You will die fast your first couple attempts! You will progress and still die! You will run out of oxygen! You will run out of water! You will run out of food! ... After a couple of hours you will finally get the hang of it, but just until you realize you didn't. And once you did okay-ish with your first 'real' colony you will just die again. You next colony will be bigger better and stronger for sure. Nope, you just died again due to germs. I did so many colonies and I could always think about at least 1 thing I could still improve on. The content itself is not that much, you will get/see everything that's in the game within a couple of hours. But getting the hang of everything and improving yourself/the colonies is on a whole other level. I really recommend this game to everyone who likes sweet/lovely graphics and really loves a good building and simulation game. Observing your colony, optimizing walk ways, hording resources, growing, dying... Starting all over again. You won't get a perfect/sustainable base. You will have lots of fun trying to get one though.

You will notice that almost none of the top reviews have more than 50 hours. That in itself speaks for itself how terrible and disappointing this game is.
First off, if you think 50 hours is worth 35 dollars, then hats off to you, buy this game. If you enjoy having games, especially games with open world, that has a lot of replayability, dont buy this game. The game gets old incredibly fast. I had bought this game while it was in Alpha, and i had hoped that new content would be added that would make the game much more interesting. Boy was I wrong and I will never EVER again support another developer with game that is in alpha or beta.
Now why does this game get old fast?
Firstly the game is completely static. Economies never change except for specific events where suddenly prices suddenly spikes up or down depending on the station. It also means if  you want to make money trading, all you need is 2-3 nearby stations and finding out a profitable trade route. Sounds fun you say? try doing it 500 times. Sure you make money, but it gets old and boring as ♥♥♥♥. The map, factions, and borders are completely static as well. My first game I spent about an hour exploring the map only to realize that there was no point in exploring new systems. The only benefit is new ships that may or may not be better than the one you own now. Plus majority of the♥♥♥♥♥♥that is available in different planet is available everywhere, so why even bother visiting another system? you cant conquer it, you cant buy unique rare items and trade it elsewhere and since price stays similar in most region that there is no point in making long trips to different planets. Why bother exploring in a big♥♥♥♥♥open world map? There is no point and there is no encouragment from the game to do so unless you have the money to buy new ships.
Secondly there is literally nothing to do in this game. Since Economy, Diplomacy and borders remain completely static, you have literally no impact in the game. You can have the most powerful or biggest and the baddest ship in the whole map, but whats the point? All you can do is shoot down other ships with it or break asteroids. You will spend 2 mins breaking asteroids when you realize that your cargo is already full. There is no point to mining when you make barely any money and can carry literally nothing cuz the cargo space is just tiny. Why bother upgrading your ship? Why bother buying a new ship? Why bother doing anything at all? These are the question i ask my self whenever i turn this game on.
Thirdly jobs are ♥♥♥♥ing horrible. There are couple assassination jobs, but they are either too easy or too annoying to do. At some point they are ever more pointless, because assassination offers literally nothing other than monetary compensation. Other jobs break down to transporting cargo, VIP or assisting other ships or patrol. They give you a good sum of money, but again they are incredibly repetitive with you making zero impact in the game. Most people grind for that awesome gear or item, but in this game, you grind so you can be even more bored and stop playing the game.
The only saving grace in this game is the modding community. I played the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of playing as the Imperial Stardestroyer.
The last thing that really ♥♥♥♥ing grinds my gears is the developers. ♥♥♥♥ you, I bought this game for you in Alpha, hoping and expecting great things, now that you got your cash you release ♥♥♥♥ing DLCs? are you ♥♥♥♥ing serious? ♥♥♥♥ you. Now I know your company is only ripping off of EVE popularity.

Here's some gameplay:
City Climber is a short but very entertaining physics game. The music is catchy, although loops a little on longer levels and the controls are well implemented, allowing both controller and mouse input depending your preference. I like to use the mouse as it allows precise movement of the arms, left and right mouse buttons control grip for their repsective hands.
The game isn't very long, it currently has 14 levels which are somewhat replayable due to a speed runners leaderboard and also a challenge mode which has 3 challenges spread across 30 stages (3x10). I wouldn't recommend for anyone looking for a lengthy experience but it has allot of charm, is well polished and the controls are allot of fun to grapple with.
There is also a character customiser where you can change the colour of your character and also add various headwear such as pirate hats and spy glasses, these are unlocked as you progress through the game.
There is multiplayer support, the story mode (14 levels) has a co-op mode where two players each control an arm. You need two controllers for this, one can use mouse whilse the other uses a pad. There is also turn based party play where up to four people take turns to plough through the levels in a hope to out pace their friends. It's a nice addition to have multiplayer in the game and it adds some replayability.
All in all I recommend the game, it's cheap and chearful but could benefit from some workshop support.

Yooka Laylee is a collectothon platformer basically taking the almost complete seat from banjo kazooie's design. Flat out, if you like Banjo Kazooie, DK64, Ty the tasmanian tiger, You're very likely to like this. However; at the same time you're not completely blinded by nostalgia, it gives you those warm fuzzy feelings that you get when you play your favorite platformer today, yet its not fully there.
I also would like to say, Yooka laylee is not a bad game, and anyone who tells you that is near blind, however it does have LOTS of flaws. Its still a great game in its own right, its just you're not fully nostalgia blind like you are when you play a game from your childhood. Those same games SUFFER immensely from the same issues Yooka has. (Terrible minigames, bad camera angles, oddly slippery controls at times, wonky feel and so on). I will be adding to my review later, but as someone who loves Banjo, DK64 and so on and still loves platformers to death, I know as much as the next guy looking in that all these games have immense flaws. During their time, yeah. They were stellar(besides DK64's glaring issues, still a great platformer). Yooka Laylee is like a game that was meant to be out well over 10 years ago.
POSITIVES:
- The soundtrack. Its amazing, some songs should be toned down a tiny bit sound wise, but its great. Definitely reminds me of Banjo in this regard.
- The control of Yooka/laylee is great in some aspects, in others.. It hurts(mainly during rolling).
- The levels are great so far, if not only for their design. I hear they get kind of worse later on though(will edit later if)
- Progression is amazing. Level and move progression is done amazingly, and this is how it should be done if this game gets a sequel, this is by far the most updated feature of the game. The linear progression of other collectothon games hurts, but this one is miles better in this regard.
- Its great visuals/performance. I haven't had a lick of performance issues. I've tried this on two different computers and both run it fine while one having pretty good specs and the other.. not really having the best.(Heading on I think 4-5 years old, with dated hardwware in it as soon as I got it)
- A semi modern but still the same way it was collecto-thon! Its great if you liked it in the first place.
- Great characters, funny personalities. as well as full of british humour.
NEGATIVES:
- OH GOD. THE CAMERA. In the toolbox this thing was alright, much better than what it is in game. Why, WHY did they mess it up. I hope they fix this later.. It hurts the game a bit(as it did with all games from that era) However, I might add q, and e seemed to fix a lot of the problems I had personally, but still is terrible in general. using q and e to move it did help.
- Non rebindable?(I haven't tried rebinding the keys because it worked fine. I also remember seeing options for it anyway.. so I don't know, this is other peoples word, not mine).
- Rolling movement is slippery, although it somewhat makes sense. not having as much control while in that state. However, it feels awkward with how yooka is normally on the ground. Why? I don't know, it was also an issue in the toolbox.
- Some soundtracks being too loud. Capital B's lair is stupid loud, and I'm not sure why.
- So far, the minigames have been annoying to me. They were bad in banjo and any other platformer, and they're bad here. I imagine there is some fun to be had, but like those games they are the least enjoyable part to me. They haven't overstayed their welcome, but they haven't made me happy either.
- Enemies are painfully average, but you do have a number of ways dealing with them. I kind of wish there was bosses like DK64 personally, they weren't hard or anything, but a slight fight would've been nice.(banjo also suffers from this).
- Wheres banjo threeie. Where. OH yeah, building cars. I forgot. whoops. Ugh... Hate that damn game.
-CONCLUSION-
Its a good game, with issues that could be fixed, at least the more glaring ones. I suggest picking it up if you like platformer-collectomaniac type games. Definitely not bad, but I'd probably give it a 7 when its being nice and a 6 when its in the bad area. Its a game that was meant to be out a long time ago, not now. Like. 2002 maybe. Most people are nostalgia blind, and I love banjo myself and everything else from that era.. and I miss playing them to this day. But they have just about the same glaring flaws that this one has, even with the improvements to progression.
