So I've been reading through some of these reviews and it's hard to believe what's being said..
"The colors and world design are mediocre / too bright for my eyes"
"The character voices are too annoying for me to sit through"
"The keyboard support for this spiritual successor to Banjo Kazooie doesn't feel good"
"This isn't Banjo Kazooie.. they messed this one up"
Dear lord, some of these people really don't read what they've written before they post a "review" of the game. Did you play the original banjo kazooie on your keyboard / mouse? Were the bright polygons too much for you back then since half the game was practically flashing you in the face? Just how badly were the character voices annoying you when it was the exact same style in every N64 predecessor made by this team? Did you moan about the world design during the original when it incentivized you to explore and discover characters / rewards / cool little tidbits? "This isn't banjo kazooie.." DID YOU READ THE NAME OF THE GAME YOU BOUGHT??
Yooka-Laylee is the spiritual successor to the Banjo Kazooie games, made by many of the veterans of the 3d rare platformers on n64 (Like Donkey Kong 64), and this game was made for those who have been itching to get some more of their fill of fun characters, collecting, exploring themed worlds, and enjoying the music of David Wise / Grant Kirkhope. If you're looking for a game where you can have a couple chuckles from some fun character writing, bouncy / bright soundtracks, running around (...platforming.) and playing little mini - games while traversing through worlds that can be expanded upon (Upon expanding the first world for the first time, it felt like I had another solid hour or two of gameplay within that world), and return back to the N64 feels of video games, this is it. Upon playing for around 5~ hours, I felt the same immersion within the game that my younger self felt playing the Banjo Kazooie games. I know I'm really into a game if I'm actually chuckling from the in-game dialogue. Also, bonus points for keeping it somewhat non-linear through choosing to unlock new worlds, or offer a huge expansion on the previous world you've already unlocked! It's great knowing that I have the choice to play through the game however I'd like to, and that I'm not nudged towards my next choice.
However, I'm not going to claim this game as perfect because it does have it's faults. I didn't really get the whole quiz show they threw at me because while it was reminiscent of tackling Grunty's castle in the original BK, it felt oddly stuck in there and took way too long for it's first appearance. It's also off-putting to see how easy it is to take down certain enemies, as if they were bowling pins waiting to be taken down by you, the spinning lizard/bat bowling ball. Some people may not enjoy certain aspects of the controls since again, they're reminiscent of N64 platformers which admittedly, aren't perfect and can be considered slightly sloppy. I'm not going to recommend this game to anyone playing on keyboard and mouse because frankly, I'm not going to bother trying to see how the spiritual successor of Banjo Kazooie plays on a K/M; It's a goddamn controller game. Finally, I wouldn't be able to recommend this game to people who dislike repetitive / nasally voices since some of the characters can come off as annoying to any newcomers for this genre.
Would I recommend this game though? If you grew up playing platformers in the 90's / early 00's, then absolutely. This game is a blast waiting to happen. I've been waiting for a game like this for over a decade, and I'm so glad it's finally here.

This game seems really polarizing but as someone who has played a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of banjo kazooie and can easily deal with bad cameras, this is a pretty goddamned solid experience. There is far less polish than that of past rare games but I still feel as if it retains a lot of the fun.

It's really a nice platformer with a fair amount of the charm and humor the old Banjo games had.
Overall, the first hour or two of gameplay is a nostalgia trip for BK and BT players, but the rest of the game holds up well on its own.
*Things to note:*
The camera issues a lot of people are reporting are overblown, but that doesn't mean they don't exist. The camera's a little stiff and sometimes feels like it follows behind the player a little too aggresively, though this is rarely an issue and just something you'll get used to as you play. If you need to look around a lot, just stop moving and the camera will move completely freely. I also had the camera get stuck behind scenery a couple of times, but it fixed itself within a second or so both times, so no biggie. My suggestion is to max out the camera sensitivity so you can control it more easily and avoid it getting stuck without interupting gameplay.
Controls can't be remapped. This is fine for controllers, but it's a huge missing feature for keyboard/mouse or disabled players. If you really need controller remapping though, Steam's Big Picture Mode has you covered, just go into the Steam settings while in BPM, pull up the controller settings, turn on mapping support for your controller of choice, and then use the "Steam Controller Configuration" menu that's visible before launching a game.
World 3 is a bit confusing to find. Find and go under the gate in Waterworks to reach it.

Hitman is an action adventure stealth video game developed by IO Interactive and published by Square Enix.  Hitman is the sixth entry in the Hitman series but is a prequal rather than a reboot of Codename 47 (2000) or a direct sequal to Absoultion (2012).
Hitman is IO Interatvies attempt at remaking the franchise for the next generation of Hitman games.  Once again to take the role of Agent 47 at the start of his career with ICA under his handler Diana Burnwood, as you did in Codename 47 but with a new story.  The game stands on its own feet in terms of missions and is not a dirrect remake of the original.  However where the game falls short is the story itself.  Not that it isn't good so far, but it is short.
Absolution had something like 21 levels giving you an interactive story to play thru.  Hitman was released with only three levels if you count the two training levels, the same two training levels we were given to play in Beta.  The story is substituted with cut scenes to provide background on your assignments as well as intel you gather while in mission.  The game will release five more levels throughout 2016 for a total of six main missionsand two tutorial levels.  With only six main levels planed for the game, the main story is short no matter how well done it may turn out.
The story is extremely short and tries to make up for this in level design and bonus content.  The levels have been designed to be an open sandbox where you are provided with numerous methods of assassinating your targets.  Where the level design fails is that the maps themselves are still rather small and lack the feel of other open world games in the action adventure stealth genre, like Assassin's Creed games.  Had IO Interactive went with larger maps say, a quater of Paris in AC Unity and allowed us to actually explore the city and pick up contracts all over the city, then being limited to six maps excluding the tutorial missions would be enough for to provide a satisfying story and exeprience.
The bonus content is quite good providing you do not get overly bored with the same level to run them on over and over again.  Contracts mode is back from Absoultion and improved upon.  Escalation mode has been added which is similar to doing contracts made by others only the requirements continue to become more and more challenging with each completion.  Elusive targets is something new to the live game feature which is a plus to gameplay.  In Elusive Targets, you have a limited time to kill targets until they are gone and no longer available.
Due to the bonus content of this game being interactive online with the community, there is an Always Online DRM feature to this game which has caused waves of disapproval.  If you choose to play offline, you are extremely limited in your choices to play the game.  So much so that while I am not overly bothered by online DMRs, I do see a design flaw  that causes problems for people trying to enjoy Hitman.
Being offline not only limits how you play the single player game, if you happen to be disconnected from a mission do to your isp or the server, your mission is ended, you lose all of your progress and must start over.  Now for a training mission that really isn't that big of a problem however if you just spent 40 mins reconing targets in the main mission and get killed before finishing the mission or your recon, the issue becomes a much larger one.  Why a save feature was not implemented here so you could continue to play offline if you DC'd I have no idea but it was a bad decision.
The graphics are next generation and look good at 4k resolutions.  Considering how many NPCs are in each level, that is an accomplishment.  However, don't expect Rise of the Tomb Raider or Division quality graphics here because it isn't to either games level of fedelity when playing on ultra settings.
The graphics do not require a beast of a machine to run, but they do have issues.  The graphical issues at play once again with a Square Enix game is that it is not optimised for SLI/Crossfire.  Although it will run in SLI/Crossfire the performance improvements are little to none.  Like most games designed for consoles and ported for PC , the game is not optimized above 60 fps.  The target always seems to be between 30-60 fps for consoles which causes issues for more and mroe PC gamers as we move to higher quality monitors supporting 75, 90, 120, 144 hz and above monitors. Once you go above 60 fps in Hitman you take hits in performance and visual quality.
The game play and controls feel exactly like you would expect a Hitman game to feel like if you have played any of the other Hitman games. The controls work very well and I did not experience and bugs with them.  The game play felt smooth if you exclude graphical hickups due to pooor optimazation and driver support. The Menu could have been better for tacking opportunities but other than that I liked the menu, hud, and UI.

Indi games are a prime example.  We are willing to rate these games on a different scale overlooking many flaws because the game was independently developed/produced. Who we are is not just what we appear to be on the outside. When you think of Garfield, you may think of a lazy cat lounging next to some of that sweet, sweet lasagna and otherwise not caring about a single thing that doesn't involve naptime. However, what you believed Garfield to be will be crushed in this harrowing tale of smashing our limiters and truly becoming who we are behind the mask that society gives us to live by, Garfield Kart.
In Garfield Kart, you play as any one of the Garfield cast in thrilling and chaotic go-kart rides through insane and strategically-involved tracks everywhere from Egypt to industrial Zimbabwe. After racing you can customize your racer with special items such as hats, spoilers and new karts. The items you buy effect your driver performance, and some item sets are made specifically for a certain driver. Stacking a full set of driver-specific items onto the driver they were meant for makes you very powerful, and in the world of Garfield Kart, you either get good or die hard.
During your gameplay you may wonder why some characters act out of place according to the setting of the original comics they come from. The nurse (Liz) turns from helpful hand of medicine into a competitive matriarch who crushes the enemy beneath her iron go-kart, and even Garfield himself acts out of his usual lazy character. All of the people in Garfield Kart seem to be only alike to their comic counterparts only in appearance (and even that is questionable once the hats start rolling in). How could this be? You may wonder to yourself how these characters could be so unlike their original bases, until you realize one day that they are not different at all.
Garfield Kart isn't just a tale of a friendly competition between some friends (and also that stupid grey cat who keeps hitting me with aliens RIGHT BEFORE I FINISH THE FINAL LAP IN FIRST NERMAL I WILL END YOU), but the tale of self-actualization and the breaking of societal norms through sport. Garfield himself abandons the mask so forced upon him by society to become his true self. The character customization store is just another way to self actualize, with every set of items for each character representing who they really are in the dark. When you finish a set of items for a character, you successfuly break society's pre-determined path for this character and allow them to be themselves once more. This is also why the completed sets make your characters much more powerful.
Garfield Kart is a triumph of the gaming industry, and is more akin to a work of art that focuses on the trials and tribulations the people of today go through to become their true selves. I think we can all take a page out of Garfield Kart's book, and strive not only to be the best we can be, but to also become who we know we are deep inside.

Firstly, I'll confess, I bought this almost immediately after watching Markiplier's first Let'sPlays of it. lol
Something about it, just so goofy and exciting, silly and challenging. I love games with slightly grindy tedium... like Minecraft. Thing is, I'm normally not so fond of 2D layouts like this. Resource-management and building theme aside, this was a special case for me. And I've played Don't Starve, as well. I was terrible at it, it was stressful in an unrewarding way, and the lack of being able to enclose yourself in something securely had me giving up on that game after less than a week. But I notice, this game does the opposite. You're trapped, trying to dig your way out (despite there not technically being an "out"... yet), which is a fun reversal.
Now, don't get me wrong.
I absolutely suck at this game.
Honestly? I barely manage to survive past 40 days or build any big machines that purify and recycle your "less sanitary" resources, so my efficiency is pretty low in the long run.
But you know what?
I don't even care. lol
I don't think I've ever run across a game in 25+ years that was ever as fun to just keep failing and trying again and again. I learn something new each time, and the world seeds can leave me in a dry pit to die in a handful of cycles, or I might get lucky enough to find a place so rich with food and water and oxygen readily available, that I don't even need to make any advanced machines for dozens of cycles.
I think this game emphasizes to me that I'm personally more of an explorer, or an artistic builder... not so much a calculator/computer. And I'm probably never going to be like those players whom've built perfect systems that last 300+ cycles. (I've seen these. Wow.) So I think I'm kind of hoping that with future updates, they might not only have an actual end-goal option, such as reaching the surface and having to build transmitters to call for help, or maybe terraform the surface of whatever rock they're on to keep going at whatever pace they like.
10/10, I'm technically failing to conquer this game, but having the best time ever while doing it. lol
EDIT: I've made it to over 100 cycles with no advanced technology greater than a coal generator! HUZZAH! I started a new save though, left that one where it was because I'm not likely to be able to keep up with it very well. lol

This is the most overhyped game I can ever remember playing.  It's not only a step back from the first Borderlands, it's uninteresting, frustrating, and tedious.  There is a large amount of content in the game, but overall the experience isn't worth more than $5, in my opinion.  The enemies are cheap, overpowered, and unintelligent.  If you're not fighting monsters that can destroy 90% of your HP/Shield in 1-2 hits, you're fighting invisible teleporting monsters that move faster than your bullets.  Seriously, the speed of bullets in this game will make you feel like a monster 100 feet away is actually a mile away.
I'll sum up the story in one word:  boring.  Every single story mission sounds straight forward to begin with, but when you reach your objective, 100% of the time something will go wrong and you'll end up backtracking and doing a whole bunch of other stuff to accomplish what seem like simple goals.  Menial tasks is story missions.  Unbelievable.  There were three times in the course of hundreds of lines of dialogue that made me laugh.  90% of the dialogue was written with the intent of being funny, but it's not.  The "comedy" feels forced and unnatural.  The game tries way too hard to be comedic and the whole effort just seems like the writers were trying to manufacture memes.  The most memorable character from the first borderlands is barely even featured in this game and has become just another uninteresting NPC.
This is not an RPG (it has quests but you might as well call every game where you fetch a key an RPG), it's an FPS where there is no strategy in taking down your opponents.  More importantly, it's a loot-grinding game much like Diablo 3.  I hope you like Twitter, because if you want weapons that will actually let you progress through the story without doing dozens of side-quests, you'll need to watch their Twitter account so you can get good loot.  In the course of this game, I saw two purple rarity weapons.  Follow them on Twitter and you can get a key that will give you more than that.  Don't want to do that?  Hope you like side quests.
Let's talk again about the enemies.  Invisible, teleporting enemies that can also run faster than your bullets do not make good enemies.  They are annoying ones.  There are probably a dozen, maybe as many as 18 different enemy types (not counting bosses).  Many of the enemies will simply spawn all around you when you enter an area.  That makes the game challenging, but not in a fun "I can do this!" kind of way.  It's more like, "Why the hell did all of these dudes emerge from huts once they had me surrounded?  Why can't I enter or blow up the huts and approach areas like I don't want to be killed?  Why did anyone think this would be fun?"  The vast majority of the encounters you will face are difficult because the enemies are so much more deadly than the player.  It can take hundreds of bullets to kill a single enemy, but that same enemy may only need to hit the player twice to kill them.
The AI is almost nonexistant.  Enemies spawn all around you, occasionally take cover, and usually just walk towards the player without any regard for their own safety.  Enemies do not flank the player except by accident.  There are TONS of kamikaze enemies, but even the ones that aren't kamikazes prefer to be right in the player's face, shooting the hell out of you.  This is a good strategy for them because they are ridiculously bullet resistant, but it's cheap.  In short, the enemies are cheap and annoying in almost every instance.
The heart of this game is about loot.  99% of the loot you will see will not be an upgrade and will be sold.  In the first Borderlands, I felt like I was getting upgrades all the time.  In this game, even the big upgrades feel weak.  Elemental damage weapons are more prevalant in this sequel, but interesting weapons have been removed.  There are no shotguns (at least that I ever saw) that shoot bouncy projectiles, but there are weapons that explode when you reload them.  After the first few hours of the game, it will feel like no weapon upgrade is enough to deal with the cheapness of the enemies you will face.  You will look at the stats, you will say to yourself "Now this is what I needed!" and after 15 minutes, the weapon will feel weak again.  The guns do look VERY cool.  Too bad they're not.
The classes are just tweaks of the first game's classes.  Pathetic.  I tried really hard to like this game and was excited because I enjoyed the first Borderlands quite a lot, but I was very disappointed.
3/10 - Too much hype, cheap enemies, boring characters/story, social media is part of game design, and bad loot.  HOPE YOU LIKE TWITTER.

Don't be fooled by the 30 factions, there are essentially 2 - good or bad, and even then being "bad" is difficult due to how reputation is managed.
The gameplay is alright, but the most effective way of making money is SLOWLY towing in captured ships to salvage them. Cargo is incredibly limited on anything but freighters, but why would you ever fly a freighter? There is no sandbox or dynamic economy to speak of, so there's not point in being a pacifist. Regions are locked to one faction, the map is entirely static and the campaign is laughable. Large ships are only marginally slower than tiny ships, and no ship ever reaches the size of even the smallest EVE Online capital ship, so piloting a "fighter" is essentially the same as a carrier.
Still, I love this game.
The music is fantastic, the fetch quests are in an atmospheric enough universe that I don't mind the skinner box, the modding tools seem to be very powerful so a few of these issues could (or are already fixed). The ships don't look all that great (I don't think any game is going to reach the same level of lore and style as EVE Online), but I still love piloting them.
I love it, but I wouldn't recommend it if you don't have a specific itch.

This game is a TRUE open world space RPG. I really love this game, despite is few shortcomings.
Freedom: Full freedom to do whatever you want, wherever you want, whenever you want is why this game is great. You can become a full time miner and collect minerals, you can ferry goods from station to station and trade for money, you can capture enemy ships and DRAG them back to your base to sell.
Combat: Perhaps the best part of this game is the combat system. It is really like a 3d dogfight in space ships. Do not expect a true space physics, but the combat system is one of the most fun I have played. You actually fly the ship yourself and shoot the weps yourself. Direct full energy to shields to survive, weps to destroy, or engines to run like hell!
RPG: You gain levels as you go. You can kill ships for small XP or do missions for more XP. You can level up each of your 4 special skills, get bonuses to your "profession", and buy new ships at higher levels, each with their own special traits.
Glitches: I have had about 10 full crashes in 24 hours of playtime. I have many out of memory errors when I still have lots in task manager, although the game still runs, for a while... In game glitches are more frequent but less noteworthy.

The few misgivings I have are minor but I feel are worth pointing out:
- I encountered a hitch in the music at least twice. There were minor audio hiccups when transitioning between zones where the music shifts, but they were noticeable. Nothing that directly impacts gameply, but still.
- Swimming controls are a smidge wonky, diving and ascending still feel like they have too much input lag.
- The game's a bit easy. I understand that the game is primarily trying to please the old audience, but I also think they're not trying to scare away the new blood. I am very pleasantly surprised with this game. The humor is on point and the soundtrack is nostalgic af. If you don't want to play a N64-era-inspired game, then don't pick this up. All the negative reviews the game gets for being "outdated" are counterintuitive if the game's purpose is to be "out-dated."
Many of the new characters come close to the charm of Banjo-Kazooie. Yooka and Laylee's abilities are very unique and fresh. The structure of the game is open-ended; you can either advance to new worlds or expand your current one, all at your own pace. You also pick which moves to learn first.
The game looks great, controls great, and sounds great. Sure, there are a few minor bugs I've noticed, but nothing big enough to take away from the experience.
As to be expected, a controller is a must.
All-in-all: I am one very satisfied customer

Hitman is an action adventure stealth video game developed by IO Interactive and published by Square Enix.  Hitman is the sixth entry in the Hitman series but is a prequal rather than a reboot of Codename 47 (2000) or a direct sequal to Absoultion (2012).
Hitman is IO Interatvies attempt at remaking the franchise for the next generation of Hitman games.  Once again to take the role of Agent 47 at the start of his career with ICA under his handler Diana Burnwood, as you did in Codename 47 but with a new story.  The game stands on its own feet in terms of missions and is not a dirrect remake of the original.  However where the game falls short is the story itself.  Not that it isn't good so far, but it is short.
Absolution had something like 21 levels giving you an interactive story to play thru.  Hitman was released with only three levels if you count the two training levels, the same two training levels we were given to play in Beta.  The story is substituted with cut scenes to provide background on your assignments as well as intel you gather while in mission.  The game will release five more levels throughout 2016 for a total of six main missionsand two tutorial levels.  With only six main levels planed for the game, the main story is short no matter how well done it may turn out.
The story is extremely short and tries to make up for this in level design and bonus content.  The levels have been designed to be an open sandbox where you are provided with numerous methods of assassinating your targets.  Where the level design fails is that the maps themselves are still rather small and lack the feel of other open world games in the action adventure stealth genre, like Assassin's Creed games.  Had IO Interactive went with larger maps say, a quater of Paris in AC Unity and allowed us to actually explore the city and pick up contracts all over the city, then being limited to six maps excluding the tutorial missions would be enough for to provide a satisfying story and exeprience.
The bonus content is quite good providing you do not get overly bored with the same level to run them on over and over again.  Contracts mode is back from Absoultion and improved upon.  Escalation mode has been added which is similar to doing contracts made by others only the requirements continue to become more and more challenging with each completion.  Elusive targets is something new to the live game feature which is a plus to gameplay.  In Elusive Targets, you have a limited time to kill targets until they are gone and no longer available.
Due to the bonus content of this game being interactive online with the community, there is an Always Online DRM feature to this game which has caused waves of disapproval.  If you choose to play offline, you are extremely limited in your choices to play the game.  So much so that while I am not overly bothered by online DMRs, I do see a design flaw  that causes problems for people trying to enjoy Hitman.
Being offline not only limits how you play the single player game, if you happen to be disconnected from a mission do to your isp or the server, your mission is ended, you lose all of your progress and must start over.  Now for a training mission that really isn't that big of a problem however if you just spent 40 mins reconing targets in the main mission and get killed before finishing the mission or your recon, the issue becomes a much larger one.  Why a save feature was not implemented here so you could continue to play offline if you DC'd I have no idea but it was a bad decision.
The graphics are next generation and look good at 4k resolutions.  Considering how many NPCs are in each level, that is an accomplishment.  However, don't expect Rise of the Tomb Raider or Division quality graphics here because it isn't to either games level of fedelity when playing on ultra settings.
The graphics do not require a beast of a machine to run, but they do have issues.  The graphical issues at play once again with a Square Enix game is that it is not optimised for SLI/Crossfire.  Although it will run in SLI/Crossfire the performance improvements are little to none.  Like most games designed for consoles and ported for PC , the game is not optimized above 60 fps.  The target always seems to be between 30-60 fps for consoles which causes issues for more and mroe PC gamers as we move to higher quality monitors supporting 75, 90, 120, 144 hz and above monitors. Once you go above 60 fps in Hitman you take hits in performance and visual quality.
The game play and controls feel exactly like you would expect a Hitman game to feel like if you have played any of the other Hitman games. The controls work very well and I did not experience and bugs with them.  The game play felt smooth if you exclude graphical hickups due to pooor optimazation and driver support. The Menu could have been better for tacking opportunities but other than that I liked the menu, hud, and UI.

Recommendations are very subjective and while I can find many flaws in a game, ultimately our hyped expectations for a game is what determines our level of satisfaction.  Indi games are a prime example.  We are willing to rate these games on a different scale overlooking many flaws because the game was independently developed/produced.  While Hitman was a disappointment to me in many areas such as level design, story, and optimization I do find it fun, challenging, and rewarding to play.  Therefore dispite the games flaws and my own disappointments, I do recommend Hitman if you are a fan of the series and are aware of the always online DMR.

Star Wars fan or otherwise, the Jedi Knight series (JKII:Outcast and JK:JAcademy) has one of (if not decisively) the best swordfighting mechanics to date, on par with the likes of Rune and Severance. For this alone, they are worth playing.

If you want more acrobatic swordplay and are tired of the alternative's (Chivalry:Medieval Warfare / War of the Vikings) equally solid but slower pace, this is the one to try.

JA is fun and very entertaining: you shoot lightning bolts, force grip and cut your enemies down by the dozens and wreak havoc in general. Until you get to the end part of the game when 99% of the enemies are sith / jedi characters grouped in twos, threes or fours. At that point the game just ends up being tedious work - lure one of them close, kill, heal, repeat.

Have you ever wanted to be a Jedi? The Force isn’t strong enough in real life for you to be one? Well then, this game is good enough to satisfy that need. If you never wanted to be one, then this game will show you its charm anyway and afterward, you’ll fall in the former category. Despite its outdated look,  the gameplay is engaging and the story has the SW charm to it. This game has the original trilogy’s atmosphere, but it has more action.  Despite its predecessor, the level design won’t get you lost and there is less linearity, as you can select your gender, race, lightsaber fighting style and its shape and choice you make in the (near)end, whether to stay in the light or give into the dark and the consequences feel strongly(the protagonists attitude changes, some die, some get hurt, everything is awesome). There are some great moments for a Star Wars fan, such as fighting alongside Chewbacca, force choking Boba Fett, or taking a station down with Wedge Antilles.
The gameplay involves lightsaber fighting(this is what made the Jedi Knight series famous) that inspired the combat of Blade Symphony, as there are many duels. Aside from those instances, chopping arms and heads of stormtroopers that actually can aim is really entertaining.  Jumping on walls, then on your adversaries is a good example of how fluid the combat can be. There are three types of force powers: light sided ones,  which involve sustaining health by healing and protection, and turning your enemies into allies, the universal ones like force push, pull, speed, sense and lightsaber throw and there are the dark sided ones, which are damaging and risky, as you’ll enter modes that strengthen you while draining your health, exposing yourself with force choke or force lightning, though the latter, when upgraded to its zenith, means pushing everyone out of the room while having bolts all over them.  You also have an arsenal of weapons to your disposal, that have primary and secondary types of firing.
The story has its charm, as you start up as a student and end up being a Jedi Knight, there are many iconic characters and there is Kyle Katarn, the hero of the other Jedi Knight games.  The plot isn’t really intriguing, but it has its mystery. 80% of the game you’ll be doing missions that don’t seem to be related to the plot, but more to being a Jedi, that is keeping the peace in the Galaxy.
The game last for about 8 hours, provided you tend to be alive most of the time. For Star Wars fans it’s a treat and some don’t exaggerate when they call it the best Star Wars game; while it’s a matter of taste, this game ends up on being on the favorites list. For newcomers, it’s enough to make them understand why people go crazy over Star Wars. The game isn’t complex, but is good enough to spend time with it and enjoy doing so.

The problems I have with this game are the same I have with Just Cause 2. Avalanche Studios (the devs) excel at making a blend of GTA and Skyrim-like repeatable-events systems. The games are not bad,  by any means, but your tolerance for what the game offers may vary. The core gamepaly loop is enjoyable, but beomes quite repeatable.
Within the first two hours, I felt very on-rails, with a lot of "gather this" prompts for variosu items. My main problem settling into the game is that what the "tutorial" begining teaches you, it doesn't do a good job of. There were several times where what the tutorial meant for me to learn was not clearly comminicated, thus creating frustration and sometimes restarts of sections.
That aside, the game looks amazing, even on may aged rig. I run am currently running an Intel 2500k CPU, GTX 660 GPU, 16GB DDR3 1600MHz RAM, 7,200 RPM HDDs. The game runs great at near-maximum level (only ambient occlusion is tuned down to HIgh) at 50fps+ to a capped 60fps framerate. Game runs smooth and feels great.
I am enjoying the game, but it is not without flaws, and I will update this review as I play more.

it's a reasonably large sandbox with very little to differentiate any of the areas, and very little to do in any of them. There are a few bugbears, like cars phasing out of existence when they're out of view, and the lack of varied side-quests, but the main one for me is that you cannot drive into the fortresses, and you cannot accrue a proper convoy of cars - instead, you can only see them in a menu system, which frankly, fails to immerse. Also, there are no bloody bikes. In a Mad Max game. No bikes. Mad Max.
There is absolutely no replay value to this game, and I would certainly not recommend it.

Very mixed on this game, but I just want to say I'm a huge fan of Banjo Kazooie, Tooie, DK 64, Conkurs Bad Fur Day - I love them all and I've played them all at least 3 times over. I wouldnt recommend this game but I wouldnt say dont buy it. It's just like meh. I cant see myself playing this game for hours on end in one session, if you can then that's great. I just can't, it get stale pretty quick and traveling from one piece of the map to the next is exhausting. Stuff seems to spread out, it doesn't feel like there's a lot to do just a lot of traveling to do. Is it fun? Yes it was, but I got bored after awhile and needed a break. The camera is a presistent issue that limits my experience greatly, half my attention is adjusting the dodgey camera so I can actually play, which in itself is exhausting as well.
There's a lot of dialogue, soo much dialogue that I found it was just annoying and skipping through it all. Like I said before the levels are huge which I loved in Banjo Tooie, but in this game it didn't seem rewarding. It felt more of a nusiance and learning the level was difficult and clunky. The flow is very messy in that regard too, I can't find stuff, it just feels like an open world where objectives are placed at random. Additionally the puzzles dont fit in the world, it just feels like odd segmented parts where you go once and never return.
There's plenty of content though, I'll probably get around to playing the whole game maybe even collecting everything. But right now, the game feels like a chore.
Just wanted to add there's plently of pros to this game, like the music and the beautiful maps you'll play. I just feel like the few cons are so heavy weighted that it drags down the whole experience. As I play the cons become more apparent and more of an annoyance. I honestly love the golden age of rares games, I wish I had the same experience but the polish of this game just isn't there.

Basically the same as 'Jedi Knight II: Jedi Outcast' in controls, looks and feel only with more RPG like features:
This time around you get to choose your character and become a Jedi, starting with a light saber and then developing your force skills along the way. Upon starting a new mission you can choose a new Force power to upgrade (up to 3 points, each level making it stronger) from either the light or dark side. The Core Force Powers (speed, Jump, saberskills and sense [see enemies/items/secrets through walls]) are upgraded within set times between Main-Plot related missions. Along the way you loose your light saber and get to build a new one, but this time you get to choose. 1 LightSaber, Dual-Saber or Saber-Staff. Each Saber has its own unique pro's and con's and Special Moves.
All in all a good game, if you can get passed the (rather well) aged graphics!

I've played this game twice and it made me cry both times. This is by far the best game of 2015, the best game of this decade and probably the decades to come. Every boss fight changes the size of the battlefield and adds a brand new mechanic. Every boss fight is uniqe and exciting and fun, pure fun. Story never fails to suprise you and it always gets more and more epic. And like I said this game made me cry countless times in both of my playthroughs. It doesn't have limits that crack when you push them. Everything is thought of, you can't crack this game even by hacking. It's a masterfully-crafted and a solid experiance that everyone on earth needs to play. It'll stel your hearth then crush it, repair it and give it back to you better then ever. Max Payne lives in a world where thugs jump up to get shot down, where every few hours a grimly hand-painted comic book panel appears to aid him in narrating his life, and where a rogue cop on the edge with nothing to lose isn't something to snicker at.
Appearing in the post-Half Life "Gee do you think our shooter should have a story or something?" boom, MP is all about being dryly noir while providing you the player with an excuse to shoot as much of the population of New York as your trigger finger can stand. While games like Stranglehold and FEAR would later perfect the slow motion shoot-dodge-in-bullet-time antics seen here, Max Payne delivered them first.
Back in 2001 there was this real craze for people dodging bullets in slow motion (and if you think about this REAL HARD you'll work out why) and using it as the core gameplay mechanic added something rich to the whole experience.
That said, this game is retro-hard.
You'll want to abuse Quicksave here.

Both Batman: Arkham Asylum and Batman: Arkham City are excellent games. Batman: Arkham Origins continues on - riding the coat-tails of the previous games. That's not a jab at the developers, but I do imply a certain level of laze.
They did have every resource to draw upon from the previous games, which they obviously used (I'm looking at you various sections of Gotham City!). There are plenty of spots that echo their more decrepit counterparts in the prior games.
The combat is the same, the animations are the same, the core gameplay is the same. The issue of "been-there, done-that" sort of permeates the game. The developers really needed to try add to the gameplay in more significant ways. I suspect that their reasoning was probably affected by the fact that this is a prequel, and radical additions/deviations wouldn't make much sense.
The story is decent, the voice-acting is quite good (even with the replacing of Kevin Conroy, and Mark Hammill), and many of the character designs are very good as well, though not quite as dynamic as the previous games. I did find that for some reason, there were many spots that I should've been able to grapple or glide to (and would've, in the previous games), but couldn't. which was somewhat irritating.
On a more positive note, I really appreciate that the Riddler puzzles are significantly less annoying this time around. I hate having to jump through hoops just to acquire unlockable goodies. That feels less like being a detective, and more like a trained monkey that jumps through hoops. I also enjoyed the addition of the Electrocutioner's electric mittens, which made fighting hordes a bit easier.
But I still can't shake the feeling that while Batman: Arkham Origins is a good game overall, it could've been a GREAT game if they just pushed the envelope. Batman: Arkham City added to the scale and spectacle of Batman: Arkham Asylum. Batman: Arkham Origins feels like a few small steps back. Logically, it should be, but it didn't have to be that way.
All-in-all, like Dead Island: Riptide, and Saints Row IV, I get the impression that many games developers are pushing sequels that really aren't sequels. More like "samequels" - more of the same, with nothing really added to the experience. Batman: Arkham Origins could've very well been DLC, rather than a full-price game.
Unfortunately, as of this writing, there's a game-breaking bug when trying to solve the Burnley Comm Tower mission. There are several work-arounds/exploits players have tried, which haven't worked for me. I hope it gets fixed soon.

Prison Architect is just the kind of crafting/ management sim that is quite easy to get addicted to. In it, players oversee the design and construction prison buildings, placing various objects and designating rooms that AI staff members and prisoners interact with. Numerous game mechanics are used to make the prison population adequately contented, punished, rehabilitated, and profitable. Since many game functions are not very intuitive and budget management can be difficult for new players, reviewing developer updates is highly recommended:
. Despite Prison Architect's seeming complexity and learning curve, it is relatively accessible and has a surprising amount of polish for an alpha, even when considering  the game's 5+ year lifespan. The art style is appealing and consistent, virtually no game-ending bugs are to be found, and success can be achieved easily while mastery, cannot.
TL;DR: management sim, complex but functional, excellent dev support, addictive, 84%, worth a buy

From the sound of the clacking of balls, to the feeling you get when you jump-swerve-combo shot your way to victory, this game delivers. The physics are spot-on, the variety of games is ideal, and pretty much everything else serves this game sweetly.
The only downside I've found so far is the frontend UI. It feels clunky and ported from a console (perhaps it is). Once you start playing though, the controls are very intuitive and, with a bit of practice, you'll be slinging super trickshots off with ease before you know it.
There are a bunch of "special rules" type games to play too, Endurance being the most exhilarating/frustrating. Here, you have to keep potting balls whilst playing to a timer. The longer you take, the more balls are added to the table, eventually maxxing out and ending your game.
The camera views are terrific, with full control either 3D or overhead. The graphics are everything you'd want from a pool game, and most important of all, the balls behave as they should.
Seriously, this is near-perfect for a pool game. The dodgy front-end aside, this is the best virtual pool experience you'll find on the PC today. Highly recommended.

The sixteen tracks are all fun and interesting. Four of them take place at the airport. Another few take place in egypt, some are in the snow with snowmen and pine trees. Others take place on a farm where cows live, but there are no cows, because Garfield loves to eat things. That is why there are no cows. Garfield and other characters have eaten so much that they are the same size and height as Jon who is a human, but Garfield is Bill Murray. Odie is played by Rhea Pearlman (great aunt of Ron Pearlman and Danny DiVito's wife) and Sheldon (Cooper?) in this game and it must have cost a lot of money to get the celebrity voice acting. I'm just kidding there isn't celebrity voice acting, just bad voice acting that you get to hear a lot.
Before each race you get to buy what cheats you want to use. These cheats cost money, but not micropayments. Instead you need to grind for the cash you need to buy stuff. Playing the same races over and over before you can buy that chick magnet car you always wanted, but Nermal drives. Cheats really help you compete in the 155 CC races so you can finish in 6th and final place a few seconds less than you would normally.
This game comes with a stop watch, because during the races, they don't keep time for you. You need to do that yourself. With a stop watch. I then write down my best times for the grand prix mode so I have them always. There is a time trial, but why would I ever use that to keep track of time when I'm only racing against a UFO? That's right Garfield Kart has UFOs and so many of them that they should be identified by now. You race against one in the time trial, which makes it more of a race with an actual time instead of the real races with no time. Then you also find them in the real races as a way to crash the first place racer, so its always best to be in second place until the end, where winning matters. You play to win.
I will recommend it to all my friends no matter what their age. We all know and love Garfield. He is the best cat and Felix would end up in 6th place if he raced Garfield, because Garfield can drive a truck in this game but Felix can just sack race. Garfield is a great game and will continue to be the standard bearer for Bill Murray and Jennifer Love Hewitt games. Someone should make a sequel with Alvin & the Chipmunks.

The User Reviews are correct - Mad Max is an over-looked gem of a game.
At first glance you'd think you were playing another canned, boring formula game such as "Rage" employed.  But Mad Max is much, much more fun and interesting, well-polished and balanced.
The inspiration to keep playing comes from the need to upgrade your car and fighting abilties by collecting scrap, parts, and completing open-world objectives, such as clearing "camps."  Camps are fun, because there is some real variety to their types and layouts, and assortment of enemies...and the hand-to-hand combat is fun, well-done, and shows that it's not just another FPS action game.
And that's the key - you battle enemies and overcome obstacles in the game, in a variety of ways...your car, its harpoon, sniper and shotgun options (with very limited ammo so you use them spaingly, as they're tied to set hot-keys), or you can toss a lighted gas can, or use a melee weapon if there's one lying around (temporarily).
You essentially take-over various areas of the map, leading up to the final confrontation with Gas Town, which is the key to survival, dominance, and easy-living in the desert.  But it will also take a buffed-out car and abilities to do it.
The driving is fun and well-done, although the camera can be a tad wonky when fighting or driving, it's tolerable and otherwise similar to any other modern game in that regard.  Your main car (Magnus Opus) is heavy and loud, and comes from 3-4 different models of your choice (they are not drastically different).
Finally, the voice-acting is fantastic! What a surprise to experience Ace voice actors and characters in a game, makes such a big difference to the game's charm and sense of immersion.  Chum, your mechanic assistant, is a classic video game character who is constantly jabbering warning you of on-coming enemies in the distance.  He's  a great, whacky character, and have nothing but praise for his voice actor, seriously one of the best voice-over jobs and writing I've ever experienced in a game.
The environments are detailed and immersive (for a desert), the storms are crazy cool, and the sunsets are great to drive around in.  Roads are faster than the shiftier, deeper sand off the road, cars spin accurately in the dirt.
Got this for $10 on sale, and maybe that makes me a bit biased, but the game deserves more praise from the gaming media than it has received.

So this game has single handedly reinvigorated my hope for the future of gaming. I had been concerned that gaming would be reduced to one good release annualy followed by mediocre to poor sequels of other games, or great ideas that simply dont tickle the sweet spot that gaming used to when I was growing up. This game is not for everyone, It comes from an age of gaming that seems to have been long forgotten, ignored by money grubbing cash cows hardly worried about making platformer games and instead prioritize FPS after FPS simply because thats what is popular and racks in the endless fountains of money. This however is a game i decided to buy day one, and I havent been willing to do that in ages. I purchased this title for $40 and it is worth every penny. I am a fan of platformers, I grew up playing N64 as a kid and had purchased the Banjo Kazooie, as well as Banjo Tooie when it was re released into Xbox 360. Those games are some of the best games who's gameplay had been ignored until i caught wind of this game. Sure, its an obvious clone but its supposed to be. it is a very late 90's platforming banjo kazooie clone with nearly identical feels from camerawork, cutscenes, and even characters. People judge this game based on writing, but you dont play a platformer expecting to have your heartstrings tugged by the writing. Thats as irrational as hating a Mario game because "muh it didnt have enuf splosions and swears". This game has the same text feel with the grunts of all the characters like banjo kazooie, the jigsaw pieces have been replaced with pages of a mystic book, there are feathers, learned moves, jumping, an enemy with an absurd evil plan which feels as conveluted as it does classic platformer, and it even has dialogue directly stating its a clone of another game. as said in a review i read before this one, if you dont like Banjo Kazooie, then it isnt for you. To anyone who wants a new Banjo kazooie experience, buy this game immediately.

Spec Ops:
The Feels is a gritty 3rd person shooter set out to put players through emotional torment as they question their actions while gunning down supposed allies. The purpose of the game is to smack those who have the mindset of "war is awesome, I want to sign up in the military because games like Battlefield and Call of Duty make it look so cool" and show them the horrors of what being a soldier could be like, the consequences, the dark corners of a war. Soldiers can make really stupid decisions that can cost innocent lives and the repercussions could damage them mentally, something that Spec Ops is able to capture spectacularly well. That's the beauty of this game, you are not here to play just another military shooter, you're here for an experience that can only be understood once you played it. There are no heroes, no villains, just men with guns.

Prison Architect is just the kind of crafting/ management sim that is quite easy to get addicted to. In it, players oversee the design and construction prison buildings, placing various objects and designating rooms that AI staff members and prisoners interact with. Numerous game mechanics are used to make the prison population adequately contented, punished, rehabilitated, and profitable. Since many game functions are not very intuitive and budget management can be difficult for new players, reviewing developer updates is highly recommended:
. Despite Prison Architect's seeming complexity and learning curve, it is relatively accessible and has a surprising amount of polish for an alpha, even when considering  the game's 5+ year lifespan. The art style is appealing and consistent, virtually no game-ending bugs are to be found, and success can be achieved easily while mastery, cannot.
TL;DR: management sim, complex but functional, excellent dev support, addictive, 84%, worth a buy

If you want a full game right now, DO NOT BUY THIS! You will have to wait until Jan 17 for the fully finished product with all episodes.

It does however autosave like every three minutes, so you don't lose much progress when it does disconnect, which in my experience (with a stable internet connection) has happened once in three hours.
DX-12 does not function fully with this game at the minute. It crashes at random points and the only thing you can do to resolve this is use DX-11 till the first proper patch fixes it. It's not that big a deal, it's one setting to change. People need to quit whining about it.

Things that Black Ops II did right:
-You are able to select your weapon load out before each mission, which is a first for the series. This is nice because you can easily try new weapons and combinations, or to play with your familiar favorites, rather than whatever the mission happens to give you.
-Branching story-ish. There are a few moments in this game where you get to make a choice. Sometimes you don’t even realize it’s a choice. This was actually very well done, and after going through the game once, going back and seeing how all the different events could have worked out to give you different endings was quite interesting.
-The side missions in the campaign in which you play as nameless soldiers, and get to command a battle was actually a really neat idea. It was a good effort, but the controls felt like a port from a console game, rather than optimized for PC.
Not-so-right:
-The story (as with damned near every Call of Duty game). It makes no sense. The characters are not sympathetic. Ultimately, you end up not caring. Again, the super-long, super-unskippable cutscenes just add to the boredom that replaying any part of the campaign will bring. It’s a quintessential string of set-pieces campaign, with minimal input from the player. When you do get full control, your levels are narrow and linear. Ultimately, if I wanted to actually PLAY a Call of Duty experience, I would not choose this one.

Gameplay?  Above average TPS à la Gears of War.  Solid, precise aim and feel.  Clunky-ish cover/vault/melee system, but effective enough that you won't die too much to it.  Two-weapon system, no real restrictions beyond ammo/grenade caps.  Fantastic world effects -- sand behind that window?  Yes, you can totally shoot it out and watch it knock an enemy over.
Execution?  Great.  Beyond the standard waves-of-enemies-then-move-on strategy, you have snipers to outsmart, and companions to instruct (that actually do what you ask -- most of the time).  There's a large quantity of particular scenes that are just wonderful.  The scene with a flashing light -- you'll know when it happens.  The scene where a sandstorm is pushing your team back, and you have to make a mad dash for safety.
But this game ins't amazing because of those.  It's amazing because of... well...
The story.  A terrifying morality simulator.  Absolutely wonderful character development.  A team you actually want to keep safe.  A common enem--wait, just kidding.  It absolutely smashes all the clichés you'd expect out of the genre and setting.  Actual choices that have quite an impact.
If not for some stupid issues -- blah graphics settings, horribly rigid control scheme, a tendency to just hang for no discernable readon, and some stupid  barricades with incorrect hitboxes -- it'd be one of the best shooters I've played.  Don't let those negatives detract you from this game, though.  Play it, if only for the story.

Star Wars “The Phantom Menace” was the most disappointing thing since my son. I mean, how much more could you possibly ♥♥♥♥ up the entire backstory to Star Wars?! And while my son eventually hanged himself in the bathroom of a gas station, the unfortunate reality of the Star Wars prequels is that they’ll be around… forever. They will never go away.
They can never be undone.
If someone who’s under the age of like 20 says his least favourite film in the series is “The Empire Strikes Back” because it was “the most boringest one”, then I suggest you shut this review off right now before I carefully explain how much of a ♥♥♥♥ing idiot you are.
So where do I possibly start?
Nothing in “The Phantom Menace” makes any sense at all. It comes off like a script written by an 8 year old. It’s like George Lucas finished the script in one draft, like turned it in, and they decided to go with it without anyone saying that it made no sense at all, or was a stupid, incoherent mess.
I guess at this point who’s gonna question George, or tell him what to do? He controls every aspect of the movie. He probably got rid of those people that questioned him creatively a long time ago. (Han Solo getting tortured)
I also think that everyone just assumed that a Star Wars prequel would be an instant hit, regardless of what the plot was.
Really… how hard could it be to screw up? It’s like screwin up mashed potatoes. You boil the water, you pour in the packet.
Number 1: The Characters
The biggest and most glaring problem with the Phantom Menace is the characters. This is like the most obvious part of movie making, but I guess I gotta explain it when talking about this turd. (Jar-Jar stepping in turd)
So let’s start at Movie Making 101 shall we?
You see, in most movies the audience needs a character to connect with. Typically this character is called a “Pro-ta-gawnist”.
When you’re in a weird movie with like Aliens, and monsters, and weirdos, the audience really needs someone who’s like a normal person like them to guide them through the story. Now this of course doesn’t apply to every movie, but it works best in the sci-fi, superhero, action, and fantasy genres.
I picked a few examples to illustrate this point: Marty McFly, John McClane, Billy Peltzer, Sarah Connor, Neo, Charlie Bucket, Peter Parker, Cliff Secord, Johnny Rico, Rocky Balboa, and Kevin Bacon.
So in addition to being like an everyday kinda schlub, usually the pro… prutugunist is someone that’s down on their luck, in a bad place in their lives, or someone who everything just doesn’t always go perfectly for them. Eventually they’ll be confronted with some kind of obstacle or struggle that they gotta deal with. If we like them, we hope they succeed. The drama in the film is the result of us rooting for them against opposition. Eventually our prumurmrurm will find themselves in the lowest point where it seems like all is lost, but eventually they’ll pull through and conquer whatever force opposes them. It’s satisfying when our hero gets ahead from where they started off at. They make like a change. This is called an “Arc”.
Often too, they’ll get the girl in the end as icing on the cake.
Now I need to explain that I don’t think that all movies should be the same, or conform to the same kind of structure, but it works well in certain kinda movies. So unless you’re the Coen Brothers, David Lynch, Paul Thomas Anderson, Stanley Kubrick, Alfred Hitchcock, Lars Von Trier, David Cronenberg, Gus Van Sant, Quentin Tarantino, John Waters, Wes Anderson, Sam Peckinpah, Terry Gilliam, Martin Scorsese, Werner Herzog, or Jim Jarmusch, you really shouldn’t stray away too far from this kind of formula.
Especially if you’re making a movie that’s aimed at children, and has a cartoon rabbit in it that steps in the poopy. This is all of course completely applicable to the original Star Wars film, and the character of Luke Skywalker. This was accomplished even without all the wonders of modern CGI.
Now with all you’ve just learned, in this video that I have made for educational purposes, I want you to tell me who the main character of “The Phantom Menace” is.
I can tell you it’s not the Jedi. They were just on some kind of boring mission that they didn’t really care about. Plus they were ♥♥♥♥ing boring themselves.
It wasn’t Queen Amidala, cuz she was some foreign Queen who the movie was certainly not really about specifically either.
You might be thinking that it’s Anakin, cuz he was like a slave and saved the day at the end by accidentally blowing up the starship, but the audience doesn’t meet Anakin until 45 minutes into the movie. And then the things that are happening around him are pretty much out of his control or understanding.
If a protagonist has no concept of what’s goin on or what’s at stake, then there’s no real tension or drama… without that there’s no story.
So the conclusion is that there isn’t one.
Before the movie opened I was really excited to hear that Scottish actor “Ewan McDonald” was going to be playing Obi-Wan Kenobi. I thought that was a great choice, and he’d be perfect as the lead of this movie. But he wasn’t really… He just sat on the ship and complained a lot.
So YOU may like the characters, y’know, if you’re stupid.

I started playing as a Pacifist when I started the game. It was a fun journey, but I got stuck on a boss fight that I couldn't get through (Muffet, the spider boss). So I switched to Genocide for fun. I liked the boss fights but it was too repetitive and it took a long time to grind monsters just to make a proper run. I haven't completed the game yet on either route, so maybe I'll take back some things, but anyway, I just wanted to share my ups and downs for this game.
+Upsides
Beautiful story. Has a strong ending that affects those who are willing to embrace it.
Love the characters (Except Alphys), I've grown attached to them.
Pacifist makes you learn about all the monsters and become friends with the bosses (possibly).
I love dodging attacks and feel satisfied with a bit of a challenge.
Flowey is a fun enemy too.
Nice and funny puns and unique dialog/narration.
Cool art style of retro gaming.
-Downsides
Overall structure isn't really what people hope for. The example of what I mean is, is that you're given very easy puzzles, and some of them are solved for you which is a complete waste of time.
No changeable difficulty settings
If you play genocide, all puzzles are solved for you, and enemies are way to easy to kill. It's just like 1 to 3 hits until you win, and then you go against a boss, like Undyne The Undying and the attacks are overwhelmingly hard to dodge. Basically the transition is unstable as f*** if you ask me.
In Pacifist, Alphys won't stop updating her status, and won't shut the hell up while I try to do my puzzles. Don't you find it creepy to have a fan girl forcefully make your profile follow hers on whatever site they use?
The Genocide seems to be easier than Pacifist one.
You can't gain EXP when sparing monsters in Pacifist, so you can't get a little more health to withstand more hits from bosses like Muffet.
I could be missing some +'s and -'s, but overall, I do recommend this game, even if there are many flaws. I think that $10, or maybe even less, is definitely worth it. I hope you can say the same.

OVERVIEW-- 9.8/10
Easily the best game I have ever played. Story and characters are so well made it seems like it could be real. This game made me legitimately laugh out loud at times, and cry at others. The "Reset" button is nothing more than a button. I rate the game 9.8 out of 10. Read on for my full review.
CHARACTERS AND STORY-- 9.7/10
Like I said, the characted are incredibly well done. They have such different personalities that are consistent throughout the story.
The reason Frisk, the human who you, the player, shows no emotion is most likely so that you can react in your own way, rather than being told how to react.
The story is a rater cliche topic. Humans and mosters lived in harmony, had a battle, humans won. However, the way it is developed through the game, especially if you read the books in the Home, Libarby, and New Home, is unique.
GAMEPLAY ELEMENTS-- 9.5/10
There are a few different things to consider here. The puzzles are a big factor in the game, especially Snowdin. However, I don't think that Toby Fox, the creator of Undertale, put a lot of effort into them, or, more likely, it reflects Papyrus' rather goofy attitude.
However, five, or four if you played the Genocide Run, soul modes are particularly impressive aspects of the game, each presenting their own unique challange.
The reset button. I have never seen anything like this. In my opinion, this is a stroke of genius from Toby Fox. The reset button never truly resets the game. The characters remember you, your blunders, your choices. This is, once again, a stroke of genius from Toby.
GRAPHICS AND SOUNDTRACK-- 9.1/10
Let me just remind you that Undertale was an Indie game. For the graphics, Toby Fox had help from Mangolina Porter and Temmie Chang, but all of the songs in the soundtrack were original compositions. Impressive.
For the art, I'll just be honest-it kinda stinks. But this is a 2-D retro style game. Also this means that Undertale is incapable of lagging.
The music. Wow. Just wow. 10/10 soundtrack. The OST (Original Sound Track) holds so much emotion and meaning. It's amazing, and well worth its price.
FANBASE-- 0/10 DISCLAIMER: THIS DID NOT AFFECT MY FINAL DESICION
Yes, the fanbase is cancerous. They all want you to play the pacifist route. This is not what the game is meant for people! If Toby Fox wanted that, he would not have made a "Fight" button. The game if for YOU to explore. If you looked up how to do a pacifist run before getting your first few neutral endings, than you did it wrong.
FINAL THOUGHTS
Wow, did you read all of this? Good, you only have a bit left.
Overall, this game is wonderful, and well worth its price of ten USD ($10). I thouroughly enjoyed playing this game and finishing all four endings. There are so many hidden features, I wouldn't be able to fit it all in this review, and besides, they're for you to find out. This is where I leave you! Have fun and stay determined!

I purchased this game under the impression that it was going to be an open world space simulation RPG (as tagged). To some extent, it does meet these criteria, but only just so. The presentation leads you to believe that there is a depth of customization to the gameplay, that you are let loose in a huge galaxy to your own devices and you will be able to mold the whole experience to your liking.
Unfortunately, It doesn't really happen that way. The whole world is completely static, and feels lifeless. There
factions, LOTS of them (despite what a preliminary flight across the map would lead you to believe). Rather than having them interact with one another in any sort of dynamic and interesting way, however, it's just good guys and bad guys.
Progression is totally linear. You grind the same 3 or 4 missions over and over again, level up, buy better equipment for your ship, rinse and repeat.
After the first couple of hours, you will have experienced everything that the game has to offer. I trudged on, though, thinking that surely it can't possibly be that boring. I really hated the idea that I wouldn't even be able to get my money's worth out of a game like this. I wanted to believe that maybe the developers just aren't finished with it yet, and future updates will yield more interesting content.
Wrong again.
Today held the announcement of a new DLC, which of course costs
money (the game is terribly overpriced to begin with). I was willing to give the developers a chance until I saw this. I cannot in good conscience recommend this game to anyone, even if it were deeply discounted.

I've played every Hitman game since Silent Assassin and absolutely loved the series, until the huge disappointment that was Absolution. Absolution threw the sandbox mechanics out the window and turned the game into a frustrating pseudo Splinter Cell. The real highlight of the series was Blood Money, and many fans including myself saw that as the last true Hitman game.
Fast forward to 2016 and IO Interactive has, for the most part, listened to its fans. The Blood Money sandbox we all know and love has returned largely intact, including a save system that actually cooperates (saving the state of all items and NPCs, not just your position). The big map is replaced by a less intrusive "Instinct Mode", similar to Batman's detective mode in the Arkham series. The disguises actually work as intended - for the most part, identically dressed NPCs will not be auto-suspicious, but there will be a few odd individuals (helpfully highlighted with white dots) who "know everyone else" and will get suspicious the way they did in Absolution. In this way, the disguise system has managed to strike a reasonable balance between being too-forgiving (Blood Money) and near-useless (Absolution). Also, there's no Instinct meter to drain any more. Hurray!
For now, there are only two training levels plus one story level thanks to the decision to make the game "episodic". Not to worry - all the levels have a VERY high degree of replayability, encouraging you to keep going back to explore different options (unlike Absolution). You can place a non-lethal rat poison your target's drink, causing him to make a beeline for the nearest washroom, where you're probably lying in wait to drown him in the toilet bowl. You can drop a chandelier on his head when he's unaware. You can knock out the VIP he's supposed to meet, steal the VIP's clothes, and then assassinate him during a private meeting. You can do it old-school, finding a vantage point with a silenced sniper rifle and then putting one in his head. You can break out the automatic weapons and go on a psychotic killing spree. You can plant remote explosives (or even trick NPCs into delivering them for you) and finish the job from a comfortable distance with a single button press. And that's not all the possibilities!
Replaying a level and scoring more and more points each time will also unlock new equipment for when you start, along with new ways to spawn in the level (i.e. spawn inside the kitchen wearing a chef disguise, instead of going through the front door in your suit). I do wish you had the ability to equip poison vials right from the get go without having to unlock it first though.
One of the few things Absolution did well was to smooth out the control system, and that's carried over for the most part. Character movement is fluid and button prompts ensure that you don't accidentally punch the air when trying to grab an NPC in a headlock from behind. Unfortunately, someone at QA forgot that a PC keyboard has more than 100 keys - meaning there's currently no ability to bind equipment to number keys, and you have to hold down a key and scroll around to equip items (console port!). Hopefully a patch will address this.
On the technical side, things certainly could be much better, but I'm not complaining too much after the horror that was Batman Arkham Knight. I'm getting 40-80 fps on a GTX970 at 2560x1440 with textures on high, FXAA-only, and shadows on low. Dropping to 1080p allows me to lock it at vsync (60fps) with few drops. Given that Nixxes (the porting company) did a great job with previous titles like Tomb Raider, Deus Ex HR, and even Absolution, I have faith that they'll get their act together with patching. At the end of the day, it's still a very fun game and the performance is tolerable.
Sadly, the animations (or lack thereof) are quite lazy considering the AAA budget. Like in Absolution, most items are just magically conjured out of thin air when you equip them. Even Blood Money at least tried to show Agent 47 reaching into his shirt/suitcoat to pull out something. Large items like assault rifles are stuck on your back instead of disappearing into thin air, which is a slight improvement. I'd like to see 47 put handguns into holsters when wearing an appropriate uniform - this was done in PSP games 10 years ago, seriously. It would certainly help the immersion.
Overall, the new Hitman is a very fun game that fixed most of its predecessors problems and has largely given the fans what they want. Wait for a few patches, and then pick this game up. You won't regret it.

In conclusion, this game feels like a shell. I think in its current state this game would be a good mobile game for 1.99 because of the very little options and awkward gameplay. But for roughly $20 CAD on steam? Yikes.

Things that Black Ops II did right:
-You are able to select your weapon load out before each mission, which is a first for the series. This is nice because you can easily try new weapons and combinations, or to play with your familiar favorites, rather than whatever the mission happens to give you.
-Branching story-ish. There are a few moments in this game where you get to make a choice. Sometimes you don’t even realize it’s a choice. This was actually very well done, and after going through the game once, going back and seeing how all the different events could have worked out to give you different endings was quite interesting.
-The side missions in the campaign in which you play as nameless soldiers, and get to command a battle was actually a really neat idea. It was a good effort, but the controls felt like a port from a console game, rather than optimized for PC.
Not-so-right:
-The story (as with damned near every Call of Duty game). It makes no sense. The characters are not sympathetic. Ultimately, you end up not caring. Again, the super-long, super-unskippable cutscenes just add to the boredom that replaying any part of the campaign will bring. It’s a quintessential string of set-pieces campaign, with minimal input from the player. When you do get full control, your levels are narrow and linear. Ultimately, if I wanted to actually PLAY a Call of Duty experience, I would not choose this one.

When I first played this on Xbox, I got it for $30 and expected it to be another generic third-person shooter. How wrong I was. Spec Ops: The Line is a thoughtful, polished and well-crafted rollercoaster ride through the doomed city of Dubai. If you can make it through the 1st hour of generic gunplay, you'll have excellent story developments to easily make up for that (honestly) quite boring initial hour.

tl;dr;
If you enjoy colony-management games, this entry is well-worth the cost of admission.  Good for multiple playthroughs; good foundation; plenty of room for expansion; very few bugs.
Although not complete (as it is still in Early Access), this game entertains for hours.  Finding the correct balance among the multitude of requirements is difficult but not impossible; this conveniently lends itself toward a scenario of multiple playthroughs, each of which I found thoroughly entertaining.
The technology tree is well-established, but does have room for improvement; particularly, as one reaches the final stages of colony improvement; this is a result of the game not being in a completed state.  The developers are actively updating and expanding this with each new version, and they do a great job of communicating with and involving the community in regard to new technology features.
I have been playing with the Oil and Germ updates in place and found both to be valuable and entertaining extensions to the base gameplay mechanics.  I have seen a number of reviews complaining about the Germ upgrade, but personally, I found the germs to add a valuable level of depth to the game.  Perhaps, Klei could consider making their difficultly adjustable, and if players prefer that they be kinder (or more vicious), they could tweak the resilience of the germs or something of that nature.
I have found very limited bugs in the game: sometimes, when I'm ready to shut-down, it doesn't want to close and has to be force-killed; and in one game, I encountered a single tile (a ventilation bridge, in case that information is useful to someone at Klei) that I couldn't seem to destroy; other than that, this game played like a well-tested release.
Performance has been flawless the entire time I have played.  I have saturated most floors of my colony with equipment of one form or another; I run the game on a 6-core AMD with a GeForce 750; and have seen minimal framerate loss.

Prison Architect is the first game that got me into buying Alpha/Beta games.  What a joy it has been to progress with this game and its updates.
This game pretty much has it all.  You get the simulation by building your own prison.  This can be done very easily or (if you intend to have alots of prisoners who are hard criminals) this can be very hard.  The game includes fincial managment, but not to a level of frustration.
You start off in a small prison where one of the prisoners is being put to death.  Your first job is to make a death row cell for them.  You easily learn the basics of the game as you start to build.  Once this is done, you're left on your own to build, create, destory, and exapnd.
It is up to you if you want to reform your prisoners and give them jobs, education and other skills.  Or as Warden you can keep them locked up tightly unable to have any freedoms.  Gangs fight often and snitches get stiches real quick!  Find a few CIs to help you keep the hard to handle prisoners under control.
Train your guards, hire some guard dogs, and build a nice security system.  Your limits are boundless, truely.
And don't let the Alpha scare you away.  The game bugs are fixed quickly and any updates make you seem like you've gotten a brand new game.
Enjoy!
