Trader, Warrior, Pirate, Explorer, Bounty Hunter, Miner, Smuggler - a few of the things you can be in the Gemini Sector.  This game puts you in the boots of a newbie starship captain in one of the most volitile areas of human colonization, and it's your choice as to what you will do with your newfound freedom.  Will you avenge your father and find out why he was killed in the storyline?  Will you go off and discard your past in the free-roam sandbox mode?  The choice is yours.
You start out with a very basic gunship, but the game doesn't limit you to one ship like some others (Darkstar One, X-Rebirth), but instead gives you the option to upgrade and upgun in one of several ship classes.  Do you like the thought of zipping around in a fast, maneuverable stealth corvette?  You've got several to choose from.  Maybe you'd prefer to roll into a hostile area in one of the mighty dreadnaughts or carriers and outgun everything in the zone (except perhaps another dreadnaught or carrier)?  You can do that, too.  Or you'd like to be a trader, working your way from your starter ship to a freighter, and then a freightliner, ferrying cargo, buying cheap and selling high.  Again, your choice, but remember to pack guns to keep the pirates off your back, as they have the same choice in ships as you do!
You'll do all of this in a *very* good-looking setting that has NPC ships doing their own thing according to their own agendas.  My personal favorite example of this was the time I was attacked by a group of pirates.  I was in a destroyer, which is fairly middle-of-the-pack in speed-to-guns/armor, and flying with a group of trader ships.  The pirates jumped us, I engaged...and the traders *bolted!*  Left me there and ran, as they weren't going to stick around and slug it out with pirates that outgunned them (being businessmen in freighters rather than naval officers in warships, it seemed their AI told them to GTFO).  Just as I was swearing to hunt them down (if I survived this and didn't have to reload halfway across the map), security forces from the nearby station arrived with battleships and cruisers and what was a brutal last stand became a lopsided pirate turkey shoot.  Brilliant!
Starpoint Gemini does a lot of things right, and the devs have shown a lot of interest and support in the community.  There were a few bugs on first release, but continual support has polished this into a real gem most space-sim fans will enjoy greatly.  9/10

Great potential, but rather incomplete.
This game should not be released as a completed game yet. There are many aspects of the game that are not implemented. Enemies cannot board your ship, though you can purchase upgrades to defend against this. Fighters, bombers and inteceptors all act the same, and there are no enemy fighters. Some structures have hit points, but you can't actually do anything to them. Graphics occasionally glitch or break. Ship class balance doesn't exist. Mission-critical enemies can't be targeted with auto-fire and fighters won't attack. Raising and lowering reputation with various factions doesn't seem to have much impact on the game. The list goes on.
That said, it's still quite fun for a while. Despite occasional (very rare) glitches, the graphics are beautiful. The soundtrack is relaxing, if a bit unvaried. Customizing a ship for long, mid or short range combat can be rather fun. The controls take a bit of getting used to, but work smoothly once you get the hang of them. The ability to capture enemy ships with the choice of keeping or selling them is always a plus in my book.
As much as I wanted to love this game, though, it fell short. The story had some interesting points, but was short and overall dull. Side missions were worthless and repetitive, with very low rewards and only a handful of variants. The bad grammar in the text and horrible fake accents in the voice acting detracted from the otherwise just passable story. There's really no incentive to explore all that much; I did simply because I always do in games, but found it didn't provide anything of worth to do so.
If the developers ever finish the game, it could be decent, perhaps even great. In its current state, it will get hopes up and then let you down with the disapointment of spending money and time on something that needs quite a bit more time in development. Here's to hoping I can switch to recommending this game in the future.

The only complaints from many of the critics reviewing this game are about how it isn't much different than Arkham City. That complaint, to me, is one of idiocy. Arkham City was perfect, so instead of attempting to alter perfection, the developers kept everything good about Arkham City and improved upon it.
This game features a younger, harder Batman with a bigger temper. The storyline is much darker in a way that feels more akin to the Dark Knight movies while still maintaining the Arkham atmosphere. The combat feels smoother, faster, but mostly the same (which is good). The predator sections haven't changed at all (they didn't need to).
Detective mode is now more interesting than Arkham City's. You now analyze clues at crime scenes in order to reconstruct crimes from start to finish. Also, there's no longer the need to run around with detective mode on through extended portions of the game in order to follow trails.
As far as graphics go, the game at ultra settings are a huge leap over Arkham City--especially utilizing all the Nvidia-exclusive graphics technologies. The game also doesn't have the optimization issues that Arkham City had, so it runs at 60fps stable at ultra.
In conclusion, if you enjoy the previous Arkham games, you'll enjoy this one just as much, if not more.

Then you can carefully approach your targets when they are in the bathroom if they just happened to drink something... unfortunate and either garrotte them or (my personal favorite) drown them in the toilet and then dump their body in a closet. If you're showier, you can also rig some ceiling displays to come down right on the head of your target, or alternatively rig gas pipes to explode or expose some wires so your target is electrocuted when he steps in a puddle. The numbers of ways of going about your appointed tasks is truly impressive and shows the devs put some serious thought into the execution here.
The downsides for me are rather small but still there; it requires you to be always online (which is fine for me but I imagine not everyone has that same luxury so if you have a spotty internet connection I might hold off) And the episodic format of the new Hitman means that you will be very familiar the mission very quickly as the rest of the episodes haven't been released yet so I'm unsure if the replayability can extend for as long the devs can hope before more episodes arrive.

An honest open letter to the negative reviewers of Yooka Laylee,
Hi! I am calling out to the common sense of gamers far and wide on the relentlessly scathing reviews on this glorious game. The devs are industry professionals that have poured their hearts and souls into this project. If nothing else that should be acknowledged regardless of your opinion of them in the recent PR stuff regarding JonTron and Refunds. As of this post, I am nearly 9 hours into the game and have been blown away by how faithful they were to the genre.
But back on track, I'd like to address some of the major topics you guys have brought up. While I am by no means an expert on the topic and do not claim to be, I hope to shine a realistic light on these "issues".
To those claiming the camera is too clunky/moody. I BEG the question, have you ever played an N64-era platformer? Because as someone who played through all of Banjo-Kazooie in preparation for YL, I can attest that this set-up is pretty spot on when compared to BK/BT. Because in all honesty, the devs said from the get-go that they were going to "...create a spiritual successor to our most cherished work from the past!" (
) Which to my understanding means making an N64-esque game for the modern consoles.
To those claiming the level design is incoherent. I would like to bring to your attention that this is a staple of the genre, get over it. There is no getting around that. Platformer levels are all over the place because you are supposed to WANT to explore every nook and cranny.
To those claiming the "voices" are annoying. Really? These are same devs that pretty much coined the gibberish SFX and text thing and you are put off by that? Come on people...
To those claiming the game has performance issues. Yes, it has bugs. This is, put simply, the result of one simple fact. This game was  NOT made by a AAA company. Say it with me, this game was  NOT made by a AAA company. While yes, the Kickstarter was immensely successful, QA is simply not a problem you can throw money at and just magically get a bug-free game. This situation is unavoidable for a team of this size, period, end of story.
To those claiming the game is dated. You are absolutely, 100%, without a shadow of a doubt, correct. And that was completely the point. If you don't like that you should have read the headline of the game description a little closer. Sorry.
The real headline that everyone seems to be missing is that these guys faithfully brought back a genre that had one foot in the grave. All of these "issues" come with the package. Get over it and enjoy this beautifully flawed game, or continue to gripe. Either way, no one who shares my point of view will care if you keep griping, they'll be too busy enjoying the game.
Sincerely,
Galbjorn
P.S. To any devs that manage to end up seeing this, you have my heartfelt thanks and gratitude.

Yooka-Laylee is honestly up there with all the great collecathon platformers. It takes all the gameplay mechanics from Banjo-Kazooie and gives you much larger and organic-feeling levels to use them in. Updating some of the mechanics, like lowering the number of different collectibles, is very welcome.
What really stood out to me, apart from gorgeous visuals and amazing music, was the freedom you're given to explore the level. No longer are there invisible walls and slippery rocks you can't stand on, now you can climb anything in any way you want. See a tiny ledge that could help you jump somewhere? Go ahead, jump on it. Thanks to this you feel like you're thinking outside the box, coming up with your own solutions to the platforming challenges, which is always welcome.
As for negatives, sometimes the controls for the transformations feel a bit off and make some platforming harder than it should be, but it's nothing you can't get used to. Also, having to unlock all the moves annoyed me a bit, especially that without them you can't 100% the stages right away, but it just meant I had to get over my have-to-collect-everything-now OCD and just return to the previous stages later.
Speaking of stages, yes, they are much much larger than in the old games, but your movement speed is also much faster so that's not an issue. After spending about 10-15 minutes in each, you won't have any trouble navigating them thanks to a decent number of memorable landmarks and high spots from where you can take a good look at the level.
Overall, a must-buy for any 3D platformer fan, even at a full price.

I started this game up with little expectations as it like just just a cheap TPS with decent graphics and a surprisingly acclaimed story by a well known gaming writer. Figured the story would be o.k enough to justify the price, so I bought it during a sale.
To put it bluntly, yes, gameplay wise it is as GENERIC of a TPS or any shooter for that matter. Guns have little to no punch, enemy AI is basic but otherwise predictable and unchallenging, and weapon variety is decent but limiting with the 2 weapon loadout system... but, BUT... the story...
Let me just say the STORY for this game is the REAL SELLING POINT, far above the gameplay. You play Captain Walker accompanied by his boyband of I swear must be Ice Cube and Matt Damon impersinators. They at first seem uninteresting with that classic "HOO RAAAWWW" mentality games like Call of Duty suffer from. As the story progresses they get broken down, beaten up, shot, stabbed, burned, and tortured until only a husk of a human being survives.
The stuff these guys go to is the stuff of knightmares and it culminates to shocking revelations, and mental barriers being broken one by one. As each character commits atrocious acts of violence they lose whatever humanity stuck with them at the beggining, degrading into savage killing machines who literally cause the city to burn by the end of it.
I dont wish to spoil too much, but it is a serious trip.
I repeat DO NOT buy this game if you are looking for a satisfying TPS like Vanquish, Gear of War. Space Marine, Uncharted, Last of Us, etc. Instead BUY THIS GAME if you want a jaw dropping and heart wrenching story that characterises the horrors of War in a very Apocolypse Now esque manner with brutality, savagery, and sheer gut wrenching violence NO MILITARY SHOOTER HAS EVER DONE outside of some obscure Vietnam games.
11/10... would feel like a terrible person again.

I've always had a soft spot for pool games, but I've been dissappointed with the offerings available. Nothing's come close to making pool a fun experience on PC since 3D Ultra Cool Pool. Until Now.
This game is excellent. How to sum it up... the amount of polish is excellent, graphically stunning, smooth audio tracks and high fidelity, well-placed SFX, but most importantly, the physics engine. It's a trick shot game, where emphasis is placed on being able to perform crazy trick shots in a regular game of 8-ball, 9-ball, or any of the other games. Sure, it's weird to do those all the time IRL. Sure, you can choose to not do them and just play straight shots... but it's fun. Fun with a capital F.
Many previous games I've played seemed like an exercise in potluck or else purely strategy with aiming guides being perfect. With this game, some unexpected things do happen, but they've always seemed deserved to me. Hit the cue ball with max force at the wrong time and it might fly off the table. You can also knock other balls of the table.
I haven't yet tried online matchmaking, having only played with Steam friends, but I can say that playing with friends is very nicely done. Inviting a friend is very easy, it works with the Steam invite system you've likely already used. During an opponent's shot, you can walk around the table in first person view and see what they're doing, with WSAD and mouse.
The game controls excellently. There's no "Hot Shots Power Meter", and getting the power just right is possible, and you can take your time on it, but it's not as precise as just dialing it in. I find it's a great balance between skill and the precision needed for the kinds of trickshots the game sells itself on.
The amount of single player content is phenomenal, with new unlocks of ball sets and table decals, as well as pool cues, coming frequently, a little tiny bit at a time. It keeps the game fresh. Whoever hosts an online match can use his unlocks, so it's a fun way of showing how far you've gotten to new players. The single player is so good, I sometimes prefer it to multiplayer, simply to get more "hats and crates."
In short - Best pool simulation game I've ever played. Even better than 3D Ultra Cool Pool, if you could count that as a "simulation." (And look up 3D Ultra Cool Pool by Sierra if you want a different kind of pool game, it's very old, but it still has it's charm.)

Ever wanted a star wars game where you can play as an FPS or third person hack and slash. Well look no further cause this is the game for you. Star wars Jedi knight: Jedi academy is the fourth game in the jedi knight series. The campaign sets you up as a student of the new jedi academy run by Master Luke Skywalker. You basically complete missions while also trying to figure out the motives of a mysterious sith cult. There are over 20 missions available.
Gameplay involves intense combat, some platforming and puzzle solving. You start of with a light sabre and limited force powers. As you play, you will unlock new sabres, weapons and force powers. The lightsabre combat looks amazing, especially when you face the sith guys (really flashy). Other weapons include: Rifles, sniper, rockets, shotgun, grenades and pistol. Each weapon has a secondary fire mode such as scope, grnade launcher, charged shot, auomatic fire etc. You have limited ammunition available for guns and will need to restock via containers or looted from corpses. With each mission you complete you can select a new force power to level up/learn. You can only choose light and dark force powers to learn and upgrade, with the neutral powers upgrading naturally as you progress though the story. Besides the sith, you also face other foes such as stormies, jet troopers, thugs, rancor and wampas.
The level design is amazing. Each mission you do, sets you in a unique place with different objectives available. The level of detail of the levels are great as there are plenty space to move around and secrets to find.
The sound is also good. Besides the awesome star wars soundtrack that we are accustomed to from the movies, the voice acting in this game is good as well.
Besides the single player campaign, there is also a multiplayer mode available. In multiplayer you and 15 other players face off in arenas. Everyone has lightsabres and a few guns. There are also bots available (up to 15) that you can play with should the multiplayer be dead (which unfortunately it is). You can choose a large variety of characters to play as/face off including stormies, boba fett, Luke etc. Furthermore, you can customise you lightsabre colour, hilt, fighting style (dual, single, attached sabres) as well as force powers. There are a variety of game modes including: deathmatch, team deathmatch and capture the flag. In the arenas, you can find power ups, health packs as well as new guns to play with.
I highly recommend this game for fans or star wars or people who want good hack and slash game. Worth every cent.

As a cart racing game this one is pretty generic but perfectly fine, however the PC port is a disaster. No matter what graphical preset I selected or resolution, this game would drop to sub 30 FPS on a consistent basis. Some tracks would see single digit FPS drops in places. And it's not just the low FPS, it's the insane dips and spikes. If you have a good PC, in the span of 15 seconds you will go from 100+ FPS down to 10 FPS. The framerate is all over the place, making the karts impossible to control at times. And the specs given are completely off base with the games actual demands. My PC slaughters the recommended specs. I have an fx 8350 Black Overclocked, an RX 480 with 8gbs VRAM and 16 gbs of Ram. I can't even maintain a solid 30 on the lowest graphical preset with Garfield Kart, so the idea that a dual core 2ghz CPU, and 256 mbs of VRAM could run this thing, is laughable. So unless you have quad sli 1080's with a G-Sync monitor to negate the massive dips and spikes, you might want to steer clear of this one. It's a shame that the port is unplayable, because the actual game was pretty good.

Looking for that purr-fect kart racer? Look no further than Garfield Kart! If you're a fan of a certain lasagna-loving, Monday-hating tubby fella (and who isn't!) then you owe it to yourself to check this little under-the-radar gem out. Sure, the production value isn't quite up to par with that of another well-known kart racer that, let's be honest, is becoming a little long in the tooth, but the sheer amount of enthusiasm the developers have for our favorite feline franchise is evident in every nook and cranny of this lovingly crafted title. Beautiful 1080p graphics and a whimsical color pallete bring Garfield's world to fluid, 60-fps life and it's a truly sublime experience to finally race through the environments that Jim Davis let us escape to for so many years. The power up items are all clever nods to the comic - Garfield's favorite pasta dish (if you're a true fan, enough said on what this could be!) allows him and his friends to perform heart-pounding, tooth gritting boosts to the karts - as well as to the player's heart rate as the adrenaline starts to surge! The famous (or infamous?...) spring is also present, enabling players to finally re-enact all of their favorite spring-related antics from the comic strip. Character and kart customization options allow for endless replayablility, plus playing dress-up with our furry friends is a joy in and of itself (ever wish you could just slap a chef's hat on Odie? Wish no more, your prayers have been answered!).
I could go on, but hopefully if you've read this far I've already convinced you to give this game a shot. If you have even the slightest interest in Garfield, Kart racing, or video games in general then don't let this one pass you by!

1. It is far too complex to be enjoyable, you will spend most of your time building pipes, wires, and pumps.
2. There is no point to the game beyond pure survival.
3. The base building concept seems like it would be amazing, but it is tedious and often ruined by one small miss-step.

ONI has only slightly missed its mark.  The game could EASILY be corrected by simplifying a few of the concepts.  ~Honestly, your characters can build a supercomputer but not a space heater?
~Why not just make a junction tile that has pipes and wiring built in for those of us that dont want to mess with it? Just the let pumps determine what goes where, example: turn pump "A" on and then set pump "B" as the exit source, as long as the pumps are connected by tiles the pumps will work ... done.
~Why cant your characters throw away jugs of urine? They just sit on the floor and the characters wont sweep them up.
~The characters need to vaccum up items off the floor like 10x faster, honestly, junk everywhere all the time.
~Nobody gets hypothermia from falling into water for 2seconds, andcharacters should not stay hypothermic.
~Add easier filter systems
This is one of the few games that I just want to be easier and far less tedious. I dont mind that the characters can get heat stroke or hypothermia, but it is annoying that it happens so much. You make one small mistake, or a toilet breaks, and your characters go to the bathroom on the floor ... or, more than likely they will go to the bathroom in your water supply.
I just wanted a neat base building game, but this is micromanaged survival.

I tried really hard to like this game, then I tried really hard to dislike this game, and I pretty much failed at both.  This is one of those games where Steam's "either, or" rating system just doesn't work.
If you don't count RTS or 4x games, this is technically my first space sim.  It is most definitely not my first sandbox game.  I will review it as a gamer, not a space sim fan.  If you're looking for comparisons to other titles in the same genre, look elsewhere.
Visually, the game is beautiful.  I hesitate to say whether or not it's poorly optimized.  I kept getting the occasional 1 second frame hangs, especially going through cloud formations.  My PC isn't new, but I can run the latest games on at least High settings ultra-smooth.  It seemed very odd to me to have lagg on a game like this.  The graphics here won't take your breath away, but they're better than you'd hope for your average space game.
The soundtrack is "spacey" enough and forgettable.  It does the job, nothing  more.  The voice acting ranges from bad to so-so, with the exception of one character who only gets some scenes leading up to the end.
When you get your first ship right off the bat, you are thrown into a vast galaxy.  There are several methods of fast travel, but you'll be hoofing it through most areas.  You'll be excited wondering what awaits you.  Stellar phenomena?  Pirates?  Epic battles?  Wretched hives of scum and villainy?  Alien races?  Strange worlds?
The game has most of these things.... Sorta.  "Sorta" is the pervasive theme of most elements of the game.
Is the UI good?  Sorta.  You gain four keys for your class abilities, and four more for equipment loadouts.  Most of the time, you want to open the page that accesses your cargo bay so you can throw junk out to make room for the good stuff, and there is inexplicably and inexcusably no hot key for this.  Nor the equipment menu.  Nor really any goddamn menu at all as far as I'm aware.  You have to click EVERYTHING.
This is also the place to mention that space is disorienting as hell.  Maybe it should be.  The game is very bad at steering you to points of interest.  Flying itself is nice and smooth, it's when you want to go somewhere specific that the trouble starts.  Most of the time you will use waypoints via the star-chart, because finding out which direction you're supposed to go is intrusively bad.  The map itself operates on a two-dimensional plane which will get you where you're going, and is your only hope.  The minimap is a sphere, but is restricted to local scans.  It was very interruptive to have to open the star chart EVERY time you want to go somewhere.  The game also obnoxiously eclipses many starbases with side mission icons, making them impossible to click to place a waypoint.  If you happen to be nearby, say salvaging bad guys near the station, you'll find yourself wheeling the ship in all directions just to find the base a asteroid's-throw away.  Not a common occurrence, but Irritating in the extreme.
Is the combat gripping with dogfights in space and epic battles?  Sorta.  I can't imagine what the game was like before it had autofire, because no ship but the largest ones is going to charge straight in.  This means weaving and bobbing, trying to disperse damage amongst fresh sides of the ship.  Most of the time enemies will be off-screen when they blow up.
You never know when your day is about to be wrecked by a random encounter.  The ratings given to enemies when they have been targeted will tell you their strength relative to yours - except they are completely arbitrary.  I have danced around and beaten "Impossible" ships and gotten thoroughly schooled by "Weak" ships.  So much for that feature.
That wouldn't particularly be a problem if you could save when you wanted.  You can ONLY SAVE WHEN DOCKED AT A BASE.  Just... what the hell?  It's such an arbitrary device to add tension to an otherwise boring encounter system, and when you get cheapshotted because you didn't grind enough is nothing but a source of aggravation.
Are the side missions interesting?  Sorta.  Most of them are not worth the payout and time investment.  They give you reputation.  While having a bad reputation as a pirate would be interesting, having a good reputation from being lawful means nothing.  If you're at a station, and all the ships there are neutral, and a pirate de-cloaks, they'll attack the pirate.  If they're your allies because you have good reputation, they'll do exactly the same thing.  I personally witnessed no significant advantage of reputation in the game whatsoever.  There were also lots of times when my "allies" did fu*kall to help me and I was on my own.
Are the ships/loadouts good?  There are several weapon types, and each weapon brand in particular has its own stats and three different tiers.  You probably COULD spend lots of time tweaking your loadouts, but frankly it isn't really necessary.  Ships themselves are hideously expensive, which brings me to....
Money and grinding.  The game has many commodities, but the difference between an average price and the best price is usually less than a few hundred credits - and possibly quite a bit of travel.  Chump change compared to what you'll need to get better stuff.  What could have been a vibrant trading system is utterly useless.
So is mining.  Space is full of many different kinds of rocks.  The best ones are crystal at 1800 a pop (always in dangerous areas)--- but decent salvage of ships can run 6k a piece for certain items.
Salvage is where it's at, and it will STILL take forever to make decent money until you get one of the larger ships with a bigger cargo hold so you don't have to return to base every ten damn minutes.  Technically you can send troops to board enemy vessels and drag it back to a base to sell or keep.  Not once was I successful at this.  I don't know what internal values were assigned to the troopers, but minus officer bonuses, all troopers are technically the same.  In 40 hours I never captured a ship.  Ever.
Is the story good?  Sorta.  It's overworked and tries far too hard to sound deep and complex, but is ruined by poor delivery and bland events.  You won't really care about anything that's going on, and before you know it it's over.  Most of my time stat was spent grinding so I wouldn't get my♥♥♥♥♥kicked on story missions.  The game sets itself up so hard for a sequel that the last battle feels like any other, and there's technically no real ending whatsoever.
The community seems really nice.  The devs are still actively working on this game post-release.  One of them told me so himself.  They're still trying to add content so that everything in that giant galaxy isn't virtually the same.  In a game like this, you could theoretically carve out your own story, but the game has no infrastructure whatsoever to do that.  It's just grinding, ships, and blowing up people who shoot at you.  There are no people outside of the story cutscenes, you can't even get out and walk around.  There's a history of the war of the previous game, and absolutely nothing else.  There's plenty of ROOM to make your own story, but nothing to do it WITH.
And yet, in spite of everything I just said, I will probably check in on this game after some serious time has passed.  See if the devs make good on their promises of content.  If you like grinding, or have a special chubby for space or ship battles, this could be your game.  It better be enough, because that's all there is.  For now.

If you can somehow ignore the always online DRM (which is just idiotic in a singleplayer game) and the performance issues which will likely be fixed soon... this is, in my opinion, the best hitman game ever made.
HITMAN does everything right, it really is what Absolution should have been. Don't let the mixed reviews fool you as most of the negative reviews are due to one or all of the following reasons:
1. Always online DRM
2. Episodic release
3. Performance issues even when using really powerful hardware
4. "Handholding" which means waypoints to stuff like disguises and such related to assassinating your target in a specific way, instinct = wallhack...
So.. ignoring all of the stuff I listed above... This game is good. It is REALLY good.
There is a lot of ways to assassinate your targets. Want to drown them in a toilet? No problem. Bash someone in the face with a battleaxe? You can do that. Seriously, there is a ton of ways to kill people. HITMAN brings back the freedom from blood money and refines it. The AI is still really dumb, but thats just the way it has always been in all hitman games and honestly it is an important part of what makes hitman so fun to play.
One of the more controversial features is the opportunity system. Sometimes you can overhear NPCs talking about stuff like how a certain lighting rig looks very poorly made and how it could possibly fall onto anyone standing below it. This triggers an opportunity which you can follow if you want to,
. Some people (including me) find these opportunities to be slightly too disruptive and they do kind of lock you onto a certain path. You see if you follow an opportunity, the game will guide you through the steps necessary to assassinate your target. And by guide you I mean it will place waypoints around the map pointing to required disguises and other stuff like that. This is great for players who are not familiar with previous hitman games but I am betting almost every hitman veteran will want to ignore these opportunities.
Contracts mode makes a return from Absolution. This mode is very good and brings a lot of replayability. In this mode the game makes a note of who you kill, how you kill them and what disguise you are wearing when you do so. Then you can challenge other players to repeat your steps. Fun!
Escalation mode is a new addition to the series. In it you must assassinate a target with a given weapon and disguise and then make your escape. After this you can proceed to escalation level 2 in which there will be additional objectives and conditions that you must meet in order to complete the level. Additional targets and "Pacifying anyone will fail the mission" are good examples.
Elusive targets are a feature that is not yet live. It is said that elusive targets will be available for a short time and if you manage to assassinate them and get away with it, you will be rewarded with cosmetic stuff like suits from previous hitman games. Saving is disabled during this event and if you fail... the target will get away and you will not get another chance at them! A pretty cool addition.

For now I can tell everyone that there are too many technical difficulties to recommend this game to anyone really, as a huge fan of the Hitman franchise, having episodic releases bothered me a little bit.

I am a huge fan of the Arkham games, and even though this game comes from a different developer, I gotta say that this is a great game and a worthy addition to the Arkham franchise.
Story:
The story is absolutely fantastic.
The game takes place about 5 years before Arkham Asylum.
You play as a younger, less refined Batman trying to find and stop Black Mask who put a bounty of 50 million dollars on his head, which automatically attracts 8 of the most talented assassins in the DC universe such as Deathstroke, Deadshot and Bane.
Even though the title says "Arkham Origins", it doesn't have anything to do with Arkham, and it's definitely not an origin story. In this game, Batman meets his ultimate adversary, The Joker, for the first time, and many other villains and allies as well.
Gameplay:
Despite the fact that this is not Rocksteady who developed the game, it shouldn't come as a surprise that the the gameplay is exactly the same as in Arkham City, simply because Rocksteady's work is remarkable and irreplaceable, and it should never be changed. There's a few new gadgets, and I have one minor complaint about the new Shock Gloves that I don't like the idea of because it's too overpowered. You are able to clear a room full of guys in matter of seconds with those. Good thing is, you get them pretty late in the game and they need to recharge. Aside from a few new types of enemies and the new gadgets, everything is the same, and that's good. You don't try to fix something if that's not broken.
Visuals:
The visuals are excellent, and are slightly better than Arkham City's.
The game has a lot of bugs though, and some of them are extremely annoying and sometimes they will not let you continue in your mission. For example: I encountered a major frame rate bug near the end of the game, even though my computer was able to run the game on maximum settings smoothly. I eventually managed to fix it.
Aside from that, the animations look great and fluid, except for the weird lip movement in dialogue scenes (not cinematic).
Multiplayer:
The multiplayer can be fun at times, but it's not polished.
There are 3 teams, Joker's gang, Bane's gang and Batman and Robin. Both gangs are fighting each other while Batman and Robin need to take both gangs out.
It has a lot of potential but it's not well executed.
Still, it's always fun to play as Batman and do inverted takedowns on helpless victims.
Summary:
Definitely a great addition to the Arkham series like I said, WB Games Montreal did a great job with the writing on this game and the new Batman and Joker voices are a great replacement, especially Joker's which is portrayed by the famous Troy Baker.
I give this game an 8/10, the things that really bugged me were the multiplayer and the great number of bugs, I wouldn't mind waiting a few more days and get a bug free game instead.

So far this game is everything I hoped it to be and more. It's easy to understand the nostalgia one would feel playing this game and comparing it to Banjo-Kazooie. However, don't mistake Yooka-Laylee as simply a BK clone. It is a fun and enjoyable game in its own right. The puzzle aspects of the game are familiar to those who have played 3D Platformers or the BK series but it doesn't, at this point, feel repetitive albeit, as is common in games like this, they are a bit gratutious; this is the nature of the beast though. Graphics are fun and suitable but aren't as detailed or intensive as other recent releases. Having said that I have found myself just standing on a vista and surveying the worlds as they are quite beautifully constructed. The executive mode is, from what I can tell, a full screen mode of sorts that the devs (steam community post) have said may not run smoothly on all PCs. Keep this in mind and run normally if you experience any hassles. The audio is probably the main thing that reminds me of Banjo-Kazooie. It's light, it's fun, it's catchy. The story is fairly simple - your book has been stolen and you must get it back. Queue dramatic search for pages from the book and battles against a evil mastermind (Grue?) and his minions across multiple worlds (books). I can't finish the review without acknowledging the elephant in the room; the camera. It's not great. But is it game breaking? No. At time of writing you will find yourself fighting the camera everyone now and then. My experience has been that this is worse when near walls and other solid objects. Whilst annoying it is bearable (not a banjo-kazooie pun unless you want it to be).
Anyway, to summarise, Yooka-Laylee is a fun 3D platformer with a good combination of graphics, audio and story to keep you well entertained. Those of you who have played Banjo-Kazooie before will find similarities and much to love in this game. New gamers wanting a fun adventure platformer will similarly enjoy themselves.

I wanna start by saying I'm one of the biggest fans of the original games for the N64. I love the Banjo games and I'd be the first one to say that I wanted this game to be good, I wanted Banjo back.
But perhaps my hopes, all our hopes, were misguided. See, what we wanted wasn't just Banjo Threeie. What we wanted was that same magic feeling that the Banjo games gave us, that same burst of charm and wonder, which this game sorrowfully lacks. And now that we've grown up and had more gaming experiences, a game that so shamelessly feels like nothing but a pretty looking remaster of a game nearly two decades old feels rather dated. The evolution isn't there, the bar was raised, and Yooka Laylee has neither the ambition nor the talent to meet it.
Sure the charming writing is there, but a lack of restraint really makes the fourth wall breaking less special. It's like as soon as the game starts it's saying "Oh hey, you're playing a video game, do you know that? LOL I'm so clever for making that observation haha!" Unlike the originals, which saved the fourth wall jokes for times when it's actually funny or poignant. The characters are recycled between levels instead of having new ones show up which actually fit the levels they are in. The camera and the controls often feel like they would rather fight you instead of let you experience the world. The levels are disjointed and boxed in rather than sprawling and interconnected, and the fact that they need to be "expanded" by playing in them seems completely unnecessary: You waste time to exit and re-enter the level to get the full experience. Dumb restrictions and petty annoyances like the stamina meter or loud and obnoxious voice acting add up over time and continuously grade away at your patience until it's nothing but buyer's pity and your nostalgia driving you to complete the game.
Its got its heart in the right place, but at the end of the day Yooka Laylee is pretty much just a mediocre 3D platformer with pretty visuals and a comedic tone. I wanted a true return to glory, and instead I am playing what feels more like a fan tribute of it's predecessor from 1998, but even then ends up just being worse.

What is this game like? It's a 2d platformer speedrunner that's frustrating, to put it simply. ...but for some reason, it keeps making me come back to it. I never thought I would like this game, but once my friend bought if for me and I gave it a try, it had the strange affect of being somewhat addictive. Honestly, it is such a challenge on these levels, that it makes you want to see how well you can do. It's hard to explain, but it's definitely got to be one of the most difficult platformers EVER.
I wouldn't fault this game for its difficulty, in fact, it handles the difficulty well and relishes in it. You not only die a lot, but it expects you to, and makes respawning as quick and painless as possible (forcing you to watch the death-splat animation and then a 1 second pause as punishment for dying).
BUT that said, the game is not without fault. There are at least a few glitches, including the game crashing sometimes when you press the "Esc" key. (ie: when trying to back out to the overworld) I also did find Meat boy would go through walls -forcing him to die- occasionally, but while that may sound bad, those glitches are rare and can only occur when in special mode (pressing "Shift") and jumping.
But the Pros outweigh the Cons in this game. The quirky humor and great music are what really bring this thing together, though. (And the barebones story.) Give it a try...but don't be surprised if you want to punch some babies while playing it. :)

I am a Garfield fan and was really looking forward to Garfield Kart being a good game and it really could have been but unfortunately this is a lazy port of the 3DS version with partial controller support that only works when driving. The mouse is needed when going through the menu and starting each round.
There are framerate issues and they get worse on some areas of each map, even on low graphics settings. Lowering the resolution also does not help the problem.
I was also sad to see Garfield Kart's description says Single Player. Yup, not even local multiplayer. :/ Seriously?, even Hello Kitty and Sanrio Friends Racing has Co-op and Local Co-op, and that game is worse than this. >.>
Also, there are no achievements and no cards drops.
Each characters speech is very limited and Garfield's favorite words seem to be "Whoo hoo!", since that's all he seems to say throughout each round.
On the positive side, the detail of the game looks good. There are plenty of characters, karts, helmets, spoiler parts and boosters to unlock and choose from. On the tracks you will find shortcut paths, speed boosts and awesome power-ups and weapons to collect and stack.
This game has the potential to be so much better but it's a shame the devs were lazy with the PC port.
If not for the problems mentioned above, I would have given Garfield Kart a positive review because it really could be fun.
If you are a fan of Garfield, save your money and follow this game to hopefully get a notice of an update that fixes Garfield Kart's current problems.

This game sucks. It's boring, repetitive, generic, and uninspired.
Remember in the movies how Max would drive to different enemy camps to clear out the bad guys there like he was Batman? Remember how the big bad villains used to mark their territories with flaming towers that Max would spend most of his time driving around to find so he could pull them down with a harpoon?
No?
This isn't Mad Max. It's a lazy GTA/Batman/Far Cry rip-off. You spend under 10% of the game doing what Max does in the movies - fighting in your car. The rest of the game has you following a tedium of tasks that play like every other AAA 'open world' game out there. You drive to enemy encampments, clear a few waves of lesser enemies then defeat the boss in a fistfight. That's the game. That's it. Oh wait no - there's all the flaming towers to pull down.
Why not blow up camps to lure the bosses out on to the road? Why not have elongated, elaborate car battles, like in the movies? The only time you ever truly feel like you're playing a Mad Max game is when you take on convoys, and there's just a few of those. Other than the occasional race you use your car to drive from point A to B and then fistfight.
Some of the other things I hate about this game:
- Aside from growing a beard, the only visual options for Max's face are an oil smear and blue paint which seems to reference Braveheart. Seriously? No cool wasteland hats/helmets? Play any Fallout game FFS.
- The second boss was the same model/mechanics as the first, except he was covered in pink paint. Whoa, stand back! Plus there's only about four real variations on the enemy cars.
- Play this for an hour or two and you've experienced pretty much the full extent of the game. Seriously.
- The bulls^^^ linear character and car progression. You get to build ONE car. Why couldn't you have a garage and the ability to build dozens? Why couldn't captured enemy cars be broken down into meaningful components instead of just more f^^^ing SCRAP? Why do you have to blow up the enemy cars to be able to loot them?
- The absolutely pathetic item and fuel management. You are unable to carry/store a melee weapon in your car, and only one gas can. Worse, you can't even check how much fuel is inside the can. In the movies Max sponges gas off the asphalt. The game says 'yeah, we'll include fuel as a mechanic, but we'll make it as irrelevant as any of the other actual Mad Max content.'
- There's no motorcycles. I repeat - there are NO motorcycles in a Mad Max game. Go f^^^ yourselves.

I wanna start by saying I'm one of the biggest fans of the original games for the N64. I love the Banjo games and I'd be the first one to say that I wanted this game to be good, I wanted Banjo back.
But perhaps my hopes, all our hopes, were misguided. See, what we wanted wasn't just Banjo Threeie. What we wanted was that same magic feeling that the Banjo games gave us, that same burst of charm and wonder, which this game sorrowfully lacks. And now that we've grown up and had more gaming experiences, a game that so shamelessly feels like nothing but a pretty looking remaster of a game nearly two decades old feels rather dated. The evolution isn't there, the bar was raised, and Yooka Laylee has neither the ambition nor the talent to meet it.
Sure the charming writing is there, but a lack of restraint really makes the fourth wall breaking less special. It's like as soon as the game starts it's saying "Oh hey, you're playing a video game, do you know that? LOL I'm so clever for making that observation haha!" Unlike the originals, which saved the fourth wall jokes for times when it's actually funny or poignant. The characters are recycled between levels instead of having new ones show up which actually fit the levels they are in. The camera and the controls often feel like they would rather fight you instead of let you experience the world. The levels are disjointed and boxed in rather than sprawling and interconnected, and the fact that they need to be "expanded" by playing in them seems completely unnecessary: You waste time to exit and re-enter the level to get the full experience. Dumb restrictions and petty annoyances like the stamina meter or loud and obnoxious voice acting add up over time and continuously grade away at your patience until it's nothing but buyer's pity and your nostalgia driving you to complete the game.
Its got its heart in the right place, but at the end of the day Yooka Laylee is pretty much just a mediocre 3D platformer with pretty visuals and a comedic tone. I wanted a true return to glory, and instead I am playing what feels more like a fan tribute of it's predecessor from 1998, but even then ends up just being worse.

Yooka-Laylee, the rebirth of the 3D platforming genre, has finally arrived.
And I am loving it.
As of writing this review, I have put in 8.6 hours into the game, so I can't judge every nook and cranny of the game just yet. However, I can and will give you my "general gist" review. This is also being written by a long-time fan of Banjo-Kazooie (and collect-a-thons in general), and a backer since the very beginning.
Yooka-Laylee is (as mentioned above) an attempt to revive the 3D plaforming genre of video games, such as the likes of Donkey Kong 64 and Banjo-Kazooie. Made by the same developers that made those games, the package is complete: quirky British humor, an animal-buddy duo, a villain with crooked teeth (that sadly doesn't rhyme), large open worlds and boat loads of collectibles to get your hands on. Also, the game's music is composed by the three legendary composers Grant Kirkhope, David Wise, and Steve Burke. While some tracks are not in the same style/consistancy despite being played in the same world, this game will have you humming the same tunes for days.
There are two hub worlds (Shipwreck Creek and Hivory Towers) and five main worlds, with a total of 20 Pagies, 200 quills, 5 Ghost Writers, One Health Increaser, One Power Increaser, One Play Coin, and One Mollycool (yes, the pun is intentional) per main world. Let's just say you'll be busy for quite some time.
There is also a multiplayer mode where you can play some arcade-styled minigames with a group of friends. I haven't tried this out yet, so I'll come back and edit this once I do that.
Now, I've seen people jump on the negative review bandwagon quite a few times. The negative points mostly come from technical issues, such as frame drops, camera problems, etc. However, I have a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ laptop running this game on my system's deafault setting of "Fastest". The game runs perfectly fine for me. In regards of the camera, I didn't have a problem with it at all. Either I'm just oblivious to the so called "issues" or people just don't know how to keep their camera in order.
Other negative points include the sections where it's not a platformer anymore. For example, the Kartos minecart sections. I actually kinda enjoyed those sections since it takes a brief break from the platforming action and delivers something a little more fresh (depending on your definition) to the table. Think of them as 2D versions of the minecart sections from Donkey Kong 64.
Then there's the Rextro 64 minigames. I will call these sections my least favorite. While interesting in concept, the loose controls on most of them just bring the experience down for me. I'm just hoping it isn't too chaotic in the multiplayer modes...
All in all, Yooka-Laylee is a good game. If you're a fan of Banjo-Kazooie? Go for it! If you're not a fan, then you may wanna stay away.
If you're still on the fringe because of all the bad reviews its been getting, I just say play it for yourself. FORM YOUR OWN OPINION.

Despite what it attempts to play its self off as, Spec Ops: The Line is most definitely not your typical military shooter. The first 20 minutes or so you spend walking around viewing the devastation of the sandstorms, now a common occurance in Dubai, and you also run into some "terrorists" who are just generic Arabian men. After you wade a bit more into this game's depth, however, there is a twist that makes the game so much more interesting and complex. The rest of this masterpiece display the harshness of a desert environment, some incredibly hard decisions to make- with horrible consequences no matter what, and the mental effects on your character because of those decisions.
The third-person shooter gameplay is solid, and I found it incredibly gritty-It matched the theme of Spec Ops perfectly. Overall, I would definitely recommend this game because it has all the complexity that a lot of games don't have, with incredibly satisfying gameplay, to boot.

I am going to give an honest review on this game:
COD: Black Ops II is probably one of the best Call of Duty games.  Treyarch really knows how to connect with their community and work with them to make a game for everyone!  The new singleplayer create-a-class system was pretty interesting, and it made me want to complete those extra missions to unlock weapons and allowed me to choose my approach how I wanted to.  Besides that, the story was very interesting and the strike force missions were cool side missions, with multiple endings.  The multiplayer is the part of COD that gets the most hate.  The multiplayer on Black Ops II was probably the smoothest experience I have ever had with any COD multiplayer.  Even when playing at 150 ping I feel like I am playing at 2!  The pick 10 system and scorestreaks were great new additions to the game!  The zombies, while I have never been a fan of in the past, really addicted me into its story and was very fun to play with friends.
Pros:
+: Singleplayer story was very well played, with new loadout systems and strike force missions
+: Multiplayer is very smooth and is obviously well-optimized for PC
+: Zombies is well put together and new survival mode makes it better for those nostalgic zombie players
Cons:
-: Multiplayer seems kind of like a futuristic DLC for Black Ops 1 in a full game, easibly overlookable
My overall rating for this game is 9.5/10.  I would recommend waiting until this game is on sale, but it is definetly worth the $60.
Note: I have only 1.7 hours on steam, but over 500 on Xbox.  I recently became a full-time PC gamer, so I have not played alot of this game on Steam but from what i have played, it was amazing!

What is this game like? It's a 2d platformer speedrunner that's frustrating, to put it simply. ...but for some reason, it keeps making me come back to it. I never thought I would like this game, but once my friend bought if for me and I gave it a try, it had the strange affect of being somewhat addictive. Honestly, it is such a challenge on these levels, that it makes you want to see how well you can do. It's hard to explain, but it's definitely got to be one of the most difficult platformers EVER.
I wouldn't fault this game for its difficulty, in fact, it handles the difficulty well and relishes in it. You not only die a lot, but it expects you to, and makes respawning as quick and painless as possible (forcing you to watch the death-splat animation and then a 1 second pause as punishment for dying).
BUT that said, the game is not without fault. There are at least a few glitches, including the game crashing sometimes when you press the "Esc" key. (ie: when trying to back out to the overworld) I also did find Meat boy would go through walls -forcing him to die- occasionally, but while that may sound bad, those glitches are rare and can only occur when in special mode (pressing "Shift") and jumping.
But the Pros outweigh the Cons in this game. The quirky humor and great music are what really bring this thing together, though. (And the barebones story.) Give it a try...but don't be surprised if you want to punch some babies while playing it. :)

I rate the game Borderlands 2 (including game of the year edition and its associated expansions) 3.5/5. Pretty Good. I played Zero, the assassin character.
This is a fun action-oriented, hub-based first-person-perspective game with comic book style graphics and relatively few bugs (though it does still have a few). The game mechanics and leveling system is generally excellent (except for a few frustrating situations usually involving overly difficult boss situations) and the action is visceral. The 5 different playable characters and numerous add-on expansions give the game excellent replayability and the music is at least pretty good throughout (and utterly brilliant in places). Adding to the replayability The highly varied nearly infinite combinations of weapons and items allow for a great and unique playing experience every time you play and something similar should be done in actual adventure games to give each item more of a unique feel.
That said, the sound is mediocre and the action gets highly repetitive (with enemies coming back again and again after each area has already been cleared of enemies) resulting in a seemingly never-ending miasma of action-oriented sections which ultimately become exceedingly tedious. The humor is clownish, absurd and random throughout and very hit and miss (mostly misses here). There are good pieces of dialogue here and there but these snippets are too few and too far between.
This game can potentially be played cooperatively though unfortunately there are many areas (especially in several of the add-ons) where the game clearly intended for you to play cooperatively with others (a difficult thing to do now considering the age of this game) making these areas either nearly impossible or totally impossible. Many of the sidequests have pretty bad bugs and the game routinely presents objectives in a confusing manner causing the player to wonder (what am I supposed to do again?). The game's main plot is interesting but the sidequests are totally amoral and the ethics of your character (or rather, the total lack thereof) do not seem to matter at all in this game world one way or another causing me to be less intellectually captivated in this game than I otherwise could have been. But despite everything wrong with this game, it does get a lot more right but it might be best to only focus on the main quests only unless you are a truly big fan of this game.Pretty Good overall despite several weaknesses, the greatest of which is the game constantly bringing back previously defeated enemies back to life.

As an Early Acess game that recently leaved alpha, you first should understand that this game will have a long road ahead, the team behind has very ambitious plans to what every player will be able to do in the final product. Don't Starve and Oxygen not Included can't be compared for scale of development, ONI is a much more complex and intricated system that take in consideration real world dynamics such Physics and Thermonadynamic, everything can be used or have some type of interaction, simple or complex.
Taking this in consideration, klei team at the moment is developing more core mechanics and increasing the complexity of what can be done for the current stage of the game. As an player you can see this as steps towards the right direction, you cannot reach a end game objective without having the tools to take you there (at least to a game much more related to Rim World than Don't Starve).
Currently the upgrades are released on a 5 week schedule, with a pre-release branch available 2 weeks earlier to anyone interested in helping solving more eminent bugs (or having a lot of curiosity about). Updates ares almost daily depending on the stage of the current patch, so yeah, there are bugs because this is an early acess, but they listen to the community and bring sollutions very quickly.
Not every element on a upgrade will satisfy you, bring your opnion and share with the others.
, is a good place for that.
If you don't like the lack of a final stage/ objective, but is very passionate in developing solutions and test your skills in making a susteinable world, give this a shot, in the long run you will have supported an awesome game.
If not, than wait, maybe with more robust final objective you can have a blast playing this too.
Or, save the money, never is a bad time to think better about what you're spending your money on.
Just please, don't support an early acess game without understanding what you are getting, there are plenty of information in the web to help you, this way you help yourself and the others interested in buying this.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
TL'DR : Awesome game, long road ahead to be complete. Much more complex than Don't Starve ( in the same stage, not taking in consideration DLC's), not same type of game, can't be compared. Support if you understand what you are getting. Support if you like to have a good challenge.

I've now 100% completed the game with a save file time of 20 hours. My initial feelings of the game didn't change after seeing the rest of it. I don't think it's a particularly bad game, but why would I recommend a game that isn't fun? Yooka-Laylee doesn't challenge your abilities with its puzzles or platforming so much as it challenges your patience.
The game controls well for the most part with only intentionally-annoying features standing out. Transformations and movement-modes that don't let you make sharp turns even when stopped (especially the snow plough) are very annoying. The world 5 boss highlighted this very well as the only real challenge was properly controlling your character. Overall though, the game plays well, and once you unlock flying the game is a lot better. I'd suggest any new player rush to flying rather than staying in 1 world for too long running in circles.
Each world has its good and bad elements, but world 1 was was definitely the least annoying. World 2 and 5 were by far the most annoying, and worlds 2, 3, and 4 were pretty ugly. World 1 was also the most pretty and charming level. Most of the collectables were pretty reasonable to find and obtain, though there were some quills and casino coins hidden in very unfun places that dragged out finishing a world. If you were to hide 10 easter eggs in my backyard it might be fun for my kids to hunt for them, but if you burried 2 eggs 6-feet in the dirt and didn't tell them, they might not have fun after the first 8. The level design overall is pretty lazy, but that kinda fits with the rest of the game. I have a hard time believing the team responsible for this game is very creative when almost everything in the game is so obvious. Puzzles like activating visually distinct objects in the right order are the perfect example of what I consider lazy. The worlds are full of elements like these that seem to fulfill the requirement for game length and "content" without passing the test of "is this interesting?" or "is this fun?"
Mini-games and puzzles were one of the weakest elements of gameplay. Rextro's game and the mine-cart runs were entirely not fun, and when the requisite score for those was anything but a joke, it was annoying replaying these games. Fulfilling puzzles or "quests" to unlock pagies was rarely entertaining. Getting the keys from the 4 pigs on world 5 is a great example of an awful filler objective. There's no challenge in it, yet it's tedious. Some of the mini-games that are challenging might entertain some, but I think most people would be annoyed like I was.
The quizes are insanely stupid and the game would have been better without them.
In contrast, exploration was the best part of the game. The first half of every world where you're running around grabbing quills and naturally stumbling upon challenges is great (even if the challenges themselves aren't). When you've completed the obvious ones though, finding the rest is annoying. For finding missing quills and other powerups, the hunter tonic helps give you the power to finish, but it doesn't make it easy. There's no compass telling you where the nearest item is, you just have to exhaustively search the entire world with the benefit of slightly better perception in your viscinity.
There's not much to say about the plot. I think for the most part it's stupid by design and meant to be silly, but that doesn't make it good or interesting. It's bad and it has an excuse, but it still doesn't make the game better.
The characters are the biggest disappointment and downfall of the game. Theoretically, Yooka-Laylee is a potentially cute, fun little game full of bright colors and humor, but this potential is poorly realized. The art of the characters is fine and not what I'm talking about. The voiceovers are mostly annoying, and I'm not wholly against the concept of nonsense pseudo-speak the characters use (I have fond memories of Goblin's Quest 3), but for the most part these don't sound like speech sounds. If the speech was nonsensical syllables strung together it would have been a lot better.
The biggest problem with the characters is the dialog. There was no emotion evoked in me from any of the dialog or cutscenes in this game other than cringe. It feels like watching a TV show for Toddlers along the lines of Dora or Teletubbies. I can't even describe the personality of the characters other than Laylee is a snide prick towards everyone. The main characters like to predict their victory. The fat pig is a fat pig. The bad guy taunts you. None of this is done well, and the unskippable dialog and cutscenes put a spotlight on this, the worst element of the game.
Overall, Yooka-Laylee is alright if that's what you want to play. I haven't played Banjo, and maybe I need to so that I can compare this to it, but I don't think this game stands up to the likes of Mario 64 and the Crash Bandicoot series. I don't think anyone's wrong for liking this game, I just didn't like it myself. Overall I'd say it's a 5/10. It's competent with some problems and bugs, but it's not exemplary at all. In the end what really matters with a game is that it's fun, and while I don't have any desire to refund this game, nor do I regret buying it, I think there are much better ways to spend your time and money.

This is basically Banjo-Threeie. There is really not much new here, and that's not a bad thing. It's got all the humour/innuendos, puzzles, characters, and charm Banjo Kazooie/Tooie has. But since it has all the old stuff all the problems come along with it. The camera is not great, and neither is the shooting/aiming. I don't really care though since it's just so much fun. I was a Kickstarter Backer and only paid $15 USD for this so it's definitely well worth it for me. Is it worth $40 USD? That's really up to you in the end.  If you like old school Rare games, this is for you. If you don't, then it's not.

I'll cover the game, but first I need to talk about the developers.
This game is helmed by the best company/team I've ever encountered in a long time. They work & worked very hard on this SG2 which was even a joy to play incomplete in the earlier betas - constantly (like to the point of how do you get any work done?) reading, replying, and participating in forum discussions. They entertain ideas for how to approach planned features & possiblities of integrating new ones. This game is far from done in their eyes, and we are all excited to see how SG2 evolves over the long run.
Oh yeah, the game: The graphics are awesome. The difficulty is varied enough to appeal to everyone (I'm in the extreme club, and find it quite challenging at times). You feel the constant itch to explore as available ship components, slot enhancements, crew officers, mercenaries, and new ship models differ between areas - and buying a ship direct from the manufacturer is cheaper than buying 3rd party from a different faction.
Don't want to or can't buy a ship (because that faction hates you)? Grind rep and switch sides, or just board and capture the ship for yourself. Want to mine asteroid fields? You can do that. Want to capture ships and sell them for millions? You can do that too. Want to hunt down obsure achievements? They're here.
And this game is only going to get better.
Positive
+ Awesome community
+ Gameplay rewarding proper piloting
+ Mod support (check out sound, graphics, and UI mods)
+ Craftable rare drops (blueprints) that feel as good in use as they are frustrating to get
+ Power management
+ Huge map
+ Wormholes!
+ Great music
+ Interesting campaign storyline
Neutral
+/- Slow start - it's very hard to begin classing up in ships, especially for new players. There are guides, but there is a bit of a grind. I like the payoff feeling from earning your way. Others will just go get a mod that gives them 1 billion credits. I suggest learning.
Negative
- Voice acting (there is a mod that improves a bit).
- Illegal goods priced roughly equivalent to expensive legal goods.
- Trade market prices could be more varied for better profits.
- Few factors past pool numbers for shields and hulls.
- Unrealistic aggro (2 gunships will "think" they can take on your dreadnought and rip you out of cruise speed).
What can I say. The game is just great!

Campaign done, here's *thoughts*.
Good:  To start off with, the music in SG2 is pretty great.  That's the first thing that hits me, and it's always good whenever I've booted the game.  A bit more variety would be nice too, after a while of free-roaming, it might get a little stale, but that goes for most games, really.
Bad:  The dialog and cutscenes are terrible.  No, really REALLY terrible.  The dialog is cliche, and *hideously* over-acted.  And those accents?  AND NO SKIP??  And the game doesn't really pause during these tedious, cliche, dragging, unskippable cutscenes.  I've seen better cutscenes in pretty much any other game.
Good:  Ships.  Mostly.  They're all quite recognizable, and have a lot of variety.  Once you know the ships, you can see a silhouette of most of them from most angles, and be able to ID the specific ship, or at least class.  Nexus ships a couple others in particular are EASY to spot.  Transports less so, but their class is obvious, so no matter.
Bad:  Firing arcs.  These are SPACE ships, they should have minimal blind spots.  They are not floating in an ocean, they need coverage above and below.
Bad:  There is a single "best" weapon, DPS-wise?  The stats show that, anyway.  Beams tickle, the only NPC weapons that seem to DO anything are rails and plasma.  This balance state made it out of early access?
Bad:  Map and space design.  Freelancer got this right, and they had space with "too much" stuff in it.  The SG2 single solar system is both incredibly too small and insanely crowded.  It would be fine for say, underwater on an ocean planet, but for "outer space" it's just crowded.  And the "movement" field for dust floating past makes it feel like a fish tank with a broken filter and a bunch of pooping fish.
Space Engineers and EVE and to a lesser extent Freelancer made the game FEEL spacious.  SG2 is a lot of LARGE factions crammed into a small fish tank with a bunch of stuff floating in the water.
Bad:  I finally managed to get a ST-drive, yay!  ...Only to find that it doesn't actually work?  *All* the things should be working before the EA tag comes off.  At least implemented in some state.

I am going to give an honest review on this game:
COD: Black Ops II is probably one of the best Call of Duty games.  Treyarch really knows how to connect with their community and work with them to make a game for everyone!  The new singleplayer create-a-class system was pretty interesting, and it made me want to complete those extra missions to unlock weapons and allowed me to choose my approach how I wanted to.  Besides that, the story was very interesting and the strike force missions were cool side missions, with multiple endings.  The multiplayer is the part of COD that gets the most hate.  The multiplayer on Black Ops II was probably the smoothest experience I have ever had with any COD multiplayer.  Even when playing at 150 ping I feel like I am playing at 2!  The pick 10 system and scorestreaks were great new additions to the game!  The zombies, while I have never been a fan of in the past, really addicted me into its story and was very fun to play with friends.
Pros:

+: Multiplayer is very smooth and is obviously well-optimized for PC
+: Zombies is well put together and new survival mode makes it better for those nostalgic zombie players
Cons:
-: Multiplayer seems kind of like a futuristic DLC for Black Ops 1 in a full game, easibly overlookable
My overall rating for this game is 9.5/10.  I would recommend waiting until this game is on sale, but it is definetly worth the $60.

So, after reviewing
(that was sarcasm for those who don't get it) I may as well go ahead and review Black Ops 2, also since I directly had some comparisons done with Ghosts. This is mostly on multiplayer.
So yep, Black Ops 2, not just that it is a pretty solid CoD-game with solid mechanics, it's also a pretty good PC-Port. Treyarch sure did a great (maybe even the best) job since the last CoD-game with a proper server browser and freedom (that being CoD4 and World at War - Black Ops 1 was not such a good port performance-wise). It may rely on matchmaking as seen since Modern Warfare 2, but uses dedicated servers instead of player-hosted servers. Also, quite a neat amount of PC-related settings to optimise the game or even give it better-than-consoles graphics and a FOV-Setting!
Also runs at a rock-solid 120+ FPS here (can be set to have a maximum FPS cap of 200 FPS) with no drop-downs below that on max settings, while looking just a tad bit worse than Ghosts - which by itself runs at a varying 45-90 FPS at most times... So yeah, ports-wise it's a great CoD.
Sadly though, the bad taste of Modern Warfare 3 (which was awful, port-wise) probably kept a lot of people from getting Black Ops 2.
Still has a good-enough playerbase now to easily find TDM matches, too.

This game is truly unique entry in military shooter genre, as I’m sure many will tell you it’s not fun but I think they should take a step back with that statement. This game has fun gameplay, the controls are quick and responsive and the guns have a feeling of impact when you shoot. I think the reason behind the "it’s not fun" statement is that you can have fun and run around and kill people with reckless abandon, but the game will stop you and say "Having fun? Why don’t you look at the suffering you just caused?" This game is not shy about making you look like a monster. There is a point in this game were you do something really, REALLY  bad, and when I had done that I needed to take a step back, turn off the game and remember it was all just a game and not real. But that part still sat with me lingering in my mind as I try to sleep that night. I did not play the multiplayer, but that’s not what I wanted this game for. This is a work of art, I have always enjoyed military shooters but this one really understands the psychological torment that can be inflicted to one’s mind in times of war. This game deserves a lot of recognition for what it accomplishes and a great step towards furthering games as an artistic medium.

Everyone thought that this game was doomed. A new developer, no Kevin Conroy, and no Mark Hamill. Everyone thought this game was a quick cash-in. Everyone was wrong.
Arkham Origins didn't set out to fix what wasn't broken. It took the Arkham City formula and expanded on it. Combat's a bit more refined, investigations are far more detailed, you've got more of Gotham to explore. It also borrowed from the best of Arkham Asylum. I won't spoil how.
But the real selling point to the game is the story.. and my God, the story and presentation put this game up there as the best in the Arkham series for me. Incredible cinematic style through a story with twists and turns make this an epic wild ride. The voice actors all deserve major kudos, but none moreso than Roger Craig Smith as Batman and Troy Baker as The Joker.
Seriously, Baker's Joker is insanely awesome. The voice just radiates madness and chaos and murder while being able to channel Mark Hamill's performance to the point that you'll find yourself forgetting it's not Hamill anymore. There's a real sinister, monsterous glee to the voice. I can't understate how bloody incredible it is.
Visually, the game is a step up from Arkham City. Textures are higher quality, things have a great crispness and clarity. Framerates were very steady for me on the highest settings with FXAA. Audio is great, too. Combat impacts sound bone-crushingly painful. The music has a dark Christmas-y tone to it like right out of Batman Returns. It fits.
The game world is Old Gotham and New Gotham.. as in the area that would one day become Arkham City, and the newer part of the city across the bridge. Retreading the Arkham City area doesn't feel lazy or repetitive, and you'll enjoy seeing the place before it all hit the fan. Lots of nods and references to what came before (or will come, I guess).
And there's a lot to do in this game. Side missions keep coming as the story progresses. There's never nothing to do. Really.
That's not to say the game is flawless. There are one or two game-breaking glitches right now in the PC version but WB Montreal is aware of it and they should be taken care of shortly. Combat can be a little annoying from time to time as you find yourself unable to counter incoming attacks that you know you hit the button in time for, but I had the same problem in Arkham City and it might just be a personal skill issue.
If you beat the game, you unlock New Game Plus, and if you beat that you get access to I Am The Night mode which introduces a sort of perma-death. Worth checking out if you're in for a challenge.
The game does have a multiplayer mode to go with it but I haven't played it yet. It has nothing to do with the single player campaign, at least, so take it as you will.
I -HIGHLY- recommend this game for everyone. Look past your doubts. WB Montreal did justice to the Batman/Arkham legacy. It's worth your time and money to experience this. It's a real joy.
