All we have at the moment is the paris mission but so far I like the level alot.  The open style gameplay is back like the older games had and the level is the most open and large I have seen other than the Japan missions in SA and they were pretty much empty.  The disquise system is not only better than the bad one from absolution but it is an improvement over the old games.  It has the realistic element that allows people like a security team leader to see that you are not part of his team but leaves the rest of the workers clueless so you can have fun.  Thanks to the sections that only allow certain personell it is both fun and challenging.
Graphics on the Paris level are great.  Shadows look soft when cast from high sources and hard when cast up close.  No line where shadows switch from low to high in your face like GTA 5.  Lights are fantastic and they have a very soft CG quality to them plus god rays look nice but not overdone.  The character models look high poly and the crowds of people are huge.  Texture quality is good but not great.  The textures do have a fantastic art style to them and really the whole art design is fantastic like it has been in all the previous games for the series.
The kills in this game are fun and a bunch of options are available.  Some of the illusion of free will is disturbed by the triggered nature of the kills.  In Blood Money you had a few scripted accident kills but you were given more options to take the target out however you wanted as they walked around the game.  In the Paris mission both targets are followed by body guards everywhere other than the bathroom and they won't go to the bathroom unless you poison them.  Every room that a target will go in has people in them which forces you to either poison the target or kill them in front of others.
Personally I like what they have done and I think it is fun and adds more gameplay to the mission if you have to knock out and hide certain civilians and body guards before taking out the target  but I wouldn't mind if thy had a few spots in the level where NPC's randomly walk through an area  but if you are patient or get lucky you maight catch a target alone for just enough time to pull  off the kill  without getting cought.  This can be done in a few spots for the male target if you take out his body guard first but the female target must have characters removed from rooms before the kill unless poison is used.  As of writing this I have only seen the first mission so this may improve in future missions plus with contracts mode you can assign target that will allow this form of gameplay on your own.
So far the performance has been really good at 1080P with everything maxed out other than supersampling.  My FPS is always locked at my TV's refresh rate of 60Hz.  I am using a 6700K CPU and a single 980TI superclock for graphics.  I have SLI but it's not working currently.   The game will run slower and have lag spikes if I don't disable SLI from the control panel.  My hope is that SLI will be supported so I can use 4K resolutions in the future.  One last thing I forgot to mentino initially.  Avoid DX12 until they fix it.  It causes odd slow downs and game freezing for me.  So I have been playing in DX11.  Also I am using a Samsung m.2 hardrive which is pretty fast so the load times for me is 12 seconds for the level and 6 seconds to load a save.  This could be considerably worse for slower drives which i have heard complaints about.  If you are reading this and you own a  fast hardrive you won't have to worry about load times.

It really does hurt to do this, but for $40 there are just way better games out right now.  The camera is constantly wrested from your control at inopportune moments, bugs like floating enemies and
put a real damper on the fun.
The game is of course adorable and it looks wonderful, the music is amazing, but the accusations of boneheaded level design are unforutnately true.  You'll often spend 10+ minutes scaling obstacles, maybe falling off a couple times and climbing back up, only to discover that you lack an ability or key or expansion to reach the prize.  You can't help but feel frustrated that the game doesn't have the decency to put its gating mechanics at the beginning of these long obstacle courses so that you don't waste so much time for nothing.
The camera is often overly busy, as though the game really doesn't want you manually controlling it as though the right analog stick hasn't been invented yet.  There's even a dedicated camera reset button on the right trigger which is a really strange sight in 2017, and if you're not using a Steam Controller with jump bound to the right pad click you're probably going to be forced to use that camera reset button a lot.
Speaking of which, I most certainly hope you're using a controller because this game won't even let you rebind your keybindings.  You can't use simultaneous mouse and gamepad input either, so I highly recommend rebinding your controls through the Steam Configurator to get something somewhat reasonable.  Over the shoulder third-person segments don't even let you shoot by pulling the right trigger, so mode shifts are practically a must for comfortable controls.
It's tragic, because there is so much to love about this game and what it could have been.  I'm a huge Banjo-Kazooie fan and while I feel like I got my $10's worth out of the Kickstarter I don't feel like I can really recommend this game for full price.  Maybe if later patches address some of the technical issues and provide more options, maybe if the game introduces the Steam Controller API so that controller players can rebind their controls per segment or minigame, then this game might be worth buying if you're nostalgic for the old Rare platformers, but until then you should wait until this game hits the bargain bin.

Playtonic have made a game with the scale of Banjo-Tooie but less than the content of even Kazooie, wherein you will be a hundred times more invested in fighting the camera than what few enemies there are.
In all seriousness, consider this a thumbs sideways. It's mediocre. It's not the irredeemable trash fire that Jim Sterling would have you believe, but it feels aged and rusty. The former Banjo team put a lot of effort into the aesthetic of the game... and yet the environments still have that unmistakable uncanny feel of "made in Unity". The levels are huge, and yet are largely bereft of unique landmarks or enemies or puzzles. There ARE enemies and puzzles, of course, but the scale of the game feels like they built everything up first, started trying to fill it in, and ran out of budget.
The premise isn't overly gripping -- the villain is mostly just a stereotypical corporate overlord. He's a jerk, for sure, but doesn't seem altogether invested as an actual villain. The true driving force of the game, the magic book that can be used to rewrite the fabric of reality, seems like more of a side project and only has its purpose revealed to you by one of the talking collectibles as an afterthought. Wait, what?!
There are, of course, numerous gameplay elements cribbed directly from the Banjo games... for better and for worse. The transformations are here, but insofar are
to play as rather than an entertaining novelty. The dialogue has lost what little subtlety it ever had, and very dryly delivers a torrent of forced puns and witticisms that rarely (but do sometimes) hit their mark. Playtonic seem to realize that Grunty's Furnace Fun was really memorable, but unfortunately forgot that the actual quiz part of it was kind of horrible to play. This time, you get the awful quiz part (multiple times through the game as filler, rather than at the end where it made more sense), without the parts that actually made it memorable. Features such gems as "how long have you been playing the game for?" with about a 15 minute margin of error.
I will say I really like the music; Kirkhope is in good form here, as is David Wise. The voices are alright, and the controls aren't bad. The worlds look fine. The characters are animated well. The googly eyed enemies now being some sort of horrifying symbiote that latches onto nearby inanimate objects is a genuinely clever new twist, but the fact that these bog-standard grunts have invulnerability phases is neither communicated well, nor a good combat mechanic. The graphics, controller, and audio options are unfortunately sparse, general optimization is passable but could've been better, the camera (even with launch day patch) has somehow regressed to some sort of inferior version of Mario 64's camera and WILL get you killed at some point, I saw an enemy fall through the floor as I was writing this, and after one play session I'm left less with an eagerness to progress, and more of a dull exhaustion.
It's a serviceable collectathon that tries desperately to ride on the coattails of its nostalgia factor, yet ironically might be better received by the crowd who've never played the Banjo games for comparison. I'd still give it a cautious recommendation on sale, but given that Bayonetta has suddenly launched on the same day, it's hard not to think of more enjoyable games available for cheaper.
PS: Crouching while cloaked lets you redirect lasers and focus light beams with your tail. This mechanic is neither explained nor hinted at anywhere.

Borderlands 2 is a first-person shooter set in the colourful world of Pandora. You choose from one of the four Vault Hunters (or classes): Commando, Siren, Gunzerker or Assassin. The main villain is Handsome Jack and it is your job to stop his diabolical plan through leveling, shooting and looting.
Story: The story in Borderlands is pretty straightforward. Handsome Jack has attacked the Vault Hunters and declared his scheme to use Eridium (a power source) to unlock the Vault. As you progress through the game, he will often talk as you are completing the main story missions and what he says is normally charming and most of the time, outrageous. Personally, I believe Handsome Jack is one of the most charismatic villains in all of gaming and his true intentions will be made clear as you move closer to the end of the game. In my opinion, the game's narrative is interesting and very humorous.
Graphics: This is where Borderlands stands out from the rest of the FPS crowd. Sick of dark and washed out colours from games such as Call of Duty or Killzone? Then say no more, Borderlands is the complete opposite. The game's cel-shaded graphics work really well to bring life and personality to the game. The games environments are lush, full of detail and are extremely vibrant in colour (which complements the light tone of the story). Monster designs are creative and the weapon design innovative. Borderlands 2 definitely leaves a lasting impression on me.
Gameplay: Now this is where the game excels. Unlike other first-person shooters where you often go through missions linearly, Borderlands encourages open-world gameplay. This involves you being able to complete many side-quests in addition to the main story and this adds a substantial amount of replayability to the game. There are countless hours of shooting fun to be had. Also, the gameplay is similar to that of Diablo where you can gain levels and when you kill monsters, you can pick up various loot such as weapons, skins, modifications or shields. Finding that epic loot is definitely very addictive and very fun. Top-notch stuff.
Overall, Borderlands 2 is an excellent game that was clearly made with alot of hard work, passion and creativity. It stands above other similar games for it's immense replay value, various character classes, charm and above all, it's addictive loot-based gameplay.

Let’s cut to the chase; Mad Max is bland and generic. Which, for a series with themes of anarchy and madness, and with multiple films containing fairly fresh and original ideas, is a really odd thing to have to say. There’s very little here that hasn’t been done before and done better, and the more you whittle away at the game, the more readily this becomes clearly apparent. The end result is a game which rapidly loses its appeal for each hour that passes, and one that has no real reason to stick around in your memory for the long term.
To pick apart why this is the case, you only need to look at the core structure of the game. It’s a case of going to one location to scout out points of interest in the area, and then going to those points of interest and clearing them out. Do that over and over again, and finally the area will be free of any ‘threat’ and you can move on to the next area and do it all again. If this seems familiar, it’s because you probably recognise it as that classic ‘Ubisoft formula’ game style that’s been used in countless titles in the past few years; Watch Dogs, Assassin’s Creed, Far Cry, you could go on. It’s not the only idea to be mundanely recycled, either. The whole hand to hand combat system, for instance, is incredibly close to that of the Batman franchise, right down to the counters and combo meter. It’s so confusingly similar, that given a few hours you’d be forgiven for wondering why Mad Max himself isn’t wearing the cape and cowl.
There’s nothing technically wrong with the re-use of such elements, especially considering they work; but it’s just so tiring to see them so lazily recycled here, especially in conjunction with a franchise such as this. It’s a potentially forgivable grievance, but dig a little deeper into more specific gameplay elements, and you’ll see just how flat this whole experience is. For instance, collecting scrap for upgrades is vital to making progress, but you soon learn if there’s a slight annex or route off the (completely linear) path through enemy bases, there’s going to be scrap there.  It’s not even open to questioning – it’s simple fact. Such cliché gameplay elements roll on– if there’s a door that needs explosives to open, there’s guaranteed to be some sort of combustible extremely close nearby. If you need fuel for a generator, there’s going to be cans of it within ten feet of your location. This last one is particularly laughable – the game goes on about the scarcity of fuel, but you can pick up a fuel can that’s required for some purpose, and IMMEDIATELY see another one spawn in its place. It’s possible to stack about 5 or 6 cans up just by picking up the new spawn and immediately dropping it. It’s absurd.
The whole issue with this cookie cutter generic gameplay and the desire for the game to hold your hand only goes to fly in the face of the game’s (and the franchise as a whole) ideas of survival as a whole. Early on, you’re told to keep fuel for your car close at hand lest you get stranded, and keep your canteen full of water as it’s your only means of refilling health. It’s a neat concept in theory  – desperately trying to cling on to your last supplies as they slowly dwindle away – but you soon realise both these supplies are practically everywhere. In all my time playing, I don’t think I’ve refuelled my car once. It’s not even come close to starting to run out. Water also becomes meaningless when you realise death only drops you a few minutes back with a miraculously full life bar. It’s all just so painfully bland, so much so that the end result just makes you want to smash your head into the keyboard.
Is there any positives? Well, yeah, actually. Car combat is a little weird and doesn’t work perfectly, but it’s damn fun all the same, which is what you’d sort of expect from anything relating to Mad Max. The car harpoon is the obvious highlight – using it to rip off parts of your opponent’s vehicles until they are a mere shell, and then boosting into them for a glorious finale of explosive pyrotechnics. You could, of course, just cut out the middle man and harpoon your foe straight out the driver seat, dragging them merrily along behind you before whipping them into the nearest brick wall for a gristly finale. It’s delightfully vindictive fun that only gets more fun the more you upgrade your car into the perfect killing machine.
The game itself is also visually stunning. The wasteland is an eerie place just to drive around, dust and sand whipping away at your feet, elegant arcs being carved through the sand as you get into your car and roar away. When you encounter your first storm, the screen filling with debris and your speakers roaring with the sound of the wind, it’s a genuinely terrifying and immersive experience. HUD clutter ruins the effect somewhat, but you can go into photo mode (it in itself good fun to play around with) and eradicate that nuisance, as long as you don’t mind not knowing where anything else for a while. It’s a visual spectacle that does capture the spirit of a destroyed and ravaged world in a weird and wonderful way.
Overall, though, it’s really, REALLY hard to recommend Mad Max. Fans will get something out of it – that goes without saying – and if you know exactly what you’re going into and don’t expect much from the whole affair, there is fun to be had. Overall, though, the rest of us will find a game that’s ticks all the right boxes mechanically, but lacks any soul whatsoever. And all things considered, that’s... Well, mad.

For Steam's Only (current) Pool Game, Pool Nation sets a high bar for any Billiard-themed game that wants to show up on Steam. The physics for this game are top notch with the ability to perform jump, swerve, bounce and multiball trick shots are but a minute's time and a precice accurate eye, away. And there is nothing more relaxing to me than taking time to set off the perfect shot, and rub it in the Computer's proverbial face.
Positives: The Graphics are AMAZING. (I know what you are thinking: "How The [Expletive] could a Pool game have good graphics?!") Well, to put it this way, imagine the shiniest piece of metal to ever grace your eyes. A shine so great you could literally ogle at your perfect image in its reflections. That is how the game looks. It's that good.
Negatives: With great graphics, comes great disk space. The ammount of data that was put into making this game look and feel soo good, creates alot of memory. The size of this game is atleast 5x the expected size of what someone would think a Pool game would be, numbers-wise. It is pretty damn big for a 'simple' Pool Game.
Grey Areas: The AI. I like to compare the AI in this game slightly similar to the AI in Worms Revolution. How? They both are perfectly accurate when they try, but when they mess up, they mess up HARD. The nicer part about the AI in Pool Nation, though, is that the AI will give you a large break when you first start to play. And the chances of your Computer Counterpart getting a perfect 8 ball streak win against you is almost impossible. But rest assured, there will be no mercy if you can't learn to pocket well.
But after touching upon all these needed areas, Pool Nation is definately a must have for cheap, simple, yet enjoyable for many-a-time-gaming. Overall Ranking of games I've played: (9/10 because Left 4 Dead 2 & Kingdom Hearts still have my ties for 10/10 of all time).

An outstandingly simple but well-executed game, Pool Nation does one thing but it does it very very well. Actually, that's not really accurate, because there are a great many components of the game that work seamlessly together, including the lobby, multiplayer connection, freeplay for practicing for a no-stress way to improve your game, and a wry sense of humor. The ability to play on your own in the lobby while waiting for friends to connect is one example of a small feature that makes a world of difference.
The other wonderful thing has been the active and friendly development staff who have been available online to answer questions, address bugs, and take suggestions for improvements and changes. All in all a wonderful effort at a great price, and I hope the devs are able to continue to support it and continue bringing their level of quality control to their next game.

Another abysmal port. More abysmal controller support.
After having a lot of fun with this on my console, I grabbed it on Steam. Unfortunately like several "controller enabled" titles here, the input progarmming is only half complete. Instead of having a fully functional control mapping feature, it simply picks up input devices and automatically assigns them to functions in the game. This means that if you have other controllers besides a gamepad, like throttles and sliders, menus and views will constantly scroll or move until you find the offending device and unplug or otherwise disable it.
This is a fun little game, but I have no desire to constantly unplug or reconfigure controllers just to play, only to have to reconfigure again to play games which use those controllers.
On top of this, there was no consideration for alternate resolutions (such as multiple monitor setups). The 3d portion of the game functions, but 2d elements such as splash screens fail to scale properly, making them unreadable.
Either make PC games or don't make them. I have no interest in a product that not only doesn't fully support my platform, but forces me to disable features of the platform in order to make the product usable.

Max Payne is a classic that proves one thing: they don't make 'em like this anymore. Given that it came out in 2001, that's probably obvious, but bear with me here. The style of the game consistently straddles the line between grittiness and campiness. It is at once a darkly humorous, self-aware love letter to film noir and a prime example of late 90s/early 2000s "badass". It has a certain essence that its higher-production-value sequels lack, despite their other qualities, and I imagine the story has something to do with it as well.
Even the nature of the protagonist clues you in to these qualities. I mean...his name is
. He wears a trenchcoat at all times. His face, for all the range that it displays in the neat graphic novel 'cutsenes', is modeled in a permanent state of incontinence whenever you see it in-game.
The story starts off relatively rote, placing you in the seedy underbelly of New York street crime. Even then the two-bit underlings you're fighting give off an exaggerated air, like they're the distillation of every criminal stereotype given just enough believability to conceivably be for real. When you're done with them, things start escalating and eventually get pretty crazy, even for neo-noir. Through it all however the game still manages to make you feel like a one-man army waging a war of desperation, probably because it makes quite clear the odds Mr. Payne is facing, and that's how it remains compelling.
Max Payne is a fairly difficult game. That's the other half of the "they don't make 'em like they used to" equation, not that the modern trends of accessibility and a range of difficulties for different types of players are bad things. The default difficulty however is dynamic - the game makes itself easier when you die and makes itself harder if you're blowing through it like one-ply. It doesn't take effect if you quickload in a hopeless situation or immediately after you die, which I naturally only learned after beating the game. I'd recommend playing it on the dynamic difficulty, and to not be afraid of saving if you need to. The end result is that there's a fair bit of game here, despite no multiplayer: I'd say the whole campaign will last you 10 to 12 hours on your first playthrough.
While the gunplay definitely improved with Max Payne 2, it's still fairly good here. This game was one of the first to model bullets as actual projectiles in flight instead of instant hitscan deathrays, and you'll need to take advantage of that by leading your shots, and outright dodging enemy volleys with your movement abilities. Speaking of which, movement in Max Payne is almost as fun as the shooting (aside from the odd platforming bit anyway) and they combine to create a rewarding combat system that still holds up today for those who don't mind some challenge.
Overall, Max Payne is worth playing if you're into noir or old games and looking for something to sink your teeth into.

I was introduced to this by markiplier's lets play series and i hadn't really been a fan or interested in this genre before, but the cuteness of the characters and flexible learning curve has been the main reason i took a chance on this game.
So on to the review !
It's addictive, swallows time up like a black hole and is really fun!  The game gives you basic tools at the start and like evolution it gradually improves your options through research, this then opens up a somewhat daunting spec tree of kit to build.
Which then leads into manipulating the biomes to suit your needs and if your lucky on the random map generator you can get very helpfull resources early on.
The game allows you to customize the dupes overall wellbeing from stress and illness to low to high or make it so they aren't affected at all, like a slightly more indepth version on difficulty.
It can be slow at the start while you're working things out and researching, but once you get the food/toilets/showers/power/  last but not least oxygen generation sorted, i found you get a lot of freedom to explore the map and discover new things.
During this build up of a base you will discover these dupes are DUMB and frankly suicidal.. if you tell a dupe to dig over a gap/hole/pit and aren't planning ahead with ladders/tiles or leaving stepping 'stones' for them they have this uncanny ability to dig where they stand and promptly fall in... The game has improved the alerts you get when a dupe is in distress, so you have a chance to save them, using the job menu you can select what dupes do and set priority level.
You start with 3 dupes which can be changed by a random generator and name them how you want, within reason, but be carefull if you do name them as you might get overly attached to them and over react when they get in trouble.
As you build out your base you will get the chance to select a new dupe from a set list of 3. But you can change them by saving before looking and reloading the save (might get patched).
Dupes have strengths and a weakness and a reaction to stress, strengths are usually an increase of 1 or 2 set skills, the weakness is usually one skill this dupe doesn't do at all, or they have a bad habit or medical condition like falling asleep randomly or breaking wind.  If stress is active they will react by doing something like smashing equipment or vomiting.
Some of those problems can be countered or even exploited via decor/general improvements to the base using stress relieving tech.
Pretty much every need is covered and the game still has more to come !
Buy it, start small think big !

Seriously, this is the definitive Jedi experience. After creating your own padawan from a number of races, skin tones and costumes (with more choices through mods), you undergo training with Kyle Katarn as your master and complete missions all over the galaxy in any order, gaining new jedi abilities and lightsaber fighting styles along the way. The main plot of the game unfolds and changes depending on decisions you make toward the end of the game.

I was raised on Dark Forces, Dark Forces II (Jedi Knight) and Jedi Outcast. This switch to third person view and the more generic "I am a nameless random Jedi" character you play instead of Kyle Katarn makes the game not very compelling to me. I played about 4-5 hours of it (pre-Steam) back in the old days, got bored with it, and forgot about it.
The upside is that it is, of course, much prettier than the older games. 3rd person view means lightsaber dancing looks cooler.
But overall, for me it was the most forgetable of all Star Wars games, namely due to my lack of interest in who I was playing (who can be customized up the wazoo, at least for a 90's era game). But Asypr/Lucasart's wish to make the game like an RPG, without the RPG elements, were its downfall. You play and watch Star Wars for the story and for the characters, not (just) the gameplay and the graphics.

I think the "Intro Pack" to the game is worth the money, for $15 you get enough to play for hours. I see myself replaying it over and over again until the next episode is released.

Ok this is my edited review. I'll try and be semi-objective as I have interacted with the dev's, their moderator and the community for some time. But please read on and judge for yourself.
Spg2 is a tactical space combat sim. I joined in EA and didn't play it for long due to hardware limitations on my account but liked the idea of a big massive universe where the player doesn't end up being the "King of the Hill" but just a small piece of a bigger universe. And Spg2 filled that need for me.
This is not the most epic game I've ever played and I didn't expect it to be. But from a small ~10-ish Croation developer team I've been surprised. Not only have these guys made their own engine which shows beatiful graphical capability but they also constantly updated the game for almost a year after release with steady patching and a nice and cheap DLC while being constantly (I can't express how crazy these dev's are when it comes to listen to player feedback and troubleshooting with the community, it's unheard of) active on forums and responding to any bug report they received and fixing it with each new update. This is more than half the reason I'd buy any game they'd ever release.
Well about the game; There are more in-depth Space Games out there, more epic stories to be told. But this game doesn't pretend to be any of that. It knows it's limitations as a huge space universe where the player is just a small piece of the puzzle. And it does that extremely well. Imagine being in a single-player MMO ( yeah kind of contradictory) but that's how this game treats you. You're nothing more special than the next dude around. You won't change the Universe all by yourself but you're just a small part in a bigger scheme. I love that sense of relating to your own existence in the world.
How many games dares that anymore? In an age where we all feel we're the turning point and center of the Universe this game is a fresh breath teaching us the Universe doesn't resolve around us but we're just here to try to survive and do the best we can.
There's no classic story arch to this game. You don't end up feeling like you're the king of the world. You're just a captain in the void trying to fend for him or herself. That's it. And from a philosophical perspective I love that notion. Too many games rub your need for being the "one and only". Not this game. This is reality expressed through a game. You're not gonna matter more than others but still need to claim your place in the world. That's beautiful and invigorating and  ... well poetic in some sense.
There's a story (campaign) in the game that lends itself to the lore created in Spg1. But former knowledge of that is not required. I am still on the last mission of that storyline but that's not the reason I play Spg2. I don't relate that much to the story as such but enjoy the stories I can make with my own captains more.
The game lets you choose between story and freeroam missions at a whim. You can always wander off to do randomly generated missions even when playing the campaign (campaign has a fixed character while freeroam lets you generate your own male/female character) and explore as you see fit. My preference and love for space was to be more of a "freelancer" doing randomly generated missions for different factions making friends and enemies along the way depending on my choice of the missions I'd carry out for different factions (help one faction=lose reputation with another faction and vice versa).
The game can be a grind for some, other cherish that type of neverending possibilities and in Spg2 the ever-changing possibilities for changing your reputation and the constant randomly generated missions can keep you playing this for hours on end.
Some days I just log in, cloak my ship and enjoy the scenery. Other days I just log in to take my temper out on whatever faction I'm currently in bad standing with and make them suffer.
For a better description of the game check some videos on Youtube or other reviews. I'm still sold on this thing and the constant updates, a very nice and cheap DLC plus the upcoming FREE DLC makes me wanna recommend this game to everybody. Best and coolest development team I've ever meet and a hell of a positive and friendly community.
This game is Steam History for the books. The reason I still get into EA from time to time is because of these guys right here.
This is a game made by gamers to gamers. And a hella lot of respect for their interaction, back-and-forth, constant updates and pleasent attitude.
If you're in doubt visit the forum. These guys are the future of gaming and a pinnacle of how developers can make gamers trust and cherish them again (yeah plenty of jaded gamers out there seeing bigger companies♥♥♥♥♥♥all over their customers or make highly dubious decisions).
Edit: It should be noted that this game twists a few familiar concepts of games and how to progress the best possible way. There's not much "hand-holding" here but the forum is pretty active to anyone needing a tip or two on how to get the most of it and learn those "different" mechanics/understanding from what other games usually bring. So remember to pitch in with questions if there are any or you don't understand something. The early game in particular can be a bit rough for new players but once they get a hang of it it's really not that hard to understand.

For the "tl;dr" crowd:  7/10
Almost 80 hours in, I found the game to be enjoyable for a space sim.  Many similarities to the "X" franchise (I have over 200 hours in "X2: The Threat"), but somewhat "lighter" in comparison.
Game mechanics are adequate (stations, planets, commodities, equipment, etc,), and do not get in the way of game play.  Conversely, they are not "deep" (no stock exchange, no station building/owning, no empire building), so there comes a point where it becomes routine and a bit boring.  I only played a "Gunner", and did not engage in all of the the game's offerings (mining, bounty hunting, etc.).
I found leveling to be almost too easy.  I would expect higher levels to become asymptotically harder to achieve, but the experience points required to level seemed to be rather linear.  After 78 hours of simultaneous freelance and story line, I was at level 79 ("Fleet Admiral"), where the story campaign was only requiring level 40.  If you want the story line to remain challenging, you should probably stick to it until it is complete, and then freelance.
Graphics are above average.  I always play with everything on high, so the space junk, asteroids, nebulea, visual effects, etc. really added to the immersion.  One of the bright points of the game engine is that
.  You fly through space, going from one grid tile to another, without having to transition in any way.  The only transitions in the game happen with the Jump Gates, T-Drive or Wormholes, which one would expect.
Combat is enjoyable, with enough going on to keep it interesting.  It doesn't take long, however, to know when enemies will ambush you, what specific loadout will let you take down a Hero, etc.  I rarely died in the game, and when I did, it was typically when there were just too many enemies concentrating their fire on me (and no allies in the vicinity to pull aggro for me), or when I accidently left my "Fire At Will" mode engaged and approached a station with enemies docked.
It is a 1.2 release as of this writing, and I have still experienced a few bugs.  The most ubiquitous is a "Maintenence" mission not completing following combat enroute (either by ambush or just encountering enemies along the way).  One that just hit me, that caused me to stop playing, was my entire equipment inventory suddenly disappeared after a T-Drive jump and an ambush when I materialized.  I went to change my equipement loadout (swap the T-Drive with Energy Shield for the fight), and my rather robust equipment inventory was just gone!  I tried several things, but I couldn't get it back, and decided that was enough.
I recommend the game to anybody who enjoys this genre (my favorite), and who is looking for a less-stressful diversion from the higher-order space simulations.

-Camera still bad, can't imagine how it was before update. It's like having a drone on a leash and trying to run through a dense forest without having the drone crash while it sometimes randomly teleports away.
-Unresponsive controls/Level design doesn't fit your moveset. Some parts are just needlessly iffy/too precise leading to frustration. Especially the parts where you have to use the roll are just not satisfying.
-Uninspired "challenges". Very much been there, done that. Also there are quite some where you can skip/cheat the challenge by jumping on surrounding geometry to get around obstacles (Like the wind turbines) or by bruteforcing yourself through it which makes it less of a challenge.
-Minigames feel like baby's first Unity game. I have seen more polished/fun games in 48 hour game making contests...
-Having part of the worlds locked till you expanded the world leads to dead ends that waste your time. Like for example spending a good 5 minutes to climb the tower in the first level only to see that there is absolutely nothing there till you expand. Happened multiple times. Luckely after world 1 you probably won't have to enter an unexpanded world again if you collect enough pagies.
-The game can't go 5 seconds without either treating you like an idiot or *wink* *wink* "reference lol* I just try to skip the text as fast as possible because most of it's sooooo mundane.
-Mandatory quizes! It's not that difficult but the punishment is incredibly annoying. Why did the quiz have to be a billion(10) questions long?? Especially annoying if you accidently press a button the moment the answer window pops up and thus lose a life. Why make the dialog slow and the answer part fast as ♥♥♥♥?!?
-Transformations are just... meh. Slow, boring abilities. Should have just been left out of the game.
-Inconsistant graphics ranging from good to rocks that belong in a ps2 game and standard Unity terrain.
tl;dr Just play Banjo Kazooie.

Updated Summary: The game is a 8/10 for me. It's solid, but has it's flaws. I highly recommend a controller no matter what. If you love 90's 3D platformers then it's a great buy at $40 USD, but if you only have a slight interest in platformers then wait till it hits the $10-$20 range.

I'll have to play through the game fully before I can say if it's worth it at "X price" or give a final score, but it's a 8/10 so far for me. Oh and I am using a controller for this, haven't tried keyboard/mouse, but it's a 3D platformer and it should be played with a controller.
Positive(s);
* Graphics are beautiful and zero performance issues for me
* Game mechanics are solid and fluid
* World design is amazing
* Written dialogue is hilarious
Neutral;
* Camera can be wonky in certain areas(forced perspectives), but the majority of the game it's fine so far.
* Can't skip cutscenes nor certain dialogue sequences.
* Update: Mini-bosses for the worlds were "ok", expected a bit more from them.
* Update: A few more worlds would have been appreciated, but hopefully DLC will fix this going forward.
Negative(s);
* Voices can get annoying at times, but can be skipped in most dialogue events while still reading the text.
* No online co-op or multiplayer, maybe in a future patch(?), but it's not the 90's anymore and most of my gaming friends are too far away to do some jolly cooperation with.
* Update: Lack of options with keyboard/mouse support, no B key assigned. Controller HIGHLY recommended.
*Update* April 14th
So I just finished the game(both defeating the end boss and collecting everything and getting all the achievements). In-game time was 18 hours and 35 minutes from start to finish.
I'm happy with the end boss fight and the feeling of having collected everything on my own is such a huge satisfaction that most video games do not give nowadays. I'd say if you loved Banjo and other 3D platformers growing up then the $40 USD price tag is fair, but if you're only semi-interested in the genre then wait until it hits $10-$20 USD.
It's a very solid game and I'd still give it a 8/10. If it had online co-op and a few more worlds with fixes for KB/M controls and voice options then I'd say it's a 9-10/10.
Also since I was a backer, I just want to say thanks to Playtonic for bringing this game to life. Seeing my name in the end credits was a joyful experience and a great end to this game for me.

The aesthetics are good and the music is amazing. Sadly, the story, controls and lack of clear objective or paths ruins this game for me. I can barely even play the game, and from what I've played, I know I won't finish the whole game.
The max mouse sensitivity is still abysmally low, and turning can take up to 2 meters of in-game floor to complete. There is no precise turning at all. Everything seems to be a fight against the game's ♥♥♥♥♥♥ controls
Not only that, but for keyboard users, forget knowing any of the controls. you can't rebind them, and they are NEVER stated properly. The entire control setup for the game is obscured and unknown.
Further, the cameraman is on ♥♥♥♥ing cocaine if I've ever seen it. This is some of the worst 3rd-person camera work ever. Imagine Super Mario 64, and make it even worse.
The biggest issue is controls and the camera. I can get past everything else and praise this game. I can get past a mediocre story, a lackluster "big bad" etc etc, but I can't get past the controls. It's a non-starter. When your controls are worse than the Nintendo 64 game that inspired your game, you must know that you've ♥♥♥♥ed up. Until they're fixed, I can only downvote this.

THE GAME ITSELF IS GREAT, BUT THE BUSINESS MODEL SUCKS DONKEY♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
Since things have changed a bit (as of November 2017), and since I can not give a middle-kind-of-thumb, I decided to recommend this game. IOI have managed to escape the claw of Square-Enix and are now working on the second Season. I would like to support them, however, I still don' support the always online, which is still ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Below my review that I haven't changed otherwise.
The reason is simple: This is a single player game that forces you to be online all the time. And no, the offline mode is NOT adequate. You simply get only half of the game if you play online. PERIOD. In the Beta everyone thought "yeah, online, metrics, bugfixing", but nobody expected - nor was told - that it would be like that in the full release. I had applied for a refund, but I didn't get it. So I am here to stay and play the game, even if it disconnects me and takes several retries before I can resume playing. And the loading times in the main menu are a joke. There are still lots of bugs. And while I can run the game on max settings (without SuperSampling) at 1680x1050 with an average of 90fps with my R9 390, I encounter regular slowdowns to under 25fps.
But what I want to say is: NO MONEY FOR SQUARE ENIX
The business practice shown here is but a huge middle finger to any honest gamer and had I known that BEFORE, I wouldn't have bought it, at all. Should the ever remove the always online, I will give it a recommendation and tell everyone to buy three, but until then, stay away and don't support this.
I really wish I could, because now for the actual review of the game itself:
It looks great. The world has so much detail going on. The NPC dialogue is marvellous, funny, great, awesome and some other words of joy you can insert [HERE]. The levels are now sandboxes, unlike the tube levels in Absolution.
You can devise so many ways to get your hit and if you have done everything, you can do some more. Just go to youtube and look what kind of crazy♥♥♥♥♥♥people are doing even without glitches. The prebuilt events are great nevertheless, like shooting a cannon or breaking a heart or doing it old school spy style.
I don't like that there are no difficulty levels anymore, because simply turning off the crutches is just not the same, because if I cave in, I can simply turn them back on. That takes a bit from the challenge in my opinion. Same with feats and opportunities. Feats basically tell you the hits, so turn them off! Opportunities should also be turned off, they are merely a step by step guide for the hits. I think a Hitman game doesn't need this kind of handholding.
Disguises work pretty well, they are not as broken as in Blood Money anymore and not as useless as in Absolution (or SA, in certain levels), but you now just have SOME people who might find you suspicious, who are more distrusting in that new one eighty bald guy who came today instead of my colleague.
All in all, this is the Hitman I love and if they can keep (or even raise) this level of quality, this will be the best Hitman game to date. And if they ever decide to NOT ♥♥♥♥ their customers in the♥♥♥♥♥ I will recommend it wholeheartedly to everyone.

I'll admit, this game might not be as powerful as it was before I heard it played upon expectations of the player considering the cloning of CoD singleplayer campaigns, but it was powerful either way! Left me thinking for a long while about it, how you, the player, and the character you control are responsible for the actions in game, how traumatizing PTSD is, how war can be actually hell... I wrote this last one off of Capcom's big book of clichés... and that from Yahtzee...
Spec Ops: The Line tells you about a squad of three man who go into the city of Dubai that recently suffered a huge sandstorm. Before said enviromental hazard occurred, the 33rd Battallion was stationed there in order to organize an evacuation that failed. Your buddy characters are Alphanso Adams (the "aww hell naw" guy) and John Lugo (the cracka sniper) and the generic burly white dude captain is Martin Walker, who you'll be controlling! Along the way into Dubai, you'll venture into the terror of war, questionable choices and dive into confusing insanity. Right now you may be thinking: "shouldn't games be fun?". They can be, but what they also can also be simoultneosly or not, is compelling. Horror games aren't necessairly just fun, they're interesting due to their mystery and opression they give to the player. Such method is used by Spec Ops: The Line. Do you feel ok for performing the acts that the game tells you to do and should you feel guilty for doing them wheather you wanted to do it or not...? That you'll have to answer... the question is worth 70% of your grade...
Unfortunatly, I can't say much without spoiling the story otherwise from saying that it's fantastic and screws with your mind aside from some minor plotholes. I do love the choices you make in the game, instead of Mass Effect-style of: good, bad and neutral choices. Instead, you get grey and debatble choices that don't really lead to any happy ending and it's all done mechanically instead of a cutscene which I friggin' love it! The best way to transmit story in gaming is through mechanics since you yourself are in control of the character. There is no other medium that can accompish that! Some choices may not have an impact to the gameplay but at least they build up properley the illusion that they may have. What I feared about the game is that it would only develop its narritive through cutscenes rather through interactivity, but that wasn't true.
The plot twist is quite amazing, as good as that of Bioshock 1! If you haven't played that game, you should! It's one of those that you could've spotted it if you paid close attention to the story. The plot twist was so good that it desearved its own paragraph in my review!
The game left me very curious about it and I did some reasearch on it out of free will. There's a lot under this game and you know, this could be used for schools if games weren't considered "only for children". It's acessible in both of its gameplay and story, you get to explore many metaphors and secrets of the narritive at the same time. Certainly be better than a book that does not follow the rules of grammar even though for 12 straight years you've been taught to obey said rules but you'll still be forced to analyze said book because f**k you (the book is called: "Memorial dos Conventos"). Sorry, I just had to this a small rant.
As for the gameplay, like I said, it's a chest-high wall simulator. You regenerate HP, use generic weapons (that have good weapon feedback at least since they kick a lot), hide between cover so you can suck on your thumb while the screen cleans itself from all of the jam and use shemactical manuveurs to get an advantage over your enemy. You can use the tactical button to flash your enemies or frag them or have them eliminated by your team mate in one button. But these only appear in contextual situations. You also can revive them, but they can't revive you because REASONS! Or maybe there's as an actual secret reason towards it.
During the combat, you can also shoot down on your enemies: sand. However, this is rare and amist the tension of the combat, such traps will be easily avoided.
As for enemies, there's nothing much to hype about, you have the regular dudes, crazy psychos trying to stab you, shotgunners (nothing more annoying then a storm of bullets to your face), special shemelta squad troopers (that act the same way as the regular soldiers), snipers (aimbot hax!) and of course, JUGGERNAUTS (bullet sponge)! The plot twist to this is that you'll be fighting american soldiers who are just doing their job, they're just normal people that you'll be forced to kill. Overall, there are third person shooters that are much better than this like Mass Effect.
There are also stealth sections that require you to use your teamates to take out enemies immediatly without any trouble. But they're far too short and lack depth. I would like if they would extend but I guess it was their objective to make the game as generic as possible in order to shock the player later on. Still, I think it was already generic with its combat, so it'd be great if it could vary things up with the stealth sections. If this game was released nowdays in between the other games that have tacked on stealth, because developers can't think of anything else, then I guess the shock effect would be better pulled off assuming these stealth sections were longer.
You can also perform executions to finish off downed enemies, it's unecessary but looking at the enemy in pain whilst they're downed just makes you want to be merciful and take them out immediatly. The executions do become more violent along the way and if you play the game you'll know why...
Technically, it's a preety good PC port, it runs well, looks good, controls ok but there are issues. The explosions effects are really bad and the .ini files are encrypted. All issues can be solved with the PCgamingwiki. The game may be griddy and dark, but the bright yellow and orange colours have a lot of charm to it. It looks like both the visual aesthetic and the actual content itself contrast themselves. Finally, the lighting affects are preety good, but it depends on the filter you choose. Not sure why that's something important you have to choose at the start of the game.
There's also multiplayer which is preety much a desert town (get it... desert town... like Dubai...) and COOP which I have not tried yet. I don't think you'll miss much with multiplayer, even the dev said they didn't want it in the game but 2K ordered them to make a multiplayer mode.
In conclusion, this game will leave a mark in my memory and it'll surely leave one in yours. Do not spoil yourself with walkthroughs, you'll punish yourself from a good game with an actual good interactive  gaming experience! I recommend it!

At first glance this game seemed to have everything I wanted from a RPG/space sim combo, but what started out as an enjoyable experience quickly turned into an exercise in frustration. The game seems to suffer from major balance issues and design flaws.
The class system doesn't really contribute much to the gameplay as the only difference between the three classes are 4 skills which hardly seem to affect gameplay other than an animation on activating a skill.
Regarding balance, I've played all three classes in campaign and freeroam mode and once you reach around level 12 the game seems to go out of sync with what your character is able to do. All combat missions have enemies rated as 'Impossible' to defeat and unless there happens to be friendlies in the area you're pretty much doomed. It also seems impossible to stay alive longer than a few seconds in hostile space as you'll be swarmed by enemies against which you stand no chance. So the sandbox is in reality confined to space in the vicinity of friendly stations.
Combat is clunky as most of the time you'll be battling the camera view instead of the enemies who will be off-screen for the majority of the fight. This means that manual combat isn't an option.
Making money to buy better ships is also a bit of a chore as it takes forever to make the roughly 2 million credits you'll need to buy your first decent ship. What seems to be the fastest way to make some money is by boarding and selling enemy ships which is also made almost impossible by friendly NPCs tending to blow up the ship you're trying to capture with all your troops on board.
All in all I'm rather disappointed to be so let down by this game as on the surface it really has the potential to be excellent.

After 28 hours, I've finished SG2 on normal difficulty. I've mixed feelings about this game. Since I got it at a reduced price and it managed to enthral me long enough to finish it, I hesitantly recommend this game.
I'll give you a list of things that, in my opinion, are well done (from + to +++) or bad (from - to ---).
Stability: +++
I've encountered not a single crash. Good work.
Bugs: +
There are some minor bugs but no show stopper. Most of the bugs are only slightly annoying or are gone once you restart.
Graphics: ++
Not cutting edge, but there are some nice visual effects that improve immersion.
Audio: +
Ok, but nothing eartshaking.
Character development: -
I didn't feel that there's anything that I really want to "reach" with my character, except maybe getting better ships. The skills are dull and consist mainly of "tier 1 gives you +8% dmg", "tier 2 gives you 16% dmg" and so on.
HUD: --
Bad HUD. You want to know what kind of ship you've just locked as a target? Well, better turn your giant Dreadnaught around and find out that it was just some tiny gunship that gets destroyed by your automatically firing canonns before you can take a look at it. You can't really scroll out while flying your ship, so that your view is basically reduced to what's in front of you.
Aiming / Target selection in combat: ---
They really dropped the ball here. You either enable automatic fire, which means that all your guns fire at will at a target of their chosing (no focus fire), or you take over manual control over your ship's weapons and try to hit your designated target. Unfortunately, this is so badly implemented that you will stick to auto fire 99% of the time.
Missions: -
You level up and get money from missions by activating the star map and click on a mission marker that has become available there. Missions are the entire content of the game. If you play the campaign, these mission markers may either be part of the main mission or they are a side mission. If you play in free mode (no campaign just pure exploration), there are no main mission markers. The side missions are repetitive as hell. Go there, kill that, finished. Go there, repair that, finished. Go there, take the item and bring it elsewhere, finished.
Role playing / Character immersion: --
Nope. No. There's none of that here, move along.
Fights: +
Fights are often balanced, sometimes not, but generally they are somewhat fun. Have a "meh" from me here.
Traveling: --
Pirates. Pirates, everywhere. Have you ever played an MMO where some frenzied rabbit may bite your horse and rip you out of travel mode so that you have to squish that little bug with one hit and then wait until you can enter travel mode again? Well, SG2 gives you some nostalgia here.
Campaign: -
The campaign is nothing special. You character is rather lethargic and just stumbles from one event into another. You can't make any choices either. The ending is rather unspectacular. I was like "and now? that's all or what?". There are no epic story fails, though.
Replay value: --
SG2's replay value is the same as the reeat value of a pizza.
Customization options of your character and ship: +
You can't customize your charakter except for his skills, but there are some nice options to personalize your ship, which is nice.
Modifications: ++
The fan base is strong in this one. There are some decent mods out there that give you new ship skins or that modify game values.
If you can get SG2 for less than $15 and like the genre, go for it.

Rust is honestly one of the best survival games out - and much like other survival games out there it takes time to understand the basics of resource griding and crafting. Rust in my honest opinion is best played with a group of people, if you're going solo try pick a smaller pop server until you get some experience.
The basis of rust is -
1. Resource Grind
2. Crafting your base
3. Survival
4. PVP / Raiding other bases
You're going to find out very quickly that in most servers shoot on sight is going to be standard, don't expect to go into a server and expect your first encounter is going to be friendly, it most likely won't be. People want your resources, especially in the early grind.
Servers will reset depending on the admin, allowing everyone to restart new. This can vary between a week or a month.
The game from my short time of play-time has shown me the dev's are continiously developing the game which is good, a few veteran's of rust have said over the last few months alot of updates have been happening and the player count is impressive.
Beware though, as like every other survival game out there - hackers can be a problem.
Also servers sometimes have a tendency to have memory leaks which can cause mass lag - but other then that it runs well for the most of the time. Also regarding servers, check when the restart of a server will happen, there is nothing quite like spending a whole day upgrading a base and then finding out the server resets the next day.
With a GTX 1080 I can have this game with most of the high settings although crop in can be a pain at times with my FPS dropping from 100 to 10 in a matter of seconds regarding loading.
In anycase, a sold game and worth the asking price. Hopefully the game will continue to develop and expand whilst fixing the issues.

I honestly tried to give this game a chance, but the problems stretch far beyond a technical level. The game feels like it had a lot of love put into it, but it lacks the polish of Banjo-Kazooie that it tries to recreate. So many game design flaws hinder this game including:
* Lacking the musical score that helped give Banjo-Kazooie its charm and life
* The controls are not always as 'tight' and 'perfect' as some say Banjo's are (terribly inconsistent and at times extremely frustrating)
* Frequent segments of the game involve waiting
* Worlds feel segmented, disjointed and nowhere near as natural as one might hope for
* Clunky and frustrating minigames break up the action and immersion on a constant basis
* NPCs are uninteractive and feel like set decoration rather than actual characters
* Constant reuse of NPCs from previous levels giving the feeling of a lack of progression
* Levels are divided by black holes in the wall that serve as checkpoints that make you more frustrated than relieved to respawn there
* The first boss fight is absolutely atrocious feeling so repetitive and uninteractive (even unmoving like the NPCs which make everything seem lifeless)
* The game is extremely easy with the only challenge being to collect the overabundance and oddly placed collectables
* Significantly less time clearly went into polishing the minigames (again which appear much too often) and it shows making constant interruptions stopping the well-made platforming that you likely bought the game for
The pros are far less, but I will list them here:
* The game looks amazing with its vibrant visuals and dynamic use of color
* The main characters (Yooka and Laylee) are absolutely beautfully designed
* Some of the music is just as wonderful as what the Banjo-Kazooie games had to offer
* Lots of collectables (although unlike Banjo-Kazooie the placement of said collectables doesn't feel nearly as natural and even feels like a chore to find some things)
I strongly recommend if you want this game to get it on sale. It's disappointing to me that over two million dollars produced such an unpolished product. In my opinion it is not worth its asking price and would be reasonably priced at twenty dollars rather than forty. If you like platformers and can get this game for twenty dollars then by all means go for it. Me? I waited in anticipation for this game and at least expected something decent and did not get it.

It's an old game, so any computer that was made 2007 or later should run it great. You'll need a few unoffical files to get it running, but afterwards, it's fine.
For a dated game, you'll notice that the game doesn't have HD graphics or anything. But any Star Wars fan (such as myself) will tell you that these Jedi Knight games developed by Raven are, by far, the best Star Wars games out there. The lightsaber combat is engaging and you can run around with a single lightsaber with your choice of fighting style, use dual-wield lightsabers, or channel your inner Darth Maul and use a staff. There's a plethora of force powers to use, even the movie ones such as Jedi Mind Trick and Force Choke. While the multiplayer side is most likely dead, the singleplayer experience is fine on its own.
But the best part is the modding community. Adding mods is almost as easy as downloading files from the Steam Workshop, and Star Wars fans are probably the most creative people out there. You can play as Darth Vader for your Sith needs, or give the game a comedic effect and saber people as Homer Simpson, Duffman, or even Bender. There is a singleplayer mod that allows you to romp around as Jack Sparrow. If you wish the game had more up-to-date graphics, somebody has created an HD texture overhaul, and there is also a Widescreen mod to make the game fit a 1920x1080 monitor properly.
Overall, I give this game a 9/10. It's definitely a unique experience with or without mods and even if you aren't a fan of Star Wars, you can still have a great time with this game. If you love Star Wars, you'll love this.
Oh, and grab the source code. What is in there is hilarious.

In brief, Pool Nation is possibly the best pool game you have ever and will ever play in your life, and I don't say that lightly.
The gameplay is flaweless, and suited for both the beginner pool player and the expert ball shark alike, with the game's aim assist proving an excellent means to adjust difficulty. The gameplay itself is incredibly fun and addictive, probably moreso than an actual game of pool, as once you master the controls (an easy task), you can control your ball quite precicely, and pull off all sorts of trick shots with ease. This simplicity does not translate to a lack of difficulty though, as the AI can keep up quite easily.
Adding to these mechanics is a huge variety of game modes. The two basic types of match, 9 ball and 8 ball, make up most of the game's tournament, but there are also different specialty games to play with the AI, online or with friends locally, as well as an endurance game mode where you race against the computer to pocket balls as they constantly appear on the table.
Perhaps the best thing about Pool Nation is that all the above detail comes bundled with an amazing visual style. There are a dozen sets of pool balls, cues and table patterns, and 4 locations to play in, all rendered in a surreally clean and beautiful setting that wouldn't be out of place in a sci-fi film. The gloss and polish of the visuals will keep you coming back for more time and time again.
So if you have even the slightest interest in playing pool on a computer, you cannot possibly do better than this game. At least, until a sequel comes out, perhaps.

I see a lot of complaining that the game is slow, mostly from people who have never played the card game before. The reason that there's a pause while the heroes are moving through each room of your dungeon is because it gives the other players about 3 seconds to decide if they're going to interfere with your dungeon and play cards against you. Spell cards and certain rooms can only be played if certain conditions are met, so sometimes you need 3 seconds to realize your room can activate. So it's not a flaw of the port, it's an inherent rule in the gameplay.
That said, this port is not perfect. I have not experienced UI issues like others have mentioned, but I might also be less annoyed since I've played the card game and know my way around after a few runs with the AI.
Bottom line is - if you enjoy the physical card game then you will like it. If you're looking for a fast paced card game, this isn't it. You need to think through your choices, try to tailor your dungeon to attract certain heroes, mess with your opponents and try to stop them from scoring points, and try to setup combos and place rooms optimally. That's called strategy.

Boss Monster is very fun once you understand the gameplay and mechanics. This is a very accurate recreation of the Table top edition of the game; as they advertised. The DLC is worth getting from the start if you're a fan of the game; but also worth getting after you've played long enough to understand the base game. The game is a bit slow with it's wait times; a mechanic built with multiplayer in mind specifically. The tutorial is a bit lacking, but the rules are simple enough.
There aren't any variations on the rules in the Digital release; something that the original rule book had a section on. Including modes suh as; 'I Choose You' (Draw 2 Bosses and pick one) or the 'Hard Mode' (Removes all 4 HP heros).
Pros:
~ It is a very well made and fun game
~ It looks very nice
~ Has a card database to read up on cards
~ Lots of referances to enjoy
~ Good DLC
~ Perfectly priced
Cons:
~ Games take a long time to complete
~ Not the easiest to get into for newcomers
~ Tuutorial isn't the best for learning
~ Music is nice; but can be grating after too long
~ The Multiplayer community if beyond dead

A return to form. After Absolution, I should have been more hesitant with this game. But I'm glad I wasn't. This game picks up right where Blood Money left off. The two tutorial levels are more open than you'd expect, and the main Paris level is massive and up there with Blood Money's best. For an early level, it sets a high bar that I hope the later ones will be able to expand upon more creatively.
It might seem lacking in content now, even for 15 dollars, and I'd advise anyone who opposes to multiple replays of the same level to hold off. But to me, Hitman has always been about coming up with new fun ways to take out the target. And Paris offers many options that I won't spoil. The opportunities system does spoil them, however, so turn that off right away. Don't look at any of the challenges until you've started running out of ideas. They offer an interesting form of progression though, in the form of getting new ways to start each mission and new tools to bring with you.
As for new ideas, the escalation mode offers increasingly complicated requirements for taking out the same target each time you play it. It can feel a bit repetitive if you do it all in one sitting, but it's still a ton of fun once it gets going. And I'm really looking forward to the upcoming elusive mode You have one chance to take out a brand new NPC on an existing map. The hit will be on a timer, and if you fail, the mission is gone. The target won't be marked on instinct mode or the map. It's up to you to find them based on clues and a photo in your briefing. It sounds like a true test of your skill as an assassin.
The contracts mode is back from Absolution, which will really shine in these open maps. For those who don't know, it allows players to make a new mission on an existing map by targeting a specific NPC with the option to require certain uniforms or kills. There are so many side stories going on that you might never even notice following the main targets, so this will really give a chance to become intimately familiar with a level. Speaking of which, I just want to mention the ambient and contextual dialogue is fantastic. NPCs have so much going on and so many reactions to what you can get up to. I've had fun just listening to every guard give a different reaction to every disguise you try to bring into a restricted area. The vampire magician outfit especially, which I'm expecting great contracts involving
Now for the cons. The always online system can only lead to frustration when you get kicked out and can't load any online saves. The game is still playable offline, but it keeps those saves separate. Thankfully, I've only been kicked once and the servers will likely become more stable. Many have had optimization issues, though I'm going to be that guy who says it works fine on my machine. I've experienced a few bugs here and there, like slide tackling a guy through the floor, but nothing gamebreaking and nothing a quick reload can't fix when the game autosaves frequently.
And back to the episodic model. I understand it'll put people off, but I sort of like that it gives time to thoroughly explore each map. If they keep up this quality, I won't mind coming back every month to put in another 10+ hours. And for the people who want to hold off for the finished product, you'll have a true successor to Blood Money waiting for you.
To all the people comlaining about "Performance issues" and "Bad framerates" and "Horrible optimization".. Go to Task Manager and set HITMAN to "HIGH" on priorities. Thank you, and enjoy the game :)

I pre-loaded the game and have been playing it since and while it is a good game it's not on a par with Arkham City in my opinion. The first thing I noticed was how well the game performed and how much crisper the visuals looked, which I was very happy about as Arkham City's frame rate was a touch patchy at its highest settings (I'm a PC player). However once I got out in the city I realised that the reason for the increased performance was due to just how much the visuals had been dialed back rather than any optimisation. The PhysX features are almost non-existant compared to the previous games and a lot of the detail appears to be missing. It's not a deal breaker  but Arkham City had a much denser setting and still managed to perform well even if you couldn't max out the graphics settings.
The city itself doesn't seem very interesting either. Aside from random robberies there is no sign of life anywhere, the setting just seems a bit soulless. There is also a very long bridge that you will need traverse regularly (unless you fast travel) and I can only surmise that it is there to hide loading. Aside from that it looks sound enough but lacks character, the thrill of discovery and the easter eggs of the last game (although on the other hand it does feel a Tim Burton's Batman Returns at the start).
As far as gameplay it's pretty much the same deal as the last game. The fighting is still fun however I have noticed the camera now has a tendency to stick to walls and ceilings, and can get muddled when fighting mobs. This was never an issue in previous games, at least from what I remember.
The bosses so far have also been pretty mundane. [MILD EARLY GAME SPOILER] Crock is the first boss you fight and can be beat in a repetitive "stun, punch, punch, punch, punch, QTE, dodge" manner with goons dropped in to prologue the fighting. I realise this is the first "boss" in the game but it still could have been done better and should have for what is such an intimidating character. The next boss I thought in a pit also looked pretty intimidating so imagine my surprise when ONE solitary kick to the head ended the confrontation. Boss fights weren't Arkham City's strong point either but it should have at least been improved on.
The map system could also use some work as whilst it will tell you which area you need to go it doesn't get any more specific than that. Running around a building several times trying to find the correct entrance does not feel very "Dark Knight".
By contrast however the new Detective Mode is pretty awesome. It still holds your hand but being able to play out a crime scene in real time is pretty satisfying.
Admittedly most of that does sound pretty negative. I'm not saying the game is bad, it's definitely worth picking up. But it's probably the weakest entry so far and there is no reason to go out of your way to pick this up if you haven't already played Arkham City (although I suppose a lot of the faults in this game would be less visible if you bought this first).
So far its a 7/10 for me.

Full Review (It's not that long!)
Yooka Laylee is a spiritual successor to Banjo Kazooie made by the same developers. It has a lot of heart, and fans of the originals will love Yooka Laylee, but it has the same issues the old games did.
The Good
-Entire new game of BK-style gameplay
-Yooka and Laylee are great characters in their own right
-The game is beautiful
-YL controls well and has a variety of moves.
-It's more Banjo Kazooie.
The Bad
-Camera can be wonky at times, as in BK
-Rolling isn't as precise as the Talon Trot
-Worlds can be confusing to navigate in their upgraded forms, as they're very large.
-Rextro's games can be frustrating
-It's more Banjo Kazooie
The Meh
-Jontron was in it but now he's not and it's made a fair amount of people mad.
All in all, I like Yooka Laylee for all its flaws and strengths. I'd wait for a sale or play Banjo Kazooie if you were never really a fan of the genre, but want to get into it. If you liked the first, you should find this a fun addition to your library.
